t1.a: Climate stabilization requires management of current and historical CO2 emissions, in parallel with the rapid expansion of renewable and low carbon energy sources. Avoided CO2 emissions – a key ingredient in climate stabilization – can be achieved by carbon capture at point sources, or by substituting fossil energy generation with renewable energy. Negative CO2 emissions – a second necessary ingredient in climate stabilization – are achieved by methodologies that remove CO2 from the atmosphere and oceans. One such technology, direct air capture of CO2 (DAC), is highly scalable but requires further cost-reducing innovation. In this talk, I will discuss the unique challenges associated with DAC and forecast how the future of DAC technology development may evolve in the coming years. CO2 conversion to fuels or chemicals will also be considered, envisioning pathways for carbon circularity.

t2.k: Biomass; Metal oxides; Composite materials; Electrode materials; Electrochemical capacitors; Energy storage
t2.a: This talk presents our recent progress in the development of advanced electrode materials for energy-storage applications, with a particular focus on nanomaterials and their composites, including biomass-derived porous carbons, nanostructured metal oxides, and carbon/oxide hybrid materials. These materials are synthesized using various approaches, such as sol–gel processing, hydrothermal synthesis, electrospinning, and related techniques. Their structural, morphological, and physicochemical properties are systematically investigated using a combination of laboratory- and synchrotron-based characterization techniques to establish correlations between material structure and electrochemical performance. The energy-storage properties of the developed electrodes in aqueous electrolytes are evaluated using cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). Finally, the practical potential of these materials is demonstrated through the straightforward fabrication of energy-storage devices employing the developed electrodes as cathodes and anodes. The results highlight promising strategies for designing high-performance, cost-effective, and sustainable electrode materials for next-generation energy-storage technologies.

t3.a: The development of sustainable electrochemical energy storage devices relies heavily on the simultaneous improvement of power density, energy density, materials, kinetic performance, and durability. Although considerable attention has been focused on developing new electrode stoichiometries, the decisive factors are, in fact, the interfaces, which critically influence charge transfer, charge storage mechanisms, ion transport, and electronic structures. Therefore, rational design principles are required to engineer these interfaces, thereby offering an alternative strategy to overcome the intrinsic limitations of conventional electrode materials. This article presents an interface-based approach to developing advanced electrode materials for electrochemical energy storage, focusing on atomic-layer and thin-film engineering, heterostructure formation, and electrochemical characterization. Representative electrode architectures incorporating specifically designed Schottky junctions and metal-p-n heterojunctions are analyzed to establish relationships between interfacial electronic structure, charge-transfer processes, and electrochemical charge-storage behavior. The discussion also addresses charge-storage mechanisms, electrode architecture, and the translation of material-level design principles into functional energy-storage devices. It has been observed that engineered interfaces substantially modify electronic structures, interactions between the electrolyte and the electrode surface, and charge storage pathways in transition-metal-based electrode materials. Schottky junctions have preferentially enhanced the pseudocapacitive contribution by controlling ion movement during charge and discharge processes; simultaneously, the formation of metal-p-n heterojunctions has enabled further control over charge transfer and storage mechanisms, leading to compelling design principles for fine-tuning these mechanisms and improving electrochemical performance. These results demonstrate that interfaces offer greater control over critical descriptors to address the competing demands of energy density and power capability in hybrid electrochemical storage systems. Furthermore, the findings underscore the importance of understanding interfacial phenomena beyond conventional material descriptors such as composition and surface area. Interface engineering is a powerful materials design strategy for controlling charge storage mechanisms and developing advanced electrochemical energy storage systems. The evolution from atomic-level surface modification to engineered heterojunctions and functional electrode architectures demonstrates how interfaces can be intentionally designed to couple different charge storage processes. This approach offers the opportunity to develop durable, scalable, and high-performance materials and devices for sustainable electrochemical energy storage.

t4.k: Lithium Ion Battery; Layered Oxide (NM); Doping Strategy
t4.a: Layered transition metal oxides are widely used as high-energy-density cathodes because of their high capacity, operating voltage, and rate capability. Co-free layered oxides have recently gained attention as cost-effective alternatives to conventional Co-containing cathodes. However, cobalt removal often causes structural instability, sluggish kinetics, and rapid capacity fading, requiring effective stabilization strategies. High-valence transition metal doping can strengthen the transition metal–oxygen framework and suppress irreversible phase transitions. However, dopants such as Zr and Mo exhibit substantial mismatches in ionic radius and oxidation state with the host metals, hindering their uniform incorporation into the layered lattice. Their resulting segregation at grain boundaries or local regions limits the effectiveness of the doping strategy. An organic additive-assisted co-precipitation strategy was developed to achieve homogeneous dispersion of Zr and Mo by suppressing dopant segregation during synthesis and calcination. In this work, we investigate a high-valence transition metal doping strategy for a Co-free layered LiNi0.9Mn0.1O2 cathode and develop a highly dispersed doping approach to achieve homogeneous distribution of Zr and Mo throughout the secondary particles. The improved dopant dispersion effectively enhances structural integrity, suppresses microstructural degradation, and promotes more stable electrochemical reactions during repeated cycling. As a result, the doped cathodes exhibit significantly improved cycling stability and rate capability compared with conventionally doped materials. These findings demonstrate that controlling dopant dispersion is as important as dopant selection itself and provide a practical design strategy for developing high-performance Co-free layered oxide cathodes for next-generation lithium-ion batteries.

t5.k: Solid Polymer Electrolyte; Lithium Metal Battery; Wide-temperature Operation
t5.a: Solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs) are promising materials for solid-state lithium metal batteries because of their high safety and excellent processability. However, their practical application is restricted by limited ionic conductivity and unstable electrode/electrolyte interfaces, especially under low-temperature. A fluorinated ether-assisted semi-interpenetrating polymer electrolyte based on polyethylene glycol dimethyl ether (PEGDME) was developed to regulate the Li⁺ solvation environment through molecular-level interactions. The electrolyte was characterized by physicochemical analyses, while its electrochemical performance was evaluated using lithium symmetric cells, LiFePO₄ and NMC811 full cells, and prototype pouch cells over a wide temperature range. The molecular interaction effectively reduced polymer chain ordering and weakened Li⁺ coordination, leading to enhanced ionic transport and the formation of stable inorganic-rich interphases. The optimized electrolyte exhibited improved ionic conductivity, higher lithium-ion transference, intrinsic flame retardancy, and an expanded electrochemical stability window. Cells employing this electrolyte demonstrated superior cycling stability, enhanced rate capability, uniform lithium deposition, and stable operation from ambient to sub-zero temperatures. This molecular solvation engineering strategy simultaneously improves ionic transport and interfacial stability, providing an effective approach for developing safe, durable, and wide-temperature solid-state lithium metal batteries suitable for practical high-energy storage applications.

t6.a: Electrolytes in lithium batteries continuously evolve under electrochemical, thermal, and chemical stresses, altering the composition and properties of the liquid phase. However, this dynamic “stressed electrolyte” environment remains less understood than solid-phase degradation. We investigated a chemically stressed ether-based electrolyte, 1 M LiFSI in DME, after 24-hour exposure to metallic lithium. Liquid chromatography–quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry was used to identify soluble degradation products, while cryogenic electron microscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy were used to analyze interfacial structures formed on Cu current collectors. FSI⁻ anions underwent cascading degradation reactions, producing highly polar fluorosulfonate- and imide-derived species. Unexpectedly, these soluble products showed strong oxidative reactivity toward nominally inert Cu current collectors. They reacted spontaneously with the Cu₂O surface and generated a chemically formed “premature” SEI, or pre-SEI, without any applied electrochemical potential. The pre-SEI contained amorphous inorganic species and nanoscale Cu clusters, which significantly altered subsequent SEI formation and Li metal cycling behavior. These findings show that electrolyte stress alone can chemically activate and transform solid interfaces. Liquid-phase degradation chemistry is therefore a critical but overlooked driver of interfacial evolution and battery performance.

t7.k: Sodium-ion Batteries; Cathode Materials; High Energy Density
t7.a: The rational design of structurally stable and high-voltage cathode materials is critically important for the advancement of next-generation sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). Among various cathode materials, Prussian blue analogs (PBAs) have attracted significant attention owing to their open framework structure, rapid Na + diffusion pathways, low-cost synthesis, and tunable redox chemistry. However, conventional manganese-based Prussian blue, Na 2 Mn[Fe(CN) 6 ], suffers from severe Jahn-Teller Distortion (JTD), high crystal water content, and structural instability during repeated sodium insertion/extraction processes, leading to rapid capacity degradation and poor cycling durability. To address these challenges, we report a novel non-metal doping strategy through the incorporation of ethylenediamine (En) into Na 2 Mn[Fe(CN) 6 ] via a facile co-precipitation method, resulting in a chemically engineered Na 2 MnEn[Fe(CN) 6 ] framework for high-performance sodium-ion batteries. The incorporation of ethylenediamine effectively reduced the coordinated/interstitial water content within the Prussian blue framework and suppressed Jahn-Teller distortion of Mn centers, thereby significantly enhancing structural robustness and interfacial stability during long-term electrochemical cycling. In addition, En doping modulated the electronic structure and increased the interlayer distance, enabling stable high- voltage electrochemical operation over an extended voltage range of 2.0-4.2 V compared to pristine Na₂Mn[Fe(CN)₆] (2.0-4.0 V). Benefiting from the synergistic effects of reduced water content, suppressed lattice distortion, and improved framework stability, the optimized Na 2 Mn[Fe(CN) 6 ] cathode delivered a high specific capacity of 130 mAh g -1 with outstanding cycling durability. The charge storage mechanism and structural evolution were systematically investigated using structural, spectroscopic, and electrochemical characterization techniques. The findings demonstrate that organic ligand-assisted non-metal doping is an effective strategy to overcome Jahn–Teller distortion and improve the long-term stability of manganese-based PBAs for advanced sodium-ion battery applications. Further results will be presented in the conference.

t8.k: Lithium Trifluoromethanesulfonate; Lithium Bis(oxalate)borate; Trimethyl Phosphate
t8.a: The practical application of lithium metal batteries (LMBs) is still severely limited by safety concerns such as lithium dendrite growth and the flammability of conventional electrolytes. To address these critical issues, this study proposes cooperative dual-salt electrolytes utilizing lithium trifluoromethanesulfonate (LiOTf) and lithium bis(oxalato)borate (LiBOB) in a non-flammable trimethyl phosphate (TMP) solvent for high-stability and safety LMBs. The optimized Li[OTf/BOB]-55 electrolyte significantly reconstructs the Li+ primary solvation shell. This unique structural modification promotes the preferential reductive decomposition of LiBOB at higher potentials and operates synergistically with LiOTf decomposition products, thereby forming a robust dual-layer inorganic–organic composite solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on the lithium metal anode. The inner layer is enriched with inorganic species such as Li2CO3 and LixBOy that facilitate ionic conduction, while the outer elastic organic polymeric layer imparts mechanical toughness. This highly stable and elastic SEI effectively suppresses the continuous consumption of the TMP solvent and blocks lithium dendrite propagation at the microscopic level. The optimally proportioned electrolyte endows the batteries with outstanding electrochemical performance: Li//Li symmetric cells achieve an ultra-long stable cycle life of over 1700 hours and tolerate a critical current density of up to 1.25 mA cm-2, while Li//Cu cells deliver a high average coulombic efficiency of 91.83%. In application evaluations, Li//LiMn2O4 cells utilizing this electrolyte realize a remarkably long lifespan of 1600 cycles at a high rate of 500 mA g-1. Furthermore, the system exhibits excellent temperature adaptability and interfacial stability across a wide temperature range from −20 °C to 60 °C. The proposed non-flammable dual-salt electrolyte design, enabled by solvation structure engineering, offers a highly practical and promising strategy for the development of next-generation safe LMBs.

t9.k: Metal-air Batteries; Gas-phase Electrochemistry; Air-breathing Batteries
t9.a: Conventional electrochemical energy storage technologies are largely built upon solid electrodes and liquid electrolytes. Expanding electrochemical systems beyond these traditional phases by incorporating gaseous components offers new opportunities for developing lightweight, high-energy, and sustainable energy storage technologies. In particular, gas-phase electrochemical systems can utilize abundant gaseous species such as oxygen and carbon dioxide as active reactants, potentially reducing dependence on transition-metal-based cathode materials while enabling fundamentally different electrochemical architectures. This presentation provides an overview of our recent research on electrochemical energy storage systems involving gaseous reactants, products, and electrolyte phases. Materials design, interfacial engineering, electrochemical characterization, and advanced cell configurations are explored to understand and control reactions occurring at dynamic solid–liquid–gas interfaces. Recent advances in air-breathing battery systems will be highlighted, including strategies to regulate gas-related reaction pathways and improve electrochemical reversibility. In addition, a new atmospheric open electrochemical architecture based on aeroelectrolytes will be introduced. The delivery of electrolyte microdroplets directly to electrode surfaces enables dynamic electrochemical interfaces and provides an alternative platform for operating electrochemical reactions under open atmospheric conditions. The integration of gas-phase components into electrochemical energy storage offers opportunities to move beyond conventional closed-cell configurations and established battery chemistries. Advances in interfacial control, functional materials, and unconventional cell architectures may enable new directions for high-energy and sustainable energy storage. Collectively, these developments highlight gas-phase electrochemistry as an emerging platform for future energy storage technologies.

t10.k: Silicon Thin-film Anodes; Mesh Patterning; Polymeric Buffer Layer
t10.a: Silicon thin-film anodes offer an exceptionally high theoretical capacity for next-generation lithium-ion batteries. However, continuous films on rigid current collectors accumulate severe planar stress during the ~300% volumetric expansion upon lithiation, leading to cracking, delamination, and rapid capacity fading beyond a critical thickness. To address this mechanical bottleneck, this work proposes a dual-stabilization strategy that combines micron-scale mesh patterning with compliant polymeric buffer layers to alleviate film stress. A patterned silicon thin-film platform was first established using an environmentally friendly poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) binder. The abundant polar groups of PAA enable strong interfacial adhesion, while the patterned geometry provides sufficient lateral buffer space. Two patterned architectures were designed: (i) conformal deposition of silicon over a pre-patterned buffer (MRP) to form three-dimensional stress-relief channels, and (ii) segmentation of silicon into discrete micro-islands (PMR). Systematic investigations across various mesh densities revealed a non-monotonic relationship between geometric density and electrochemical stability. Among the investigated architectures, the optimized 250-mesh PMR configuration accommodated volume expansion laterally into inter-island gaps, maintaining robust interfacial adhesion and delivering an exceptional capacity retention of 98.5% after 200 cycles at 0.5C. Moreover, the 250-mesh PMR design exhibited outstanding rate capability, delivering a high discharge capacity of approximately 1321.4 mA h/g even at 20C (retaining 46.2% capacity relative to 0.2C). These results demonstrate that binder-assisted patterning effectively decouples silicon film thickness from cycle-life limitations by alleviating mechanical stress and interfacial failure. The patterned amorphous silicon thin-film platform established in this work provides a robust geometry–interface engineering framework for future pre-lithiation strategies and the development of high-rate lithium-ion battery anodes.

t11.k: Banana peel waste; cellulose; chitosan; reduced graphene oxide; triboelectric nanogenerator; waste-to-power; sustainable energy harvesting
t11.a: The development of bio-based triboelectric materials from agricultural waste offers a promising route toward sustainable mechanical energy harvesting. Herein, banana peel waste was valorized into cellulose and integrated with chitosan to construct flexible triboelectric composite films, while reduced graphene oxide (rGO) was introduced as an interfacial modifier. Rather than solely exploiting rGO as a conductive filler, this study investigates its role in regulating the surface morphology, interfacial polarization, and charge retention of the cellulose/chitosan matrix and their consequent effects on triboelectric charge generation. The influence of rGO loading on the chemical structure, surface topography, wettability, dielectric properties, electrical conductivity, and surface charge characteristics was systematically investigated and correlated with the triboelectric performance of the resulting devices. An optimum rGO content is expected to promote surface roughening, interfacial polarization, and charge trapping, leading to enhanced transferred charge and electrical output. In contrast, excessive rGO incorporation may induce aggregation and conductive pathways, thereby increasing charge dissipation and reducing the triboelectric response. The structure–surface–charge–performance relationships established in this work provide mechanistic insight into the design of waste-derived cellulose/chitosan triboelectric materials and demonstrate a sustainable waste-to-power strategy for self-powered electronics.

t12.a: Endogenous bioelectric signals regulate cell migration, proliferation, and tissue regeneration during wound healing, creating a need for electrical stimulation platforms that can operate without wired electrodes. Piezoelectric materials can convert remotely applied ultrasound into localized electrical signals, offering a promising approach for wound-healing-related biointerfaces. Here, we developed three-dimensional porous poly(vinylidene fluoride-trifluoroethylene) (P(VDF-TrFE)) scaffolds using sugar cubes as sacrificial templates. Pore structure was controlled by varying sugar particle size and polymer solution concentration to produce coarse and fine scaffolds. Their structural, mechanical, dielectric, and piezoelectric properties were evaluated. Polydopamine (PDA) coating was applied to improve surface wettability, and alginate-extracellular matrix (ECM) composites were incorporated to provide biochemical support. Cellular responses under ultrasound stimulation were assessed using in vitro assays with NIH-3T3 fibroblasts. Sugar templating produced interconnected porous scaffolds with distinct pore architectures. The fine scaffold exhibited higher stiffness and stronger piezoelectric responses than the coarse scaffold, generating 0.609 V under compression and 0.390 V under ultrasound stimulation. PDA coating improved surface wettability, and the PDA-coated fine scaffold under ultrasound stimulation achieved scratch closure values of 60.4% and 84.8% at 12 and 24 h, respectively. Alginate-ECM incorporation further enhanced cell viability and proliferation. These results demonstrate that porous P(VDF-TrFE) scaffolds can convert ultrasound-induced deformation into piezoelectric stimulation while supporting favorable cellular responses. This platform shows potential as a multifunctional ultrasound-responsive piezoelectric biointerface.

t13.k: Triboelectric Nanogenerator; Dielectric Engineering; Dual-dimensional Conductive Fillers
t13.a: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert mechanical energy from contact and vibration into electrical energy. Conductive nanofillers can improve TENG performance by increasing interfacial polarization and dielectric permittivity. However, one-dimensional multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) readily form conductive networks, causing dielectric loss and charge leakage, whereas zero-dimensional silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) require relatively high concentrations to achieve sufficient dielectric enhancement. A dual-dimensional conductive network was designed by incorporating MWCNTs and AgNPs into the dielectric layer. MWCNTs were used to establish efficient polarization pathways, while AgNPs were introduced between the nanotube networks to promote localized interfacial polarization without excessive electrical connection. The filler concentrations were optimized by evaluating dielectric properties and TENG output performance. The optimized composite containing 1.2 wt% MWCNTs and 1 wt% AgNPs exhibited an increased dielectric constant while maintaining a favorable dielectric loss tangent. The resulting TENG produced an open-circuit voltage of 164 V and a short-circuit current of 31.2 μA. These values corresponded to 2.02-fold and 2.55-fold improvements, respectively, compared with the unfilled device. The complementary combination of one-dimensional MWCNTs and zero-dimensional AgNPs effectively enhanced interfacial polarization while suppressing excessive conductive network formation. This dual-dimensional filler strategy provides a practical approach for improving the electrical performance of high-output TENGs.

t14.k: Electrospinning; Polyacrylonitrile; Multi-walled carbon nanotubes; Titanium dioxide; Triboelectric effect; PM2.5 filtrations; Nanofibrous membrane
t14.a: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is a major air pollution problem and can cause serious health effects. Developing air filtration materials with high filtration efficiency and low airflow resistance is therefore important for effective PM2.5 removals. In this work, polyacrylonitrile (PAN)-based nanofibrous membranes containing multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) and titanium dioxide (TiO₂) were prepared by electrospinning for PM2.5 filtration and triboelectric applications. The effects of PAN concentration, MWCNT and TiO2 contents, and electrospinning conditions on the morphology, fiber diameter, elemental composition, and porous structure of the nanofibrous membranes were investigated. The membranes were characterized using field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) analysis. Their triboelectric properties were also examined by evaluating charge generation and charge retention on the membrane surface. PM2.5 filtration performance was evaluated based on filtration efficiency, pressure drop, and quality factor (QF). The results showed that the material composition and electrospinning conditions significantly affected the fiber morphology and porous structure of the membranes. The incorporation of MWCNTs and TiO2 also changed the electrical and surface charging characteristics of the nanofibrous membranes. These changes were related to the ability of the membranes to capture PM2.5 particles, indicating that surface charging can contribute to particle removal in addition to physical filtration by the fibrous network. Overall, the results demonstrate that controlling the composition and electrospinning conditions is an effective way to tailor the morphology, triboelectric properties, and filtration performance of PAN/MWCNT/TiO2 nanofibrous membranes. The developed membranes show potential as high-performance filtration materials for PM2.5 removals with reduced airflow resistance.

t15.a: Gunshot residue (GSR) analysis is important for forensic science to identify suspects especially in firearm-related crimes. The increasing use of lead-free ammunition has highlighted the need for alternative forensic markers beyond traditional inorganic gunshot residue components such as barium (Ba), antimony (Sb) and lead (Pb). Diphenylamine (DPA), a major stabilizer in smokeless gunpowder and one of the most abundant constituents of organic gunshot residue (OGSR), has emerged as a target for firearm discharge identification. This work presents the first feasibility study of a surface-engineered liquid-solid triboelectric sensor (LS-TES) for selective and ultrasensitive detection of DPA. The solid-sensing interface of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) is engineered by using stearic acid (SA)-functionalized silica (SiO2) and octadecyltriethoxysilane (OTES) to enhance the selectivity toward π-alkyl interaction and hydrophobic molecular-recognition. Upon contact and separation between the liquid droplet and the engineered PTFE surface, the coupled mechanisms of triboelectrification and electrostatic induction generate characteristic electrical signals. The presence of DPA in solution induces significant changes in both the open-circuit voltage (VOC) and shirt-circuit current (ISC), reflecting alterations in the triboelectric charge transfer process. The LS-TES exhibits a concentration-dependent response with distinguishable signal waveforms and provides a linear variation in electrical output over the ultra-low DPA concentration range of 10-200 ppb. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the modified LS-TES for ultrasensitive DPA detection, enabling reliable discrimination of trace analyte levels, and highlight its promise as a future analytical platform for OGSR investigation and forensic analysis.

t16.a: Ionic thermoelectric generators have attracted considerable attention for low-grade waste-heat harvesting because of their thermovoltage arising from the thermodiffusion of mobile ions. Polymer/ionic-liquid ionogels, in particular, have attracted substantial scientific and technological interest as ionic thermoelectric materials owing to their quasi-solid-state processability and tunable thermoelectric response, which are distinct from those of conventional thermoelectrics. However, because the thermovoltaic behavior of ionogels is governed by complex factors including ion–ion interactions and interfacial environments, tailoring these interactions through a systematic material-level approach is essential to further enhance their thermoelectric performance. Ionic thermoelectric generators based on engineered ionogels are fabricated from a polymer/ionic-liquid system, in which the ion–ion interactions and interfacial environments are tailored through a systematic material-level approach to modulate the thermovoltaic response. The thermoelectric characteristics are evaluated by analyzing the interfacial interactions between the ionogel and the mobile ions under a controlled thermal gradient. The engineered ionogels are expected to exhibit a modulated thermovoltaic response through the tailored ion–ion interactions and interfacial environments, demonstrating that the thermoelectric performance can be enhanced by a material-level design of the polymer/ionic-liquid system. The relationship between the engineered interfacial environment and the resulting thermovoltaic behavior will be presented and discussed in detail. This work is expected to provide material-level insight into ionic thermoelectric generators based on engineered ionogels, offering a useful strategy for the design of high-performance devices for future energy-harvesting electronics.

t17.a: Laundry is a dominant source of microplastic emission, and retrofit drain filters intercept fibres only after they have entered the drain flow, so the fraction they retain is bounded by the pore size that can be sustained without clogging. Enlarging the particles before they reach the filter is therefore an attractive route. Electrocoagulation aggregates microplastics effectively, but it has been applied to laundry wastewater almost exclusively as a batch treatment of separately collected effluent, and at beaker scale. In continuous flow the internal reactor geometry governs residence time and floc capture, yet it has rarely been designed systematically. Vial-scale screening on real laundry wastewater was used to separate the roles of the electrical parameters, applied voltage and electrolysis time, from the geometric parameters, inter-electrode distance and electrode area, on both flat and nanostructured aluminium electrodes prepared by glancing-angle deposition. The resulting design rule was translated into a single objective, minimizing the area-averaged velocity in the electrode section, which was optimized over five geometric variables by Bayesian optimization coupled to computational fluid dynamics. The optimized module was fabricated and mounted directly in the drain line of an operating household washing machine, and the discharged solids were size-fractionated through a filter train and compared against the untreated drainage and against an intuitively designed module. Aggregation collapsed onto the charge passed rather than onto voltage or electrolysis time separately, so that conditions delivering matched charge produced matched capturable fractions. Because electrolysis time cannot be imposed in continuous flow, this rule was recast as a flow-design objective. The resulting optimum was constraint-active, filling the available installation envelope, and was insensitive to the remaining shape variables, indicating that the design tolerates fabrication variation. Mounted on the operating machine, the optimized module raised the filter-capturable mass fraction of the discharged microplastics well above both the untreated drainage and the intuitively designed counterpart, with the coarsest size fraction showing the largest relative gain. The delivered coagulant dose remained bounded below that of the vial experiments, so the improvement followed from the internal flow design rather than from a larger aluminium input. Nanostructured electrodes showed a further improvement that depended on the operating condition, pointing to the electrode surface as a second and independent lever. Internal flow design and electrode surface structure act as separable levers on microplastic aggregation, and simulation-guided optimization of the flow path alone is sufficient to move a household drain line from a regime in which almost nothing is filter-capturable to one in which most of the discharged mass is. The module installs into an existing drain without a collection tank or an external separation stage, demonstrating a route to source-level mitigation of microplastic emission.

t18.k: Self-Sustained Electric Field; Droplet Manipulation; Programmable Microfluidics
t18.a: Power-independent droplet manipulation is essential for resource-limited microfluidic systems, yet conventional electrical approaches require high-voltage supplies, wired electrode arrays, and active switching circuits. Here, we demonstrate an electret-enabled electrophoretic platform driven by a self-sustained electric field for autonomous microdroplet charging and multifunctional manipulation with substantially reduced dependence on continuously powered high-voltage hardware. Fluorinated ethylene propylene films were corona-charged to fabricate emitters with quasi-permanent surface charges. Charged droplets were generated by electrostatic induction using a concentric emitter–nozzle geometry. Surface potential, droplet charge, detachment behavior, and motion were characterized using an electrostatic voltmeter, Faraday-cup electrometry, and optical imaging. Theoretical modeling and finite-element simulations related emitter geometry and field distribution to droplet size, charge, and electrostatic force. Spatial charge patterning encoded passive guidance functions. The emitters maintained stable kilovolt-level surface potentials and generated droplets with controllable polarity and charges of approximately ±300 pC, with stable charging sustained for more than 500 consecutive droplets. Droplet charge was regulated by emitter potential, nozzle diameter, and geometry, while velocity increased with charge magnitude and field strength. The platform demonstrated polarity-selective attraction and repulsion, contactless transport, three-dimensional levitation, parallel transport, controlled merging, charge-selective flotation, and autonomous classification. Patterned emitters further enabled spontaneous self-alignment and repeatable routing along predefined trajectories without real-time electrode switching. Electret-mediated electromechanical coupling provides a robust, scalable, and hardware-minimal strategy for droplet manipulation. The platform supports programmable microfluidic functions while reducing power and circuit requirements, offering a practical route toward autonomous diagnostics, wearable biointerfaces, and low-power biochemical processing.

t19.a: The development of cost-effective and acid-stable HER and OER electrocatalysts is essential for the implementation of proton exchange membrane (PEM)-based water electrolysis at gird scale. In this presentation, I will introduce the development of scalable Ru-based HER (core–shell RuP) and OER (RuNb oxide) catalysts using scalable synthetic methods, including flame-assisted synthesis and spray coating followed by calcination, respectively. These catalysts were subsequently integrated into a practically relevant PEM water electrolyser. When integrating Ru catalyst prepared at this scale into a practical proton-exchange membrane electrolyser (2 × 100 cm−2), it sustains 200 A (1 A cm−2) at a moderate cell voltage (1.8 V) with a stability over 1,500 h. A scalable Ru-based catalyst platform for PEM water electrolysis featuring low-cost synthesis, excellent acid stability, and high performance. The technology enables large-area PEM electrolysers to operate at industrially relevant current densities with long-term durability, providing a promising solution for cost-effective green hydrogen production.

t20.a: Organic semiconductors (OSCs) are promising photocatalysts for solar-driven hydrogen evolution because of their strong visible-light absorption, tunable electronic structures, and synthetic versatility. Beyond molecular energetics, however, photocatalytic performance is strongly influenced by nanoscale molecular packing, which governs exciton diffusion, charge separation and transport, recombination, and interfacial reactions. Although packing–property relationships are well established for OSC thin films, their translation to photocatalytic nanoparticles (NPs) remains challenging. Organic NPs are typically produced by rapid solvent exchange or reprecipitation under nonequilibrium conditions. Molecules can therefore become kinetically trapped in disordered or metastable structures before reaching thermodynamically favored crystalline states, making it difficult to control crystallinity, packing geometry, and molecular orientation. Here, we investigate how molecular organization within OSC NPs regulates photophysical processes and photocatalytic hydrogen evolution. By combining molecular design, controlled NP formation, direct structural characterization, and time-resolved spectroscopy, we correlate NP crystallinity and packing orientation with exciton and charge-carrier dynamics and hydrogen-evolution performance. Our results demonstrate that photocatalytic activity cannot be fully explained by molecular energetics or thin-film morphology alone. Instead, the internal molecular packing of NPs should be regarded as a key design parameter for efficient organic photocatalysts.

t21.k: PEMFC Durability; EIS Analysis; Nonlinear Impedance
t21.a: The commercialization of polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cells is limited by the durability of the membrane electrode assembly rather than by its peak performance, and degradation proceeds through several strongly coupled pathways including platinum dissolution, carbon-support corrosion, ionomer degradation, and loss of water management. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy is the standard non-destructive in-operando tool, but every fitted resistance is degenerate: a single parameter responds to several mechanisms at once and sometimes in opposite directions. The protonic resistance of the catalyst layer, for example, decreases when the layer thins yet increases when the ionomer degrades or the cell dries, so that the three contributions can cancel one another. The nonlinear response, in contrast, is governed by the curvature and asymmetry of the current-voltage relation rather than by its slope, and therefore carries information that the linear response cannot contain. Harmonic methods have been developed mainly for model electrodes and batteries, and quantitative protocols that resolve which material component of the membrane electrode assembly is degrading in an operating fuel cell are not yet established. Here we report a harmonic impedance protocol for operating fuel cells. A large-amplitude sinusoidal potential is superimposed on a controlled DC operating point, and the current response is acquired as a time series and decomposed by an integer-period rectangular Fourier transform, so that no window correction is required and a noise floor, and hence a signal-to-noise ratio, is obtained for every harmonic. Two normalizations make the harmonics comparable between states. The amplitude is referred to the electrode-side perturbation corrected for the ohmic drop, which defines the second- and third-harmonic indices as HR2/Velec and HR3/Velec squared, and the frequency is referred to the characteristic frequency taken from the linear impedance at the same DC point. The protocol is applied to 25 cm2 single cells at 80 C subjected to a dynamic load-cycling accelerated stress test under sub-saturated humidity, with transmission-line analysis of the linear impedance under hydrogen and nitrogen, cyclic voltammetry, and polarization curves acquired at the same checkpoints. Controlled humidity and DC-potential excursions are used as reference perturbations. Comparison at a fixed frequency is shown to be misleading because the characteristic frequency shifts by a factor of 2.5 over the stress test; only after normalization do the harmonic spectra become comparable, and the normalized curves still do not collapse, indicating that the harmonics carry state information beyond the linear time constant. At a matched normalized frequency, the second-harmonic index increases by 33% over 15,000 cycles while the electrochemically active surface area decreases by more than 40%, so this index is not a simple surface-area proxy. It collapses by a factor of five for a 50 mV negative shift of the DC point, which a Butler-Volmer description cannot reproduce and which instead points to the potential-dependent surface state of the catalyst. The third-harmonic index, in contrast, changes by less than 1% over the same 15,000 cycles but decreases by 48% when the cell is dried from 100% to 30% relative humidity, behaving as a hydration-selective probe. Measurement limits are also quantified: the cell-to-cell scatter of the second harmonic is 24%, and the signal-to-noise ratio of the third harmonic falls to between 3 and 7 in part of the frequency window. Amplitude- and frequency-normalized harmonics provide observables that respond along directions different from those of the linear parameters and from each other, the second harmonic tracking the catalyst surface state and the third harmonic tracking hydration. This suggests a two-dimensional readout in which a measured impedance change may be assigned either to a reversible hydration change or to irreversible catalyst-layer degradation. Work in progress extends the protocol with amplitude sweeps to verify amplitude invariance, DC-potential maps, humidity calibration ladders, and mechanism-selective accelerated stress tests using replicate cells, with the aim of establishing a standardized harmonic protocol that identifies, non-destructively and during operation, which material component of the membrane electrode assembly - the platinum catalyst, the carbon support, or the ionomer - is degrading.

t22.k: Atomic Layer Deposition; Ni3FeN/CoN Heterostructure; Oxygen Evolution Reaction
t22.a: The development of earth-abundant and durable bifunctional electrocatalysts with precisely engineered interfaces is essential for advancing alkaline water electrolysis. Transition-metal nitrides offer attractive electronic properties for electrocatalysis, while atomic layer deposition (ALD) provides precise control over ultrathin surface coatings and heterointerfaces. In this work, an ALD-engineered Ni3FeN/CoN heterostructure was developed on 3D nickel foam to enhance electrochemical water-splitting performance, with particular emphasis on oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity. Ni3Fe layered double hydroxide (Ni3Fe LDH) was directly synthesized on nickel foam through a hydrothermal reaction using a 3:1 Ni/Fe precursor ratio at 120 ºC for 10 h. A conformal CoOX thin film was subsequently deposited onto the Ni3Fe LDH surface by atomic layer deposition. The resulting precursor was subjected to ammonization under an NH3/Ar atmosphere at 500 ºC for 1 h, yielding a Ni3FeN/CoN heterostructure. The electrocatalytic properties were evaluated toward OER and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in alkaline electrolyte OF 1M KOH using polarization, Tafel, electrochemical impedance and electrochemically active surface area analyses. Overall water-splitting performance and durability were further investigated under galvanostatic conditions. The ALD-engineered Ni3FeN/CoN electrode exhibits pronounced OER activity, requiring overpotentials of 209, 245, and 270 mV to deliver current densities of 10, 50, and 100 mA cm-2, respectively, with a Tafel slope of 86.9 mV dec-1. The electrode also demonstrates HER activity with overpotentials of 136, 227, and 259 mV at 10, 50, and 100 mA cm-2, respectively, corresponding to a Tafel slope of 105.5 mV dec-1. Electrochemical analyses reveal favorable charge-transfer characteristics and a high electrochemically active surface area. When operated as both electrodes, the catalyst achieves overall water splitting at 1.61 V at 10 mA cm-2 and 1.95 V at 100 mA cm-2 under iR-uncompensated conditions. Furthermore, stable operation is maintained for 10 h at 10 and 100 mA cm-2, demonstrating excellent durability. The enhanced OER performance is associated with the synergistic interaction of Ni and Fe within the nitride framework and the ALD-engineered CoN interface, which can facilitate charge transfer and interfacial water activation. An ALD-enabled Ni3FeN/CoN heterostructure was successfully developed as an earth-abundant bifunctional electrocatalyst for alkaline water electrolysis. The precise deposition of the ultrathin cobalt-containing layer provides an effective strategy for engineering the surface/interface of Ni-Fe nitride catalysts, resulting in particularly strong OER activity and durable overall water-splitting performance. The results highlight ALD interface engineering as a promising and scalable approach for developing advanced transition-metal nitride electrocatalysts. Furthermore, possible electrochemical surface reconstruction of the nitride heterostructure into catalytically active oxyhydroxide species provides an important direction for future investigation of the underlying OER mechanism.

t23.k: Chlorine Evolution Reaction; Atomically Dispersed Catalyst; Active Site
t23.a: Chlorine (Cl2) is one of the world’s most important commodity chemicals, with widespread applications across the chemical industry. Industrial Cl2 production relies almost exclusively on the chlorine evolution reaction (CER) at the anode of chlor–alkali electrolyzers, where platinum group metal (PGM)-based mixed metal oxides (MMOs), exemplified by dimensionally stable anodes (DSAs), have served as benchmark catalysts for more than half a century. However, DSAs face inherent limitations arising from their reliance on scarce and expensive PGMs, as well as limited chlorine selectivity caused by the competing oxygen evolution reaction. Over the past decade, CER electrocatalysis has undergone remarkable advances with the emergence of alternative catalysts, including non-PGM metal oxides, atomically dispersed catalysts (ADCs), and organic molecular catalysts. In 2020, we reported atomically dispersed Pt–N₄ sites supported on carbon nanotubes as a highly active and selective CER electrocatalyst. Building on this work, we have pursued three complementary research directions: (i) expanding the compositional diversity of atomically dispersed CER catalysts, (ii) identifying the catalytic active sites and elucidating the reaction kinetics and mechanisms of ADCs, and (iii) integrating ADC-based CER electrocatalysts with complementary cathodic catalysts to develop new electrochemical systems for value-added chemical production. In this presentation, I will highlight our recent advances in these areas and discuss future opportunities for atomically dispersed catalysts in chlorine electrocatalysis.

t24.k: Titanium Oxycarbide; RuPt Alloy; Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
t24.a: The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), a fundamental process in water electrolysis, is highly dependent on the performance of noble-metal catalysts, including platinum (Pt) and ruthenium (Ru). The catalytic activity and durability of these metals are strongly influenced by the properties of their supporting materials. Titanium carbide (TiC)-based supports have attracted considerable attention for their excellent electrical conductivity, high corrosion resistance, and strong metal–support interaction (SMSI). Nevertheless, conventional synthetic approaches to TiC often involve complex procedures and hazardous fluorine-based reagents, yielding materials with limited surface area and porosity. To address these limitations, using highly porous metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) as precursors for TiC-based supports is a promising strategy to improve electrocatalyst performance. In this study, mesoporous titanium oxycarbide (TiOC) was synthesized via direct pyrolysis of a titanium-based metal–organic framework (MIL-125) at temperatures of 800°C, 900°C, and 1000°C, yielding TiOC-T materials (where T denotes the pyrolysis temperature). These TiOC-T materials served as supports for RuPt alloys prepared by a combination of wet impregnation and hydrogen reduction. By adjusting the pyrolysis temperature, TiOC-1000 exhibits higher Ti–C content and a greater number of defective Ti3+ sites. Notably, TiOC-1000 exhibits a high surface area with mesoporous structure. After RuPt deposition, RuPt/TiOC-1000 retains the Ti–C structure and displays a pronounced SMSI effect. Furthermore, intermetallic interactions between Ru and Pt are observed, thereby enhancing HER performance in both acidic and alkaline conditions. These findings establish that MOF-derived mesoporous TiOC serves as an efficient support for RuPt alloys, significantly enhancing catalytic HER activity and stability.

t25.a: The development of efficient and sustainable hydrogen production technologies has become increasingly important for the transition to a carbon-neutral society. Water electrolysis is regarded as one of the most promising approaches, but its widespread implementation requires electrocatalysts with both high catalytic activity and long-term operational durability. This study focuses on the rational design and comprehensive evaluation of advanced electrocatalysts for water electrolysis. Material synthesis, structural and physicochemical characterization, and electrochemical performance analyses were systematically combined to investigate catalytic behavior and durability under relevant operating conditions. The designed electrocatalysts exhibited improved electrochemical performance and enhanced stability compared with conventional systems. The integrated evaluation also provided valuable insights into the relationships between catalyst structure, interfacial properties, and electrochemical performance, offering general guidelines for catalyst optimization. This work demonstrates a comprehensive approach for the design and evaluation of advanced electrocatalysts for water electrolysis. The findings provide a broader understanding of catalyst design principles and contribute to the development of highly efficient and durable electrochemical energy conversion technologies.

t26.a: Proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) is a promising technology for green hydrogen production; however, its commercialization is hindered by the high cost and scarcity of iridium (Ir)-based oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalysts. Developing low-Ir anodes with high activity and long-term durability is therefore essential. This presentation provides an overview of the development of low-Ir anodes through the rational design of advanced supported and nanostructured Ir catalysts, highlighting strategies to reduce Ir loading while maintaining high activity and long-term durability. Low-Ir anodes were developed through the rational design of supported and nanostructured Ir catalysts. Mesoporous and hierarchical multiporous Ta₂O₅ supports were engineered to enhance Ir dispersion and strengthen metal-support interactions. Subsequently, a hollow dual-phase IrOx (HDP-IrOx) catalyst comprising amorphous IrOx and crystalline IrO₂ domains was designed to overcome the activity–durability trade-off. The Ta₂O₅-supported catalysts improved Ir utilization through enhanced electron transport, a larger electrochemically active surface area, and stabilization of favorable Ir oxidation states, enabling an MEA with an anode loading of only 0.2 mg/cm² to achieve 2.5 A/cm² at 1.89 V. The optimized HDP-IrOx catalyst further improved mass transport and structural robustness through its hollow dual-phase architecture, delivering stable PEMWE operation for over 1100 h at the same Ir loading (0.2 mg/cm²) with minimal voltage degradation. The combination of strong metal-support interactions and dual-phase nanostructural engineering provides an effective strategy to maximize Ir utilization while achieving high activity and excellent durability. These design principles offer a practical pathway toward scalable, low-Ir PEMWE anodes for economically viable green hydrogen production.

t27.k: Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis (AEMWE); Catalyst-Coated Membrane (CCM); Membrane Surface Patterning
t27.a: Catalyst-coated substrate (CCS) has been widely employed for membrane electrode assembly (MEA) fabrication in anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE). However, limited membrane/electrode interfacial compatibility often results in increased interfacial resistance and reduced electrochemical performance. Although studies on catalyst-coated membrane (CCM)-based MEAs for AEMWE remain relatively limited, increasing attention has recently been paid to CCM fabrication as a promising strategy to improve interfacial contact and cell performance. In addition, membrane surface texturing (or patterning) has emerged as an effective approach to further enhance membrane/electrode interfacial characteristics. Since CCM fabrication has already been well established in PEM fuel cell technology, it provides a promising platform for application to AEMWE. This presentation introduces recent advances in CCM fabrication for AEMWE, focusing on membrane surface patterning and catalyst layer deposition using conventional spray coating, newly developed direct ink coating, and decal transfer processes. The influence of membrane surface morphology and fabrication methods on catalyst layer formation, membrane/electrode interfacial contact, electrochemical performance, and durability is discussed. The combination of membrane surface patterning and optimized CCM fabrication significantly improves membrane/catalyst interfacial compatibility, resulting in reduced interfacial resistance, enhanced mass transport, and improved reaction kinetics. Furthermore, the synergistic effects of patterned membranes and advanced CCM fabrication processes lead to enhanced MEA performance, lower ohmic resistance, and improved long-term durability. The integration of membrane surface engineering with CCM fabrication provides an effective strategy for developing high-performance MEAs for AEMWE. These approaches offer practical guidance for scalable MEA manufacturing and accelerate the commercialization of next-generation anion exchange membrane water electrolysis systems.

t28.a: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations combined with a genetic algorithm (GA) structural search were performed to elucidate the structural and catalytic roles of Co dopants in hydrated V2O5 nanobelts (V2O5·nH2O NBs). A theoretical V2O5·nH2O model was first constructed by placing H2O molecules between V2O5 layers according to the experimentally determined hydration level, followed by GA optimization to identify the most stable water configurations. The optimized model reproduced the experimentally observed interlayer distance and its contraction after Co incorporation. Comparative calculations for interlayer- and lattice-doped CoVO models showed that interlayer Co doping is thermodynamically more favorable and better matches the experimental XPS results, including partial reduction of V species and Co2+-like oxidation states. Electronic-structure calculations further revealed that Co doping eliminates the small band gap of pristine V2O5·nH2O, suggesting enhanced electronic conductivity. OER free-energy calculations on exposed surface models demonstrated that Co incorporation significantly lowers the theoretical overpotential by modulating the adsorption energies of oxygen-containing intermediates. In particular, Co dopants weaken the excessively strong intermediate binding of pristine V2O5·nH2O, thereby improving the OER energetics. These results indicate that atomically dispersed Co species in V2O5·nH2O simultaneously promote charge transport and optimize surface reaction energetics.

t29.k: Triethyl Phosphate; Lithium-metal Batteries; Nonflammable Electrolytes
t29.a: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) offer ultrahigh theoretical energy density but are limited by electrolyte flammability and lithium dendrite growth. Although triethyl phosphate (TEP) improves safety as an intrinsically flame-retardant solvent, its poor electrochemical stability toward lithium metal causes continuous decomposition and interfacial degradation, restricting its practical application. In this study, an intrinsically nonflammable electrolyte is proposed. Through optimization of dual-salt and mixed-solvent compositions, an electrolyte comprising LiFSI, LiBOB, TEP, and FEC in a molar ratio of 0.8:0.2:2:2 was developed. TEP serves as the primary solvent, while lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) provides ionic conductivity. Lithium bis(oxalate)borate (LiBOB) is introduced to enhance the structural stability and mechanical strength of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) is incorporated as a preferential film-forming additive. Electrochemical analyses confirm that the designed electrolyte maintains intrinsic nonflammability while promoting the formation of a stable, ion-conductive, and mechanically robust SEI layer on the lithium metal anode. The resulting SEI suppresses continuous TEP decomposition and mitigates interfacial corrosion. In Li//Li symmetric cells, the electrolyte exhibits a low initial overpotential and stable cycling for over 500 h. In Li//Cu asymmetric cells, a Coulombic efficiency of 77.2% is achieved. Furthermore, Li//LMO half-cells deliver an initial discharge capacity of 93.2 mAh g⁻¹ and maintain 97% Coulombic efficiency after 10 cycles. Overall, this work provides a feasible strategy to improve the interfacial stability of phosphate-based electrolytes for safer, high-energy-density lithium metal batteries.

t30.a: Electrochemical CO₂ conversion is promising for sustainable chemical production, but its efficiency depends strongly on electrode composition, interfaces, and surface stability. This study compares catalyst design strategies for low-temperature CO₂ reduction and high-temperature solid oxide electrolysis. Zirconium-containing bismuth catalysts were evaluated for aqueous CO₂ reduction to formate. Their structure and electrochemical behavior were analyzed to clarify the role of Bi–ZrO₂ interfaces. CuFe₂O₄ cathodes were examined before and after high-temperature CO₂ electrolysis using electrochemical measurements, low-energy ion scattering, and TOF-SIMS. In the low-temperature system, zirconium incorporation formed Bi–ZrO₂ heterointerfaces that modified the local reaction environment and improved formate selectivity. In the high-temperature system, CuFe₂O₄ showed changes in surface composition and elemental distribution during electrolysis. These surface changes were associated with phase stability and electrochemical performance. Across both systems, CO₂ conversion was controlled not only by bulk composition but also by interfacial structure and operation-induced surface evolution. Designing stable interfaces and controlling surface reconstruction are therefore key strategies for improving the efficiency and durability of CO₂ electrolysis electrodes over a wide temperature range.

t31.k: Wearable Sensors; Flexible Electronics; Hybrid Direct Bonding
t31.a: The realization of imperceptible and reliable skin-integrated electronics demands a holistic strategy that simultaneously tackles material-level degradation, interfacial mechanical mismatch, and sustainable energy autonomy. Conventional wearable sensing systems suffer from fundamental trade-offs: polymer adhesives commonly used for device integration introduce significant viscoelastic signal drift and parasitic interface resistance; multilayer assemblies fail under repetitive mechanical deformation; and lightweight energy harvesters undergo rapid ambient degradation under operational stresses. In this invited talk, we present an integrated framework that bridges environmentally robust ultraflexible optoelectronics, adhesive-free low-temperature hybrid direct bonding, and body-coupled wireless power delivery to establish high-fidelity, drift-free, and autonomous on-skin sensory platforms. We established a coordinated hierarchy spanning functional materials, seamless integration, and system architecture. At the component level, intrinsic stability was realized by engineering ultraflexible perovskite solar cells with dual hole-transporting layers and 15-nm atomic layer deposited AlOx moisture barriers, developing organic photovoltaics on 3.6-µm UV-filtering polyimide substrates with indium-doped electron transport layers, and utilizing 5-µm single-crystal silicon piezoresistors to eliminate viscoelastic relaxation. At the integration level, a low-temperature (85 °C) hybrid direct bonding method (LBPW) combining water-vapor plasma activation and the water-plasticizer effect was established to simultaneously achieve atomic-level Au-to-Au metallic diffusion and parylene-to-parylene fusion bonding across the entire interface without adhesive interlayers. The engineered ultraflexible components demonstrated outstanding performance and durability: perovskite solar cells achieved a power conversion efficiency of 20.3%, a specific power of 27.2 W g⁻¹, and record ambient air stability while retaining >95% efficiency after 1,000 bending/folding cycles, while UV-filtering substrates extended organic solar cell 1-sun operational lifetime after 4,000 cyclic bends. Concurrently, direct Au–Au bonding of ultrathin silicon piezoresistors eliminated the ~15% viscoelastic drift seen in adhesive-based sensors, maintaining stable sensitivity over 10,000 cycles for precise gesture tracking in data gloves. Crucially, the adhesive-free LBPW bonding unified these heterogeneous materials with high resolution (5-µm line/space, contact resistance of 0.33 mΩ cm⁻²) and robust shear strength, enabling 3D-stacked organic photodetector/light-emitting diode photoplethysmogram (PPG) sensors that conform to 0.5-mm bending radii with <3% resistance change after 10,000 cycles. By organically linking advanced ultraflexible optoelectronics, adhesive-free hybrid direct bonding, and body-mediated energy distribution, this platform overcomes long-standing constraints in flexibility, electrical fidelity, and operational lifetime. This comprehensive materials-to-systems architecture provides a versatile foundation for next-generation skin-conformal healthcare diagnostics, robotic sensory skins, and unconstrained human-machine interfaces.

t32.k: Wearable Sensors; Piezoelectric Nanogenerators; Self-powered Energy Harvesting
t32.a: Wearable and skin-integrated sensors are rapidly emerging as key technologies for continuous healthcare monitoring, assistive systems, HMIs, and IoT platforms. However, conventional rigid sensing components are mechanically incompatible with the soft, curved, and continuously deforming surfaces of the human body. Therefore, developing materials that simultaneously offer flexibility, stretchability, sensitivity, mechanical durability, environmental stability, and skin conformability is essential. Moreover, minimizing dependence on external batteries is important for long-term wearable operation. This invited talk presents our progress in designing flexible and stretchable piezoelectric materials that directly convert biomechanical deformation into electrical signals, enabling self-powered wearable and skin-integrated sensing. Our materials strategy involves integrating functional piezoelectric ceramics, metal oxides, transition-metal sulfides, BaTiO3-based nanostructures, carbon nanomaterials, MXenes, and engineered heterostructures with mechanically compliant PDMS and PVDF polymer matrices. Composition optimization, heterointerface engineering, interfacial polarization, charge separation, microcrack engineering, and filler–polymer interactions were employed to enhance electromechanical transduction while preserving device flexibility. The resulting flexible piezoelectric nanogenerators (FPENGs) were evaluated under controlled mechanical forces and different environmental conditions and subsequently integrated into wearable and skin-attachable configurations. More recently, we extended this approach toward resilient and stretchable dual-hydrogel architectures by combining self-healing conductive hydrogel electrodes with bio-derived BaTiO3-containing piezoelectric networks. These materials and device architectures enabled sensitive detection of subtle physiological signals as well as large biomechanical movements. DyW@MoS2-based FPENGs were utilized in smart masks for real-time respiratory monitoring, whereas microcrack-engineered f-MWCNTs/BaTiO3 composites provided enhanced acoustic sensing. AgZn(MoO4)(WO4)–PDMS sensors enabled differentiation of voluntary and involuntary eye blinks and demonstrated eye-controlled human–machine interaction. ZnWO4/BaTiO3 smart gloves enabled self-powered Morse-code communication through finger movements, while MXene/f-MWCNTs/BaTiO3 devices attached to the throat captured vocal-cord vibrations for voice recognition and speech-to-text applications. Our recent resilient and stretchable hydrogel FPENG operated across an ultrawide force range of 0.01–883 N and maintained electromechanical functionality under varying humidity, temperature, and chemical environments, enabling biomechanical sensing, handwriting recognition, and real-time communication. Collectively, these studies demonstrate the evolution of our materials design from conventional flexible ceramic–polymer composites toward heterointerface-engineered, microstructured, stretchable, self-healing, and environmentally resilient sensing platforms. The findings emphasize that rational materials chemistry combined with interface and mechanical-architecture engineering can substantially improve electromechanical transduction without sacrificing mechanical compliance. These advances provide promising pathways toward battery-free, skin-conformal wearable sensors and intelligent HMIs for healthcare, assistive communication, personal safety, and next-generation IoT technologies.

t33.a: Conventional Ag/AgCl and metal electrodes often cause wearing discomfort and are susceptible to motion artifacts because of their limited breathability and mechanical mismatch with skin, while existing PEDOT film- and textile-based electrodes remain constrained by optical opacity, substrate dependence, and insufficient moisture permeability. Here, we developed a transparent, free-standing, and skin-conformable bioelectrode by wet-spinning PEDOT fibers, aligning them into an open-grid architecture, and applying sulfuric acid treatment to induce irreversible self-fusion while enhancing electrical conductivity. To improve skin conformability and reduce interfacial impedance without compromising breathability, the self-fused grid was sandwiched between electrospun poly(vinyl alcohol)-poly(acrylic acid) nanofiber layers infused with a glycerol-based electrolyte. The resulting electrode exhibited over 98% optical transparency, a sheet resistance of approximately 100 Ω sq⁻¹, and stable electrical performance over 10,000 deformation cycles at strains of up to 35%. It also demonstrated low skin–electrode interfacial impedance, high moisture permeability, and reliable electrocardiography and electromyography recording for up to three days, with a signal-to-noise ratio reaching 30.9 dB. When applied to the face, the electrode enabled accurate electrooculographic eye tracking and clear differentiation of facial muscle activity associated with smiling and anger. These results demonstrate that substrate-free, self-fused PEDOT fiber grids combined with breathable nanofiber encapsulation can provide an imperceptible, mechanically robust, and user-friendly epidermal interface for long-term physiological monitoring and facial muscle movement detection.

t34.a: An ultimate goal of biological measurement is to monitor the states of a living body in a non-invasive, continuous, and accurate manner without disturbing the natural functions or activities of the living body. Because sensors in direct contact with biological tissues are inevitably exposed to physical disturbances caused by physical contact, considerable efforts have been made to minimize the effects of sensors [1]. In temperature measurement, for example, it is preferable to reduce the heat capacity or thermal conductance of a sensor in order to suppress the effect of heat transfer from the object to the sensor [2]. Furthermore, mechanical compliance with electronics is extremely important for biological objects. The skin is soft and has a three-dimensional structure. Flexible and/or stretchable sensors have been proposed to reduce the effects of modulus differences between the skin and the electronics [3]. We developed nanomesh-based on-skin electronics with ultrathin, porous, and soft structures for a small area of the skin, as well as a textile EMG monitoring system using coaxially shielded conductive yarns. Nanomesh electrodes could attach directly to the skin without additional adhesives because of their high gas permeability and soft structure. Stable contact was maintained for more than one week without detectable skin irritation. Nanomesh pressure sensors on the fingertip could measure finger manipulation with negligible influence on tactile sensation [4]. The textile EMG system could record EMG signals from widely distributed muscle groups of the body. The shielded yarn reduced external noise, and the noise level was below 0.1 mV even under noisy conditions [5]. These results show that soft and permeable electronics can measure biological signals while reducing the influence of the devices on the skin. Nanomesh and textile devices can be useful for biological monitoring from a small area such as the fingertip to a large area of the body. 1. D. Kim, et al, Science 333, 838 (2011). 2. R. Webb, et al., Nat. Mater. 12, 938 (2013). 3. J. Park, et al., Sci. Adv. 1, e1500661 (2015). 4. S. Lee, et al., Science 370, 966 (2020). 5. S. Lee, et al., Sci. Adv. 11, eadx4518 (2025).

t35.a: The rapid growth of smart healthcare and personalized medicine has created increasing demand for flexible and wearable sensors capable of continuously and reliably monitoring physiological signals and human activities. Beyond the selection of functional materials, mechanical and structural design plays a critical role in determining key sensor characteristics, including sensitivity, linearity, dynamic range, stability, hysteresis, and response speed. In this talk, I will present our recent efforts toward mechanics-driven design of flexible and wearable physical sensors and their integration into smart healthcare and medical systems. First, various micro- and nano-structured pressure and strain sensors will be introduced, illustrating how engineered deformation mechanisms can substantially improve sensing performance. Examples include porous elastomer–carbon nanotube composites exploiting structural elasticity and percolation, bio-inspired gradient structures enabling tunable sensitivity and broad linear sensing ranges, thermoformed three-dimensional electronics for customizable tactile sensing, and auxetic mechanical metamaterials combined with piezo-transmittance for highly stable and self-powered strain sensing. Bio-inspired interfacial designs for mechanically robust hybrid flexible electronics will also be discussed. These sensing technologies are further translated into system-level healthcare applications, including real-time blood-pressure estimation, large-area body-pressure mapping, motion and exercise monitoring with machine learning, and wearable sensing integrated with augmented-reality interfaces. Particular emphasis will be placed on pressure-injury prevention, where wireless and battery-free pressure/temperature sensors have been developed for beds and wheelchairs, together with sensor arrays and feedback-controlled mattresses for continuous monitoring and active pressure redistribution. Wearable NFC-based optoelectronic platforms for health-condition monitoring will also be presented. Collectively, these studies demonstrate how rational mechanical design across multiple length scales can provide a powerful route toward high-performance, conformable, and intelligent sensing platforms for next-generation healthcare and medical applications. Prof. Inkyu Park received his B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. from KAIST (1998), UIUC (2003) and UC Berkeley (2007), respectively, all in mechanical engineering. He has been with the department of mechanical engineering at KAIST since 2009 as a faculty member and is currently a full professor and KAIST Endowed Chair Professor. His research interests are micro/nanofabrication, smart sensors for healthcare, environmental and biomedical monitoring, and flexible & wearable electronics. He has published more than 235 SCI journal articles (48+ cover articles) and 50+ patents in the area of MEMS/NANO engineering, and his publications have been cited more than 24,685 times (h-index=72) as of Aug 2026. He is a recipient of HP Open Innovation Research Award (2009-2012), KAIST Prize for Academic Excellence (2021), KAIST Grand Prize for Technology Innovation Award (2019), Top 10 Nanotechnology of Korea (2023), and Minister Award from Ministry of Science and ICT (2023). He is also a fellow (academician) of Korean Academy of Science and Technology (KAST) and a general member of National Academy of Engineering of Korea (NAEK). At present, he holds the position of editor for Sensors and Actuators B: Chemical (Elsevier), a top-ranked SCI journal in the field of chemical sensor technology.

t36.a: Biomimetic flexible sensors with skin-like softness and high sensitivity have attracted significant attention for applications in human–machine interfaces, robotic skins, and wearable healthcare systems. Despite substantial advances in soft materials and sensing mechanisms, achieving multifunctionality, environmental robustness, and seamless integration with the human body remains challenging. Biological sensory systems offer valuable design principles because their highly evolved micro/nanostructures enable sophisticated sensing functions and adaptive responses to external stimuli. We developed a series of biomimetic structural design strategies based on micro/nanostructured polymer composites for high-performance soft sensing and bioinspired information processing. The designs were inspired by the hierarchical structures and functions of human fingertips, the frequency-selective response of the cochlea, stimuli-responsive color-changing structures in nature, and biological synapses. These concepts were implemented in multifunctional electronic skins, frequency-tunable triboelectric acoustic and haptic sensors, colorimetric tactile sensors, and biodegradable artificial synapses. The fingertip-inspired electronic skins enabled highly sensitive discrimination of multiple mechanical and thermal stimuli, including normal pressure, shear, stretching, bending, static and dynamic forces, and temperature. Cochlea-inspired triboelectric sensors incorporating hierarchical ferroelectric composites provided frequency-tunable acoustic and haptic sensing for dual-mode human–machine interfaces. Bioinspired colorimetric tactile sensors quantitatively visualized external forces through distinct chromatic changes. Furthermore, the biodegradable artificial synapse operated at sub-millivolt levels, reproduced key synaptic behaviors, and enabled a bioinspired reflexive system capable of stimulus-dependent learning and reflex-like responses. These results demonstrate that biomimetic structural engineering provides a versatile strategy for integrating diverse sensing, visualization, and information-processing functions into soft material platforms. By translating structural and functional principles found in biological sensory systems into engineered materials and devices, this approach offers promising opportunities for next-generation wearable electronics, robotic skins, and adaptive human–machine interfaces.

t37.a: Building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) technologies offer promising solutions for urban power generation. Among these, transparent luminescent solar concentrators (TLSCs) are exceptionally well-suited for BIPV applications because they combine high average visible transmittance (AVT) and a superior color rendering index (CRI) with excellent aesthetic qualities. However, their power conversion efficiency (PCE) and light utilization efficiency (LUE) are often constrained by the wavelength selectivity of the harvested solar spectrum. Furthermore, achieving high photoelectric performance remains challenging due to severe spectral overlap between absorption and emission, which triggers detrimental self-absorption losses. Fluorescent organic molecules featuring excited-state intramolecular proton transfer (ESIPT) have emerged as highly attractive luminophores to address this bottleneck. Thanks to their characteristically large Stokes shifts, ESIPT fluorophores effectively eliminate self-reabsorption to significantly boost optical efficiency. This talk highlights recent advancements in the development of novel ESIPT fluorophores and their integration into high-performance TLSCs. Specifically, we discuss a series of HBB- and HBI-based ESIPT dyes that exhibit intense keto orange-red emission, yielding high thin-film photoluminescence quantum yields (42–100%) and minimal spectral overlap integrals (0.30–0.79%). When coupled with silicon solar cells, these TLSC-PV devices achieve impressive optical efficiencies of 4.15–9.37% and PCEs ranging from 0.46% to 2.21% under AM 1.5G illumination. Notably, they deliver a high external quantum efficiency (8.74–21.47%), an excellent CRI of 99, and an outstanding AVT of 92%, reflecting both efficient light harvesting and pristine transparency. Finally, alternative molecular designs and near-infrared (NIR) absorbing dyes will be discussed and compared.

t38.a: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have attracted worldwide attention due to their remarkable power conversion efficiencies. However, their operational stability remains a major obstacle to commercialization. Among the various degradation pathways, the accumulation of trapped charges, where a device operates, plays a fundamental role in initiating perovskite degradation. Trapped charges generate local electric fields, which leads to lattice distortions, lower ion migration barriers, and facilitate defect-mediated decomposition. These coupled processes progressively deteriorate photovoltaic performance.
