In this presentation, we discuss the fundamental mechanisms of trapped charge-driven degradation in wide bandgap(WBG) PSCs, in which halide segregration actively takes place in the presence of trapped charges. To mitigate accumulation of trapped charges, we introduce a maximum stability point tracking (MSPT) strategy as an operating protocol, which dynamically operates PSCs at conditions that minimize trapped charge accumulation while maintaining efficient power generation. Unlike conventional maximum power point tracking (MPPT), MSPT significantly suppresses degradation by reducing charge-induced lattice perturbations and ion migration. As a result, wide-bandgap PSCs exhibiting rapid performance loss under MPPT operation maintain over 90% of their initial efficiency for more than 700 h under continuous illumination. The presented results highlight trapped charge accumulation as a central degradation driver in PSCs and demonstrate that stability can be substantially improved not only through materials engineering but also through intelligent operational control. These findings provide new insights into the design of durable perovskite photovoltaics and establish operation-aware stabilization strategies as a promising pathway toward commercially viable PSC technologies.

t39.k: Carbon Electrode; Perovskite Solar Cells; Sustainability
t39.a: Carbon electrode-based perovskite solar cell modules (C-PSMs) represent a promising pathway to advance the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), specifically to provide affordable and clean energy (SDG 7), foster industry innovation and infrastructure (SDG 9), and promote responsible consumption and production (SDG 12). In this work, we introduce a novel, cost-effective free-standing carbon electrode with self-encapsulation, superhydrophobic properties, as well as outstanding flexibility, produced via an all low-temperature process. This innovative carbon electrode, characterized by a low sheet resistance of ~ 4 Ω/cm², effectively solves the lateral resistance issue commonly encountered in large-area modules, thereby enabling stable, efficient, and mechanically robust device operation. Using a combination of P1 (laser scribing), P2 (tape marking), and P3 (engraved free-standing carbon electrodes ), perovskite modules were fabricated on 5x5 cm² substrates (active area ∼10 cm²). The modules achieved a power conversion efficiency of 7.82% under 1 sun illumination (with Voc = 5.64 V), and 10.64% under LED 1000 lux illumination (with Voc = 4.63 V). These findings demonstrate the strong potential of carbon-based approach for scalable fabrication of durable, high-performance, adaptable, and cost-effective perovskite solar modules, supporting progress toward sustainable eco-commercialization.

t40.a: Ambient-air processing remains one of the central unresolved challenges for scalable perovskite solar cells manufacturing: uncontrolled humidity and oxygen exposure disrupt nucleation and crystallization kinetics, producing small grains and high defect densities that limit efficiency and operational stability. These challenges are especially pronounced in wide-bandgap compositions relevant to tandem and semi-transparent solar cells. We address this by designing additive molecules that actively participate in perovskite crystallization and defect chemistry under open-air conditions. Wide-bandgap CsFA perovskite films were processed entirely under ambient, high-humidity conditions using two additive classes: a urea small-molecule Lewis-base additive combined with gas-quenching, and natural polysaccharide (starch) additives that isolate macromolecular topology as a variable independent of small-molecule chemistry. Devices were fabricated with low-cost, vacuum-free carbon electrodes. Adduct formation and film defect chemistry were characterized by FTIR, DFT, and standardized operational stability protocols (ISOS-L-1). Urea forms a urea–perovskite adduct that extends the annealing window from 1.8 to 5.3 minutes, enabling reproducible wide-bandgap film formation at 40% relative humidity — conditions under which conventional processing typically fails. Starch-based devices reach 16.17% efficiency with double the T80 lifetime of urea-based controls, showing that operational stability is governed by polymer topology rather than grain size. We are extending this additive-design framework to several sulfur-containing, redox-active molecules, targeting phase-segregation suppression in wide-bandgap systems. Small-molecule reactivity and macromolecular topology emerge as distinct, complementary design levers for defect control in ambient-processed, wide-bandgap perovskites. This framework, paired with a scalable carbon-electrode architecture, offers a materials-design route toward humidity-tolerant, tandem-compatible perovskite solar cells.

t41.k: Inverted perovskite solar cells; Interfacial reaction; ALD-NiO
t41.a: In inverted perovskite solar cells (i-PSCs), thin films of NiO as hole transport layers (HTLs) have been widely used due to their p-type characteristics, wide bandgap, and low cost. However, Ni≥3+ at the surface of NiO film deprotonates cationic amines and oxidizes halide anions, thereby promoting the formation of PbI₂-rich barriers that impede efficient hole extraction at the perovskite/NiO interface. It limits the hole transporting and enhances charge recombination, thus resulting in a loss of open-circuit voltage (Voc). Herein, we systematically analyze the changes in FAI-NiO and α-FAPbI₃-NiO powder mixtures upon heating, as well as the interface evolution of perovskite/NiO films under thermal treatment. Based on X-ray Diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analyses, we identify the presence of PbI₂ at the perovskite/NiO interface. Based on these insights, we further explore a strategy for depositing molecular interlayers on top of atomic layer deposited (ALD) - NiO. Furthermore, compared to devices with bare NiO, NiO-based devices incorporating the interlayers exhibit improved Voc and fill factor (FF), as the interlayers can prevent detrimental interfacial redox reaction at the perovskite/NiO interface and optimize the energy level alignment between perovskite and NiO. Consequently, introducing the molecular interlayer leads to significant improvements in device performance: Me-4PACz increases the average power conversion efficiency (PCE) to 21.73%, while 3PATAT-C3 results in a 23.12% enhancement, compared to devices employing NiO alone as the hole transport layer (HTL). With this strategy, the inverted PSCs were systematically fabricated and compared across active areas of 0.06, 0.25, and 1 cm2. A novel 3D model was developed to link fill factor losses to grain boundary area within the perovskite layer, establishing a direct connection between film microstructure and upscaling behaviour. These findings highlight ALD-NiO as a promising route for scalable PSC fabrication that can guide the design of more efficient, large-area perovskite devices for future commercialization and tandem photovoltaic applications. It will be also discussed on direct experimental evidence that inevitable strain induces static Rashba effects, offering new insights into strain engineering for high-performance perovskite optoelectronics and potential quantum applications. References [1] Shin, S., et.al, and Shin, H., “Uneven Strain Relaxation in Formamidinium Lead Triiodide (FAPbI3) Films upon Aging”, ACS Energy Lett. 9, (2024) [2] Xu, Y, et.al, Wakamiya, A., and Shin, H., “Molecular Bridge on Buried Interface for Energy Level Alignment in Inverted Perovskite Solar Cell with Efficiency over 25%” ACS Energy Lett. 10 (2025) [3] Jeong, H.J., et. al., Wakamiya, A., Saeki, A. Sung, J., and Shin, H., “Anisotropic Strain-induced Centrosymmetry Breaking in Cubic Formamidinium Lead Iodide (a-FAPbI3) Thin Films”, Adv. Energy Mater. (2026) [4] Gibson, A., Wang, C., Amornkitbamrung, U., In, Y., Han, S., Jeong, H.J., Jung, H.S., and Shin, H., “Scalable Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells Enabled by Atomic Layer Deposition”, EES Solar (2026) [5] Wang, C., Amornkitbamrung, U., Xu, Y., Rhee, R.J.K., Gibson, A., Jeong, H.J., In, Y., Song, J., Wakamiya, A., and Shin, H., “Buried Interfacial Engineering in Metal-Halide Perovskite/NiO Heterostructures through Direct Observation of Interfacial Reactions”, ACS Energy Lett. (2026)

t42.k: Organic Photovoltaics; Nonfullerene Acceptors; Electron Paramagnetic Resonance
t42.a: Light energy conversion is a fundamental process that underpins numerous natural phenomena and technological applications. Our research has focused on organic photovoltaics (OPVs) with the goal of improving solar energy conversion efficiency through molecular design and mechanistic understanding. We have developed a wide variety of dyes and redox shuttles for dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSCs), as well as donor and acceptor molecules for bulk heterojunction (BHJ) OPVs, to elucidate the fundamental factors governing photovoltaic performance. In particular, we have clarified the intricate relationships among molecular structure, molecular packing, film morphology, excited-state dynamics, charge-transfer processes, and device performance. Our studies have addressed: (1) inclined adsorption geometries of dyes on TiO₂, (2) methylene-bridge-fused molecular structures for high-performance DSSCs, (3) the effects of copper-based redox shuttles in DSSCs, (4) isomeric effects of fullerene acceptors, (5) long-lived excited states in non-fullerene acceptor (NFA) films, (6) charge-transfer dynamics in two-dimensional layered materials covalently functionalized with photoactive molecules, and (7) electron–hole separation distance distributions as physically measurable descriptors that quantitatively correlate molecular packing with charge generation, charge recombination, and voltage losses in OPVs. This presentation will provide an overview of these studies and demonstrate how rationally designed model systems can reveal the fundamental design principles governing high-performance organic photovoltaic materials and devices.

t43.k: Organic Tandem Solar Cells; Intermediate Connection
t43.a: Intermediate connections in organic tandem solar cells typically consist of multiple charge-transport and recombination layers, which complicate device fabrication and may introduce additional optical and electrical losses. Here, we demonstrate a structurally simplified organic tandem solar cell employing a single-layer intermediate connection by extending an interfacial engineering strategy originally developed for metal–semiconductor–metal (MSM) organic solar cells. In MSM devices, selective modification of the photoactive-layer surfaces enables efficient charge extraction without conventional electron- and hole-transport layers, substantially reducing device complexity while maintaining power conversion efficiencies exceeding 18%. Based on this concept, tetrahexylammonium iodide (THA-I) was applied as a surface treatment to the PM6:L8-BO and PM6:Y6 photoactive layers rather than being deposited as a separate physical layer. The THA-I treatment provides the required interfacial charge selectivity, allowing M-PEDOT:PSS alone to function as the single physical intermediate connection between the front and rear subcells. This architecture successfully integrates the charge-selective and electrical-connection functions required for tandem operation without additional physically deposited charge-transport layers in the intermediate connection. These results demonstrate that surface-selective interfacial modification provides a practical route toward substantially simplified fabrication of high-performance organic tandem solar cells.

t44.k: Pre-blended perovskite powder, Stable perovskite precursor solution, Perovskite crystallization.
t44.a: Perovskite solar cells have been studied for decades and now offer high efficiency and stability, yet a low-cost, scalable, and reproducible fabrication route remains a key barrier to commercialization. Here, we address this challenge by fabricating perovskite micro-polycrystalline powders through a solvent-free mechanochemical synthesis process. Using industrial-standard ball milling, pre-formulated micro-polycrystal powders can dissolve readily in standard or green solvent systems, providing a simplified, ready-to-use route to precursor solution preparation for thin-film fabrication. We show that this solvent-free ball-milling approach enhances perovskite precursor solution stability without any chemical additives, an effect attributed to the formation of an iodoplumbate-cation framework. Using in situ photoluminescence (PL), in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD), PL lifetime measurements, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and nanomechanical/conductive atomic force microscopy (AFM), we demonstrate that films derived from these powders exhibit favorable formation dynamics, earlier nucleation, faster growth, and pronounced Ostwald ripening, yielding high-quality, high-modulus perovskite thin films. This approach is validated in two device architectures: small-scale carbon-based solar cells fabricated via spin coating and large-scale metal-based solar modules fabricated via slot-die coating. Together, these results establish pre-formulated, micro-polycrystal powder synthesis as a scalable, simple, and versatile platform for high-performance perovskite photovoltaic production.

t45.a: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) face critical challenges owing to their intrinsic instability under harsh environmental conditions. Although various strategies have been explored to enhance stability, their effects remain temporary. Herein, we designed dendrimers that serve as volatile reservoirs, enabling repeated self-healing while simultaneously enhancing power conversion efficiency (PCE). We introduced dendrimers with appropriate and effective functional groups into lead halide perovskites (LHPs) to impart self-healing properties while achieving a high PCE. PSCs incorporating these dendrimers exhibited a PCE exceeding 26% (certified PCE: 26.0%), surpassing the PCE of pristine PSCs (~24%). Furthermore, these dendrimer-based PSCs retained over 96% of their initial PCE for 1000 h under controlled conditions (25 ± 1 °C, 60 ± 5% relative humidity (RH)). Interestingly, the dendrimer-based PSCs retained 90% of their initial PCE even after undergoing repeated exposure to high humidity conditions (60 ± 1 °C, 85 ± 5% RH) and dry conditions (25 ± 1 °C, <20% RH) for 10 cycles. We further elucidated the origin of the dendrimer-derived LHP self-healing mechanism through chemical analyses and molecular simulations. These results demonstrated the effectiveness of dendrimers as volatile reservoirs, which enabled sustained self-healing and enhanced the stability and performance of the LHP. we introduced a novel approach to address the intrinsic instability issues of PSCs by incorporating a self-healing feature within LHPs. We have elucidated the self-healing mechanism of PSCs using organic additives, which is supported by solid evidence.

t46.a: Crystal growth and defect engineering have become central research topics in the development of metal halide perovskite solar cells (PSCs). A fundamental understanding of the underlying mechanisms has contributed substantially to recent advances in both the performance and operational stability of PSCs. In this presentation, I will discuss our recent efforts to understand crystal growth and defect passivation mechanisms in both solution- and vapor-deposited halide perovskites. Based on these insights, we have developed a series of growth- and passivation-engineering strategies, including vapor-assisted processing, to fabricate perovskite thin films with excellent optoelectronic quality. Through comprehensive in situ and ex situ characterization, we elucidate the mechanisms governing phase evolution, crystallization, and defect passivation. Building on these fundamental insights, I will discuss our research directions toward efficient, reproducible, and scalable perovskite photovoltaics.

t47.k: Perovskite microcrystal powder, Aqueous synthesis, Perovskite solar cell
t47.a: Perovskite powders have been synthesized via various methods, such as inverse temperature crystallization (ITC) and antisolvent precipitation. Although these methods offer good purity, several drawbacks remain, including the use of toxic solvents, low product yield, and complex processing procedures. These challenges call for the development of an improved and more sustainable synthesis approach. In this work, we present an environmentally friendly process for synthesizing perovskite microcrystal (MC) powder by tuning the solubility of the precursor using green solvents like water-based solvent and less toxic additives. We first optimized the process for preparing triple-cation MC powder. No impurities or residuals from the MC synthesis were detected, and the composition of the MC was confirmed for both its organic and inorganic components. The larger colloidal size observed in the MC solution likely indicates the presence of a pre-formed 3D perovskite scaffold, which facilitates perovskite film formation and results in high crystallinity. Interestingly, the MC powder also exhibits improved stability in solution, film and device forms. The MC perovskite was employed to fabricate low-cost with carbon-based NIP and metal-based PIN perovskite solar cells (PSCs); both architectures achieved good power conversion efficiencies (PCEs). This aqueous synthesis enhances both the stability and performance, paving the way for simplified and sustainable future production of perovskite solar cells.

t48.k: Graded perovskites, SnO2 nanocrystals, Intrinsic stability, Acceleration testing.
t48.a: Perovskites are prone to degradation in elevated-temperature environments. Although perovskites can be encapsulated to protect against oxygen, moisture, and ultraviolet light, they cannot avoid exposure to high-temperature environments. To improve the intrinsic stability of perovskites and prolong the lifetime of perovskite solar cells, in this work, we fabricated strained perovskite films induced by a salt-rich electron transport layer (ETL) and investigated the thermal stability against conventional perovskite counterparts. The developed perovskite exhibits a predicted lifetime of two years under ISOS-D-2 thermal aging, whereas the conventional perovskite exhibits a predicted lifetime of one year. Moreover, the developed technique results in graded structures, from I-rich to Br-rich perovskite phases, as tracked by in situ photoluminescence (in-situ PL) spectroscopy. In situ X-ray diffraction (in situ XRD) is employed to closely monitor the material evolution under elevated temperatures, specifically the phase transition between the perovskite phases and PbI₂, revealing their intrinsic thermal stability, while grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction (GIXRD) enables depth-resolved profiling of the perovskite films from surface to interface. Furthermore, the developed perovskite exhibits improved interfaces through perovskite anchoring into the ETL, as demonstrated by enhanced fill factor (FF) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) characterization.

t49.k: Functionalized Graphitic Carbon Quantum Dots; Interfacial Band Alignment; HTL-free Perovskite Solar Cells
t49.a: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have gained research and industrial attention over the past decade as a scalable, cost-effective alternative to silicon photovoltaics, particularly in carbon-based, HTL-free configurations. However, this architecture still suffers from a poor perovskite/carbon-electrode interface, both physically and electronically, presenting limited solid–solid contact and band-alignment mismatch. Among interface modification materials, graphitic carbon quantum dots are a promising candidate owing to their adjustable surface chemistry and tunable optoelectronic properties. This work synthesizes functionalized graphitic carbon quantum dots (f-g-CQDs) as a perovskite/carbon interlayer and uses ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy to map how surface functionalization controls interfacial energetics, with the goal of tuning band alignment while improving physical contact at the interface. FTIR and XPS of in-house synthesized g-CQDs show abundant surface hydroxyl groups, providing a versatile platform for molecular grafting. This surface chemistry measurably tunes the interfacial energetics of the MAPbI₃ film: bare g-CQDs deepen the surface work function from 4.13 to 4.34 eV, with ionization energy increasing from 5.55 to 5.95 eV. Functionalization with an electron-donating group reverses this trend, increasing functional-group concentration lowers the work function monotonically from 4.04 to 3.49 eV while widening the EF–VBM separation from 1.60 to 1.85 eV, giving a total work-function tuning range of 0.85 eV across the series. These results demonstrate that g-CQD surface chemistry can shift the perovskite work function over a wide range. Because a rigid interfacial dipole would shift EF and the valence band edge together, the additional 0.25 eV widening of EF–VBM indicates n-doping at the interface, making the surface less p-type and raising the hole-extraction barrier. This indicates that an electron-withdrawing group is required to shift EF in the favorable direction for band alignment, which should ultimately improve device PCE. Further characterization will be discussed in the poster.

t50.a: In this talk, I will summarize the recent research on phase engineering of nanomaterials (PEN) in my group, particularly focusing on the rational design and synthesis of novel nanomaterials with unconventional phases for various promising applications. For example, by using wet-chemical methods, for the first time, we have successfully prepared novel Au nanostructures (e.g., the hexagonal-close packed (hcp) 2H-Au nanosheets, 4H-Au nanoribbons, and 4H/fcc and fcc/2H/fcc heterophase Au nanorods), epitaxially grown metal nanostructures on the aforementioned unconventional Au nanostructures and 2H-Pd nanoparticles, and amorphous/crystalline heterophase Pd, PdCu, Rh and Rh alloy nanosheets. By using gas-solid reactions, metastable 1T'-phase group VI transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), e.g., WS2, WSe2, MoS2, MoSe2, WS2xSe2(1-x) and MoS2xSe2(1-x), have been prepared. Impressively, the 1T'-MoS2-supported single-atomically dispersed Pt (s-Pt) atoms with Pt loading up to 10 wt% exhibit superior performance in hydrogen evolution reaction. Importantly, 1T'-TMD monolayers can be stabilized on 4H-Au nanowires, which have been used for ultrasensitive SERS detection. Moreover, the salt-assisted 2H-to-1T' phase transformation of TMDs have been achieved, and the phase transformation of TMDs during our developed electrochemical Li-intercalation process has been observed. Impressively, the lithiation-induced amorphization of Pd3P2S8 has been achieved. Currently, my group focuses on the investigation of (crystal) phase-dependent physicochemical properties, functions and applications in catalysis, (opto-)electronic devices, clean energy, chemical and biosensors, surface enhanced Raman scattering, water remediation, photothermal therapy, etc., which we believe are quite unique and very important not only in fundamental studies, but also in future practical applications. Importantly, the concepts of phase engineering of nanomaterials (PEN) is proposed.

t51.a: Since the seminal report of 9.7%-efficient, stable solid-state perovskite solar cells (PSCs) in 2012, perovskite photovoltaics have rapidly evolved into one of the most promising next-generation solar technologies. Intensive research on the optoelectronic properties of organic-inorganic lead halide perovskites has driven a remarkable rise in power conversion efficiency (PCE), with certified values now exceeding 27% in single-junction devices and even higher efficiencies of about 35% in tandem configurations. Achieving such performance requires precise control over precursor solution chemistry, crystallization pathways, defect passivation, and interfacial energetics. In particular, sub-stoichiometric additives and advanced interface materials play key roles in regulating film formation, suppressing non-radiative recombination, and enhancing operational stability. More recently, the field has entered a transformative phase characterized by a broad transition from conventional n-i-p structures to p-i-n architectures, rapid advances in perovskite tandem solar cells, and significant progress in device durability. Despite these achievements, several critical challenges remain for large-scale commercialization, including long-term stability under real-world conditions, scalable manufacturing, materials reliability, and module integration. This talk will highlight key scientific breakthroughs driving advances in efficiency and stability, discuss emerging device architectures and materials strategies, and address the remaining barriers that must be overcome to translate perovskite photovoltaics from laboratory success to industrial deployment.

t52.k: Lithium batteries, mixed ion-electron transport, layered oxide cathodes, X-ray microscopy
t52.a: Lithium-ion and electron transport through battery electrodes critically determine rate capability, polarization, and reaction uniformity during electrochemical operation. In practical NCM electrodes, ionic and electronic fluxes propagate through spatially distinct pathways and are subjected to non-uniform electrochemical driving forces. Variations in particle morphology, characteristic dimensions, spatial connectivity, and interfacial properties consequently generate heterogeneous potential and concentration distributions throughout the electrode. Resolving these local transport processes remains challenging because experimentally measured electrochemical responses generally reflect the convoluted contributions of ionic transport, electronic conduction, and interfacial charge-transfer reactions. Here, we develop an integrated experimental and theoretical framework to identify and spatially resolve these coupled processes in practical NCM electrodes. Transmission X-ray microscopy (TXM) and projection X-ray microscopy (PXM) are employed to reconstruct the three-dimensional electrode architecture and quantify particle morphology, dimensions, and spatial connectivity. The extracted structural parameters are subsequently incorporated into an augmented transmission-line model and analyzed in conjunction with electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. By explicitly considering geometrically constrained transport pathways and carrier-selective interfaces, the model provides a physical interpretation of non-ideal impedance responses and predicts the spatial redistribution of lithium under different operating rates. More importantly, this framework enables the spatial decoupling of polarization associated with lithium-ion transport, electronic conduction, and intrinsic charge-transfer kinetics. The resulting correlation between three-dimensional electrode architecture and local electrochemical processes provides a quantitative basis for identifying the dominant kinetic limitations governing rate-dependent polarization in NCM electrodes.

t53.a: Silicon (Si) is a promising anode material for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), but it suffers from severe volume expansion during repeated cycling. This induces particle pulverization and the loss of electrical contact, leading to rapid capacity degradation. Since conventional linear polymer binders cannot effectively withstand this stress, there is a critical need to develop multifunctional binders that offer both strong interfacial interactions and self-healing properties A multifunctional self-healing polymer binder, PAA-APDS, was synthesized by incorporating 4,4’-dithiodianiline (APDS) crosslinkers into a poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) backbone, introducing dynamic disulfide bonds. This binder was mixed with Si nanoparticles and SiOx@C active materials to fabricate anodes. The electrochemical performance, mechanical strength, adhesion properties, and lithium-ion diffusion behavior were systematically evaluated through half-cell and pouch-type full-cell tests. The PAA-APDS binder forms a robust 3D network via multiple hydrogen bonds and dynamic disulfide bonds, providing superior adhesion strength (6.5 N) to the copper current collector and spontaneously repairing microcracks. As a result, the Si/PAA-APDS electrode exhibited an exceptional capacity retention of 94.91% after 300 cycles, alongside a 2.1-fold increase in the $Li^+$ diffusion rate compared to pristine PAA. Moreover, an NCM622||SiOx@C/PAA-APDS20 pouch full-cell demonstrated stable practical applicability, maintaining 72.62% capacity retention after 50 cycles. The dynamically crosslinked PAA-APDS binder effectively dissipates mechanical stress caused by Si volume changes and prevents the structural collapse of the electrode. By successfully combining strong interfacial adhesion with intrinsic self-healing capabilities, this binder design provides a highly effective and practical strategy for ensuring the long-term stability of next-generation, high-energy-density silicon-based LIBs.

t54.k: Insertion material, structural defect, high capacity, phase transtiion, electrolyte
t54.a: Ni-rich layered oxides such as LiNiO2 are attractive positive electrodes, but suffer from capacity degradation at high voltages due to Ni migration. Recent studies show that non-stoichiometry and antisite defects play a critical role, and defect engineering enables highly reversible pure Ni-based layered materials without metal substitution.2 In parallel, Co-/Ni-free Mn-based electrodes are important for cost-effective electric vehicles.2–5 While typically synthesized by energy-intensive milling, nanostructured LiMnO2 with high energy density (~800 W h kg–1) has recently been obtained through conventional calcination, demonstrating scalability. For safety, solid electrolytes are promising, but electrode volume changes complicate interface stability. Dimensionally invariable cation-disordered rocksalt oxides address this issue, achieving excellent reversibility with solid electrolytes.6, 7 Overall, defect-engineered and nanostructured lithium insertion materials are central to the development of safe, high-energy, and practical Li-ion batteries. References (1) I. Konuma et al., and N. Yabuuchi, Energy Storage Materials, 66, 103200 (2024). (2) A. Kanno et al., and N. Yabuuchi, ACS Energy Letters, 8, 2753 (2023). (3) Z. Yanjia et al., and N. Yabuuchi, Advanced Energy Materials, 14, 2304074 (2024). (4) Y. Miyaoka et al., and N. Yabuuchi, ACS Central Science, 10, 1718 (2024). (5) M. Shinoda et al., and N. Yabuuchi, Journal of The American Chemical Society, 147, 26238 (2025). (6) I. Konuma et al., and N. Yabuuchi, Nature Materials, 22, 225 (2023). (7) T. Ohno, Y. Ugata, and N. Yabuuchi, Journal of Materials Chemistry A, 14, 385-393 (2026).

t55.k: Polymalonamide; Poly(ethylene Oxide) (PEO); Solid Polymer Electrolyte (SPE)
t55.a: Poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO)-based solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs) are attractive for all-solid-state lithium batteries, but PEO crystallization limits ion transport and electrochemical performance. This study employs polymalonamides (PMs) with tunable diamine structures as functional modifiers to regulate PEO-based SPE properties. Two PMs were synthesized from short-chain hexamethylenediamine (PM-HDA) and polyetheramine JEFFAMINE XTJ-500 (PM-XTJ) and incorporated into PEO/LiTFSI electrolytes. Structural, thermal, mechanical, and electrochemical properties were evaluated, followed by cycling tests in LiFePO₄|SPE|Li cells. PM incorporation reduced PEO crystallinity, while β-carbonyl and amide groups promoted lithium salt dissociation and restricted anion mobility, respectively. The rigid PM backbone reinforced mechanical strength, suppressing lithium dendrite penetration. SPMH-3 (20 wt% PM-HDA) exhibited a Li⁺ transference number of 0.287, supported faster charge−discharge kinetics, and retained 93.4% of its capacity after 100 cycles. SPMX-2 (10 wt% PM-XTJ) delivered an initial capacity of 166 mAh g⁻¹ with 87.6% retention after 300 cycles at 0.2 C, demonstrating an alternative balance between ion transport and mechanical integrity. Diamine structure and PM content can be tailored to balance ion transport and mechanical integrity in PEO-based SPEs, offering a versatile molecular design strategy for safe, durable, high-performance solid-state lithium batteries.

t56.a: Rechargeable aqueous batteries are promising high-safety alternatives to lithium-based batteries for stationary energy storage. However, aqueous zinc-iodine batteries (ZIBs) face challenges such as Zn dendrites, side reactions, narrow electrolyte potential windows, and polyiodide shuttling. Strategies include designing dual-function electrolytes to stabilize both Zn anodes and iodine cathodes, using hydrogel electrolytes for interface optimization, and promoting stable four-electron reactions. These approaches improve the durability and energy density/capacity of aqueous ZIBs by stabilizing electrode interfaces and enhancing electrochemical reactions. Electrolyte and interface engineering are promising strategies for developing durable, high-energy aqueous ZIBs. These advances could support the development of practical ampere-hour-level ZIBs.

t57.a: Organic cations in ionic liquid electrolytes have generally been regarded as passive species, while electrolyte design has primarily focused on Li-anion coordination. However, the role of cation-anion interactions in determining solvation structures and interfacial reactions remains poorly understood. The coordination environments of ionic liquid electrolytes were investigated using spectroscopic analyses and computational simulations. Based on the identified cation-anion interaction mechanism, ether-functionalized pyrrolidinium cations were designed to modulate ionic interactions and regulate Li+ solvation structures. Increasing Li salt concentration weakened cation-anion interactions and generated unprotected organic cations, leading to reductive decomposition and irreversible capacity loss. In contrast, the ether-functionalized pyrrolidinium cation behaved as a weakly interacting "lone cation", promoting Li-FSA aggregate formation without volatile diluents. This cation-engineering strategy enabled anion-rich solvation structures, inorganic-rich interphases, and improved Li metal reversibility and cycling stability. Cation-anion interactions fundamentally govern solvation chemistry and interfacial stability in ionic liquid electrolytes. The proposed lone-cation concept establishes organic cations as active design parameters for controlling Li⁺ solvation and electrolyte performance, providing a new design principle for advanced ionic liquid electrolytes in Li-ion and Li metal batteries.

t58.k: Zinc Electrode; Energy Storage; Aqueous Electrolytes
t58.a: Recent research on aqueous Zn-based energy storage devices, such as Zn-air batteries, Zn-ion batteries and hybrid Zn-ion capacitors, has shifted gradually toward neutral or even strongly acidic electrolytes, which leverage the more intrinsically reversible Zn2+/Zn redox couple to extend cycling life. An electrospun polyimide (PI) nanofabric film onto the Zn substrate promotes a pre-desolvation process, effectively and partially desolvating the hydrated zinc ions from [Zn(H2O)6]2+ to [Zn(H2O)4]2+ before approaching Zn surface. A defect-engineered MOF-801 coating creates a confined interfacial microenvironment, where the hydrophobic pore entrances can exclude bulk water and the defect-derived –COOH/–OH groups selectively trap hydronium. We introduce the indium ion to stabilize the Zn electrodes in highly acidic electrolytes. The [Zn(H2O)4]2+ ions reaching the Zn surface can accelerate the charge transfer process with a reduced activation energy for zinc deposition from 40 to 21 kJ/mol. The PI nanofabric film can serve as a protective barrier which suppresses the side reactions at the electrode. The MOF-protected Zn symmetric cells can achieve stable cycling for longer than 1,660 h at 1 mA cm-2 in the pH 0 electrolyte. The strategy further enables the record performance in Zn–PbO2 (2.35 V), Zn–MnO2 (502.8 Wh kg-1), and Zn-ion hybrid capacitors (30,000 cycles), extending the operational pH boundary of aqueous electrochemistry. During Zn plating, indium accumulates at the electrode surface to form a protective In–Zn alloy, which alleviates the HER via weakening the hydrated proton adsorption and promotes preferential growth of the Zn (002) facet, enabling highly reversible Zn plating/stripping. Zn||Zn symmetric cells exhibit an extended cycling life approaching 3000 h (at pH 1.13), while acidic Zn||MnO2 coin cells deliver a record-high discharge plateau of ~1.95 V with stable cycling over 1100 cycles. Our approaches pave novel avenues for high-performance zinc metal electrodes in the aqueous zinc-based energy storage devices.

t59.k: NCM811; X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy; Oxidation State
t59.a: Lithium nickel cobalt manganese oxide (LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2), commonly known as NCM811 is important material to be used as cathode for Li ion rechargeable batteries. Therefore, synthesis methods such as coprecipitation and hydrothermal are frequently used. This work explores synthesis of NCM811 using sol-gel method by taking metal nitrates as starting materials, known as nitrate method. For synthesis, citric acid was used as host and precursor was annealed at 300 (amorphous phase), 500, 700 (crystalline phase with minor impurity), 800, 900 (crystalline phase) and 1000oC (deteriorated crystalline phase). Scanning electron microscopy studies exhibit stoichiometric ratio of Ni, Mn and Co ions. Ni, Co & Mn L-edge near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) measurements exhibit the characteristic spectral features in the respective spectra that are affected by the annealing temperature. Annealing temperature also influences the oxygen-metal interactions which is reflected by the O K-edge NEXAFS measurements. Ni and Mn ions exhibit no change of their respective oxidation state as inferred from the Ni and Mn K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure measurements (XANES) measurements; however, onsets of local atomic structural changes are observed from these measurements. Annealing temperature influences the oxidation state of Co ions as evidenced from the Co K-XANES measurements. Quantitative analysis of extended X-ray fine structure measurements reveals the annealing temperature induced changes in metal-oxygen/metal radial-distance and coordination. Therefore, this work elaborates the successful synthesis of NCM811 from the metal nitrates by adopting sol-gel processing and highlights the role of thermal treatment for achieving the crystalline phase of NCM811.

t60.k: Battery, electrolyte, solvation, thermodynamics, lithium, sodium
t60.a: The electrolyte plays a critical role in lithium and sodium batteries. In particular, ion solvation critically impacts electrolyte properties and the battery performance. Solvation thermodynamics is at the foundation of solvation phenomena, but our understanding of it and how it impacts solvation structure, electrolyte properties and the battery performance remains elusive. In this talk, I will begin by introducing potentiometric methods to experimentally probe solvation free energy of Li+ in battery electrolytes. Then I will discuss our recent studies on the factors that govern solvation free energy. I will highlight the comparison between dielectric constant and donor number to describe solvation behavior. I will conclude by introducing methods to measure Na+ solvation energy and discussing the key differences between solvation of lithium and sodium ions.

t61.a: Compact, battery-free power sources are highly desirable for environmental monitoring and regenerative medicine, particularly under low-frequency mechanical vibrations. However, harvesting sufficient energy from weak ambient vibrations remains challenging because of the limited power density and scalability of miniaturized energy harvesters. We developed a compact inertia-driven triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) platform incorporating a resonant inertia structure and multi-stacked, surface-treated TENG arrays. The platform was designed to amplify low-frequency ambient vibrations and enable scalable energy harvesting within a miniaturized form factor. The harvested energy was integrated with a Bluetooth Low Energy system-on-chip (BLE SoC) for wireless CO₂ monitoring using pipeline vibrations. In addition, the TENG was coupled with bioresorbable electrodes to generate motion-modulated electrical stimulation for regenerative electrotherapy. The miniaturized TENG, with a volume of 2 cm³ and a weight of 4.9 g, achieved a root-mean-square power output of 0.5 mW at 13 Hz. The harvested energy successfully powered a BLE SoC for periodic wireless CO₂ monitoring, demonstrating battery-free environmental sensing from pipeline vibrations. For biomedical applications, the inertia-driven TENG generated motion-dependent electrical waveforms that restored endogenous electric fields and enhanced cell migration, exosome secretion, angiogenesis, and epidermal maturation in vitro and in vivo. This work demonstrates a compact and scalable inertia-driven TENG platform capable of converting low-frequency mechanical vibrations into usable electrical energy for autonomous sensing and regenerative electrotherapy. The integration of vibration energy harvesting, wireless environmental monitoring, and bioresorbable electroceuticals highlights the potential of the platform for sustainable infrastructure and battery-free healthcare systems.

t62.a: Soft and wearable electronic devices have attracted considerable interest for applications in continuous health monitoring, biomedical engineering, and human–robot interaction. Among various device architectures, fiber-based electronics offer unique advantages owing to their one-dimensional geometry, mechanical flexibility, and compatibility with conventional textiles. Fiber-form devices can be seamlessly integrated into clothing for unobtrusive wearable sensing, while their small cross-sectional dimensions and needle-like geometry also enable direct interaction with or implantation into biological tissues. These characteristics make fiber electronics a versatile platform that can bridge wearable electronics and implantable bioelectronics, particularly when combined with biocompatible and biodegradable materials. We developed multifunctional fiber-based electronic devices by integrating conductive nanomaterials, soft functional materials, and bioresorbable components onto fiber and microfiber platforms. For wearable applications, highly conductive nanoparticle-based fiber electrodes were utilized to construct textile-integrated pressure, strain, and shear sensors capable of detecting diverse mechanical stimuli. For biomedical applications, electronic sensing sutures were designed to combine biochemical sensing, including local pH monitoring, with electrical stimulation for electroceutical therapy. In addition, fully biodegradable fiber electronic devices were fabricated using biocompatible and bioresorbable materials to enable temporary sensing and therapeutic functions without requiring permanent implantation. The developed fiber devices demonstrate that a one-dimensional soft electronic platform can support multiple sensing and therapeutic functionalities across wearable and biomedical environments. Fiber- and textile-based mechanical sensors enabled sensitive detection of pressure, deformation, and shear forces while maintaining mechanical compliance suitable for wearable interfaces and interactive robotic systems. Multifunctional electronic sutures provided simultaneous biochemical monitoring and electrical stimulation, offering a route toward active wound monitoring and treatment directly at the tissue interface. Furthermore, biodegradable fiber electronics maintained functional electronic characteristics during their intended operation while providing the potential to physically disappear after use, thereby addressing important limitations associated with chronic foreign-body implantation and surgical device retrieval. Fiber-based soft electronics provide a promising platform for integrating sensing, stimulation, and transient functionality into mechanically compliant and geometrically versatile devices. By extending fiber electronics from textile-integrated mechanical sensors to multifunctional electronic sutures and biodegradable implantable systems, this work highlights a unified strategy for developing next-generation interfaces between electronic devices, the human body, and robotic systems. Such multifunctional fiber platforms may ultimately enable seamless wearable health monitoring as well as minimally invasive and transient biomedical technologies.

t63.k: Triboelectric nanogenerators; Liquid-Solid Interface; Gallium liquid metal; Gouy-Chapman limit.
t63.a: Liquid–solid triboelectric nanogenerators (LS-TENGs) offer considerable potential for harvesting energy from moving droplets, yet their performance is typically restricted by ion-mediated interfacial screening governed by the Gouy–Chapman–Stern framework. Here, we introduce a gallium-based metallic liquid–solid triboelectric nanogenerator (Ga-LS TENG) that circumvents this conventional electrochemical regime by shifting the dominant interfacial process from ionic electric-double-layer formation to bulk-electron-mediated polarization. By coupling gallium-based liquid metal (GLM) with PTFE, we show that interfacial charge generation is controlled primarily by highly localized electronic screening rather than Debye-length-dependent ionic redistribution. Comparative measurements using deionized (DI) water demonstrate that GLM delivers substantially greater electrical output despite exhibiting a larger static contact angle, reaching an open-circuit voltage of 384 V and a short-circuit current of 182 µA. Finite-element modeling together with electrostatic force microscopy reveals enhanced electric-field localization and increased interfacial charge density at the GLM–PTFE interface. Furthermore, a coupled wettability–electrostatics framework indicates that partial Cassie-like wetting, combined with atomic-scale interfacial capacitance, enables charge accumulation beyond that attainable through conventional ion-screened interfaces. These findings establish bulk-electron-mediated interfacial polarization as an alternative mechanism for liquid–solid triboelectric charge generation and provide a new pathway toward high-power droplet-based energy harvesting.

t64.a: Piezocatalysis enables this conversion by generating polarization charges in piezoelectric materials under mechanical deformation, thereby driving surface redox reactions. The demonstration of piezocatalytic activity in single- and few-layer MoS₂ nanoflowers in 2016 represented an important milestone in extending piezocatalysis from conventional bulk ferroelectric oxides to two-dimensional semiconductors. Since then, 2D piezocatalysts have been increasingly investigated for hydrogen evolution, ammonia synthesis, and environmental remediation because of their abundant active sites, short charge-transport distances, and strong sensitivity to strain. Nevertheless, further advances in mechanistic understanding, material stability, energy-conversion efficiency, and scalable system design are still required. Two-dimensional piezocatalysts and their heterostructures were synthesized using hydrothermal, solvothermal, and interfacial assembly methods. Their structures, compositions, and electromechanical properties were characterized by electron microscopy, spectroscopy, piezoresponse force microscopy, and electrochemical measurements. Piezocatalytic hydrogen evolution, ammonia synthesis, and pollutant degradation were evaluated under mechanical stimulation, photoirradiation, or their simultaneous application. Mechanically induced polarization promoted charge separation, directional carrier transport, and interfacial redox reactions. Further coupling with photoirradiation produced synergistic improvements in catalytic performance by suppressing charge recombination. Advanced heterostructures and defect-engineered materials provided additional active sites and optimized reaction pathways. Two-dimensional piezocatalysts provide a promising platform for converting ambient mechanical energy into chemical energy. Their strain-responsive polarization, abundant active sites, and tunable interfaces enable hydrogen evolution, ammonia synthesis, CO2 reduction, and wastewater treatment. Future efforts should focus on improving material stability, mechanochemical conversion efficiency, mechanistic understanding, and scalable reactor design to advance practical self-powered energy and environmental applications.

t65.a: A piezoelectric energy generating device that produces electricity using plasmon-enhanced solar radiation pressure (SRP) is developed. The SRP is greatly enhanced on the operational region of the device with a unique craterlike structure, and direct current is generated successfully on the device. By optimizing the material and thickness of top electrode, a maximum power density of 7mW cm−2 is obtained. In addition, by using Raman measurements, Finite difference time domain simulation, and COMSOL Multiphysics analysis, it is confirmed that the SRP is greatly amplified on the operational region with the nanoscale surface roughness due to resonance between the incident light and surface plasmons. By increasing the rotational speed of an optical chopper used to measure the change in the output characteristics of the device, and comparing this with the simulated result, it is found that the constant charge produced by the piezoelectric effect

t66.k: Liquid-solid Triboelectric Sensor; Albumin Detection; Chronic Kidney Disease
t66.a: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive and globally prevalent condition, yet it remains clinically silent until advanced stages. Urinary albumin is an established early biomarker of kidney dysfunction; however, most current detection platforms require complex instrumentation, external power sources, or multi-step biochemical protocols, limiting their suitability for point-of-care pre-screening. Here, we report a self-powered, antibody-functionalized liquid-solid triboelectric sensor (LS-TES) for selective albumin detection in artificial urine. The sensor is constructed from mechanically roughened polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) coated with emeraldine-salt polyaniline (PANI@ES) and subsequently immobilized with anti-human serum albumin (anti-HSA) antibody, forming a bioresponsive triboelectric interface. Among three PANI oxidation states examined, the PANI@ES form exhibits the highest electrical conductivity and optimal antibody-anchoring capability, yielding the largest open-circuit voltage (VOC) response. Under optimized droplet conditions, the m-PTFE/PANI@ES/AB LS-TES produces a concentration-dependent decrease in VOC and ISC over the albumin/artificial urine concentration range of 50-250 ppm, with a linear response (R2 = 0.9957) and an estimated (extrapolated) detection limit of 10.4 ppm in artificial urine matrix, obtained by linear extrapolation beyond the experimentally tested concentration range (50-250 ppm). The sensor demonstrates excellent selectivity against common urinary interfering species including creatinine, glucose, urea, NaCl and KCl at physiologically relevant concentrations, and retains over 80% of its initial response after 20 days of ambient storage. These finding presents the first demonstration of antibody-mediated molecular selectivity in a self-powered LS-TES platform, providing a simple, low-cost, and label-free route toward pre-screening of proteinuria associated with CKD.

t67.k: Hybrid Nanogenerator; Lead-free Piezoelectric; Self-powered Sensor
t67.a: The rapid expansion of IoT and wearable electronics—growing at ~22% annually toward tens of billions of units—demands sustainable, flexible power sources beyond conventional batteries, which suffer from limited lifespan, maintenance burden, and hazardous waste. Harnessing electromechanical coupling, nanogenerators convert human motion and ambient vibration into electricity, yet individual piezoelectric (PENG) and triboelectric (TENG) mechanisms are each limited in either current or voltage. This work presents a synergistic hybrid strategy spanning lead-free inorganic ceramics through to fully organic, biodegradable systems for self-powered sensing. Lead-free BaTiO₃ was engineered across morphologies—nanoparticles and salt-flux-derived nanowires and nanorods—and integrated into PDMS or biopolymer matrices with conductive (Ag, carbon nanotube) and dielectric 2D fillers. Bio-based devices employed chitosan–protein composites and pure γ-glycine fillers, combined with soft bacterial-cellulose electrodes and self-charge-pumping (SCP) circuits. Coupling the tribo-negative PDMS matrix with ferroelectric BaTiO₃ dipoles yielded 60× voltage and 32× current enhancements (~320 µW/cm²), confirming constructive PENG–TENG superposition. In chitosan/BaTiO₃-nanorod TENGs, tetragonal ferroelectric polarization elevated surface charge density, while a soft electrode minimized the air gap and an SCP module recirculated charge, raising output to ~247 V and 1568 µW/cm². In organic systems, glycine-rich domains broke centrosymmetry to generate polar moments; at the 50 wt% percolation threshold, an interconnected γ-glycine network maximized stress transfer and interfacial polarization, delivering ~79 V while retaining biodegradability. Integrating synergistic PENG–TENG coupling, nano-architecture engineering, and biodegradable-materials design enables high-performance yet sustainable self-powered devices for wearable sensing and green IoT.

t68.a: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) are a promising self-powering technology that harvests electricity from ambient mechanical motion. However, their output generally deteriorates at high humidity because adsorbed water molecules dissipate surface charge and electrostatically screen induction. Hydrophilic biopolymers could instead convert moisture from a detriment into a driving force, but polysaccharides suffer from low dielectric constants and weak triboelectric tendencies that limit their practical output performance of TENGs. Here we fabricated freeze-dried cryogel films using sodium alginate (SA), a brown-algae-derived biopolymer containing abundant hydroxyl and carboxyl groups. The resulting porous and rough surface enhanced triboelectric charge generation. TEMPO-oxidized cellulose nanofibers (CNFs), containing both amorphous and crystalline domains, were incorporated to reinforce the mechanically fragile cryogel, and the resulting SA/CNF (SC) networks were ionically crosslinked with Cu2+ to form egg-box junctions. Cu2+ crosslinking strengthened intermolecular junctions and markedly increased water uptake, because each ion binds carboxylate groups while retaining four coordination sites for dynamic bonding with water. As a result, SC cryogel TENGs amplified rather than lost their output at 80% relative humidity. Absorbed water raised both the dielectric constant and the ionic conductivity, enhancing charge induction, while its intrinsic tribopositivity shifted the cryogel to be more tribopositive than nylon. Humidity therefore drives, rather than degrades, the performance of SC cryogel TENGs, simultaneously resolving the poor mechanical robustness and moisture vulnerability of conventional cryogels. This work establishes a design principle for sustainable, high-performance biopolymer TENGs and suggests broad applicability of humidity-adaptive polysaccharide architectures in self-powered energy harvesting and environmental sensing systems.

t69.k: Ultrasound Energy Transfer; Template Grain Growth; KNN
t69.a: Ultrasonic wireless energy transfer is a promising power-delivery approach for implantable medical devices because it enables deep-tissue transmission while avoiding the short range and electromagnetic interference associated with electromagnetic induction. However, high-performance piezoelectric receivers commonly contain lead, whereas lead-free alternatives generally exhibit insufficient piezoelectric properties. A lead-free KNN-based piezoelectric ceramic fabricated by templated grain growth (TGG) was employed as an ultrasonic receiver and compared with a randomly oriented ceramic. The d33*g33 figure of merit, output voltage, angular dependence, and load-resistance-dependent power were evaluated. A low-resonance bending-mode design was also adopted to improve compatibility with commercial transducers, together with an array configuration, a flexible polymer medium, and a hydrogel coupling layer for enhanced tissue adhesion and acoustic impedance matching. The TGG ceramic exhibited a d33*g33 value approximately 4.5 times that of the randomly oriented sample. At an applied voltage of 250 V, its peak-to-peak output voltage reached 61.1 Vp-p, compared with 16.2 Vp-p for the random sample, representing a 377% increase. Although output decreased with increasing angular misalignment, the TGG sample maintained approximately 23 mW higher power across all measured angles. At a 250 Vp-p input, the maximum output power was 27.0 mW, versus 4.1 mW for the random sample, corresponding to a 659% improvement. TGG-based texture engineering substantially enhances the ultrasonic energy-conversion performance of lead-free KNN receivers. Combined with resonance optimization, array integration, and flexible acoustic coupling, this approach offers strong potential for biocompatible implantable wireless power systems.

t70.k: Bacterial cellulose; Heat-driven triboelectricity; Titanate nanotubes; Thermal response; Triboelectric nanogenerator
t70.a: Bacterial cellulose (BC) is a promising sustainable material for flexible electronics, but its electrical response during temperature changes is not well understood. Here, we study the triboelectric response of BC/titanate nanotube (BC/TNT) composites during rapid heating and cooling. Composites containing 3 and 10 wt% TNT were compared with pristine BC. Adding TNT increased the triboelectric output, with the transferred charge increasing from 12.2 μC for BC to 20.5 μC for BC/10TNT. The electrical output also changed with temperature. During cooling, the voltage and current decreased, while during heating they increased. This response became stronger with increasing TNT content. For BC/10TNT, the output voltage changed from about 39 to 90 V during the temperature transition. Infrared imaging showed that TNT also improved heat spreading across the BC film. In addition, the composite produced a measurable voltage when a temperature gradient was applied. These results show that BC/TNT composites can respond to both mechanical contact and changing temperature, making them promising materials for self-powered thermal and motion sensors and flexible electronic devices.

t71.k: Ultrasound-driven Triboelectric Nanogenerator; Bioelectronics; Materials Engineering
t71.a: Ultrasound-driven triboelectric nanogenerators (US-TENGs) are attractive wireless power sources for implantable bioelectronics because their electrical output can be tailored to distinct therapeutic functions. However, energy storage and battery charging benefit from high current and power delivery, whereas electric-field-mediated stimulation can require substantially higher voltage. A single material design, therefore, is unlikely to satisfy the diverse electrical output requirements of various bioelectronic applications. We developed a two-track materials strategy for US-TENGs. A perfluoroalkoxy alkane (PFA)-based architecture was designed to enhance high-voltage output through mechanically amplified vibration and vibration-mode conversion under ultrasound excitation. In parallel, a poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-trifluoroethylene) [P(VDF-TrFE)]-based triboelectric layer was employed as a high-permittivity platform to increase device capacitance and tune its electrical characteristics toward the ideal load-matching regime, thereby maximizing transferred charge, current, and electrical power. The two material systems produced distinct electrical operating regimes. The PFA-based device preferentially enhanced voltage by increasing effective triboelectric displacement through vibration amplification and mode conversion, making it suitable for high-electric-field actuation. In contrast, the P(VDF-TrFE)-based device increased capacitive charge transfer and delivered higher current and power, providing a more favorable output profile for energy storage and battery charging. These results establish a function-oriented materials design framework for US-TENGs in which mechanical mode engineering and dielectric engineering are selectively employed to maximize distinct electrical output characteristics for different bioelectronic applications. These strategies provide a practical route toward application-specific ultrasound-powered implantable systems.

t72.k: High Entropy Alloy; Hydrogen Evolution; Synthesis
t72.a: Nanoparticles (NPs) containing multiple elements in a single phase have recently attracted much attention as new types of nanomaterials, such as catalysts. In particular, alloys containing more than five elements at almost equal ratios, called high entropy alloys (HEAs), have been intensively studied all over the world in recent years. We synthesized new HEA NPs and studied their catalytic properties based on their electronic structures. (1-7) For example, platinum-group metal HEA NPs (PGM-HEA NPs) consisting of Pd, Pt, Ir, Rh, and Ru were synthesized by a chemical reduction method and tested their electrochemical hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activities.(3) Furthermore, we also developed a flow-synthesis reactor to synthesize them with high reproducibility and efficiency. (4, 5) PGM-HEA NPs showed very high electrocatalytic activity toward HER in both acid and alkaline solutions, which is higher than that of a commercial Pt catalyst.(3) Furthermore, we also succeeded in synthesizing new HEA NPs consisting of all eight noble-metal-group elements (NM-HEA NPs). We revealed that the local density of states (LDOS) of every surface atom in NM-HEA is different.(2) Some atoms of the same constituent element in HEA NPs have different LDOS profiles, whereas atoms of other elements can have similar LDOS profiles. This may provide an interesting result that the NM-HEA NPs showed 10.8-times higher activity for the hydrogen evolution reaction than Pt/C, even though NM-HEA NPs are formed from PGM-HEA and three HER-inactive elements, Os, Ag, and Au. In addition to the synthesis of the HEA NPs and their electronic structure and catalytic properties, we will discuss machine learning approaches to optimize the synthesis conditions and metal compositions and to understand the catalytic mechanism in the presentation. References [1] D. Wu, K. Kusada, H. Kitagawa, et al., JACS, 2020, 142, 13833–13838. [2] D. Wu, K. Kusada, H. Kitagawa, et al., JACS, 2022, 144, 3365–336 [3] D. Wu, K. Kusada, H. Kitagawa, et al., Chem. Sci., 2020, 11, 12731–12736 [4] K. Kusada, H. Kitagawa, et al., J. Phys. Chem. C, 2021, 125, 458–463 [5] H. Minamihara, K. Kusada, H. Kitagawa, et al., JACS, 2022, 144, 11525–11529 [6] H. Minamihara, K. Kusada, H. Kitagawa, et al., JACS, 2023, 145, 17136–17142. [7] S. Hanabata, K. Kusada, H. Kitagawa et al., JACS 2024, 146, 181−186.

t73.a: Advancing anion exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs) is critical for efficient and scalable hydrogen production. This presentation highlights interfacial engineering strategies that integrate catalyst design, electrode fabrication, and advanced electrochemical diagnostics to improve AEMWE performance and durability. A highly active platinum-group-metal-free oxygen evolution electrode was developed by immobilizing metal nitrides within reconstructed oxy(hydroxide) surfaces, enabling rapid surface reconstruction and enhanced OER kinetics in alkaline media. In parallel, an in-situ ionomer-free catalyst-coated membrane (m-CCM) fabrication method was introduced to create intimate electrode–membrane interfaces, improving catalyst utilization while reducing interfacial resistance. To elucidate degradation mechanisms, a three-electrode MEA diagnostic platform was implemented to independently probe anode and cathode processes under realistic operating conditions. The analysis reveals that cathode processes predominantly govern the early degradation of AEMWEs. Finally, the extension of advanced electrochemical analysis, including distribution of relaxation times and three-electrode MEA configurations, to related systems will be discussed.

t74.k: Wet Nonaqueous Zinc-ion Battery; MnO2 Cathode; Interfacial Stability
t74.a: Wet nonaqueous electrolytes improve Zn-metal reversibility in zinc-ion batteries (ZIBs), but the instability of MnO2 cathodes remains a major limitation because of Mn dissolution-redeposition, interfacial reconstruction, and irreversible byproduct formation. This study explores intergrowth engineering as a cathode-design strategy to simultaneously enhance bulk structural adaptability and cathode-electrolyte interfacial stability. An intergrowth-type MnO2 (I-MnO2) containing intimately integrated δ-like layered domains and γ-related motifs was therefore developed and compared with conventional δ-MnO2 in a wet nonaqueous Zn system. I-MnO2 was synthesized through a Mn-Al precursor-assisted co-precipitation route followed by persulfate oxidation, with a Mn precursor ratio of 4:1, while δ-MnO2 was prepared hydrothermally as a reference. Cathodes containing MnO2/Super P/PVDF (7:2:1) were evaluated in Zn||MnO₂ cells using 0.5 M Zn(CF3SO3)2 in DMSO/DMF/H2O (47.5:47.5:5.0 wt%). Electrochemical behavior was investigated by galvanostatic cycling, CV, EIS, and GITT. Structural and interfacial evolution was examined using TEM/HRTEM, XRD, Raman, FT-IR, bulk operando Mn K-edge XANES, in situ grazing-incidence XANES, Mn fluorescence tracking, and operando XRD. The optimized I-MnO2 exhibited a δ/γ intergrowth architecture and substantially improved electrochemical durability compared with δ-MnO2. It delivered discharge capacities of 147-96 mAh g-1 at 0.05-0.5 A g-1, retained approximately 97% capacity after 500 cycles, and maintained about 84% retention after 2500 cycles. Operando XANES revealed highly reversible bulk Mn redox, while GI-XANES and Mn fluorescence measurements demonstrated enhanced Mn retention and suppressed dissolution at the cathode interface. Operando XRD showed reversible framework expansion and partial loss of layered ordering rather than severe structural collapse. In contrast, conventional δ-MnO2 exhibited stronger interfacial reconstruction and irreversible ZnO formation during cycling. Intergrowth engineering effectively stabilizes MnO2 cathodes under wet nonaqueous Zn-storage conditions by coupling reversible bulk structural evolution with controlled interfacial chemistry. The δ/γ intergrowth framework accommodates redox-induced structural rearrangements while improving Mn retention and suppressing irreversible byproduct formation, resulting in markedly enhanced long-term cycling stability. These findings establish intergrowth engineering as a practical strategy for designing durable Mn-based cathodes beyond electrolyte optimization alone. Sulfate-associated local environments may additionally contribute to stabilization, although their precise role, together with possible effects of residual Al and morphological differences, requires further investigation.

t75.k: Hierarchical NiFe LDH; Florine Doping; Saline Water Oxidation
t75.a: The rational design of hierarchical electrocatalysts is crucial for advancing saline water oxidation, a key technology for sustainable hydrogen production. This work demonstrates a novel strategy where a fluorine-doped NiFe layered double hydroxide on nickel foam (F-LDH/NF) is transformed into a multi-level hierarchical catalyst (R-F-LDH/NF) via a targeted in-situ electrochemical process. This reconstruction creates core-shell nanosheets with a robust LDH core and a mesoporous, amorphous NiFeOOH surface, maximizing active site exposure and mass transport. The resulting catalyst exhibits exceptional OER performance in saline alkaline media, requiring only 262 mV to achieve 200 mA cm-2 with outstanding durability. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that fluorine incorporated in the precatalyst could serve three crucial functions. It enhances chloride repulsion at the surface for stability in saline electrolytes, triggers potential-driven desorption to initiate reconstruction into a defect-rich active phase, and optimizes the OER energetics of the resulting γ-NiFeOOH shell by stabilizing key reaction intermediates. This work provides a clear pathway for engineering advanced catalysts through controlled structural and chemical evolution.

t76.k: Solid Oxide Fuel Cell; Oxygen Reduction Reaction; Thermal Expansion Coefficient
t76.a: The performance of low-temperature solid oxide fuel cells (LT-SOFCs) is critically constrained by sluggish oxygen reduction kinetics and thermal expansion mismatch between cathode and electrolyte materials. Here, a dual-site engineering strategy is employed to develop a novel perovskite oxide cathode, Ce0.05Sr0.95Co0.8Nb0.1Ta0.1O3−δ (SCCNT05), that achieves both thermal compatibility and electrochemical functionality. A-site substitution of Ce4+ into the SrCo0.8Nb0.1Ta0.1O3−δ (SCNT) lattice contracts the unit cell, resulting in a significantly reduced thermal expansion coefficient (TEC) of 14.42 × 10−6 K−1, well-matched with ceria-based electrolytes. Despite a moderate increase in area-specific resistance (ASR) to 0.429 Ω·cm2 at 500 °C, Ce doping markedly enhances structural stability by suppressing oxygen vacancy formation, as confirmed through thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). This synergistic design offers a promising pathway toward structurally robust and efficient LT-SOFC cathodes.

t77.a: Applying an external magnetic field to electrochemical reactions is recently an interesting topic among the electrocatalysis community. Earlier studies have shown that the water oxidation reaction (also called oxygen evolution reaction, OER) can be promoted by an external magnetic field through the promoted bubble removal on the electrode surface. However, that is for the case under the high overpotential and high current applied. In 2019, it has been reported that the promotion of OER in alkaline by applying the field is related to the magnetism of the electrode materials. On the other hand, theoretically, the OER needs to consider the triplet O2 formation, which involves the spin-polarized electron transfer. The spin-polarized electron transfer can be achieved by ferro(i) magnetic catalysts, however, which may not be easily proved experimentally. That is because in principle, an external magnetic field is not necessary for spin-polarized electron transfer on ferro(i)magnetic materials. It is also unclear about the reaction pathways with a consideration of spin-polarized electron transfer. The pH dependent enhancement has further generated confusion about the relation between magnetic field enhanced OER and the theoretical expectation. In addition, some magnetic catalysts do not exhibit any improvement under the magnetic field. All these phenomena have created a scientific puzzle, appealing to the community. In this talk, I will briefly discuss the progress of this field and several important experimental findings for solving the puzzle. The critical roles of magnetization, pinning effect, and pH dependent increment will be discussed in detail. In addition, the revealed spin promotion effect can be extended into other reactions. Examples will be discussed.

t78.k: Low-carbon Hydrogen; Hydrogen Ecosystem; Biogas to Hydrogen
t78.a: Thailand has abundant biomass resources and renewable energy potential that can support domestic low-carbon hydrogen production. Integrating hydrogen pathways based on biogas, biomass, and renewable electricity can enhance energy security, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and demonstrate practical applications for decentralized clean-energy systems. ENTEC is developing an integrated hydrogen ecosystem demonstration site that combines three complementary production pathways: biogas-to-hydrogen conversion, renewable-electricity-powered water electrolysis, and biomass-to-hydrogen technologies. The concept is designed to link local feedstock utilization with low-carbon hydrogen production, storage, and end-use applications. Produced hydrogen will be evaluated for power generation and energy supply within the ENTEC building, providing a real-world platform to assess technical performance, operational integration, and utilization strategies. A biogas-to-hydrogen reactor has been developed and demonstrated with a hydrogen production capacity exceeding 20 L/min. In parallel, ENTEC is establishing a laboratory-scale facility to test water electrolysis supplied by solar photovoltaic electricity. This facility will enable investigation of renewable hydrogen production under variable solar generation conditions and support the integration of hydrogen production with building-scale energy applications. Biomass-to-hydrogen development is also being considered as an additional pathway for utilizing Thailand’s agricultural residues and expanding the flexibility of the proposed ecosystem. NTEC is advancing a hydrogen ecosystem demonstration site that harmonizes low-carbon hydrogen production from biogas, renewable electricity, and biomass with practical hydrogen utilization. The initiative will provide an integrated testbed for technology validation, operational learning, capacity building, and future scale-up. It is expected to support Thailand’s transition toward a resilient, resource-based, and low-carbon hydrogen economy.

t79.k: Lithium Metal Batteries; Dimethylacetamide; Dual-salt Electrolyte
t79.a: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) are promising next-generation energy storage systems due to their high theoretical energy density. Here, dimethylacetamide (DMAc) was strategically selected as the solvent because, as a tertiary amide, it lacks active N-H protons that react with lithium, ensuring excellent chemical stability with the lithium anode. On this baseline, single- and dual-salt electrolytes using lithium nitrate (LiNO₃) and lithium bis(oxalate)borate (LiBOB) were systematically investigated and further optimized with 5 wt% vinylene carbonate (VC). The electrochemical performance was evaluated in Li//Li symmetric cells, Li//Cu asymmetric cells, and Li//LiMn₂O₄ half-cells. At a current density of 0.5 mA cm⁻², single-salt electrolytes (1n LiNO₃or 1n LiBOB in 4n DMAc) and the VC-free dual-salt control short-circuited within 120 hours Li//Li symmetric cells. In sharp contrast, the optimized 0.8n LiNO₃ - 0.2n LiBOB - 4n DMAc + 5 wt% VC electrolyte enabled an outstanding stable cycling lifespan of over 480 hours Li//Li symmetric cells. Furthermore, this VC-modified dual-salt system maintained a steady coulombic efficiency of ~80% for 50 cycles in Li//Cu cells. Crucially, the Li//LMO half-cells exhibited exceptional stability with a capacity retention of over 90% after approximately 450 long-term cycles. This dramatic enhancement is ascribed to the strong synergistic effect among LiNO₃、LiBOB and VC, which facilitates the formation of a dense, uniform, and mechanically robust solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer on the lithium anode. This interface effectively suppresses dendrite proliferation and mitigates parasitic side reactions, offering a viable pathway toward safe, high-performance amide-based LMBs.

t80.a: Hydrogen holds the promise as green energy carriers for global scale storage of renewable energy, e.g., solar and wind, enabling the continuous usage of these diffusive and intermittent energy sources. Electrochemical energy-conversion devices such water electrolysers, CO2 electrolysers and fuel cells are cornerstone technologies for decarbonisation and hydrogen economy, which requests highly efficient, low cost, and robust catalyst materials to reduce its current levels of energy consumption and cost. However, currently there is a gap between lab-scale research and industrial scale application, effectuated by catalysts, cell design, and operation conditions. This talk highlights the current challenges and opportunities for electrochemical energy-conversion devices, from materials and device engineering perspectives. I will showcase our efforts in developing Earth-abundant electrocatalysts for oxygen evolution reactions (OER), hydrogen evolution reactions (HER), oxygen reduction reactions (ORR), CO2/CO reduction reactions, as well as operando methodologies for understanding the catalytic processes and degradations in membrane electrode assemblies The commercialisation of some our work for industry also will be introduced to highlight the significance of material design from atomic to macroscopic to industrial scale.

t81.a: Alkaline water electrolysis using earth-abundant electrocatalysts is a promising approach for converting renewable energy into hydrogen. However, achieving both high catalytic activity and long-term stability remains challenging. Understanding and controlling the dynamic evolution of catalyst surfaces during electrolysis is therefore crucial for developing durable water-splitting electrocatalysts. A high-performance antiperovskite metal nitride was synthesized through a facile hydrothermal process followed by thermal nitrogen diffusion. High-valence elements (Fe, Mo, P, V, and W) were incorporated into the metal nitride to modulate its electronic structure and enhance electrical conductivity. The electrocatalytic activities toward the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) were evaluated in alkaline media. In situ operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and complementary structural and surface characterizations were employed to investigate charge-transport properties and catalyst evolution during electrolysis. Overall water-splitting performance and durability were evaluated using a two-electrode configuration with the modified metal nitride serving as both cathode and anode. The high-valence-element-modified metal nitrides exhibited substantially enhanced HER and OER activities compared with the pristine metal nitride, resulting in improved overall water-splitting performance. In situ operando impedance measurements provided evidence of enhanced charge-transport characteristics. The modified catalyst also demonstrated efficient overall water splitting and excellent long-term durability. Mechanistic investigations revealed dynamic surface reconstruction during electrolysis, resulting in the formation of an active hydroxide/metal-nitride interfacial layer that facilitates water dissociation and catalytic reaction kinetics. High-valence metal centers promote interfacial charge redistribution, contributing to accelerated reaction kinetics and improved catalytic stability. These findings demonstrate that dynamic surface evolution and electronic-structure modulation play critical roles in determining the activity and durability of metal-nitride electrocatalysts.
