The resulting hydroxide/metal-nitride interface provides an effective platform for developing robust and efficient electrocatalysts for alkaline water electrolysis.

t82.k: Electrocatalyst; Water Electrolysis; Single Crystal Electrode
t82.a: The development of highly active and durable electrocatalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is essential for efficient hydrogen production by polymer electrolyte membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE). Ir oxides are currently the most practical OER catalysts in acidic media, but their scarcity and high cost remain major barriers to large-scale deployment. Ru oxide is an attractive alternative because of its intrinsically high OER activity, yet its insufficient electrochemical stability under acidic conditions severely limits practical application. Therefore, establishing design principles that simultaneously improve catalytic activity and corrosion resistance is a key challenge for PEMWE anodes. In this talk, I will present our recent studies on surface-structure effects on electrocatalysis for OER based on single-crystal thin-film electrodes prepared by arc-plasma deposition method. First, by using RuO₂ and IrO₂ thin films with controlled surface orientations, we found that the electrochemical stability under acidic OER conditions depends strongly on crystal plane, and that RuO₂ and IrO₂ exhibit distinct orientation dependences in corrosion behavior. We then extended this model-electrode approach to Ti-doped RuO₂(110), where Ti incorporation improved both OER activity and stability while markedly suppressing Ru dissolution. Structural and spectroscopic analyses showed that Ti doping induces anisotropic geometric and electronic modifications in the near-surface region, demonstrating that the OER performance of noble-metal oxides is governed not only by composition but also by the geometric surface atomic arrangement and its response to doping. The results demonstrate that the single crytstal electrode can be a powerful platform to clarify the surfae structure effects on the activity and stability of OER electrocatalysts.

t83.a: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) are promising next-generation energy storage systems due to the high theoretical capacity and low electrochemical potential of lithium metal. However, their practical application is hindered by electrolyte instability and unstable electrode/electrolyte interfaces. In this study, a DMPA-based electrolyte was developed using lithium Bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) and N,N-dimethylpropionamide (DMPA) at a 1:4 molar ratio with 5 wt% fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) as a film-forming additive. The baseline electrolyte exhibited stable Li plating/stripping in Li//Li symmetric cells for 90 h with low overpotential. In Li//Cu cells, Coulombic efficiency (CE) exceeded 80% during the first 9 cycles and reached 91.7% at the fifth cycle. The Li//LMO half-cell delivered an initial discharge capacity of 110.7 mAh g⁻¹ with an initial CE above 99%. However, the CE gradually declined after the 53rd cycle, indicating insufficient long-term interfacial stability. To address this issue, a dual-salt strategy is proposed to regulate the Li⁺ solvation structure and tailor the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). By modifying anion–solvent interactions, this approach is expected to form a more robust inorganic-rich SEI, suppress lithium dendrite growth, and improve cycling stability. The study provides insights into electrolyte design for high-performance and durable LMBs.

t84.a: Ultrathin organic electronics based on polymer films offer excellent mechanical conformability for applications such as wearable and on-skin sensing. To realize multifunctional flexible electronic systems, heterogeneous integration is essential because different functional devices often require distinct materials, substrates, and fabrication conditions. Integrating separately fabricated devices therefore enables each component to be optimized independently without imposing process constraints from monolithic fabrication. However, conventional adhesive-based integration increases the local thickness and stiffness of bonded regions, degrading the intrinsic flexibility of ultrathin devices. Here, we demonstrate an adhesive-free direct bonding method for metal electrodes on thin polymer films using water-vapor-plasma-induced surface activation. The process enables direct bonding of gold/gold and silver/silver electrodes under ambient air at room temperature without an additional adhesive layer. The bonded interfaces exhibit low contact resistance while maintaining mechanical flexibility. Furthermore, electrodes with a 10 μm line-and-space pattern were successfully bonded, demonstrating applicability to high-resolution interconnections. This plasma-activated bonding approach provides a promising platform for flexible heterogeneous integration of independently fabricated electronic devices.

t85.k: Synaptic Transistors; Conjugated Polymers; Two-Dimensional Perovskites
t85.a: Our group develops functional polymers and hybrid perovskites for optoelectronic devices such as thin-film transistors, photo-memory, LEDs, and solar cells. We emphasize the interplay between material structure and properties, aiming to connect fundamental chemistry with device performance. We employ controlled synthesis of solution-processable semiconductors and explore interface engineering to enhance efficiency. Our strategy includes designing conjugated polymers and Sn-based two-dimensional perovskites for transistor memories, extending these concepts toward synaptic transistors. This dual approach integrates molecular design with device optimization. We have demonstrated organic materials tailored for dielectric and active layers, enabling organic synaptic transistors with promising neuromorphic behavior. Careful engineering of interfaces further improves performance. Sn-based two-dimensional perovskites show strong potential in memory and synaptic applications, offering new opportunities for high-performance, energy-efficient electronics. In summary, our work highlights how functional polymers and two-dimensional Sn-based perovskites can advance memory and synaptic transistor technologies. By combining synthesis, interface design, and device engineering, we open pathways toward neuromorphic systems and next-generation optoelectronic devices.

t86.k: Intrinsically Stretchable Polymer Semiconductors; Polarimetric Organic Photodetectors; Photoplethysmography Sensors
t86.a: Intrinsically stretchable polymer semiconductors are promising materials for wearable and skin-integrated electronics because they can accommodate large mechanical deformation while maintaining their optoelectronic properties. However, simultaneously achieving high charge carrier mobility and mechanical stretchability remains challenging because molecular ordering that facilitates efficient charge transport often compromises mechanical compliance. Furthermore, exploiting the mechanically induced structural evolution of these materials to introduce additional optoelectronic functionalities remains relatively unexplored. Intrinsically stretchable polymer semiconductors were designed to achieve a balance between efficient charge transport and mechanical compliance. Their charge-transport characteristics and mechanical properties were systematically investigated under tensile deformation. Controlled mechanical stretching was further employed to induce molecular orientation and optical anisotropy in the polymer thin films. The stretched and uniaxially oriented thin films were subsequently utilized as photoactive layers in polarization-sensitive organic photodetectors, and their potential for wearable optical sensing was evaluated through photoplethysmography monitoring. The developed polymer semiconductors exhibited high charge carrier mobility exceeding 0.1 cm2 V−1 s−1 while maintaining stretchability beyond 200%. Mechanical stretching induced pronounced molecular orientation, resulting in strongly anisotropic optoelectronic properties with a polarization dichroic ratio approaching 4.0. The resulting polarimetric organic photodetectors enabled polarization-sensitive photodetection without the use of external polarizers, thereby avoiding the optical losses associated with conventional polarizer-based configurations. The polarization-selective photoresponse was further exploited to suppress motion-induced interference in photoplethysmography monitoring, enabling more reliable physiological signal acquisition under dynamic conditions. These results demonstrate that mechanical deformation of intrinsically stretchable polymer semiconductors can be utilized not only to achieve mechanical compliance but also to engineer molecular orientation and polarization-dependent optoelectronic properties. This approach provides a versatile materials and device strategy for polarizer-free photodetection and motion-tolerant photoplethysmography sensors, highlighting the potential of intrinsically stretchable polymer semiconductors for next-generation wearable and skin-integrated sensing technologies.

t87.a: Wearable electronics are emerging as versatile platforms for continuous health monitoring, personalized healthcare, and human-machine interaction. Integrating flexible optoelectronic and bioelectronic devices further enables energy harvesting, optical sensing, and physiological signal acquisition within lightweight, conformable systems. In these devices, flexible electrodes are critical interfaces governing light transmission, charge transport, mechanical coupling, and communication with biological tissues. However, conventional electrodes are vulnerable to deformation, moisture, sweat, and biological fluids, leading to delamination, electrical degradation, and reduced signal fidelity. Here, we present interface-engineering strategies for stable flexible organic optoelectronic and bioelectronic devices. Liquid-metal electrodes simplify device architectures and provide mechanically compliant charge-collection interfaces for ultraflexible organic photovoltaics. Fluorinated conductive polymers, including PEDOT:F, regulate electrode energetics and enable stable solution-processed charge transport. PEDOT:F is further integrated with silver nanowire networks to reinforce nanowire junctions, improve adhesion, and suppress aqueous degradation. These approaches support flexible optoelectronic devices, wearable heart-rate sensors, and ultrathin implantable neural interfaces that operate reliably under mechanical deformation and in complex biological environments. The results establish stable electrode interfaces as a common foundation connecting energy harvesting, optoelectronics, and bioelectronics for durable wearable and implantable systems.

t88.k: Organic Electronics; Flexible Sensor; Helth Care
t88.a: Robust polymeric nanofilms can be used to construct gas-permeable soft electronics that can directly adhere to soft biological tissue for continuous, long-term biosignal monitoring. However, it is challenging to fabricate gas-permeable dry electrodes that can self-adhere to the human skin and retain their functionality for long-term health monitoring. We have succeeded in developing an extraordinarily robust, self-adhesive, gas-permeable nanofilm with a thickness of less than 1 µm. The nanofilm can self-adhere to the human skin by van der waals forces alone, for 1 week, without any adhesive materials or tapes. The advantageous features of its thinness, self-adhesiveness, and robustness enable a gas-permeable dry electrode comprising of a nanofilm and an Au layer, resulting in a continuous monitoring of electrocardiogram signals with a high signal-to-noise ratio for 1 week. In additon, we have successfully fabricated ultrathin stretchable organic thin-film transistors on this nanofilms. This organic transitors shows the multi-scale conformability which was enabled through the reduction of the total device thickness to ~2.6 µm, through substrate reinforcement and direct fabrication of the OTFT islands. The devices operated stably under stretching, with less than 7% mobility change at 100% strain, or under crumpling where the minimum bending radius reached 3 µm. The device structure, processes, and design guidelines proposed in this study can be applied to other substrates or island materials. Thus, these methods could be utilized to enhance conformability of other types of stretchable devices or to enhance the durability of ultrathin devices while maintaining low bending stiffness.

t89.a: Flexible and stretchable electronics have demonstrated high skin conformability, enabling long-term healthcare monitoring with comfort-of-wear and high signal integrity. However, the device's appearance sometimes psychologically disturbed its use in daily life, especially on the face, which is the source of useful signals, including EEG, EMG, and EOG. In this presentation, we demonstrate fully unperceivable skin electrodes that do not alter the optical or mechanical properties of bare skin. The invisible skin electrode consists of an optical adjustment substrate and a transparent, stretchable electrode. The optical adjustment substrate is a 200-nm-thick composite film of SEBS elastomer TiO2 nanopowders. The transparent electrode is a random network of silver nanowires. The high optical and mechanical invisibility on the skin was confirmed by a series of physical characterizations and sensory experiments. Furthermore, we verified that the appearance of the electrodes psychologically affects the wearers' emotions and the signals obtained through the devices, which we call appearance artifacts. Still, our unperceivable electrodes didn't leave any appearance artifact. We also constructed a system using unperceivable electrodes and measured EEG, EOG, and EMG signals, whose signal quality was comparable to that of conventional gel electrodes. The invisible wearable devices truly harmonize human and electronics. In addition to the unperceivable electrodes, we will also cover recent topics related to soft electronic materials and devices.

t90.a: Electronic textiles are emerging as a promising platform for wearable systems because electronic functions can be incorporated directly into lightweight, deformable, and breathable fabrics. In particular, emissive e-textiles can provide visual information without attaching conventional planar display modules to garments. However, realizing practical textile displays requires light-emitting devices that are compatible with conventional weaving processes while simultaneously providing pixel-level addressability, environmental stability, and electrical integration with driving electronics. Fibertronic devices, in which electronic components are formed along or within one-dimensional fibers, offer an attractive route toward intrinsically integrated textile displays. Here, we present a systematic development of OLED-based fibertronic platforms, ranging from individually addressable OLED strip fibers to encapsulated full-area emissive textiles and TFT-integrated OLED fibers. Strip-shaped OLED fibers were fabricated using flexible polymer fibers with patterned conductive electrodes and pixel-defining barrier structures. Phosphorescent OLED stacks, metallic base/contact pads, and polymer barriers were sequentially formed on the fibers, which were subsequently woven with conductive fibers to construct electrically addressable textile matrices. For enhanced environmental stability and enlarged emissive coverage, multilayer thin-film encapsulation was integrated with the OLED fibers. To overcome the limitations of passive-matrix operation, oxide thin-film transistors (OxTFTs) were integrated with OLED pixels through a transferable thin-film process incorporating bottom encapsulation, via formation, TFT fabrication, OLED pixel definition, top encapsulation, and subsequent transfer onto flexible fibers. The patterned OLED strip fibers enabled pixel-level emission after weaving with conductive fibers and successfully demonstrated passive-matrix addressing and rapid electrical on/off operation. The woven OLED textile maintained light emission under substantial textile deformation, demonstrating the mechanical compatibility of the fiber-based architecture. Encapsulated OLED fibers also maintained operation during water exposure and repeated bending tests. The transferable-device approach enabled direct integration of OxTFTs and OLED pixels on strip fibers without significant degradation of the OLED EL characteristics after transfer. The integrated OxTFTs exhibited a reasonable switching performance, enabling gate-controlled OLED emission. These results establish a scalable fibertronic strategy for transforming OLEDs from discrete fiber-shaped emitters into electrically addressable and environmentally stable textile display systems. The combination of pixelated OLED fibers, woven electrical interconnections, multifunctional thin-film encapsulation, and integrated TFT driving elements provides a pathway toward intrinsically integrated wearable displays rather than conventional displays mechanically attached to fabrics. Further advances in chemical and mechanical reliability, abrasion resistance, and long-term operational stability will be important for practical wearable implementation.

t91.k: Carbon Electrode; Perovskite Solar Cells; Passivation
t91.a: Carbon-electrode based perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs) have emerged as promising next-generation photovoltaics owing to their low cost, excellent stability, and compatibility with low-temperature fabrication. Replacing vacuum-deposited noble metal electrodes with carbon electrodes enables energy-efficient manufacturing while enhancing long-term device durability. In addition, MA-free CsFA perovskites integrated with carbon electrodes offer a sustainable platform for scalable photovoltaic technologies. This work summarizes recent progress in sustainable MA-free CsFA C-PSCs, focusing on the transition from laboratory-scale devices to scalable mini-modules through entirely low-temperature processes. Emphasis is placed on passivation strategies, including defect passivation, grain boundary modification, and interface engineering at the electron transport layer (ETL)/perovskite, perovskite/hole transport layer (HTL), and HTL/carbon interfaces. These approaches effectively suppress non-radiative recombination, mitigate ion migration, improve charge extraction, and enhance long-term operational stability under both one-sun and indoor illumination. Recent advances in free-standing carbon electrodes and scalable module fabrication further demonstrate practical pathways toward cost-effective manufacturing and commercialization. Collectively, these developments support sustainable photovoltaic technologies that contribute to Affordable and Clean Energy (SDG 7), Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG 9), and Climate Action (SDG 13).

t92.a: Vacuum thermal evaporation is a promising solvent-free and scalable technique for perovskite solar cells (PSCs), offering precise control over film thickness and uniformity. However, rapid crystallization during vacuum deposition often results in excessive nucleation, small grains, and high defect densities, which become particularly detrimental in ultrathin perovskite films. We therefore developed a vacuum-compatible dry additive strategy to regulate crystallization during film formation. Diphenyl sulfoxide (DPSO), a volatile Lewis base, was co-evaporated with PbI₂ and MAI during the deposition of MAPbI₃ films. DPSO transiently coordinates with perovskite precursors to suppress rapid nucleation and was subsequently removed by mild post-deposition annealing at 80 °C. Fully vacuum-evaporated PSCs with perovskite thicknesses of 350, 200, and 150 nm were fabricated and characterized using SEM, XRD, XPS, UV–vis spectroscopy, J–V measurements, and EQE analysis. DPSO effectively suppressed nucleation and promoted the formation of larger, more crystalline perovskite grains with improved film continuity. While the efficiency improvement was modest for 350 nm devices, with a maximum PCE increasing from 17.25% to 18.04%, the effect was pronounced in ultrathin devices. At 200 nm thickness, DPSO-assisted devices achieved a PCE of 16.90%, compared with only 3.24% for the control, while a 150 nm DPSO-assisted device maintained a PCE of 11.45%. In addition, unencapsulated DPSO-treated devices retained approximately 94% of their initial efficiency after 720 h of ambient storage. The dry DPSO additive strategy provides an effective means of controlling nucleation and grain growth in fully vacuum-evaporated perovskite films. This approach enables efficient and stable ultrathin PSCs while preserving the advantages of solvent-free vacuum processing, offering a promising route toward scalable, lightweight, and semitransparent perovskite photovoltaics.

t93.k: Fs-TAM; Perovskite Thin Films; Charge Carrier Dynamics
t93.a: ﻿Additive and interfacial engineering have substantially improved perovskite solar-cell performance by controlling crystallization, morphology, defects, and carrier transport. However, their effects on spatial charge migration and spin transport remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigate caffeine-engineered 3D perovskites and chiral 2D–3D perovskite heterostructures to elucidate how structural and molecular engineering governs charge and spin transport. ﻿Pristine and caffeine-treated perovskite films were examined using femtosecond transient absorption microscopy to visualize carrier migration across flat and wrinkled regions. Separately, 2D–3D heterostructures incorporating enantiomeric RNEA and SNEA spacer ligands were studied using circular-polarization- and pump-energy-dependent transient absorption spectroscopy to probe interfacial spin-selective charge carrier dynamics. ﻿Caffeine altered perovskite crystallization and promoted wrinkle formation. In pristine films, Type-II band alignment between wrinkled and flat regions drives long-range lateral carrier migration toward favorable flat domains. In contrast, caffeine treatment suppresses this lateral intergrain transport and promotes carrier transport perpendicular to the film plane, thereby facilitating carrier extraction in solar cells. In 2D–3D heterostructures, RNEA- and SNEA-based interfaces exhibited opposite circular-polarization-dependent transient responses, providing evidence for chirality-dependent spin-selective carrier dynamics. Pump-energy-dependent measurements further revealed that the spin-selective response varies with the initially excited electronic states of the 2D perovskite, highlighting the active role of the chiral organic spacer in mediating interfacial spin filtering through the CISS effect. ﻿These results demonstrate that mesoscale morphology and molecular chirality provide complementary control over charge and spin transport in perovskites. Structural engineering directs carrier migration, whereas chiral interfaces enable spin filtering, offering a unified strategy for high-performance photovoltaic and spin-optoelectronic devices.

t94.k: Copper Coordination Compounds; Photocapacitor; Battery-free IoT
t94.a: Copper coordination compounds, from extended polymers to discrete redox shuttles, provide earth-abundant, solution-processable building blocks for every layer of an autonomous indoor energy system. Photocapacitors that monolithically integrate photovoltaic harvesting with supercapacitive storage on a single substrate are emerging as a key architecture for battery-free IoT, yet their performance has been limited by inefficient charge-selective contacts and narrow spectral harvesting [3]. This talk traces how copper coordination chemistry addresses these bottlenecks from the molecular to the system level. First, mixed-valence Cu(II)/Cu(I) dithiocarbamate–halide coordination polymers are introduced as dopant-free hole conductors. Switching the bridging halide from bromide to iodide enhances Cu–I valence-band conjugation, reducing the computed effective hole mass from 94me to 6me and raising conductivity over two orders of magnitude to 1 mS cm−1. In carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells the iodide polymer reaches 13.8% PCE nearly double that of doped Spiro-MeOTAD and retains >94% efficiency over 50 days under ambient humidity [1]. Second, we leverage discrete Cu(tmby)2 redox shuttles in dye-sensitized solar cells (DSCs) that exceed 30% PCE under 1000 lux and couple them with polyviologen/carbon asymmetric supercapacitors on a shared PEDOT electrode to form three-terminal photocapacitors. Under ambient light these devices deliver 920 mV and 18% overall charging efficiency, sustaining a three-layer edge-AI network for 72 hours outperforming commercial a-Si modules 3.5-fold in inference throughput and reaching 93% CIFAR-10 accuracy at 0.81 mJ per classification [2]. These results demonstrate how tuneable redox potentials and solution processability in copper coordination compounds propagate from molecular design through device integration to system-level energy autonomy for battery-free computing.

t95.k: Perovskite Solar Cells; Indoor Photovoltaics; Green Antisolvent
t95.a: Carbon-based perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs) offer an exceptionally short energy payback period, which can be further optimized by adopting a hole transport layer-free (HTL-free) architecture. These advantages are narrowing the gap between laboratories and the commercial scale of C-PSCs. Although pioneering studies have demonstrated comparable performance of carbon electrodes in HTL-free C-PSCs, the perovskite layer has rarely been tailored to operate solely on the electron transport layer (ETL). This is because the HTL-free C-PSC structure leads to electronic band energy mismatches between perovskite/carbon and imbalanced charge transport at the perovskite/ETL interface. In this study, we modulated the (111) and (100) perovskite facets at the buried interface and enhanced the in-plane crystal orientation using the molecular structure of an antisolvent. This antisolvent structural tuning significantly improved the electronic band alignment at the ETL junction. Furthermore, residual PbI₂ formed on the top surface of the perovskite film effectively facilitated 2D/3D defect passivation. As a result, the optimized devices achieved an outstanding indoor light power conversion efficiency (PCE) of up to 32.31%. The cells also exhibited excellent long-term operational stability, retaining over 98% of their initial PCE after more than a year of continuous testing under the standard ISOS-D-1 protocol. Beyond device performance, this strategy aligns with environmentally friendly manufacturing practices, as the alternative antisolvent provides a safer and greener processing route compared to conventional toxic solvents.

t96.a: Tin-lead perovskite solar cells are considered strong candidates for narrow-bandgap single-junction devices and as bottom cells in all-perovskite tandem solar cells. In p–i–n structured tin–lead perovskite solar cells, PEDOT:PSS has often been used as a standard hole transport layer. However, its acidic and hygroscopic characteristics, along with unwanted interfacial reactions, can restrict both device performance and long-term stability. Because of this, NiOₓ has gained attention as a promising inorganic hole transport layer due to its stability and compatibility with processing. That said, NiOₓ still suffers from several issues, including relatively low electrical conductivity, less-than-ideal energy level matching with tin–lead perovskites, and interfacial recombination at the NiOₓ/perovskite boundary. These factors can impede charge extraction and carrier transport. In this work, a multifunctional organic molecular dopant was introduced into NiOₓ to enhance both its electrical properties and its interfacial behavior. With this doped NiOₓ, the resulting tin-lead perovskite solar cells showed improved short-circuit current density and fill factor compared with devices using pristine NiOₓ. The multifunctional dopant is expected to tune the buried NiOₓ/perovskite interface by interacting with defects on the NiOₓ surface and by adjusting the interfacial environment during perovskite formation. These changes help promote hole extraction, lower interfacial charge-transport losses, and strengthen interfacial contact—ultimately boosting current generation and fill factor. Overall, this study shows that molecular doping of NiOₓ is an effective strategy for engineering the HTL to improve tin-lead perovskite solar cell performance. The proposed method offers a promising route toward efficient narrow-bandgap perovskite solar cells and effective all-perovskite tandem bottom cells.

t97.a: Tin–lead perovskites (TLPs) offer near-optimal band gaps for single-junction and tandem photovoltaics but suffer from spontaneous Sn2+ oxidation and imbalanced charge transport. Controlled p-doping can accelerate hole extraction, yet conventional p-dopants further oxidize Sn2+, creating a fundamental conflict between doping and stability. We designed a bifunctional copolymer additive, poly(pyrrolidinium-Jeffamine) hexafluorophosphate (PPJ-PF6), directly blended into the TLP precursor solution. The polypyrrolidinium backbone electrostatically anchors PF6− anions at defect-rich grain boundaries for controlled, non-destructive p-doping, while the Jeffamine polyether segment coordinates undercoordinated Sn2+ sites and kinetically suppresses Sn2+ → Sn4+ conversion. Polymer–perovskite interactions were verified by DFT calculations, FT-IR, and 1H NMR, and inverted (p-i-n) solar cells were characterized by XPS, KPFM, in-situ GIWAXS, and photovoltaic analysis. PPJ-PF6 reduced the Sn4+ fraction from 32.7% to 18.7% and produced a beneficial Fermi-level downshift that operates only when PF6− is retained within the polymer scaffold. Trap-assisted recombination was suppressed (diode ideality factor 1.52 → 1.29) with enhanced hole mobility and reduced hysteresis, delivering a champion PCE of 22.8% from a 21.4% baseline. Unencapsulated devices retained approximately 80% of their initial efficiency after 500 h, and single-molecule reference additives lacking either segment underperformed, confirming the cooperative mechanism. Bifunctional polymer scaffolds that decouple dopant delivery from lattice protection enable oxidation-safe p-doping of tin–lead perovskites, offering a generalizable design principle for next-generation multifunctional additives in low-bandgap perovskite optoelectronics.

t98.a: Single-crystalline perovskites offer superior electronic, dielectric, and optoelectronic properties, but their scalable integration remains challenging because conventional solution-based synthesis provides limited control over crystallographic orientation, interfaces, and wafer-scale uniformity. Vacuum deposition provides a promising pathway toward deterministic growth by enabling precise control of composition, surface reactions, and crystallization kinetics. We developed complementary vacuum-based approaches for single-crystalline perovskite synthesis. Epitaxial vapor deposition was employed to directly grow high-quality crystalline frames, while a sequential vapor-phase conversion strategy was used for hybrid halide perovskites. In the latter, crystalline inorganic precursor frameworks were first deposited and subsequently converted through controlled incorporation of volatile organic species, enabling regulation of phase formation and crystallographic orientation. These approaches enabled highly crystalline perovskite films with controlled interfaces and preferential crystallographic orientations. For hybrid perovskite, the intermediate crystalline framework governed the conversion pathway and produced strong orientation selectivity, including a dominant (111), (100), and (110) texture. More broadly, the results demonstrate that decoupling precursor crystallization from subsequent chemical conversion provides an effective means of controlling nucleation, orientation, and defect formation in vacuum-grown perovskites. Vacuum deposition can provide a scalable and deterministic route toward single-crystalline perovskite thin films. By controlling epitaxy, intermediate phases, and vapor-phase conversion kinetics, this approach establishes a general framework for integrating high-quality oxide and hybrid perovskites into next-generation electronic and photonic devices.

t99.k: Carbon-based perovskite solar module, Dual-layer carbon electrode, Free-standing graphite film, Sheet resistance, Lamination
t99.a: Carbon back electrodes make perovskite solar cells cheaper and more stable than those using evaporated Au or Ag, but they are far more resistive, and the resulting series resistance limits the fill factor at one sun. The difficulty is that a single carbon layer has to do two jobs at once: good contact with the perovskite calls for a carbon-black-rich paste, while good lateral conduction calls for large graphite flakes and little binder, so improving one degrades the other. In this work we separate the two functions into two layers that are optimized independently. The contact layer (C foundation) is a graphite/carbon-black paste coated directly on the hole-transport layer for best adhesion, while the conducting layer (C framework) is a free-standing graphite film made from graphite flake and aqueous binder along with high pressure treatment. Solar cells were made with contact layers of two different optimized thicknesses, showing promising conversion performance. The same electrode is being applied to series-interconnected modules. The process requires no vacuum steps and can readily be transferred to roll-to-roll production.

t100.k: Perovskite Solar Cells; Deep Eutectic Solvent; TiO2
t100.a: Carbon electrode-based perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs) have attracted significant attention as a cost-effective and stable alternative to metal-electrode devices, owing to the excellent chemical stability and low fabrication costs of carbon materials. However, their performance is often limited by interfacial defects and suboptimal charge extraction at the TiO2 electron transporting layer (ETL). Herein, an effective interfacial engineering strategy is introduced using a deep eutectic solvent (DES) composed of choline chloride and urea to passivate the TiO2 surface. The DES treatment induces strong interfacial coordination, effectively passivating oxygen vacancies and optimizing the surface electronic properties for improved charge transfer. Consequently, enhanced charge extraction and suppressed non-radiative recombination are achieved, as evidenced by reduced trap density. In addition, the modified surface promotes improved perovskite crystallinity with more uniform grain distribution and better interfacial contact. As a result of these synergistic effects, the DES-modified C-PSCs achieved a notable power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 15.84%, a significant improvement over the 14.50% obtained by the control devices. This work highlights DES-assisted passivation as a highly effective yet straightforward strategy for advancing high-performance C-PSCs through tailored interfacial engineering.

t101.a: Metal-halide perovskites offer exceptional potential for next-generation photovoltaics, but their long-term stability under realistic operating conditions remains a major challenge. In particular, partial shading of series-connected solar cells and modules can induce severe reverse-bias conditions, leading to degradation and potentially catastrophic failure. In this talk, I will present how an understanding of resistive switching in perovskites can be translated into a new device concept that directly addresses this reliability challenge. I will first discuss the fundamental mechanisms governing resistive switching in perovskite devices. Through detailed device investigations, we show that switching is not mediated by distributed conductive nanofilaments, as commonly assumed, but instead occurs within highly localized regions that form during initial device operation. By introducing a light-assisted patterning approach to precisely define these regions, we eliminate the need for an energy-intensive electroforming step and demonstrate perovskite memristors with low operating voltages, extremely low leakage currents, long data-retention times, and stable operation over millions of switching cycles. These insights provide the basis for exploiting resistive switching as an intrinsic functionality within photovoltaic devices. Building on this understanding, I will introduce the Memsol concept: a perovskite solar cell with an integrated memristive element that functions simultaneously as a self-regulating protection and bypass mechanism. Under reverse-bias conditions caused by partial shading, the integrated memristor automatically switches to a low-resistance state, protecting the solar cell from degradation. Under normal photovoltaic operation, it returns to a high-resistance state, thereby preserving the solar cell's performance. Reverse-bias and shading experiments, including demonstrations on multi-cell strings, confirm robust and autonomous protection without the need for conventional external bypass components. Together, these results demonstrate how fundamental insights into ionic and electronic processes in perovskites can be translated into innovative photovoltaic device architectures. The Memsol concept provides a pathway toward intrinsically protected perovskite solar cells and modules and illustrates how multifunctional device concepts can address critical reliability challenges in next-generation photovoltaics.

t102.k: Halide Perovskites; Wide Bandgap; Tandem Solar Cells
t102.a: Wide-bandgap halide perovskites are suitable as top cells in tandem solar cells. However, their applications are limited by large Voc losses and insufficient photostability. In this talk, I will introduce our work from the following three aspects. 1) We used lead-based additives to regulate the crystallization of wide-bandgap inorganic perovskites and realize homogeneous halide distribution throughout the film depth; 2) We designed the interfacial properties of buried contacts to achieve selective coordination with Pb-halide species in hybrid perovskites and synchronize halide incorporation during crystallization; 3) We elucidated the mechanism governing phase segregation under light illumination by clarifying the role of carrier-selective contacts. In CsPbI2Br solar cells, we achieved 1.25V Voc and >16% efficiency, owing to homogeneous halide distribution and suppressed nonradiative carrier recombination. In 1.67 eV hybrid perovskites, by realizing homogeneous phase formation, suppressing ion migration, and improving carrier transport, we achieved 1.26V Voc and >24% efficiency; when paired with a silicon bottom cell, the tandem device achieved >34% efficiency. We also found that phase segregation in inorganic perovskites is governed by hole-extraction dynamics rather than solely by intrinsic instability. Our work demonstrates that homogeneous halide distribution in wide-bandgap halide perovskites is critical for realizing high-performance single-junction and tandem solar cells. By developing suitable additives and controlling the interfacial properties of buried contacts, homogeneous halide distribution can be significantly improved. We also prove that hole extraction is critical to light-induced phase segregation; therefore, designing efficient hole-extraction materials is important for future applications.

t103.k: Indoor Photovoltaics; Emerging Nanomaterials; Sustainable Energy Harvesting
t103.a: Indoor photovoltaics (IPVs) offer a promising route to sustainably power the rapidly expanding ecosystem of Internet-of-Things devices by harvesting ambient light and reducing reliance on disposable batteries. Emerging functional nanomaterials are opening new pathways toward high-performance IPV devices, including lead-free perovskite derivatives. However, realizing the sustainability potential of these technologies requires more than the development of new absorber chemistries and advances in device and fabrication engineering. Emerging materials must be evaluated over their full life cycle, while IPV devices must be designed, characterized, and benchmarked using physically meaningful approaches that remain valid across diverse indoor-lighting conditions. Addressing these challenges is essential for translating advances in functional nanomaterials into reliable and genuinely sustainable energy-harvesting technologies. This presentation brings together research spanning functional nanomaterials, device engineering, environmental assessment, and the design, characterization, and benchmarking of IPV devices. Lead-free, pnictogen-based perovskite-inspired nanomaterials were developed as absorbers for IPVs. Their environmental implications were evaluated using comparative life-cycle assessment (LCA), comparing lead-based and lead-free halide perovskite and perovskite-derivative IPVs while accounting for impacts across the full life cycle and assessing their environmental benefits relative to conventional battery-powered devices. In parallel, systematic experimental and analytical investigations were conducted to establish physically grounded approaches to IPV design, characterization, and benchmarking. These studies identified limitations in commonly used metrics, testing conditions, and methods for cross-study comparison. Building on these insights, a universal, spectrum-aware, and device-aware framework for IPV design, characterization, and benchmarking was developed. Pnictogen-based perovskite-inspired absorbers demonstrate that lead-free nanomaterials can deliver indoor photovoltaic efficiencies competitive with established IPV technologies, highlighting their potential for indoor energy harvesting. However, the LCA results show that environmental sustainability cannot be inferred from elemental toxicity alone. When material production, processing, device fabrication, use, and end-of-life are considered, the relative environmental performance of lead-based and lead-free technologies becomes substantially more nuanced than a simple lead-free-versus-lead-based comparison suggests. The design and characterization studies further show that commonly used IPV practices—including reliance on human-vision-based illumination metrics, inappropriate or insufficiently calibrated light sources, and single-illuminant benchmarking—can introduce substantial, device-dependent inaccuracies and compromise comparisons between technologies. These limitations can be addressed through a spectrum-aware framework that connects the illumination spectrum to optimal IPV design and enables consistent comparison of device performance across diverse lighting conditions and materials. The resulting framework provides predictive design metrics and a locus-based approach for benchmarking devices across realistic illumination scenarios, while a complementary device-aware error framework enables quantitative assessment of characterization accuracy. These results demonstrate that sustainable IPV development requires the integration of functional nanomaterials, physically grounded device design, accurate characterization, rigorous benchmarking, and life-cycle assessment. Emerging nanomaterials can provide promising routes toward lower-toxicity and high-performance indoor energy harvesting, but their true technological and environmental value depends on how they are designed, measured, compared, and evaluated across their life cycle. Together, these advances establish a general framework for translating functional nanomaterials into reliable, environmentally meaningful IPV technologies.

t104.k: Optical Fiber Sensor; Molecularly Imprinted Polymer (MIP); Methamphetamine Detection
t104.a: Rapid and reliable detection of methamphetamine (Meth) is important for forensic and drug-screening applications. Although rapid screening kits are widely available, their typical cut-off concentrations of approximately 1 ppm may limit screening at lower Meth concentrations. Molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) provide target-tailored recognition sites and can be integrated with optical fiber sensors for label-free detection. In this work, we systematically optimize the Meth-MIP recognition interface of an optical fiber sensor for low-concentration Meth detection and extend its analytical evaluation to structurally related compounds and competitive mixed-analyte conditions. Meth-MIP formulations were prepared by varying the methamphetamine template concentration while maintaining methacrylic acid (MAA) and ethylene glycol dimethacrylate (EGDMA) concentrations. The pre-polymerization mixtures were dip-coated onto silanized coreless fibers and photopolymerized under UV irradiation to form five MIP layers. Following template removal, the 4-cm MIP-coated sensing region was spliced between two single-mode fibers to form an SMF–NCF–SMF structure. Sensor performance was evaluated over 0.01–0.10 ppm Meth using wavelength shifts in the transmission spectrum, with at least five replicate measurements at each concentration. The optimized MIP interface was characterized by SEM, AFM, and FTIR and evaluated against structurally related compounds, including amphetamine, pseudoephedrine, MDA, and MDMA. Binary-mixture experiments were further conducted to investigate the sensor response to Meth in the presence of interfering compounds. The optimized sensor was further evaluated in artificial oral fluid to assess its performance in a matrix relevant to non-invasive drug screening. Optimization of the Meth-MIP formulation led to the selection of a Meth:MAA:EGDMA ratio of 1:4:20, providing a favorable balance of sensitivity, linearity, and detection limit. The optimized sensor achieved a sensitivity of 12.36 nm/ppm (R² = 0.97) and a calculated LOD of 0.01 ppm, approximately 100-fold below the 1 ppm cut-off commonly used in rapid Meth screening kits. Morphological characterization revealed a MIP coating thickness of 118.15 ± 5.45 nm, while FTIR showed spectral changes associated with template removal. The optimized sensor exhibited its highest response toward Meth, followed by amphetamine (10.70 nm/ppm), pseudoephedrine (6.22 nm/ppm), MDA (4.76 nm/ppm), and MDMA (2.43 nm/ppm), while no detectable spectral response was observed for MDEA or MDPV under the tested conditions. Competitive binary-mixture experiments further revealed interferent-dependent changes in the Meth response, highlighting the importance of evaluating molecular recognition under competitive rather than isolated-analyte conditions. Systematic engineering of the Meth-MIP recognition interface enabled low-concentration Meth detection with an LOD of 0.01 ppm, substantially below the 1 ppm cut-off commonly used in rapid screening kits. Beyond analytical sensitivity, evaluation against structurally related compounds and competitive mixtures provided insight into the recognition and interference behavior of the MIP sensing interface under increasingly complex analytical conditions. Together with evaluation in an oral-fluid-relevant matrix, this work advances MIP-functionalized optical fiber sensing toward sensitive, label-free Meth screening using non-invasively collected oral fluid.

t105.k: Organic Non-volatile Floating-gate Photomemory; Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor; Artificial Neural Network
t105.a: Programmable inverters using non-volatile floating-gate photomemories as the basic building blocks instead of field-effect transistors enable the manipulation of the threshold voltage by photon, giving an additional degree of freedom for applications in integrated circuits. However, the development of organic photo-controllable inverters remains rare due to challenges such as solubility issues for film stacking and the immaturity of photo-recordable devices. Especially, the development of organic non-volatile floating-gate photomemories (ONVFGPs) with n-type charge-transporting layers still lags the p-type ones due to the shortage of proper solution-processable charge-trapping materials and charge-transporting materials pairs. Herein, photo-crosslinkable polystyrene-b-poly(methacrylic acid) (PS-b-PMAA)/5,10,15,20-tetraphenyl-21H,23H-porphine zinc (ZnTPP) with anti-kasha’s rule is adopted as the charge-trapping layer for ONVFGP. Both the second and first excited states of ZnTPP participate in the photo-induced charge transfer and thus realize the state-of-art photo-programming time of 0.1 seconds for ONVFGP. The transfer curve of the derived photo-programmable inverter can be fine-tuned by a broad spectrum spanning from 405 nm to 830 nm and lead to six output states at least for the same input signal. Both the second and first excited states of ZnTPP participate in the photo-induced charge transfer and thus realize the state-of-art photo-programming time of 0.1 seconds for ONVFGP. The transfer curve of the derived photo-programmable inverter can be fine-tuned by a broad spectrum spanning from 405 nm to 830 nm and lead to six output states at least for the same input signal.

t106.k: Liquid Crystals; Colloidal Transport; Reconfigurable Soft Matter
t106.a: Transporting microscopic particles (colloids) without electrodes or pumps is central to lab-on-a-chip and micro-robotic technologies. In liquid crystals, fluids whose rod-shaped molecules align along a common direction, defect lines called disclinations trap colloids, acting as rails for micro-cargo. The challenge is to rewire these rails on demand and keep the new layout. We built nematic (5CB) cells with a photopatterned bottom surface that templates vertical disclination lines and a photoswitchable azobenzene top layer. The top alignment was switched with ultraviolet (365 nm) or visible (450 nm) light. Silica microspheres (10 μm) served as cargo. Landau–de Gennes simulations, a continuum model of liquid crystal alignment, mapped the stable network states. Ultraviolet light reoriented the top surface from perpendicular to in-plane, and vertical lines reconnected with new partners, changing which lines are connected to which. Visible light restored the surface but not the network. The rewiring persisted. Simulations found two stable states, the initial vertical array and a lower-energy reconnected network. The light-switched surface decided whether a local disturbance could carry the system between them. During rewiring, trapped microspheres were carried and handed off between lines, advancing in steps. The network thus behaves like a mechanical ratchet, advancing in one direction only, and carries cargo with light as the sole input. This electrode-free platform points toward low-standby-power devices for micro-cargo manipulation and reconfigurable photonics. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, RS-2024-00411809).

t107.k: Molecular Memristor; Local Learning; Energy-efficient Neuromorphic Computing
t107.a: On-chip learning aims at neuromorphic hardware that updates its own parameters at the edge, where memory, power and bandwidth are scarce. Existing artificial synapses implement mostly Hebbian or spike-timing-dependent rules, which are two-factor and cannot solve credit assignment in goal-directed tasks. Biology resolves this chemically: neuromodulators broadcast reward, error and novelty to many synapses at once. Chemistry encodes such signals in molecular structure, concentration and diffusion, variables unavailable to electrical wiring, yet artificial synapses remain almost exclusively electrically gated. Au/SAM//GaOx/EGaIn molecular junctions bearing photoresponsive and alkanethiolate monolayers were characterized under optical and voltage pulse trains at sub-volt bias. Chemically mediated fluidic synapses sharing a common electrolyte delivered a global modulatory signal, and measured synaptic parameters were used to parameterize a reinforcement learning task. Junctions operated at sub-volt bias with tunnelling-limited currents, placing switching energies well below those of filamentary devices. Photoresponsive junctions showed paired-pulse facilitation and a continuous short- to long-term potentiation transition, supplying an eligibility trace whose decay constant is set chemically; bias polarity switched responses between excitatory and inhibitory over 10³ cycles. Terminal-group chemistry tuned intrinsic switching stochasticity. In fluidic synapses, one modulator injection reached every junction simultaneously, and simulations driven by the measured characteristics adapted faster than two-factor devices under changing task statistics. Molecular and chemical junctions deliver ultralow-power memristive elements whose energy cost, temporal dynamics and modulatory access derive from chemistry rather than circuit design. Chemical broadcast of a third factor, impractical to wire electrically, positions them as primitives for adaptive edge-learning hardware.

t108.k: BNNT; Electro-optic Devices; Liquid Crystal Alignment
t108.a: The rational design of the highly aligned one-dimensional nanomaterials has emerged as a promising anisotropic functional material for the next generation of electronics and photonics devices. Among them, Boron nitride nanotubes (BNNT) are the material that is structurally similar to the carbon nanotube, but is an electrical insulator, chemically stable, and exhibits superior mechanical properties. The surface morphology and unidirectional orientation of the BNNT were investigated using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM). The role of the unidirectionally aligned BNNT in inducing alignment of liquid crystal (LC) is evaluated after filling the LC in a BNNT-based cell. The electro-optical properties are investigated using the Polarizing Optical Microscope (POM) and electrical switching measurement. The highly aligned BNNT show excellent structure anisotropy and effectively align the LC molecules through synergistic effect of anisotropic nanotube topology and epitaxial-like interfacial interactions between aromatic LC molecules and the curved BN lattice. This demonstrates the uniform optical texture and reversible switching of the LC molecules, emphasising the potential of highly aligned BNNT films as electrically insulating anisotropic interfaces. This work establishes that the anisotropic nanostructure and electrical insulating properties of the BNNT provide a promising alternative to polymers and CNT-based alignment layers for the LC-based electro-optic devices. Beyond the LC-based devices, the anisotropic structure can also be explored for photonics, flexible electronics, and thermal management systems. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, and RS-2024-00411809).

t109.k: Semiconducting Polymers, Molecular Design, Electronic Skin (E-skin), Artificial
t109.a: Our research is fundamentally driven by molecular design and interfacial science, aiming to control polymer structures and their interactions to achieve targeted functions. This talk highlights how we apply these core principles to develop advanced polymeric materials for nature-inspired applications, focusing on two representative directions: electronic skin and artificial photosynthesis. Skin, as the largest organ in the human body, performs multiple functions such as pressure and temperature sensing, stretchability, and self-healing. Mimicking these properties, electronic skin (e-skin) has emerged as a promising field that integrates material flexibility with sensory capabilities. In this context, we design organic and polymeric materials with tailored architectures to achieve stretchable, self-healing, and conformable sensors that emulate skin-like behaviors. Our approach emphasizes the importance of controlling molecular mobility, dynamic bonding, and interfacial compatibility. In parallel, we draw inspiration from natural photosynthesis to develop polymer-based photocatalysts for solar-driven hydrogen production via water splitting. By fine-tuning polymer backbones, energy levels, and nanostructures, we create polymer dots (Pdots) and bulk materials capable of efficiently harvesting visible light. This part of the talk will discuss our strategies in conjugated polymer design, the role of hydrophilic/hydrophobic interfaces, and mechanistic insights into charge separation and reaction kinetics. Through these two platforms—e-skin and artificial photosynthesis—we demonstrate how molecular design and interfacial control can converge to enable innovative functions, offering pathways to address grand challenges in sustainable energy and wearable electronics.

t110.a: All-inorganic perovskites are promising photoactive semiconductors for optoelectronic and solar-to-chemical applications owing to their strong visible-light absorption, efficient emission, and favorable carrier-transport properties. However, their measured optical and photoelectrochemical responses are often complicated by coupled photophysical and interfacial processes. In particular, reabsorption-mediated spectral distortion can obscure intrinsic photoluminescence behavior, while inefficient interfacial charge extraction can limit photoelectrochemical performance. Inorganic perovskite based photoactive systems were investigated using steady-state, temperature-dependent, and time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy, together with photoelectrochemical and electrochemical analyses. Optical measurements were used to assess emission redistribution associated with photon propagation and reabsorption. Conductive scaffold-integrated perovskite architectures were further examined under non-aqueous photoelectrochemical conditions to evaluate photoinduced charge extraction, interfacial resistance, and operational response. The optical response revealed that apparent emission features can be strongly affected by reabsorption and effective optical path length, leading to spectral redistribution that may mimic changes in intrinsic recombination pathways. In parallel, direct integration of CsPbBr3 with a conductive framework promoted photoinduced carrier extraction and improved interfacial charge-transfer behavior compared with control configurations. Complementary photoluminescence dynamics and electrochemical measurements consistently indicated that both photon transport and interfacial charge dynamics play crucial roles in the observed device-level response. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing intrinsic material properties from geometry- and interface-induced effects in CsPbBr3 perovskite systems. The study provides a framework for interpreting reabsorption-affected emission and interfacial charge-transfer behavior in strongly light-absorbing perovskite semiconductors.

t111.k: Waste valorization; Ethanol oxidation; Ni-BDC metal–organic framework; Acetate production; Hydrogen evolution
t111.a: Converting food waste into value-added chemicals while producing hydrogen offers a promising strategy for more sustainable electrochemical manufacturing. Here, low-purity ethanol obtained from bread fermentation is directly converted to acetate while H₂ is produced at the cathode through paired ethanol oxidation and hydrogen evolution (EOR||HER). A Ni-based benzenedicarboxylate metal–organic framework (Ni-BDC-MOF) was constructed on nickel foam and systematically modified with –NH₂, –NO₂, and –Br linkers to tune the electronic properties and redox behavior of Ni active sites. Among these catalysts, Br-functionalized Ni-BDC exhibited the most favorable Ni²⁺/Ni³⁺ redox transformation, facilitating the generation of active NiOOH species and selective ethanol oxidation. The optimized Ni-BDC-Br delivered a 90.7% Faradaic efficiency for acetate at 1.435 V versus RHE. Operando XANES/EXAFS together with potential-dependent Raman spectroscopy revealed reversible changes in the Ni coordination environment and supported a Ni³⁺-mediated oxidation pathway involving ethoxy- and carbonyl-containing intermediates while limiting C–C bond cleavage. Incorporation of the catalyst into an EOR||HER electrolyzer reduced the required cell voltage to 1.88 V, approximately 14% lower than that of conventional OER||HER electrolysis. Notably, the system retained its activity with unpurified bread-fermentation ethanol containing approximately 0.74 M ethanol (4.3 vol%). Furthermore, photovoltaic coupling enabled hydrogen production using renewable electricity without additional external power input. Overall, this study demonstrates linker engineering as an effective approach for controlling MOF electronic structure and reaction selectivity, while providing an integrated route for simultaneous food-waste valorization, acetate production, and renewable hydrogen generation. This approach avoids feedstock purification and reduces energy demand for integrated simultaneous chemical production pathways.

t112.a: Achieving net zero requires materials that can convert light, manage charge, sense environments and be manufactured at scale. This keynote will examine how nanoscale materials design can accelerate that transition, linking fundamental nanoscience to deployable technologies for a resilient, electrified and connected society. Carbon-based and hybrid organic–inorganic nanomaterials provide a powerful design space because their morphology, interfaces, transport pathways and optical response can be engineered across length scales. Examples will include carbon nanotubes, graphene, perovskite and organic semiconductor hybrids, quantum-dot and nanocomposite architectures, diamondlike carbon superlattices and bioinspired ultra-black coatings. These materials enable enhanced light harvesting and charge extraction in next-generation photovoltaics; flexible and stretchable large-area electronics; high-sensitivity photodetectors and radiation sensors; self-powered sensing platforms; and low-power devices for distributed monitoring. The lecture will place these device innovations within the broader materials challenge of building renewable-energy systems that are efficient, durable, scalable and affordable. A central theme is that future energy materials must be multifunctional and manufacturable, operating not only as high-performance components but as integrated building blocks for clean-energy infrastructure, autonomous sensor networks, smart buildings, environmental monitoring, healthcare technologies and sustainable manufacturing. By connecting functional nanomaterials, scalable processing and system-level energy thinking, this keynote will outline a materials-led pathway from laboratory discovery to renewable-energy ecosystems. The emphasis will be on how nano-engineered carbon and hybrid materials can move beyond individual devices to support deployable technologies capable of meeting climate, societal and technological demands across regions, sectors and communities, including emerging economies where resilient decentralised energy can transform opportunity.

t113.k: Atomic Layer Deposition; Reactant Chemistry; Surface Modification
t113.a: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is a versatile materials synthesis technique that enables atomic-scale thickness control, with applications in next-generation memories, solar cells, and catalytic coatings. Metal precursor chemistry has been widely studied, but how reactants affect ALD growth remains largely unexplored. This gap limits process optimization based on reactant selection. This study analyzes how reactants affect ALD growth behavior. ZnO was grown as a model system using diethylzinc (DEZ) as the precursor, with H2O or O3 as the reactant. ZnO was also deposited on substrates with differing ozone activation. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to clarify the underlying surface reaction mechanism. H2O gave a consistently higher growth rate than O3 at all temperatures, independent of dose. O3 showed the opposite trend: growth rate decreased with dose at low temperature but increased with dose at high temperature. Growth rates also varied significantly across substrates, supporting surface modification as a key factor governing ALD growth behavior. DFT results show that O3 modifies the surface in ways that either suppress or promote growth, depending on temperature and dose, enabling the surface to be engineered through these parameters. This substrate-dependent surface modification enables area-selective deposition, offering an alternative to conventional lithographic patterning. By simplifying photolithography and etching processes, this approach reduces the use of chemicals such as photoresists, developers, and etchants, offering an eco-friendly route to device fabrication. Beyond ALD, these insights into reactant–surface interactions may also help control metal surface reactivity in catalytic or energy systems.

t114.a: Despite extensive exploration of metal tellurides for energy storage, achieving synergistic charge transport and redox kinetics in bimetallic telluride electrodes remains challenging. In this work, CuTe-CoTe/NiCoSe₂ core-shell nanostructures are synthesized to offer a conductive core with Faradaic redox capacity. BET analysis shows that growth of shells decreases surface area (23.9 to 11.9 m² g−1) and micropore volume, but increases average pore diameter (8.5 to 14.7 nm) and larger mesoporous interparticle voids (median pore diameter: 20.0 to 28.5 nm), which promotes rapid penetration of electrolyte and ion transportation. In the three-electrode configuration, the optimized electrode is able to deliver a specific capacitance of 870 F g−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1. An asymmetric device with activated carbon provides 586 F g−1, energy density of 40 Wh kg−1 at 352 W kg−1. The study here shows a design approach for telluride-based core-shell electrodes where the conductivity and the redox activity are separated in space, and pore architecture is optimized for ion transport. Core-shell structure is a scalable and cost-effective solution for advanced energy storage technologies.

t115.a: There is increasing interest in harnessing sunlight to drive the synthesis of molecular fuels and chemicals, including in particular water photolysis to yield molecular oxygen and hydrogen. This can be achieved either through the coupling of photovoltaic cells and electrolysis, or through direct sunlight conversion by photoelectrodes or photocatalysts, the latter being the focus of this talk. Metal oxides are the material of choice for most such devices, due to their potential stability to oxidative degradation, low cost and scalability. However for metal oxide based photoelectrochemical and photocatalytic systems for solar energy conversion, a key challenge for efficient operation is the efficient separation and stabilisation of photogenerated charges, and thereby the minimisation of undesired recombination losses. This challenge is particularly great for water splitting systems because of the long charge lifetimes required to drive catalysis. My talk will introduce recent advances in the development of metal oxide photoelectrochemical and photocatalytic devices, and then go on to cover examples of recent work from my group addressing the charge carrier dynamics of these devices which are critical determinants of device efficiency. I will discuss how our kinetic studies give insight into material design, and the opportunities and challenges for technological application of solar driven synthetic chemistry.

t116.a: Electrochemical interfaces govern ion transport, reaction kinetics, mechanical stability, and parasitic reactions in rechargeable batteries. Rational control of these interfaces is therefore essential for developing high-energy, durable, and safe battery systems. We designed interface-focused material architectures across four battery platforms. Directional and layered LLZO frameworks were fabricated using graphene oxide templates and integrated with polymer matrices to form composite solid electrolytes. Hierarchical rGO@NiMn2O4@silicene-flower anodes were constructed to accommodate silicon expansion and regulate interfacial reactions. Metal phosphide-functionalized carbon nanotube aerogels were employed as three-dimensional current collectors to generate a Li3P-rich interphase for lithium-metal deposition. For aqueous zinc batteries, PVDF-HFP/PEO coatings were applied to zinc-powder anodes as ion-conductive protective binders. The oriented ceramic networks enhanced ionic transport and mechanical integrity compared with randomly dispersed composites. The silicon architecture retained 533.5 mAh/g after 500 cycles at 4.0 A/g and delivered 361.1 mAh/g at 16.0 A/g. The Li3P-rich interface reduced lithium nucleation overpotential and enabled Coulombic efficiencies above 99% for over 1000 cycles. The polymer-coated zinc anodes suppressed corrosion and hydrogen evolution, promoted uniform Zn deposition, and operated stably for over 1200 h at 5 mA/cm2. These studies demonstrate that coordinated control of ion-conducting pathways, interphase chemistry, and chemo-mechanical stability provides a versatile strategy for advancing solid-state, lithium-ion, lithium-metal, and aqueous zinc batteries.

t117.k: Solid Polymer Electrolyte; TEMPO-oxidized Cellulose Nanofiber; LiNi0.83Co0.12Mn0.05O2 Cathode
t117.a: The practical deployment of poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO)-based solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs) with Ni-rich cathodes is hindered by coupled limitations in ion transport, mechanical integrity, oxidative stability, and cathode–electrolyte interfacial degradation. Here, we develop a coordinated bulk–interphase engineering strategy that couples molecular-weight-regulated TEMPO-oxidized cellulose nanofiber (TOCN)-reinforced SPEs with a compliant and passivating poly(butylene oxide)/lithium bis(oxalato)borate (PBO/LiBOB) interphase on LiNi0.83Co0.12Mn0.05O2 (NCM83) cathodes. Compared with PEG3350, PEO200k forms a more cohesive TOCN–polyether network and increases the oxidation onset potential from approximately 4.8 to 5.2 V. The optimized TP28_PEO200k electrolyte exhibits an ionic conductivity of 9.53 × 10-5 S cm-1 and a Li-ion transference number of 0.24 at 60 °C. Li|TP28_PEO200k|Li symmetric cells sustain stable Li stripping/plating for at least 1200 h at 0.15 mA cm-2 and 60 °C. At the cathode, infiltration of a mixed PBO/LiBOB precursor throughout the porous NCM83 electrode generates a mechanically adaptable and chemically passivating interphase. During cycling, the cathode interfacial resistance increases from 258 to 667 Ω in the pristine cell but only from 161.8 to 376.7 Ω in the modified cell, corresponding to 47.4% lower resistance accumulation. Consequently, the modified cell retains 72.18% of its initial capacity after 100 cycles at 0.2 C and 60 °C, compared with 63.15% for the pristine cell. Post-mortem electron microscopy and Ni K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy further reveal suppressed intergranular cracking and reduced local Ni-environment changes. This work establishes a multiscale design framework that balances polymer-network ion transport and mechanical stability while suppressing chemo-mechanical degradation at high-voltage cathode interfaces, thereby enabling more stable solid-state lithium-metal batteries.

t118.k: Coordination–Transport–Interface; Electrochemical Energy Storage; Operando Characterization
t118.a: Electrochemical energy materials are commonly evaluated using isolated descriptors such as ionic conductivity, capacity, redox potential, and catalytic activity. However, these metrics often fail to predict durability under practical operating conditions because degradation develops through a coupled causal chain involving local coordination chemistry, species transport, and dynamic interfacial evolution. A Coordination-Transport-Interface (CTI) framework is proposed to interpret and design electrochemical energy systems across multiple length scales. Evidence from three electrochemical energy-storage systems, hard-carbon anodes for sodium-ion batteries, aqueous organic redox flow batteries, and manganese dioxide cathodes for zinc-ion batteries, was synthesized within a common Coordination–Transport–Interface framework. The cross-system analysis integrated electrolyte coordination, ion and molecular transport, membrane and electrode processes, device-level performance, and operando or in situ characterization of interfacial evolution. In hard carbon, nanoconfinement acts as an electrolyte-state selector that modifies local ion pairing, desolvation, electrolyte reduction, and interphase survival. In aqueous organic redox flow batteries, molecular properties propagate to electrolyte viscosity, mass-transfer limitations, membrane partitioning, crossover, and cell- and stack-level performance. In manganese dioxide cathodes, in situ grazing-incidence X-ray absorption spectroscopy reveals reversible redox behavior in the bulk but partially irreversible accumulation of Mn2+ and Mn3+ species at the interface. This surface layer obstructs Zn2+ transport, increases overpotential, and contributes to capacity fading. Favorable bulk properties alone do not guarantee a durable electrochemical device. The CTI framework provides transferable design rules, minimal descriptor sets, operando evidence strategies, and reporting practices that connect molecular chemistry with electrode and system performance. Treating durability as a causal chain rather than a single metric offers a more rigorous approach to material comparison, failure diagnosis, and the development of reliable electrochemical energy systems.

t119.k: Carbon Fiber Composite; Organic Electrode; Structural Battery
t119.a: Electrification of transportation has become essential for mitigating climate change and realizing a sustainable future. Although electric vehicles (EVs) are increasingly replacing internal combustion engine vehicles, their market growth has recently stagnated due to limited driving ranges and the need for frequent charging. However, unlike fossil fuels, simply adding more battery packs substantially increases the total weight of a vehicle, which can further restrict driving range, due to the relatively low energy density of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). To address these issues, structural batteries (SBs), which can simultaneously store electrical energy and carry mechanical load, have been introduced. By integrating energy-storage functionality into structural composites, SBs can considerably reduce both the mass and volume of the overall system. Herein, we propose a novel structural battery electrode design: a carbon fiber-reinforced redox-active polymer (CFRRAP) consisting of CFs bound by a redox-active polyimide (PI) instead of an epoxy resin. A series of PI-based CFRRAPs is prepared via a conventional hand lay-up process by varying the loading of conductive carbon additives. After thermal imidization, the thermoplastic PI resin tightly binds CFs, enabling the PI-based CFRRAPs to bear high mechanical loads comparable to those of conventional epoxy-based CFRP composites. Simultaneously, the CFRRAPs can store electrical energy as cathodes via reversible redox reactions of carbonyl groups in the PI matrix, accompanied by the insertion/de-insertion of Li-ions. We investigate their charge/discharge mechanism and mechanical failure mode through various analysis methods. Notably, the CFRRAP outperforms conventional structural cathodes in both electrochemical and mechanical performance, achieving a multifunctional efficiency greater than 1.

t120.k: Lithium Batteries; Fast Charging; Lean Electrolyte
t120.a: Battery design principles established under conventional testing conditions often fail in demanding battery configurations, including fast charging, lean electrolyte, anode-free cells, and high-energy-density lithium metal-based batteries. Understanding how interfacial phenomena evolve under these practical conditions is essential for developing next-generation batteries. Our research combines electrochemical analysis, advanced interfacial characterization, and molecular simulations to reveal how electrolyte chemistry governs interphase formation and lithium deposition under practical operating conditions. Based on these mechanistic insights, we develop electrolyte and interphase engineering strategies tailored for demanding battery environments. Our studies uncovered previously unrecognized interfacial mechanisms limiting battery performance under practical conditions. These insights led to multiple electrolyte engineering strategies that suppress lithium corrosion, regulate interphase evolution, enable dendrite-free lithium plating, and improve reversibility across fast-charging, lean-electrolyte, and anode-free lithium-metal batteries. Our work establishes that design strategies for practical batteries requires condition-specific interphase engineering rather than conventional optimization. These findings provide new design principles for translating lithium-metal batteries from laboratory demonstrations to practical high-energy applications.

t121.k: Na-ion Battery; Computational Screening; Machine Learning
t121.a: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are a cost-competitive alternative to lithium-ion batteries, with sodium precursors ~50× cheaper. But SIB cathodes (e.g., NaFeO₂) need high-voltage operation to reach LIB-comparable energy density, which accelerates interfacial degradation—making a fast-ion-conducting, stable protective coating essential. We screened the Materials Project (~200,000) and GNoME (~2,200,000) databases (consistent PBE+U) through a cascaded filter: thermodynamic stability (E_hull), Na content with hazardous/expensive elements excluded, electrochemical stability window (3–4.5 V), and interfacial compatibility with NaFeO₂. Surviving candidates were evaluated for Na⁺ migration barrier/MSD and elastic moduli using the Orb_v3 machine-learning potential, with rxn-ca for synthesizability. The full workflow ran on a single RTX-5070 GPU in ~3 weeks. Fast Na⁺ conductors were strongly enriched in NASICON-type frameworks (P–O 50.7%, P–Si–O 26.8%). Na₃Fe₂(PO₄)₃ emerged as a leading coating: low barriers (E_a ≈ 0.11 eV), balanced ductility, electrochemical inertness in the coating role, and simple solid-state synthesis. From GNoME, the previously unreported Na₄TiV₂O₉ was identified, with rxn-ca supporting its synthesizability. An MLP-accelerated pipeline reduced millions of structures to a compact set of oxide/phosphate coatings, highlighting NASICON-type Na₃Fe₂(PO₄)₃ and novel Na₄TiV₂O₉ for experimental validation—all on a single consumer GPU. The main limitation is modest reliability of ML elastic-constant prediction.

t122.k: Stretchable Solar Cells; Polymer Solar Cells; High Stretchability
t122.a: Considering the technical standards (e.g., mechanical robustness) required for wearable electronics, which are promising application platforms for organic solar cells, the development of fully stretchable OSCs (f-SOSCs) should be accelerated. First, the mechanical requirements of f-SOSCs, in terms of tensile and cohesion/adhesion properties, are summarized along with the experimental methods to evaluate those properties. Second, important studies to make each layer of f-SOSCs stretchable and efficient are discussed, emphasizing strategies to simultaneously enhance the photovoltaic and mechanical properties of the active layer.
