For example, I present material design strategies to enhance the mechanical robustness and power conversion efficiencies (PCEs); i) incorporating a high-molecular weight polymer acceptor as an electro-active additive into binary blends, ii) design of hydrogen-bonding incorporated polymers, and iii) design of block copolymerized electroactive polymers. With these contributions, the f-SOSCs with over 14% PCE and excellent stretchability are developed. In addition, I will present an example of strain-induced power enhancement using these f-SOSCs. KEYWORDS Stretchable Solar Cells; Polymer Solar Cells; High Stretchability; Power Conversion Efficiency; Maximum Power REFERENCES 1) Seo, S. et al. Adv. Mater. 2023, 35, 2300230 2) Park, J. et al. Adv. Mater. 2022, 34, 2207544 3) Wan. Q et al. JACS 2023, 145, 11914 4) Lee, J. W. et al. Joule 2024, 8, 204 5) Lee, J. W. et al. Joule 2025, 9, 101792 6) Lee, J. W. et al. Energy Environ. Sci. 2025, 18, 3325 7) Lee, J. W. et al. Energy Environ. Sci. 2022, 15, 4672

t123.k: High-Power Ultrasonics; MHz Range; Elliptical Focusing Reflector
t123.a: High-power ultrasound has been widely used in various applications, including ultrasonic cleaning, machining, and sonochemistry. For more than a century, Langevin-type transducers have played a central role in the development of high-power ultrasonics. However, their operation has been primarily limited to a single resonance mode in the tens-of-kilohertz range. This study proposes a new approach to extend high-power ultrasound into the MHz and multimode range. We have developed ELIPS (ELliptical reflector for hIgh-Power ultraSound), which utilizes elastic-wave mode conversion and focusing by an elliptical reflector. MHz longitudinal waves generated by a relatively large piezoelectric transducer are converted into transversal waves and simultaneously focus inside a metallic structure, enabling highly concentrated acoustic energy to be delivered to a small resonator. Using ELIPS, strong MHz vibration was successfully excited in a 1.3 mm-diameter rod, generating MPa-level ultrasound from its tip into water. The focusing and mode-conversion mechanism was further extended to surface acoustic wave excitation without using a piezoelectric single-crystal substrate. ELIPS has also been applied to acoustic-radiation-force-based separation of red blood cells from whole blood. These results demonstrate a new generation of high-power ultrasonic transducers operating in the MHz range and in multiple vibration modes, extending high-power ultrasonics beyond the conventional capabilities of Langevin-type transducers. This work introduces the principle and recent developments of ELIPS, opening new possibilities for next-generation high-power ultrasonics.

t124.k: pyroenergy harvesting, ferroelectric, harvester, power output, Olsen cycle.
t124.a: Two-thirds of global electricity consumption is ultimately wasted as heat across industrial, commercial, residential, and transportation activities. Recovering this waste heat is critical for achieving sustainable electrification. Thermoelectric generators are currently the leading solid-state technology for direct heat-to-electricity conversion, with state-of-the-art modules reaching efficiencies of 8.5% for low-temperature harvesting; however, they rely on spatial temperature gradients of several hundred kelvin, limiting their applicability to many low-grade heat sources. Pyroelectric materials offer a complementary approach, converting temporal temperature variations, rather than static spatial gradients into electrical energy. While conventional pyroelectric conversion, based on temperature-induced polarization changes, typically yields modest energy densities and limited power output, several thermodynamic cycles (Ericsson, Brayton, Stirling, and Olsen) have been explored to enhance harvested energy. Among these, the Olsen cycle demonstrates the highest energy-harvesting capability by exploiting the large polarization variation of ferroelectric materials near their phase transition. In this invited talk, we discuss the energy harvested in benchmark ferroelectric materials and present their implementation in a pyroelectric energy harvester, reporting the resulting power output.

t125.a: While 3D printing offers broad industrial utility by enabling complex geometries, fabricating high-performance piezoelectric devices remains challenging. Ceramic materials deliver superior properties but are difficult to process, whereas polymer composites are highly shapeable but suffer from low piezoelectric output. To resolve this trade-off, we utilize direct ink writing (DIW) to print complex piezoelectric architectures using Sm-PMN-PT powder. Crucially, a post-shaping sintering process is introduced to completely eliminate the polymer binder, preventing the performance degradation typically caused by residual matrix materials. The resulting pure ceramic devices retain remarkable piezoelectric performance, achieving an exceptional figure of merit (FOM), a benchmark value among DIW-fabricated piezoelectric ceramics. We validate this approach by integrating the printed components into conformal ultrasonic transducers for nondestructive testing. These devices adapt seamlessly to curved surfaces, generating symmetric guided waves that drastically improve defect detection and signal clarity. Overall, this study presents a highly viable strategy for manufacturing geometrically versatile, high-performance piezoelectric devices for advanced inspection technologies.

t126.k: 2D materials; nanogenerators; piezotronics; energy harvesting devices
t126.a: The rapid development of solution-processable two-dimensional (2D) nanomaterials has opened new opportunities for scalable fabrication of flexible and multifunctional electronic devices. In particular, 2D materials such as borophene and transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), including MoS2, have attracted considerable attention because of their unique structural, electrical, optical, and piezoelectric properties. In the present study, few-layer crystalline borophene and MoS₂ nanosheets were successfully synthesized through a facile solution-based chemical exfoliation approach under low-temperature conditions, enabling high-yield and solution-processable 2D nanomaterials. A Borophene – MoS2 nanosheet heterostructure based flexible nanogenerator was developed for efficient mechanical-energy harvesting. The heterostructure was fabricated directly on a flexible conducting substrate, providing a lightweight and mechanically flexible platform for self-powered electronics. The developed device exhibited an exceptional output performance, generating an open-circuit voltage of approximately 22 V and an ultra-high current density of 34 µA cm⁻² under low pressure. The enhanced energy-harvesting capability is attributed to the synergistic effects of the high piezoelectric response of the 2D nanosheets and efficient interfacial charge transport across the borophene-MoS2 heterointerface. Furthermore, the device demonstrated a pronounced variation in output voltage under ultraviolet (UV) illumination. This light-responsive behavior highlights the potential of the borophene–MoS₂ heterostructure for integrating mechanical-energy harvesting with optical sensing. We will also discuss the 2D WS2 and MXene based piezoelectric nanogenerators and their applications toward next-generation flexible, self-powered UV nanosensors and wearable electronic systems. Ref: Charu Sharma, Avanish Kumar Srivastava & Manoj Kumar Gupta, 2D borophene–MoS2 nanosheet heterostructure as a flexible piezoelectric nanogenerator for self-powered piezotronic sensing, Communications Materials volume 6, Article number: 120 (2025)

t127.a: Liquids exhibit the triboelectric effect, enabling significant charge transfer and long-term charge storage. However, practical applications have been constrained by two fundamental bottlenecks: (i) the absence of standardized quantification methods, owing to interference from extrinsic factors such as temperature, flow rate, and viscosity; and (ii) inherently weak electrical signals (~10 V), which obscure critical liquid-specific information within noise. To address these challenges, we developed a gas‑regulated liquid column flow method using programmable mechanical shear. With liquid mercury as a probe, we standardized the quantification of contact electrification charge densities for approximately 50 organic and inorganic solutions under controlled conditions, establishing a reliable liquid triboelectric series. Separately, inspired by the dynamic suction‑spray mechanism of an elephant’s trunk, we designed a bio‑inspired gas–liquid two‑phase flow architecture that shears continuous flow into high‑velocity microdroplets. This amplified output voltage from ~10 V to ~900 V (over 100‑fold enhancement). The enhanced signals were combined with a hybrid CNN‑LSTM deep learning framework for liquid analysis. The standardized quantification confirmed a co‑driven mechanism of ions and electrons in liquid contact electrification. The bio‑inspired flow architecture enabled systematic dissection of electron transfer, molecular polarization, ion migration, and screening effects in charging dynamics. Leveraging the amplified signals, the CNN‑LSTM model achieved 97.25% accuracy in self‑powered liquid identification and 99.13% accuracy in high‑resolution concentration prediction, with a detection limit down to 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹, using minimal training data. This work overcomes the long‑standing bottlenecks in liquid triboelectric studies by establishing both a standardized quantification methodology and a signal‑amplification strategy. The integrated approach—from fundamental mechanism elucidation to intelligent application—provides a new paradigm for real‑time, in‑situ liquid analysis, with broad potential for environmental, biomedical, and industrial monitoring.

t128.k: Droplet-based Electricity Generator; Biomimetic Surface; Slippery Surface
t128.a: Droplet-based electricity generators (DEGs) have emerged as promising technology for harvesting energy from droplets. Since DEGs operate based on the contact and separation of droplets from a dielectric surface, developing a hydrophobic or superhydrophobic surface is essential for efficient droplet removal. Consequently, tailoring surface wettability is a key strategy to enhance DEG performance and expand its applicability. To fabricate a superhydrophobic surface, natural lotus leaves were replicated via a ultraviolet replication process and the structure was utilized as a mold to imprint the dielectric layer through thermal nanoimprinting. For the slippery surface, polysilazane was used as a Si layer, and PDMS brushes were deposited using a layer-by-layer method. This coating relied on sulfuric acid as a catalyst and ambient moisture to rapidly bond the polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) brushes to the surface. Using a biomimetic approach was employed to successfully fabricate a DEG with a superhydrophobic surface. As a result, not only was the energy output increased, but the operational droplet volume range was also widened. However, high-potential-energy droplets prone to breaking or bouncing can disrupt stable harvesting. To address this, we introduced a slippery hydrophobic surface. This modification enabled droplets to maintain their volume even after the impact, ensuring stable energy output regardless of drop location. This work demonstrates that the performance and functionality of DEGs can be significantly enhanced through precise control of surface wettability. In this regard, our approach paves the way for the practical implementation of DEGs.

t129.a: (Invited Speech: This abstract is just one parts of whole presentation) Flexible and self-powered pressure sensors based on ion transport in hydrogels have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation wearable electronics; however, they remain limited by inefficient ion migration, narrow sensing ranges, and poor low-frequency energy harvesting capability. Herein, we present a structurally engineered hydrogel-based piezoelectrochemical sensing platform that integrates ion-diode-inspired bipolar architectures, template-assisted three-dimensional microstructures, and directional conductive microchannels to simultaneously enhance ion transport efficiency and electromechanical performance. By incorporating anisotropic PVDF/carbon microchannel skeletons and templated porous/interconnected networks into polyelectrolyte hydrogels, the device achieves guided and accelerated ion migration, resulting in an enhanced rectification behavior and improved stress-induced electrochemical response. The optimized system demonstrates a wide pressure sensing range, high sensitivity, rapid response/recovery, and excellent mechanical durability, along with notable power density for self-powered operation. Furthermore, the ion-diode mechanism enables effective harvesting of ultralow-frequency mechanical energy by modulating the built-in potential and space charge region under external stimuli. The device is further validated in practical applications, including tactile sensing arrays, pressure mapping, and real-time physiological monitoring. This work provides a comprehensive design strategy that synergistically combines structural engineering and ionotronic principles, offering a viable pathway toward high-performance, multifunctional, and low-frequency-responsive self-powered sensing systems for advanced wearable and human–machine interfacing technologies.

t130.k: Triboelectric nanogenerator, Geopolymer, Pathway block, Cabon nanotubes, Bismuth Oxyiodide
t130.a: The rapidly increasing global demand for sustainable energy technologies has intensified the search for distributed energy harvesting (EH) systems capable of converting ubiquitous mechanical stimuli into usable electrical power, and triboelectric nanogenerators (TENG) have emerged as a promising platform. Here, we propose a geopolymer-based triboelectric pathway block designed for direct conversion of footstep-induced mechanical energy to electricity, enabling sustainable EH system from pedestrian traffic. The device is constructed from metakaolin geopolymer (MG) and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), while a synergistic filler-engineering strategy is introduced through the incorporation of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and bismuth oxyiodide (BiOI). CNTs establish conductive percolation networks that facilitate charge transport, whereas BiOI functions as a highly polarized piezo-photocatalytic component that promotes interfacial polarization, charge trapping, and electric-field-driven charge separation. Comprehensive structural, electrical, and dielectric characterizations reveal a strong correlation between filler composition, interfacial charge dynamics, and triboelectric performance. The optimal CNT loading of 2 wt% (MG/CNT2.0) produced an open-circuit voltage (VOC) of 80.8 V, a short-circuit current (ISC) of 6.8 A, and a maximum output power (Pmax) of ~663 W (powder density ~73.6 W/cm2). Further incorporation of 0.05 wt% BiOI resulted in the highest triboelectric output, yielding a VOC of ~112.6 V, ISC of ~19.3 A (current density (J) ~2.14 A/cm2), and Pmax of 1,155 W (powder density ~128.3 W/cm2). The developed geopolymer-based triboelectric pathway block demonstrates a scalable and environmentally sustainable strategy for integrating energy-harvesting functionality into civil infrastructure, offering a viable route toward self-powered smart cities and next-generation distributed energy systems.

t131.a: Efficient conversion of mechanical energy into direct current (DC) remains challenging for conventional triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), where triboelectric charge retention and electrical conductivity are often in competition. Ionic tribomaterials provide an alternative pathway because mobile-ion displacement, redistribution, and polarization can dynamically regulate the magnitude and direction of generated charges. We modified conventional dielectric polymers, including poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC), into DC-generating tribomaterials by incorporating ionic plasticizer components. The resulting ionic DC TENG (iDC-TENG) was evaluated under contact–separation, sliding, and rotary modes. The effects of electrode work function, operating frequency, load resistance, ionic properties, and mechanical configuration were investigated. The iDC-TENG converted mechanical motion into continuous DC output through a mechanism governed by contact electrification and electrode polarization. Stable charge directionality was maintained across multiple mechanical configurations. Electrode polarization and ion mobility played central roles in determining the polarity and magnitude of charge transport. Modulation of ionic composition, exploration of alternative ionic/polymeric materials, and optimization of device architectures further improved output performance, long-term stability, and adaptability under different mechanical conditions. This work establishes ionic polymer tribomaterials as a promising platform for direct mechanical-to-DC energy conversion.Their practical capability was demonstrated by directly powering electronic devices and charging capacitors without external rectification, highlighting the potential of ionic tribomaterials for mechanical energy harvesting and direct DC power delivery. By bridging the advantages of polymer-based TENGs and tribovoltaic systems, iDC-TENGs provide a versatile and scalable strategy for sustainable energy harvesting and a foundation for next-generation DC-output triboelectric devices.

t132.k: Nanogenerator; Water Energy; Electrical Double Layer
t132.a: Converting rain, spray, and small waves into electricity is attractive for sustainable micro-power because water dynamics are ubiquitous. Real-world deployment is hindered by low repeatability, orientation sensitivity, and unstable output under stochastic droplet arrivals. Motivated by battery-free distributed sensors, this project develops scalable devices that transform discontinuous water inputs into stable electrical output. Using interface and impedance matching, we address the mismatch between micro-energy sources and electronics and enable deployment across diverse scenarios. We develop a switchable triboelectric nanogenerator (s-TENG) that performs polarity-agnostic rectification, achieving rectification effectiveness ≈133 without external circuits, simplifying wearable power modules. Last but not the least, we extend the switching scheme to waves with a floatable droplet electricity generator (FDEG) using asymmetric electrodes and instantaneous switching: a single unit delivers ~107.6 μA (1.2 kW m⁻³; 31.2 mC m⁻³), and parallel arrays reach 1.2 mA at 0.28 Hz with omnidirectional stability. Together, these devices establish design rules and scalable module-to-array strategies for reliable, on-site micro-energy.

t133.k: Invisible Information Carriers; Triboelectric Decoding; Electrical Surface Patterning
t133.a: Pattern-based identification systems are widely used for information storage and object recognition, yet conventional optical codes remain visually exposed and rely on optical scanners or externally powered readers. This study presents a transparent and reconfigurable triboelectric barcode (Tri-barcode) for optically invisible and self-powered identification. A customized mask is first placed on a fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) film to define the regions to be patterned. Electrical surface patterning (ESP) based on corona discharge then selectively injects charges into the exposed regions, forming charge-concentrated bars (C-bars) without altering the surface morphology or optical appearance. For decoding, the patterned film interacts with a free-standing sliding triboelectric reader. Relative motion converts each C-bar width into a characteristic time interval between positive and negative voltage peaks. The Tri-barcode exhibits a visible-light transmittance of 95.05% and retains a surface-potential contrast of 1.45 kV after seven days. The electrical patterns can be erased and rewritten on the same substrate. Spatial-to-temporal signal conversion enables discrimination among 250 barcode configurations without an external power supply. A convolutional neural network-assisted personal identification system achieves 99.7% accuracy. In addition, real-time robotic object classification and manufacturing process detection demonstrate the applicability of the Tri-barcode to smart factory systems. This study demonstrates a reconfigurable and optically invisible triboelectric barcode enabled by surface-charge patterning. By storing information in erasable electrical patterns and decoding it through self-generated triboelectric signals, the proposed platform improves resistance to straightforward image-based duplication and enables self-powered intelligent identification.

t134.a: Self-powered energy harvesters based on natural biomaterials are gaining interest for bio-integrated electronics. Conventional piezoelectric materials such as PZT and BaTiO3 perform well but are toxic and brittle. Glycine, the simplest amino acid, exhibits β-phase piezoelectricity comparable to that of conventional materials, yet β-glycine is thermodynamically metastable, hindering large-area, phase-selective synthesis. We report a meniscus-driven self-assembly strategy that kinetically stabilizes β-glycine over large areas. In a dip-coating configuration, a hydrophilic substrate is withdrawn from aqueous glycine solution, and the balance between solvent evaporation and crystal-growth kinetics is tuned via pulling speed and concentration. Phases were identified by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and Raman spectroscopy; piezoelectric properties were assessed by piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM). A flexible glycine piezoelectric nanogenerator (PENG) was fabricated to evaluate practical performance under bending. Rapid evaporation with reduced concentration suppressed the β→α transformation within a defined kinetic window, producing uniform, highly oriented β-glycine domains; XRD and Raman confirmed phase purity at high pulling speeds and low concentrations. PFM and second-harmonic generation revealed a non-centrosymmetric structure with pronounced in-plane anisotropy. The aligned crystals showed an effective lateral piezoelectric coefficient of 11.7 pm/V, locally reaching 65.9 pm/V, exceeding most reported biomolecular piezoelectrics. A vertical-electrode β-Gly-PENG delivered 0.2 V open-circuit voltage, 23 nA short-circuit current, and 0.065 nW maximum power at 50 MΩ, with stable output over 10,000 cycles and above 80% relative humidity. COMSOL simulations reproduced the bending-induced potential. This kinetic-stabilization route for metastable biomolecular crystals offers a scalable platform for self-powered, bio-integrated applications and broadens the design space for bio-piezoelectrics.

t135.a: Solar cells operating in industrial environments suffer from persistent contamination by oily volatile organic compound (VOC) residues that conventional superhydrophobic coatings cannot effectively repel, resulting in sticky dust accumulation and progressive efficiency loss. Here, we present a springtail-inspired hyperbolic domed star grid (HDSG) surface that simultaneously provides multiaxial oil repellency and enhanced photovoltaic performance in a single scalable coating. The HDSG integrates three synergistic structural features: (i) hyperbolic sidewalls generated by capillary wrapping of polyurethane acrylate (PUA), creating a Laplace pressure barrier that suppresses oil infiltration; (ii) a disconnected star-grid architecture that inhibits lateral liquid imbibition even in the presence of structural defects; and (iii) dome-shaped pillar tops acting as broadband microlenses while minimizing oil residue after droplet detachment. Under sticky dust contamination, oil-assisted self-cleaning achieved 100% removal efficiency at a tilt angle of only 20°. When integrated onto thin crystalline silicon (c-Si) solar cells, the HDSG coating increased the peak power conversion efficiency from 16.2% to 18.1% while producing broadband external quantum efficiency enhancement across 400–1100 nm through a microlens-mediated light-trapping effect. These results demonstrate a scalable bioinspired surface that integrates durable oil self-cleaning, defect-tolerant liquid repellency, and broadband optical enhancement for next-generation photovoltaic systems operating under realistic environmental conditions.

t136.k: Liquid Metals; Supercapacitors; Perovskite Solar Cells
t136.a: Gallium-based liquid metal alloys (GaLMs) retain their liquid state at room temperature while exhibiting high electrical and thermal conductivity, low toxicity, and remarkable deformability. These attributes make them promising materials for flexible and stretchable electronic applications. However, precise control over their interfacial interactions with substrates remains a major challenge. In particular, the combination of a high-surface-tension liquid phase and an adhesive oxide skin gives rise to complex surface behavior, making it difficult to form uniform and mechanically stable thin films. In this work, we present a robust strategy for fabricating smooth GaLM films and patterns using microstructured metallic features. These structures promote the spontaneous spreading of oxide-free GaLMs through capillary-driven imbibition. We also investigate the wetting behavior of GaLMs on textile substrates and demonstrate their application as current collectors in stretchable supercapacitors. The interplay among textile architecture, wetting dynamics, and electrical resistance is systematically examined. In addition, we demonstrate the use of GaLMs as cathodes in perovskite solar cells, where the surface oxide, beyond its role in electrical conduction, contributes positively to device performance. Notably, the liquid metal electrodes can be readily recovered through mild acid treatment, offering a practical pathway toward efficient recycling of perovskite solar cells. Overall, this work establishes GaLMs as versatile, deformable, and recyclable electrodes by elucidating and harnessing their interfacial behavior in energy-storage and photovoltaic applications.

t137.k: Atomic Layer Deposition; Solid Oxide Cell
t137.a: Reversible solid oxide cells (RSOCs) are promising platforms for bidirectional energy conversion, operating as fuel cells for power generation and as electrolysis cells for hydrogen and synthetic fuel production. Their high operating temperatures (≥700 °C) enable rapid electrode kinetics, high ionic conductivity, and efficient power-to-gas conversion for large-scale, long-duration renewable-energy storage. However, practical deployment is hindered by sluggish oxygen reduction and evolution reactions and insufficient oxygen-electrode durability. We address the conventional activity–stability trade-off through interface engineering at the electrode–gas and electrode–electrolyte interfaces using scalable semiconductor manufacturing techniques, particularly atomic layer deposition (ALD). This talk highlights an ALD-enabled stabilization strategy based on an ultrathin Hf-derived surface modification of an LSCF oxygen electrode. Å-level thickness control and conformal coating of porous electrodes suppress Sr segregation and particle coarsening. During operation at ≥700 °C, the Hf-containing layer undergoes near-surface cation redistribution to form an in situ Hf–Fe–Co surface, enhancing both catalytic activity and structural stability. The resulting RSOCs deliver peak performances of 1.5 W cm⁻² in fuel-cell mode and 1.1 A cm⁻² in electrolysis mode at 750 °C, and demonstrate stable operation for 100 h in a three-cell (10 × 10 cm²) stack at 700 °C. Combined physicochemical characterization and density functional theory calculations reveal the mechanisms underlying the improved performance. These results demonstrate that ALD-based surface engineering provides a scalable, industrially viable route to high-performance and durable RSOCs.

t138.k: Hierarchical Nanostructures; Scalable Manufacturing; Electrochemical Energy Storage
t138.a: The demand for high-performance electrochemical energy storage necessitates advanced electrode materials. Conventional manufacturing often involves toxic solvents, high temperatures, and complex, energy-intensive processes. Thus, low-cost, scalable, and high-efficiency manufacturing technologies for nanostructured materials are critical to overcome sluggish ion transport and structural instability. We present facile manufacturing strategies for hierarchical nanostructures, including the carbonization of eco-friendly polyvinyl alcohol via iodine treatment, the one-step electroreduction of silver halides, and the bromine-mediated electrodeposition of copper frameworks. We also introduce a scalable microneedle-assisted perforation for dry-processed thick electrodes and a low-temperature (150–180°C) organo-silver ink treatment for 3D scaffolds. These manufacturing approaches produced highly tunable nanostructures with specific surface areas up to 650 m²/g and precise feature sizes, such as 0.55 nm sub-nanometer pores and ultrathin (<90 nm) metallic ligaments. These optimized morphological properties yielded remarkable electrochemical enhancements. Transition metal oxide-decorated 3D frameworks exhibited ultrahigh specific capacities (e.g., 630 mAh/g at an extreme 10 C rate) and exceptional long-term stability. Furthermore, structurally engineered thick electrodes achieved high areal capacities of 11 mAh/cm², while conformal Ag nanoseeds (20–50 nm) lowered Li nucleation overpotentials from 22 mV to 7 mV, ensuring dendrite-free cycling. These scalable fabrication methods provide highly controllable and robust nanostructured frameworks. Such advanced structural engineering techniques offer an effective, cost-efficient pathway for developing next-generation electrochemical systems.

t139.k: Direct Catalyst Coating; PEMFC; Crack Formation
t139.a: Direct catalyst coating on ion-exchange membranes has attracted increasing attention as a simplified membrane electrode assembly (MEA) fabrication process by eliminating the decal-transfer step. Although the conventional decal-transfer method is widely adopted in commercial production, it inevitably involves additional backing films and transfer processes, which may introduce incomplete catalyst transfer, adhesion variability, and increased manufacturing complexity. Direct coating offers a promising alternative; however, the high water uptake and dimensional swelling of ion-exchange membranes during coating frequently result in membrane deformation, poor coating uniformity, and degraded electrode quality. In this study, a swelling-controlled direct ink coating process was developed through systematic optimization of ink rheology, solvent composition, coating parameters, and drying conditions. The influence of deionized (DI) water content, rheological behavior, and solvent balance on membrane swelling, catalyst-layer morphology, and coating stability was comprehensively investigated. Furthermore, drying protocols were optimized to minimize membrane deformation while maintaining homogeneous catalyst distribution and strong electrode adhesion. The optimized process enabled uniform catalyst-layer formation directly on the membrane without the need for a decal-transfer process, significantly suppressing membrane swelling during fabrication. The resulting MEAs exhibited improved coating quality and excellent structural integrity, demonstrating that simultaneous control of ink formulation and process conditions is essential for reliable direct coating. This work provides a practical manufacturing strategy for scalable MEA fabrication and offers a viable alternative to conventional decal-transfer technology for next-generation electrochemical energy devices.

t140.a: Energy conversion devices require efficient and low-cost electrocatalysts to reduce reaction overpotentials and improve reaction kinetics. Localized structures can enhance catalytic activity by regulating key reaction steps. Electrocatalysts including biaxial-strained 2D materials, single-atom arrays, and high-entropy nanosheets were synthesized and applied to alkaline hydrogen evolution and CO₂ reduction. Data-driven approaches were also used for catalyst discovery. The engineered nanoscale structures enhanced intrinsic catalytic activity by promoting water dissociation and intermediate adsorption/desorption. These effects also improved overall device performance. Nanoscale structural engineering is an effective strategy for developing high-performance electrocatalysts. Data-driven discovery can further accelerate the development of efficient and low-cost catalyst materials.

t141.a: Meeting the growing global demand for clean and sustainable energy requires the continued development of advanced functional materials for energy conversion, storage, and catalysis. The performance of these materials is governed by their atomic arrangements, electronic configurations, and interfacial dynamics under operating conditions. Establishing clear relationships between these fundamental properties and catalytic behavior is therefore essential for the rational design of high-performance energy materials. Synchrotron-based X-ray absorption and emission spectroscopies were employed as element-specific probes of the local atomic and electronic structures of chemically complex alloy nanostructures, with particular emphasis on high-entropy alloys. In situ and operando measurements were integrated with complementary structural characterization and computational modeling to monitor catalyst evolution and elucidate interactions among constituent elements under realistic reaction conditions. The combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that subtle changes in local coordination environments, charge distribution, and interelement interactions can strongly influence catalytic activity and stability. In high-entropy alloy catalysts, the diverse local atomic configurations generate distinct electronic environments and active sites that cannot be readily predicted from the properties of individual constituent metals. Operando synchrotron measurements further enable the identification of reaction-induced structural transformations, active catalytic phases, and dynamic charge-transfer processes. Energy-tunable and element-specific synchrotron X-ray techniques provide powerful tools for establishing atomic-level structure–property relationships in multimetallic catalytic systems. Their integration with complementary experimental and computational approaches offers critical mechanistic insights into catalyst function and provides a foundation for the rational design of advanced materials for sustainable energy conversion.

t142.k: Photoelectrochemical (PEC) Water Splitting; Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD); Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER)
t142.a: Photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting offers a sustainable route to green hydrogen production by directly converting solar energy into chemical fuel. However, incomplete light absorption, rapid charge carrier recombination, and inadequate material stability continue to limit practical PEC performance. A black silicon (b-Si) based ZnO/MoS2 heterostructured photocathode was developed to integrate enhanced light harvesting, charge separation, and catalytic activity. Vertically aligned b-Si nanowires were fabricated by metal assisted chemical etching (MACE) to improve broadband light absorption, An n-type ZnO layer was deposited by spin coating to facilitate type-II charge separation, while MoS2 was deposited by chemical bath deposition to provide catalytically active edge sites for hydrogen evolution. Titanium based oxide/nitride interlayers were introduced using atomic layer deposition as active and passive interfacial layers to improve charge transport and corrosion resistance. The b-Si substrate exhibited broadband visible-NIR light absorption exceeding 80%. The multilayer b-Si/ZnO/MoS2 photocathode showed enhanced photocurrent density and improved operational stability in acidic electrolyte. The titanium-based interlayers further supported interfacial charge transfer and improved protection against corrosion. Combining b-Si light harvesting nanostructures with ZnO/MoS2 heterojunctions and atomic layer deposited titanium-based interlayers is a promising strategy for developing efficient and durable photocathodes for PEC hydrogen production.

t143.k: Alkali Thermal Treatment; Hydrogen Production; Food Waste
t143.a: The surge in general waste, and food waste in particular, poses significant environmental challenges. According to the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), approximately 931 million tons of food waste were produced in 2019, contributing 8–10 % of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Therefore, developing diverse food waste treatment methods that are both environmentally friendly and economically efficient has become a critical imperative. Driven by the rich organic composition of the food waste, this study aims to upcycle it as a sustainable biomass resource for hydrogen (H2) production via alkaline thermal treatment (ATT). Unlike conventional gasification methods, ATT operates at relatively low temperatures and selectively produces H2 while capturing carbon dioxide (CO2) as solid carbonates. Herein, sodium hydroxide (NaOH) was utilized as an alkaline catalyst to facilitate the highly selective conversion of the food waste into H2. Our process enables the simultaneous conversion of abundant waste into high-purity H2 energy and mitigation of GHG emissions via in-situ CO2 immobilization. At an optimized food waste : NaOH ratio of 1:3 (w/w), a maximum H2 yield of 44.02mmol/(dry-ash-free)-g-food waste was achieved. Furthermore, the effects of nitrogen (N) derived from protein structures and various metals inherent in the food waste sludge were systematically investigated to assess the feasibility of upscaling the reaction using a rotary kiln reactor. These findings demonstrate that alkali-catalyzed ATT serves as a promising dual-functional strategy, converting abundant food waste into clean hydrogen while simultaneously capturing CO2, thereby offering a scalable and carbon-neutral waste-to-energy solution.

t144.a: Methane dehydroaromatization (MDA) is a promising catalytic process that directly converts methane into high-value aromatic hydrocarbons. MFI-type zeolites are widely used as MDA catalysts because their microporous structure suppresses the formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), while their Brønsted acid sites promote olefin oligomerization and cyclization. However, the practical application of MDA is limited by low methane conversion (~10%) and rapid catalyst deactivation caused by coke deposition. Recent studies have suggested that, in addition to external Mo species and Brønsted acid sites, silanol groups generated from framework defects may also contribute to coke formation. Adjacent silanol groups form silanol nests, which strongly adsorb PAHs and facilitate their accumulation, leading to coke deposition. Nevertheless, the relationship between the amount and distribution of silanol species and catalytic performance remains unclear. In this study, silanol defects were controlled using several desilanol strategies, including W-containing MFI one-pot synthesis and post-treatments with ethylenediamine (EDA), ammonium hexafluorosilicate ((NH₄)₂SiF₆), and ammonium fluoride (NH₄F). The physicochemical properties and catalytic performance of the prepared catalysts were systematically evaluated. Among the investigated approaches, the W one-pot synthesis significantly reduced the silanol concentration and increased benzene yield and catalyst lifetime compared with the conventional catalyst. In addition, coke deposition decreased. These results suggest that controlling silanol defects is an effective strategy for suppressing coke formation and improving MDA catalyst performance. Further studies will investigate the relationship between specific silanol species and coke formation to establish design principles for highly stable MDA catalysts.

t145.k: Tantalum Oxynitride; Phase Purity Control; Photoelectrochemical Solar Water Splitting
t145.a: Tantalum oxynitride (TaON) is a promising visible-light-responsive photocatalyst for solar water splitting. However, its practical application is limited by challenges in selectively synthesizing phase-pure, thermodynamically stable β-TaON under processing-sensitive conditions, where competing phase evolution and intrinsic factors, such as crystallinity, stoichiometry, charge-carrier mobility, and recombination dynamics, influence performance. Here, the control of phase purity and the modulation of optoelectronic properties are introduced as complementary strategies to enhance the photoelectrochemical performance of β-TaON. β-TaON was synthesized by ammonolysis of Ta2O5 under controlled oxygen partial pressure, while vanadium doping was introduced to modulate the electronic structure. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and experimental characterization were used to correlate nitrogen incorporation, band-structure modulation, light absorption, and charge-transport properties. An oxygen flow rate of 0.25 L/h enabled the formation of phase-pure β-TaON within a narrow synthesis window. Controlled phase evolution also allowed β-TaON/Ta3N5 heterostructure formation, improving light absorption, charge separation, and interfacial charge transfer, leading to higher photocurrent density and favorable band alignment for water oxidation. Vanadium doping retained phase-pure β-TaON up to 10 at.% V, while higher V contents induced a redshift of the absorption edge and reduced the bandgap from 2.72 to 2.38 eV. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed substitutional incorporation of V5+ at Ta5+ sites, and theoretical results indicated reduced electron effective mass, enhanced n-type conductivity, and favorable band-edge shifts at moderate doping levels. These findings highlight complementary pathways for regulating phase composition and electronic structure in β-TaON, offering new insights for the design of efficient oxynitride-based materials for solar fuel production.

t146.k: CO2 Capture; Blended Amines; Absorbent Screening
t146.a: Aqueous amine absorption is one of the most mature technologies for post-combustion CO2 capture; however, conventional amine solvents still face trade-offs among absorption kinetics, cyclic capacity, regeneration energy, and long-term stability. Blending amines with complementary characteristics provides a promising strategy to overcome these limitations, although identifying optimal formulations from a vast compositional space remains experimentally intensive. This study presents a systematic, data-driven framework for developing blended amine absorbents, integrating high-throughput experimental screening, AI-assisted formulation optimization, durability assessment, physicochemical characterization, and bench-scale validation. More than 100 individual amines were pre-screened based on literature and patent surveys and key physicochemical properties, including vapor pressure, boiling point, viscosity, and toxicity. Selected amines were prepared as 30 wt% aqueous solutions and evaluated under an identical protocol using multiple fast-screening reactors operated in parallel. Simulated flue gas was continuously introduced into batch solvents, while the outlet CO2 concentration was monitored by NDIR analysis to determine time-resolved CO2 loading. Absorption and desorption rates, rich and lean loadings, cyclic capacity, completion times, heat of reaction, and relative desorption energy referenced to 30 wt% MEA were evaluated. Vapor-liquid equilibrium measurements were additionally conducted to determine working CO2 capacity and estimate regeneration energy. Promising candidates were further assessed for oxidative degradation and corrosion, including the effectiveness of degradation and corrosion inhibitors. Experimental data for blended formulations containing three or more amines were subsequently integrated with an AI model for iterative formulation optimization. Selected formulations were validated in a 2 Nm3/h bench-scale unit (BSU) by evaluating CO2 removal efficiency and regeneration energy at different liquid-to-gas ratios. Thermophysical and transport properties required for process design and simulation were also experimentally characterized. Screening of individual amines provided a consistent experimental database for designing blended formulations. More than 100 blends, initially formulated using three components serving as primary absorbent, secondary absorbent, and promoter, were evaluated using the same performance metrics. The accumulated data were used to train an AI model, which proposed new compositions for subsequent experiments. The newly acquired experimental data were periodically fed back into the model, enabling iterative refinement of formulation selection and extension of the search space to blends containing four or more amines. This approach identified multiple formulations that simultaneously achieved CO2 absorption rates comparable to 30 wt% MEA and substantially lower energy requirements for solvent regeneration. The most promising formulations showed estimated regeneration energies of approximately 50-55% of the 30 wt% MEA benchmark. The integration of parallel high-throughput screening with iterative AI-guided formulation design enabled efficient exploration of a large compositional space that would otherwise require extensive trial-and-error experimentation. By prioritizing promising formulations for subsequent experiments, the proposed approach can substantially reduce development time, manpower requirements, and material consumption while maintaining experimental validation as the basis for solvent selection. Combined with durability assessment, physicochemical characterization, and bench-scale validation, this framework provides a practical route from molecular-level solvent screening to process-relevant evaluation. The resulting blended amines demonstrate the potential to retain MEA-level absorption kinetics while substantially reducing the energy penalty associated with CO2 capture.

t147.a: Photocatalytic water splitting is a sustainable method to produce green hydrogen, but charge recombination limits the performance for these materials. Methods such as doping, facet engineering, and tandem systems have been utilized to reduce charge recombination, all of which relies on inducing an electric field within the photocatalyst to increase electron-hole separation. Here we propose an alternative approach to reduce charge recombination by inducing ferroelectric polarization into the photocatalyst. Our results demonstrated improved performance for water splitting in both particulate and photoelectrochemical systems. Additionally, the performance can be controlled and modulated by the direction of the electric field where water oxidation can be either suppressed or enhanced. The internal electric field is also visually demonstrated via controlled surface silver deposition where silver particles are reduced only on one facet of the photocatalyst when the internal electric field is present, but removal of the electric field yields sporadic aggregation of silver particles.

t148.a: The global environment is challenged by excessive consumption of fossil fuels and resources, which perturbs the nature’s sustainable cycles of various chemical elements such as C, N, O, and H. As solar energy is the major driving force of the global cycles of these key elements, photo(electro)catalysis is an ideal engineering method to mimic and restore the nature’s element cycles. The photochemical conversion of H2O, CO2, N2, and O2 has been intensively investigated employing various methods among which photo(electro)catalysis using semiconductor materials has been established as the most popular method. This talk will introduce several examples of photocatalytic, photoelectrochemical (PEC), and electrocatalytic conversions of C, N, and O compounds and discuss their environmental implications. The photocatalytic and photoelectrocatalytic processes have been applied to denitrification, de-NOx, and nitrogen fixation reactions but the successful performance is limited. The direct conversion of nitrogenous pollutants to dinitrogen and dinitrogen to ammonia without using chemical reductants is an ideal solution but difficult to be realized. Here we introduce various engineered photo(electro)catalytic systems that selectively interconvert among C and N compounds. As for O conversion, some examples of photocatalytic and photoelectrochemical systems for sustainable production of H2O2 through O2 reduction will be introduced. A PEC system enabled continuous H2O2 production over 100 h even under a bias-free condition. Finally, some recent advances in carbon capture and conversion through photo- and electrocatalytic technologies are presented and discussed.

t149.a: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is an important chemical used in the agricultural, medical, and chemical industries. However, the conventional anthraquinone process is energy consuming with a high carbon footprint. Electrocatalytic H2O2 production through the two-electron oxygen reduction reaction has emerged as an alternative for green H2O2 generation. In this study, a salt-free electrocatalytic H2O2 production system based on a three-compartment flow cell was developed. H2SO4/Na2SO4 was used as the supporting electrolyte in the cathodic and anodic chambers, while ultrapure water was circulated through the middle chamber to enable the accumulation of salt-free H2O2. The produced H2O2 was applied during the irrigation of bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis). The effect of the middle-chamber water volume was investigated using 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 L of ultrapure water and the H2O2 concentrations reached 6527, 3970, 3138, and 2133 mg L-1, respectively, at 6h, demonstrating that a smaller middle chamber volume enhanced H2O2 accumulation. The produced H2O2 was applied during the irrigation of bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis). Early-stage H2O2 application improved biomass and shoot growth. Under seawater irrigation, H2O2 application improved bok choy's salinity tolerance, enhancing plant survival, shoot growth, and biomass. Microbial community profiling revealed that H2O2 irrigation enriched bacterial taxa adapted to oxidative stress. Furthermore, the seawater irrigation selectively favored salt-tolerant bacterial populations. This study presents an alternative approach to producing high-purity H2O2 for agricultural applications.

t150.a: The local reaction environment plays a critical role in determining the selectivity, efficiency, and durability of electrochemical and photoelectrochemical processes. Yet these environments are dynamic and difficult to control: local ion concentrations, pH, reactant availability, interfacial interactions, and transport can evolve substantially under operating conditions. Here, we will discuss how engineering and probing these microenvironments can provide a common framework for understanding and improving reactions ranging from CO2 conversion to nitrate reduction. Microenvironment control can promote challenging carbon–carbon coupling reactions. In photoelectrochemical CO2 reduction, defect-engineered Cu catalysts coupled with a covalent organic framework (COF) on a metal-halide perovskite photocathode create an environment that enhances CO2 accumulation and modifies local cation interactions. This coordinated control of light absorption, catalysis, and the reaction environment enables C2+ formation at low applied bias, including ethylene production close to its thermodynamic potential. Beyond selectivity, however, the evolution of the microenvironment can become a major determinant of durability. In CO2 electrolyzers, changes in local pH and ionic composition can drive carbonate salt precipitation within gas-diffusion electrodes, progressively altering transport pathways and causing performance losses. We combine electrochemical studies with neutron-based characterization to probe water and salt distributions within operating electrodes and connect these spatially evolving environments with device performance and degradation. For electrochemical nitrate reduction (NO3RR), ionomer-based modifiers on Cu catalysts are used to alter the catalyst-electrolyte interface. Cation-exchange ionomers reshape the local ionic environment and regulate the ionic composition, resulting in enhanced selectivity toward NH3. The reduced sensitivity of Faradaic efficiency and current density to electrolyte flow further suggests that these confined interfacial environments can stabilize conditions favorable to multistep reaction pathways. By combining control of interfacial chemistry with operando probes of evolving reaction environments, we aim to establish relationships between local chemical and transport phenomena, reaction selectivity, and long-term device stability across electrochemical and photoelectrochemical systems.

t151.a: The design of chiral surfaces is one of the most crucial topics in modern chemistry, particularly in catalysis as they can be used to selectively produce chiral compounds, which can exhibit a positive effect on the biological activity for one enantiomer, whereas the other one even shows toxicity. Previously, we have successfully designed chiral encoded PtIr alloys which showed excellent performance as both electrocatalysts and heterogeneous catalysts for asymmetric synthesis of chiral model compounds via either electroreduction or hydrogenation of prochiral molecules. To extend the applications of chiral encoded PtIr electrocatalysts, we report in this contribution a novel strategy for the enantioselective electrochemical synthesis of chiral compounds from carbon dioxide (CO2). Chiral mesoporous PtIr alloys, imprinted with chiral enantiomers, were prepared by electrodeposition from Pt and Ir salts in the simultaneous presence of non-ionic surfactants and chiral templates, which were used as mesoporogens and enantiomers, respectively. After electrodeposition, both surfactants and chiral templates were removed completely. The cleaned electrodes were used as electrocatalysts for asymmetric synthesis. The chiral imprinted PtIr alloys deposited on nickel foam were then applied as electrocatalysts for the electrocarboxylation of aldehyde with CO2. When using pulse electrosynthesis, an acceptable enantiomeric excess (ee) (> 50 %) was obtained for synthesizing the respective enantiomers. This first example illustrates a novel concept for the asymmetric synthesis of chiral compounds using chiral encoded metals as electrocatalysts for electrocarboxylation.

t152.a: Photochemical reduction of CO₂ into fuels and chemicals offers a sustainable route to mitigate carbon emissions while valorizing CO₂ as a carbon resource. However, its practical implementation is limited by the lack of well-designed material interfaces that couple efficient light absorbers with active CO₂ reduction catalysts while enabling effective charge separation and rapid electron transfer. Further integration with CO₂ capture remains challenging because captured CO₂ species generally exhibit low reactivity. Here, we report a ternary hybrid photocatalyst with tailored interfaces that enhances solar-energy utilization for photochemical CO₂ reduction. The photocatalyst consists of cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc) molecules assembled on multiwalled carbon nanotubes (CNTs) decorated with nearly monodisperse cadmium sulfide quantum dots (CdS QDs). Upon visible-light irradiation, the CdS QDs generate electron–hole pairs, while the CNTs rapidly extract and transport photogenerated electrons from CdS to CoPc at a rate approximately 37 times faster than charge recombination within CdS. The transferred electrons are subsequently utilized by CoPc to selectively reduce CO₂ to CO at a high rate. Time-resolved and in situ vibrational spectroscopies reveal the interfacial charge-transfer dynamics and catalytic reaction pathways. Beyond serving as efficient electron-transport highways, the strong broadband light absorption of CNTs generates localized photothermal heating, which activates amine-captured CO₂ in the form of carbamates and enables its direct photochemical conversion without additional external energy input. This multifunctional architecture integrates light harvesting, charge transport, molecular catalysis, and photothermal activation of captured CO₂, providing a strategy for coupling CO₂ capture with solar-driven CO₂ conversion.

t153.a: Colloidal semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) have made great strides in commercial applications, initially in display and lighting, and more recently in food and energy end markets. These materials exhibit tunable photoluminescence in the visible and near-IR, with near unity quantum yield, making them ideal for spectrum/color optimization. Moreover, for applications in sunlight, their scalable synthesis (enabling low cost) and good stability, both in terms of field us and manufacturing, enable QDs to be deployed at scale in cost-sensitive applications like solar energy and agriculture. UbiQD, a materials technology and QD manufacturing company spun out of Los Alamos National Laboratory, has pioneered the industrialization and scale-up of these materials, starting with critical end uses related to spectrum optimization for greenhouses and solar modules. In this presentation, UbiQD’s CEO will share an overview of how quantum dots are being used to enhance spectral quality of sunlight for improved photovoltaics (energy) and photosynthesis (food), and how this is driving a new 10x scale of “mass production”. New manufacturing techniques and supply chain incentivization are critical for this new regime for QDs. For greenhouse agriculture, crop yield enhancements of up to 20-40% have been reported (including recently in a published USDA-funded study) by shifting the peak of incident sunlight closer to the peak of chlorophyll, around 600 nm. In certain types of solar modules , with specific configurations, spectral response can more than double. These applications will be highlighted, as well as advancements in commercialization.

t154.k: Semiconductor Nanocrystals; In-situ Transmission Electron Microscopy; Degradation
t154.a: Structural degradation is a major factor limiting the structural stability and practical application of semiconductor nanocrystals. However, because degradation proceeds through nanoscale, transient, and spatially heterogeneous pathways, its microscopic mechanism is difficult to resolve using ensemble-averaged measurements alone. Direct observation under liquid environments is therefore essential for identifying intermediate states, local reaction pathways, and crystallographic anisotropy during degradation. In this talk, I will present our recent studies on degradation mechanisms of semiconductor nanocrystals using in situ liquid-phase transmission electron microscopy. By imaging individual nanocrystals in real time under controlled liquid environments, liquid-phase electron microscopy enables direct visualization of structural transformations. In CdS nanocrystals, liquid-phase TEM reveals that crystalline nanocrystals undergo structural decomposition through transient amorphous intermediates, indicating that water can destabilize the crystal lattice before complete degradation. In contrast, metal halide perovskite nanocrystals exhibit a degradation pathway governed by their ionic lattice and facet-dependent surface polarity upon water exposure. These studies demonstrate that liquid-phase electron microscopy is a powerful platform for uncovering material-specific degradation mechanisms in semiconductor nanocrystals. These direct nanoscale observations will provide design principles for improving nanocrystal stability.

t155.a: Cadmium-free InP quantum dots (QDs) are promising emitters for next-generation quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (QLEDs). However, their performance, especially in the green and blue regions, is limited by core-shell interface defects and lattice mismatch-induced strain, which suppress photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) and device efficiency. Herein, we present three strategies to overcome these challenges. To address interfacial defects, a halogen-mediated diffusion approach effectively passivates oxidation-induced trap states, elevating the PLQY of green-emitting InP/ZnSeS QDs to 86%. Subsequently, a Zn(Ac)2-based doping strategy mitigates lattice strain by facilitating Zn2+ incorporation into the InP core, improving the lattice alignment with the ZnSe shell. This approach produces green InP/ZnS QDs with a PLQY exceeding 90%, enabling the fabrication of a green QLED with an external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 26.3%. Finally, for blue emission, a chloride ion-assisted dynamic surface passivation method promotes uniform ZnS shell growth on small-diameter InP cores (<1.8 nm) by modulating precursor kinetics across crystal facets. This yields blue-emitting QDs with a PLQY of 75% and a narrow emission linewidth (FWHM of 43 nm), culminating in a record EQE of 4.1% for a blue InP-based QLED. Collectively, these strategies provide a robust pathway for engineering high-performance, heavy-metal-free QDs for QLEDs applications.

t156.a: The synthesis of colloidal gallium nitride (GaN) quantum dots (QDs) is limited by the instability of organic ligands at the high GaN crystallization temperatures. We report a top-down, defect-driven fragmentation strategy that yields high-purity colloidal GaN QDs at 50 °C and ambient pressure. The process is mediated by nitrogen-containing organic solvents that lower the energy barrier for native point defect segregation to the crystal surface, inducing controlled structural subdivision. Defect extraction is evidenced by the progressive suppression of deep-level defect luminescence and the emergence of sharp, quantum-confined emission with a full width at half maximum of 38.8 nm. Direct observation of crystal fragmentation via identical-location transmission electron microscopy corroborates the mechanism. Post-synthesis analysis reveals extensive crystallite subdivision and the formation of surface Ga2+ states. This strategy offers a scalable route to high-quality GaN QDs and establishes a generalizable framework for the defect-mediated synthesis of nanostructures from other chemically robust semiconductors. We have also developed highly sensitive lateral flow analysis (LFA) kit based on surface-engineered ligands, synthesized through a self-assembly of quantum dots and polystyrene-co-poly(acrylic acid), composed of a highly emissive QD core and a brush-shaped multifunctional ligand shell. We controlled the orientation of the antibodies conjugated on the QDs. In order to acquire the LFA results conveniently, a smartphone-based reader with a 3D-printed optical imaging module was developed. Through a proof-of-concept experiment, the diagnostic performance of our sensing platform was validated with a pregnancy test kit. Our LFA application can potentially be expanded to diagnosis other diseases by simply changing the antibody pair in the kit.

t157.a: Freestanding nanocrystal quantum dots (NQDs) promise next-generation optoelectronic applications ranging from color-saturated displays to low-threshold lasers, enabled by cost-effective solution-processing methods. Recent studies have revealed that the structural features of NQDs govern carrier dynamics within individual NQDs and NQD assemblies, thereby exerting a significant impact on the performance of optoelectronic devices. In this talk, I present how the structural features of NQDs correlate with their optical properties and device performance. Specifically, I examine the optical and electrical properties of NQDs — including single-exciton and multi-carrier dynamics — in relation to their size and shape, and relate these properties to the performance of corresponding devices. I introduce recent achievements in high-performance light-emitting diodes enabled by structurally engineered NQDs, demonstrating how control over NQD structure translates into improved device-level performance. I conclude by discussing the state-of-the-art of NQD-based optoelectronic applications, along with their potential and limitations for practical realization.

t158.a: Near-infrared to visible photon upconversion holds great promise for a diverse range of applications. Current photosensitizers for triplet-fusion upconversion across this spectral window often contain either precious or toxic elements, and have relatively low efficiencies. Although colloidal nanocrystals have emerged as versatile photosensitizers, the only family of nanocrystals discovered for near-infrared upconversion is the highly-toxic lead chalcogenides. Here we report zinc-doped CuInSe2 nanocrystals as a low-cost and lead-free alternate, allowing for near-infrared to yellow upconversion with an external quantum efficiency reaching 16.7%. When directly merged with photoredox catalysis, this system enables efficient near-infrared-driven organic synthesis and polymerization, which in turn solves the issue of reabsorption loss for nanocrystal-sensitized upconversion. Moreover, the broadband light capturing of these nanocrystals allows for very rapid reactions under indoor sunlight. Extending the reach of "solar synthesis" into the near-infrared may realize the century-long dream of conducting high added-value chemical transformations using sunlight.

t159.a: Present-day liquid lasers rely on organic dyes, which suffer from triplet-state losses and photodegradation and thus require continuous circulation. Colloidal quantum dots (QDs) are attractive alternative gain media, but fast non-radiative Auger recombination of multicarrier gain states has prevented lasing from QD solutions. Core/multishell CdSe/ZnSe/CdS/ZnS QDs were designed so that optical gain originates from a hybrid direct/indirect biexciton with trion-like, strongly suppressed Auger decay. Structures were characterized by transmission electron microscopy, ensemble and single-dot spectroscopy, and femtosecond transient absorption. Lasing was tested using static (non-circulated) toluene solutions (14 μmol L-1) in a 1-mm quartz cuvette inside a wavelength-tunable Littrow cavity pumped by 2.33 eV, 5-ns Nd:YAG pulses. The hybrid biexciton exhibited a lifetime of >13.5 ns, roughly an order of magnitude longer than in conventional CdSe-based QDs, and 60–76% emission efficiency. The QDs displayed a ~300 meV gain bandwidth, peak material gain of 1,110 cm-1, and gain lifetimes up to 3.0 ns, lowering the critical lasing concentration to ~10 μmol L-1. Static solutions produced directional, linearly polarized lasing above a 44 mJ cm-2 threshold and grating-controlled tunability spanning 634–575 nm for two QD core sizes. Output remained stable over 5 h of continuous operation, whereas rhodamine 6G degraded within 1 h. The QDs enable stable, broadly tunable liquid-state lasing without a circulation system, establishing QD solutions as a practical alternative to laser dyes for optofluidics, lab-on-a-chip diagnostics, and compact photonic devices.

t160.a: Quantum dots (QDs) have been widely employed in fluorescence-based bioimaging and sensing biomarkers owing to their excellent photostability arising from quantum confinement and their large surface area that facilitates conjugation with bioactive molecules. However, most biomarker detection studies and commercial assays to date have relied on quantum dot beads (QBs)—aggregates of numerous QDs—rather than exploiting the fluorescence of individual QDs. While QBs offer strong fluorescence signals, their submicron-to-micron size raises concerns regarding sedimentation during assay processes and limits their suitability for nanoscale particle–protein interactions. Here, we present single-QD-based immunoassays for protein detection, where individual QDs are surface modified and directly conjugated to antibodies. Bioorthogonal chemistry enables controlled, site specific coupling between QDs and antibodies, producing conjugates with a compact overall size and well-defined stoichiometry. The resulting single-QD–antibody conjugates allow for the highly sensitive detection of target molecules and, when integrated with complementary platforms such as magnetic nanoparticles, enable the simultaneous multiplexed detection of biomarkers. This approach combines the nanoscale precision of single-QD probes with platform versatility, offering a promising strategy for sensitive, multiplexed fluorescence immunoassays.

t161.k: Self Driving Lab; Halide Perovskites; Qunatum Dots
t161.a: Quantum dots are key materials for unlocking potential of next-generation display and sensor applications. Alloyed halide perovskites have emerged as promising alternatives to current material systems but suffer from stability and toxicity challenges. Discovering new stable and bright compositions with complementary surface terminations for any emerging material system is challenging. Here, we demonstrate a novel concept combining automated robotic synthesis and Bayesian optimization algorithms to accelerate discovery of perovskite quantum dots. We address the challenge of discovering the thermodynamic balance between bright and stable ternary halide compositions by balancing formation and surface energies. Our workflow consists of an automated high-throughput colloidal synthesis platform that enables measurement of optical properties and mapping of solid solution stability across 3,000 halide perovskite anion-exchange alloyed compositions. We show that nanocrystal size, and thus surface energy, is critical in modifying perovskite miscibility boundaries. Smaller nanocrystals suppress halide segregation and associated interfacial defect formation, producing homogeneous ternary alloys that are thermodynamically forbidden in bulk form yet highly luminescent. This approach establishes miscibility as a tunable design parameter and demonstrates nanoscale miscibility engineering as a synthetic strategy for stabilizing metastable compositions. We have integrated this high-throughput workflow into a fully operational autonomous laboratory governed by Bayesian optimization algorithms. This autonomous platform bridges the gap between digital predictions and physical reality, accelerating discovery and precise synthesis of complex perovskite nanocrystal architectures.

t162.a: Perovskite nanocrystals (NCs) are highly promising emissive materials for next-generation displays due to their outstanding optical properties. Recently, trivalent metal doping has been widely utilized to tune the optical properties of perovskite NCs. In this study, CsPbBr₃ NCs were post-treated with trivalent metal solution. Despite the post-treatment, the PL emission of the CsPbBr₃ NCs remained unchanged. The XRD and TEM results revealed that the trivalent metal was not incorporated into the CsPbBr₃ NCs. However, the maximum PLQY of the post-treated CsPbBr₃ NCs significantly increased from ~58% to ~90%. Furthermore, the post-treated CsPbBr₃ NCs demonstrated superior structural stability under ambient conditions. Our result demonstrates that post-treated CsPbBr₃ NCs with trivalent metal does not involve the substitution of Pb²⁺, but instead enhances the PLQY and structural stability through defect passivation.

t163.a: Halide perovskite quantum dots (PQDs) are promising color-conversion materials for micro-LED displays because of their high photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs), narrow emission bandwidths, and tunable optical properties [1]. Among them, mixed-cation Cs1-xFAxPbBr3 PQDs exhibit enhanced phase stability compared with conventional CsPbBr3 PQDs [2, 3]. In this study, high-quality Cs1-xFAxPbBr3 PQDs were synthesized using a dual-solvent-assisted reprecipitation method under ambient conditions, eliminating the need for high temperatures, inert atmospheres, and hazardous solvents. The synthesized PQDs displayed high PLQYs and narrow emission spectra. Low-temperature photoluminescence analysis revealed reduced nonradiative recombination and weaker electron-phonon coupling compared with PQDs prepared by conventional methods. Encapsulated PQD films demonstrated excellent environmental stability under ambient conditions. Furthermore, white light-emitting devices were successfully fabricated by integrating the PQD films with commercial red phosphors and blue LED chips. These results highlight the potential of Cs1-xFAxPbBr3 PQDs for stable and efficient display applications. References [1] J. Chen, H. Xiang, J. Wang, R. Wang, Y. Li, Q. Shan et al., ACS Nano, 15 (2021) 17150-17174. [2] L. Yang, Y. Zhou, H. Xiang, S. Yuan, Q. Shan, S. Zhang, et al., Adv. Optical Mater. 12 (2024) 2401482. [3] S. A. Lu, K. K. Gupta, C. H. Lu, Appl. Surf. Sci. 715 (2026) 164457.

t164.a: Quantum dots have been investigated as fluorescent sensors and markers in many environmental problems. In our group at Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand, we have synthesized various types of quantum dots including CdSe/ZnS, CdTe, InP/ZnS, silicon and carbon QDs for tackling environmental problems existing in our region. After suitable surface modifications, these quantum dots were used in fluorescent sensing and detection of various pollutants including heavy metals, pesticides, and antibiotics. These fluorescent detections could become crucial tools for environmental monitoring and safety practice in Thailand.

t165.a: Human skin sensing of mechanical stimuli originates from transduction of mechanoreceptors that converts external forces into electrical signals. While imitating the spatial distribution of those mechanoreceptors can enable developments of electronic skins capable of decoupled sensing of normal/shear forces and strains, it remains elusive. In this talk, I will introduce a three-dimensionally architected electronic skin (denoted as ‘3DAE-Skin’) with force and strain sensing components arranged in a 3D layout that mimics that of Merkel cells and Ruffini endings in human skin. Microfabrication techniques allow formation of a lithographically defined multilayered electronic device consisting of laminated force and strain sensing arrays, which was transformed into biomimetic 3D configuration through precisely controlled mechanical assembly. A heterogeneous encapsulation strategy of the 3D architected device ensures that the surrounding soft materials of force and strain sensing components have similar mechanical properties to those of Merkel cells and Ruffini endings in the skin. This 3DAE-Skin shows excellent decoupled sensing performances of normal force, shear force and strain. Integration of the 3DAE-Skin with data acquisition/processing modules aided by deep learning algorithms allows development of a tactile system capable of normal/shear force sensing with spatial resolution comparable to human skin, as well as simultaneous modulus and curvature measurements through a simple touch of an object. Demonstrations include rapid modulus measurements of fruits, bread and cake with various shapes and degrees of freshness. Furthermore, the 3DAE-Skin is integrated with a multifunctional porous interface to develop a 3D closed-loop wound administration patch capable of multimodal sensing and on-demand therapy, markedly accelerating scald wound healing in vivo. The bioinspired 3D architected designs, heterogeneous encapsulation strategies, and microfabrication technologies allow for the development of 3DAE-Skin that mimics the spatial arrangement of Merkel cells and Ruffini endings in human skin, as well as the skin’s multilayer geometrical/mechanical characteristics. The capabilities to quantitatively assess the contact state and the object information in real time also have important implications for human-machine interactions, humanoid robots, smart prostheses, and auto inspection instruments.

t166.a: Wearable human–machine interfaces (HMIs) provide a direct pathway for translating human intention and physical interaction into machine-readable signals. Achieving practical HMIs requires soft, mechanically compliant electronic systems together with scalable computational approaches that maintain reliable performance under dynamic human motion. This presentation introduces two wearable HMI platforms based on soft bioelectronics. The first is a silent speech interface that captures facial strain patterns during articulation using ultrathin crystalline silicon strain gauges integrated with deep learning algorithms for nonacoustic speech recognition. The second is a soft, ultrathin electronic skin based on electrical impedance tomography (EIT), which combines stretchable materials with computational image reconstruction to enable high-resolution tactile sensing using a minimal number of electrodes. The silent speech interface accurately recognizes silently spoken words by directly mapping facial skin deformation to linguistic commands, overcoming key scalability and stability limitations of conventional electromyography-based approaches. The EIT-based electronic skin achieves robust three-dimensional tactile mapping and enables reliable real-time machine control even under large mechanical deformation and partial device damage. Together, these studies demonstrate the progression of wearable HMIs from intention-based communication to physically interactive interfaces. The convergence of soft materials, wearable electronics, and data-driven computation provides a scalable framework for next-generation wearable bioelectronic systems. This presentation also discusses future opportunities for integrating multimodal sensing and artificial intelligence to further enhance practical human–machine interaction.

t167.a: Escalating climate change and urban heat island effects poses increasing heat-related risks to human beings, while current thermoregulation strategies relying on centralized air conditioning systems are highly energy intensive. One innovative method to reduce the impact on health is developing wearable technology for diagnosis, treatment, and aftercare rehabilitation. Currently, the adoption of wearable sensors and therapeutic materials onto the human body remains challenging because of device bulkiness, power supply restrictions, and ergonomic comfort limitations. In this talk, I introduce a strategy of incorporating thermal management and sensing capabilities into wearing textiles by nano- to macro-scale material design and multilevel textile engineering from fiber to fabric. First, I will introduce an advanced spinning technology for regenerated silk fibroin spinning. Then, I will introduce spectrum-selective hierarchical fabric for personalized radiative cooling, with emissivity dominant in the atmospheric transmission window to minimize the net heat gain from the surrounding buildings and ground. Lastly, I will share textile strain sensors for self-powered biomechanical and human respiratory signal monitoring. A smart wearable sign language translation system that combines yarn sensing array and machine learning algorithms will be introduced. At the end of the talk, I hope I can convince that the smart textiles could promote the human being better adapting to the climage change.
