t168.a: Non-invasive sweat biosensing has emerged as a promising strategy for non-invasive biochemical monitoring, yet translation into reliable, wearable platforms require innovations in microfluidic engineering, assay chemistry, and system integration. In this seminar, I will present a series of wearable and point-of-care microfluidic technologies engineered to expand the biochemical scope and practicality of sweat diagnostics. First, I will introduce a skin-interfaced, adhesive-free microfluidic band that enables time-dynamic monitoring of sweat biochemistry during exercises for personal fitness evaluation. Three key innovative colorimetric assays are introduced here: a colorimetric timer that tracks sweat collection time, a nanoplasmonic lactate assay, and a dye-conjugated silica nanoparticle pH sensor. Second, a wearable lateral flow assay platform with integrated bioelectronic iontophoresis circuit allows time-sequenced sweat stimulation for monitoring of cortisol concentrations. The use of gold nanoflower enables highly sensitive cortisol quantification down to the picomolar range. Finally, I will present a sweat microcapsule that interfaces with a lab-on-a-disc ELISA system for fully automated folate quantification. Series of human participant studies demonstrate the feasibility of sweat diagnostics for personal fitness, stress, and nutritional status. We demonstrate for the first time that sweat pH is an excellent non-invasive alternative to blood lactate for the personal fitness evaluation by studying the response of sweat pH to exercise intensity, sampling location, and varying subject fitness levels. Monitoring cortisol represents another interesting application for wearable sweat diagnostics where it reflects daily cycle, acute stress, and disruption to the daily cycle by jet lag. Additionally, sweat contains various nutrients such as folate, which is a vital nutrient for pregnancy. Together, these technologies outline a pathway toward accessible, multiplexed, and user-friendly biochemical monitoring, illustrating how microfluidics can bridge the gap between laboratory-grade analytics and wearable healthcare.

t169.k: Flexible neural bioelectronics; Seamless integration; Clinical applications
t169.a: Flexible electronics are advancing digital healthcare and intelligence. When integrated with neural sensing and modulation technologies, they enable flexible neural bioelectronics that bridge human and machine intelligence. This presentation explores the development and applications of flexible neural bioelectronics. Beginning with a comprehensive finite deformation theory that elucidates the climbing habits of twining plants, we establish fundamental insights into their attachment mechanisms. Leveraging this understanding, we propose a 3D twining electrode that can naturally self-climb onto nerves driven by 37 �C normal saline from a temporarily flattened 2D configuration. In vivo experiments demonstrate its potential for peripheral nerve stimulation and recording in neuroscience. Extending these principles, we introduce twining-inspired in-ear bioelectronics, named SpiralE. Utilizing electrothermal actuation, SpiralE adaptively expands and spirals along the auditory meatus, ensuring conformal contact while facilitating communication with the outside world. Visual and auditory Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) paradigms confirm that SpiralE achieves reliable EEG sensing, supporting wearable and discreet BCI control. Additionally, we present multifunctional bioelectronics with switchable rigidity and reconfigurable shapes, enabled by a fast thermal response shape memory polymer substrate. Taking advantage of its ability to be implanted through a small incision and recover in limited spaces to envelop biosurfaces, animal experiments demonstrate its efficiency in the comprehensive diagnosis of epilepsy and pericardial effusion. Furthermore, this presentation covers the development of magnetic resonance-compatible electrodes based on conductive polymers and stretchable multilevel mesh electrodes, discussing their applications in clinical brain diseases such as epilepsy and brain tumors. Overall, the development of flexible neural bioelectronics, with their excellent biocompatibility, multimodality, and environmental adaptability, heralds a new generation of bio-electronic hybrid systems, driving innovation in basic neuroscience and clinical applications.

t170.a: Soft wearable sensors, known for their unique deformability and biocompatibility, offer a promising way to continuously monitor plant physiology. By integrating miniature spectral sensors with temperature-and-humidity sensing on modulus-gradient PDMS substrates with liquid-metal circuits, we developed soft wearable systems that continuously acquire in-situ spectral and microclimatic data from different plant organs, including leaves and fruit. On leaves, this platform diagnoses five plant stress types, including nutrient deficiencies and pest attacks, with 99.2% accuracy, detecting nutrient deficiency over 10 days earlier than conventional computer vision methods; on fruit, a stretchable, ring-shaped variant tolerant of over 65% circumferential strain tracks the ripening process, classifying maturity stage with 98.67% accuracy. Yet these diagnoses remain black-box correlations rather than interpretable physiological insights, leaving users unable to trace their causal basis or translate them into management decisions. To close this gap, we coupled the sensing platform with a knowledge-guided reasoning framework built on a large language model, transforming raw multimodal signals into mechanistic diagnoses and actionable recommendations. In a real potassium-deficiency experiment, this reasoning-augmented system detected stress on day 4, seven days earlier than the machine-learning framework, and its intervention recommendations guided the plant to full recovery by day 12. Together, these soft wearable systems and the reasoning framework transform raw multimodal signals into mechanistic diagnoses and actionable recommendations for continuous plant physiology monitoring.

t171.a: During the recent pandemic, many biosensors were developed for virtual clinics, a concept that patients do not need to visit hospitals personally to receive diagnosis and treatment. For instance, they can measure physiological parameters such as Photoplethysmogram (PPG) at home and upload those data to clouds for analysis. If such a biosensor can detect NIR (near-infrared) light, it can also capture vein images for biometric authentication. The vein pattern is underneath the skin surface, so it is more difficult to counterfeit than the fingerprint. In this study, we have developed sheet-type image sensor with low-noise organic photodiode. The developed sheet-type image sensor is fabricated by densely integrating a high-efficiency readout circuit using an active matrix of a low-temperature polysilicon thin film transistor and an organic photodiode that uses a highly efficient organic semiconductor as a photosensitive layer. The weak light detectability allowed the capture of artery information from deep tissue during vein imaging and enabled the removal of additional light source to utilize only near-infrared in the indoor ambient as light source. In addition, the high-speed capability allows us to visualize the blood perfusion image by combing time series data and singular value decomposition (SVD) method. We successfully developed a conformable organic image sensor that enables high-resolution and high-speed reading. The flexible imager can capture high-resolution images of fingerprints, veins, and pulse waves. The developed flexible imager has potential applications in the field of biomedical engineering to perform highly accurate measurements.

t172.a: Recent advances in soft bioelectronics have attracted considerable attention due to their potential applications in personalized, bio-integrated healthcare systems. A primary challenge in this field arises from the mechanical mismatch between conventional rigid electronic devices and the soft, dynamic nature of human organs. To address this challenge, novel materials for soft, stretchable electronic devices have been developed, offering mechanical and chemical properties more compatible with in vivo cellular environments. Despite these advances, current stretchable conductive materials typically exhibit lower conductivity than commercial implantable devices, which leads to higher power consumption and more frequent battery replacement. This talk introduces a sustainable power supply solution for soft implantable bioelectronics to overcome these limitations. An all-solid-state thin-film lithium-ion battery, combined with parity-time symmetric long-range wireless power transfer, represents a promising approach. This system eliminates the need for periodic battery replacement, thereby significantly reducing the physical and economic burdens on patients. Key technological challenges and future research directions will also be briefly discussed. Ongoing efforts in developing unconventional materials and bioelectronic systems are expected to have a profound impact on addressing unmet needs in clinical medicine.

t173.k: Fine-Particle Air Filtration; Nanoparticle; Nuclear-Enabled Biofuel
t173.a: The first author (WT) joined the Chemical Engineering Department, Chulalongkorn University, two years after its establishment in 1976 and resigned in 2003 to join the newly established National Nanotechnology Center as its founding executive director. In 1981, WT et al. pioneered an innovative super-efficient 3-D Monte-Carlo method to simulate “A Stochastic Model for Deposition of Aerosol by Convective Brownian Diffusion on a Dust Loaded Fiber” and presented it at the International Symposium on Powder Technology, Kyoto, Japan. The methodology was successfully extended to the cases of polydisperse aerosol and a dust-loaded electret fiber. Subsequently, WT et al. extended his research areas to the production and applications of nanomaterials, including carbon nanomaterials, and nanoparticle synthesis and characterization. To reduce carbon emissions and mitigate the impacts of climate change, it is highly effective to enable fossil-fuel replacement and elimination of abundant agricultural wastes by transforming them into biofuels using nuclear technology. The second author (WL) proposed the application of Dr. Charles Forsberg’s vision and strategy to obtain nuclear-enabled biofuels for Thailand. A super-efficient Monte-Carlo simulation was developed to track the trajectories of submicron particles around a dust-loaded fiber instead of the governing Langevin’s equation. Various kinds of nanomaterials were synthesized and characterized successfully. Integration of Nuclear Energy, Hydrogen Technology, and Bioenergy for Bio-fuels Production was proposed by WL. A comprehensive overview of the research achievements of WT at CU was presented along with WL’s supplement on nuclear-enabled biofuels. This presentation was made to commemorate the 50th Anniversary of the ChE Dept, CU.

t174.a: Understanding the characteristics, both physical and electrochemical, of two-dimensional (2D) materials is crucial for the advancement of various electrochemical devices such as energy storage systems, electrocatalysts, ions selective membranes, and wastewater treatment technologies. To achieve this goal, controlled synthesis of 2D materials plays a vital role. In this study, we focus on the structural control achieved through liquid phase exfoliation of bulk materials, specifically: (i) graphite-graphene, (ii) transition metal dichalcogenides, and (iii) heterostructure formation. This involves material handling techniques and recycling of waste generated during the synthesis process. Furthermore, the exfoliated materials were utilised in diverse applications including supercapacitors (including electrode materials and binders), electrocatalysts, and removal of ions for wastewater treatment. To delve deeper into the complex realm of materials science and electrochemistry, we incorporated data science methodologies such as machine learning and statistical tools. Through simple data analysis, valuable electrochemical insights were derived, paving the way for the design of machine learning algorithms—an innovative approach in this field. To the best of our knowledge, this integration of data science as well as the materials synthesis in the context of 2D materials holds great potential for their development and application in various fields.

t175.k: Overall Water Splitting; Two-Dimensional Metal Organic Frameworks; Photocatalysts
t175.a: Photocatalytic overall water splitting offers a promising route toward sustainable hydrogen production. However, single-step excitation systems suffer from severe kinetic bottlenecks in both the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Overcoming these limits typically requires complex, site-selective dual-cocatalyst deposition alongside durable blocking layers to prevent unwanted back-reactions. Here, we introduce a conductive, two-dimensional metal–organic framework (2D MOF) as a multifunctional, single-component cocatalyst. Deposited onto SrTiO<sub>3</sub>:Al via a one-step self-assembly process, this framework drives steady overall water splitting with an apparent quantum efficiency of 31.5% at 350 nm, successfully suppressing reverse reactions without requiring additional blocking layers. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and theoretical analyses reveal the mechanistic origins of its activity. This work establishes conductive 2D MOFs as an all-in-one platform for designing efficient, streamlined solar-to-hydrogen conversion systems.

t176.a: While carbon dioxide (CO2) is a primary driver of the greenhouse effect, it holds significant potential as a sustainable carbon feedstock due to its abundant availability from industrial sources of fossil-fuel power plants and steel and cement manufacturing. However, the primary obstacles to its utilization lie in its thermodynamic stability, which necessitates harsh reaction conditions—such as elevated temperatures and pressures—for chemical activation. This talk addresses the conversion of carbon dioxide to carbon materials using NaBH4 as a reduction agent at moderate conditions and their applications for battery electrodes. Hierarchical porous carbon was synthesized via CO2 reduction in the presence of the reduction agent, utilizing CaCO3 nanoparticles as a template. The resulting carbon material exhibits a hierarchical porous architecture, boasting a high specific surface area of 1000 m2/g and a pore volume of 3 cm3/g. This exceptional porosity can accommodate a large volume of active sulfur within the cathode of Li-S batteries. Additionally, a sheet interlayer was fabricated to form a composite paper composed of porous carbon and a CNT/CNF layer. By dispersing Fe-based molecular catalysts and sulfur active materials within this porous carbon electrode, the shuttle effect can be significantly suppressed through enhanced chemical interactions. DFT simulations elucidated the thermodynamic effects of the Fe-coordination on lowering both the energy change of the redox steps and the activation barrier for lithium-ion diffusion. Finally, this presentation will introduce the direct conversion of CO2 into crystalline carbon materials and discuss their applications in electrochemical conversion and energy storage.

t177.k: Intelligent Energy; IoT; Artificial Intelligence; Energy Optimization
t177.a: Energy efficiency has traditionally focused on reducing consumption through equipment upgrades, operational controls, and energy-saving initiatives. However, in increasingly complex industrial environments, a more fundamental question must be addressed: Do we truly understand where energy is being consumed, why it is being consumed, and whether that energy is creating the expected operational value? This presentation introduces the concept of Intelligent Energy, an approach that moves beyond conventional energy monitoring toward data-driven understanding, prediction, and continuous optimization. The fundamental principle is simple: we cannot improve what we cannot see. Internet of Things (IoT) technologies make energy visible by connecting machines, equipment, and operational processes with sensors and measurement systems. Instead of viewing energy consumption only as an aggregate figure, organizations can observe how individual pumps, motors, HVAC systems, lighting, and other assets consume energy under actual operating conditions. Energy data alone, however, does not explain performance. Two machines performing the same task, under the same load and for the same operating time, may consume significantly different amounts of energy. Understanding this difference requires combining energy measurements with operational data such as temperature, vibration, runtime, load, equipment condition, and environmental factors. This richer data context enables organizations to identify patterns, detect abnormal behavior, uncover hidden inefficiencies, and ask better operational questions: Where is energy being wasted? When does abnormal consumption occur? Why does it happen? What action should be taken? Artificial Intelligence (AI) extends this capability from visibility to intelligence. By analyzing patterns across energy and operational data, AI can support anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, root-cause analysis, forecasting, and optimization. Organizations can therefore move from reacting to historical information toward anticipating problems before they become failures, reducing unnecessary energy consumption while simultaneously improving equipment reliability and operational performance. The ultimate objective is not simply to create more dashboards or collect more data. A dashboard does not save energy; action does. Sustainable improvement emerges when organizations close the loop between sensing, analyzing, deciding, acting, and continuously learning from the results. This transforms energy management from passive monitoring into an ongoing optimization process. Most importantly, intelligent energy is not driven by technology alone. Effective transformation requires the integration of human experience, IoT data, and AI intelligence. Technology provides visibility and insight, while people provide operational knowledge, judgment, and the ability to turn those insights into meaningful action. The journey toward sustainable industrial operations can therefore be summarized in three imperatives: Make energy visible. Make data intelligent. Make every action count.

t178.k: Functional polymers; Molecular engineering; Photocatalytic hydrogen evolution;
t178.a: Functional polymers offer a versatile platform for energy applications because their molecular structures, electronic properties, and interfacial functionalities can be precisely tailored through molecular design and synthesis. By engineering polymer backbones, side chains, functional groups, and intermolecular interactions, their optical, electronic, ionic, and physicochemical properties can be systematically controlled for different energy conversion and storage processes. In this presentation, we will discuss our recent efforts in the molecular design and synthesis of functional polymers for both energy production and energy storage. For energy production, conjugated polymers and polymer dots (Pdots) are developed as photocatalysts for visible- light-driven hydrogen evolution, where molecular engineering enables control over light absorption, charge generation and transfer, interfacial interactions, and catalytic processes. For energy storage, functional polymers are designed to regulate ion transport, molecular interactions, and electrode/electrolyte interfaces, providing opportunities to improve the performance and stability of battery and related energy-storage systems. Through these examples, this presentation will highlight how molecular and polymer engineering can establish structure–property–function relationships, providing a general design framework for developing functional polymer materials for next-generation energy production and storage technologies. Polymer dots; Energy storage.

t179.k: lithium-ion battery, silicon anode, polymeric binder, supramolecular chemistry, mechanically interlocked polymer, fast charging
t179.a: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are rapidly expanding into electric vehicles and energy storage systems, where both higher energy density and fast-charging capability are increasingly demanded. Silicon (Si) anodes can meet these demands owing to their high specific capacity, yet their volume change of up to 300% during cycling causes particle pulverization, electrode delamination, and continuous solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) growth. Although binders account for only a small portion of an electrode, they have emerged as a critical component for addressing these mechanical challenges. In this presentation, I will first introduce how supramolecular chemistry and mechanostereochemistry, which preserve the structural integrity of biological systems, can be translated into binder design for Si anodes. Binders based on reversible noncovalent interactions enable self-healing of broken interparticle connections, while mechanically interlocked molecules such as polyrotaxanes act as molecular pulleys that dissipate stress. However, noncovalent interactions are confined to where two functional groups meet and thus become spatially inhomogeneous as the electrode density increases, a key parameter for high volumetric energy density. In the second part, I will present our recent work on a poly(acrylic acid) binder with mechanically interlocked crosslinks (MI-PAA) that overcomes this limitation. Its topologically entangled network undergoes rotation, elongation, sliding, and rocking motions at the crosslinks, providing spatially homogeneous mechanical strength and elasticity and enabling global stress relaxation across the entire electrode. As a result, MI-PAA preserves surface porosity and electrode integrity during calendering to a high electrode density of 1.6 g cm−3, and suppresses electrode swelling and SEI growth during cycling. Si-graphite full cells with MI-PAA retained 78.2% of their capacity after 200 cycles (vs. 60.1% for SBR/CMC) and 77.0% after 100 cycles under 3C fast charging (vs. 58.6%), reaching 80% state of charge in 17.6 min. This topological approach offers a versatile design strategy for high-energy, fast-chargeable Si anodes and other mechanically fragile energy storage systems.

t180.k: Self-healing rubber; gloves; autonomous; chemical resistance; supramolecular polymers
t180.a: Protective gloves offer an exciting platform for chemical engineers to translate molecular understanding into innovations with societal impact. This presentation explores how colloid and polymer engineering can advance glove functionality, durability and sustainability, drawing on research from Monash Colloids and Polymers Research Group. Self-healing rubber is highlighted as an emerging approach, using reversible interactions within polymer networks to repair damage and potentially improve protective performance. The talk connects molecular design and interfacial behavior to material performance and manufacturing needs while exploring the challenges of translating laboratory discoveries into practical glove technologies. It will also consider how industry partnerships can guide research priorities and help bridge material development with scalable production processes. Collaborations with prominent researchers of Chulalongkorn University’s Chemical Engineering Department and Thailand Synchrotron Light Research Institute will also be briefly discussed, demonstrating how shared expertise and advanced characterization support materials innovation. Celebrating the Department’s 50th anniversary, this talk aims to encourage young chemical engineers to connect curiosity with industrial needs, embrace multidisciplinary collaboration and explore how discoveries at small scales can contribute to safer protection and more sustainable materials for society. References D. Y. S. Low, S. Mintarno, J. Supramaniam, K. W. Tan, B. H. Goh, S. Manickam, S. Y. Tang, J. Ind. Eng. Chem., 2025, 300-307. D. Y. S. Low, J. Supramaniam, B. H. Goh, S. Manickam and S. Y. Tang, Adv. Funct. Mater., 2024, 34, 2401345. D. Y. S Low, J. Supramaniam, W. D. Leong, A. Soottitantawat, T. Charinpanitkul, W. Tanthapanichakoon, S. Manickam, K. W. Tan, B. H. Goh, S. Y. Tang. Mater. Today Sustain., 2023, 100545. J. Supramaniam, D. Y. S. Low, S. K. Wong, B. F. Leo, B. H. Goh, S. Y. Tang, Chem. Eng. J., 2021, 437,135440. Speaker introduction: Dr Patrick Tang Siah Ying is an Associate Professor and also Leader of Colloids and Polymers Group at Monash University Malaysia. His fields of research focus on sonochemistry, self-healing polymers, rubber and glove technologies, cellulosic nanomaterials, functional coatings and controlled delivery. Dr. Patrick is an active author, with five book chapters and several high impact publications. He is currently supervising six full-time PhD students and acting as an associate supervisor for another four. In 2014, he was honoured with the prestigious IChemE Malaysia’s Young Chemical Engineer Award. In 2019, he was the recipient of Visiting Professorship of Chulalongkorn University and conducted his collaborative research at the Center of Excellence in Particle Technology. Presently, Dr. Patrick’s Colloids and Polymers group is working actively on the micro/nanoencapsulation of natural products for modern nutraceutical and pharmaceutical applications. On polymer side, his team concentrates on the development of new self-healing rubber and functional glove products with tunable properties. His patented self-healing glove inventions have earned him several awards in both national and international innovation exhibitions. Additionally, he has established several collaborative industry-driven projects on self-healing rubber, glove innovations and renewable energy technology.

t181.k: Trehalose; Saccharomyces cerevisiae; stress-induced fermentation; whole-cell
t181.a: Trehalose is a non-reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose units that acts as a cellular osmolyte, stabilizing proteins and membranes and enhancing microbial survival under environmental stress. Because of its exceptional stabilizing properties, trehalose is widely used in food, pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and biotechnology products; however, current industrial production relies mainly on starch-based enzymatic conversion, which suffers from limitations in enzyme stability, substrate specificity, and process robustness. Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a GRAS yeast extensively used in food and beverage fermentations, naturally accumulates trehalose in response to ethanol, osmotic, and thermal stresses, making it a promising whole-cell catalyst for more sustainable trehalose production. In this work, we developed a stress-induced, two-stage fermentation strategy for trehalose production by S. cerevisiae and systematically evaluated the impacts of ethanol-induced osmotic stress, elevated temperature, and cell physiological state on trehalose biosynthesis. In the first stage, cells were cultivated in a high-glucose (100 g/L) cell production medium to obtain high biomass and ethanol levels, and late-log-phase cells were then transferred to a trehalose production medium containing 100 g/L glucose with varied ethanol concentrations and incubated at 45°C. The combined osmotic and thermal stresses significantly enhanced trehalose formation, with 37.5 g/L ethanol giving the best performance; under these conditions, extracellular trehalose reached 0.47 g/L with a yield of 0.26 g/g and productivity of 0.08 g/L·h, while intracellular trehalose reached 1.35 g/L (0.003 g/g cell). These results demonstrate that deliberate design of synergistic stress conditions in a two-stage process can markedly improve trehalose production in S. cerevisiae and highlight the importance of matching stress profiles to the physiology of the whole-cell catalyst. To support process intensification and future strain engineering, we integrate chromatographic and metabolomic analyses to monitor central carbon metabolism and trehalose-pathway intermediates during the stress-induction phase, enabling identification of key regulatory nodes and bottlenecks. Overall, this study establishes a food-grade, yeast-based platform for stress-induced trehalose production and provides a mechanistic framework for optimizing whole-cell bioprocesses for high- value functional carbohydrates in food and bioprocessing applications. catalyst; metabolomics; food bioprocessing

t182.k: multiphase catalytic hydrogenation, CO2-dissolved expanded liquids (CXLs), biphasic CXL–water system
t182.a: The development of chemical conversion systems with low environmental impact and minimal energy consumption is essential for advancing next-generation green technologies, calling for innovative alternatives to conventional processes designed primarily for large-scale chemical plants. Achieving this goal requires not only highly active catalysts capable of promoting reactions under mild conditions but also reaction media that enhance catalytic activity and product selectivity. In this study, we explore a unique catalytic reaction medium composed of two ubiquitous liquids: water and oil. In particular, we highlight the distinctive properties of CO2-dissolved expanded liquids (CXLs), formed by pressurizing the organic phase with CO2, and their role in multiphase hydrogenation reactions. CXLs enhance the solubility of coexisting gases, such as H2, O2, and CO, thereby facilitating chemical reactions involving these gases. Owing to these unique properties, CXLs have attracted considerable attention as promising reaction media for novel multiphase catalytic reactions. One example demonstrating the effectiveness of this reaction medium is the selective hydrogenation of aromatic compounds. Under H2 pressure, the hydrogenation of benzonitrile over a Pd catalyst yields benzylamine as the major product. However, subsequent reactions between the resulting primary amine and imine intermediates lead to the formation of secondary amines as byproducts. In contrast, conducting the reaction in a biphasic CXL–water system enables the selective production of benzylamine with an exceptionally high selectivity of 99%. This remarkable selectivity arises from the synergistic effects of CO2 and water. The primary amine rapidly reacts with CO2 dissolved in the CXL phase to form a carbamate, thereby suppressing undesired side reactions. Simultaneously, the transfer of the resulting species into the aqueous phase across the liquid–liquid interface facilitates product removal and promotes turnover. A more direct demonstration of the effectiveness of biphasic CXL–water system is the synthesis of formic acid through liquid-phase CO2 hydrogenation. In this reaction, the CXL phase enhances H2 solubility in the organic solvent, thereby facilitating CO2 hydrogenation. Meanwhile, the preferential transfer of the resulting formic acid into the aqueous phase, driven by its high polarity, promotes product removal and accelerates turnover. Although these reaction systems are still in the early stages of development, they hold considerable promise for enabling sustainable and energy-efficient chemical conversion technologies under mild reaction conditions.

t183.a: The Integrated Carbon Capture and Conversion (ICCC) process represents a promising catalytic approach for producing syngas from CO₂ and CH₄ by integrating gas separation and reaction within a single system. However, fluctuations in the composition and feed ratio of gases supplied from the flue gas unit can significantly affect process performance. To address this challenge, a Ratings concept workflow based on density functional theory (DFT) is implemented through a two-stage protocol. The first stage, Catalyst Identification, evaluates catalyst properties and predicts catalytic performance using reactivity (RT-R) and stability (RT-S) ratings. These ratings are calculated from activation energy data obtained experimentally or through DFT calculations. The second stage, Catalyst Optimization, focuses on improving catalyst performance by identifying suitable operating conditions while accounting for catalyst deactivation over time. In addition, a “coking boundary” is established to prevent operation under conditions that favor carbon deposition. Sensitivity analyses of temperature and feed composition show that most catalysts are more strongly affected by changes in temperature than by variations in feed ratio, highlighting the importance of accurate temperature control for effective process optimization. Spin-polarized periodic density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) was employed together with Projector Augmented-Wave (PAW) pseudopotentials and a plane-wave basis set. Brillouin-zone sampling was carried out using the Monkhorst–Pack scheme, with first-order Methfessel–Paxton smearing applied for electronic occupations. Activation energies for individual elementary reaction steps were determined using the climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method. The reaction mechanism was developed under the assumption that surface reactions constitute the rate-limiting processes. Forward and reverse rate constants were calculated using the Eyring equation, with corrections for zero-point energy (ZPE), entropy (S), and internal energy (U). A pseudo-steady-state hypothesis (PSSH) was applied to surface intermediates without invoking the most abundant reactive intermediate (MARI) approximation. Adsorption–desorption equilibrium was assumed for gaseous CO and H₂. Catalyst reactivity and stability were subsequently evaluated on the basis of dry reforming of methane (DRM) reaction rates and the competing mechanisms of coke formation and removal. The Ratings concept provides a systematic framework for optimizing the ICCC process through two consecutive stages. In the first stage, Catalyst Identification, promising catalysts for the DRM reactor are screened using RT-R and RT-S ratings. Derived from activation energy data, these ratings quantify catalyst reactivity and stability relative to a selected reference catalyst and therefore provide a convenient performance coordinate for catalyst comparison. In the second stage, Catalyst Optimization, a database-assisted online optimization system is used to determine operating conditions that can maintain catalytic performance as deactivation progresses. The optimization strategy involves two major control actions. First, temperature adjustment is applied when syngas production declines, with sensor measurements used to determine and implement a revised reactor temperature setpoint. Second, feed-ratio tuning is performed by adjusting the flow rates of makeup gases in response to changes in the inlet gas composition. Sensitivity analysis indicates that temperature has a greater influence on process performance than feed-ratio variations, identifying temperature control as the dominant parameter for effective optimization. The integration of an online optimization module enables rapid and reliable determination of operating setpoints for both feedback and feed-forward control strategies. Furthermore, incorporating a defined “coking boundary” allows the reactor to operate within conditions that minimize carbon deposition. This approach can therefore help extend catalyst lifetime while improving the operational stability and robustness of the ICCC process.

t184.k: Graphite Intercalation Compounds; Two-Dimensional Nanoparticles; Selective Hydrogenation
t184.a: Several metal chlorides can be intercalated between graphite layers to form graphite intercalation compounds (MClₓ-GICs). Upon reduction of the intercalated metal chlorides, two-dimensional metal nanoparticles can be formed because the graphite layers sterically hinder the growth of metal particles. Here, we report the preparation of two-dimensional noble-metal nanoparticles, including platinum nanosheets and iridium nanodisks, by hydrogen reduction of the corresponding metal chlorides intercalated between graphite layers, and their catalytic properties. Platinum or iridium chloride was mixed with graphite powder pretreated under a high-pressure chlorine atmosphere, followed by hydrogen reduction to produce metal-intercalated graphite (M-GIC; M = Pt or Ir). TEM observations revealed that platinum nanosheets, with thicknesses of 1–3 nm and widths of several hundred nanometers, were arranged parallel to the graphite layers in Pt-GIC. The nanosheets contained many hexagonal holes with straight edges, suggesting that their structure was strongly influenced by the graphite layers. In Ir-GIC, disk-like iridium nanoparticles with a thickness of approximately 2 nm and a width of 9–10 nm were intercalated between the graphite layers. Both Pt-GIC and Ir-GIC showed higher selectivities toward cinnamyl alcohol in the hydrogenation of hydrocinnamaldehyde than spherical platinum and iridium particles supported on the graphite surface. Noble-metal nanoparticles confined between graphite layers exhibit catalytic properties distinct from those of conventional metal nanoparticles supported on the graphite surface. In this presentation, we will also discuss the synthesis and catalytic properties of bimetallic nanoparticles formed between graphite layers.

t185.k: Delta-MnO2/C Composites; Zinc-ion Batteries; Spent Alkaline Batteries
t185.a: Billions of alkaline batteries are discarded every year, and most end up in landfills together with their manganese. Conventional recycling routes rely on multi-step acid leaching, pH adjustment and purification, which consume hazardous chemicals (H2SO4, HCl, NaOH) and generate secondary waste streams. Here, we present a one-step hydrothermal process that converts spent alkaline battery black mass directly into δ-MnO2/C cathodes for zinc-ion batteries, with KMnO4 as the only added reagent. The black mass acts as both the manganese source and the reductant; without it, KMnO4 alone yields no MnO2. Compared with the previously reported route (6:1 KMnO4:MnSO4), the optimized KMnO4:black-mass ratio of 3:1 halves the oxidant demand, eliminates the virgin MnSO4 precursor and lowers the total reagent input by ~48%, giving a simple E-factor of 2.59 and a manganese utilization efficiency of 42.64%. The product is phase-pure δ-MnO2 with a BET surface area of 69.62 m2/g, 2.2 times that of the reference-route material (31.42 m2/g), and a 44% lower charge-transfer resistance (25.69 vs. 45.47 Ω in DMSO). Against a MnSO4-derived control prepared and tested under identical conditions, the recycled cathode delivered 96% of the capacity in DMSO (140.12 vs. 146.43 mAh/g at 0.1 A/g) and 90% in aqueous ZnSO4 (127.87 vs. 142.26 mAh/g), and retained ~80% of its capacity after 300 cycles at 1.0 A/g in DMSO, versus ~71% for the control. Spent alkaline batteries can therefore replace virgin manganese salts in δ-MnO2 cathode synthesis while reducing oxidant use, offering a simple route from battery waste to energy-storage materials.

t186.a: Magnon valves are fundamental building blocks for magnon-based memory and logic devices, providing switchable on/off control of magnon transport. Such valves can be realized using thermally driven magnon currents, for example through the spin Seebeck effect. Beyond proof-of-concept demonstrations, a central challenge in developing practically relevant magnon valves is to improve the on/off ratio and the contrast between the two magnetic states. In this talk, we present our recent efforts toward addressing these challenges. To enhance the on/off signal ratio, we optimize ferromagnetic insulator (FMI)/spacer/FMI trilayer structures and explore spin-detection layers with efficient spin-to-charge conversion. To achieve clearer separation between the on and off states, we further develop a new exchange-bias structure that pins one of the FMI layers. The refined all-insulating magnon valve achieves a state-of-the-art on/off ratio together with a pronounced contrast between the two magnetic states. This work demonstrates the first all-insulating magnon valve that combines efficient magnon-current modulation with robust magnetic-state control, paving the way toward practical magnonic memory and logic devices.

t187.k: Flexible Actuatator; Π-Electronic Systems; Martensitic Transition
t187.a: π-Electronic molecular crystals offer an unusual combination of mechanical compliance and stiffness originating from anisotropic intermolecular interactions. Easy-glide planes along π-stacked molecular layers provide structural flexibility, while close molecular packing supports a high elastic modulus, making these crystals attractive building blocks for mechanically active systems. Temperature-dependent crystallographic, thermal, and mechanical analyses were employed to correlate molecular packing, anisotropic lattice deformation, and macroscopic thermomechanical responses. Particular attention was given to molecular rearrangements associated with martensitic transformations and anisotropic thermal expansion within the crystalline state. To translate these intrinsic properties into functional devices, meniscus-guided microtransfer molding (MG-μ-TM) was developed to assemble π-electronic molecular crystals into large-area, crystallographically oriented microstructured films. The resulting crystalline architectures were further integrated with compliant substrates and passive layers to construct flexible actuators and robotic devices. Structural analyses revealed that the anisotropic intermolecular interactions of π-electronic crystals enable pronounced and highly directional thermomechanical responses, including large transformation strain associated with cooperative martensitic transitions and continuous deformation driven by anisotropic thermal expansion. MG-μ-TM enabled these molecular-level responses to be preserved and spatially organized within interconnected crystalline microstructures, allowing intrinsic lattice deformation to be effectively translated into macroscopic motion. The resulting devices exhibited large reversible actuation and substantial mechanical output, while integration into bimorph and other mechanically programmed architectures enabled bending, gripping, and temperature-responsive shape changes. These results establish a molecular-to-device relationship connecting π-electronic packing, anisotropic thermomechanical deformation, and macroscopic actuation. π-Electronic crystals therefore provide a promising materials platform for lightweight flexible actuators and soft robotic systems.

t188.k: Single-crystalline 2D Metal Nanosheets; Omni-directional Assembly; Conductive Films
t188.a: Single-crystalline two-dimensional (2D) metal nanosheets are promising building blocks for next-generation conductive films owing to their high electrical conductivity, mechanical flexibility, and solution processability. In particular, their grain-boundary-free crystalline nature provides an effective pathway for charge transport, while their 2D geometry enables versatile assembly into functional film architectures. However, the development of scalable strategies that integrate nanosheet synthesis, controlled assembly, and device implementation remains essential for their practical application. Single-crystalline 2D metal nanosheets were synthesized through solution-based approaches and subsequently assembled into conductive films with controlled intersheet connectivity. Omni-directional assembly was employed to construct densely interconnected nanosheet networks with isotropic electrical pathways. The assembled films were further engineered into hierarchical porous architectures to modulate their mechanical properties while retaining efficient electrical conduction. Finally, single-crystalline Ag nanosheet films were integrated into oxide thin-film transistor platforms to evaluate their applicability as functional conductive layers for electronic devices. The solution-synthesized 2D metal nanosheets exhibited well-defined single-crystalline structures, providing highly conductive building units without grain-boundary-limited charge transport. Omni-directional assembly produced densely connected nanosheet networks with isotropic electrical conduction while maintaining an ultrathin and mechanically compliant film structure [1]. Structural reconfiguration into hierarchical porous architectures further enhanced mechanical deformability without significantly compromising electrical conductivity, enabling stable electrical performance under stretching and multifunctional operation in device-level systems [2,3]. Moreover, the scalable assembly process enabled direct integration of single-crystalline Ag nanosheet films with oxide thin-film transistors, where the nanosheets served as effective conductive layers for precise threshold-voltage engineering [4]. The results demonstrate that controlling the crystallinity, assembly direction, and hierarchical architecture of 2D metal nanosheets provides a versatile materials strategy for high-performance conductive films. The combination of single-crystalline charge-transport pathways, controlled nanosheet connectivity, mechanical compliance, and scalable solution processing offers practical design guidelines for the development of stretchable electronics and large-area electronic devices.

t189.k: Polymer Gate Dielectric; Flexible Electronics; Field-Effect Transistor
t189.a: Background Flexible electronic devices require polymer gate dielectrics with excellent insulating properties, mechanical flexibility, and low-temperature processability. In particular, both the bulk dielectric properties and semiconductor/dielectric interfacial properties strongly affect the performance and operational stability of field-effect transistors. Therefore, systematic material design and evaluation are essential for developing reliable polymer gate dielectrics. Methods Various polymer gate dielectrics, particularly soluble polyimides, were designed and evaluated through experimental and computational approaches. Their surface, bulk, dielectric, and electrical properties were systematically characterized and correlated with field-effect transistor performance. In addition, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to investigate molecular structure–dielectric property relationships and predict dielectric constants. Results The molecular structure of polymer gate dielectrics significantly influenced their dielectric properties, semiconductor/dielectric interfaces, and transistor characteristics. Optimized polymer dielectrics enabled high-performance and electrically stable FETs while maintaining excellent mechanical flexibility. Furthermore, DFT calculations successfully reproduced experimental trends in dielectric constants, demonstrating their potential for efficient screening and optimization of polymer insulators. Conclusions The results demonstrate that polymer gate dielectrics can be systematically optimized by combining molecular design, material characterization, device evaluation, and computational prediction. This integrated approach provides an efficient strategy for developing reliable polymer insulators for next-generation flexible and solution-processed electronic devices.

t190.a: Two-dimensional (2D) materials have attracted considerable attention for next-generation electronics, optoelectronics, sensing, and energy technologies owing to their unique electrical, optical, and mechanical properties. In particular, graphene has been extensively investigated as a transparent conducting electrode for flexible and stretchable electronics. However, despite substantial progress, achieving high electrical conductivity through scalable, reliable, and stable doping remains a key challenge for the practical use of graphene and other 2D materials. In this presentation, I will discuss our progress in doping strategies for large-area graphene and other 2D materials. Our earlier studies demonstrated dual-side doping strategies that significantly improve the electrical conductivity, uniformity, and long-term stability of graphene transparent electrodes [1,2]. More recently, we have developed a dry doping approach based on the controlled modification of surrounding polymer layers, enabling effective carrier modulation without conventional wet chemical doping processes [3]. This approach enables highly uniform conductivity enhancement while maintaining high optical transparency and long-term stability. Beyond graphene transparent electrodes, we are further exploring this approach as a versatile strategy for controlling the electrical properties of 2D materials and devices.[4] In particular, functional polymer layers can provide not only carrier modulation but also additional functions, including passivation of 2D semiconductor devices. These studies highlight the potential of advanced doping strategies for extending the practical applications of graphene and other 2D materials. References: [1] M. J. Im et al., “Sandwich-doping for a large Schottky barrier and long-term stability in graphene/silicon Schottky junction solar cells,” ACS Omega 6, 3973–3979 (2021). [2] M. J. Im et al., “High uniformity and stability of graphene transparent conducting electrodes by dual-side doping,” Applied Surface Science 605, 154569 (2022). [3] S.-K. Hyeong et al., manuscript in preparation. [4] H. Choi et al., manuscript in preparation.

t191.a: The continuous scaling and three-dimensional integration of semiconductor devices require new material and interface engineering strategies beyond conventional covalently bonded semiconductor platforms. van der Waals (vdW) materials offer unique opportunities for next-generation semiconductor technologies owing to their atomically thin nature, dangling-bond-free surfaces, and the ability to form heterogeneous structures without conventional lattice-matching constraints. In this presentation, I will introduce our ongoing research program on stacked van der Waals semiconductors, which aims to establish fundamental material, process, interface, and device technologies for highly integrated three-dimensional semiconductor architectures. Particular emphasis will be placed on several key research directions currently being pursued in our group, including the scalable synthesis of high-quality vdW semiconductor materials, engineering of vdW interfaces, and reduction of contact resistance in two-dimensional semiconductor devices. In particular, vdW contact approaches utilizing layered contact materials provide an effective route to suppress interface-induced electronic states and reduce carrier injection barriers, addressing one of the major limitations of 2D semiconductor devices. These studies demonstrate how vdW materials and interfaces can provide a versatile platform for overcoming critical material and integration challenges in conventional semiconductor technologies and enabling future high-density, low-power, and vertically integrated semiconductor systems.

t192.k: Strain-insensitive Sensors; Stretchable Electronics; Wireless Electronics
t192.a: Skin-integrated electronic systems must undergo repeated stretching and deformation while maintaining stable electrical, sensing, and optical performance. However, tensile strain can alter the conductivity of interconnects, the characteristics of semiconductor devices, the resonance of radio-frequency (RF) components, and the geometry of stretchable displays. In capacitive touch and pressure sensors, in-plane strain can also generate unwanted signals that interfere with the detection of out-of-plane pressure. These strain-induced changes remain a fundamental challenge to reliable and practical skin-integrated electronics. We developed materials and device-level design strategies to minimize the influence of mechanical deformation on electronic performance. These approaches combine strain-stable functional materials, mechanically optimized device architectures, and material-property engineering that compensates for deformation-induced changes. We further explored geometric design strategies that preserve critical device dimensions or electrical responses during stretching. These concepts were implemented across semiconductor devices, RF components, stretchable displays, and capacitive touch and pressure sensors. The developed approaches enabled multiple classes of stretchable electronic devices to maintain stable electrical or optical characteristics under tensile deformation. Semiconductor devices and RF components exhibited reduced strain-induced changes in electrical response and operating frequency, respectively. Stretchable display architectures were designed to suppress deformation-induced variations in pixel geometry, while capacitive sensors minimized interference from in-plane stretching during pressure sensing. Together, these results demonstrate that strain invariance can be achieved through coordinated engineering of materials, device structures, and mechanical deformation. Strain-invariant operation represents an important step toward reliable skin-integrated electronics that can function independently of body motion and mechanical deformation. Combining functional-material engineering with deformation-aware device design provides a broadly applicable route to stable stretchable electronic systems. Remaining challenges include large-scale integration, manufacturing compatibility, long-term mechanical reliability, and extension of these concepts toward highly integrated, multifunctional skin-interfaced platforms.

t193.a: The chemical energy stored between seawater and river water, the so-called osmotic energy (or blue energy), can be harvested by an ion-selective membrane. However, previously reported membranes suffer from insufficient ion selectivity and inferior transmembrane ionic flux (low conductance), thus impeding practical application. For example, the output osmotic power density reported by most of existing ion selective membranes is typically below the commercial benchmark of 5 W/m2. Taking the inspiration from electrocytes in electric eel, which consist of a large number of sub-nanoscale rectified ion channels that allow unidirectional ion transport with amplified flux, we engineered two types of sub-2 nm-scale covalent-organic framework (COF) and metal-organic framework (MOF) based ionic diode membranes for osmotic energy harvesting. We show that the two COF and MOF-based heterogeneous membranes can rectify ionic current even in high salt concentration. We then probe application of these membranes in harvesting energy from salinity gradients. Notably, in addition to ultrahigh ion selectivity, these sub-2 nm-scale ionic diode membranes can achieve an unprecedented power density, higher than the commercial benchmark bandgap and outperforms all the state-of-the-art ion selective membranes. Our works would open up new avenues of using pinhole-free COF and MOF membranes towards next-generation highly selective and ultrahigh-performance sustainable energy harvesting.

t194.k: Conjugated Polymers; Block Copolymers; Stretchable Semiconductors
t194.a: Organic semiconducting polymers have attracted considerable attention for flexible and wearable electronics. However, simultaneously achieving high charge-transport performance, mechanical flexibility, and multifunctionality remains a major challenge because structural features that enhance charge transport often compromise mechanical robustness. Developing new molecular design strategies is therefore essential for next-generation organic electronic materials. We present a topology-engineering strategy using polyisobutylene (PIB) soft segments to develop multifunctional conjugated polymers. By evolving molecular architectures from linear block copolymers to molecular claw-type branched polymers, we demonstrate how polymer topology governs morphology, mechanical properties, and device performance. ABA triblock copolymers of poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) and PIB served as model stretchable semiconductors, where hierarchical phase separation maintained charge-transport pathways while improving deformability. Extending this strategy to n-type poly(naphthalene diimide-alt-bithiophene) (PNDI2T)-based ABA triblock and (AB)n multiblock copolymers effectively suppressed crack formation under strain while preserving electron transport. We further developed molecular claw-type PNDI2T tribranched multiblock copolymers containing three-armed star PIB segments. Their branched topology suppresses backbone aggregation and enables highly efficient sorting of semiconducting single-walled carbon nanotubes (>99.9% purity), yielding polymer/nanotube composites for optoelectronic memory devices. These results establish PIB-based topology engineering as a versatile platform for multifunctional semiconducting polymers in advanced organic electronics.

t195.k: Bi-MOF-assisted Photocatalysis; S-Scheme; Interfacial Charge-transfer Modulation
t195.a: The rising frequency of persistent organic pollutants in aquatic ecosystems, particularly antibiotics like sulfanilamide, diclofenac, aspirin, levofloxacin, and etc, raises major ecological and public health issues due to their chemical stability and propensity to cause antibiotic resistance. Conventional wastewater treatment techniques are typically inadequate in eliminating these micropollutants, emphasizing the critical need for improved remediation solutions. Recent research has shown that metal-organic framework (MOF)-supported composite photocatalysts can effectively manage antibiotic contamination in water systems. Their structural integrity, close interfacial contact, and homogenous component distribution were thoroughly tested utilizing a variety of characterization methods and a simple chemical production method. The integration of Bi-MOFs along with Bi₂S₃/TiO₂ and formation of S-Scheme heterojunctions benefited structural stability and improves charge separation, increasing the formation of reactive oxygen species and levofloxacin degradation. Photocatalytic kinetic analysis, time-resolved photoluminescence measurements, and radical trapping investigations show that photogenerated electrons, superoxide radicals (O₂•⁻), and hydroxyl radicals (•OH) play key roles in degradation. PL quenching efficiency and Relative carrier lifetime estimation suggested Bi-MOF/Bi₂S₃/TiO₂/NF Quenching efficiency of 64%, with Lifetime factor of 2.79. The suggested composites Strongest charge separation and enhanced photocatalytic activity is principally due to reduced charge recombination, increased light absorption, and effective band bending afforded by the heterojunction architecture. These findings demonstrate the promising potential of MOF-based photocatalysts for the scalable and effective removal of levofloxacin from polluted water systems.

t196.k: Boron Nitride Nanotubes; Photocatalysis; Charge Mediation
t196.a: Electrical conductivity has long been considered essential for charge mediation in photocatalysis. Consequently, conductive materials, metal cocatalysts, and semiconductor heterojunctions dominate current strategies for suppressing charge recombination. Here, we challenge this paradigm by demonstrating that an electrically insulating material can instead mediate charge separation through interfacial polarization. Polarization-active boron nitride nanotube (BNNT)-ZnO heterostructures were synthesized via in situ growth of ZnO nanocrystals on BNNTs. Their structural and interfacial properties were characterized using electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, photoluminescence (PL), and time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL). Photocatalytic degradation and radical-scavenging experiments were performed to evaluate charge-transfer behavior and identify the dominant reactive oxygen species. The intimate BNNT-ZnO nanointerfaces suppressed electron-hole recombination and prolonged carrier lifetime compared with pristine ZnO. Radical-scavenging experiments identified superoxide radicals (•O₂⁻) as the dominant reactive species, indicating more efficient utilization of photogenerated electrons. Rather than transporting charges through electrical conductivity, BNNT mediates carrier dynamics through its intrinsically polarized B-N lattice, generating localized electrostatic fields that spatially separate photogenerated electrons and holes. This polarization-driven mechanism enhances photocatalytic reaction kinetics while maintaining excellent cycling stability. This work overturns the conventional assumption that electrical conductivity is indispensable for charge mediation, establishing polarization-active insulating nanointerfaces as a new paradigm for photocatalyst design. By establishing BNNT as a polarization-driven charge mediator, this study introduces a new design principle for engineering semiconductor nanointerfaces beyond conventional conductivity- and band-alignment-based strategies. Funding: This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, and RS-2024-00411809).

t197.k: Self-Assembly; Block Copolymer; Covalent Organic Framework
t197.a: The rational design of functional nanomaterials requires precise control over molecular interactions, self-assembly, and nanoscale architectures to achieve targeted properties and functions. In this presentation, we highlight our recent efforts in developing functional polymeric materials ranging from complex self-assembled nanostructures to porous organic polymers, with emphasis on the relationships among molecular design, supramolecular interactions, structural organization, and sustainable applications. Polymer-based hybrid systems containing molecular nanoparticles, particularly polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane (POSS), provide versatile platforms for understanding how molecular geometry and intermolecular interactions govern the formation of diverse and complex nanostructures. These molecular-level design concepts are further extended to conjugated microporous polymers (CMPs), covalent organic frameworks (COFs), and related porous organic materials with tunable pore structures and tailored functionalities. Through rational selection of molecular building blocks, their interfacial interactions, electronic properties, and adsorption characteristics can be systematically regulated. Representative applications in CO₂ capture and conversion, photocatalytic hydrogen evolution, energy storage, and environmental remediation will be discussed. These studies demonstrate how molecular and supramolecular design can bridge complex self-assembly and functional porous materials toward sustainable energy and environmental technologies.

t198.a: Aqueous organic redox flow batteries pairing anthraquinone-2,7-disulfonate (AQDS) with bromine offer a potentially low-cost route to grid-scale energy storage. Increasing active-species concentration is the conventional strategy for improving energy density, yet the resulting performance loss is commonly attributed to reduced ionic conductivity. Here, we combine long-term flow-cell testing with molecular simulations to show that molecular association and the resulting transport limitations, rather than conductivity alone, can govern this concentration ceiling. Flow cells with 16 cm2 nitrogen-doped carbon-felt electrodes were cycled at 30 mA cm-2 using 0.5 M AQDS(NH4)2 against NH4Br. One cell completed 1000 cycles over 81.8 days at a fixed 17.5% depth of charge, maintaining an end-of-charge voltage of 1.34-1.40 V, with coulombic and energy efficiencies of 92.6% and 71.6%, respectively. A cell using a choline-chloride catholyte achieved 96.9% coulombic and 74.1% energy efficiency over 378 cycles before an abrupt charge-voltage runaway, preceded by a detectable voltage signature about 15 cycles earlier. Polarization measurements yielded an area-specific resistance of 2.3-2.6 Ω cm2 and a peak power density exceeding 139 mW cm-2 at 200 mA cm-2. Increasing the anolyte concentration to 0.7 M reduced coulombic and energy efficiencies by 7 and 5 percentage points, respectively, despite lower impedance. Molecular dynamics and density functional theory calculations explain this counterintuitive behavior: the oxidized species forms strongly associated, contact-stacked assemblies, whereas the reduced species remains comparatively dispersed, causing the anolyte structure to evolve with state of charge. Equilibrium Green-Kubo analysis further gives a zero-shear viscosity of 3.25 ± 0.25 mPa s at 1.0 M, 41% higher than non-equilibrium estimates. These results identify molecular association and mass transport as key constraints on concentration scaling in AQDS-based flow batteries and show that transport parameters used in cell models should be determined at zero shear and for each redox state.

t199.k: Thin Lithium Electrode; High Energy Density; Prelithiation Agent
t199.a: High-energy-density and high-performance lithium batteries are urgently needed. Surface-engineered stabilized lithium metal powder (SLMP) is synthesized using a simple, safe, and energy-efficient method that eliminates the need for high temperatures and hazardous molten lithium handling. By optimizing the processing parameters, we successfully engineers a tailored surface pro-tection shell, enabling the dual functionality of SLMP as both an anode material and a prelithiation reagent. The synthesized SLMP is employed to fabricate a thin Li electrode (LiSLMP) via a binder-free slurry casting method. The resulting electrode exhibits excellent stability in dry air and strong mechanical durability, as confirmed by bending, coiling, and adhesion tests. Compared to conven-tional lithium foil, a LiSLMP-based symmetric cell exhibits significantly improved interfacial stability and uniform lithium stripping/plating, maintaining stable voltage hysteresis for approximately 700 hours of cycling and achieving a high critical current density of 25 mA cm−2. A full cell paired with a LiNi0.6Mn0.2Co0.2O2 cathode demonstrates superior electrochemical performance, including excellent high-rate capability (130 mAh g⁻¹ at 1500 mA g⁻¹) and outstanding cycling stability (95% retention after 100 cycles). A three-electrode study reveals reduced anode polarization, which results in improved cell charge-discharge capacities, especially at high rates. Moreover, precise control over LiSLMP thickness enables a tunable areal capacity and predictable cycle life. This advancement also contributes to enhanced battery energy density and safety. Additionally, using SLMP as a prelithia-tion agent for Si/C anodes significantly improves the initial coulombic efficiency from 72% to 92%. In conclusion, above attributes position the developed SLMP as a key enabler for high-energy-density and high-performance lithium batteries.

t200.k: Covalent organic frameworks, porous materials, and lithium ion conductivity, and solid-state electrolyte
t200.a: Guest diffusion in bulk covalent organic frameworks (COFs) is fundamentally limited by misaligned layers in two-dimensional (2D) frameworks and discontinuous 1D channels in 2D and 3D COFs across crystallite boundaries. Here, we report new triptycene-based 3D COFs, HKU-2-PEGn (HKU: The University of Hong Kong; n = 2 or 4), featuring orthogonally interconnected channels and tunable polyethylene glycol (PEG) functionality that mitigate the diffusion limitations. These COFs contain channels up to 4.8 nm in width and a total of 67 channels larger than 5 Å (13 crystallographically unique) distributed along multiple crystallographic directions, facilitating channel connectivity between randomly oriented crystallites. Lithium-ion (Li+) transport in bulk samples of these COFs exhibits high diffusion coefficients across a wide range of Li+ concentrations, comparable to those of commercial liquid electrolytes, demonstrating that large, multichannel crystalline architectures effectively mitigate the diffusion anisotropy inherent to low-dimensional channels in COFs.

t201.a: Numerous high-capacity cathode and anode materials have been proposed for the development of high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries. However, their practical application remains challenging because large structural and interfacial changes during cycling often result in poor reversibility and limited cycle stability. Although material-based strategies, including elemental doping and surface coating, are important for improving electrode stability, the formation of stable electrode–electrolyte interfaces is also critical for sustaining electrochemical performance. In this study, electrolyte engineering was employed to regulate both the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI). Ether-based electrolytes containing various lithium salts were systematically investigated to modify the interfacial chemistry. In particular, the electrolyte formulations were designed to form a stable and robust SEI on the lithium-metal anode, thereby suppressing continuous electrolyte decomposition and stabilizing lithium-metal cycling. A dual-salt electrolyte formulation promoted the formation of a stable interphase on the lithium-metal surface. The modified interfacial chemistry facilitated more uniform lithium deposition and reduced undesirable interfacial reactions during repeated plating and stripping. As a result, the dual-salt electrolyte improved the reversibility and cycling stability of lithium-metal battery systems. These results demonstrate that rational electrolyte formulation is an effective strategy for stabilizing electrode–electrolyte interfaces and improving lithium-metal reversibility. Electrolyte engineering, particularly through the use of dual-salt systems, can complement conventional electrode-material design strategies and contribute to the development of high-energy-density lithium-metal batteries.

t202.a: Functional nanomaterials with intrinsically new and tailored properties are key elements for developing of eco-friendly optoelectronic devices such as solar cells, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), printed electronics, semiconductor-based sensors, etc. Recent progress of novel devices designs has led to significant advances in the fundamental understanding of functional nanomaterials. For example, perovskite solar cells have attracted a lot of attention thanks to their high efficiency, low cost, and ease fabrication using solution techniques such as spin-coating and printing. Development of chemical and biological sensors for selectively detecting multiple components in real time still remain a major challenge at the nanotechnology frontier of healthcare. Next generation display devices also require novel functional nanomaterials for reliable and efficient performance that can be easily processed using printing technology. In this talk, functional nanomaterials and composites based on metal, metal oxide and graphene will be lectured for the development of stable and efficient composites-based perovskite solar cells, high performance chemical and biological sensors for simultaneously detecting multi-analytes, and nanoinks of electronic materials for flexible optoelectronic devices.

t203.a: Solid-state batteries have attracted significant interest as a safer, higher-energy-density alternative to conventional Li-ion batteries, positioning them as a key technology for sustainable energy storage solutions amid the urgent need to mitigate global warming. Among emerging cell architectures, anode-free designs have gained particular attention for their potential to simplify manufacturing processes and further increase energy density. However, when paired with anode-free configurations, in situ-formed thin Li-metal anodes (< 50 µm) exhibit mechanical behaviors during electrochemical cycling that are distinct from those of thicker Li-metal foils. These differences become especially pronounced during lithium stripping, where thin Li layers are increasingly susceptible to void formation, ultimately limiting discharge capacity. Li-metal anodes were formed in situ on LLZO and stripped under various conditions. FIB-SEM, EIS, XPS, and other characterization techniques were employed to analyze void formation in the in situ-formed Li layer in comparison with thick Li foil stripping. In situ-formed Li anodes were then cycled at varying depths of discharge (DOD) to investigate the effect of DOD on the progressive growth of voids during cycling. Finally, strategies to enhance stripping capacity while suppressing void formation were explored by engineering surface roughness and modifying discharge protocols through the application of intermittent current. FIB-SEM, EIS, and XPS analyses revealed that in situ-formed thin Li anodes developed pronounced voids at the Li/LLZO interface during stripping, in contrast to thick Li foils, which maintained more uniform contact and delayed void formation. Cycling at varying depths of discharge showed that increasing DOD accelerated the progressive growth of voids, leading to a corresponding decrease in accessible stripping capacity with continued cycling. Engineering the surface roughness of the in situ-formed Li layer improved initial contact area and mitigated early-stage void formation, while modifying the discharge protocol through the application of intermittent current further suppressed void growth and enhanced stripping capacity, particularly under high-rate conditions. This work demonstrates that void formation at the Li/LLZO interface, exacerbated by increasing depth of discharge, is a critical factor limiting the stripping capacity of in situ-formed thin Li-metal anodes in anode-free solid-state batteries. Surface roughness engineering and intermittent current protocols were shown to be effective strategies for suppressing void growth and improving discharge performance, offering practical pathways toward realizing high-energy-density anode-free solid-state batteries.

t204.k: All-solid-state Batteries; Electrode Design; High Energy Density
t204.a: The widespread adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) as alternatives to fossil fuels to facilitate a greener and more sustainable future is the most remarkable technological development of recent years. Nevertheless, the exponential increase in energy demand has given rise to significant concerns regarding the safety of batteries, which necessitates urgent consideration. While conventional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) employ flammable liquid electrolytes, they have demonstrated susceptibility to thermal runaway incidents, which present significant safety hazards and necessitate a fundamental transformation in energy storage technologies. All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) have emerged as a promising alternative that is able to revolutionize the energy storage industry. One of the primary obstacles that greatly hampers the performance of ASSBs is the issue of point contact between the solid electrolytes and the active materials. This problem stems from poor interfacial adhesion and restricted intimate contact between the two components, impeding effective charge transfer and ion diffusion. The presence of non-conductive interfaces, voids, or delamination zones hinders the efficient diffusion of lithium ions, resulting in increased interfacial resistance and restricted usage of active materials within the electrodes. Furthermore, the issue of solid contact contributes to the localized stress concentration and mechanical strain that occurs during charge-discharge cycles. In this presentation, the concepts of intimate contact in both the anode and cathode will be discussed.

t205.k: Lithium Metal Battery; Protectiv Layer; Transfer-printing
t205.a: Next-generation energy storage heavily relies on lithium metal batteries (LMBs) due to their unparalleled theoretical energy density. However, the commercial viability of LMBs remains fundamentally hindered by severe morphological instabilities and continuous thermodynamic degradation at the anode-electrolyte interface, leading to active lithium depletion and uncontrolled dendritic growth. To overcome these interfacial challenges, an advanced design employing a hybrid composite protective layer was developed. An ionically conductive cross-linked polymer network was synergistically integrated with rigid inorganic fillers to establish a resilient artificial interphase on the lithium substrate. To prevent the premature degradation of the pristine lithium surface during cell assembly, a solvent-free transfer-printing methodology was adopted for the layer application. The tailored composite structure exhibited exceptional dual-functionality. The highly stiff inorganic constituents acted as a robust physical barrier to suppress dendritic protrusion. Concurrently, the flexible organic matrix ensured continuous interfacial contact and promoted homogeneous lithium-ion distribution via segmental chain dynamics. This engineered boundary layer effectively mitigated continuous solvent depletion and supported the evolution of a structurally sound solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI). Consequently, electrochemical evaluations demonstrated significantly reduced voltage polarization, highly reversible stripping/plating behaviors, and dramatically extended operational lifespans under continuous cycling. This materials-driven interfacial engineering approach successfully mitigates the critical instabilities of lithium metal anodes. By combining a scalable solvent-free application technique with a dual-functional composite framework, this strategy provides a robust and practical solution for deploying durable, high-energy-density energy storage system

t206.a: Isomerism can influence molecular properties despite identical chemical compositions. However, its effect on electrolyte chemistry for aqueous zinc batteries has received limited attention. Here, fumaric acid (FU) and maleic acid (MA), two geometric isomers, were investigated as electrolyte additives in aqueous ZnSO₄ electrolytes. Electrochemical measurements, spectroscopy and theoretical calculations were used to compare their interactions with water, Zn²⁺ and the Zn interface. FU and MA showed different hydrogen-bonding behavior and Zn²⁺ coordination due to their different molecular configurations. FU showed stronger interactions with Zn²⁺ and modified the solvation environment and Zn deposition behavior. As a result, improved cycling stability was obtained in Zn symmetric cells and Zn||MnVO full cells. These results suggest that molecular isomerism can affect electrolyte and interfacial chemistry in aqueous zinc batteries. Isomer selection may therefore provide an additional parameter for electrolyte design.

t207.k: Oxygen Reduction Reaction; Interfacial Proton Activation; Double Activation
t207.a: Proton-coupled ORR underpins metal–air batteries and H₂O₂ electrosynthesis, but catalyst design mainly tunes active sites while neglecting local proton delivery to oxygen intermediates. Polypyrrole (pPy) was coupled with Co, Mn, Cu, Ni, Fe, and Zn monoxides.
