ORR was examined by pH-dependent RRDE, dopant control, in situ Raman, operando Co K-edge XAS, Pd-membrane H-cell, and Zn–air battery tests. pPy lowered ORR overpotentials across both 4e⁻- and 2e⁻-biased oxides, with stronger promotion at lower pH. Mechanistic probes showed proton transfer from pPy, not oxide-site reconstruction, as the main origin. Polymer-assisted proton delivery enables double activation: oxide sites activate oxygen intermediates while pPy supplies protons. This pathway-tolerant strategy improves ORR to H2O2 and Zn–air battery performance.

t208.k: Interface Engineering; Materials Design; Energy Storage Systems
t208.a: In this rapidly moving era, the demand for sustainable energy systems has brought the need for advanced energy materials capable of governing the charge/ionic transport while maintaining the structural integrity via stable surface/interface electrochemical reactions. Although, researchers have made significant progress in materials counterpart, initiating from electrode’s combination to possible working electrolyte’s, however, the crucial interfacial aspect is being explored in the last few years from performance point of view. The interface engineering in these advanced material systems serve as a bridge between material component construction and their delivered performance. Thus, it is imperative to understand the importance of these electrode interfaces, so that they can be tailored to expediate enhanced electrode-electrolyte interactions through hetero-nanointerfaces designing, defect engineering, surface engineering and surface passivation effect. The present topic also discusses the strategies and techniques providing basic insights into interfacial aspects and their role in transforming the materials technologies to develop next generation energy storage devices.

t209.a: Zn batteries (ZBs) are considered promising next-generation energy storage systems because of their high safety and low cost. However, their practical application is hindered by poor reversibility and non-uniform Zn deposition, which compromise long-term cycling stability. In this presentation, several electrolyte engineering strategies for improving the performance of ZBs are introduced. In particular, approaches to suppress side reactions involving species other than Zn ions in the electrolyte are discussed. Electrolyte engineering significantly improved Zn reversibility and deposition uniformity. As a result, our ZBs achieved Coulombic efficiencies and cycling stability that surpassed previously reported results. Although practical commercialization of ZBs remains challenging, we believe that advances in electrolyte engineering will bring Zn batteries one step closer to practical applications.

t210.k: Cobalt-free Cathode; Air Calcination; Lithiation Kinetics
t210.a: LiNiO2 (LNO) offers the highest capacity attainable in the Ni-rich layered cathode family without cobalt, but its synthesis has relied on pure-oxygen calcination at moderate temperatures (~650 oC) to suppress oxygen release and maintain the Ni3+ oxidation state, which adds processing cost. We establish an air-calcination route to Nb-doped LNO by resolving how calcination atmosphere, temperature, and Nb incorporation govern lithiation and microstructural evolution. At 650 oC, incomplete densification leaves intragranular nanopores irrespective of atmosphere, and the lower oxygen partial pressure of air additionally slows lithiation: spatially resolved STEM-EELS of the Ni oxidation state reveals unlithiated, precursor-like regions retained within particle interiors, a stagnation that deepens upon Nb doping. Raising the calcination temperature to 750 oC overcomes this kinetic limitation - nanopores are eliminated and the layered phase forms completely even in air - but at the expense of primary-particle coarsening. Nb doping suppresses this growth, preserving a uniform radial microstructure with homogeneously incorporated Nb, and further stabilizes the layered framework against high-voltage degradation. The optimized air-calcined Nb-LNO delivers 244.3 mAh g-1 at 0.1 C and retains 86.7% of its capacity after 100 cycles at 0.5 C (2.7-4.3 V, coin cells). By eliminating the oxygen atmosphere required for Ni-rich cathode production, this route lowers both raw-material and processing costs of cobalt-free, high-energy cathodes.

t211.a: Prospects of the lithium redox-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) as a viable cathode process for the electrosynthesis of ammonia from dinitrogen and hydrogen or water are yet to be comprehensively and reliably understood. While enabling practical ammonia yield rates and faradaic efficiencies under model conditions, integration of the high-performance Li-NRR cathodes into practical electrolyser designs presents an ongoing challenge. To identify factors limiting the Li-NRR performance, our group investigates the process using a suite of advanced online and in situ characterisation techniques. This presentation will particularly focus on our recent studies of the Li-NRR cathodes by in situ X-ray radiography, neutron reflectometry and high-resolution multi-nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Our results suggest that the Li-NRR and the preceding formation of the solid-electrolyte interphase on the cathode are accompanied by a range of undesirable processes both at the electrode surface and within the electrolyte solution. These processes contribute to the irreversible degradation of some of current most prominent Li-NRR systems based on the tetrahydrofuran and diglyme solvents and lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide and borohydride electrolytes. Improvements in the stability of the Li-NRR-based electrosynthesis systems require new cathode designs, including those enabling operation at more positive potentials to exclude the Li0-induced degradation. A strategy to achieve such operation will be highlighted.

t212.k: Li-mediated Nitrogn Reduction; Hybrid Electrolyte System; Bipolar Palladium Membrane
t212.a: Li-mediated nitrogen reduction (Li-NRR) offers a promising route to electrochemical ammonia synthesis, but its reliance on water-sensitive non-aqueous electrolytes has hindered the direct use of water as a sustainable proton source. This fundamental incompatibility remains a major barrier to achieving the ultimate goal of electrochemical ammonia synthesis producing NH3 directly from N2 and H2O. In this presentation, we introduce a hybrid electrolyte system that couples Li-NRR in an organic solvent catholyte with water oxidation in an aqueous anolyte, thereby enabling the direct use of H2O as the proton source for NH3 synthesis. This system requires selective proton transport from the aqueous anolyte to the organic solvent catholyte while minimizing the water crossover. We first demonstrated that cross-linked ion-exchange membranes can diminish water crossover during proton conduction by the entrapment of bulky anions, but the usage of ion-exchange membranes cannot completely block the water crossover because of their water-mediated ion transport mechanism. Thus, we subsequently introduced a bipolar palladium membrane to transport protons through reversible proton absorption, lattice hydrogen diffusion, and proton desorption. In a continuous-N2-fed Li-NRR electrolyzer, the bipolar palladium membrane enabled water-fed ammonia synthesis with a Faradaic efficiency of 51% and stable operation for 12 h under potential cycling. These results establish water oxidation as a viable proton source for Li-mediated NH3 electrosynthesis. The progression from polymeric ion-exchange membranes to a bipolar palladium membrane overcomes the conductivity–selectivity trade-off of the conventional polymeric membranes and provides a general strategy for coupling incompatible electrochemical reactions under strict compartmentalization.

t213.k: Dinitrogen Activation; Asymmetric-site Catalysts; Electrochemical Ammonia Synthesis
t213.a: Ammonia (NH3) is essential to global agriculture and is increasingly considered a promising hydrogen carrier and carbon-free fuel. However, activating dinitrogen (N2) under mild conditions remains one of the most difficult challenges in catalysis. Beyond the strength of the N≡N triple bond, the high symmetry and nonpolar nature of N2 limit molecular polarization, directional adsorption, and selective electron transfer into antibonding orbitals. Consequently, conventional average energetic descriptors may not fully capture the pathway-dependent and site-specific interactions that govern N2 activation. This presentation will first discuss the thermodynamic, electronic, and kinetic origins of N2 inertness, with particular emphasis on symmetry breaking as a general activation strategy. Asymmetric catalytic environments can impose nonequivalent interactions on the two nitrogen atoms, thereby promoting N2 polarization, directional charge transfer, and subsequent N–N bond weakening. Such asymmetry may arise from low-coordination sites, defects, single-atom promoters, bimetallic motifs, interfacial structures, or local electric fields. The second part will highlight recent progress in electrochemical ammonia synthesis under ambient conditions. Advances in lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction include continuous-flow reactor development, electrolyte optimization, stable anode design in organic media, and mechanistic understanding of proton shuttles, enabling ammonia synthesis with a Faradaic efficiency of up to 61%. Calcium-mediated nitrogen reduction will also be introduced as an alternative pathway, supported by quantitative 15N2 isotope-labelling analysis and a Faradaic efficiency of approximately 40%. Together, these results connect fundamental N2 activation principles with practical electrochemical ammonia synthesis and suggest new strategies for designing selective, efficient, and scalable nitrogen reduction systems operating under mild reaction conditions.

t214.a: Electrochemical nitrogen reduction offers a promising route towards sustainable ammonia production under ambient conditions. Although lithium-mediated systems have been unequivocally demonstrated to produce ammonia, further progress is limited by low energy efficiency, competing side reactions and an incomplete understanding of how electrolyte composition governs reaction selectivity. Electrochemical nitrogen reduction was investigated using lithium-mediated systems across a wide range of electrolyte formulations. Electrochemical measurements were combined with cryogenic electron microscopy, infrared spectroscopy, electrochemical mass spectrometry, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS), quantitative chemical titration and density functional theory to elucidate the relationships between electrolyte composition, interfacial chemistry and reaction performance. Ammonia selectivity was found to be governed primarily by the relative chemical potentials of lithium ions and proton carriers in the electrolyte. This simple thermodynamic descriptor unifies the influence of salts, solvents and proton donors on the competition between nitrogen reduction, hydrogen evolution and lithium passivation. In contrast, the solid electrolyte interphase primarily suppresses overall reaction rates by passivating lithium, rather than directly determining product selectivity. These findings establish quantitative design rules for electrolyte engineering in lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction. More generally, they provide a mechanistic framework for developing more selective and energy-efficient electrochemical ammonia synthesis and offer guidance for identifying alternative redox mediators capable of operating at substantially less negative potentials.

t215.k: Ammonia Synthesis; Lithium-mediated Nitrogen Reduction; Electrolyte Engineering
t215.a: Ammonia has recently attracted considerable attention as an energy carrier. However, the Haber–Bosch process, the conventional method for large-scale ammonia production, requires harsh reaction conditions involving high temperatures (400-500 ℃) and pressures (up to 200 bar), resulting in substantial energy consumption (∼1% of global energy use) and carbon dioxide emissions (∼1% of global energy use). Consequently, the development of sustainable ammonia synthesis routes has become increasingly important. Among various approaches for green ammonia synthesis, electrochemical nitrogen reduction (NRR) has emerged as a promising alternative. Lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction (Li-NRR) has gained significant attention due to the strong reducing power of lithium, which enables activation of the highly stable N≡N triple bond. Recently, the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formed during the lithium plating step has been recognized as a critical factor governing reaction selectivity by regulating ionic transport and electronic conductivity at the electrode interface. Since the SEI originates from electrolyte decomposition products, extensive electrolyte engineering strategies have been explored to tailor its composition and properties. Notably, the formation of anion-derived SEI is considered a promising strategy for improving Li-NRR performance owing to its favorable lithium-ion conductivity and enhanced interfacial stability. In this study, we investigated electrolyte engineering for SEI modification in Li-NRR through both solvent and additive approaches to promote the formation of anion-derived SEI. Introducing a small amount of dimethyl sulfide (DMS) to the electrolyte altered the physicochemical structure of the SEI with Li2SO4 and Li2S resulting in improved lithium-ion conductivity and mechanical strength. This sulfur-derived SEI led to more stable cell potential for up to 20hr than the base electrolyte (10hr). Additionally, cationic ionomer additives mitigated anion repulsion at the electrode interface, promoting anion enrichment within the electric double layer (EDL). This facilitated the formation of anion-derived SEI and enabled ammonia faradaic efficiency of up to 90%. To further increase anion participation in interfacial reactions, solvation blending strategies were employed to introduce steric hindrance effects that weaken Li⁺ solvation and generate anion-rich solvation structures. In parallel, artificial SEI layers were investigated to achieve uniform Li plating and promote anion-derived SEI formation. Collectively, these approaches demonstrate the importance of electrolyte and interfacial engineering in tailoring SEI chemistry toward enhanced Li-NRR performance. Finally, to address the remaining challenge of low energy efficiency in Li-NRR, we propose an integrated ammonia synthesis platform coupled with water splitting, providing a promising pathway toward sustainable and energy-efficient ammonia synthesis.

t216.k: Li-NRR; Ammonia Synthesis; Solid Electrolyte Interphase
t216.a: Lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) is a promising route to sustainable ammonia synthesis, but its efficiency and stability are limited by morphological inhomogeneity of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). This study investigates in situ polymerization as a strategy to mechanically reinforce the SEI. 1,3,5-Trioxane was added to a LiBF4/THF-based electrolyte in Li-NRR systems. The resulting interphase was analyzed using complementary mechanical, morphological, and chemical characterization, and ammonia production was quantified by independent analytical methods. Trioxane-derived polymeric species were incorporated into the LiF-rich SEI, producing an organic–inorganic interphase with a higher modulus and a more uniform morphology. At the optimized trioxane concentration, the ammonia Faradaic efficiency (FE) reached 76.1%, a 23.4 percentage-point improvement over the base electrolyte, without additional overpotential and a FE of 79.9% was maintained during an 8 h cycling test. Co-designing polymeric organic and inorganic SEI components improves interphase integrity, suppresses parasitic charge loss, and provides a general strategy for efficient and stable ammonia synthesis. Reference Energy & Environmental Science, Accepted, DOI: 10.1039/D6EE01256F

t217.k: nonaqueous electrolysis; flow electrolyzer; reaction environment; Li-NRR; CO2 reduction; gas diffusion electrode; multicarbon electrosynthesis
t217.a: Electrochemical conversion of small molecules, such as N2 and CO2, offers a promising route to sustainable chemical synthesis. In nonaqueous flow electrolyzers, reaction selectivity is governed not by catalyst identity alone, but also by the reaction environment—the coupled interfacial and transport conditions surrounding the active interface. These coupled factors determine the local reactant concentrations, lifetimes of reactive intermediates, and ultimately control product selectivity. A central challenge is therefore to control the formation and fate of reactive intermediates by coordinating interfacial chemistry and mass transport under continuous operation. Here, we address this challenge in N2-to-NH3 and CO2-to-multicarbon electrosynthesis, revealing how reaction-environment engineering can redirect reaction pathways in nonaqueous flow systems. In lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction (Li-NRR), the gas diffusion electrode must simultaneously sustain N2 transport and accommodate Li deposition at the gas-liquid-solid interface. We find that conventional carbon paper is poorly matched to these requirements because its tortuous pore network promotes electrolyte flooding, while graphitic domains consume charge through parasitic Li+ intercalation before metallic Li deposition is established (Fig. 1). To decouple these structural and chemical limitations, a carbon-coated macroporous metal mesh (Ni@C) was constructed as a model gas diffusion electrode. The open pore architecture maintains gas accessibility, whereas the low-graphitization carbon interface suppresses Li+ storage and accelerates the transition to metallic Li deposition. This combined regulation increases the NH3 Faradaic efficiency (FE) from approximately 20% to 59%, demonstrating that efficient Li-NRR requires coordinated control of gas transport and Li interfacial chemistry rather than optimization of either factor alone. We further extend this reaction-environment concept to continuous nonaqueous CO2 electrolysis. In this system, selective C–C bond formation depends strongly on how activated CO2 intermediates evolve within the local electrochemical environment. By regulating proton delivery, water availability, and CO2 transport, the reaction can be directed toward multicarbon oxygenates, particularly oxalic and glyoxylic acids, rather than conventional C1 pathways. Control of the local CO2 supply further regulates the balance between C-C coupling and subsequent conversion of C2 intermediates, providing a route to tune product partitioning under continuous-flow operation. Together, these studies establish reaction-environment engineering as a general strategy for controlling intermediate formation, evolution, and product selectivity in nonaqueous flow electrosynthesis. Fig. 1. Design principles for carbon-based GDEs in continuous-flow Li-NRR. a, Schematic illustration of gas–liquid distribution and Li+ intercalation on the carbon paper electrode. b, Schematic illustration of gas–liquid distribution and Li deposition on the Ni@C electrode. c, Comparison of NH3 FE and Li+ intercalation capacity between carbon paper and Ni@C electrodes.

t218.k: Alkali Metal Hydrides; Complex Hydrides; Ammonia Synthesis
t218.a: Alkali hydrides (AH) can supply both electrons and hydrogen to activate N₂. As semiconductors, they undergo photolysis under UV irradiation to generate electron-rich surfaces. These features render AH catalytically active for ammonia synthesis. Catalyst preparation and testing procedure can be referred to our publication. We found a distinct reaction between N₂ and LiH, i.e., 4LiH + N₂ = 2Li₂NH + H₂ (R1). N₂ is reduced to N³⁻. Hydridic H in LiH is oxidized to H₂ and N–H species. Li bonds with NH forming stable Li₂NH. Li₂NH can be hydrogenated to NH₃ and LiH following reaction R2: Li₂NH + 2H₂ = 2LiH + NH₃ (R2). Reactions R1 and R2 form a loop for N₂ + 3H₂ = 2NH₃. This process is fundamentally different from the conventional TM-mediated routes. AH can synergize with a variety of transition metals via forming AH–3d metal composites or A–[RuH]₆ complex hydrides , enabling efficient thermal catalytic ammonia synthesis. Interestingly, LiH undergoes photolysis under UV illumination to form electron-rich color centers. Upon co-feeding N₂ and H₂, a multi-component Li–N–H surface forms, exhibiting a unique photoresponse that enables investigation of the wavelength dependence of the reaction potential and kinetics. We demonstrate that wavelength-specific excitation selectively modulates the kinetics of distinct reaction steps in LiH-mediated photo-driven ammonia synthesis, thereby decoupling the scaling relations that constrain thermal catalysis. Under combined UV–vis illumination, NH₃ yield, surpassing the thermodynamic equilibrium limit, can be achieved. Semiconducting AH can create a multi-component, dynamic and electron-rich reacting environment to activate and convert N₂ to NH3.

t219.a: The ammonia cycle, encompassing sustainable ammonia production and utilization, has emerged as a promising platform for carbon-neutral energy storage and nitrogen conversion. Despite rapid advances in catalyst development, the molecular mechanisms governing lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction (Li-NRR) and photoelectrochemical ammonia oxidation (PEC-AOR) remain poorly understood because of the dynamic evolution of catalyst surfaces and interfacial reaction environments under operating conditions. Direct experimental observation of reaction intermediates and interfacial chemistry is therefore essential for establishing rational design principles for efficient ammonia conversion systems. This presentation introduces operando attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS) as a powerful platform for real-time analysis of electrochemical interfaces. Time-resolved operando measurements were combined with electrochemical characterization to monitor transient reaction intermediates, solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) evolution, and interfacial microenvironment changes during both Li-NRR and PEC-AOR. For Li-NRR, operando ATR-SEIRAS directly visualized the dynamic formation, dissolution, and spatial evolution of the SEI, revealing the critical roles of LiOH, lithium alkoxides, and carbonate species in regulating lithium plating, nitrogen activation, and ammonia production. These findings demonstrate that the SEI continuously evolves throughout the reaction rather than acting as a static passivation layer. For PEC-AOR, operando spectroscopy identified transient NHx intermediates and elucidated the reaction pathways responsible for selective N₂ formation. Operando ATR-SEIRAS provides direct molecular-level insights into both ammonia production and oxidation by revealing the dynamic evolution of reaction intermediates and interfacial chemistry under working conditions.

t220.a: Ammonia is an essential chemical for fertilizers, chemicals, and emerging carbon-neutral energy systems, yet its production remains largely dependent on the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process. Electrochemical ammonia synthesis has attracted growing interest as a sustainable alternative, enabling nitrogen conversion under ambient conditions using renewable electricity. In this talk, I’ll introduce recent progress in electrocatalytic ammonia synthesis from various nitrogen-containing feedstocks, including NO, NO3⁻, N2, and urea. Our studies focus on catalyst design strategies aimed at enhancing ammonia selectivity and production rates through controlled surface chemistry, active-site engineering, and reaction environment optimization. Efficient electrochemical conversion of N-containing molecules to NH3 is demonstrated, highlighting the importance of catalyst structure in governing reaction efficiency and stability. These results illustrate the versatility of electrochemical nitrogen conversion pathways and underscore their potential for sustainable ammonia production and nitrogen resource utilization.

t221.a: Photocatalytic water spitting and CO2 reduction using water as an electron donor are promising reactions to solve resources, energy, and environment issues. We have developed various photocatalysts for water splitting and applied them to photocatalytic CO2 reduction using water as an electron donor. In the present paper, various metal oxide and sulfide photocatalysts, and semiconductor photoelectrodes for water splitting and CO2 reduction are introduced. Photocatalytic reactions were conducted using a gas-circulation system and a gas flow system with a high-pressure mercury lamp and a Xe lamp. Products were determined with gas chromatograph. RhCrOx/SrTiO3;Ir,Sb,Al has arisen as a visible light responsive photocatalyst for water splitting under VIS light irradiation. A Ag/NaTaO3:Ba photocatalyst gave ca. 90% of the selectivity for CO formation by the CO2 reduction accompanied with water oxidation to form O2 in an aqueous medium. A Rh-Ru/NaTaO3:Sr photocatalyst continuously produced CH4, H2, and O2 under UV irradiation. The selectivity for CH4 formation based on the number of reacted electrons was about 10%. Photocatalytic CO2 reduction using water as an electron donor under visible light irradiation were successfully achieved by a Z-scheme photocatalyst using bare (CuGa)0.5ZnS2 powder as a CO2-reducing photocatalyst. The selectivity for the CO formation of the Z-schematic CO2 reduction reached 10–20% even in an aqueous solution and without loading any cocatalysts on the (CuGa)0.5ZnS2 metal sulfide photocatalyst. Photocatalytic water splitting and CO2 reduction were achieved using powdered photocatalysts. A cocatalyst strongly affected the selectivity for the photocatalytic CO2 reduction.

t222.a: Rationally designed nanostructures can offer enhanced intrinsic activity and improved long-term durability, paving the way toward advanced, application-ready systems. Among metal@semiconductor composites, yolk@shell nanocrystals are widely adopted motifs, which incorporate a deliberate void between the yolk and the shell. The confined space can function as a nanoreactor, where concentration gradients across a permeable shell facilitate reactant/product diffusion. The hollow geometry enhances light harvesting through cavity-induced scattering and trapping. Moreover, both the inner and outer shell surfaces are accessible, maximizing the density of active sites and enabling cooperative inner–outer surface catalysis. By leveraging these features, yolk@shell nanocrystals have emerged as a versatile, high-performance catalysis platform, particularly attractive for photocatalysis. One of the most representative case studies is Au@Cu7S4 yolk@shell nanocrystals synthesized via a Kirkendall-effect-assisted anion exchange starting from Au@Cu2O core@shell templates. Upon sulfidation with S2-, unequal outward diffusion of Cu+ and inward diffusion of S2- generated a central void while converting the shell to Cu7S4, yielding the yolk@shell architecture. The apparent quantum yield (AQY) measurements showed activity enhancements for Au@Cu7S4 across both visible and near infrared (NIR) regions. This broad response arises from dual plasmonic effects. Au supports visible-range SPR, while non-stoichiometric Cu7S4 exhibits a lower-energy, NIR SPR. Yolk@shell nanocrystals have shifted photocatalyst design from materials discovery to interface engineering. Evidence shows that performance is governed less by composition alone than by how geometry and interfaces regulate photon management, charge transport, and mass transfer. Overall, metal@semiconductor yolk@shell nanocrystals have reshaped photocatalyst design for sustainable solar hydrogen production.

t223.a: In two-electron oxygen reduction reaction, the utilization of high-purity dioxygen feedstock will increase the production cost of hydrogen peroxide; while air is an abundant dioxygen source, so the direct air electrocatalytic conversion is expected to offer the green and low-cost synthesis of hydrogen peroxide However, the application of this technology has been limited by Le Chatelier's Principle: as comparison to high-purity dioxygen feedstock (100%), the dioxygen level in atmospheric air has been diluted by dinitrogen and other molecules, which dramatically decreases to 21%, so leading to left shift of the reaction equilibrium, thereby compromising the overall hydrogen peroxide productivity. Consequently, in the conventional concept, dioxygen has played a negative synergistic effect in the catalytic process, where the direct air conversion would generate hydrogen peroxide at much lower productivity as comparison to high-purity dioxygen counterpart. In this research, we have observed an abnormal catalytic phenomenon, where the spin iron-based functional unit catalyst can promote direct air-to-hydrogen peroxide conversion with a productivity surpassing by 1.42 times of high-purity dioxygen counterpart. Further mechanism study reveals the positive synergy of dinitrogen component in air, which can absorb on the catalyst and promote dioxygen activation, elongating the O=O bonding length from 1.31 Å to1.41 Å, thereby promoting dioxygen reduction process This work will attracted broad readership in catalysis and materials

t225.a: Indoor lighting accounts for a substantial fraction of global energy consumption, underscoring the urgent need for effective energy-recycling strategies in this domain. In this work, we report a high photocurrent density of 163 μA cm⁻² at 0 VHg/HgO using a cadmium sulfide quantum dot/titanium oxide (CdS/TiO₂) photoelectrochemical (PEC) water-splitting system specifically optimized for indoor illumination (2000 lux). To address the inherent instability of CdS/TiO₂ in aqueous environments, a phosphate (Pi) passivation layer was introduced on the photoanode surface, markedly enhancing stability by leveraging its negatively charged nature to facilitate hole extraction. Furthermore, a wireless, bias-free artificial leaf system was realized by coupling the Pi@(CdS/TiO₂) photoanode with a three-dimensional mesoporous nickel (3D-Ni) electrocatalyst, enabling sustained hydrogen generation. Collectively, this study advances the development of quantum-dot-based photoelectrodes for indoor PEC applications and provides a promising route toward sustainable hydrogen production under ambient lighting conditions.

t226.k: Atomically Precise Copper Clusters; CO₂ Electroreduction; Carbon-neutral Fuels
t226.a: Electrochemical CO₂ reduction powered by renewable electricity can produce carbon-neutral fuels and chemicals, but catalyst design is often empirical because conventional nanoparticles contain heterogeneous active sites. Atomically precise copper clusters provide defined metal cores and ligand shells, enabling direct structure–function correlations. A series of thiolate-protected copper clusters was synthesized by controlled reduction and structurally resolved by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Ligand identity, nuclearity/geometry, surface ligand vacancies, and dimensional assembly were systematically varied. CO₂ electroreduction products were quantified by gas chromatography and NMR, while spectroscopy, microscopic analyses, and density functional theory elucidated catalytic states and pathways. Aromatic-ligated Cu₁₄ clusters delivered formate with a Faradaic efficiency of approximately 40%, exceeding that of aliphatic-ligated analogues through enhanced structural stability and electronic modulation. For Cu₁₁ clusters, changing the ligand shifted selectivity from formate (about 45%) to hydrogen (about 82%); increasing the core to Cu₁₈ reduced formate selectivity. Introducing ligand vacancies into Cu₅₈ reorganized adjacent Cu sites and afforded methanol selectivity above 50%, whereas the intact cluster mainly produced CO. Furthermore, hierarchical assembly of Cu₇ clusters into a porous two-dimensional framework increased formate selectivity from 23% to 39% and suppressed hydrogen evolution. Ligands, core geometry, defects, and dimensionality operate cooperatively to control electronic structure, intermediate binding, and the reaction microenvironment. This integrated, atomically precise design principle offers a rational route to selective CO₂-to-fuel conversion catalysts.

t227.a: Bi-based oxides, including Bi2O3, Bi2O2CO3, BiOCOOH, and BiOCl, have emerged as promising photocatalysts for CO2 reduction because of their tunable electronic structures and surface chemistry. However, their photocatalytic performance is often limited by rapid charge recombination and insufficient chemisorption and activation of CO2. Herein, we demonstrate simple ethanol- and glycerol-mediated solvothermal strategies for the one-step synthesis of Bi2O3/Bi2O2CO3/BiOCOOH and rGO/Bi/BiOCl ternary heterophase photocatalysts, respectively. Their phase compositions and structural evolution can be readily regulated by tuning the Bi precursor concentration. In the Bi2O3/Bi2O2CO3/BiOCOOH system, multiple intimate heterophase interfaces promote charge transport and separation, while the Bi2O2CO3/BiOCOOH components facilitate CO₂ and H₂O chemisorption and activation, enabling efficient utilization of photogenerated charge carriers. In the rGO/Bi/BiOCl system, BiOCl serves as the primary light-harvesting component, while rGO enhances CO2 accumulation at the catalyst surface and temporarily conducts electrons away from BiOCl to suppress charge recombination. Metallic Bi clusters provide active sites for CO2 chemisorption and activation through reversible oxidation and reduction during photocatalysis. Importantly, the distinct surface environments of the two heterophase systems regulate their CO₂ reduction pathways and product distributions. The Bi2O3/Bi2O2CO3/BiOCOOH heterophase favors CO formation through -COO- intermediates, whereas metallic Bi sites in rGO/Bi/BiOCl promote deeper reduction and C-C coupling toward CH4 and C2H4 formation. These results demonstrate that engineering the composition and interfacial structure of Bi-based heterophase photocatalysts can simultaneously regulate charge-carrier dynamics and CO2 activation, and product selectivity.

t228.k: Alkaline Thermal Treatment; Mixed Plastic Wastes; Clean Hyrogen Production
t228.a: The recycling of commingled plastic waste remains a persistent challenge, since conventional approaches rely heavily on manual or mechanical sorting and typically employ energy-intensive, high-temperature gasification routes that release large quantities of CO₂. In this work, we introduce an alternative, low-carbon route based on alkaline thermal treatment (ATT) that converts unsorted mixtures of common plastics—polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyethylene (PE), and polypropylene (PP)—directly into high-purity hydrogen without any prior feedstock separation. In contrast to earlier studies that target single-polymer feeds or demand extensive pre-processing, our approach achieves uniform hydrogen generation across heterogeneous plastic mixtures while operating at markedly reduced reaction temperatures and minimizing the release of carbon-based gas byproducts. The central innovation lies in overcoming the inherent chemical inertness of polyolefins (PE and PP) through a straightforward oxidative pretreatment step prior to ATT. This treatment installs oxygen-containing functionalities along the polymer backbone, which markedly increases their susceptibility to alkaline conversion and allows PE- and PP-rich streams to react as readily as more oxygen-rich polymers such as PET. We further optimized the ratio of NaOH to plastic feedstock to maximize both hydrogen yield and product selectivity. To rationalize these experimental observations, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed, showing that the introduced oxygen functionalities reduce the activation barriers governing hydrogen-forming reactions in alkaline environments—offering a molecular-level explanation for the improved reactivity of oxidized polyolefins. A complementary life-cycle assessment (LCA) shows that the combined benefits of lower operating temperatures, in-situ carbon capture, and elimination of the sorting step translate into a substantially reduced environmental footprint relative to conventional thermochemical recycling. Taken together, these results outline a practical and scalable strategy for converting real-world, mixed plastic waste streams into a clean hydrogen fuel with built-in carbon management.

t229.a: Semiconductor nanocrystals have shown facet-dependent behaviors in electrical conductivity, photocatalytic activity, light absorption and emission, magnetism, piezoelectric and ferroelectric responses, and piezocatalytic activity. The origin for the emergence of all these phenomena can be attributed to considerable facet-specific lattice deviations in the surface layer region of a crystal, plus slight cell constant changes for different particle shapes, as revealed by synchrotron XRD patterns and fast Fourier processing of HR-TEM images. This surface layer should affect charge transport across a particular crystal face. The photogenerated superoxide radicals can be utilized to catalyze some organic oxidation reactions, and facet effect can strongly influence product yields. Moreover, facet-dependent piezocatalytically produced charge carriers and radicals can also degrade dye molecules and generate hydrogen in pure water. Photocatalytic organic reactions are carried out by irradiating Cu2O or SrTiO3 crystals in a solution of reagents. The generated superoxide radicals are involved in the reaction mechanism. For piezoelectric hydrogen evolution, ultrasound agitates the particles in water, and the excited electrons reduce protons to form hydrogen. The photogenerated electrons, holes, and superoxide radicals are utilized in reactions including arylboronic acid hydrogenation, aryl sulfide oxidation, oxidative amine coupling, aromatic thioamide cyclization, disulfide formation, benzimidazole formation, benzothiazole formation, and thio-ene reaction. SrZrO3 octahedra are notably more efficient than rhombic dodecahedra and cubes in piezocatalytic hydrogen evolution. Cu2O rhombic dodecahedra or particles and particles with certain shapes have been found to give notably higher product yields in these organic transformation reactions. This is presumably due to more efficient charge transfer to water and oxygen to produce radicals for certain crystal faces, which is linked to lattice deviation. Particle shape control is also important in piezocatalysis.

t230.k: Carbon Mitigation; CO2 Affinity; Electrochemical Upcycling
t230.a: The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (e-CO2RR), powered by renewable electricity, offers a highly promising route to valorize captured greenhouse gases into valuable industrial feedstocks. However, utilizing low-concentration CO2 directly from emission sources without undergoing energy-intensive purification and concentration process remains a major technical challenge. Herein, we report on the development of MWCNT|CuPc‐CoPc‐modified gas‐diffusion electrodes (GDEs) featuring molecular‐level dispersion of cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc) and copper phthalocyanine (CuPc) on the multi‐walled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) support via a facile H2SO4-assisted impregnation method. The introduction of CuPc effectively mitigates the detrimental - stacking and aggregation of CoPc molecules, allowing a high molecular-level dispersion of active sites on the MWCNT support. During electrolysis, in situ CuPc demetallization yields metal-free phthalocyanine (H2Pc), which exposes buried CoPc sites and significantly increases the fractional active site accessibility. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and CO2 temperature-programmed desorption confirm that the synergistic electronic interactions among CoPc, MWCNT, CuPc, and the in situ formed H2Pc optimize the catalyst's d-band center, resulting in a moderate, highly favorable CO2 binding affinity and an enhanced overall CO2 adsorption capacity (91.5 mol g-1). Owing to these structural and electronic advantages, the optimized electrode exhibits exceptional e-CO2RR performance across a wide range of CO2 concentrations (20~98%). Notably, an efficient single-pass conversion of CO2 to CO is achieved, yielding a high CO yield of 65.7 ± 2.3% and an energy efficiency of 54.8 ± 1.9% using 20% CO2 at an ampere-level current. Furthermore, the developed electrode demonstrated robust stability, maintaining CO faradaic efficiency > 80.4% over 72-h electrolysis under a simulated biogas atmosphere. These findings demonstrate the potential of molecularly engineered, multi-metallic phthalocyanine configurations for highly selective and stable conversion of low-concentration carbon emissions, paving the way for scalable carbon mitigation and alternative energy storage technologies.

t231.k: Hydrogen, Chemical hydrogen storage, Thermocatalysis, Formic acid dehydrogenation, Pd catalyst, Electrochemistry
t231.a: Hydrogen storage is pivotal for the sustainable management of energy harvested from intermittent renewable sources via water electrolysis. However, current strategies based on physical storage (e.g. compression and liquefaction) present significant economic challenges with regard to long-term storage and long-distance transportation infrastructure. Chemical hydrogen storage is a promising alternative due to its high chemical stability, low toxicity, high availability and compatibility with existing industrial infrastructure [1, 2]. This approach relies on catalytic (de)hydrogenation reactions between hydrogen and carrier molecules on a heterogeneous surface to achieve sustainable hydrogen storage cycles through circular chemical processes [1]. However, thermocatalytic (de)hydrogenation reactions are thermodynamically and kinetically challenging and require a process at a high temperature (>200 °C) [2]. Addressing these challenges requires a fundamental understanding of catalyst-molecule interactions through operando analysis and the design of advanced catalytic interfaces. Electrochemistry offers a unique opportunity to enhance thermocatalytic (de)hydrogenation in chemical hydrogen storage. Recent studies have explored the integration of electrochemical concepts into thermocatalytic processes. For example, open-circuit potential has been used to study the kinetics of formic acid (FAD) dehydrogenation on palladium (Pd) surfaces, where the kinetics of the reaction are explained by the mixed potential theory of two electrochemical half-reaction couples.[3, 4] Furthermore, the presence of charged species at the interface between the catalyst and the molecule (i.e. the electrochemical double layer) has been shown to modulate the work function and significantly improve non-Faradaic thermocatalysis. This phenomenon is known as the electrochemical promotion of catalysis (EPOC).[5–7] Nevertheless, there have been few systematic studies of the EPOC effect in the thermocatalytic (de)hydrogenation process, despite this being critical for improving the energy efficiency of chemical hydrogen storage. In this study, we investigate how electrochemical interfaces (under both Faradaic and non-Faradaic conditions) can be used to promote thermocatalytic (de)hydrogenation on Pd catalyst material. By probing key electrochemical parameters that govern the catalyst-molecule interface, we demonstrate how the electrified solid-liquid interface can influence catalytic performance, i.e. activity, selectivity and stability. Furthermore, we identify critical design principles for engineering these interfaces to effectively steer thermocatalytic or electrocatalytic pathways towards advanced hydrogen storage systems.

t232.a: Developing advanced electrocatalytic systems for efficient electrochemical CO2 reduction (e-CO2RR) at industrially relevant current densities under environmentally benign conditions is important but remains challenging. Herein, we report Au@Cu2O (n) core@shell nanocatalysts with outstanding e-CO2RR performance at -200 mA cm-2 in near-neutral media, where the Cu2O shell thickness is tuned by adjusting Au seed solution volume (n mL). The Au@Cu2O (n) nanopowders were synthesized, where the Cu2O shell thickness was modulated by adjusting the volume (n mL, n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) of Au core seed solution (0.25 mM) added to a solution containing a fixed concentration of Cu2+ ions. In 1.0 M KHCO3, the thin-shelled Au@Cu2O (n= 5) nanocatalyst achieves an exceptional Faradaic efficiency (FEC2+: 50.6 ± 3.3%) and an energy efficiency (EEC2+: 29.1 ± 1.3%) for C2+ products, outperforming its thicker counterparts (e.g., Au@Cu2O (n= 2); FEC2+: 19.6 ± 2.7%, EEC2+: 8.9 ± 0.9%) and individual control components. This enhanced performance stems from strong core@shell electronic interactions that modulate copper oxidation state (OSCu) and preserve the core@shell architecture. Intriguingly, iodide addition triggers divergent, shell-thickness-dependent effects. Iodide modulates both structural reconstruction and OSCu of the Au@Cu2O (n= 2) nanocatalyst, boosting C2+ product selectivity (SC2+) fourfold. Conversely, iodide disrupts the electronic synergy of the Au@Cu2O (n= 5) nanocatalyst, driving the OSCu away from the optimum and suppressing SC2+. These findings underscore the importance of cooperatively engineering interfacial electronic properties and electrolyte microenvironments for bimetallic core@shell electrocatalysts to drive efficient e-CO2RR at circumneutral pH.

t233.k: Metal Carbonate; CO2 Conversion; CH4 Conversion
t233.a: The escalating accumulation of greenhouse gases, primarily carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4), necessitates innovative catalytic strategies for their utilization as sustainable C1 building blocks. Transforming these thermodynamically stable molecules into value-added liquid chemicals, such as acetic acid, represents a critical challenge in modern heterogeneous catalysis. Conventional indirect conversion methods, including dry reforming of methane (DRM), are highly endothermic and require elevated temperatures (>630 °C) to achieve thermodynamic favorability. Furthermore, the direct coupling of free gas-phase CH4 and CO2 to form acetic acid is fundamentally restricted by an unfavorable positive Gibbs free energy change. To overcome these inherent thermodynamic limitations, alternative reaction pathways must be explored. Recent advances indicate that altering the chemical state of CO2 from a free gas-phase molecule to a stabilized, carbonate-bound species significantly alters the energetic landscape of the coupling reaction. By utilizing solid-state metal carbonates (MCO3) as pre-activated CO2 reservoirs, the entropic penalty associated with gas-phase coupling is mitigated, presenting a novel avenue for direct C-H bond activation and subsequent carboxylation. This strategy shifts the paradigm from traditional gas-phase catalysis to surface-mediated, solid-gas interactions, enabling the direct synthesis of valuable oxygenates under milder conditions. The proposed reaction pathway, CH4(g) + MCO3(s) → CH3COOH(g) + MO(s), was initially validated through computational thermodynamics using phonon calculations to determine Gibbs free energy changes. Experimental investigations were conducted using a continuous flow fixed-bed reactor operating at varying temperatures and pressures up to 30 bar. A diverse array of metal carbonates, including magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium, cobalt, nickel, copper, zinc, manganese, and cerium carbonates, was screened. To establish a reversible catalytic cycle, transition metal oxides, specifically Co3O4, were utilized. Furthermore, to mitigate structural deformation during repeated adsorption-desorption cycles, a core-shell nanostructure (Co3O4@mSiO2) was synthesized and evaluated for cyclic stability and sequence-dependent activation behavior. Theoretical calculations confirmed that utilizing metal carbonates (MCO3) as CO2 reservoirs shifts the direct coupling of CH4 and CO2 into a thermodynamically favorable regime. Experimental screening revealed that only specific metal carbonates, namely CoCO3, CuCO3, and ZnCO3, successfully mediated the conversion of CH4 to acetic acid. The reaction exhibited a distinct volcano-shaped temperature dependence, indicating that optimal acetic acid yield requires a precisely synchronized temperature window where carbonate activation, which occurs near the temperature of CO2 desorption, aligns with CH4 activation. Pressure optimization demonstrated that moderate pressures, such as 20 bar, selectively produced acetic acid, whereas higher pressures of 30 bar led to excessive surface coverage, diverging the pathway toward methanol and acetone. Mechanistic studies highlighted that carbonate-bound CO2 reaches a highly reactive state immediately prior to thermal desorption. Concurrently, adjacent metal sites activate CH4 into methyl-like species (*CH3). The direct coupling of this activated carbonate and the methyl intermediate facilitates targeted C-C bond formation. To transition this stoichiometric process into a reversible catalytic cycle, Co3O4 was employed to sequentially adsorb CO2 and activate CH4. While bare Co3O4 suffered from severe structural and crystalline deformation during repeated CO2 adsorption-desorption cycles, encapsulating the oxide within a mesoporous silica shell (Co3O4@mSiO2) provided robust structural integrity, maintaining stable acetic acid yields over extended cycles. Furthermore, product selectivity was highly dependent on the activation sequence; introducing CO2 prior to CH4 favored acetic acid formation, as confirmed by in-situ FT-IR showing distinct bidentate and monodentate carbonate species interacting with activated methyl groups. This study successfully demonstrates a novel paradigm for transforming inert greenhouse gases into valuable liquid chemicals by utilizing metal carbonates as pre-activated CO2 reservoirs. By synchronizing the thermal desorption of carbonate with C-H bond activation, the inherent thermodynamic limitations of direct CO2 and CH4 coupling are effectively bypassed. The development of robust core-shell Co3O4@mSiO2 architectures further enables a stable, reversible catalytic cycle. Ultimately, this carbonate-chemistry-coupled C-H activation approach provides a highly versatile, scalable, and thermodynamically viable pathway for carbon utilization, contributing significantly to sustainable chemical synthesis.

t234.a: Efficient electrocatalysts for the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) are essential for realizing a circular carbon economy. Here, single-atom catalysts (SACs) and dual-atom catalysts (DACs) based on metal–nitrogen-doped carbon (M–N–C) materials were developed using zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF)-derived supports. Eco-friendly synthesized two-dimensional ZIF-8 nanosheets (ZIF-8-NS) served as optimal supports for SAC fabrication. After incorporation of a Ni precursor and pyrolysis at 950 °C under N2, the resulting Ni-NC-NS exhibited excellent CO2RR performance with nearly 100% Faradaic efficiency (FE) toward CO production. To achieve high metal loading while preventing aggregation, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) was introduced as a strong metal-chelating ligand. This strategy suppressed Ni nanoparticle formation and enabled a high Ni loading of ~2.7 wt%. The resulting high-loading Ni SACs achieved a CO FE of 96.6%, a CO partial current density of –120.2 mA cm–2, and maintained FE above 90% over a wide potential range from –0.4 to –0.9 V versus RHE. The asymmetric Ni–N3C1 coordination structure optimized the balance between *COOH formation and *CO desorption, thereby enhancing catalytic activity. Furthermore, Cu/Ni dual-atom catalysts (Cu/Ni-NC) anchored on N-doped carbon were developed to maximize synergistic interactions between two metal atoms. With an optimized Cu–Ni atomic distance of ~4.08 Å, the DACs achieved nearly 100% CO FE at −0.9 V versus RHE in an H-type cell and 96.3% at −0.4 V in a flow cell, outperforming single-metal counterparts. Ni based single/dual atom decorated catalysts for electrochemical CO2 conversion was well demonstrated.

t235.k: nanocrystals; defects; interfaces; assembly; CO₂ capture; electrocatalysis
t235.a: Nanocrystals occupy a distinct materials regime in which surface energy, elastic strain, defect formation, electrostatics, and interfacial interactions can become comparable in magnitude. This sensitivity creates opportunities to engineer material responses that are difficult to realize in conventional continuous solids. Our recent work has focused on using nanocrystals both as finite three-dimensional model systems and as modular building blocks, with particular emphasis on how growth history, structural defects, and interface geometry govern subsequent catalytic, thermal, and electronic responses. Across epitaxial core-shell nanocrystals and ordered nanocrystal assemblies, we aim to move beyond viewing defects and interfaces as unavoidable imperfections and instead treat their geometry, connectivity, and statistical distribution as design parameters. By combining atomic-resolution characterization, correlative spectroscopy, automated population-level metrology, and controlled assembly, we seek to connect local structural motifs with collective function. This framework provides a route toward predictive design of adaptive catalysts, electrochemical materials, and energy-efficient electronic systems based on nanocrystal architectures. Applications to CO₂ capture and conversion will be discussed, focusing on how engineered interfaces can couple CO₂ adsorption with electrochemical reaction pathways.

t236.k: Catalyst Design; Ammonia Production; Hydrogen Carrier
t236.a: Ammonia is an essential chemical feedstock and a promising carbon-free hydrogen carrier. However, conventional ammonia production remains highly energy-intensive, while its sustainable utilization requires efficient catalytic oxidation. Electrochemical nitrogen-cycle reactions offer opportunities to integrate renewable electricity, pollutant remediation, chemical production, and energy conversion under mild conditions. We developed a series of advanced electrocatalyst design strategies for electrochemical ammonia production from nitrate and subsequent ammonia utilization. These strategies include heterostructure construction, cationic and anionic composition engineering, morphology-controlled binder-free electrodes, multimetallic alloys, and high-entropy materials. Electrochemical analysis, in situ spectroscopy, theoretical investigation, and flow-cell or zero-gap evaluation were combined to establish relationships among catalyst structure, interfacial kinetics, selectivity, and device performance. We developed a series of advanced electrocatalyst design strategies for electrochemical ammonia production from nitrate and subsequent ammonia utilization. These strategies include heterostructure construction, cationic and anionic composition engineering, morphology-controlled binder-free electrodes, multimetallic alloys, and high-entropy materials. Electrochemical analysis, in situ spectroscopy, theoretical investigation, and flow-cell or zero-gap evaluation were combined to establish relationships among catalyst structure, interfacial kinetics, selectivity, and device performance. These studies demonstrate that catalytic performance cannot be optimized solely by selecting an active element. Coordinated control of composition, defects, morphology, interfaces, and reaction systems is required to achieve efficient and durable ammonia production and utilization. This integrated materials-to-device approach provides a framework for sustainable ammonia-based energy technologies.

t237.k: Electrochemical CO2 Reduction; Electrocatalysts; Catalyst Reconstruction
t237.a: The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) converts CO2 into value-added fuels and chemical feedstocks, providing a promising pathway toward carbon-neutral and sustainable chemical manufacturing. Heterogeneous electrocatalysts play a central role in CO2RR by activating CO2, facilitating proton and electron transfer, and stabilizing key reaction intermediates. Among them, Cu-based catalysts have attracted particular attention because of their unique ability to promote C-C coupling through *CO dimerization, producing multicarbon (C2+) chemicals such as ethylene (C2H4) and ethanol (C2H5OH). Despite extensive efforts in rational catalyst design, simultaneously achieving high efficiency, selectivity, and productivity toward C2+ products remains a major challenge. One critical obstacle is catalyst reconstruction under operating conditions, which alters the engineered surface structures and active-site configurations that govern catalytic performance. Here, we systematically investigate the fundamental principles governing the reconstruction of Cu-based electrocatalysts during CO2RR. We identify a reconstruction mechanism driven by the selective and continuous dissolution and redeposition of metal atoms. Comprehensive in situ characterization reveals that *CO-induced dissolution-redeposition dynamics, together with miscibility-governed atomic rearrangement, dictate catalyst reconstruction and phase evolution. These dynamic structural transformations regulate both C1/C2 selectivity and the distribution between C2H4 and C2H5OH. We further demonstrate that electrolyte pH modulates reconstruction dynamics and propose actionable strategies for steering catalyst reconstruction toward targeted CO2RR pathways. These findings establish a mechanistic framework for predicting and controlling electrocatalyst reconstruction and provide new design principles for efficient and selective CO2 conversion.

t238.a: Flexible and wearable sensors play important roles in applications of electronic skin, healthcare, and human-machine interfaces. Thin-film transistors (TFTs) are the core electronic components for constructing large-area, active-matrix flexible sensor arrays with high spatial resolution. Metal oxide semiconductors (MOSs) based TFTs hold great promises for emerging applications in active-matrix flexible sensor arrays by virtue of their high optical transparency, large-area uniformity, sound electrical performance, and capability of being fabricated via low-temperature solution-based processes. Based on the low-cost, solution-processed MOS TFTs, we successfully developed flexible active-matrix sensor arrays, where each sensor pixel is monolithically integrated with one or more TFT devices. In this way, each sensor can be arbitrarily accessed and controlled by TFTs, providing fast-switching speed and high density. With the TFT back-panel, we reshape the flexible tactile sensors by transforming the passive, static, and dispersed sensors into active, dynamic, and highly integrated sensor arrays.

t239.a: Active materials have enabled significant advancements in medical diagnostics, military defense, and environmental remediation. Despite this potential, conventional non-electronic active materials face substantial bottlenecks, including poor spatiotemporal controllability, limited functional versatility, and overly complex fabrication processes. To address these limitations, we propose a versatile bio-hybrid active matter platform created by integrating a multifunctional liquid crystal (LC) droplet system with motile bacteria. In this study, we demonstrate that an asymmetric LC droplet in a preradial configuration—characterized by the unilateral localization of a point defect—serves as a sophisticated template for the asymmetric self-assembly of nanoparticles coated with bacterial antibodies. This specific topological arrangement induces anisometric bacterial binding on the droplet surface, breaking the systemic symmetry and triggering sustained directional motion of the droplet. The propulsion of these bacteria-fueled LC droplets can be finely tuned and reconfigured through the phase transition or molecular reorientation of the LC medium. These mechanical outputs, coupled with the bacteria's response to external stimuli like thermal fluctuations and light irradiation, allow for high-level command over active transport. Furthermore, the innate chemotactic dynamics of the integrated bacteria promote the autonomous transport of LC droplets toward designated targets. Our results confirm their efficacy in complex tasks, such as scavenging environmental pollutants and the controlled release of therapeutic agents, providing a promising blueprint for next-generation autonomous micro-robotic systems.

t240.a: Medical bioelectronics are evolving towards systems that adapt to physiological needs, function only for a clinically required period and then disappear or disengage without further intervention. This presentation will describe a materials-driven strategy that combines transient implants with adaptive skin interfaces for closed-loop bioelectronic medicine. The first part will trace the development of a wireless, bioresorbable cardiac pacing platform. A bioresorbable dynamic covalent polyurethane was developed to provide the softness, stretchability, interfacial stability and biofluid resistance required for operation on the moving heart. These material and device concepts enabled a fully implantable, leadless and battery-free pacemaker, which was subsequently integrated with skin-mounted sensors, wireless power delivery and algorithmic control to create a transient closed-loop system capable of monitoring physiological status and adapting pacing therapy. Reliable closed-loop operation, however, also depends on stable communication with the body through wearable interfaces. The second part will introduce an adaptive skin-interfaced hydrogel designed for prolonged electrophysiological monitoring under motion, perspiration and repeated use. Its potential will be demonstrated in wearable monitoring and human–machine systems requiring sustained biosignal quality. Together, these studies highlight how transient implants and adaptive skin interfaces can work as an integrated platform that senses, responds and ultimately withdraws when treatment is complete.

t241.a: Recent advances in soft materials, robotics, and manufacturing technologies have inspired many innovations in biomedical engineering like wearable electronics, implantable sensors, and new intervention methods. Soft acoustic materials possess extraordinary acoustic properties for long-distance wireless sensing and communication without the addition of electronic components or metal electrodes. To address the grand challenges in understanding the interfaces between human and medical devices, I will show our recent progress in the development of the medical devices using soft acoustic materials. Examples will be involved in this talk include: metagel ultrasonic sensor for wireless monitoring of physiological signals like strain, pressure, temperature, pH. Achieving multimodal and decoupled physiological signals is beneficial for an intricate and precise depiction of bodily health. Besides, wireless sensor in the form of embedded ultrasonic soft sensors (EUSS) is integrated with miniature machine, magnetic actuators, to address sensing-actuation challenges.

t242.a: High-precision molecular sensing at flexible bioelectronic interfaces is essential for dynamic health monitoring and personalized medicine. However, the complex cascade transduction of biomolecular signals, together with the mechanical mismatch between conventional electronics and soft biological tissues, compromises the sensitivity, stability, and functional integration of flexible biosensing systems. Effective regulation of biomolecular cascade transduction across flexible bio-interfaces is therefore critical for developing reliable and intelligent molecular sensing technologies. We systematically investigated biomolecular cascade transduction at flexible bio-interfaces from signal amplification, transduction stability, sensing–feedback integration, and intelligent information processing. Mechanochemical coupling was introduced to amplify molecular recognition signals; interfacial and cascade transduction processes were engineered to improve sensing stability under complex physiological conditions. Integrated sensing–computing–feedback architectures were further developed to connect molecular signal acquisition with adaptive responses, while artificial intelligence algorithms were incorporated for multimodal data fusion, pattern recognition, and predictive analysis. A mechanochemical transduction strategy was established to couple mechanical deformation with molecular recognition, enabling highly sensitive molecular sensing. Regulation of cascade transduction improved the spatiotemporal stability of flexible biosensors under dynamic physiological conditions. An integrated sensing–feedback cascade further enabled modality-compatible bio-signal sensing, information processing, and intelligent feedback within a unified interface. In combination with artificial intelligence, multimodal molecular and physiological signals could be fused and interpreted for intelligent recognition and predictive decision-making. This work establishes a systematic framework for regulating biomolecular cascade transduction at flexible bioelectronic interfaces, advancing flexible biosensors from individual molecular sensing toward stable, integrated, and intelligent sensing–computing–feedback systems. These advances provide a scientific and technological foundation for next-generation wearable and implantable bioelectronics and their translation toward intelligent diagnostics and personalized healthcare.

t243.a: Structural color arising from optical interference in nanometer-scale thin films provides a power-efficient alternative to pigment- and emission-based color, but optical sensing and reflective display have typically been developed as separate device classes. Integrating both functions in one flexible, low-power platform would enable conformable "optical skins" that report their environment while doubling as a battery-free display. We fabricate lithography-free metal–insulator–metal (Fabry–Pérot) thin-film cavities on soft polymer substrates, in which an ultrathin, lossy absorbing layer narrows the reflection band to produce high-purity, wide-gamut structural color from a compact planar stack. Functional layers, such as phase-change or electrochromic media, are incorporated into the cavity to enable active, low-voltage color modulation. The optical response is characterized spectrally and as a function of viewing angle, and the mechanical robustness is assessed under repeated bending. Because the reflected hue is set by the optical path length of the cavity, external stimuli—mechanical strain, humidity or vapor swelling, temperature, or analyte binding—produce a clear, reversible color shift that can be read out by eye or camera without external power. The same cavity, when combined with functional layers, switches its displayed color under low-voltage electrical control while remaining vivid under ambient light without a backlight, and the films retain their optical response after repeated bending on curved, deforming surfaces. y unifying colorimetric sensing and reflective display in a single interference architecture, this approach removes the traditional separation between sensor and display and does so in a mechanically flexible, battery-free form. Drawing on bioinspired strategies for durable structural color, the platform points toward multifunctional, low-power optical skins for wearable sensing, anti-counterfeiting, and next-generation reflective displays.

t244.k: Organic Bioelectronics; Ultraflexible Electronics; Neural Interfaces
t244.a: Seamless integration between electronic systems and biological tissues requires bio-interfaces that combine extreme thinness, mechanical compliance, biocompatibility, and operational stability in complex aqueous and physiological environments. However, traditional bio-interfacing technologies suffer from fundamental trade-offs between electrical performance, tissue mechanical matching, long-term barrier protection against biofluids, and sustainable power supply. Here, we present recent breakthroughs in advanced organic biomaterials, microstructural engineering, and device architectures to establish imperceptible, chronic, and self-powered bio-integrated electronic platforms. We established a comprehensive suite of soft biomaterials and scalable integration strategies: 1. A solution-processed biphasic percolation network combining fluorinated conjugated ionomers with metal nanowires for aqueous-insensitive transparent conductors; 2. A conductive hydrogel featuring an interfacial percolation architecture fabricated via controlled in-plane swelling and dry, soft-protective etching for all-organic neural electrodes; 3. Elastomer-assisted multidimensional phase separation and liquid metal (EGaIn) blade/spray-coating for waterproof optoelectronics and universal trilayer device integration; 4. Biocompatible adhesive–nonadhesive interleaving mechanics and wet-volatile surface-adhesion methods for body-mounted living cyborg insect systems. The transparent BIPIN conductor exhibited superior stability across diverse aqueous media (pH 4.6–8.6), enabling simultaneous electrophysiological recording and deep two-photon cortical neurovascular imaging without optical distortion. The hydrogel demonstrated an exceptional in-plane electrical conductivity of up to 2,500 S cm⁻¹ and low tissue impedance (8.9 kΩ at 1 kHz), enabling an all-organic, 9-µm-thick 128-channel electrocorticography (ECoG) array with chronic in vivo recording stability exceeding 550 days and minimal inflammatory response. Furthermore, 3.2-µm-thick water-resistant organic photodetectors maintained linear photoresponse and high detectivity during prolonged underwater immersion for continuous photoplethysmogram (PPG) sensing. Finally, integrating ultra-flexible organic photovoltaics with organic transistors or on-body modules enabled autonomous cardiac signal detection and wireless locomotion control of living cyborg insects with an output power of 17.2 mW without hindering natural mobility. These advanced biomaterial paradigms and structural design strategies successfully overcome long-standing electrical, mechanical, and environmental limitations at biotic–abiotic interfaces. This platform establishes a robust technological foundation for next-generation imperceptible wearable diagnostics, chronic high-density neural interfaces, and energy-autonomous bio-hybrid systems.

t245.k: Lithium Recovery; Electrochemical Membrane Separation; Graphene
t245.a: Electrochemical separation with two-dimensional laminar membranes offers an energy-efficient route to recover lithium from brines and spent lithium-ion batteries. Graphene oxide (GO) membranes are especially promising because their ångström-scale interlayer nanochannels sieve ions by size and charge, but their use is limited by hydration-induced swelling and by an inherent permeability–selectivity trade-off. This talk presents a unified strategy that uses aluminosilicate (AS) sol nanoparticles as a versatile design element to engineer the interlayer architecture of GO membranes, progressing from structural stabilization to nanochannel design that decouples selectivity from transport. We first show that subnanometer AS sols crosslink GO layers into swelling-resistant, hydration-stable membranes, enabling continuous lithium recovery by redox-mediated electrodialysis with a Li⁺/Fe³⁺ selectivity of ~42. Controlling AS particle size then reveals that spacer size simultaneously tunes the vertical interlayer spacing and the in-plane channel geometry, giving non-monotonic transport in which Li⁺ permeability peaks at an intermediate spacer size while selectivity is highest at the smallest. Finally, using AS sols as both interlayer crosslinkers and in situ vapor sources, we build a dual-scale architecture that interlaces narrow ion-selective galleries with expanded transport highways, raising Li⁺ permeability more than fivefold while retaining high divalent-ion selectivity (Li⁺/Ni²⁺ ≈ 246), with molecular dynamics simulations confirming the selectivity mechanism. Together, these studies trace a clear design progression: stabilizing the laminate, tuning a single spacing scale, and finally engineering two coexisting scales. They establish AS-based interlayer engineering as a general design principle for high-performance lithium-selective membranes.

t246.k: Goldschmidt's Tolerance Factor; New Simple Material Model; Halide Perovskites for Photovoltaics
t246.a: In 1926, Victor Moritz Goldschmidt (1888 – 1947), regarded as the founder of both modern geochemistry and crystal chemistry, introduced Goldschmidt’s tolerance factor (GTF). This year, 2026, represents GTF's special centennial year of recognition and extensive use to date. GTF, a unitless quantity and correlation relation, is mathematically expressed as the ratio of the lattice parameter determined using the A-site and C-site atom radii to that of the lattice parameter determined using the B-site and C-site atom radii within the "ideal" perovskite where A-site and B-site are cations and C-site is an anion, respectively. In comparison, the new "simple" material model is based on physical constraints of the perovskite. Using coordination dependent radii of Shannon, a scoring system is used to evaluate both GTF and NSMM. Recently, GTFF has been shown to be less effective than the coin-flip, which is significantly less effective than the new simple material model (NSMM), for a priori predicting whether-or-not a perovskite will form for a given composition. Here, we continue to discuss NSMM and compare it with GTFF, through numerous examples, about 3300 potential "simple" perovskites, as limited using Shannon coordination dependent radii. NSMM is shown to outperform Goldschmidt's tolerance factor by roughly several academic letter grades, roughly 15 to 25% higher score, when using Shannon coordination dependent radii. Adjustment, lowering of the anion radii and increasing of the cation radii to preserve distance, can be used to increase NSMM scores to roughly another 10%. Whence NSMM is a superior model and Goldschmidt's tolerance factor can be modified or discarded.

t247.a: The development of environmentally sustainable organic electronic devices using renewable biomaterials has attracted growing attention in recent years. Biomass is now regarded as a promising feedstock for sustainable functional materials. In this paper, we explore the use of dimethyl 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate (PDC-DE), a lignin-derived small molecule, as a functional additive in the p-type semiconducting polymer poly(diketopyrrolopyrrole-thiophene) (PDPP4T) for organic field-effect transistor (OFET)-based memory devices. Incorporation of 15 wt% PDC-DE into PDPP4T significantly improved charge storage characteristics and broadened the threshold voltage shift. These enhancements are attributed to the additional charge-trapping sites introduced by the biomass-derived additive. In contrast to additive-free devices, where the memory window progressively decreased owing to trap filling during repeated gate voltage sweeps, PDC-DE-containing devices exhibited a gradual enlargement of the memory window through successive programming and erasing operations, suggesting the emergence of electric-field-induced charge trapping. Furthermore, the modified OFETs successfully demonstrated synaptic behaviors. Excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) measurements revealed both paired-pulse facilitation and pulse-number-dependent long-term potentiation, closely emulating essential signal-processing characteristics of biological synapses. These results indicate that PDC-DE not only improves memory retention but also imparts reliable neuromorphic functionality to OFET devices. The present strategy highlights the potential of biomass-derived functional additives for realizing sustainable organic electronics with advanced memory and neuromorphic capabilities, paving the way toward next-generation bio-inspired electronic systems.

t248.a: Aloin is a naturally occurring bioactive compound widely associated with several pharmacological properties, while excessive exposure may cause undesirable effects, highlighting the need for reliable and sensitive methods for its determination. In this study, we developed a simple and effective fluorescent sensing platform based on bovine serum albumin-templated gold nanoclusters (AuNCs@BSA) for the rapid and selective detection of aloin. The AuNCs@BSA nanoclusters were synthesized using bovine serum albumin (BSA) as a stabilizing and templating agent and sodium borohydride as a reducing agent. The resulting nanoclusters exhibited excellent aqueous dispersibility and stable fluorescence characteristics, providing a suitable platform for analyte recognition. Upon interaction with aloin, a pronounced fluorescence quenching response was observed, enabling quantitative detection over a concentration range of 1–250 μM, with a detection limit of 1.12 μM. The sensing response was attributed predominantly to static quenching in combination with the inner filter effect, indicating an effective interaction between aloin and the AuNCs@BSA system. Notably, the probe exhibited a visible color change, while static quenching and the inner filter effect were the main fluorescence quenching mechanisms. The AuNCs@BSA probe was successfully applied to aloin detection in natural samples, demonstrating its potential for simple, rapid, sensitive, and visual aloin monitoring.

t249.k: Electrocatalysis, Nitrate Reduction Reaction, Ammonia Electrosynthesis, CuSnOx, Faradaic Efficiency, Interface Engineering.
t249.a: The electrochemical reduction of nitrate (NO3-RR) to ammonia (NH3) at ambient conditions presents an attractive and sustainable substitute for the carbon-heavy and energy-intensive Haber-Bosch method. In concurrently, it tackles the pressing worldwide issue of extensive nitrate pollution in industrial discharges and aquatic environments. Among various non-noble electrocatalysts, binary copper-tin oxides (CuSnOx) have attracted significant interest due to the synergistic interaction in which Cu active sites promote initial NO3 adsorption, while Sn adjusts the local coordination environment and enhances the generation of active hydrogen (*H) species through water dissociation. Nevertheless, attaining nearly total product selectivity continues to be a significant challenge owing to intense kinetic competition originating from the detrimental hydrogen evolution process (HER) and the buildup of multi-step intermediates. In this study, we introduce a CuSnOx nanocatalyst that is optimised for composition and interface, directly fabricated on conductive nickel foam substrates by a swift, scalable interfacial crystallisation method. Utilising the systematic electronic modification between Cu and Sn positions, the customised CuSnOx exhibits remarkable electrocatalytic performance and unparalleled selectivity for ammonia electrosynthesis. The optimised CuSnOx electrocatalyst, functioning in alkaline nitrate-rich electrolytes, attains a remarkable NH3 Faradaic efficiency (FE) of ~ 97 % at -0.5 V versus RHE and a high NH3 yield rate of 67 mol h-1 cm-2 , thereby minimising both HER and intermediate nitrite production.
