Thorough electrochemical characterisation and kinetic evaluations demonstrate that the refined Cu/Sn interfacial atomic ratio significantly modifies the d-band center, improving the adsorption energies of crucial nitrogenous intermediates (*NO3→*NO2→*NH3) and reducing the inherent energy barrier for hydrogenation of intermediates. Moreover, the resilient binder-free three-dimensional structure provides the catalyst with exceptional electrochemical longevity via prolonged chronoamperometry electrolysis, exhibiting no observable structural deterioration or active-phase separation. This research illustrates the critical importance of binary oxide electronic engineering in attaining near-quantitative selectivity, providing a feasible and sustainable design approach for enhanced electrocatalytic nitrogen circularity.

t250.a: Photoinduced energy and electron transfer processes offer a convenient way to convert light energy into electrical or chemical energy. These processes remain the basis of operation of thin film solar cells, light emitting devices and optoelectronic devices, and solar fuel generation. Furthermore, modulating the interfacial transfer of electrons and holes following bandgap excitation is a critical factor in determining the effectiveness of photocatalysis. We have synthesized CsPbX3 (X= Br and Cl) quantum dots of different bandgap through size quantization as well as by varying Br:I composition. The energy and electron transfer processes between CsPbX3 QDs and a molecular acceptor have been probed through transient absorption and emission measurements. The analyzed data provides insight into the kinetics and mechanism of energy and electron transfer processes Bandgap tuning achieved through compositional changes allowed us to modulate singlet and triplet energy transfer pathways in such assemblies. With careful selection of semiconductor nanocrystal donor and one or more chromophores, it is possible to induce down conversion or up conversion of incident photons. Such a strategy of building semiconductor-molecular arrays has potential applications to tailor the emissive properties of optoelectronic and display devices. Bandgap engineering of QDs achieved through composition and size quantization, has allowed us to demonstrate precise control over photoinduced interfacial charge transfer processes. The forward electron (and hole) transfer to surface-bound probe molecules is dependent on the thermodynamic driving force, viz., the energy gap between the band edge and the acceptor’s redox potential. Using Marcus theory, we correlate the rate constants of electron transfer to surface-bound probes with the the energy gap. The role of bandgap engineering in enhancing the selectivity and efficiency of photocatalytic systems will also be presented. Photoinduced energy and electron transfer between semiconductor donor and a molecular acceptor can be tuned through bandgap engineering of quantum dots. By integrating upconversion or singlet fission processes of such semiconductor-molecular hybrids in solar cells can further improve the efficiency of harvesting low energy photons. Similarly, by modulating forward electron and hole transfer process through bandgap engineering allows tuning of photocatalyic properties.

t251.k: lithium-ion battery recycling; direct regeneration; order retention; repair window; black mass; fluorine management; green chemistry
t251.a: Lithium-ion battery (LIB) recycling is still benchmarked mainly by elemental recovery yield, purity, and cost. As cathodes shift toward cobalt-lean, LiFePO4 (LFP), and sodium-ion chemistries, these endpoint metrics become insufficient, because routes with similar recovery yields can retain very different amounts of manufacturable structure. Here, we present an order-retention framework that treats the hierarchical order of a spent cell, across the pack, cell, electrode, particle, and interphase scales, as a recoverable asset. The framework comprises three linked tools. A reset-level taxonomy places pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy, thermal conditioning, and direct regeneration on a continuum of irreversible reset depth. A reversibility ledger classifies end-of-life disorder as repairable, conditionally repairable, or effectively irreversible. A repair window bounds the conditions under which direct regeneration remains selective. From published data, we propose approximate repair-window boundaries: lithium inventory loss below 20–30%, total Cu below 1 at% with no metallic Cu, fines (<10 µm) below 20–25 wt%, fluorine below 1–2 wt% in removable form, and rock-salt reconstruction shallower than 5–10 nm. These boundaries are indicative and are intended to be refined as standardized data accumulate. Applied to a published industrial LiNi0.6Co0.2Mn0.2O2 (NMC622) black mass, the ledger identifies a conditionally repairable feed: the layered lattice is retained, but the fluorine load (about 4.3 wt% bulk PVDF) and a fines fraction of about 55 wt% lie outside the window. The same dataset shows that pyrolysis at 600 °C lowers surface fluorine to about 2 wt% but partially resets particle structure, which indicates that milder fluorine management is needed before relithiation. Within this framework, unit operations act either as order filters or as entropy amplifiers, and fluorinated binder and electrolyte residues are the dominant amplifiers. Because reagent, energy, water, and fluorinated-emission burdens increase with reset depth, order retention serves as a green-chemistry design metric. It also turns route selection into a matching problem between the incoming disorder state and the reset depth that a route imposes. Reference: S. Eeamtak et al., Green Chem., 2026, 28, 15843–15869. DOI: 10.1039/d6gc03171d Acknowledgement: This work was funded by the National Research Council of Thailand (NRCT), Grant No. N11A670659. Preferred symposium: Symposium 2, Advanced Materials for Electrochemical Energy Storage (alternative: Symposium 10)

t252.a: Electrochemical nitrate reduction (NO₃RR) offers a sustainable route to ammonia, but its efficiency is constrained by sluggish proton-coupled hydrogenation kinetics and poor selectivity at low overpotentials. Cu drives selective NO₃RR yet suffers from a rate-limiting NO₂⁻-to-NH₃ step. We present two complementary strategies—heterogeneous active-site coupling and interfacial-water engineering—to overcome these bottlenecks. A Co–Cu mixed single-atom/cluster catalyst (Co–Cu SCC) was synthesized by ligand-calcination pyrolysis and characterized by AC-HAADF-STEM, XPS, and FT-EXAFS. Separately, an inverse Cu–CeO₂ catalyst was fabricated by impregnation and probed by in situ ATR-SEIRAS and ab initio molecular dynamics to resolve interfacial water dynamics. Performance was evaluated in H-type and membrane-electrode-assembly cells. The Co–Cu SCC exhibited tandem catalysis in which Cu sites catalyze NO₃⁻-to-NO₂⁻ and Co sites catalyze NO₂⁻-to-NH₃, bypassing each site's rate-determining step and delivering 91.2% NH₃ Faradaic efficiency at –0.3 V vs. RHE, with stable multigram NH₄Cl production. The inverse Cu–CeO₂ catalyst restructured interfacial water, enriching both labile free water and four-hydrogen-bonded networks that accelerate proton relay, achieving 83.9% FE at –0.35 V and a 14-fold improvement at –0.05 V vs. RHE. Both site-level tandem coupling and interfacial-water structuring lower kinetic barriers for proton-coupled hydrogenation, establishing dual design principles for efficient, selective ammonia electrosynthesis.

t253.k: solar hydrogen production, photocatalysis, yolk@shell nanocrystals
t253.a: This presentation highlights the structural engineering of yolk@shell nanocrystals for sustainable solar hydrogen production. Yolk@shell nanocrystals consisting of a mobile Au yolk encapsulated within a permeable, hollow semiconductor shell possess several unique structural and functional characteristics that make them attractive platforms for photocatalysis. The mobility of the Au yolk can induce a micro-stirring effect that enhances local mass transport, while the nanoreactor-like void facilitates the diffusion of reactants and products, thereby accelerating reaction kinetics. Meanwhile, the metal/semiconductor interface between the Au yolk and the semiconductor shell promotes directional charge separation and suppresses carrier recombination, contributing to enhanced photocatalytic performance. To further optimize photocatalytic efficiency, structural engineering strategies involving precise control over void size and shell thickness have been developed to regulate photon harvesting, charge transfer, and molecular transport. This presentation will discuss several representative yolk@shell systems to demonstrate how these structural parameters govern photocatalytic behavior and to highlight the versatility, efficiency, and potential of yolk@shell nanocrystals for sustainable solar hydrogen production.

t254.k: Green Ammonia; Solar Energy; Thermochemical Cycle
t254.a: Ammonia is an important chemical for fertilizer production (70% of its 240 million-ton annual output) and a promising carbon-free fuel. However, the conventional Haber-Bosch process for ammonia synthesis consumes ~2% of global energy and emits ~1.8% of CO₂. Solar-driven thermochemical ammonia production offers a sustainable alternative, using renewable energy to decarbonize fertilizer production. This approach employs redox-active metal oxides (e.g., perovskites like SrFeOx) in a two-stage process: oxidation by air followed by thermal reduction using concentrated solar energy. The resulting high-purity nitrogen, combined with solar-derived hydrogen (from water-splitting via electrolysis, thermochemical, or photocatalytic methods), produces green ammonia, a fully renewable fuel and fertilizer precursor. A key advantage is the surplus oxygen generated during nitrogen and hydrogen production, which can be integrated into nitric acid plants (e.g., the Ostwald process) as oxygen-enriched air. This can boost nitric acid output and reduces capital costs. Techno-economic assessments show optimal oxygen injection could cut costs by ~€0.41 million. Currently, green ammonia’s viability is hindered by high green hydrogen prices, but CO₂ pricing could soon make it economically feasible. This work highlights the potential of solar-powered ammonia synthesis, emphasizing the synergy between renewable nitrogen/hydrogen production and oxygen utilization in nitric acid synthesis. By leveraging solar energy and byproduct integration, this method could reduce emissions and costs in fertilizer production, paving the way for sustainable agriculture and energy solutions.

t255.k: Neat Hydrous Hydrazine; Hydrogen Carrier; Rhenium Catalyst
t255.a: Hydrogen is central to a sustainable energy future, but its low volumetric density and safety concerns complicate storage and transportation. Liquid hydrogen requires cryogenic conditions, while liquid organic hydrogen carriers generally require energy-intensive dehydrogenation and recovery of the depleted carrier. Hydrous hydrazine (HH, N₂H₄·H₂O) offers a carbon-free liquid alternative that could enable one-pass hydrogen generation directly at the point of use. However, complete and selective hydrogen release from neat HH under mild conditions remains challenging. Pt- and Ni-doped rhenium-based thermocatalysts (PtNi@Re) were prepared and evaluated for the decomposition of neat HH without dilution. Catalytic performance was examined at 25–80 °C in terms of conversion, hydrogen selectivity, turnover frequency (TOF), and H₂ mass activity. PtNi@Re enabled the complete decomposition of neat HH (purity >98%) under mild thermal conditions, achieving 100% H₂ selectivity without NH₃ formation. The catalyst delivered a maximum TOF of 20,396 h⁻¹ and an H₂ mass activity of 19,200 mL min⁻¹ g⁻¹. This ultrafast hydrogen release enabled direct coupling of hydrogen generation with its immediate utilization, eliminating the need for intermediate hydrogen storage and compression. The selective and ultrafast decomposition of neat HH establishes a fuel-like, one-pass approach to hydrogen delivery from a carbon-free liquid carrier. This system provides a promising basis for direct hydrogen delivery in onboard energy systems and for scalable hydrogen generation under mild operating conditions.

t256.k: Electrochemical Adipic Acid Synthesis; Hybrid Water Splitting; Nitric Acid Free Synthesis
t256.a: Electrochemical adipic acid synthesis offers a promising route to replace nitric acid oxidation with an anodic process that can be coupled with useful cathodic reactions. Nickel oxyhydroxide is an active phase for cyclohexanone oxidation, but strategies to increase the reaction rate remain important. This study explored molybdenum-containing nickel electrocatalysts and catalyst reconstruction as routes to improve adipic acid production. Undoped and chromium-, molybdenum-, or tungsten-doped Ni(OH)2 were synthesized on nickel foam by a hydrothermal method. NiMoO4·xH2O was also prepared and electrochemically reconstructed to γ-NiOOH. Electrocatalytic activity was evaluated in a three-electrode H-type cell containing 0.5 M KOH and 0.4 M cyclohexanone. Products were quantified by HPLC, while catalyst morphology and composition were examined by SEM and EDX. NiOOH reduction charge was used to compare electrochemically active nickel Among the group 6 dopants, molybdenum-doped Ni(OH)2 showed the highest partial current density for adipic acid while maintaining faradaic efficiency comparable to the other catalysts. At approximately 1.45 V vs. RHE, faradaic efficiencies reached about 80%, while OER became more competitive at positive potentials. Reconstructed γ-NiOOH derived from NiMoO4·xH2O also outperformed benchmark electrodeposited Ni(OH)2. EDX showed substantial molybdenum leaching during electrolysis. Despite their higher reaction rates, the molybdenum-containing catalysts did not show larger NiOOH reduction charges, indicating enhanced activity beyond simple active site densification. Molybdenum-induced reconstruction produces highly active nickel-based electrocatalysts for adipic acid synthesis. These findings suggest that molybdenum leaching generates a promotional effect not captured by NiOOH reduction charge alone and may enhance intrinsic site activity.

t257.a: Developing photocatalysts capable of harvesting solar energy across a broad spectral range, from the ultraviolet to the near-infrared (NIR), is essential for maximizing solar energy utilization. However, the limited availability of photocatalysts that effectively respond to NIR irradiation continues to hinder the development of efficient full-spectrum solar hydrogen production. Monoclinic TiO₂ nanowires, a relatively uncommon crystallographic phase of TiO₂, were synthesized and subsequently decorated with Au nanoparticles encapsulated by hollow Cu₇S₄ shells to construct TiO₂–Au@Cu₇S₄ heterostructure nanowires. Their structural, optical, and photocatalytic properties were systematically investigated. The TiO₂–Au@Cu₇S₄ heterostructure exhibited remarkable characteristics favorable for solar hydrogen production. The band alignment among TiO₂, Au, and Cu₇S₄ established a Z-scheme charge separation mechanism, enhancing carrier utilization while maintaining strong redox capability. Incorporation of Au@Cu₇S₄ significantly broadened the light-harvesting capability of TiO₂ into the visible and NIR regions through the intrinsic bandgap absorption of Cu₇S₄ together with the localized surface plasmon resonance of both Au and Cu₇S₄. Furthermore, the hydrophilic TiO₂ surface improved water accessibility, promoting interactions between water molecules and the photocatalyst surface. Consequently, the heterostructure achieved apparent quantum yields of 10.51% at 300 nm, 4.38% at 450 nm, 4.17% at 800 nm, and 3.66% at 1800 nm, outperforming all previously reported NIR-responsive TiO₂-based photocatalysts for hydrogen production. The present work demonstrates a practical strategy for designing full-spectrum-responsive TiO₂-based photocatalysts for solar hydrogen production. The synergistic integration of Z-scheme charge separation, plasmon-enhanced light harvesting, and heterostructure engineering provides an effective design principle for advanced photocatalytic solar energy conversion.

t258.a: Converting biodiesel-derived crude glycerol into high-value glycerol carbonate (GC) via solvent-free transesterification requires highly active and robust catalysts. Herein, we developed tunable Ca–Mg–Al layered double hydroxide (LDH)-derived mixed metal oxides (MMOs) for this sustainable transformation. The optimized mesoporous catalyst (CMA-30-600), featuring ideally balanced basicity, achieved a 55% GC yield and 99% selectivity under mild conditions (80 °C, 1 h). Furthermore, it demonstrated excellent reusability over three cycles with a mass-normalized turnover frequency of 0.62 mol·g⁻1·h⁻1. Aspen Plus process simulation confirmed the industrial viability of this route, projecting a net profit of 1148.6 USD·h⁻1. This efficient catalytic system offers a sustainable pathway to enhance the economic feasibility of biodiesel manufacturing.

t259.a: The mounting environmental concerns stemming from plastic waste accumulation have spurred a critical need for innovative and sustainable strategies to address the challenges posed by discarded polymers. Among these, polyolefins (PP and PE) stand as a prominent contributor to the global plastic waste burden, owing to their wide-ranging applications across industries. However, the conventional linear trajectory of plastic production, disposal, and waste generation is no longer tenable. This paradigm shift calls for transformative approaches that not only divert plastic waste from landfills and oceans but also harness its latent value to contribute to the creation of high-demand materials. Catalytic upcycling, especially when guided by an ingenious Ru/ZrO2 or NiW/WOx catalyst, presents an unprecedented opportunity to selectively convert polypropylene into alkanes—a fundamental class of hydrocarbons—yielding a sustainable pathway toward valuable hydrocarbon transformation. Herein, we report that through a solvent-free process, a 2.5 wt% Ru-ZrO2 or NiW/WOx catalyst converts PP and PE using H2 into 72% liquid fuels with a jet-fuel-ranged hydrocarbons selectivity at ca. 77%, along with LPG product at a ca. 28% yield. The polyolefins can be catalytically converted to jet-fuel hydrocarbons over a bifunctional catalyst.

t260.a: Electrochemical energy conversion is a surface process, yet the active material is never used alone. In a real device it forms a composite electrode with binders and electrolyte. These nominally inactive components decide where the reaction actually happens — accessible surface, wettability and triple-phase boundary, local ion transport, and the mechanical state of the interface. This talk treats that interfacial environment as a design variable in its own right. Binders bearing polar anchoring groups were designed and their adsorption on active particles and current collectors quantified by density functional theory and molecular dynamics. Mechanically adaptive interfaces based on shear-responsive polymers were characterized rheologically and followed by in-situ transmission electron microscopy during operation. Anchoring confines the polymer near the surface instead of spreading it over the surface, preserving accessible sites while improving adhesion, wettability, and ion transport, and enabling crack-free electrodes at high loading. Shear-responsive designs stiffen only when the interface is disturbed by volume change, gas evolution, or non-uniform deposition, preserving electrical contact and interfacial integrity under operation. Anchoring strength, local wettability, and mechanical adaptivity recur as the descriptors that govern composite electrodes. They are set by the composite architecture rather than by a specific chemistry, so designing the interfacial environment improves practical performance without redesigning the active material.

t261.a: Naphtha is a key intermediate product in the petrochemical industry and is widely used to produce valuable chemicals. However, conventional naphtha is primarily fossil-derived, resulting in substantial greenhouse gas emissions. Bio-naphtha offers a renewable drop-in alternative compatible with existing petrochemical infrastructure. Underutilized forest biomass is a promising carbon source, but integrated studies combining process design, techno-economic analysis, and life cycle assessment remain limited. High-temperature gasification was used to convert underutilized forest biomass into syngas. Two syngas-conditioning configurations were evaluated: external hydrogen supplementation and internal H₂/CO adjustment through the water-gas shift reaction. The two configurations were compared using process simulation, techno-economic analysis (TEA), environmental techno-economic assessment (eTEA), and gate-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA). The minimum selling price and major cost drivers were evaluated through sensitivity analysis of feedstock, utility, hydrogen, and capital costs. Environmental impacts were assessed using multiple life cycle impact assessment methods, while hotspot and eTEA analyses were conducted to identify economic–environmental trade-offs and key contributors. The two process configurations were compared in terms of bio-naphtha production, energy demand, economic feasibility, and environmental performance. Product distribution and naphtha-range hydrocarbon yield were analyzed, and TEA, eTEA, and LCA were used to identify major cost and environmental contributors and evaluate economic–environmental trade-offs. This study demonstrates the potential of underutilized forest biomass as a renewable feedstock for bio-naphtha production. The integrated process, economic, and environmental assessments clarify key trade-offs between hydrogen supply strategies and identify critical factors for improving process efficiency, cost competitiveness, and environmental sustainability in future deployment.

t262.k: Dry Reforming of Methane; Perovskite; Calcium Zirconate
t262.a: Ni-based catalysts are considered as promising choice for methane reforming owing to their economic viability and excellent C-H bond activation capabilities. However, Ni-based catalysts were prone to deactivation in high operating temperatures. Perovskite oxides were widely investigated as a catalyst. Transition metal nanoparticles can be formed on the perovskite surface through the mechanism called exsolution. These metal nanoparticles are not only highly dispersed on bulk perovskite surfaces, but also strongly interacted with the perovskite support. This study aims to reveal how structural changes of calcium zirconate derived from different synthesis methods affected their activity and stability. Ni-substituted calcium zirconates (CaZr1-xNixO3-δ) were synthesized via citric gel method, Pechini sol-gel method and mechanochemical method. During the synthesis, Ni was substituted for Zr at the B-site in amounts of 3 mol%, and the final products were calcined at 900 ℃. Structural characterization including TPR, UV-Vis, XPS revealed that the chemical state of Ni and the properties of the calcium zirconate support vary depending on the synthesis pathway, despite the identical catalyst composition. Long-term performance evaluation established that these structural variations arising from the synthesis methods exerts a critical influence on both the reaction activity and deactivation behavior during the dry reforming of methane reaction. These findings highlight that altering the synthesis method is an effective strategy to modulate the support properties and Ni chemical states in perovskite catalysts. These insights provide a rational design framework for developing highly active and coking-resistant Ni-based catalysts for efficient CO2 utilization.

t263.k: MXene/Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks (ZIFs) Heterostructures; Interface Engineering; Alkaline Water Electrolysis
t263.a: Developing efficient water splitting electrodes requires simultaneous control over electrical conductivity, catalytic-site accessibility, interfacial charge transfer, and structural stability. Zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs) provide high surface area and abundant active centres, but their limited electrical conductivity and susceptibility to structural and interfacial degradation under strongly alkaline, gas-evolving conditions can restrict their electrochemical performance. Integrating ZIFs with multifunctional conductive supports that provide both electronic transport and chemical stabilization is therefore highly desirable. MXene/ZIF heterostructures were fabricated through nitrogen-assisted interface engineering, where MXene served as an electron-transport scaffold and chemically interactive support for the ZIF phase. Nitrogen-containing surface functionalization was employed to regulate MXene surface chemistry and promote chemical anchoring and interfacial coupling with the ZIF, which was grown in situ on Ni foam through solution-phase self-assembly. The resulting electrodes were evaluated for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in alkaline electrolyte. The Engineered heterostructure exhibited enhanced interfacial charge-transfer characteristics and superior electrochemical response compared with the individual components. The MXene support provided higher electronic conductivity and stronger interfacial integration of the porous ZIF phase, while nitrogen-assisted surface modification promoted intimate coupling between the two components. The resulting architecture enabled greater accessibility of active sites and structural robustness during alkaline electrocatalysis, contributing to improved HER and OER performance and operational stability. These findings demonstrate the potential of nitrogen-assisted interface engineering to address the limitations of ZIF-based electrocatalysts. Furthermore, the study establishes a surface to interface performance relationship providing insight into balancing catalytic activity and stability in MXene/ZIF heterostructures.

t264.a: Multiphase reaction mixtures containing pressurized CO2 and/or H2O have been investigated as an interesting reaction medium for organic synthesis. An organic liquid phase pressurized by CO2 with volume expansion is referred to as a CO2-dissolved expanded liquid (CXL), and it is known that the dissolution of CO2 can facilitate the dissolution of other coexisting gases, such as H2, O2, and CO, and promote chemical reactions involving these gases. Hydrophobic activated carbon was used as the catalyst support because of the need to disperse the solid catalyst in the organic (CXL) phase. We used different reaction media with n-hexane (CXL) and/or H2O for CO2 hydrogenation. Although n-hexane forms CXL phase at a CO2 pressure of 5 MPa, the amount of HCOOH formed in the CXL phase was negligible. Meanwhile, 2.39 mmol g-1 of HCOOH was observed in the aqueous phase. Notably, the highest amount of HCOOH (11.54 mmol g-1) was formed in the mixed phase of CXL and H2O, which was present as an emulsion in the autoclave. Furthermore, the highest value obtained, 15.69 mmol g-1, was under 2 MPa H2 in the same reaction medium, indicating that optimizing the reaction conditions would further improve the HCOOH formation rate. The temperature dependence of the reaction using different CXLs showed that the amount of HCOOH increased at lower temperatures regardless of the organic solvent. The present reaction system using CXL-H2O is promising as a low-cost HCOOH formation technology without external energy such as heating.

t265.a: Biocompatible, biodegradable, and solid-state electrolyte-based organic electrochemical transistors are demonstrated. As the electrolyte is composed of all edible-level materials, which are levan polysaccharide and choline-based ionic liquid, the organic transistor fabricated on the electrolyte can be biocompatible and biodegrable. Compared to the other ion gel-based electrolytes, it has superior electrical and mechanical properties, large specific capacitance (≈40 µF cm−2), non-volatility, flexibility, and high transparency. Thus, it shows mechanical reliability by maintaining electrical performances under up to 1.11% of effective bending strain, 5% of stretching, and low operation voltage range when utilized in organic transistors. Moreover, the choline ionic liquid can modify PEDOT:PSS interface and their functions for enhanced mode operation of OECT. The measured ECG signals from the transistors, compared to signals from electrode-based sensors, has a superior signal-to-noise ratio. The biocompatible and biodegradable materials and devices can contribute to the development of many bioelectronics.

t266.k: Functional Polymer; Polymer Dielectric Film; Initiated Chemical Vapor Deposition
t266.a: Polymer materials possess the mechanical deformability required for flexible and stretchable electronics, but their intrinsically limited electrical properties and chemical functionalities should be carefully engineered to realize high-performance, functional electronic devices. Low-temperature, solvent-free initiated chemical vapor deposition (iCVD) was employed to synthesize functional polymer thin films with controlled chemical composition and functionalities. Low-temperature device fabrication processes, including thermal evaporation, were further introduced to ensure compatibility with thermally vulnerable flexible and stretchable substrates. Ultrathin high-k copolymer dielectrics were developed by balancing polar cyano functionalities and crosslinking density, enabling low-voltage flexible thin-film transistors. The same compositional control was extended to regulate conductive-filament formation in ultrathin polymer memristors, providing stable multilevel conductance modulation for in-memory computing. Molecular design was further expanded toward mechanical deformability by combining soft segments with crosslinking units. The resulting intrinsically stretchable polymer dielectrics enabled low-power stretchable transistors and active-matrix electronic skin with robust electrical operation under substantial strain and scalable monolithic integration. Functional polymer interfaces were also engineered to induce photoresponsive charge trapping, enabling flexible dual-mode memory transistors capable of nonvolatile charge storage and synaptic signal processing. In addition, vacuum-deposited polymer dielectric stacks were integrated with programmable floating gates in heterojunction transistors, producing tunable Gaussian-like electrical responses for highly parallel, low-power probabilistic inference. These results demonstrate that rational molecular, compositional, and interfacial engineering of vapor-deposited polymers can concurrently tailor electrical, mechanical, and memory characteristics, establishing versatile functional material platforms for flexible and stretchable electronics, as well as emerging computing devices.

t267.k: High-density surface electromyography; stretchable electrode patches; motion artifacts; neuromuscular Interfaces
t267.a: High-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG) records spatial muscle electrical activity during voluntary contraction and relaxation, enabling a wide range of emerging applications such as wearable health monitoring, human-machine interaction, rehabilitation assessment, and assistive communication. However, achieving reliable high-density neuromuscular interfaces under dynamic conditions remains challenging due to the inherent trade-offs among mechanical compliance, signal fidelity, and long-term wearability. In this talk, I will present large-area, stretchable, and breathable electrode patches that conform seamlessly to curved anatomical locations including the wrist, larynx, back, and chest. Systematic characterizations demonstrate stable mechanical and electrical properties under repeated deformation, with the patches effectively mitigating interfacial stress concentration and skin deformation, thereby minimizing motion artifacts even during dynamic activities. Integrated with a miniaturized wireless acquisition module and machine learning algorithms, these electrode arrays enable real-time, accurate recognition of subtle thumb movements, as well as noninvasive assessment of dysphagia, chronic low back pain, and myocardial infarction.

P1-001.k: Macroporous Ni/Al2O3; Acidity Reduction; Phosphorus Doping
P1-001.a: Dry reforming of methane is an attractive route for converting CH4 and CO2 into syngas, but Ni-based catalysts often suffer from metal sintering and carbon deposition at high reaction temperatures. This study investigates phosphorus modification as a strategy to regulate Ni–support interactions and improve catalyst stability. Macroporous alumina-supported Ni catalysts were prepared with different phosphorus incorporation sequences, including phosphorus-modified support and phosphorus-modified Ni catalysts. The catalysts were characterized by XRD, H2-TPR, XPS, TEM-EDS, Raman spectroscopy, and TGA. Catalytic performance was evaluated for dry reforming of methane at 800 °C. Introducing P after Ni loading produced the most favorable structure. 2P-Ni/MaAl exhibited the highest surface area (201.1 m² g⁻¹), the smallest reduced Ni particles (5.23 nm), and lower acidity (0.188 mmol g⁻¹) than Ni/MaAl (159.3 m² g⁻¹, 6.70 nm, 0.478 mmol g⁻¹). After 30 h, coke deposition decreased from 6.9 wt.% on Ni/MaAl to 1.5 wt.% on 2P-Ni/MaAl. During 100 h DRM, 2P-Ni/MaAl maintained ca. 92–94% CH₄ conversion, 94–96% CO₂ conversion, an H₂/CO ratio of 0.98–1.00, and a carbon balance near 99–100%, while coke formation was reduced from 9.4 to 4.0 wt.%. The results demonstrate that phosphorus modification can stabilize Ni-based catalysts by regulating Ni–support and Ni–P interactions. The formation of dynamic Ni–P-containing interfacial species promotes resistance against sintering and coke formation, offering an effective strategy for designing durable Ni catalysts for high-temperature DRM.

P1-002.k: CO2 Separation; Transient Filler; Thin-film Composite Membrane
P1-002.a: The practical deployment of polymeric membranes for carbon capture requires high gas throughput without sacrificing separation efficiency. Although polyether block amide (PEBA) preferentially transports CO2, its semicrystalline domains restrict molecular transport and limit membrane productivity. A removable-additive strategy was applied to reorganize the PEBA selective layer. Polyethylene glycol was incorporated during film formation and subsequently extracted with ethanol after coating onto a PTMSP-modified porous support. Changes in phase structure, crystallinity, free volume, layer thickness, and CO2/N2 transport were examined using spectroscopic, thermal, microscopic, and permeation analyses. Temporary incorporation of polyethylene glycol disturbed the ordered PEBA domains and altered the packing of polymer chains. Following extraction, the membrane preserved a less ordered structure while recovering its original chemical composition. This structural rearrangement, together with the formation of a sub-100-nm selective layer, substantially improved gas transport. The highest-performing membrane achieved a CO2 permeance of 2,371 GPU with a CO2/N2 ideal selectivity of approximately 45. A representative membrane also maintained a mixed-gas separation factor of 23.1 during a 50-h test. Reorganizing polymer packing during membrane formation provides an effective route to improve CO2 flux beyond that of conventionally coated PEBA. The proposed fabrication concept offers a practical platform for preparing productive composite membranes for carbon-capture applications.

P1-003.k: CO2 Methanation; Membrane Reactor; In Situ Water Removal
P1-003.a: Water accumulation during CO2 methanation can suppress complete hydrogenation, alter the surface state of Ni catalysts, and increase CO formation. Continuous dehydration within the reactor may therefore improve both catalytic activity and product selectivity, provided that the membrane remains effective at elevated temperature. Hydroxyl-polyimide hollow fibers were thermally converted into polybenzoxazole membranes and integrated with a Ni@Mg-MOF-74 catalyst bed. Membrane transport properties were evaluated from 150 to 350 °C, and CO2 methanation was conducted at 350 °C using an H2/CO2 ratio of 4. Catalyst surface chemistry and reaction pathways were examined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations. Thermal rearrangement generated diffusion pathways that enabled preferential water transport while maintaining selectivity over the major reaction gases. The membrane reactor increased CO2 conversion from 29–32% to approximately 45% and preserved high CH4 selectivity over 72 h. In the conventional reactor, conversion and CH₄ selectivity gradually declined to about 20% and 80%, respectively. Surface analysis indicated water-induced hydroxylation of Ni without membrane dehydration, while computational results showed that adjacent hydroxyl groups hindered CO hydrogenation and favored CO release. Selective water extraction stabilizes the catalytic surface and promotes complete CO2 hydrogenation toward CH₄. The polybenzoxazole hollow-fiber reactor provides an effective platform for improving the productivity and durability of high-temperature CO2 conversion processes.

P1-004.k: Ni Catalyst; Metal-support Interaction; Coke Resistance
P1-004.a: DRM converts CH4 and CO2 into syngas but conventionally requires high temperatures (700–900°C), causing Ni sintering. Low-temperature DRM lowers energy demand and mitigates sintering, but coke deposition via the Boudouard reaction becomes the dominant deactivation mechanism. Promoter addition helps stabilize Ni/Al2O3 catalysts by tuning metal-support interactions, oxygen mobility, and surface basicity. Ni/Al2O3 catalysts were modified with CeO2, La2O3, TiO2, MgO and CaO, reduced under H2 flow, and tested for DRM at 700°C for 24 h using a CH4/ CO2 (1:1) feed diluted with Ar. Performance and coke formation were evaluated via conversion measurements and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). All catalysts showed CO2 conversion of ~98–99%, exceeding CH4 conversion, indicating concurrent reverse water-gas shift activity. Basic/redox-active promoters (CeO2, La2O3, MgO, CaO) enhanced CO2 activation through greater surface basicity and oxygen vacancies. CH4 conversion decreased initially before stabilizing, reflecting surface reconstruction and intermediate accumulation. The CaO-promoted catalyst achieved the highest CH4 conversion, while the TiO2-promoted catalyst showed the lowest TGA weight loss but the fastest activity decay. CeO2-, CaO-, and La2O3-promoted catalysts showed larger weight losses, with La2O3 exhibiting two-step decomposition attributable to carbonates, complicating differentiation between coke and carbonate effects. Overall, promoter type strongly influences CO2 activation, CH4 conversion, and carbon-related surface chemistry, with coke quantity not directly correlating with deactivation rate. Rational promoter selection offers a promising route toward durable, deactivation-resistant Ni-based catalysts for sustainable low-temperature DRM and syngas production.

P1-005.a: Conventional methods of gaseous hydrogen transport are restricted by stringent safety and pressure requirements. In contrast, liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHCs) provide a safer, less toxic, and reversible medium for hydrogen storage and logistics. However, the hydrogenation of LOHCs remains dependent on high-cost noble-metal catalysts. Therefore, enhancing catalytic efficiency and reducing reliance on noble metals are critical to the commercialization of LOHC technology. This study reports the synthesis of Ni@Ru core–shell nanoparticles, consisting of a Ni core and a Ru shell, deposited onto spray-pyrolyzed γ-Al2O3 support, which serve as hydrogenation catalysts for monobenzyl toluene (MBT). The Ni@Ru nanoparticles were synthesized via a simple chemical reduction using NaBH4 at room temperature, while the Al2O3 support was fabricated by advanced spray pyrolysis, achieving both a high mass production rate (1.50 g h–1) and a large surface area (330 m2 g–1). The synthesized Ni@Ru/Al2O3 catalyst exhibits a well-defined core–shell structure, is uniformly distributed on the Al2O3 surface, and has a small average particle size of 2.6 nm. The presence of Ni induces electronic interactions with Ru, increasing the electron density of Ru and thereby promoting hydrogen activation. Moreover, the Ru shell serves as both the main active site and a protective layer, effectively inhibiting nickel self-oxidation. Notably, the incorporation of Ni not only decreases the Ru content but also enhances catalytic activity. Under hydrogenation conditions for MBT (150 °C, 50 bar), the Ni@Ru/Al2O3 catalyst achieves 100% hydrogenation within 3 hours, surpassing the performance of both the RuNi-alloy/Al2O3 and the commercial Ru/Al2O3 catalysts. These findings demonstrate the simple synthesis and high efficiency of the Ni@Ru/Al2O3 hydrogenation catalyst.

P1-006.k: Thermally Rearranged Polybenzoxazole; Membrane Reactor; In Situ Water Removal
P1-006.a: Water formed during catalytic reactions can reduce conversion, deactivate active sites, and promote undesired reaction pathways. Membrane-assisted water removal offers a continuous approach to controlling the reaction environment, but polymeric membranes capable of operating under severe thermal conditions remain limited. Hydroxyl-polyimide hollow fibers were converted into thermally rearranged polybenzoxazole membranes through heat treatment at 425 °C. The resulting hollow fibers were integrated with packed catalyst beds and evaluated in reverse water–gas shift, methane combustion, and Fischer–Tropsch olefin synthesis. Thermal properties, gas transport behavior, catalyst states, and reaction performance were examined between 250 and 440 °C. The rearranged polymer maintained its structure at high temperature and preferentially transported water over the major reactant and product gases. During reverse water–gas shift, continuous dehydration raised CO2 conversion above the calculated equilibrium value. In methane combustion, the membrane reactor sustained approximately 96% CH4 conversion for 150 h, whereas the membrane-free system declined to about 80%. During olefin synthesis, CO2 selectivity associated with the water–gas shift reaction decreased from 47.9% to 15.1%, accompanied by increased hydrocarbon production and olefin-to-paraffin ratios. High-temperature polymeric dehydration membranes can regulate catalytic environments beyond conventional catalyst modification. Their integration into reactors provides a versatile strategy for improving conversion, catalyst durability, and product selectivity in water-generating reactions.

P1-007.k: Electrochemical CO2 Conversion; Transition Metal Chalcogenide; Multi-carbon Products
P1-007.a: Electrochemical carbon dioxide conversion has attracted significant attention as a promising strategy for mitigating greenhouse gas emissions. Among various catalyst materials, copper has been widely studied due to its unique ability to produce a broad range of value-added products, including C1–C2 hydrocarbons, organic acids, and alcohols. However, catalysts for electrochemical CO2 conversion must simultaneously satisfy requirements for catalytic activity, product selectivity, and long-term stability. In practice, metallic copper suffers from rapid deactivation under CO₂ reduction conditions, which leads to the dominance of the hydrogen evolution reaction and a consequent loss of CO2 conversion efficiency. To address the deactivation of metallic Cu, extensive research has focused on maintaining Cu in a cationic state or creating oxide-derived surfaces. Recently, chalcogen elements such as S, Se, and Te have been widely explored to stabilize the oxidation state of copper while simultaneously enhancing C2+ product selectivity. In this study, we synthesized Cu chalcogenide catalysts through a facile mechanochemical process and controlled their crystallographic and chemical properties by tuning the process parameters. We further investigated the effects of catalyst crystal structure, morphology, and chemical composition on CO2 conversion performance by highlighting mechanochemical synthesis as an effective strategy for efficient CO2 reduction catalyst fabrication.

P1-008.k: Dimethyl Ether; Methanol Dehydration; Water Resistance
P1-008.a: DME is gaining attention as an eco-friendly marine fuel due to its high cetane number and low emissions, supporting IMO 2050 carbon neutrality goals. Methanol dehydration over γ-Al₂O₃ is the most common DME synthesis route, but water byproduct causes active-site poisoning and rehydration, while γ-Al₂O₃ shows limited acidity and activity below 300°C. Nb₂O₅-Al₂O₃ composite catalysts were developed to enhance low-temperature activity and water resistance via Nb₂O₅'s strong Brønsted acidity and hydrophobic surface character. Catalysts were characterized by BET, NH₃-TPD, XRD, XPS, and water adsorption isotherms, and evaluated for methanol dehydration performance at 250–300°C. Nb₂O₅-Al₂O₃ achieved ~20% higher DME conversion than pristine γ-Al₂O₃, with the gap widening at lower temperatures. Nb₂O₅ incorporation increased strong acid site density and reduced water adsorption, improving structural stability under humid conditions. Nb₂O₅-Al₂O₃ composite catalysts overcome the key limitations of conventional γ-Al₂O₃, offering a promising design strategy for low-temperature, high-efficiency DME production in green methanol-fueled marine fuel applications.

P1-009.a: Li6PS5I is a promising sulfide-based solid-state electrolyte (SSE) for all-solid-state lithium metal batteries (ASSLMBs) due to its low cost and favorable interfacial stability. However, its practical applications are limited by relatively low ionic conductivity and poor moisture sensitivity upon air exposure. In this study, we propose a halide–oxide dual-doping strategy to simultaneously enhance both ionic conductivity and air stability of argyrodite-type Li6PS5I. By partially substituting Cl− for I− and incorporating Sb2O5 as a dopant, we have synthesized a series of Li6P1–xSbxS5–2.5xO2.5xI0.3Cl0.7 (x = 0 to 0.08) solid electrolytes via a conventional solid-state process. The Cl− substitution promotes anion site disorder and facilitates Li+ transport, while Sb2O5 doping induces the formation of Sb-S and P-O bonds, suppressing H2S emission under humid conditions. The optimized composition Li6P0.98Sb0.02S4.95O0.05I0.3Cl0.7 (x = 0.02) exhibits a high ionic conductivity of 1.158 mS cm−1 and significantly improved air stability, with H₂S emission reduced by 40% under 30% relative humidity. The Li symmetric cells employing Li6P0.98Sb0.02S4.95O0.05I0.3Cl0.7 (x = 0.02) electrolyte demonstrate an excellent critical current density (CCD) of 0.52 mA cm−2 and stable cycling performance over 1000 h, which is attributed to the presence of LiI and the formation of a Li-Sb alloy for excellent interfacial stability. Furthermore, ASSLMBs incorporating the Li6P0.98Sb0.02S4.95O0.05I0.3Cl0.7 (x = 0.02) electrolyte have achieved a high initial discharge capacity of 158.4 mAh g−1 and maintained stable operation over 100 cycles. This work demonstrates that the proposed ternary doping strategy offers a viable pathway toward the development of high-performance ASSLMBs by overcoming trade-offs between ionic conductivity and air stability.

P1-010.k: CO2 Electroreduction; Metal-organic Framework; Resource Upcycling
P1-010.a: Recent studies about spent battery recycling have mainly focused on cathode recovery. In general, hydrometallurgical, pyrometallurgical, and mechanochemical processes have already reached a high level of research maturity. Among these, mechanochemical processes using ball mill machines have recently attracted attention because they minimize environmental impact by avoiding high temperatures and strong acid or base solutions. After lithium is recovered through this process, black-colored powder residue containing valuable metals such as nickel, cobalt, and manganese is generated. From a resource upcycling perspective, it is desirable to further utilize the valuable metals contained in this residue even after lithium has already been recovered. In this study, we aim to use nickel and cobalt in the residue obtained through mechanochemical technology for the synthesis of metal organic frameworks (MOFs) such as Ni-BDC (a nickel-based MOF) and ZIF-67 (a cobalt-based MOF). The synthesized Ni-BDC and ZIF-67 will be coated with polydopamine (PDA) and subsequently calcined under nitrogen gas to form a nitrogen doped carbon shell, which is expected to provide conductivity and stabilize the active sites. The catalysts developed through this approach are expected to serve as an integrated electrode material for CO2 electroreduction that simultaneously achieves resource upcycling of valuable metals recovered from spent batteries and utilization of CO2 as a resource.

P1-011.k: Carbon Nitride; Visible Light-photocatalysis; Polymer Engineering
P1-011.a: Visible-light photocatalysis has attracted increasing attention as a sustainable strategy for solar energy utilization in environmental and energy-related applications. Among various photocatalysts, graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) is considered a promising metal-free semiconductor owing to its low cost, chemical stability, and visible-light responsiveness. However, the photocatalytic activation of peroxymonosulfate (PMS) over pristine g-C3N4 remains inefficient because of limited visible-light absorption and rapid charge recombination, often requiring transition metal co-catalysts or UV irradiation. Herein, we report a polymer-engineering strategy for enhancing visible-light-driven PMS activation using metal-free poly(4-vinylphenol)-incorporated carbon nitride (PCN). Poly(4-vinylphenol)-incorporated carbon nitride (PCN) was prepared via polymer-assisted thermal synthesis. The photocatalytic activity of PCN was investigated through visible-light-driven peroxymonosulfate (PMS) activation for organic pollutant degradation. Structural, optical, and spectroscopic characterizations were performed to elucidate the effects of polymer incorporation on the electronic structure and visible-light absorption. The photocatalytic stability and reusability of the catalyst were evaluated through repeated degradation experiments. The incorporation of poly(4-vinylphenol) markedly improved the photocatalytic activation of PMS under visible-light irradiation, enabling nearly complete degradation and mineralization of 4-chlorophenol (4-CP), whereas pristine g-C3N4 exhibited negligible activity. In addition, PCN demonstrated excellent stability during repeated photocatalytic cycles and showed broad applicability toward the degradation of various organic contaminants. Spectroscopic characterizations revealed that polymer incorporation modifies the local bonding environment of g-C3N4 and enhances visible-light harvesting, leading to improved photocatalytic performance. This work provides an effective strategy for designing metal-free visible-light photocatalysts through interfacial polymer engineering and highlights their potential for sustainable solar-driven photocatalytic technologies.

P1-012.k: Yolk-Shell; Syngas to Aromatics; Hollow HZSM-5
P1-012.a: Aromatics are crucial chemical feedstocks that have traditionally been produced from crude oil, but alternative production pathways are necessary to ensure their stable and sustainable supply. Syngas conversion to aromatics via olefin intermediates is a promising alternative, as syngas-to-olefin and olefin-to-aromatics reactions share similar operating temperatures (300–400°C). Consequently, combining an Fe-based syngas-to-olefin catalyst with HZSM-5 for olefin-to-aromatics offers a viable bifunctional catalyst strategy for direct syngas-to-aromatics conversion. In this study, we designed Fe3O4@MnO2@HZSM-5 yolk-shell catalysts, in which the HZSM-5 shell suppresses sintering by acting as a physical barrier, thereby significantly enhancing catalytic performance. The Fe3O4@MnO2 core was prepared by the co-precipitation method using FeSO4·7H2O and KMnO4. This core was subsequently coated with a silica as sacrificial layer via the Stöber method using NH4OH, and finally encapsulated with HZSM-5 through hydrothermal synthesis with isopropylamine (IPA). XRD patterns of the Fe3O4@MnO2 core showed only Fe3O4 peaks due to high Mn dispersion, while EDS confirmed a core-shell-like distribution with iron at the center. For Fe3O4@MnO2/SiO2, the amorphous nature of SiO2 resulted in only the characteristic peaks of Fe3O4 being identified on the XRD pattern. TEM analysis visually confirmed successful catalyst encapsulation within the silica shell. The structural backbone for a sintering-resistant bifunctional catalyst was successfully prepared. Despite the high reduction temperature, sintering of active metal was suppressed on the Fe3O4@MnO2@HZSM-5 yolk-shell catalyst and its catalytic performance was significantly improved.

P1-013.k: BIO-HEAVY FUEL OIL; MAGNESIUN SILICATE; PHOSPHORUS
P1-013.a: Heavy lipid feedstocks pose significant challenges in the production of bio-heavy oil due to their elevated content of alkali metals (sodium and potassium) and phosphorus. These inorganic impurities lead to ash formation, boiler corrosion, and environmental emissions during combustion. To address these issues and enable the upcycling of low-quality feedstocks, the development of a multifunctional adsorbent capable of simultaneously reducing inorganic impurities, color, and polar components has emerged as a critical task. To achieve this, a high-surface-area, porous magnesium silicate was synthesized via a precipitation method. Its structural and chemical properties were optimized by controlling reaction temperature, Si/Mg molar ratio, additive composition, and stabilization conditions. Physical and chemical characteristics were systematically evaluated through PSA, SEM, and BET analyses, while the residual or incorporated concentrations of alkali metals and phosphorus were determined using ICP-AES. The synthesized magnesium silicate exhibited a spherical morphology with an average particle size of 104.0 µm and a specific surface area of 424.9 m²/g. When applied to bio-heavy oil purification, the total concentration of alkali metal ions (K, Na) decreased from 410.1 ppm to 70.8 ppm, achieving an 82.7% reduction. Additionally, phosphorus (P) was reduced from 140 ppm to below the ICP-AES detection limit (approximately 0.2 ppm), demonstrating a removal efficiency of over 99%. Precipitation-synthesized magnesium silicate serves as an efficient, economical adsorbent that removes nearly all phosphorus and substantially reduces alkali metals in low-quality bio-heavy oil feedstocks, thereby preventing ash-related operational issues and enhancing industrial boiler combustion stability.

P1-014.k: Catalytic Decomposition of Methane; Mechanochemical Synthesis; Carbon Formation
P1-014.a: Catalytic Decomposition of Methane (CDM) is a promising route for the simultaneous production of hydrogen and solid carbon without direct CO₂ emissions. Transition-metal catalysts have been widely investigated for CDM owing to their high activity for methane activation and cost-effectiveness. Since carbon is a primary product of CDM, its formation and growth behavior are closely associated with the physicochemical properties of the catalysts. In this study, transition-metal catalysts were prepared via mechanochemical synthesis to investigate the effects of different metal loading methods on methane decomposition and carbon formation. Transition-metal catalysts were prepared via mechanochemical synthesis using two different metal loading methods: one-pot synthesis and incipient wetness impregnation onto a mechanochemically synthesized support. Both catalysts were calcined under the same conditions. Catalytic methane decomposition was conducted in a 1/4-inch fixed-bed reactor. Differences in carbon formation were observed depending on the metal loading method. Metal particles were located either within the pores or on the external surface. These differences in the spatial distribution of metal particles resulted in distinct carbon deposition and growth behaviors, as demonstrated by TGA and TEM analyses. This study provides insights into the effects of metal loading methods on catalyst properties and carbon formation behavior during CDM, contributing to the design of transition-metal catalysts for hydrogen and carbon production.

P1-015.k: Methane Reforming; Solvent Effect; Ni Accessibility
P1-015.a: Ni-based catalysts are widely used for dry reforming of methane (DRM) due to their high catalytic activity and economic advantages. However, Ni sintering and carbon deposition can lead to catalyst deactivation, reducing catalytic activity and stability. A series of silica supports with high surface areas were used to promote high Ni dispersion. Among them, SBA-15 is an ordered mesoporous silica with well-defined channel structures, which allows the location and accessibility of Ni within the pores to be evaluated. This study aims to investigate how different solvents affect Ni distribution and accessibility and how these differences influence catalytic performance in DRM. Mesoporous silica was synthesized by conventional EISA method. Silica-supported catalysts with 5 wt.% Ni were synthesized by wet impregnation with different solvent (e.g. ethylene glycol, butanol, hexane) pre-treatments. After then, Ni was impregnated onto the pre-treated supports. The prepared catalysts were subsequently calcined at 700 ℃. The solvent used for pre-treatment affected Ni distribution within SBA-15. Characterization results revealed that ethylene glycol attributed to more uniform distribution of Ni inside the mesoporous channels of SBA-15 than using distilled water such as incipient wetness impregnation. In contrast, butanol and hexane resulted in relatively large Ni particles located in the outer region of the channels. The ethylene glycol-treated SBA-15 catalyst showed high conversion and maintained relatively high activity in DRM. These results suggest that controlling Ni accessibility through solvent pre-treatment provides an effective strategy for tailoring the catalytic performance of Ni-based catalysts in methane reforming.

P1-016.a: Hydrogenation reactions are essential for hydrogen storage using liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHCs), enabling safe and efficient hydrogen management. The catalytic efficiency of these reactions depends largely on the intrinsic properties of noble metals. However, comprehensive comparisons of their physicochemical characteristics and hydrogenation activities remain limited. In this work, various noble metals (M = Pt, Ru, and Pd) were deposited onto a gamma-phase alumina (γ-Al2O3) support synthesized via an advanced ultrasonic spray pyrolysis (UPS) technique based on a sol–gel process. The continuous UPS approach yields γ-Al2O3 with a high production rate of 1.5 g h–1, a microspherical morphology, high mesoporosity (0.36 cm3 g–1), and a large specific surface area (377 m2 g–1). Noble metals were deposited onto the synthesized γ-Al2O3 via NaBH4 reduction, producing uniformly distributed nanoparticles. The resulting M/γ-Al2O3 catalysts exhibit metal–support interactions (MSI) and increased surface hydroxyl groups, which promote hydrogen spillover. Importantly, H2 temperature-programmed desorption (H2-TPD) and reduction (H2-TPR) characterizations show that Ru/γ-Al2O3 possesses the highest hydrogen adsorption capacity. Moreover, hydrogen spillover occurs for both Ru/γ-Al2O3 and Pt/γ-Al2O3, whereas it is negligible for Pd/γ-Al2O3. Catalytic performance was evaluated by hydrogenating monobenzyl toluene (MBT). The catalytic activity follows the order Ru/γ-Al2O3 > Pt/γ-Al2O3 > Pd/γ-Al2O3. The synthesized Ru/γ-Al2O3 outperforms a commercial Ru/Al2O3 catalyst. In terms of stability, Ru/γ-Al2O3 maintains a particle size of 4.8 nm after a 25-hour reaction, while Pt/γ-Al2O3 and Pd/γ-Al2O3 exhibit significant metal agglomeration, with particle sizes increasing to 8.5 nm and 13.6 nm, respectively. In summary, this study presents an efficient synthesis strategy for large-scale production of γ-Al2O3 supports and demonstrates the effectiveness of the Ru/γ-Al2O3 catalyst for MBT hydrogenation in LOHC systems.

P1-017.a: Nanostructural engineering is essential for developing self-supported electrocatalyst electrodes with high activity, excellent conductivity, and long-term durability by optimizing electrode architecture and eliminating the need for binders or conductive additives. Although conventional fabrication methods, such as solvothermal synthesis, enable controlled nanostructure formation, they are limited by long processing times and scalability issues. In contrast, the molten-salt method provides a rapid and scalable route with improved crystallinity and precise multi-element incorporation, making it a promising approach for fabricating advanced self-supported electrodes. In this study, a Co₃Mo₁ phosphide/Ni phosphide/Ni foam (Co₃Mo₁-P/Ni-P/NF) self-supported electrode was fabricated via a two-step molten-salt-assisted process, where a vertically aligned Ni–P nanoarray scaffold was first formed on Ni foam and subsequently coated with a Co₃Mo₁ phosphide catalytic layer. This hierarchical structure combines the synergistic alkaline HER activity of Co–Mo phosphides with the high conductivity and structural stability of the Ni–P scaffold, resulting in enhanced charge transport, enlarged electrochemically active surface area, and improved durability. The electrode demonstrated superior HER performance under high current densities, outperformed commercial Pt/C and previously reported NF-supported transition metal phosphide electrodes, and also served as a robust scaffold for commercial Pt/C and IrO₂ catalysts. Furthermore, its excellent performance in an anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer (AEMWE) highlights the potential of molten-salt-assisted synthesis as a scalable strategy for practical alkaline water electrolysis. Preparation of Ni–P/NF: Ni foam was acid-cleaned (35 wt% HCl), washed, and dried. It was mixed with NaH₂PO₂·H₂O and phosphidized at 310 °C for 1 h under Ar/H₂ (4% H₂), followed by washing with DI water to obtain Ni–P/NF. Preparation of Co–Mo–P/Ni–P/NF: Co and Mo precursors with different Co:Mo ratios were dissolved in acetone, drop-cast onto Ni–P/NF (or bare Ni foam for Co₃Mo₁-P/NF), and dried. The electrodes were phosphidized with NaH₂PO₂·H₂O at 310 °C for 1 h under Ar/H₂, washed, and immersed in DI water to obtain the final catalyst electrodes. Co–P/Ni–P/NF and Mo–P/Ni–P/NF were prepared using only the corresponding metal precursor. Preparation of Pt/C- and IrO₂-based electrodes: Commercial Pt/C and IrO₂ catalyst inks were prepared by sonication and drop-cast onto Ni–P/NF (or bare Ni foam), followed by air drying to produce Pt/C/Ni–P/NF, IrO₂/Ni–P/NF, and the corresponding control electrodes. Preparation of Ni felt-based electrodes: Ni felt was phosphidized under the same molten-salt conditions to prepare Ni–P/Ni felt. Co–Mo–P/Ni–P/Ni felt was fabricated using the same drop-casting and phosphidation process with increased precursor amounts. Pt/C/Ni–P/Ni felt and IrO₂/Ni–P/Ni felt were prepared by drop-casting commercial catalyst inks onto Ni–P/Ni felt with catalyst loadings of 0.3 mgPt cm⁻² and 1.0 mgIrO₂ cm⁻², respectively. Corresponding bare Ni felt electrodes were also prepared for comparison. The results demonstrated that the two-step molten-salt synthesis successfully produced vertically aligned Ni–P nanoarray scaffolds, which provided a large electrochemically active surface area (ECSA), excellent electrical conductivity, and strong structural stability. Among the synthesized catalysts, Co₃Mo₁-P/Ni–P/NF exhibited the best HER performance, achieving low overpotentials and superior activity over a wide current-density range, outperforming previously reported transition-metal phosphide electrodes as well as commercial Pt/C under high-current operation. The Ni–P nanoarray also served as a versatile scaffold for commercial Pt/C and IrO₂ catalysts, increasing the ECSA by up to 4.52-fold and significantly enhancing both HER and OER activities and long-term durability compared with catalysts deposited on bare Ni foam. Furthermore, AEM water electrolysis tests confirmed that the hierarchical Ni–P-supported electrode architecture translated these advantages into improved single-cell performance and stable operation under practical membrane-electrode assembly conditions, highlighting the effectiveness and scalability of the molten-salt-derived nanoarray design. The two-step molten salt-assisted synthesis strategy developed in this study enabled the fabrication of self-supported electrocatalyst electrodes. This method enabled the formation of a vertically aligned Ni─P nanoneedle array on NF, followed by the controlled growth of a Co3Mo1-P catalytic overlayer without compromising structural integrity. The nanostructured Ni─P scaffold physically anchored the catalyst particles, thereby preventing their detachment during operation. Additionally, the Ni─P layer provided strong oxidation resistance and metallic conductivity, simultaneously contributing to structural stability and efficient electron transport. The resulting Co3Mo1-P/Ni─P/NF electrode exhibited an exceptionally low overpotential of 113.5 mV at 100 mA cm−2, outperforming previously reported TMP-based electrodes under identical conditions. The optimized Co: Mo ratio not only modulated the surface electronic structure to enhance the catalytic activity but also expanded the ECSA. Furthermore, the vertically aligned nanoneedle architecture maximized accessible active sites and facilitated rapid hydrogen bubble release, ensuring stable operation under high current densities. Beyond its intrinsic performance, the nanostructured Ni─P array also functioned as a versatile support for commercial catalysts. The integration of commercial catalysts, such as Pt/C and IrO2, onto the Ni─P/NF scaffold—an approach rarely explored—significantly improved both catalytic activity and durability. In particular, Pt/C loaded onto the nanostructured support achieved a 4.52-fold increase in ECSA and an impressively low overpotential of 55.8 mV at 100 mA cm−2 compared with Pt/C deposited on bare NF. This mechanically interlocked electrode structure effectively suppressed catalyst detachment and preserved long-term stability. Furthermore, the practical applicability of the developed self-supported electrode architecture was validated in an AEMWE single cell under membrane-based electrolysis conditions, where the synergistic Co─Mo phosphide chemistry and Ni─P nanoarray-enabled architecture translated into superior cell-level performance and stable operation under practical operating conditions. These results emphasize the importance of precise nanostructural design for high-performance and durable electrocatalysts. They also highlight the potential of molten-salt-based synthetic strategy as a scalable route for engineering robust, conductive, and industrially viable electrode platforms for alkaline water electrolysis.

P1-018.a: Sulfate-rich, high-salinity wastewaters generated from secondary battery manufacturing and hydrometallurgical recycling present a growing environmental challenge because conventional physicochemical treatment and resource-recovery processes often require substantial energy input. This study investigated marine microbial consortia as a bio-inspired platform for the low-energy synthesis of iron sulfide (Fe–S) nanomaterials through coupled Fe(III) and sulfate reduction, with particular emphasis on their time-dependent structural evolution and potential for sustainable water treatment. Marine microbial consortia enriched from coastal tidal-flat sediments were anaerobically cultivated at 30°C and near-neutral pH with ferrihydrite (30 mM) and sulfate (50 mM) as electron acceptors and pyruvate (50 mM) as the electron donor. Three representative consortia were selected from 105 enrichment cultures based on their pronounced Fe–S transformation. Substrate consumption and sulfate reduction were monitored over time, while the structural and morphological evolution of biogenic Fe–S nanomaterials was characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning and transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), selected-area electron diffraction (SAED), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Pyruvate was rapidly consumed within 1–5 days, accompanied by acetate formation and substantial sulfate reduction. The representative consortia achieved approximately 63–74% sulfate reduction during the early stage of incubation and maintained substantial sulfate removal thereafter. Concurrently, amorphous ferrihydrite progressively transformed into dark Fe–S precipitates. Time-resolved mineralogical analyses revealed a sequential transformation from amorphous ferrihydrite through intermediate Fe(III) oxyhydroxides to increasingly crystalline FeS/FeS₂ nanominerals. Electron microscopy further demonstrated the progressive development of aggregated, rod-like, and framboidal nanostructures, while elemental mapping confirmed the co-localization of Fe and S within the biogenic precipitates. These observations demonstrate controlled structural evolution of Fe–S nanomaterials under mild, biologically mediated conditions. Marine-derived microbial consortia enabled the low-energy synthesis and structural evolution of biogenic Fe–S nanomaterials through coupled Fe(III) and sulfate reduction under mild anaerobic conditions. The simultaneous sulfate transformation and formation of increasingly crystalline Fe–S nanostructures highlight a sustainable, bio-inspired route for nanomaterial production with potential applications in the treatment and stabilization of sulfate-rich industrial wastewaters.

P1-019.a: Methane reforming is an important route for syngas production, but conventional processes can require external oxygen supply and may suffer from catalyst deactivation by carbon deposition. Chemical looping reforming offers an alternative approach in which lattice oxygen from an oxygen carrier partially oxidizes methane to produce H2 and CO, followed by regeneration of the reduced carrier with air. Electronic-industry wastewater sludge may contain redox-active metals, such as Fe, Ni, and Cu, and could be valorized as a low-cost precursor for oxygen carrier development. This study proposes the use of electronic wastewater sludge as a waste-derived oxygen carrier for chemical looping reforming of methane. Electronic wastewater sludge will be washed, dried, ground, and calcined to prepare oxygen carrier materials. The elemental composition, crystalline phases, surface properties, and redox characteristics will be investigated using XRF, XRD, BET, SEM-EDS, NH3-TPD, H2-TPR, and O2-TPD. Methane chemical looping reforming will be conducted in a fixed-bed reactor at 800–900 °C. In the reduction step, CH4 will be introduced over the oxygen carrier to produce syngas using lattice oxygen. The reduced material will subsequently be regenerated under an air flow. Repeated reduction–oxidation cycles will be conducted to assess the stability of the sludge-derived oxygen carrier. Redox-active metal oxides contained in electronic wastewater sludge are expected to provide lattice oxygen for the partial oxidation of methane, leading to hydrogen-rich syngas formation. The sludge-derived oxygen carrier is expected to undergo repetitive oxygen release and uptake during the reduction and regeneration steps. Methane conversion, H₂/CO ratio, carbon deposition, and cyclic stability are anticipated to depend on the metal composition, oxygen mobility, and structural stability of the derived oxygen carrier. This study will explore the feasibility of converting electronic wastewater sludge into a functional oxygen carrier for methane chemical looping reforming. The results are expected to provide a basis for low-cost and circular syngas production using methane and waste-derived redox materials.

P1-020.k: Plastic Recycling; Hydrocracking; Ru-zeolite Hybrid Catalyst
P1-020.a: Polyolefin waste, encompassing polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), represents a significant environmental challenge, accounting for approximately 60% of plastic waste with global production exceeding 200 million tons annually [1]. Traditional mechanical recycling suffers from quality degradation and limited applicability, while incineration and landfilling pose severe environmental concerns. Catalytic hydrogenolysis offers a promising approach to chemically upcycle these polymers into valuable fuel-range hydrocarbons at moderate temperatures [1], providing an economically viable and environmentally sustainable alternative. The conversion of polyolefins to gasoline (C5–C12), wax (C13–C20), and lubricant-range products (>C20) not only addresses waste management but also contributes to circular economy by producing high-value chemicals from waste streams. However, developing efficient catalysts for selective polyolefin conversion requires systematic understanding of how catalyst properties influence reactivity and product distribution. Catalyst structure—particularly metal particle size—plays a key role in determining catalytic performance and product selectivity [2]. Yet rational design strategies remain limited, as the factors governing catalyst optimization in complex polyolefin reactions are not fully understood. To address this gap, we systematically investigated polyethylene hydrogenolysis using Ru/TiO2 catalysts with controlled metal particle sizes. Our approach involved preparing a series of Ru/TiO2 catalysts with varying metal dispersion through controlled synthesis. Polyethylene hydrogenolysis was conducted under mild conditions (270°C, 50 bar H2, 3 h), targeting the production of fuel-range hydrocarbons. Remarkably, activity exhibited a clear dependence on particle size (Fig. 1), with optimal performance achieved at intermediate particle dimensions (~2 nm). This size-dependent behavior suggests that systematic control of metal particle size enables optimization of both activity and selectivity toward valuable hydrocarbon products. These results demonstrate that rational optimization of metal catalyst structure can substantially enhance polyolefin hydrogenolysis performance, with simultaneous access to multiple value streams (gasoline, wax, lubricants). In this presentation, we will further discuss reaction condition optimization, catalyst activity evaluation across diverse polyolefin feedstocks (HDPE, LDPE, PP, and their mixtures), mechanistic insights into active sites, and catalyst reusability. These comprehensive findings underscore the critical importance of catalyst design in developing efficient technologies for plastic upcycling. We investigate catalytic hydrogenolysis of polyolefins using Ru/TiO2 catalysts to produce fuel-range hydrocarbons (gasoline, wax, lubricants). By systematically controlling metal particle size, we achieved optimal catalytic performance at intermediate dimensions. These findings provide guidance for developing catalysts that can selectively convert polyolefin waste into high-value products.

P1-021.k: Ni-exsolved Perovskite; Hydrogen Production; Biomass Gasification
P1-021.a: Biomass gasification is a promising thermochemical conversion technology for producing hydrogen(H2)-rich syngas from renewable carbon resources. However, the formation of tar and hydrocarbons during gasification can reduce gas yield and H2 production efficiency. Therefore, highly active and stable catalysts are required to effectively reform these compounds. Ni-based catalysts exhibit high activity for hydrocarbon reforming and H2 production; however, they are susceptible to deactivation caused by particle agglomeration and carbon deposition under high-temperature reaction conditions. In this study, Ni-exsolved perovskite catalysts, in which Ni species are exsolved from the perovskite lattice onto the surface, were applied to biomass gasification. This study particularly focused on the effect of precursor crystallinity on catalytic gasification performance and H2 production after Ni exsolution. LaTi0.5Ni0.5O3 (LTNO), PrTi0.5Ni0.5O3 (PTNO), and NdTi0.5Ni0.5O3 (NTNO) were synthesized and subjected to reduction treatment to induce Ni exsolution before being applied to biomass gasification. Crystalline perovskites were first evaluated to investigate the effect of the A-site cation on gasification performance. Subsequently, an amorphous precursor was prepared to investigate the effect of precursor crystallinity on exsolution and catalytic performance. The effects of exsolution temperature and gasification temperature were subsequently evaluated, and cyclic stability was assessed through repeated gasification runs. The structural and surface properties of the catalysts were characterized by XRD, H2-TPR, BET, TEM, SEM, and XPS analyses. All exsolved perovskite catalysts increased gas yield and reduced tar yield compared with the non-catalytic condition. Among the catalysts with different A-site compositions, gas yield and H2 selectivity followed the order LTNO>PTNO>NTNO. The effect of precursor crystallinity was further investigated using La-based LTNO, which exhibited the highest catalytic performance. Despite having the same nominal composition, distinct differences in gasification performance were observed depending on the precursor structure. The exsolved catalyst derived from the amorphous LTNO precursor exhibited higher gas yield and H2 selectivity than that derived from the crystalline precursor, while also showing the lowest tar yield. In addition, Ni exsolution increased H2 and CO2 selectivities while decreasing CO selectivity, suggesting enhanced H2-producing reactions, including the water-gas shift reaction. The effect of exsolution temperature was subsequently examined for amorphous LTNO. Exsolution at 750 °C resulted in only limited changes in catalytic performance, whereas treatment at 850 °C enhanced gas yield and H2 selectivity while decreasing CO and hydrocarbon selectivities. These results suggest that surface modifications induced by the exsolution temperature played an important role in promoting reforming and H2-producing reactions. Increasing the gasification temperature from 700 to 800 °C further increased H2 selectivity while decreasing the selectivities toward CO, CH4, and C2–C4 hydrocarbons. This behavior was attributed to enhanced steam reforming and cracking of tar and hydrocarbons at higher temperatures. Furthermore, the exsolved catalyst derived from the amorphous precursor maintained stable product yields and gas composition over six consecutive cycles with re-reduction treatment, demonstrating excellent cyclic stability. This study demonstrates that the A-site composition, precursor crystallinity, and exsolution conditions of Ni-exsolved perovskites play important roles in determining H2 production performance during biomass gasification. In particular, the Ni-exsolved catalyst derived from the amorphous LTNO precursor exhibited high gas yield and H2 selectivity, low tar yield, and excellent stability during repeated use.
