These findings suggest that combining an amorphous precursor with Ni exsolution can generate catalytic surface characteristics favorable for reforming and water-gas shift reactions during gasification. Therefore, amorphous-derived Ni-exsolved perovskites represent a promising catalyst design strategy for efficient H2 production from biomass.

P1-022.k: Acetylene Converter; Petrochemical Process; Catalyst Degradation
P1-022.a: Ethylene, the primary feedstock of the petrochemical industry, is produced together with trace acetylene, which poisons downstream catalysts and is therefore removed by selective hydrogenation over a Pd catalyst in an acetylene converter. As the catalyst deactivates, the reaction temperature rises steadily, leading to ethylene loss and a risk of reactor shutdown. The reactor outlet temperature, however, also reflects fluctuations caused by changes in operating conditions, so the actual extent of catalyst deactivation is difficult to assess. In this study, a pure catalyst deactivation index was defined by stepwise removal of non-deactivation factors from 4.5 years of operating data of a GS Caltex acetylene converter, and a time-series model based on this index was developed to forecast the temperature trajectory over the next 14 days, achieving an R2 of 0.91. The framework enables continuous tracking of the deactivation trend and prior comparison of temperature scenarios across operating conditions, thereby supporting both catalyst life management and operation optimization.

P1-023.a: Excessive local alkalinity during electrochemical CO2 reduction promotes carbonate formation, reducing CO2 availability and limiting current density. This study explores a silica-hydroxide cycle to regulate the reaction microenvironment and enhance CO production. Ag-SiO2 gas diffusion electrodes were prepared by spray-coating Ag and SiO2 nanoparticles and evaluated in an anion exchange membrane zero-gap electrolyzer with bicarbonate anolytes. Gas analysis, operando Raman spectroscopy, and electron microscopy were used to assess performance and investigate the role of SiO2. With 0.1 M CsHCO3 anolyte, Ag-SiO2 achieved a maximum CO partial current density of 806 mA cm-2, compared with 549 mA cm-2 for Ag alone. CO Faradaic efficiency exceeded 80% at a total current density of 1 A cm-2 and remained above 90% for 12 h at 700 mA cm-2. Mechanistic analyses supported a silica-hydroxide cycle involving reversible silica dissolution and reprecipitation, which redistributes hydroxide ions and moderates local alkalinity. The silica-hydroxide cycle alleviates CO2 transport limitations by regulating local alkalinity, enabling selective CO production at high current densities. These findings highlight a promising chemical strategy for improving CO2 electrolyzer performance.

P1-024.k: Sodium-ion batteries, Hard carbon, Boron doping
P1-024.a: Background Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are promising for large-scale energy storage owing to the abundance and low cost of sodium. Hard carbon (HC) is the leading SIB anode material, but it suffers from limited reversible capacity, poor rate capability, and low initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE). Herein, a facile boron-doping strategy is proposed to address these limitations. Methods Boron-doped hard carbon (B-HC) was synthesized by a simple solution-mixing and heat-treatment process. HC powder was mixed with 2.5 wt% boric acid in ethanol, stirred at 70 °C for 2 h, dried at 100 °C for 24 h, and annealed at 1000 °C for 2 h under Ar. The structural and chemical properties were characterized by FE-SEM with EDS mapping, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS. Electrochemical performance was evaluated in coin-type half cells using cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic charge–discharge, cycling, and rate capability tests. Results Boron was successfully incorporated into the carbon framework, expanding the interlayer spacing to ~0.40 nm and creating additional defect sites for Na⁺ storage. Consequently, B-HC delivered a discharge capacity of 364.8 mAh g⁻¹, ~11% higher than pristine HC (328.8 mAh g⁻¹), with an ICE of ~86%, stable cycling over 100 cycles, and improved rate capability. Conclusion Boron doping is a facile and effective strategy for tailoring the microstructure of hard carbon. The expanded interlayer spacing and boron-induced defects simultaneously enhance the sodium storage capacity, cycling stability, and rate performance. Therefore, B-HC is a promising anode material for low-cost, high-performance sodium-ion batteries for large-scale energy storage.

P1-025.a: The rapid growth of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) in electric vehicles and portable electronics has led to a surge in end-of-life batteries. Conventional strategies such as reuse and recycling suffer from limited economic value or high processing costs. Since loss of lithium inventory (LLI) is a dominant degradation mechanism, a direct lithium replenishment strategy offers a promising pathway to restore battery capacity while maintaining material integrity. A three-electrode pouch cell incorporating a donut-shaped lithium metal was fabricated to enable electrochemical lithium replenishment. Artificial LLI (30%) and cycling-aged cells (SOH 70–80%) were tested. Regeneration was performed by applying a 0.01C current between Li metal and the cathode. Electrochemical characterization included EIS (1 MHz–10 mHz), DCIR, OCV analysis, and cycling tests. Cells with 30% lithium depletion recovered nearly full capacity after regeneration. Aged cells showed capacity recovery corresponding to the stoichiometric difference at high SOC. EIS and DCIR results indicated minimal resistance change. Post-mortem analysis confirmed increased lithium content without structural degradation. However, regenerated cells exhibited faster capacity fade upon further cycling. Electrochemical lithium replenishment effectively restores capacity in degraded LIBs by addressing LLI. This approach provides a simple, cost-effective alternative between reuse and recycling, extending battery lifetime and enhancing circular economy potential.

P1-026.a: The growing demand for sustainable energy-storage technologies has motivated the development of simple and environmentally benign synthesis routes for electrode materials used in aqueous zinc-ion batteries and supercapacitors. Among the available electrode materials, MnO2 has been particularly attractive because of its high theoretical capacity, natural abundance, low cost, and favorable electrochemical properties. However, conventional MnO2 preparation commonly requires high-purity reagents, thermal treatment, and/or multistep processing. Here, we report an ambient-temperature synthesis of MnO2 mediated by a commercially available Korean alcoholic beverage (i.e., soju). The proposed method uses readily accessible materials and eliminates the need for elevated temperature and additional purification steps. Structural and morphological analysis confirmed the formation of MnO2 structure. The resulting MnO₂ was employed as the cathode material in a zinc-ion battery and as the positive electrode in an asymmetric supercapacitor. The zinc-ion battery delivered a specific capacity of 210 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.05 A g⁻¹ and retained 90% of its capacity after 5000 cycles, while the asymmetric supercapacitor exhibited a specific capacitance of 11 mAh g⁻¹, an energy density of 20 Wh kg⁻¹, and 96 % capacitance retention after 5000 cycles. This work establishes Korean alcoholic beverage-mediated synthesis as a facile and low-energy route for preparing MnO2 electrodes for aqueous energy-storage applications.

P1-027.a: Sodium-ion batteries have emerged as promising alternatives to lithium-ion batteries for large-scale energy storage because of the natural abundance and low cost of sodium. However, graphite stores Na⁺ poorly, making hard carbon (HC) a more practical anode. Pitch is attractive as an HC precursor because of its low cost, high carbon yield, and scalable processing, but its thermoplasticity promotes softening, particle fusion, and partial graphitization during carbonization. Pitch-derived HC was systematically engineered by varying pre-oxidation temperature, oxidation holding time, and carbonization temperature. To improve rate capability, a small amount of non-oxidized pitch was blended with optimized oxidized pitch before carbonization to form a core-shell-like heterostructure. The optimized oxidized-pitch HC exhibited a carbon yield of 62%, a first-discharge capacity of 307.6 mAh g⁻¹, and an initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) of 93.3%. Approximately 70% of the total capacity originated from the plateau region below 0.13V, indicating effective Na storage in closed nanopores. However, its highly crosslinked structure limited rapid Na⁺ transport. The heterostructured HC retained a first-discharge capacity of 289.1 mAh g⁻¹ and an ICE of 93.1%, while its 3C capacity retention increased to 87.1%, compared with 28.8% for the unmodified sample. Moreover, the heterostructured HC was also beneficial for full-cell performance. Controlled oxidation stabilized a disordered turbostratic HC structure with abundant closed pores, whereas non-oxidized pitch induced surface densification and short-range ordering. Integrating oxidation control with heterostructure engineering effectively balanced capacity, efficiency, and rate capability in pitch-derived HC anodes. This approach also preserves the processing advantages required for scalable industrial production.

P1-028.k: Aqueous Zinc–Sulfur Batteries; Hierarchical Porous Carbon; Macropore Connectivity
P1-028.a: Aqueous zinc-sulfur batteries (AZSBs) are promising next-generation energy storage systems owing to their intrinsic safety, low cost, and high theoretical capacities of Zn and S. However, the low electrical conductivity and poor wettability of sulfur, together with sluggish solid-solid conversion kinetics, significantly limit their electrochemical performance. Hierarchically porous materials can address these challenges by providing high surface area and efficient ion transport pathways, but their synthesis often requires complex multistep processes. Here, we report a one-pot synthesis strategy based on evaporation-induced self-assembly and spinodal decomposition to fabricate hierarchical N-doped porous carbon with tunable macropore connectivity. By simply controlling the solvent evaporation rate, interconnected macroporous carbon and isolated macroporous carbon were selectively obtained. Sulfur was subsequently incorporated into the porous hosts and evaluated as cathodes for AZSBs. Structural characterization confirmed the successful formation of hierarchical porous architectures with controllable macropore connectivity. By controlling the evaporation rate during synthesis, interconnected or isolated macropore structures were selectively produced without additional processing steps. Furthermore, the mesoporous and macroporous structures, pore size, connectivity, and particle morphology could be systematically tailored by adjusting the block copolymer/homopolymer ratio and precursor concentration. The interconnected porous framework exhibited improved electrolyte wettability and transport properties, facilitating electrolyte infiltration and sulfur utilization in AZSB cathodes and thereby enhancing electrochemical reaction kinetics while reducing polarization. These results demonstrate that controlling macropore connectivity through kinetic regulation effectively enhances electrolyte transport and sulfur redox kinetics, providing a scalable design strategy for high-performance AZSB cathodes.

P1-029.a: Despite their high energy density, anode-free lithium metal batteries (AFLMBs) suffer from rapid performance degradation during cycling and storage because of the absence of an excess Li reservoir. In particular, galvanic corrosion between deposited Li and conventional Cu current collector continuously consumes active Li even without an applied current. This degradation pathway is especially critical under practical operating conditions, where charged cells may remain at rest for extended periods. A grain-boundary-free Ti–Zr–Cu–Ni (TZCN) metallic glass foil was compared with Cu to determine how current-collector corrosion resistance and crystallinity affect galvanic corrosion, interfacial stability, Li reversibility, and full-cell performance. TZCN exhibited substantially lower galvanic current and suppressed Li dissolution during prolonged storage. Surface analyses revealed that TZCN promoted the formation of a thinner, more uniform, smoother, and inorganic-rich pre-solid electrolyte interphase, whereas Cu formed a more heterogeneous interphase with an organic-rich outer region. After Li plating and 15 days of rest, TZCN showed slower growth of charge-transfer resistance, and higher Li reversibility than Cu. In full cells, the performance difference was limited at an N/P ratio of 1 but became pronounced at 0.7, where TZCN delivered higher capacity retention and showed lower sensitivity to reduced Li inventory. TZCN also exhibited superior resistance to current-collector dissolution under severe overdischarge conditions. The intrinsic corrosion resistance and grain-boundary-free amorphous structure of TZCN effectively suppress galvanic corrosion and preserve active Li. These findings establish current-collector corrosion resistance and amorphous structure as key design parameters for durable AFLMBs.

P1-030.a: Overhang regions, where the anode extends beyond the cathode, are incorporated into lithium-ion batteries to compensate for electrode misalignment and mitigate edge lithium plating. Although graphite overhangs are well understood in terms of lithium storage, redistribution, and degradation, the reactivity of silicon-only and silicon-containing composite overhangs remains insufficiently clarified. Whether graphite activates neighboring silicon within the overhang and how this reactivity affects electrochemical behavior remain unresolved. Spatially resolved Raman spectroscopy was performed from the active area to the overhang, using the irreversible crystalline-to-amorphous transformation of silicon as a lithiation marker. Three-electrode cells with controlled overhang dimensions were used to correlate electrochemically inactive overhang area with anode and cathode potentials. Pure silicon electrodes retained a predominantly crystalline overhang, indicating negligible lithiation outside the cathode-overlapped region. In contrast, silicon/graphite composite electrodes exhibited amorphization of overhang silicon, with the extent increasing with graphite content and cycle number. These results indicate graphite-mediated lithium transport and charge redistribution that activate otherwise inactive silicon. Three-electrode measurements showed that a larger unreacted overhang fraction maintained a higher local anode potential, thereby increasing the average anode potential and shifting the cathode to a higher potential at a given full-cell voltage. Overhang behavior in silicon-containing anodes cannot be inferred from graphite or silicon alone. Graphite-mediated crosstalk governs silicon overhang lithiation, whereas persistent overhang inactivity alters electrode-potential balance. The resulting cathode-potential increase may accelerate electrolyte oxidation and parasitic degradation, making overhang reactivity an important design parameter for lifetime prediction and electrode optimization.

P1-031.k: Pit-controllable Protective Layer; Resistance Feedback Loop; Lithium–sulfur Batteries
P1-031.a: Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries are attractive lightweight energy-storage systems for high-specific-energy applications, but their practical operation under lean-electrolyte conditions is severely limited by Li metal anode (LMA) instability. In discharge-initiated Li–S cells, LMAs first undergo pit-forming Li stripping rather than Li plating, generating deep, spatially localized pits that deteriorate protective-layer (PL) function over prolonged cycling. Here, we propose a pit-controllable PL (PCPL) that can actively regulate Li stripping by spatially controlling pit formation. The PCPL adopts a dual-layer framework composed of PVDF-HFP outer and PEO inner layers, while incorporating lithium iodide (LiI) and iodine (I2) into the Li-facing inner layer as the pit-selective shielding (PSS) agent. At pit-nucleation sites, PSS-mediated Li2O dissolution–precipitation induces pit-selective shielding and a resistance feedback loop, promoting repassivation-controlled pit migration, and thereby regulating pit morphology and spatial distribution. The PCPL coating homogenizes subsequent Li plating and preserves its structural integrity during prolonged cycling. PCPL-coated LMAs enable stable cycling of Li–S and Li–SPAN cells under lean-electrolyte conditions (E/S = 5 µL mg−1). Beyond passive pit accommodation, our findings establish active pit regulation as a new design paradigm for durable LMA protection in high-energy Li–S cells.

P1-032.k: Line-compatible Binder Engineering; Mechanochemical PTFE Pre-defluorination; Reductively Stable Dry Anodes
P1-032.a: Dry-processed graphite anodes rely on fibrillated poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (PTFE) binders for solvent-free fabrication and mechanical integrity. However, PTFE undergoes reductive decomposition near 0.6 V during initial lithiation, consuming active lithium, generating LiF-rich by-products, and destabilizing the electrode interface. This work develops a line-compatible strategy to stabilize PTFE before electrochemical operation. A small amount of LiNO3 was introduced during the conventional kneading step, where heat and shear simultaneously induced PTFE fibrillation and partial mechanochemical pre-defluorination. Chemical and structural changes were investigated by FT-IR, XPS, solid-state 19F NMR, XRD, SEM, and mechanical testing. Density functional theory calculations and electrochemical measurements were used to evaluate electronic stabilization, interfacial reactions, and practical cell performance. Pre-defluorination generated less-fluorinated C–H-containing motifs, reduced the CF2 contribution, and increased the calculated PTFE LUMO level while preserving the fibrillar binder network at the optimized treatment level. Electrolyte uptake increased from 29.2% to 56.8%, and the characteristic PTFE reduction feature was strongly suppressed. The modified dry graphite anode achieved an initial Coulombic efficiency of 92.6% and 88% capacity retention at 3 C relative to 0.5 C. In graphite||NMC811 full cells with areal capacities of 5 and 10 mAh cm-2, approximately 70% capacity was retained after 500 cycles at 1 C/1 C and 0.5 C/0.5 C, respectively, with reduced lithium plating under fast charging. Integrating partial PTFE pre-defluorination into the existing kneading process improves reductive stability, ionic accessibility, and high-loading cell durability without additional wet processing or unit operations.

P1-033.a: Silicon-based anodes are promising for high-energy lithium-ion batteries because of their high theoretical capacity. However, their large volume expansion during lithiation causes non-uniform mechanical stress, loss of electrical contact, repeated solid-electrolyte interphase formation, and rapid capacity degradation. This study investigates pressure imaging as a non-destructive method for monitoring spatially resolved swelling and degradation of silicon-containing anodes. Pouch cells containing silicon–graphite composite anodes were operated under controlled mechanical constraint. A pressure-sensor array continuously measured the spatial pressure distribution during charge–discharge cycling. Pressure data were synchronized with voltage, current, capacity. Reversible pressure variation, irreversible pressure accumulation, differential pressure features, and spatial pressure non-uniformity were analyzed at different states of charge and aging stages. Pressure distribution imaging revealed localized regions with abnormal pressure evolution, indicating spatially non-uniform degradation. Post-mortem analysis confirmed more severe structural and interfacial deterioration in these regions. Half-cell testing showed lower residual capacity, while impedance measurements revealed increased resistance compared with normal regions. Thus, the pressure anomalies were directly associated with actual capacity loss and resistance growth in the silicon anode. Pressure distribution imaging enables non-destructive localization of mechanically and electrochemically degraded regions in silicon-containing anodes. The agreement between pressure imaging, post-mortem observations, half-cell capacity, and impedance results demonstrates its potential for diagnosing heterogeneous silicon-anode degradation before it is evident from cell-level electrical measurements.

P1-034.a: High-concentration electrolytes(HCE) can promote the formation of inorganic-rich electrode–electrolyte interphases with reduced kinetic barriers for Li-ion transport and interfacial charge transfer. However, their high viscosity, sluggish electrode wetting, and excessive lithium-salt content increase material costs and hinder practical commercialization. To overcome these limitations, ester solvents were introduced to facilitate rapid Li-ion transport under fast-charging conditions. Nevertheless, when ester solvents are designed at low concentration, they exhibit limited interfacial compatibility with graphite and insufficient oxidative stability at high-voltage cathodes, which can accelerate electrolyte decomposition, lithium plating, and interfacial degradation. Co-solvents and weakly coordinating diluents were screened based on polarity, molecular size, Li-ion coordination strength, and compatibility with ester solvents. Raman spectroscopy was used to investigate changes in the Li-ion solvation structure and anion–solvent interactions. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy(EIS) was conducted before and after cycling to evaluate the evolution of interfacial resistance at the electrodes after fast-charging cycles to examine cathode interfacial degradation. The optimized electrolyte maintained high ionic conductivity and rapid Li-ion transport of ester solvents at a sufficient level while reducing electrolyte viscosity and lithium-salt concentration. Raman spectroscopy and EIS results confirmed a modified solvation structure and reduced kinetic barriers for Li⁺ desolvation and interfacial transport. Consequently, the electrolyte suppressed polarization and interfacial resistance growth, improving fast-charging cycling stability. Molecular optimization of co-solvents and diluents provides an effective alternative to HCE design. Balancing solvation structure, interfacial resistance, and oxidative stability enables simultaneous protection of both electrodes and offers a practical strategy for fast-charging lithium-ion batteries.

P1-035.k: Lithium Ion Battery; Dry Electrode; Electrolyte
P1-035.a: Dry-processed graphite anodes are attracting attention as a promising electrode platform for next-generation lithium-ion batteries because they can simplify manufacturing and enable more sustainable electrode fabrication. However, compared with slurry-cast electrodes, dry-processed graphite anodes often exhibit limited electrolyte wetting, increased ionic transport resistance, and unstable interfacial behavior originating from their porous structure and PTFE-based binder network. These issues can hinder fast ion transport and accelerate electrochemical degradation, especially under practical cycling conditions. This study investigates electrolyte design as a strategy to improve transport properties and interfacial stability in dry-processed graphite anodes. The electrolyte systems were designed by varying lithium salts, solvents, and functional additives to control viscosity, ionic conductivity, and interfacial reactivity. Electrochemical performance was evaluated through cycling tests and impedance analysis, and the resistance components were compared to understand the effects of electrolyte formulation on bulk ion transport and electrode–electrolyte interfacial behavior in dry electrodes. Electrolyte formulation strongly influenced the performance of dry-processed graphite anodes. Low-viscosity electrolytes enhanced ion transport and reduced polarization, whereas conductivity alone did not explain the performance differences, emphasizing the roles of wettability and PTFE compatibility. Moreover, additives improved interfacial stability and cycling performance, demonstrating the need to simultaneously optimize transport and interfacial properties. This study shows that electrolyte engineering is an effective approach to addressing the transport and interfacial limitations of dry-processed graphite anodes. By correlating electrolyte properties with electrochemical resistance and cell performance, this work provides practical design guidelines for selecting electrolyte formulations suitable for PTFE-based dry electrodes.

P1-036.a: High-nickel layered NMC cathodes enable high energy density but can suffer rapid capacity fade at high cutoff voltages due to surface reconstruction and parasitic interfacial reactions. Amorphous Al₂O₃ coatings were deposited on NMC powders by powder atomic layer deposition (ALD). Coating thickness was tuned by ALD cycle number and evaluated under upper cutoff voltages of 4.4, 4.5, and 4.6 V. The optimal coating dosage increased with cutoff voltage. Lower ALD cycle counts improved cycling stability without compromising kinetics, whereas excessive coating degraded electrochemical performance. These results reveal a trade-off between initial capacity loss and long-term capacity retention. Voltage-specific optima were identified at 1, 3, and 5 ALD cycles for 4.4, 4.5, and 4.6 V, respectively, indicating that more aggressive high-voltage side reactions require absolute amount of the element for surface protection. Cutoff-voltage-dependent optimization is essential when applying nm-scale Al₂O₃ coatings to high-Ni NMC. Powder ALD enables precise and scalable control of coating thickness at the nm-scale, offering a practical route to stabilize cathode surfaces under increasingly aggressive high-voltage operation.

P1-037.k: Ni(OH)2-Ni3S2 Heterostructure; Hierarchical Nanostructures; Battery-type Electrode
P1-037.a: Nickel hydroxide (Ni(OH)2) is a promising pseudocapacitive electrode for supercapacitors (SCs), but its limited electroactive-site availability, large volume changes during fast cycling, and resulting capacitance fading hinder practical use. A binder-free strategy was developed to construct hierarchical Ni(OH)2-Ni3S2 heterostructures on nickel foam (NF) via DI water–assisted in-situ growth of Ni(OH)2 nanosheets followed by sulfurization. The structure and composition were examined by XRD, XPS, SEM/TEM, EDS mapping, and BET analysis. Electrochemical performance was evaluated in 2M KOH (aqueous) and PVA–KOH (gel) electrolytes using a three-electrode configuration, and a two-electrode quasi-solid-state asymmetric supercapacitor (QSS-ASC; Ni(OH)2-Ni3S2||AC) was assembled for device testing. Characterization confirms the formation of robust, well-interfaced Ni(OH)2-Ni3S2 heterostructures, where the synergistic coupling between interlocked Ni(OH)2 nanosheets and spherical Ni3S2 nanoparticle microclusters accelerates charge storage and mitigates diffusion limitations. The optimized electrode delivers a specific capacitance of 1300 F g−1 at 1 A g−1. The QSS-ASCs device operates at 1.6 V and achieves 127.5 F g−1 at 1 A g−1, with an energy density of 45.33 Wh kg−1 and a power density of 800 W kg−1, retaining 81.7% capacitance after 7500 cycles at 8 A g−1. Overall, this work highlights the strong potential of binder-free Ni(OH)2-Ni3S2 heterostructures grown on NF, offering a practical pathway toward durable, high-performance next-generation energy-storage systems. Acknowledgements This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, and RS-2024-00411809).

P1-038.k: Aqueous Batteries; Hydrogel Electrolytes; High Zn2+ Transference Number
P1-038.a: Hydrogel electrolytes are promising for flexible aqueous zinc-ion batteries, but freely migrating anions cause concentration polarization, parasitic reactions, and nonuniform Zn deposition. Achieving selective Zn²⁺ transport, high mechanical toughness, and a wide electrochemical stability window within one hydrogel remains challenging. A poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride)–polyacrylamide co-network was prepared by thermal copolymerization and subsequently swollen in 1 M Zn(ClO₄)₂ to exchange Cl⁻ with ClO₄⁻ at quaternary ammonium sites. Spectroscopic, microscopic, mechanical, and electrochemical analyses were combined with molecular dynamics and density functional theory calculations. Zn plating/stripping and flexible Zn||vanadium oxide full-cell performance were evaluated. Strong ammonium–ClO₄⁻ association immobilized anions and generated reinforcing ionic crosslinks. The resulting hydrogel exhibited a Zn²⁺ transference number of 0.86, ionic conductivity of 8.10 mS cm⁻¹ at 25 °C, toughness of 51.25 MJ m⁻³, and electrochemical stability window of 2.75 V. Zn||Zn cells operated for over 2000 h at 1 mA cm⁻² with a 35 mV overpotential. Zn||vanadium oxide cells delivered 350 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.5 A g⁻¹ and retained 212 mAh g⁻¹ after 3000 cycles at 5 A g⁻¹. Flexible pouch cells maintained approximately 270 mAh g⁻¹ under 0°–360° bending and retained 90.9% capacity after 300 cycles. Simulations revealed an anion-enriched Zn²⁺ solvation shell, reduced desolvation penalty, and enhanced Zn²⁺ diffusivity. Post-synthetic anion exchange simultaneously regulates ion transport kinetics, water activity, and hydrogel network mechanics, enabling a synergistic improvement in electrochemical stability and mechanical robustness. This strategy effectively suppresses parasitic reactions, enhances Zn²⁺ transport efficiency, and provides a practical and scalable route toward durable, high-rate flexible zinc-ion batteries suitable for wearable and deformable energy-storage applications.

P1-039.k: Lithium Sulfur Battery; Electrolyte; Redox Mediator
P1-039.a: Lithium–sulfur batteries (LSBs) offer high theoretical energy density but remain limited by polysulfide shuttling, sluggish sulfur redox kinetics, and the instability of metallic Li anodes. Li2S cathodes provide an attractive alternative by enabling the use of Li-free anodes; however, their practical application is hindered by the insulating nature of Li2S and the large kinetic barrier associated with its initial oxidation. A soluble redox mediator (RM) was incorporated into the electrolyte to facilitate Li2S oxidation through a solution-mediated charge-transfer pathway. The electrochemical behavior and stability of the RM were evaluated within the operating voltage window of LSBs, and its influence on Li2S activation, reaction kinetics, and cycling performance was investigated. The RM remained electrochemically compatible with the operating conditions and effectively promoted Li₂S oxidation. Its introduction decreased the initial Li2S activation voltage from approximately 3.1 to 2.6 V, substantially reducing polarization and the associated energy loss. The mediated oxidation pathway also facilitated Li2S conversion without compromising cycling stability, which remained comparable to that of the RM-free electrolyte. These results demonstrate that soluble RM-mediated oxidation provides an effective route to overcome the kinetic barrier of Li2S activation. Electrolyte engineering with suitable RMs can therefore improve reaction efficiency while preserving cycling stability, offering a promising strategy for practical high-energy Li2S-based batteries.

P1-040.k: Li-ion Batteries; Silicon Anode; SEI Layer
P1-040.a: Silicon microparticle (μSi) anodes are highly promising for lithium-ion batteries due to their high capacity, but they suffer from severe volume changes and unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation. Chemical crosstalk, such as transition-metal dissolution from cathodes, further degrades SEI stability in full-cells. A trace amount (~0.04wt%) of zinc fluoride (ZnF2) and fluorine was incorporated onto ~5μm μSi particles via an NH4F-assisted thermal decomposition strategy ZnF2/F-μSi. The physical, structural, and electrochemical properties were characterized in both half-cell and high-Ni NCMA full-cell configurations. During initial lithiation, ZnF2 decomposed to form a hierarchical SEI consisting of a mechanically robust, LiF-rich inner shell and a ductile outer Li–Zn alloy layer. In half-cells, ZnF2/F-μSi achieved 77% capacity retention after 200 cycles (compared to 27% for bare μSi) and reduced electrode swelling to 13% after 100 cycles (90% for bare μSi). In full-cell tests, the functional SEI layer suppressed parasitic reactions and transition-metal crosstalk, maintaining 70.2% capacity retention after 150 cycles at 1C. Introducing trace conversion-type materials offers a simple, scalable, and effective strategy to engineer functional, hierarchical SEI layers that stabilize high-capacity μSi anodes for practical battery applications.

P1-041.k: Zinc Metal Anode; Polyoxometalate; Artificial Interphase
P1-041.a: Zn is an attractive anode for aqueous batteries because of its high theoretical capacity (820 mAh g-1) and a deposition potential (-0.76 V vs. SHE) that lies within the stability window of aqueous electrolytes. Practical use is nevertheless limited by dendrite growth, passivation layers, and the hydrogen evolution reaction at the electrode-electrolyte interface. Artificial interphases are a direct route to address these issues, but the two available material classes are complementary rather than sufficient. Inorganic layers provide favorable nucleation chemistry yet are difficult to deposit conformally, whereas organic layers are processable but chemically and electrochemically weaker. This work asks whether a spontaneous redox reaction between the Zn surface and a strongly oxidizing inorganic cluster can be used as the layer-forming step itself, with a polymer employed to govern how that reaction proceeds. Phosphomolybdic acid hydrate (H3PMo12O40, POM) was combined with poly(ethylene glycol) dimethyl ether (PEGDME, Mn ~ 500). Two slurries were compared: 200 mg POM in 500 uL deionized water, and 200 mg POM in 100 uL deionized water with 400 uL PEGDME. Each slurry was applied to Zn foil by doctor blade at a nominal thickness of 100 um, dried at 80 C for 6 h, and washed with deionized water to remove unreacted material. The residual layer was characterized by SEM, 3D laser scanning microscopy, cross-sectional TEM with EDX line profiling, XPS, ex situ XRD, and ToF-SIMS. Zn adsorption energies on POM cluster sites and on Zn(100) and Zn(001) surfaces were computed by density functional theory. Electrochemical behavior was assessed by CV, Tafel analysis, EIS, GITT, symmetric-cell chronopotentiometry, and full cells paired with a beta-MnO2 cathode. After washing, a conformal layer 10-15 nm thick containing P, Mo, and O remained on the surface, three orders of magnitude thinner than the applied slurry, indicating that only the material chemically bound to Zn survives. The polymer-free slurry darkened within 3 s of contact, whereas the polymer-containing slurry darkened gradually over 20 s. This difference in reaction progression tracked the interphase quality. Without the polymer, acid corrosion roughened the surface (Sa 0.826 um), Mo was almost fully reduced (Mo6+ 1.7%), and ZnO formed. With the polymer, pristine Mo6+ was partly retained (6.5%) alongside Zn-POM and Mo5+ environments, no ZnO was detected, and the surface was smoother (Sa 0.629 um). DFT gave Zn binding energies of 0.366-4.020 eV on POM sites versus 0.566-0.856 eV on Zn surfaces. Charge-transfer resistance fell from 2,248 to 276 ohm and the average deposit volume from 71,754 to 16,060 um3. The coated anode sustained 9,050 mAh cm-2 in symmetric cells at 10 mA cm-2 and gave about 1.7 times the capacity retention of bare Zn in full cells. A nanometre-thick organic-inorganic hybrid interphase can be formed on Zn metal by a spontaneous interfacial redox reaction, without vacuum deposition or thermal treatment beyond simple drying. The thickness is set by the reaction itself rather than by the coating step, since the applied excess is removed by washing. Comparing the two slurry compositions shows that the outcome of this reaction is not fixed: the same reagents produce either a corroded, fully reduced surface or a smooth layer with mixed Mo oxidation states and no ZnO, depending on how the reaction environment is composed. The mixed-valence surface supplies binding sites more favorable for Zn than the metal surface itself, which is consistent with the lower nucleation overpotential and the smaller, more numerous deposits observed after cycling. Reaction control, rather than material selection alone, is therefore a usable design handle for artificial interphases on reactive metal anodes.

P1-042.a: Lithium–sulfur batteries are promising next-generation energy-storage systems owing to their high theoretical energy density and the natural abundance of sulfur. However, their practical application remains limited by sluggish sulfur redox kinetics, large electrochemical polarization, and the dissolution and migration of lithium polysulfide intermediates. These limitations can lead to inefficient sulfur utilization, polysulfide shuttling, and progressive degradation of electrochemical performance. Electrolyte additives provide an attractive approach to regulate the electrochemical reaction environment without substantial modification of the electrode architecture. In this study, functionalized cobalt phthalocyanine was investigated as a molecular electrolyte additive for improving the electrochemical behavior of lithium–sulfur batteries. Cobalt phthalocyanine and its functionalized derivative were synthesized and characterized using morphological and spectroscopic analyses to examine changes in their physicochemical properties. Their electrochemical effects were evaluated in lithium–sulfur cells using galvanostatic charge–discharge cycling, cyclic voltammetry, and polarization-related electrochemical measurements. Complementary electrochemical analyses were performed to investigate the redox behavior and shuttle characteristics of soluble polysulfide species. The influence of the functionalized additive on the lithium-metal electrode was further evaluated through lithium plating/stripping measurements and post-plating morphological characterization. Molecular functionalization altered the physicochemical characteristics and dispersion behavior of cobalt phthalocyanine in the electrolyte. Compared with the unmodified cobalt phthalocyanine and additive-free electrolyte, the functionalized additive enabled more stable charge–discharge profiles and lower electrochemical polarization. Cyclic voltammetry further revealed stronger and more distinct sulfur redox responses with reduced polarization, suggesting improved reversibility of sulfur conversion. Additional electrochemical measurements indicated modified redox behavior of soluble polysulfide species. Separately, the functionalized additive showed a stabilizing effect on the lithium-metal electrode, exhibiting lower and more stable plating/stripping polarization together with a more uniform lithium deposition morphology. The functionalized cobalt phthalocyanine exhibited favorable electrochemical behavior as an electrolyte additive for lithium–sulfur batteries. The additive reduced electrochemical polarization, improved sulfur redox behavior, and altered the electrochemical behavior of soluble polysulfide species. A stabilizing effect on lithium plating/stripping was also observed at the lithium-metal electrode. These findings suggest that molecular functionalization of cobalt phthalocyanine is a promising approach for tailoring electrolyte additives for lithium–sulfur batteries.

P1-043.k: Lithium Metal Anode; Artificial Protectice Layer; Interfacial Engineering
P1-043.a: Li metal is considered a promising electrode material for next-generation high-energy-density electrochemical storage systems owing to its exceptionally high theoretical specific capacity (3,860 mAh g-1) and low redox potential (-3.04 V vs. SHE). However, its practical implementation is limited by nonuniform Li deposition, continuous interfacial degradation, and severe morphological changes during repeated plating and stripping. Therefore, rational engineering of the electrode-electrolyte interface is essential for achieving stable and reversible lithium metal electrochemistry. Here, a hybrid Li-Ag/Li-Sb/LiF interphase was directly constructed on the Li metal surface through a facile solution-based treatment using a metal fluoride precursor. The spontaneous reaction between Li metal and the precursor simultaneously formed Li-rich alloy and LiF components at the interface. The resulting protective layer effectively regulated Li plating and stripping by combining the complementary functions of the Li-rich alloy and LiF components. The lithiophilic alloy phases promoted uniform Li nucleation and deposition, while the LiF-rich interface provided a stable interfacial environment that suppressed nonuniform Li growth. In particular, the distinct alloying characteristics of Ag and Sb contributed to reversible Li accommodation and interfacial stability during repeated plating and stripping. Consequently, the modified Li electrode exhibited reduced nucleation overpotential, uniform Li deposition, and prolonged cycling stability compared with bare Li. Structural investigations further correlated the nanoscale characteristic of the protective layer with its electrochemical behavior, providing insight into how the alloy and LiF components cooperatively stabilize the Li interface. The results demonstrate that the hybrid Li-rich alloy/LiF protective layer effectively stabilizes Li metal electrochemistry through complementary interfacial functions. This work provides a rational interfacial engineering strategy for high-energy electrochemical energy storage.

P1-044.a: Dual ion storage hybrid supercapacitors (HSCs) are considered as a promising device to overcome the limited energy density of existing supercapacitors while preserving high power and long cyclability. However, the development of high-capacity anion-storing materials, which can be paired with fast charging capacitive electrodes, lags behind cation-storing counterparts. We demonstrate the surface faradaic OH⁻ storage mechanism of anion-storing perovskite oxide composites and their application in high-performance dual ion HSCs. The oxygen vacancy and nanoparticle size of the reduced LaMnO₃ (r-LaMnO₃) were controlled, while r-LaMnO₃ was chemically coupled with ozonated carbon nanotubes (oCNTs) for improved anion storing capacity and cycle performance. As revealed by in-situ and ex-situ spectroscopic and computational analyses, OH⁻ ions are inserted into the oxygen vacancies coordinating with octahedral Mn, accompanied by an increase in the oxidation state of Mn during the charging process (or vice versa during discharge). By configuring the OH⁻-storing r-LaMnO₃/oCNT composite with Na⁺-storing MXene, the as-fabricated aqueous dual ion HSCs achieved a cycle performance of 73.3% retention over 10,000 cycles, delivering maximum energy and power densities of 47.5 W h kg⁻¹ and 8 kW kg⁻¹, respectively — far exceeding those of previously reported aqueous anion and dual ion storage cells. This research establishes a foundation for the unique anion storage mechanism of defect-engineered perovskite oxides and advances dual ion hybrid energy storage devices toward high energy and power densities.

P1-045.k: Dry Electrode; PTFE Fibrillation; Powder Rheometry
P1-045.a: Recently, dry electrode processing has attracted attention as a process for achieving high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries and thick electrodes. Dry processing can eliminate the toxic solvents and drying processes used in conventional wet processing, providing environmental and economic advantages, and is also favorable for simplifying the electrode manufacturing process. In particular, PTFE is a key binder in dry electrodes, forming fibrous structures from the nanometer to micrometer scale under high shear force and connecting active materials and conductive additives. Although the degree of PTFE fibrillation and properties of granules have a significant effect on the agglomeration, flowability, and processability of electrode powders, the physical properties of the powder at each process have not been clearly identified. In this study, the PTFE fibrillation behavior occurring during dry electrode manufacturing was quantitatively evaluated using a powder rheometer, and process-related physical property indicators for dry electrode intermediate products were established. For this purpose, the electrode powder manufacturing process was divided into three steps: mixing, kneading, and grinding, and the flow characteristics of the powder were measured at each step. Using the powder rheometer, changes in flow resistance, cohesion, and stability of the powder according to the progress of the process were compared. This study demonstrates that powder rheometer-based analysis can be a useful approach for evaluating the degree of PTFE fibrillation and changes in powder properties during dry electrode manufacturing. Through this, it is expected to provide basic physical property indicators for optimizing mixing, kneading, and grinding conditions in dry electrode manufacturing processes.

P1-046.a: The solvent-free dry electrode manufacturing process has recently been receiving significant attention due to its advantages such as thick electrode fabrication, process simplification, cost reduction, and low environmental burden. However, PTFE, a key fibrillating binder for the dry process, undergoes electrochemical reduction at the low potentials of battery anodes because of its low lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy, reacting with lithium ions. This leads to irreversible capacity loss, reduced initial coulombic efficiency, and lithium consumption in anode systems. Therefore, a fundamental understanding of PTFE reduction behavior is essential. Previous studies have reported inconsistent reduction potentials for PTFE depending on test conditions and electrode configurations. Consequently, the intrinsic reduction potential of PTFE remains unresolved, highlighting the need for a precise electrochemical analysis. In this study, various electrochemical techniques are employed to investigate the reduction mechanism and reduction potential of PTFE. Voltage ranges and current density are varied to determine whether the reduction potential of PTFE is influenced by kinetic characteristics, while PTFE content is adjusted to elucidate the contribution of PTFE binder content to irreversible capacity. The reduction behavior is analyzed under these different conditions to establish the reduction potential and characteristics of PTFE. By establishing baseline information on the reduction potential and mechanism of PTFE, this study offers fundamental guidelines for binder content optimization, voltage window design for anode stability, and the development of suppression strategies against PTFE reduction.

P1-047.a: As the demand for lithium-ion batteries rapidly increases, developing eco-friendly and safe manufacturing processes for high-performance cathode materials has become crucial. The conventional hydroxide co-precipitation method inherently relies on caustic soda (NaOH) and ammonia to synthesize cathode precursors. However, these hazardous chemicals pose significant risks to human health and the environment. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a sustainable co-precipitation process utilizing non-toxic carbonate-based precipitants, eliminating the need for harmful substances. In this work, sodium carbonate or sodium bicarbonate was employed as the precipitant instead of caustic soda. By optimizing key process parameters—such as pH, reaction temperature, and stirring speed—spherical carbonate precursors with a uniform particle size distribution were successfully synthesized. After calcination with a lithium source, the resulting cathode material exhibited a well-layered crystalline structure and electrochemical performance comparable to those produced via the conventional hydroxide route. This research demonstrates a viable, eco-friendly alternative for precursor synthesis, offering a safer working environment and contributing to the sustainability of the battery manufacturing industry.

P1-048.k: Spent Lithium-ion Batteries; Black Mass; Direct Recycling
P1-048.a: This study proposes an eco-friendly and highly efficient direct recycling process to regenerate NCM (Nickel-Cobalt-Manganese) cathode active materials directly from the black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries without conventional chemical metal extraction. Conventional hydrometallurgical recycling processes involve multi-stage leaching and separation using strong acids, which inevitably generate substantial wastewater and incur high processing costs. The cathode materials were then directly synthesized via a subsequent high-temperature calcination process to achieve successful re-lithiation into the crystal structure. The structural and morphological properties of the regenerated cathode materials were investigated using XRD and SEM, and their electrochemical performances, including initial charge/discharge capacity and cyclability, were evaluated. To address these limitations, we accurately quantified the residual transition metal (Ni, Co, Mn) and lithium content in the black mass, followed by the stoichiometric addition of a supplementary lithium source to compensate for the lithium deficiency. By bypassing the complex metal extraction steps, this direct regeneration process is expected to serve as a next-generation upcycling technology that significantly enhances economic viability and minimizes the carbon footprint of battery recycling.

P1-049.k: Dry Electrode Process; PTFE Binder; Electrolyte Affinity
P1-049.a: Solvent-free dry electrode processing has attracted significant attention as a means of addressing the environmental issues of organic solvent use, electrode non-uniformity from binder migration during drying, and the costs of the drying process, while also enabling the fabrication of thick, high-loading electrodes. However, PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), the key binder in dry processing, has a limitation in that its nonpolar structure and low surface energy result in poor electrolyte affinity, which increasingly deteriorates wetting and interfacial resistance as electrode thickness increases, undermining the advantages of dry processing. While chemical surface modification and alternative binders have been explored, PTFE's high chemical stability and unique fibrillation behavior make complete replacement difficult. In this study, we investigated the effects of PTFE's low electrolyte affinity on wetting behavior and interfacial resistance formation in NCM-based dry electrodes under various thickness and loading conditions through electrochemical analysis, examining the formation of ionic percolation pathways as a function of electrode thickness and binder content. We revealed that PTFE's limited affinity for the electrolyte directly governs the extent of ionic percolation pathway formation across the electrode thickness and identified the specific interfacial phenomena through which this affinity limitation degrades cell performance. Based on these findings, we propose an interfacial enhancement strategy incorporating a polar-functionalized co-binder to overcome the affinity limitations of PTFE and improve the electrolyte wetting and electrochemical performance of dry electrodes.

P1-050.k: Direct Recycling; NCM Cathode; Acetone-based Separation
P1-050.a: The rapid growth of electric vehicles is increasing end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and the need for sustainable recycling. Conventional hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical processes require considerable energy and can create environmental burdens. Direct recycling preserves cathode-material value, but safer separation solvents and lower-energy regeneration methods remain necessary. Spent NCM cathodes were separated from aluminum current collectors using acetone. The recovered powder was washed, relithiated through a LiOH-based autoclave process, and annealed with Li₂CO₃ under oxygen. FT-IR, XRD, ICP-OES, and coin-cell testing were conducted. Acetone achieved separation performance comparable to DMF and NMP, supporting its use as a less toxic and more volatile alternative solvent. After washing, FT-IR showed a marked decrease in the characteristic PVDF peaks, confirming effective binder removal. ICP-OES indicated an increase in lithium content and an improvement in compositional balance after relithiation. XRD revealed recovery of the I(003)/I(104) intensity ratio, sharper diffraction peaks, improved crystallinity, and fewer impurity-related peaks, demonstrating restoration of the layered structure. Coin-cell testing showed stable charge–discharge behavior, while the cycling coulombic efficiency recovered to above 99%, indicating improved electrochemical reversibility and reduced irreversible reactions. These results confirm successful regeneration at chemical, structural, and electrochemical levels. Acetone separation, washing, relithiation, and oxygen annealing effectively restored the composition, crystal structure, and electrochemical performance of degraded NCM cathodes. The proposed route therefore shows promise as a safer, lower-energy direct recycling strategy that reduces reliance on hazardous solvents while retaining the functional value of cathode materials.

P1-051.k: Biphasic Interphase; Lithium Metal Anode; All-solid-state Lithium Battery
P1-051.a: Sulfide-based all-solid-state lithium batteries (ASSLBs) are promising candidates for high-energy-density energy-storage systems, but their practical implementation is strongly limited by interfacial instability between lithium metal and sulfide solid electrolytes. Here, we report a simple ex situ surface treatment of lithium metal using zinc nitrate to construct a biphasic protective interphase for sulfide-based ASSLBs. Multi-scale structural and chemical analyses using SEM-EDS, XRD, XPS, and ToF-SIMS show that the modified interphase is compositionally differentiated, consisting of a Li3N-rich outer region and a LiZn-rich inner region adjacent to the Li substrate. Symmetric-cell measurements reveal that the treated Li exhibits more stable plating/stripping behavior and lowers interfacial resistance growth compared with bare Li, indicating mitigation of continuous interfacial degradation. Post-cycling analysis on the electrolyte side further confirms that the treated Li markedly suppresses sulfide-electrolyte decomposition. When applied to Li6PS5Cl-based full cells with a high-loading Ni-rich layered oxide cathode (4 mAh cm−2), the treated Li anode delivers stable rate capability and markedly improved cycling durability under demanding conditions. In particular, the interface-treated full cell retains more than 98% of its capacity over 100 cycles at 1C, whereas the bare-Li counterpart shows abnormal charge-capacity inflation and early shorting. These results demonstrate that a chemically simple yet functionally differentiated biphasic interphase can effectively stabilize the Li/sulfide-electrolyte interface and provide a practical interfacial-engineering strategy for sulfide-based lithium-metal ASSLBs.

P1-052.k: Li Ion Battery; Thermal Runaway; Fire Propagation
P1-052.a: Lithium-ion battery fires can propagate beyond the thermal runaway of a single cell to adjacent cells, eventually developing into large-scale fire accidents at the module level. For this reason, understanding fire propagation behavior and identifying the key risk factors associated with thermal runaway are essential for improving the safety of electric vehicle battery systems. In this study, stepwise experiments were conducted to simulate fire propagation in electric vehicle battery modules and to analyze the major risk factors related to thermal runaway. Based on this validation, the effects of aging condition, state of charge (SOC), and internal pressure were systematically investigated as major variables affecting fire propagation and thermal runaway behavior. The results showed that thermal runaway propagation between cells was strongly influenced by the rate of heat transfer from one cell to another, and that this heat transfer behavior varied depending on the cell condition. In particular, aged cells exhibited a tendency toward relatively lower hazard levels during thermal runaway. This behavior is attributed to the fact that reactive species contributing to violent combustion or explosion had already been partially consumed or transformed into other compounds through side reactions accumulated during aging. In contrast, cells at high SOC generated more severe exothermic reactions because of the increased amount of stored electrochemical energy. In addition, elevated internal pressure promoted more efficient heat transfer between neighboring cells and accelerated heat accumulation within the module, thereby resulting in faster thermal runaway initiation and propagation.

P1-053.k: Li Ion Battery; Gas Evolution; Ni Rich NCM
P1-053.a: Gas evolution in Ni-rich NCM cathodes is regarded as a critical challenge that undermines the long-term cycling stability and thermal safety of high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries. To fundamentally decouple and analyze the cathode-side reactions free from anode interference, a custom electrode reaction-induced electric reforming reactor was designed. Through this system, gas species generated solely from the interactions between transition metals and the electrolyte under high-voltage conditions can be precisely monitored in real-time. The correlation between metallic Ni formation and the increased evolution of specific gas species (namely CH4, C2H6, CO, and CO2) within practical battery environments was rigorously validated through comparative experiments in which Ni metal was intentionally incorporated into pouch full-cells. To minimize experimental variables and enhance comparative accuracy, a sophisticated cell configuration was employed, wherein Ni-added NCM electrodes and pristine NCM electrodes were simultaneously integrated into the same cell. In this setup, gas evolution was quantified and analyzed in real-time utilizing high-precision pressure sensors. Furthermore, to verify the validity of the proposed mechanism, the detailed composition of real-world gas species emitted from cycled pouch cells was analyzed via X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) and Gas Chromatography (GC). Consequently, it was demonstrated that catalytic dehydrogenation (H-abstraction) and ring-opening reactions are heavily facilitated by the exceptional adsorption affinity of this metallic Ni for hydrocarbon-based electrolytes.

P1-054.a: P2-type layered oxide Na0.67Ni0.33Mn0.67O2 (NM) has attracted considerable attention as a promising cathode material for sodium-ion batteries owing to its two-dimensional Na+ diffusion pathways and high operating voltage. However, its practical application is still limited by irreversible P2–O2 phase transition at high voltages, sluggish interfacial charge-transfer kinetics, and surface deterioration caused by electrolyte-induced side reactions. Herein, we propose a dual-modification strategy that integrates crystal-facet engineering and surface passivation to address these limitations. A molten-salt synthesis approach was used to preferentially expose electrochemically active {010} facets, shortening Na+ diffusion pathways and enhancing reaction kinetics. In parallel, a controlled gas-solid reaction with CO2 was employed to construct a uniform Na2CO3 protective layer, which mitigates interfacial side reactions and stabilizes the electrode surface. The resulting {010}-NM@Na2CO3 exhibited highly reversible structural evolution under high-voltage operation, delivering an initial specific capacity of 129.4 mAh g−1 with 83% capacity retention after 100 cycles at 1 C and retaining 88 % of its initial capacity after 300 cycles at 5 C. These findings demonstrate that combining facet control with functional surface modification offers an effective and scalable strategy for designing high-performance layered oxide cathodes for sodium-ion batteries.

P1-055.a: Commercial polycrystalline NCM cathodes experience rapid capacity fade due to unwanted side reactions with the electrolyte, which are accelerated by stress-induced intergranular microcracking along the grain boundaries due to anisotropic volume changes during charge-discharge cycling. Single-crystalline cathodes have emerged as a robust solution to alleviate these degradation pathways by eliminating grain boundaries. However, conventional synthesis of single-crystalline cathodes demands high thermal energy (elevated temperatures and extended calcination times) along with complex workflows, which impede cost-effective scalability. Moreover, such harsh thermal conditions induce detrimental structural defects, including oxygen vacancies and Li/Ni cation mixing. Although alternative strategies like molten-salt or hydrothermal methods can lower the calcination temperature, they require additional post-processing steps, such as washing or grinding. To overcome these limitations, we report a simplified synthesis methodology via spray pyrolysis that circumvents the complexities of previously reported synthesis routes and enables low-temperature synthesis of single-crystalline cathodes. Through systematic structural, morphological, and electrochemical investigations, we successfully demonstrate the fabrication of well-ordered single-crystalline NCM cathodes with minimized structural defects. Notably, the synthesized single-crystalline cathodes exhibit significantly enhanced cycling stability and capacity retention under high-voltage operation compared to the polycrystalline NCM. Consequently, the single-crystalline cathode prepared via this facile spray pyrolysis method offers a highly practical material design strategy to boost the energy density and lifespan of next-generation high-voltage lithium-ion batteries.

P1-056.k: Anode-free Lithium Metal Batteries; Interfacial Engineering; Lithium Nucleation
P1-056.a: Anode-free lithium metal batteries (AFLMBs) offer high energy density but rely on a finite cathode-derived lithium inventory that is rapidly depleted by nonuniform nucleation and growth on bare Cu, leading to unstable lithium deposits, repeated electrolyte decomposition, and inactive lithium formation. Although lithiophilic interfacial modifications can facilitate lithium nucleation, uniform and reversible deposition requires a deliberately structured interface that coordinates Li⁺ transport, site-selective nucleation, and electron delivery through a continuous conductive network. Herein, we develop a multifunctional composite interlayer comprising an ion-regulating matrix, nanoscale lithiophilic promoters, and a conductive lithiophobic network. The optimized interlayer-modified Cu achieved an average Coulombic efficiency of approximately 98% over 2-200 cycles in Li||Cu cells at 1 mA cm⁻² and 1 mAh cm⁻², outperforming bare Cu and the corresponding control interlayer without the conductive network. The improved lithium reversibility is attributed to the functionally differentiated architecture, which homogenizes Li⁺ flux, maintains electron transport throughout the interlayer, and suppresses competing nucleation on the conductive domains. These cooperative functions direct lithium deposition toward the lithiophilic sites and promote distributed nucleation with dense, lateral growth. Ongoing work extends this interfacial design to anode-free full cells under practically relevant conditions. This work provides a rational lithiophilic–lithiophobic interfacial design for improving lithium utilization toward AFLMBs.

P1-057.k: Aqueous Zinc-Ion Battery; MnO2 Cathode; Zn Doping
P1-057.a: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) are promising next-generation energy storage systems because of their low cost, high safety, environmental friendliness, and abundant zinc resources. However, the poor electrical conductivity and structural instability of MnO2 cathodes limit their cycling stability and rate capability. Herein, Zn-doped δ-MnO2 was synthesized via a solution plasma process to introduce oxygen vacancies, improve electrical conductivity, and enhance structural stability. Zn-doped δ-MnO2 was synthesized from KMnO4, sucrose, and ZnCl2 precursors with Zn concentrations of 0, 5, 10, and 30 mM. The crystal structure, morphology, and chemical states were characterized by XRD, Raman spectroscopy, FE-SEM, TEM, and XPS. Electrochemical performance was evaluated using cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, rate capability, and cycling tests. The synthesized samples—denoted as MO, ZMO5, ZMO10, and ZMO30—were categorized based on their Zn precursor concentration. Among these, ZMO5 exhibited enhanced electrochemical performance, delivering a discharge capacity of 322 mAh/g at 0.1 C, which is a significant improvement over the 260 mAh/g observed for the pristine MO. Furthermore, ZMO5 exhibited excellent cycling stability, retaining over 82% of its initial capacity after 1,000 cycles at 5 C. Zn doping effectively modulated the electronic structure of δ-MnO2, inducing oxygen vacancies that enhanced charge-transfer kinetics and structural stability. These findings demonstrate that defect engineering via the solution plasma process is an effective strategy for developing high-performance MnO2 cathodes for AZIBs.

P1-058.k: Self-Assembled Monolayers; Li-ion Batteries; 3D Structured Electrodes
P1-058.a: LiFePO4 (LFP) cathodes have attracted renewed interest owing to their thermal stability, long cycle life, and low cost. However, the intrinsically low electronic and ionic conductivity of LFP limit its C-rate capability. Three-dimensional (3D) structured electrode has emerged as an effective strategy to enhance ion transport by expanding the electrode/electrolyte interface. Nevertheless, the enlarged interface inevitably accelerates side reactions and interfacial degradation, resulting in compromised cyclability. To overcome this trade-off, we combines 3D structured electrode with an organosilane-based self-assembled monolayer (SAM) to stabilize the electrode/electrolyte interface while preserving the benefits of the 3D architecture. 3D structured LFP electrodes were fabricated using an imprinting process. A fluoroalkylsilane based SAM was subsequently formed via vapor-phase deposition. The patterned architecture and surface morphology were characterized by FE-SEM, while the formation and thickness of the SAM were confirmed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The conformal C–F molecular layer acted as an artificial cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI), serving as a molecular gate that facilitated Li-ion transport while suppressing solvent penetration and electron tunneling. The SAM coverage effectively suppressed the interfacial degradation during cycling with minimal loss of the kinetic advantage provided by the 3D architecture. The optimized electrode exhibited a capacity retention of 98.6% after 150 cycles, demonstrating significantly improved interfacial stability. The synergistic integration of 3D electrode patterning and SAM provides an effective interfacial engineering strategy to mitigate interfacial degradation while maintaining the benefits of structured electrodes. This approach offers a promising route for developing durable high-performance LFP cathodes for next-generation lithium-ion batteries.

P1-059.k: Aqueous Zinc-ion Batteries; Plasma Immersion Ion Implantation; Surface Engineering
P1-059.a: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) have attracted considerable attention because of their intrinsic safety and low cost. Among various cathode materials, MnO2 is considered one of the most promising candidates owing to its high theoretical capacity and natural abundance. However, its poor electronic conductivity and sluggish Zn2+ diffusion limit its electrochemical performance. Nitrogen incorporation has been recognized as an effective strategy for tuning the electronic structure and promoting charge transfer in transition-metal oxides. Therefore, nitrogen mixed-anion surface engineering via plasma immersion ion implantation (PIII) was employed to enhance the electrochemical performance of MnO2 cathodes. MnO2 nanoparticles were synthesized via a solution plasma process using KMnO4 as the manganese precursor and sucrose as the reducing agent. The as-prepared MnO2 was subsequently subjected to nitrogen mixed-anion surface modification through PIII. The electrochemical performance of the modified cathodes was evaluated by galvanostatic charge–discharge tests and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). Nitrogen ion implantation significantly enhanced the electrochemical performance of the MnO2 cathode. The modified electrode exhibited approximately 20% higher initial discharge capacity than the pristine MnO2 and demonstrated improved rate capability. EIS analysis revealed a reduced charge-transfer resistance and an increased Zn2+ diffusion coefficient after nitrogen implantation, indicating accelerated charge-transfer kinetics and ion transport. Nitrogen mixed-anion surface engineering via PIII effectively improves the electrochemical kinetics of MnO2 cathodes, leading to enhanced capacity and rate capability. This surface modification strategy provides a promising approach for developing high-performance MnO2 cathodes for next-generation aqueous zinc-ion batteries.

P1-060.k: Aqueous Zinc-ion Batteries; Self-assembled Monolayer; Dendrite Suppression
P1-060.a: The increasing demand for large-scale energy storage systems has accelerated the development of aqueous Zn-ion batteries (AZIBs) as safe and cost-effective alternatives to Li-ion batteries. However, their practical application is limited by the poor interfacial stability of Zn metal anodes, where parasitic reactions, including hydrogen evolution and corrosion, induce dendritic Zn growth. To address these challenges, organosilane-based self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) were employed to regulate the Zn/electrolyte interface, suppress parasitic reactions, and promote uniform Zn nucleation through molecular-level interfacial engineering. Zinc anodes were modified with fluoroalkylsilane (FAS) and (3-aminopropyl)trimethoxysilane (APTMS)-SAMs via a vapor-phase deposition. The FAS monolayer was designed to suppress water-induced side reactions by providing a hydrophobic interface, whereas the APTMS monolayer introduced zincophilic amine groups to regulate Zn nucleation. Surface chemistry was characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and electrochemical performance was evaluated. XPS confirmed the successful formation of both organosilane monolayers on the Zn surface. Compared with bare Zn, both modified anodes exhibited lower nucleation overpotential, reduced charge-transfer resistance, and significantly improved cycling stability. Among them, the APTMS-modified anode demonstrated the best electrochemical performance owing to the synergistic effect of zincophilic amine groups, which promoted homogeneous Zn nucleation, together with the interfacial barrier that effectively suppressed parasitic reactions. EIS analysis further revealed enhanced interfacial charge-transfer kinetics and reduced activation energy after SAM modification. Organosilane SAMs effectively stabilize the zinc/electrolyte interface by simultaneously regulating Zn nucleation and suppressing interfacial side reactions. In particular, the APTMS-derived interface provides an effective surface engineering strategy for achieving durable and high-performance AZIBs.

P1-061.a: Quasi-solid-state polymer electrolytes have emerged to combine the favorable ion transport and interfacial contact of liquid electrolytes with the safety and mechanical stability of solid-state systems. However, simultaneously achieving rapid and selective Li⁺ transport together with dimensional stability remains challenging. Quasi-solid-state composite polymer electrolytes were fabricated by solution-casting halloysite nanotubes (HNTs) with a thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) matrix at different ratios, followed by incorporation of a small amount of LiTFSI-based liquid electrolyte. The effects of HNT loading on morphology, swelling, ion transport, electrochemical stability, lithium plating/stripping, full-cell performance, and mechanical and thermal properties were systematically evaluated. Increasing the HNT content generated interconnected HNT-rich regions and intertubular pores, enhancing electrolyte uptake and Li⁺ transport while suppressing excessive swelling. The optimized QSCPE-70 exhibited an ionic conductivity of 1.04 × 10⁻³ S cm⁻¹ at room temperature, a Li⁺ transference number of 0.767, and stable operation in Li|Li symmetric cells for over 2500 h at 0.1 mA cm⁻². The enhanced performance was attributed to Li⁺-selective transport along interconnected HNT surfaces and improved ion flux through electrolyte-filled pores. LiFePO₄|Li full cells demonstrated stable cycling and high-rate capability, while the flexible electrolyte film retained its structural integrity under bending, folding, and twisting. A pouch cell also remained operational under bending deformation, confirming its potential for flexible energy-storage applications. HNT-assisted microstructural regulation provides continuous and Li⁺-selective transport pathways while preserving dimensional stability, mechanical robustness, and flexibility. This strategy offers a practical route toward safe, high-performance, and flexible lithium metal batteries.

P1-062.k: Aqueous Zinc-ion Batteries; Inorganic-rich SEI; Zn(002) Texture
P1-062.a: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) are promising next-generation energy storage systems (ESS) owing to their safety and cost-effectiveness. Practical implementation requires reversible Zn plating/stripping under high-current density and high-areal capacity while maintaining long-term stability. However, localized Zn2+ flux and concentration gradients at high-current density accelerate nonuniform Zn deposition and dendrite growth, thereby causing internal short circuits. Meanwhile, parasitic hydrogen evolution and corrosion continuously consume electrolyte and active Zn, accelerating interfacial degradation. Together, these degradation pathways hinder the simultaneous achievement of high-current density and stability in AZIBs. Here, we report an integrated interfacial design strategy based on the synergistic coupling of an inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and preferential Zn(002) texture. A tailored Zn(OTf)2-based electrolyte facilitates interfacial decomposition of OTf- anions, thereby forming a fluorine-rich inorganic SEI on Zn. This high-modulus SEI mechanically suppresses dendritic Zn growth, while its electronically insulating nature inhibits continuous parasitic electrolyte decomposition at the Zn surface. Concurrently, hydrogen-assisted annealing induces crystallographic reorientation toward the Zn(002) texture in the Zn anode. The low migration barrier on Zn(002) basal plane promotes two-dimensional surface diffusion and lateral Zn growth, thereby mitigating heterogeneous nucleation and dendritic deposition. Its low interfacial reactivity suppresses hydrogen evolution and corrosion, improving Zn plating/stripping reversibility. Consequently, the coupled inorganic-rich SEI/Zn(002)-textured anode enables stable operation at high current density (>5mA/cm^2), exhibiting excellent reversibility and cycling durability. These findings establish a synergistic strategy that integrates electrolyte-derived interphase chemistry with crystallographic texture engineering, providing a practical pathway toward fast-charging, long-lived aqueous zinc-ion batteries.

P1-063.k: Lithium Metal Batteries; Nanospinbar; Dendrite Suppression
P1-063.a: Uneven lithium deposition and dendrite growth remain major challenges for lithium metal batteries. Conventional static electrolytes rely mainly on diffusion and electromigration, which can produce nonuniform lithium-ion concentration near the lithium surface. This study investigates a magnetic nanospinbar-dispersed colloidal electrolyte to improve ion transport through remotely controlled convection. Rod-shaped Fe3O4@SiO2 nanospinbars were synthesized and dispersed in ether-, carbonate-, and localized high-concentration electrolytes. An external rotating magnetic field was applied to actuate the nanospinbars. Ionic transport, lithium nucleation, deposition morphology, and electrochemical cycling were evaluated using simulations, chronoamperometry, electrochemical measurements, and scanning electron microscopy. Remote nanospinbar rotation increased the apparent diffusion coefficient by 24% and reduced the lithium-ion diffusion layer thickness by approximately 30%. The convective electrolyte promoted more uniform lithium nucleation, lowered nucleation overpotential, and produced denser and less dendritic lithium deposits. In localized high-concentration electrolyte, the nanospinbar-assisted cell maintained approximately 99% Coulombic efficiency for more than 700 cycles. Lithium/NMC622 cells also showed improved cycling stability, retaining 70% capacity after more than 600 cycles. Magnetically actuated nanospinbars provide a simple approach to dynamically redistribute lithium-ion flux in liquid electrolytes. The resulting convective transport suppresses dendritic lithium growth and improves the cycling stability of lithium metal batteries.

P1-064.a: Electrolyte wetting is a time- and cost-intensive bottleneck in lithium-ion battery manufacturing, yet the mechanisms governing infiltration in realistic porous electrodes remain insufficiently understood. Three-dimensional electrode architectures of NMC622 cathodes and graphite anodes with different calendering degrees were reconstructed using X-ray computed tomography. Multiphase lattice Boltzmann simulations were performed to resolve electrolyte infiltration, saturation, pressure evolution, and trapped-air formation. Realistic structures were compared with stochastically generated electrodes, and the influence of separator wicking was evaluated. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy of symmetric cells was used for experimental validation. Calendering accelerated early-stage infiltration by increasing capillary pressure, but excessive densification narrowed pore pathways, increased tortuosity, and promoted persistent air entrapment, thereby limiting final saturation. Graphite anodes generally exhibited faster and more homogeneous wetting than NMC622 cathodes because of their larger mean pore size and lower tortuosity. Idealized spherical-particle structures showed faster, more uniform wetting and less trapped air than realistic electrodes. Stronger separator wicking enhanced initial electrolyte delivery but could outpace gas evacuation, whereas weak wicking caused supply-limited and incomplete wetting. Impedance trends were consistent with the simulated effects of microstructure and calendering on ionic transport.
