Electrolyte wetting is governed by the coupled effects of electrode microstructure, capillary forces, gas transport, and separator-driven supply. Balancing separator wicking with microstructure-enabled gas evacuation provides a practical framework for improving wetting rate and uniformity.

P1-065.a: Lithium metal anodes are attractive for next-generation high-energy-density batteries because of their high theoretical capacity and low electrochemical potential. However, their highly reactive surface is easily oxidized during storage, handling, and cell fabrication. Such surface oxidation can alter morphology, interfacial resistance, and cell performance, highlighting the need for a rapid quality-control method before cell assembly. Surface gloss measurement was used as the primary method to evaluate lithium metal oxidation. Commercial Li foils were exposed to dry-room and accelerated oxidation environments, and changes in gloss were monitored as a non-destructive indicator of surface quality. SEM, AFM, EDS, XPS, EIS, and full-cell tests were additionally used to validate the relationship between gloss degradation, surface chemistry, morphology, and electrochemical behavior. As oxidation progressed, the Li surface gradually lost its metallic silver appearance and developed whitish regions and dark spots. This visual degradation was accompanied by a clear decrease in gloss and an increase in surface roughness. Chemical analyses confirmed the formation of oxide and carbonate-containing species, while electrochemical tests showed that severe surface oxidation was associated with abnormal interfacial behavior and unstable full-cell operation. The correlation between gloss, surface composition, roughness, and electrochemical response indicates that gloss can sensitively reflect the oxidation state of Li metal. This work demonstrates surface gloss measurement as a simple, rapid, and non-destructive approach for evaluating Li metal surface oxidation. The results provide a practical framework for defining oxidation thresholds and improving Li metal quality control before cell fabrication in practical battery manufacturing processes.

P1-066.k: Spent Zn–C Batteries; Battery Upcycling; Lithium-ion Batteries
P1-066.a: The widespread use of primary zinc–carbon (Zn–C) batteries generates substantial quantities of Mn-rich black mass at the end of their service life. Previous studies have explored recycling routes ranging from conventional metal recovery to the direct conversion of spent Zn–C battery materials into electrode materials for rechargeable batteries. However, these approaches often involve energy-intensive or multi-step treatments and typically yield only a single product, leaving the waste stream underutilized. Here, we report a dual-pathway upcycling strategy that converts Mn-rich black mass from spent primary batteries into anode and cathode materials for lithium-ion batteries. Phase-pure MnO was obtained from discharge-derived Zn-containing manganese oxide (ZMO) through selective Zn removal and subsequent phase conversion. XPS and EPR analyses confirmed abundant oxygen vacancies in the resulting MnO without an additional defect-engineering treatment. The oxygen-vacancy-rich MnO delivered a reversible capacity up to 500 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.5 A g⁻¹. The MnO intermediate was further lithiated to form highly crystalline spinel LiMn₂O₄, which delivered a discharge capacity of 78 mAh g⁻¹ at 1 C and maintained 78% of its initial capacity after 500 cycles. These results demonstrate that a single waste-derived Mn precursor can be converted into two complementary lithium-ion battery materials, providing a versatile route for the broader utilization of spent Zn–C batteries.

P1-067.k: NASICON; Glaze Frit; Coefficient of Thermal Expansion
P1-067.a: NASICON ceramic electrolytes are attractive for solid-state sodium batteries, but conventional processing requires sintering above 1250°C for over 10 hours, raising cost and limiting scalability. Liquid-phase sintering additives can relax these conditions, yet coefficient-of-thermal-expansion (CTE) mismatch between the additive and the NASICON matrix often induces residual stress and surface crazing during cooling, degrading mechanical integrity. Zn-doped von-Alpen-type NASICON (NZZSP, Na3.24Zr1.48Zn0.07Si2.3P0.7O11) was synthesized via a solid-state reaction method. A CTE-matched magnesia borosilicate frit (MBF, 4.0×10-6 K-1), close to NZZSP's CTE (4.7×10-6 K-1), was added at 0.5–8 wt% and sintered at 1150°C for 1 h. Microstructure and phase were characterized by XRD, FE-SEM, nano-CT, Cs-TEM, and XPS; ionic/electronic conductivity and mechanical strength were assessed via EIS, DC polarization, and three-point bending. Na symmetric cells and Na3V2(PO4)3/Na full cells evaluated electrochemical performance. NZZSP with 0.5 wt% MBF achieved 97.2% relative density and 2.71×10-3 S cm-1 ionic conductivity, with a low activation energy of 0.204 eV, while electronic conductivity decreased to 3.15×10-9 S cm-1. CTE matching suppressed surface crazing and raised flexural strength to 88.03 MPa, over fourfold higher than CTE-mismatched frits. Na contact angle dropped to 26°, interfacial resistance fell to 25.2 Ω cm2, and symmetric cells cycled stably for over 2000 h with critical current density up to 1.0 mA cm-2. Full cells retained 88.2% capacity after 200 cycles. CTE-matched glaze-frit-assisted sintering enables the simultaneous realization of relaxed processing conditions, high densification, mechanical robustness, and stable Na-interfacial performance, establishing CTE compatibility as a key design principle for practical NASICON solid electrolytes.

P1-068.k: Garnet-type Solid Electrolyte; Hybrid Sintering Additives; All-solid-state Batteries
P1-068.a: Garnet-type Li₆.₄La₃Zr₁.₄Ta₀.₆O₁₂ (LLZTO) is a promising oxide solid electrolyte for all-solid-state lithium batteries, but conventional densification requires temperatures above 1150 °C, causing lithium loss, abnormal grain growth, and high processing costs. This study evaluates a hybrid sintering-additive strategy that simultaneously combines a low-melting transient liquid-phase sintering mechanism with a high-melting solid-state sintering mechanism to achieve low-temperature densification and improved electrochemical performance. LLZTO powder was synthesized by a solid-state reaction, calcined at 900 °C, mixed with 1.2 wt.% Al₂O₃ and 2.0 wt.% Bi₂O₃, compacted, and sintered at 1000 °C for 12 h. Phase, microstructure, thermal behavior, and sintering mechanisms were examined by X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, thermal analysis, and in situ transmission electron microscopy. Ionic conductivity and lithium-interface performance were evaluated by impedance spectroscopy and Li symmetric cells. The hybrid-additive LLZTO reached 98.1% relative density with a uniform grain size of 1.29 ± 0.51 μm. Its room-temperature ionic conductivity was 4.64 × 10⁻⁴ S cm⁻¹, 5.2 times higher than additive-free LLZTO, while the activation energy decreased from 0.41 to 0.26 eV. In situ microscopy showed Bi₂O₃-assisted transient liquid-phase sintering near 600 °C. Symmetric cells exhibited an interfacial resistance of 21.5 Ω cm², a critical current density of 1.05 mA cm⁻², and stable cycling for more than 2,000 h at 0.10 mA cm⁻². The Al₂O₃–Bi₂O₃ hybrid additive promotes low-temperature densification, suppresses abnormal grain growth, and improves ionic transport and lithium-metal compatibility. This scalable approach supports practical fabrication of high-performance garnet electrolytes.

P1-069.k: Hydrovoltaic; Energy Harvesting; Layered Double Hydroxide
P1-069.a: Hydrovoltaic energy harvesting converts ambient water movement and evaporation into electricity via streaming potential. However, conventional layered double hydroxide (LDH)-based harvesters face challenges regarding low power output, complex manufacturing, and limited mechanistic understanding of capillary wicking dynamics. We fabricated a hierarchical hydrovoltaic device by electroplating NiFe LDH (30 s) onto thermally oxidized CuO nanowires (CuO NWs) supported on a Cu mesh scaffold. The NiFe LDH/CuO NW mesh configuration created interconnected micro/nanoscale channels that facilitated rapid ionic water diffusion. The device consistently achieved a volumetric power density of approximately 250 nW/cm3. Remarkably, it maintained robust energy generation for over one month without noticeable performance degradation. Mechanistic analyses revealed that the NiFe LDH layer significantly amplified the internal potential difference, enhancing both streaming potential and ionic diffusion efficiency. Additionally, serial integration demonstrated successful modular scalability. This work presents a highly durable and scalable hydrovoltaic strategy using functionalized hierarchical nanostructures. The device highlights strong potential for real-world application in harvesting clean energy from seawater and ambient hygroscopic salts.

P1-070.k: NASICON; Mg-Ti Co-doping; Solid-state Sodium Batteries
P1-070.a: Oxide-based NASICON is a promising solid electrolyte for all-solid-state sodium batteries because of its high chemical stability and superior air stability compared with sulfide electrolytes. However, its practical application is limited by insufficient ionic conductivity, poor densification causing high grain-boundary resistance, and large interfacial resistance with Na metal. In addition, conventional NASICON generally requires sintering above 1200 °C. This study proposes an Mg2+–Ti4+ co-doping strategy for von-Alpen-type NASICON (vA-NASICON) to improve electrochemical performance while lowering the sintering. Mg–Ti co-doped vA-NASICON electrolytes were synthesized by a conventional solid-state reaction using MgO and TiO₂ as dopant precursors. Stoichiometric powders were ball-milled, dried, calcined, ground, pelletized, and sintered at 1100 °C. The effects of Mg–Ti co-doping on phase evolution, densification, ionic transport, and Na metal interfacial properties were evaluated by structural, microstructural, and electrochemical characterization. The optimized Mg–Ti co-doped vA-NASICON electrolyte exhibited an ionic conductivity of 3.1 mS cm-1, approximately eight times higher than pristine vA-NASICON (0.4 mS cm-1), together with a critical current density of 1.1 mA cm-2, significantly exceeding those of pristine (0.2 mA cm-2) and Ti-doped (0.6 mA cm-2) electrolytes. The enhanced electrochemical performance is attributed to the synergistic effect of Mg-induced Na-vacancy formation, which facilitates Na+ migration, and Ti-assisted densification and improved Na wettability, which reduce grain-boundary and interfacial resistance. The Mg2+–Ti4+ co-doping strategy synergistically enhances ionic transport, densification, and Na metal interfacial stability while enabling sintering at 1100 °C. These findings provide a practical route toward high-performance oxide solid electrolytes with reduced processing cost for next-generation all-solid-state sodium batteries.

P1-071.k: NASICON; Mg2+-Ti4+ Co-doping; Solid-state Sodium Batteries
P1-071.a: NASICON-type solid electrolytes are promising candidates for solid-state sodium batteries owing to their high Na+ ionic conductivity and excellent chemical stability. However, their practical application remains limited by high sintering temperatures, insufficient densification, grain-boundary resistance, and poor interfacial contact with Na metal. Elemental doping has been widely investigated to address these limitations, but the distinct effects of individual dopants on phase evolution, microstructural development, and electrochemical performance remain insufficiently understood. In this study, Mg2+–Ti4+ co-doping was investigated as a complementary compositional-engineering strategy to improve ionic transport, densification, and interfacial stability in von-Alpen-type NASICON solid electrolytes under reduced sintering conditions. Pristine, Mg-doped, Ti-doped, and Mg–Ti co-doped NASICON solid electrolytes were synthesized via a conventional solid-state reaction method, followed by sintering at 1100 °C for 12 h. The effects of Mg and Ti incorporation on crystal structure, phase evolution, and microstructural characteristics were systematically investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Rietveld refinement, field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). Ionic conductivity and activation energy were evaluated using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and temperature-dependent measurements. Na metal wettability, interfacial resistance, critical current density (CCD), and long-term Na plating/stripping stability were examined using contact-angle measurements and Na/electrolyte/Na symmetric cells. Full-cell performance was further evaluated using Na3V2(PO4)3 (NVP) cathodes and Na metal anodes. XRD and Rietveld refinement revealed distinct effects of Mg and Ti incorporation on NASICON phase evolution. Mg doping increased the rhombohedral phase fraction, whereas Ti doping suppressed secondary-phase formation and promoted densification. The optimized Mg0.1Ti0.05 composition exhibited an increased rhombohedral phase fraction from 17.5% to 27.2%, together with substantially reduced secondary phases. Microstructural analysis confirmed a marked reduction in residual porosity and improved grain connectivity, accompanied by an increase in flexural strength from 28.0 to 123.5 MPa. Consequently, the co-doped electrolyte achieved a room-temperature ionic conductivity of 3.08 × 10-3 S cm-1 and a reduced activation energy of 0.197 eV. Furthermore, improved Na metal wettability reduced the interfacial resistance from 4162 to 41.2 Ω cm2, while the CCD increased from 0.2 to 1.0 mA cm⁻². The optimized electrolyte also demonstrated stable Na plating/stripping for over 3000 h at 0.1 mA cm-2. In addition, the NVP-based full cell maintained a discharge capacity of 86.4 mAh g-1 after 200 cycles, confirming improved electrochemical performance. This study demonstrates that complementary Mg2+–Ti4+ co-doping effectively improves the structural, microstructural, and electrochemical properties of von-Alpen-type NASICON solid electrolytes. Mg incorporation increases the rhombohedral phase fraction, while Ti incorporation suppresses secondary-phase formation and promotes densification. These complementary effects contribute to enhanced bulk and grain-boundary ionic transport, reduced interfacial resistance, and improved electrochemical stability against Na metal. The optimized co-doped electrolyte achieves high ionic conductivity, excellent long-term cycling stability, and improved full-cell performance at a reduced sintering temperature of 1100 °C. These findings highlight Mg–Ti co-doping as a promising strategy for developing high-performance NASICON solid electrolytes for solid-state sodium batteries.

P1-072.k: Silicon-carbon Anode; Silicon Removal; Li-ion Battery
P1-072.a: Silicon–carbon (Si/C) composites are promising anodes for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries because they combine the high capacity of Si with the mechanical buffering capability of a carbon matrix. However, surface-exposed residual Si species in Si/C particles undergo large volume changes during repeated lithiation/delithiation. Commercial Si/C powder was physically mixed with NH4F at Si/C mass ratios of 1:0.1, 1:0.5, and 1:1 using an agate mortar. The mixtures were heat-treated at 300 °C for 2 h under N2 atmosphere, sequentially washed with deionized water and ethanol, and dried at 80 °C. The resulting samples were denoted as Si/C@AF-10, Si/C@AF-50, and Si/C@AF-100, respectively. The etched Si/C electrode delivers a capacity retention approximately 13 times higher than that of the Si/C bare electrode after 500 cycles in half-cells. In addition, a full cell coupled with an NCM811 cathode operates over 400 cycles at 1C, indicating the applicability of the modified anode. Cross-sectional SEM analysis after 100 cycles revealed limited electrode expansion of 37.8%, confirming improved mechanical stability and structural integrity. A simple NH4F-assisted thermal treatment effectively removed residual surface Si and silicon oxide species from Si/C particles, with increasing NH4F content promoting their removal without significantly altering the overall particle characteristics. Among the treated samples, Si/C@AF-100 exhibited markedly improved rate capability and cycling stability compared with Si/C bare. Future work will focus on doping and coating strategies to suppress side reactions associated with the increased specific surface area after NH4F treatment, thereby further enhancing the initial efficiency, electrochemical performance, and interfacial stability.

P1-073.a: Lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP) is an olivine-type cathode material derived from lithium iron phosphate (LFP) by partially substituting Mn for Fe. It retains the excellent structural and thermal stability of LFP while offering a higher energy density through the high operating voltage of the Mn2+/Mn3+ redox couple (~4.1 V vs. Li/Li+). However, the intrinsically sluggish Li-ion diffusion in LMFP, which is confined primarily to one-dimensional channels along the [010] direction, limits its rate capability. In this study, an organic chelating agent was introduced during solvothermal synthesis to regulate anisotropic crystal growth and reduce the Li-ion diffusion pathway. LiMn0.6Fe0.4PO4 was synthesized using a solvothermal method with ethylene glycol and deionized water as co-solvents. Citric acid was added with different concentrations as a chelating agent. The synthesized powder was subsequently mixed with carbon source and heat-treated under an inert atmosphere. Under the optimized chelation condition, fine and uniformly distributed particles were obtained. The resulting material exhibited discharge capacities of 148.2 mAh g-1 at 0.1 C and 138.5 mAh g-1 at 1 C. Even at 10 C, it retained 71.7 % of the capacity measured at 0.1C, demonstrating excellent rate capability. It also maintained approximately 87 % of its initial capacity after 500 cycles. These results demonstrate that chelation and facet-selective crystal growth provides an effective strategy for simultaneously regulating the LMFP microstructure and enhancing its electrochemical kinetics.

P1-074.k: Hard Carbon; Sodium Ion Batteries; Hydrothermal
P1-074.a: Starch has attracted considerable attention as a biomass precursor for hard carbon anodes in sodium-ion batteries owing to its renewability, low cost, abundant availability, and relatively high carbon content. However, direct pyrolysis of starch often causes severe volatilization and dense carbon restacking, which limit the development of disordered domains and closed pores favorable for Na storage, resulting in insufficient capacity, low initial coulombic efficiency, and sluggish reaction kinetics. In this work, an additive assisted precursor engineering strategy was developed to regulate the bulk molecular structure of starch prior to carbonization. Hydrothermal treatment with an additive promoted uniform precursor reconstruction and crosslinked network formation throughout the bulk phase. This precursor-level modification effectively suppressed excessive graphitic restacking during subsequent carbonization and guided the evolution of a disordered pseudo-graphitic framework with abundant ultramicropores and closed pores. The resulting hard carbon delivered a high reversible capacity of 316.6 mAh g⁻¹ with an initial Coulombic efficiency of 90.1%. It also exhibited excellent rate capability, retaining 209.1 mAh g⁻¹ at 2 A g⁻¹, and stable long-term cyclability with 88.2% capacity retention after 2000 cycles at 1 A g⁻¹. These improvements are attributed to the synergistic effects of bulk crosslinking, suppressed carbon layer restacking, and the formation of ultramicropore-rich closed-pore structures that facilitate efficient sodium storage and rapid ion transport. This study presents an effective precursor-level design strategy for biomass-derived hard carbon, providing a promising route toward high energy and high-power sodium-ion batteries.

P1-075.k: Sodium-ion Battery; Hard Carbon; Anode Material
P1-075.a: Hard carbon (HC) is one of the most promising anode materials for sodium-ion batteries (SIB) owing to its low cost and suitable sodium-storage behavior, yet further capacity enhancement remains a critical challenge for practical application. A biomass-derived precursor was subjected to a one-pot acid–alkali treatment to simultaneously control its pore structure and defect sites. The resulting materials were evaluated in half-cells against an untreated control, and their electrochemical performance was assessed through rate and cycling tests. The treated sample delivered approximately 19% higher reversible capacity than the untreated control, indicating that the introduced pore structure and defect sites effectively contributed to additional sodium storage. In contrast, its initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) showed a slight decrease, likely due to the increased surface area promoting irreversible reactions during the initial cycle. In the cycling evaluation, the treated sample maintained about 30% higher capacity than the control at high current rates, demonstrating enhanced rate capability and structural stability. These overall improvements are attributed to the expanded interlayer spacing and the effectively increased number of ion-storage sites induced by the one-pot acid–alkali treatment. Although an initial efficiency loss was observed, the proposed one-pot acid–alkali treatment offers an effective approach for designing high-capacity SIB anodes. With further optimization to improve initial efficiency, this method is expected to be extended toward practical anode materials. This study was supported by the Regional Innovation System & Education (RISE) program through the Chungbuk Regional Innovation System & Education Center, funded by the Ministry of Education (MOE) and Chungcheongbuk-do, Republic of Korea (2026-RISE-11-004-03).

P1-076.k: Hard Carbon; Closed Pore; Sodium-Ion Battery
P1-076.a: Hard carbon is one of the most promising anodes for sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). Its low-voltage plateau, which largely determines the achievable reversible capacity and energy density, arises from sodium storage in closed pores. However, closed-pore structures are difficult to control during carbonization, so both reversible capacity and initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) remain limited. A phosphate-based template was introduced into a biomass-derived carbon precursor (corn starch), followed by high-temperature carbonization at 1400 °C to direct closed-pore formation. The resulting hard carbon was evaluated against a template-free control by galvanostatic charge–discharge in sodium half-cells at 0.1C. Compared with the control, the phosphate-templated hard carbon delivered approximately 53% higher reversible capacity and 46% higher plateau capacity, together with an ICE improvement of about 9.5 percentage points. The enlarged low-voltage plateau indicates an increased closed-pore volume accessible for pore-filling sodium storage. These results show that phosphate-templated pore engineering effectively increases the closed-pore content of biomass-derived hard carbon and promotes reversible pore-filling sodium storage. The approach offers a simple, low-cost, and scalable route to high-capacity, high-efficiency hard-carbon anodes for practical sodium-ion batteries. This study was supported by the Regional Innovation System & Education (RISE) program through the (Chungbuk Regional Innovation System & Education Center), funded by the Ministry of Education(MOE) and the (Chungcheongbuk-do), Republic of Korea.(2026-RISE-11-004-03).

P1-077.k: Solid State Electrolyte; Gel Polymer Electrolyte; PDOL
P1-077.a: In-situ polymerized gel polymer electrolytes combine liquid-precursor wetting with solid-electrolyte dimensional stability. However, aluminum trifluoromethanesulfonate (Al(OTf)3) rapidly initiates 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) ring-opening polymerization, causing nonuniform solidification, a short handling window, poor electrode wetting, and high contact resistance. This study investigated triethyl phosphate (TEP) coordination as a method to regulate polymerization and improve processing. DOL-based precursors containing Al(OTf)3 and different TEP contents were prepared. Fluidity and solidification were monitored optically. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) compared the coordination environment and poly(1,3-dioxolane) chain formation in electrolytes containing 5, 10, and 20% TEP. Increasing the TEP content delayed solidification and extended the period during which the precursor remained flowable for dosing, electrode wetting, and cell assembly. FTIR spectra exhibited composition-dependent changes in the C-O-C stretching, C-H out-of-plane vibration, and long-chain-related regions. These changes suggest that the phosphoryl oxygen of TEP coordinates with Lewis-acidic Al centers, lowering their effective initiation activity and slowing DOL ring opening. Excess TEP retained a larger liquid fraction and prolonged polymerization during aging, indicating a trade-off between ionic transport and timely solidification. TEP coordination provides a practical method to control Al(OTf)3-initiated DOL polymerization. An intermediate TEP-to-DOL ratio is required to balance a useful liquid handling period with complete solidification. This composition-based strategy can improve precursor processability and promote uniform electrode contact in gel polymer electrolyte cells.

P1-078.k: Sodium-ion Hybrid Capacitor; Tin; Surface Modification
P1-078.a: Sodium-ion hybrid capacitors (SIHCs) are promising energy-storage systems by combining high energy density with excellent power capability. Nevertheless, developing battery-type anodes with high reversible capacity and long-term cycling stability remains a major challenge. Among various candidate materials, Sn-based anodes are particularly appealing for sodium storage because of their high theoretical capacity, superior electrical conductivity, and low operating potential. However, the severe volume changes associated with repeated sodiation and desodiation lead to continuous reconstruction of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), ultimately resulting in structural degradation and rapid capacity loss. In this study, phosphate-modified Sn nanoparticles encapsulated within an N-doped hierarchical porous carbon framework (p-Sn@C2) were synthesized via a straightforward mixing and thermal treatment process. A dual-template approach employing NaCl and Na2CO3 was introduced to regulate the Sn content and construct a hierarchical porous architecture, thereby facilitating Na+ transport and enhancing reversible sodium-storage capacity. Meanwhile, phosphate surface modification promoted the formation of a more stable SEI and improved structural integrity during repeated sodiation and desodiation. As a result, the p-Sn@C2 anode exhibited superior cycling performance, retaining a reversible capacity of 312 mAh g⁻¹ after 1000 cycles at 0.6 A g⁻¹. Furthermore, the SIHC device constructed using p-Sn@C2 as the anode and activated carbon as the cathode achieved a maximum power density of 27.5 kW kg⁻¹ and an energy density of 21.5 Wh kg⁻¹. This dual-template and surface-modification strategy offers a practical approach for designing high-capacity anode materials for developing structural and interfacial stability for sodium-based energy storage systems.

P1-079.a: Adjusting the composition of the Si/P ratio in NASICON electrolytes (NZSP) is an effective way to regulate the diffusion framework governing Na⁺ transport. In NZSP systems, increasing the Si/P ratio promotes the transition to the highly conductive rhombohedral phase and enhances grain growth. Meanwhile, Si⁴⁺ substitution for P⁵⁺ expands the lattice and increases the concentration of Na⁺ charge carriers, thereby facilitating Na⁺ transport and improving ionic conductivity. However, the effects of Si/P variation in von-Alpen-type NASICON (vA-NASICON) remain unclear. Herein, we investigate the effect of Si/P ratio on the crystal structure, microstructure, and ionic conductivity of vA-NASICON solid electrolytes. Stoichiometric quantities of Na3PO4·12H2O (Sigma- Aldrich, 98.0%), Na2CO3 (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.5%), SiO2 (Junsei Chemical Co. Ltd.), ZrO2 (Samchun Chemicals, 99.0%) were utilized as precursors to synthesize vA-NASICON Na3.1+xZr1.55Si2.3+xP0.7-xO11 (x = −0.1, 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3) ceramics via a conventional solid-state reaction method. The composition with x = 0.2 showed the best performance and reached a room-temperature ionic conductivity of 3.82 mS/cm, which is about twice higher than the x = 0 sample (1.83 mS/cm). It also achieved a relative density of 96.6%. Conversely, excessive Si substitution at x = 0.3 induced the formation of secondary phases such as Na2ZrSi2O7, which led to a substantial increase in grain-boundary resistance and a severe degradation in relative density. These results explain that precisely controlling the Si/P ratio optimizes the crystal structure and microstructure of the vA-NASICON electrolyte, thereby ultimately improving ionic conductivity.

P1-080.k: Lithium-ion Batteries; Thermal Runaway; Raman Spectroscopy
P1-080.a: Thermal runaway (TR) is a major safety concern for lithium-ion batteries as it results in rapid gas generation, pressure buildup, and the release of highly flammable and toxic species. Conventional gas analysis methods based on sampling or flowing configurations have limited ability to directly track accumulated gases under confined simulated TR conditions. In this study, we developed a vertical furnace-coupled in situ Raman gas analysis system under high-temperature simulated TR conditions, which enables uninterrupted monitoring and quantification of accumulated gases without external sampling. Using standard gas calibration, major clearly resolved TR-related gases, including H₂, CO₂, CO, CH₄, and C₂H₄, were identified and quantified. Analysis at the cell-component level revealed cathode-dominant CO₂ and transient O₂-related signals, whereas the anode-derived samples showed mainly H₂ gas evolution with some CH₄ and C₂H₄ formation. In full cells, diverse gases were generated and accumulated, and the suppression of free O₂ was observed despite the detection of oxygen in cathode-containing samples, indicating that free oxygen was rapidly consumed through reactions with electrolyte fragments, lithiated graphite, and carbonaceous species. Although the detected gas species match literature reports, the accumulated gas profiles suggest that full-cell gas evolution cannot be fully explained by the independent decomposition of individual components and is substantially affected by coupled cathode–anode crosstalk. The developed simulated TR in situ Raman platform provides an effective approach for elucidating gas generation mechanisms and evaluating LIB safety.

P1-081.k: Solid Polymer Electrolyte; Lithium Metal Battery; In-situ Polymerization
P1-081.a: Solid polymer electrolytes can improve the safety and processability of lithium batteries, but their practical use is hindered by high electrode/electrolyte interfacial resistance, insufficient mechanical strength, and low ionic conductivity. In situ cross-linking can mitigate these limitations; however, uniform infiltration of viscous precursors and stable ion transport strongly depend on the structure and surface chemistry of the supporting porous membrane. Porous membranes composed of poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), cellulose, and polypropylene (PP) were screened using electron microscopy, pore-size analysis, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, charge–discharge testing, and cyclic voltammetry. PP was selected as the base material based on its electrochemical compatibility. Three PP-based supports were then compared: a conventional porous membrane (C-PM), a single-layer porous membrane (SL-PM), and a multilayer porous membrane (ML-PM). ML-PM was fabricated by laminating electrospun poly(vinylidene fluoride) nanomembranes onto both sides of SL-PM to form a PVDF–PP–PVDF structure. A precursor containing a lithium salt, poly(ethylene glycol) dimethyl ether, a cross-linker, a thermal radical initiator, and fluoroethylene carbonate was introduced into the membranes and electrodes and thermally cured at 90 ℃. Morphology, porosity, wettability, mechanical properties, ionic conductivity, Li ion transference number, impedance, lithium plating/stripping behavior, and the performance of coin and pouch cells employing lithium metal anodes and NCM cathodes were evaluated. Rate-capability and cycling tests were conducted at 60 ℃. The PET membrane had an average pore size of 11.2 μm, and the corresponding cell exhibited abnormal behavior during the first charging process and short-circuit behavior in subsequent cyclic-voltammetry cycles, likely owing to the excessively large pores. The cellulose-supported cell showed unstable high-voltage charging and later side reactions, possibly owing to reduction and/or reaction of its surface hydroxyl groups with lithium. In contrast, the PP-supported cell showed normal initial charge–discharge behavior and reversible electrochemical reactions during repeated cycling. The porosity increased from 38.3% for C-PM to 72.4% for SL-PM, while the PVDF coating reduced the precursor contact angle from 78.86° for SL-PM to 13.06° for ML-PM. The precursor rapidly spread over and penetrated ML-PM, and cross-sectional microscopy revealed no observable voids within the cathode. At 25 ℃, the ionic conductivity increased from 5.05 × 10^-5 S cm^-1 for C-PM to 7.07 × 10^-5 and 8.20 × 10^-5 S cm^-1 for SL-PM and ML-PM, respectively, while the Li ion transference number increased from 0.32 to 0.44 and 0.48. Before cycling, the interfacial resistance decreased from 360 Ω for C-PM to 250 Ω for SL-PM and 90 Ω for ML-PM. At 1 C, the SL-PM- and ML-PM-based cells each delivered 167 mAh g^-1, compared with 36 mAh g^-1 for the C-PM-based cell. The similar rate capabilities of SL-PM and ML-PM indicate that the principal contribution of the PVDF treatment was improved wettability, uniform precursor impregnation, and cycling stability rather than a substantial increase in ionic conductivity. The ML-PM-based coin cell retained 73% of its initial capacity after 100 cycles at 0.3 C, and the SPE supported by ML-PM exhibited a yield strength of 36 MPa. In separate pouch-cell demonstrations, the ML-PM-based NCM811 cell retained 86% of its capacity after 30 cycles, NCM622 cells maintained stable operation after cutting and folding, and a four-stack pouch cell achieved an energy density approaching 300 Wh kg^-1. Controlling both pore architecture and surface wettability is essential for maximizing the performance of in situ cross-linked solid polymer electrolytes. The PVDF-PP-PVDF multilayer membrane improves precursor infiltration, ion transport, interfacial stability, and mechanical durability, providing a practical support platform for mechanically robust, high-energy lithium polymer batteries.

P1-082.k: Aqueous Zinc Metal Batteries; Lateral Zn Deposition; Zincophilic Site
P1-082.a: Aqueous Zn metal batteries are promising energy-storage systems owing to their high safety, low cost, and high theoretical capacity. However, their long-term operation is hindered by non-uniform Zn deposition and dendrite growth, together with parasitic corrosion and hydrogen evolution reactions (HER) at the Zn/electrolyte interface. Although conventional two-dimensional zincophilic layers can regulate Zn nucleation and interfacial Zn ion flux, their effects are primarily confined to the electrode surface, limiting spatial control over continuously growing Zn deposits. A three-dimensional zincophilic Sn matrix (3D SnZM) was constructed by spatially dispersing Sn-rich domains throughout an agarose matrix. The distributed Sn-rich sites were designed to provide zincophilic domains along the Zn growth pathway, enabling spatial regulation of Zn deposition beyond the initial electrode/electrolyte interface. To distinguish this three-dimensional effect from conventional interfacial regulation, the 3D SnZM was systematically compared with a surface-confined 2D Sn configuration (2D SnZI) and an Sn-free agarose matrix. Zn deposition behavior, interfacial electrochemical kinetics, and long-term plating/stripping stability were evaluated to elucidate the role of spatially distributed zincophilic sites. Structural and surface analyses confirmed the presence of Sn-rich domains distributed throughout the agarose matrix, establishing zincophilic sites beyond the immediate Zn surface. Compared with the surface-confined 2D Sn configuration and the Sn-free matrix, the 3D SnZM exhibited more regulated Zn deposition behavior and improved electrochemical reversibility during Zn plating/stripping. Cyclic voltammetry showed reduced polarization and more favorable Zn plating/stripping kinetics for the 3D SnZM. Morphological observations after Zn deposition showed that Zn growth within the 3D SnZM was less dominated by continuous protrusion normal to the electrode surface and exhibited a greater tendency toward lateral spreading. This behavior is consistent with the spatial distribution of Sn-rich domains throughout the matrix, which allows zincophilic regulation to persist as Zn growth extends away from the initial Zn/electrolyte interface. Such a three-dimensional arrangement can therefore mitigate localized tip-directed growth and promote a more spatially distributed Zn deposition pathway. Linear sweep voltammetry further showed a reduced tendency toward hydrogen evolution for the 3D SnZM compared with the control configurations, indicating improved interfacial stability in the aqueous electrolyte. Together, the regulated Zn deposition behavior and suppressed parasitic interfacial reactions contributed to enhanced cycling stability. Zn symmetric cells incorporating the 3D SnZM maintained stable plating/stripping for more than 6000 h, demonstrating the effectiveness of spatially distributed zincophilic sites for stabilizing prolonged Zn deposition. The 3D SnZM effectively regulated Zn deposition by extending zincophilic sites from the electrode surface into the three-dimensional matrix. Compared with surface-confined 2D regulation, the spatially distributed Sn-rich domains promoted lateral Zn deposition and mitigated localized, tip-directed growth as Zn propagated through the matrix. The 3D SnZM also exhibited favorable Zn plating/stripping behavior and a reduced tendency toward parasitic hydrogen evolution, contributing to improved interfacial stability and prolonged cycling. These findings demonstrate that spatially extending zincophilic regulation beyond the conventional two-dimensional interface provides an effective strategy for controlling Zn growth and stabilizing Zn metal anodes in aqueous batteries.

P1-083.a: Aqueous zinc–iodine batteries are promising energy-storage systems because of their inherent safety and favorable electrochemical characteristics. However, their practical application is hindered by unstable Zn plating/stripping and dendrite growth at the anode, as well as polyiodide formation and active-material dissolution at the cathode. Porous carbon hosts can mitigate these issues, but conventional nanostructured carbons often require complex synthesis and may suffer from limited structural stability. Here, a biomass-derived three-dimensional (3D) carbon foam was developed through a simple chemical blowing process and utilized as a multifunctional material for both cathode and anode engineering in aqueous zinc–iodine batteries. Collagen was used as a biomass-derived carbon precursor, and zinc nitrate hexahydrate was employed as a blowing agent. The precursor mixture was homogenized, dried into a gel, and rapidly carbonized under an inert atmosphere to produce ZnO-embedded collagen-derived carbon foam (ZnO@CCF). The ratio of zinc nitrate to collagen (r) was varied to control the foam morphology. Subsequent HCl treatment removed ZnO to obtain porous collagen-derived carbon foam (CCF). The structural and surface properties of the materials were characterized by SEM, EDS, XRD, BET, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, FT-IR, and TGA. CCF was used as an iodine host for the cathode, whereas ZnO@CCF was coated onto Zn foil as a protective anode layer. Electrochemical performance was evaluated using cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic charge–discharge, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, symmetric-cell cycling, and Zn–I₂ full-cell testing. The precursor ratio strongly affected the carbon architecture, and r = 1.77 produced a well-developed 3D foam structure, whereas r = 0.4 resulted in thick carbon walls with poorly developed macropores and r = 4 produced a thin sheet-like morphology after acid treatment. Removal of ZnO increased the specific surface area from 55.642 to 560.34 m² g⁻¹ while preserving the 3D framework. XPS analysis further indicated increased exposure of nitrogen-containing surface sites after ZnO removal. With a 30 wt% iodine-loading target, I@CCF delivered an initial discharge capacity of 268.92 mAh g⁻¹, compared with 157.22 mAh g⁻¹ for iodine-loaded commercial Ketjenblack. Under an identical 20 wt% iodine loading, CCF prepared at r = 1.77 exhibited a capacity of 326.34 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.1 A g⁻¹, substantially exceeding the 58.99 mAh g⁻¹ obtained with the r = 0.4 sample. For anode protection, ZnO@CCF-coated Zn maintained a relatively smooth surface after repeated Zn plating/stripping and showed improved electrolyte wettability. The ZnO@CCF-coated Zn symmetric cell operated stably for 1000 h at 2 mA cm⁻² with lower polarization than bare Zn and CCF-coated Zn. In full-cell configurations, the ZnO@CCF-coated Zn anode exhibited the highest capacity among the tested anodes and the lowest charge-transfer resistance after 100 cycles. The ZnO@CCF@Zn || I@CCF full cell also maintained stable cycling over 50000 cycles at 8 A g⁻¹. A simple chemical blowing strategy enables the conversion of collagen biomass into a structurally tunable 3D carbon foam and its ZnO-containing precursor, allowing two complementary electrode functions to be derived from the same synthesis platform. The porous CCF provides an effective iodine-hosting architecture for the cathode, while ZnO@CCF improves Zn interfacial stability and suppresses dendritic degradation at the anode. These results demonstrate a sustainable and versatile biomass-derived electrode design strategy for simultaneously addressing cathode and anode limitations in aqueous zinc–iodine batteries.

P1-084.k: Hydrophilic; Mesoporous Carbon; Evaporation Induced Self-Assembly
P1-084.a: Aqueous zinc-sulfur batteries (AZSBs) have emerged as a highly promising candidate for large-scale energy storage systems owing to their high safety, eco-friendliness, cost-effectiveness, and high theoretical specific capacity(1672 mAh g-1 for sulfur cathode and 820 mAh g-1 for zinc anode). Despite these merits, practical implementation of AZSBs is severely hindered by the low intrinsic electrical conductivity of sulfur and its reduction product (ZnS), sluggish redox reaction kinetics, poor aqueous electrolyte wettability, and significant volume changes during cycling. Conventional carbon hosts do not offer significant advantages in aqueous electrolyte wettability. Therefore, designing hydrophilic carbon hosts capable of improving aqueous electrolyte wettability to accelerate electrochemical reaction kinetics is a key strategy. Hydrophilic mesoporous carbon was synthesized via an Evaporation-Induced Self-Assembly process combined with micro/macrophase separation. Pluronic F127 block copolymer was utilized as the soft template, furfuryl alcohol (FA) as the carbon precursor, tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) as the silica source, and poly(methyl methacrylate) homopolymer (hPMMA) as the shape-directing agent. Control materials were prepared using Resol precursors. Sulfur was infused into the carbon matrices at a 50 wt% loading via thermal melt-diffusion. Morphological, structural, and textural characteristics were evaluated using SEM, TEM, XRD, Raman, N2 sorption isotherms (BET/BJH), XPS, and contact angle measurements. Electrochemical performances were evaluated using coin cells with a zinc metal anode and 2M Zn(OTf)2 + 0.2M Choline Iodide (ChI) aqueous electrolyte via Galvanostatic Charge-Discharge (GCD) and Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) tests. Microstructural characterization (SEM, TEM) verified that the carbon was successfully synthesized into a uniform oblate geometry. N2 physisorption demonstrated a high BET surface area of 1572.6 m2 g-1, a large pore volume of 1.2411 cm3 g-1, and a uniform mesopore diameter centered at 2.26 nm. XPS and Raman spectra (ID/IG = 0.87) confirmed favorable carbon crystallization with oxygen-containing functional group networks derived from the FA precursor. Significantly, Carbon from FA@S50 exhibited superior aqueous electrolyte wettability with a low contact angle of 12.0, outperforming Carbon from Resol@S50 (35.8). Consequently, Carbon from FA@S50 demonstrated outstanding rate performance and higher specific discharge capacity across various current rates, accompanied by reduced electrochemical polarization in CV analyses. An anisotropic mesoporous carbon was successfully synthesized and evaluated as a high-performance sulfur host for AZSBs. The precursor rich in oxygen functional groups, together with the disc-shaped geometry, vastly improved aqueous electrolyte accessibility. As a result, the carbon from FA@S50 cathode achieves accelerated reaction kinetics, enhanced sulfur utilization, and exceptional rate capability. This study highlights the design of morphologically controlled anisotropic carbon architectures as an effective pathway toward high-power aqueous conversion energy storage devices.

P1-085.k: Aqueous Zn–S Batteries; Multi-shelled Hollow Carbon
P1-085.a: Aqueous zinc-sulfur batteries (AZSBs) have emerged as a promising candidate for next-generation energy storage systems owing to their high safety, low cost, and high theoretical capacity. However, their practical application is severely limited by the low electrical conductivity of sulfur, sluggish redox kinetics, and substantial volume expansion (~50%) during zincation, which leads to structural degradation and rapid capacity decay. To address these issues, microporous multi-shelled hollow carbon (MMSH) nanoparticles were synthesized via a polymer phase-separation self-assembly process followed by thermal pyrolysis to serve as an effective cathode host. The engineered MMSH structure features concentric multi-shelled hollow spheres with a high specific surface area, providing necessary void spaces to accommodate volume expansion and shorten ion diffusion pathways. Structural characterization confirmed the successful formation of the multi-shelled framework and uniform sulfur distribution within the porous matrix without structural collapse. In conclusion, the MMSH cathode host successfully buffers internal stress caused by phase conversion while enhancing structural stability. This structural strategy demonstrates significant potential for high-performance sulfur cathodes, with future work directed toward evaluating full electrochemical performance and optimizing structural synthesis parameters.

P1-086.k: Next-generation Secondary Battery; Oxygen Vacancies; Nitridation And Reoxidation
P1-086.a: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) dominate current energy-storage technologies but face concerns related to flammable organic electrolytes, limited resource availability, high cost, and safety risks. Aqueous Zn–S batteries offer a safer and more sustainable alternative by using nonflammable, aqueous electrolytes and abundant zinc. In addition, sulfur provides a high theoretical capacity of 1,672 mAh g⁻¹ through the S, ZnS conversion reaction. However, the insulating nature of sulfur, sluggish conversion kinetics, sulfur loss, and unstable cathode interfaces impede efficient sulfur utilization. Here, defect-rich N-doped TiOₓ@C nanoparticles are investigated as catalytic additives to couple sulfur-species adsorption with accelerated interfacial charge transfer and conversion kinetics. TiO2@C nanoparticles were synthesized by microemulsion using cyclohexane, CO-520, ethanol, hydrochloric acid, and titanium(IV) isopropoxide (TTIP). Dropwise TTIP addition induced confined hydrolysis and condensation. The product was sequentially treated under Ar and NH₃, and reoxidized in air at varied 250–450 °C temperatures. The products were examined by TEM, XRD, XPS, BET, and UV–Vis, while CNT@S cathodes were electrochemically tested. Particles retained 8–10 nm sizes despite high-temperature treatment and nitridation. To avoid the heterogeneous TiOₓNᵧ intermediate phases that can arise from temperature-controlled partial nitridation, TiO₂@C was first fully converted to TiN@C and subsequently reoxidized to reconstruct N-doped TiOₓ@C. XRD confirmed the complete conversion of TiO₂@C into TiN@C during nitridation, followed by the reformation of a TiO₂-based phase, while XPS indicated temperature-dependent variations in retained N and Ti³⁺/oxygen-vacancy environments across 250–450 °C. Among bare, TiO₂@C-, TiN@C-, and reoxidized TiOₓ@C-additive cathodes, the 350 °C catalyst exhibited the second-highest iodine-species uptake by UV–Vis and the best electrochemical performance, delivering apparent sulfur-mass-normalized charge/discharge capacities of 2,153/2,070 mAhg⁻¹ at 0.5 Ag⁻¹, a voltage hysteresis of 0.77 V, and superior long-term cycling stability. These results suggest that the reoxidation-temperature-dependent balance among N incorporation, oxygen-vacancy density, carbon retention, and interfacial coupling promotes ZnS conversion and enhances sulfur utilization. Re-oxidation temperature is a key parameter linking defect chemistry to cathode interfacial behavior. At 350 °C, balanced N-derived sites, Ti³⁺/oxygen vacancies, and carbon coupling mitigated polarization and promoted reversible S/ZnS conversion. Incorporating a small catalyst fraction enhanced capacity and cycling stability without substantial changes to conventional electrode fabrication.

P1-087.k: Lithium-sulfur Battery; Vertically Aligned Carbon Nanotube; Binder-free Cathode
P1-087.a: Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries are promising power sources for weight-sensitive applications because of the high theoretical specific capacity of sulfur. Their practical operation, however, is hindered by the electrically insulating nature of sulfur and Li2S, sluggish sulfur redox kinetics, lithium-polysulfide migration, and nonuniform Li2S deposition at high current densities. This study investigates a lightweight, binder-free sulfur cathode based on a vertically aligned carbon nanotube (VACNT) forest directly grown on a metallic current collector. The directly grown VACNT architecture was used as a three-dimensional electron-conduction framework and sulfur host. Sulfur was incorporated into the interstitial spaces of the aligned CNT network, after which the electrode underwent a rapid post-treatment to modify the CNT surface and improve interfacial contact between sulfur species and the carbon framework. The electrochemical behavior of untreated and post-treated cathodes was compared in coin cells over a range of discharge rates. The scalability of the electrode architecture was further evaluated in a ten-stack Li-S pouch cell. The post-treated VACNT cathode delivered more than twice the discharge capacity of the untreated electrode under identical test conditions. It retained more than 70% of its 0.1C discharge capacity at 5C, 37% at 10C, indicating rapid sulfur redox kinetics and efficient active-material utilization. The improved performance is attributed to the continuous electron-conduction network, open ion-transport pathways, enhanced sulfur distribution and polysulfide affinity, and more spatially uniform nucleation and decomposition of solid Li2S. A ten-stack pouch cell with a capacity of approximately 2.2 Ah was successfully demonstrated. Integrating a directly grown VACNT framework with controlled interfacial post-treatment provides an effective strategy for mitigating the electronic and kinetic limitations of sulfur cathodes. The resulting binder-free electrode combines high-rate capability with a lightweight, scalable architecture and is therefore a promising cathode platform for high-power Li-S batteries used in weight-sensitive mobility and aerospace applications.

P1-088.a: Thermal runaway of nickel-rich lithium-ion batteries is a critical safety hazard for electric vehicles. Once initiated, a cell can escalate from venting to violent explosion, which prevents firefighters from approaching the fire and complicates suppression. Understanding what determines whether an externally heated cell merely vents or explodes is therefore essential for establishing fire-response guidance, yet the roles of the maximum applied temperature and the heating rate have not been separated quantitatively. 1 Ah NCM811 pouch cells at 100% state of charge were used throughout. Thermogravimetric analysis and differential scanning calorimetry were performed on the individual cell constituents to identify the exothermic and decomposition events of each component. Accelerating rate calorimetry was then applied to full cells to locate the onset of self-heating and runaway under adiabatic conditions. Based on these results, controlled external-heating experiments were carried out in which the maximum applied temperature and the heating rate were varied independently and then combined, with cell surface temperature and runaway behavior recorded for each condition. The combined thermal analysis identified oxygen release from the cathode near 190 °C as the decisive trigger of thermal runaway. In the external-heating experiments, the maximum applied temperature determined whether runaway occurred at all. A cell heated to 200 °C did not enter runaway even at a high heating rate, whereas cells reaching 300 and 400 °C progressed to fire and explosion. Lowering the heating rate delayed the onset of runaway but neither lowered the peak temperature nor prevented explosion. When the two parameters were varied together, a critical boundary emerged at which the cell underwent thermal runaway without explosion. Thermal runaway of NCM811 cells is initiated by cathode oxygen release near 190 °C, while the transition from runaway to explosion is governed by the coupling of maximum temperature and heating rate rather than by either parameter alone. The critical boundary identified here provides quantitative guidance on the explosion risk of nickel-rich cells under fire conditions and offers a basis for safer firefighting and cooling strategies.

P1-089.a: Commercialization of ultra-high-nickel NCM cathodes is severely restricted by safety concerns arising from thermal runaway. Thermal failure in these layered oxides proceeds as a progressive sequence that begins with lattice collapse and interfacial side reactions, advances to gas generation, and culminates in flame generation. Because each stage originates from a different structural region of the cathode, a single uniform modification is unlikely to suppress the full sequence, which motivates a strategy that targets the surface and the bulk separately. A hierarchical oxygen framework reinforcement strategy was designed by optimizing dopant positioning at both the surface and the bulk. Surface-specific Al doping was introduced as the primary defense to increase oxygen binding energy at the interface, and Nb doping was incorporated into the bulk as a secondary defense to act as structural pillars within the layered framework. Reinforcement of the surface O-Al and bulk O-Nb frameworks was validated computationally by density functional theory calculations including electronic structure analysis. Pouch full-cells were assembled with the modified cathodes, and the volume and composition of evolved gas were quantified using the Archimedes principle and gas chromatography. Thermal runaway parameters of the pouch full-cells were then compared across the modified and reference cathodes. Surface Al doping raised the oxygen binding energy at the interface and effectively scavenged reactive oxygen radicals, which inhibited early-stage gas evolution and prevented critical cell swelling near the onset temperature of about 150 °C. Bulk Nb doping stabilized the layered framework and significantly elevated the activation energy for the layered-to-rock-salt transition, which delayed the release of bulk oxygen during the growth stage near 200 °C. Density functional theory calculations confirmed the reinforced O-Al and O-Nb frameworks. In pouch full-cells, the hierarchically doped cathodes showed reduced gas emission during the early stages of thermal runaway, a substantially delayed ignition point, and a lower peak heat release rate. Positioning Al at the surface and Nb in the bulk reinforces the oxygen framework in a stagewise manner that matches the progression of thermal failure in ultra-high-nickel NCM cathodes. This hierarchical doping strategy suppresses early gas evolution, delays bulk oxygen release, and mitigates the severity of thermal runaway in pouch full-cells, offering a practical design route toward safer ultra-high-nickel cathode materials. Abstract Commercialization of ultra-high-nickel NCM cathodes is severely restricted by safety concerns from thermal runaway. Thermal failure in these layered oxides is seen as a progressive process. This process begins with lattice collapse and interfacial side reactions, leading to gas generation and eventually flame generation. In this work, a hierarchical oxygen framework reinforcement strategy is proposed to sequentially suppress this gas evolution and thermal runaway. This framework is based on strategically optimizing dopant positioning at both surface and bulk levels. Primary surface defense is achieved via surface-specific Al doping, through which oxygen binding energy at the interface is increased. As a result, reactive oxygen radicals are effectively scavenged and early-stage gas evolution is inhibited. Inhibited gas evolution hence prevents critical cell swelling at the onset temperature (~150°C). Subsequently, secondary bulk defense is implemented through Nb dopants acting as structural "pillars". The layered framework is stabilized by these shields and the activation energy for the layered-to-rock-salt transition is significantly elevated. As a result, a delayed release of bulk oxygen during the growth stage (~200°C) is achieved. Computationally, reinforcement of surface O-Al and bulk O-Nb frameworks was validated through density functional theory (DFT) calculations, such as electronic structure analysis. On the measurements side, the volume and composition of gas evolved in pouch full-cells were quantified using Archimedes principle and gas chromatography. Out of all these analyses, thermal runaway parameters of pouch full-cells with modified cathodes were compared. Overall, it is demonstrated out of this work that hierarchical doping strategy effectively reduces gas emission during early stages of thermal runaway and substantially delays ignition point, while reducing the peak heat release rate.

P1-090.k: Sodium-ion Batteries; Aluminum Current Collector; Surface Modification
P1-090.a: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) have gained considerable interest as cost-effective next-generation energy storage systems. However, hard carbon anodes suffer from repeated volume changes during sodiation/desodiation, which leads to interfacial delamination from the aluminum (Al) current collector, increases charge-transfer resistance, and accelerates capacity degradation. To overcome this interfacial instability, we engineered the surface chemistry of Al current collectors using 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES) with systematically varied concentrations (0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 wt%). The wetting behavior and surface thermodynamics were quantitatively evaluated using the Owens–Wendt–Rabel–Kaelble (OWRK) method by measuring dynamic contact angles with polar and non-polar probe liquids to deconvolute surface free energy components. Furthermore, the electrochemical reversibility and galvanostatic charge-discharge cycling stability of hard carbon electrodes fabricated on the modified current collectors were evaluated in SIB half-cells. OWRK analysis demonstrated that the optimal silane concentration (0.5–1.0 wt%) significantly enhanced the polar surface free energy component and wettability by establishing robust Si–O–Al covalent bonds, thereby maximizing interfacial affinity with the electrode slurry. In contrast, an excessive concentration (2.0 wt%) resulted in silane self-condensation and non-uniform nano-island aggregates, which degraded surface uniformity. Consequently, the hard carbon electrode prepared on the optimized APTES-treated Al collector exhibited remarkable electrochemical performance. It delivered superior capacity retention and enhanced rate capability during long-term cycling compared to the bare Al counterpart, effectively mitigating interfacial charge-transfer resistance and structural degradation. This work demonstrates that tailoring the surface free energy and chemical anchoring of Al current collectors profoundly enhances both interfacial integrity and electrochemical cycling durability. The quantitative OWRK thermodynamic analysis and associated battery performance provide critical design principles for developing robust current collector-electrode interfaces in high-stability SIBs. Acknowledgement: This research was supported by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy(MOTIE) and the Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology(KIAT) through the “Support for Middle Market Enterprises and Regional innovation Alliances (R&D, RS-2025-02633206)“ program.

P1-091.k: Lithium Metal Battery; Corrosion; Functional Separator
P1-091.a: Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) are promising for high-energy-density storage but suffer from spontaneous Li corrosion during rest. Although inorganic-rich SEIs and lithiophilic interphases have been explored to suppress parasitic reactions, repeated cycling progressively increases the electrolyte-accessible Li surface area and destabilizes the interphase. Consequently, post-cycle corrosion becomes increasingly severe, yet strategies that simultaneously control interfacial chemistry and cycling-induced surface-area growth remain limited. To address these limitations, we engineered a dual-nitrate-releasing PAN nanofiber separator designed to continuously regulate the Li metal interface during cycling. The released species promote the formation of a low-solubility inorganic-rich SEI together with a complementary dual-alloy interphase, enabling simultaneous control of interfacial chemistry and Li deposition morphology. The functional separator sustained nitrate availability during prolonged cycling and promoted the formation of an inorganic-rich SEI together with a stable dual-alloy interphase. This anti-corrosive interphase enabled dense and uniform Li deposition, limited cycling-induced surface-area growth, and effectively suppressed post-cycle Li corrosion and continuous SEI growth during rest, leading to improved calendar-life performance in Li||NCM811 full cells. Sustained dual-nitrate release enables simultaneous regulation of SEI chemistry and Li deposition morphology, thereby preserving interfacial integrity and suppressing post-cycle Li corrosion. This work establishes anti-corrosive interphase engineering as an effective strategy for mitigating cycling-amplified corrosion and extending the practical calendar life of lithium metal batteries.

P1-092.a: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) have emerged as promising alternatives to lithium-ion batteries for large-scale energy storage owing to the natural abundance and low cost of sodium resources. Among various cathode materials, layered transition-metal oxides have attracted considerable attention because of their high specific capacity and tunable composition. However, achieving homogeneous transition-metal distribution and controlled particle morphology remains critical for improving their electrochemical performance. In this study, layered oxide cathode materials were synthesized using a co-precipitation method to obtain compositionally homogeneous precursors with controlled particle characteristics. Layered sodium transition-metal oxide cathode materials were synthesized via a co-precipitation method. Transition-metal precursor solutions containing Ni, Fe, and Mn were co-precipitated under controlled pH, temperature, and stirring conditions to obtain homogeneous precursor particles. The obtained precursors were subsequently mixed with a sodium source and calcined at an optimized temperature to form the layered oxide structure. The structural and morphological properties of the synthesized materials were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Their electrochemical properties were evaluated using coin-type half-cells with sodium metal as the counter electrode. The co-precipitation method successfully produced homogeneous Ni–Fe–Mn precursor particles, which were subsequently converted into Na₁₋ₓLiₓNiFeMnO₂ cathode materials with a hybrid O3/P2 layered structure. XRD analysis confirmed the coexistence of O3- and P2-type phases, with the structural characteristics varying with Li substitution. The optimized Li-substituted composition exhibited improved structural stability and reversible Na⁺ insertion/extraction behavior. Electrochemical measurements showed enhanced capacity retention and cycling stability compared with the single-phase-dominant compositions. These results suggest that Li substitution combined with O3/P2 phase engineering is an effective strategy for stabilizing layered Na–Ni–Fe–Mn oxide cathodes and improving their electrochemical performance. The Na₁₋ₓLiₓNiFeMnO₂ O3/P2 hybrid cathode was successfully synthesized through a co-precipitation-assisted process. Li substitution promoted the formation and stabilization of the O3/P2 hybrid layered structure, contributing to improved structural stability and reversible Na⁺ storage behavior. The optimized composition exhibited enhanced electrochemical performance, demonstrating that the combined strategy of Li substitution and O3/P2 phase engineering provides a promising approach for developing high-performance layered oxide cathodes for sodium-ion batteries.

P1-093.k: Cathode Recycling; Selective Lithium Recovery; Direct Upcycling
P1-093.a: The rapid growth of lithium-ion batteries has increased the demand for sustainable recycling technologies capable of recovering valuable materials while minimizing chemical and resource consumption. Conventional hydrometallurgical processes generally rely on complete dissolution of cathode materials, followed by multiple separation and resynthesis steps. In contrast, direct recycling can preserve the value of cathode materials and reduce processing complexity. This study explores integrated wet-processing strategies for spent NCM cathodes, focusing on rapid delamination, selective lithium recovery, and direct regeneration or upcycling toward a closed-loop battery materials cycle. Spent NCM622 cathode scraps were processed through three complementary wet-recycling routes. (i) A sequential citric acid–NaOH (CA–NaOH) treatment was employed for rapid delamination of the cathode material from the Al current collector, followed by direct regeneration of the recovered NCM622. (ii) A citric acid–ethylene glycol (CA–EG) system was applied for resource-efficient delamination, followed by compositional adjustment and direct upcycling of the recovered NCM622 into Ni-rich NCM811, while preserving the Al foil for potential reuse. (iii) Formic acid treatment was used for selective pre-extraction of Li from NCM622, followed by recovery of the extracted Li as Li₂CO₃ and separation of the remaining Ni–Co–Mn-containing formate intermediates for subsequent cathode material synthesis. The recovered products were characterized by XRD, FT-IR, SEM, and ICP, and the regenerated and upcycled cathode materials were electrochemically evaluated using coin-type cells. The three wet-recycling routes demonstrated distinct advantages for the sustainable recovery and valorization of spent NCM622 cathodes. The CA–NaOH process achieved rapid delamination of the cathode material from the Al current collector while preserving the layered structure of NCM622, enabling subsequent direct regeneration with restored electrochemical performance. The CA–EG process enabled effective delamination at high solid-to-liquid ratios, substantially reducing solution consumption, while the recovered cathode material was successfully upcycled from NCM622 to Ni-rich NCM811 through compositional adjustment and thermal treatment. In addition, the separated Al foil retained its physical integrity, providing a potential pathway for reuse. In the formic acid process, Li was selectively pre-extracted from NCM622 and subsequently recovered as Li₂CO₃, while Ni, Co, and Mn were retained as formate-based intermediates suitable for subsequent cathode material synthesis. Collectively, these results demonstrate that selective wet processing can facilitate efficient separation, recovery, regeneration, and upcycling of valuable cathode constituents without relying on conventional complete dissolution. An integrated recycling framework combining sustainable delamination, selective Li recovery, and direct regeneration/upcycling was demonstrated for spent NCM cathodes. The proposed approaches enable the recovery of cathode materials and valuable constituents while reducing reliance on conventional complete leaching and multistep separation processes. In particular, direct regeneration and conversion of NCM622 into Ni-rich NCM811 provide pathways for retaining or enhancing the value of recovered materials. These results highlight the potential of selective wet processing as a resource-efficient strategy toward closed-loop recycling of lithium-ion battery cathodes.

P1-094.a: Al–Mg alloys are attractive lightweight structural materials owing to their low density, good formability, and favorable mechanical properties. However, prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures can lead to oxidation and associated microstructural degradation, limiting their long-term stability. Minor alloying additions provide a potential approach for controlling oxidation behavior through modification of the initial microstructure and phase constitution. This study investigates the relationship between alloying-induced changes in the as-cast microstructure and long-term oxidation behavior of Al–Mg alloys. A series of Al–Mg alloys containing selected minor alloying additions were prepared by conventional casting. The as-cast microstructures were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), with particular attention to the morphology, distribution, and composition of secondary phases. The alloys were subsequently subjected to long-term oxidation at 500 °C in air under identical conditions. Cross-sectional SEM–EDS analyses were performed to characterize the morphology, distribution, and penetration depth of internal oxidation. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was additionally employed for selected specimens to examine microstructural characteristics. Thermodynamic calculations were performed to predict phase formation and evaluate the stability of possible oxidation products. Minor alloying additions produced distinct changes in the as-cast microstructures, including variations in the morphology and distribution of secondary phases. Corresponding differences were observed in the development and penetration of internal oxidation during prolonged high-temperature exposure. Comparison of the experimental observations with thermodynamic calculations indicated that the oxidation behavior was influenced not only by the relative stability of oxidation products but also by alloying-induced changes in the initial microstructure. The results demonstrate that modification of the as-cast microstructure through minor alloying additions can significantly influence the long-term oxidation behavior of Al–Mg alloys. The combined consideration of initial microstructure, phase constitution, and oxide stability provides a useful approach for understanding and controlling high-temperature degradation in lightweight metallic materials.

P1-095.k: Lithium Sulfur Batteries; Metal Phthalocyanines; Polysulfide Adsorption
P1-095.a: Lithium-sulfur batteries are promising next-generation energy-storage systems because of their high theoretical energy density. However, the shuttle effect of soluble lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) and sluggish sulfur redox kinetics remain major challenges. In this study, metal phthalocyanines (MPcs) with different central metals were investigated to regulate LiPS adsorption and sulfur redox reactions. MPc were introduced onto multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) to prepare MPc/MWCNT composites. Their LiPS adsorption behavior and catalytic activities toward the sulfur reduction reaction (SRR) and sulfur oxidation reaction (SOR) were comparatively evaluated using adsorption and electrochemical analyses. The MPc/MWCNT composites exhibited distinct LiPS adsorption and sulfur redox behaviors depending on the central metal species. The differences in metal centers influenced LiPS interactions as well as the kinetics of SRR and SOR, demonstrating the important role of the M-N4 active sites in regulating polysulfide conversion. These results demonstrate that tuning the central metal of MPcs is an effective strategy for controlling LiPS adsorption and bidirectional sulfur conversion kinetics, providing useful insights for the disign of catalytic materials for high-performance lithium-sulfur batteries.

P1-096.k: Sodium-ion Batteries; Oxygen-rich Nanostructured Graphene Oxide; Hard Carbon Anode
P1-096.a: Hard carbon (HC) is considered a promising anode material for sodium-ion batteries due to its low cost, structural stability, and suitable sodium-storage characteristics. However, further improvement in its electrochemical performance is desirable for practical energy-storage applications. In this work, oxygen-rich nanostructured graphene oxide (OR-NGO) was investigated as a low-loading additive to enhance the electrochemical performance of HC anodes. OR-NGO was prepared from graphene oxide through oxidative cutting and incorporated into HC electrodes at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 wt%. The materials were characterized using XRD, Raman spectroscopy, BET analysis, and XPS. Electrochemical performance was evaluated in sodium half-cells through cycling and rate capability tests. The electrochemical performance depended on the OR-NGO content, with 1.0 wt% showing the best overall performance. After 100 cycles at 0.1 C, the 1.0 wt% OR-NGO electrode delivered approximately 25.2% higher specific capacity than pristine HC. Improved rate capability was also observed at the optimized OR-NGO content. Low-loading OR-NGO incorporation effectively enhanced the electrochemical performance of HC anodes, with 1.0 wt% providing the optimal composition among the investigated concentrations. The results demonstrate a simple additive-based approach for improving hard carbon anodes for sodium-ion batteries.

P1-097.a: The electrochemical performance of LiFePO4 (LFP) can be influenced by the structural and physicochemical properties of its FePO4-based precursor. Hydrated FePO4 precursors, such as FePO4·2H2O, can form different polymorphs depending on the synthesis conditions, and these structural differences may affect their dehydration behavior and subsequent conversion to LiFePO4. However, the relationship between the synthesis conditions and phase formation behavior of FePO4·2H₂O as an LFP precursor has not been fully clarified. FePO4·2H₂O precursors were synthesized using FeSO4·7H2O and H3PO4 as starting materials, with H2O2 used to oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+. The initial pH at the beginning of the aging process was controlled to investigate its effect on precursor formation. After reaching the target pH, the suspensions were aged without further addition of base. The crystal structure and hydration characteristics of the synthesized precursors were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The hydrated precursors were subsequently dehydrated. After ball-milling the hydrated precursors, LiFePO4/C was synthesized by calcination. The XRD patterns varied depending on the initial pH, indicating differences in the phase formation and crystallization behavior of FePO4·2H₂O. Changes in crystallinity and the appearance of different FePO4·2H₂O-related phases were observed under different pH conditions. TGA also revealed differences in the thermal dehydration behavior and hydration characteristics of the synthesized precursors. These results indicate that the initial pH influences the structural characteristics of FePO4·2H₂O formed during precipitation and aging. The initial pH is an important synthesis parameter affecting the phase formation and hydration behavior of FePO4·2H₂O precursors. The resulting precursor characteristics may further influence the properties of dehydrated FePO4 and its subsequent conversion to LiFePO4. This study provides a basis for understanding and controlling FePO4-based precursor characteristics for the synthesis of LiFePO4 cathode materials.

P1-098.a: With the expansion of the electric mobility market and the increasing demand for extended driving ranges, the development of high-capacity cathode materials has become increasingly important for improving the energy density of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). Ni-rich layered LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2 (NCM) oxides have been widely employed as representative high-energy-density cathode materials owing to their high reversible capacity. Recently, considerable research efforts have focused on ultra-high-Ni NCM cathodes, in which the Co content is reduced while the Ni content is maximized to mitigate the high cost, supply-chain concerns, and ethical issues associated with Co. However, increasing the Ni content aggravates structural instability during repeated charge–discharge cycling. In particular, lattice changes associated with the H2–H3 phase transition at high states of charge generate repetitive mechanical stress. This stress promotes intergranular microcracking within polycrystalline particles, facilitating electrolyte penetration through the cracks and accelerating interfacial side reactions, which can ultimately lead to long-term capacity fading and shortened cycle life. Therefore, a single-crystalline structure with minimized grain boundaries has attracted considerable attention as an effective strategy for suppressing microcrack formation and improving the structural stability and long-term cycling performance of ultra-high-Ni NCM cathodes. In this study, Ni0.96Co0.02Mn0.02(OH)2 precursors were synthesized via a co-precipitation method to prepare single-crystalline Li Ni0.96Co0.02Mn0.02O2 (NCM9622) cathode materials with a Ni content of 96%. Different co-precipitation conditions were employed to investigate the influence of precursor synthesis conditions on the subsequent formation of single-crystalline NCM9622.
