The synthesized precursors were mixed with LiOH and Li2SO4 and subjected to the same molten-salt-assisted heat-treatment process. After heat treatment, the samples were washed to remove residual salt species. To compensate for possible Li loss during the washing process, different amounts of LiOH were added to the washed cathode materials, followed by subsequent heat treatment to investigate the effects of Li replenishment on their electrochemical properties. The crystal structure and particle morphology of the synthesized samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), respectively. Their charge-discharge behavior, rate capability, and long-term cycling performance were evaluated using Li-metal half-cells. Although the precursors synthesized under different co-precipitation conditions were subjected to the same molten-salt heat-treatment process, differences were observed in the electrochemical properties of the resulting single-crystalline NCM9622 cathodes. In addition, after LiOH replenishment and subsequent heat treatment of the washed samples, differences in initial capacity and cycling retention were observed depending on the amount of LiOH added. Although the precursors synthesized under different co-precipitation conditions exhibited the same NCM9622(OH)2 composition, slight differences were observed in the morphology of their primary particles. In contrast, the final single-crystal NCM9622 cathode materials prepared using the same molten-salt process exhibited generally similar particle morphologies. Nevertheless, differences in long-term cycling performance were observed among the resulting single-crystal NCM9622 cathodes. This suggests that precursor synthesis parameters, including pH, NH3 concentration, stirring speed, and reaction time, may influence the subsequent electrochemical stability of the cathode materials. Meanwhile, adjusting the amount of LiOH added to compensate for Li loss during washing resulted in slight differences in the initial charge-discharge characteristics. These results indicate that the electrochemical performance of single-crystal ultra-high-Ni NCM9622 can be influenced by both precursor synthesis conditions and subsequent processing conditions, highlighting the importance of systematic process control for achieving stable long-term cycling performance.

P1-099.k: Sodium-Ion Batteries; O3-Type Layered Oxides; Co-Precipitation
P1-099.a: "Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) have attracted considerable attention as promising alternatives to lithium-ion batteries for large-scale energy storage because of the abundance and wide geographical distribution of sodium resources, which offer potential advantages in resource availability and cost. Among various cathode materials, O3-type layered oxides are particularly attractive because they contain approximately one Na per formula unit in the as-prepared, fully sodiated state, providing a large amount of electrochemically active Na+ and thereby offering the potential for a high initial gravimetric capacity (mAh g-1). In particular, O3-type NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2 (O3-NaNFM) utilizes the redox activity of Ni and Fe while incorporating relatively abundant and cost-effective Fe and Mn and avoiding costly Co, making it a promising cathode composition that combines high capacity with cost-effectiveness for SIBs. However, a high gravimetric capacity (mAh g-1) does not necessarily translate into a high volumetric capacity (mAh cm-3), which is equally critical for practical cell design. To achieve high volumetric capacity, high powder packing density and electrode density are required to accommodate more active material within a limited electrode volume, and these densities are strongly governed by secondary-particle morphology. Spherical and densely packed secondary particles are advantageous for reducing interparticle voids and improving tap density and electrode density. However, excessive growth during secondary-particle formation may lead to oversized particles, which can adversely affect ionic and electronic transport and reaction homogeneity, potentially hindering uniform electrode formation and stable electrochemical reactions. Therefore, it is important to control secondary-particle size within an appropriate range while maintaining high sphericity, compact particle structures, well-developed primary particles, and an appropriate crystal structure. In this study, various co-precipitation parameters were progressively adjusted to control the precursor morphology of O3-NaNFM. Starting from the initial synthesis condition, pH control, ammonium oxalate solution preparation, and stirring conditions were sequentially modified to improve primary-particle development and aggregation. Following the improvement in primary-particle morphology, the subsequent optimization focused on the formation and size control of spherical secondary particles. Increasing the co-precipitation time promoted the formation of spherical secondary particles but simultaneously resulted in excessive particle growth, indicating the need for further control of particle size. Accordingly, co-precipitation temperature was subsequently selected as a key parameter for regulating particle-growth behavior. This study investigates the effects of co-precipitation time and temperature on secondary-particle size, sphericity, compactness, primary-particle development, and crystal structure in O3-NaNFM, providing a basis for identifying optimal processing conditions." "Ni1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3C2O4 (NFM(C2O4)) precursors were synthesized via an oxalate co-precipitation method. Stoichiometric amounts of NiSO4·6H2O, FeSO4·7H2O, and MnSO4·H2O were dissolved in deionized water to prepare a 0.5 M transition-metal solution, which was added to a 0.5 M ammonium oxalate solution. Starting from the initial synthesis condition, the co-precipitation parameters were progressively modified to improve primary-particle development. First, pH control was introduced to maintain the co-precipitation solution at pH 7. Subsequently, the preparation procedure of the ammonium oxalate solution was modified by preparing it prior to the transition-metal solution and heating it to 70 ℃ under stirring at 450 rpm to facilitate dissolution. In the next step, continuous stirring at 300 rpm was introduced during co-precipitation to promote uniform mixing and precursor formation. The progressive introduction of these conditions resulted in improved development and aggregation of platelet-like primary particles. Based on the improved primary-particle morphology, the subsequent optimization focused on promoting the formation of spherical secondary particles. The solution feed conditions were adjusted, and the transition-metal solution was gradually fed over 11 h while maintaining the previously established pH, ammonium oxalate preparation, and stirring conditions. The extended co-precipitation time was employed to promote primary-particle growth and aggregation and facilitate the formation of spherical secondary particles. Subsequently, co-precipitation temperature was selected as the next optimization parameter to further control secondary-particle size while preserving the previously improved particle morphology. Accordingly, the co-precipitation temperature was increased to 50 ℃ while maintaining the 11 h co-precipitation time and the other established conditions. After co-precipitation, the obtained NFM(C2O4) precursors were washed and dried overnight and then mixed with Na2CO3 with a 5 wt% excess to compensate for Na loss during high-temperature calcination. The mixtures were subsequently calcined in air at 900 ℃ for 24 h with a heating rate of 5 ℃ min−1 to obtain O3-NaNFM. Particle morphology, crystal structure, and elemental composition were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), respectively. For electrochemical evaluation, electrodes were prepared using O3-NaNFM, Super P, and poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) at a weight ratio of 8:1:1. The electrodes were evaluated in sodium half-cells over a voltage range of 2.0–4.0 V vs. Na/Na+ using 1.0 M NaPF6 in EC/DMC/EMC (1:1:1, v/v/v) with 1 wt% FEC as the electrolyte." "Under the initial co-precipitation condition, SEM observations revealed limited development and aggregation of platelet-like primary particles, together with poorly defined secondary-particle morphology. Therefore, the synthesis conditions were progressively modified to improve precursor morphology. Maintaining the co-precipitation solution at pH 7, modifying the ammonium oxalate solution preparation procedure, and subsequently introducing continuous stirring during co-precipitation progressively improved the development and aggregation of platelet-like primary particles. These sequential SEM observations indicate that control of the solution preparation and co-precipitation conditions plays an important role in primary-particle formation and aggregation. XRD analysis of the samples synthesized under these conditions showed diffraction characteristics corresponding to the O3-type layered structure, while ICP-OES analysis confirmed that the Ni, Fe, and Mn compositions remained generally close to the targeted equimolar ratio across the different co-precipitation conditions. Following the improvement in primary-particle morphology, the subsequent optimization focused on promoting the formation of spherical secondary particles. SEM observations showed that adjustment of the solution feed conditions and extension of the co-precipitation time to 11 h promoted primary-particle growth and aggregation, resulting in more distinct spherical secondary particles with a characteristic size of approximately 30 μm. This result indicates that prolonged co-precipitation facilitated spherical secondary-particle formation but simultaneously led to substantial particle growth. XRD analysis confirmed the formation of the O3-type layered structure, while ICP-OES analysis showed that the Ni, Fe, and Mn composition remained close to the targeted equimolar ratio. The electrochemical properties of the cathode synthesized under the 11 h co-precipitation condition were subsequently evaluated in Na half-cells. During pre-cycling at 0.1 C, a maximum second-cycle discharge capacity of 90.22 mAh g−1 was obtained. Rate-capability testing from 0.2 to 10 C showed a gradual decrease in discharge capacity with increasing C-rate, with a more pronounced capacity loss at higher rates. However, when the C-rate was returned to 0.2 C after high-rate testing, the discharge capacity substantially recovered, demonstrating capacity recovery upon returning to a lower rate. Long-term cycling at 1 C showed a gradual decrease in discharge capacity with repeated cycling, indicating that further improvement in cycling stability is required. Although the limited high-rate and cycling performance cannot be attributed solely to secondary-particle size, the excessively grown secondary particles were considered a possible factor affecting Na+ transport and reaction homogeneity. Accordingly, co-precipitation temperature was selected as the next processing parameter to suppress excessive secondary-particle growth and further control particle size. SEM observations showed that increasing the co-precipitation temperature to 50 ℃ while maintaining the 11 h co-precipitation time and the other established conditions markedly reduced the characteristic secondary-particle size from approximately 30 to 8 μm. However, compared with the particles obtained under the 11 h co-precipitation condition, those synthesized at 50 ℃ exhibited less-developed and more irregular platelet-like primary particles, together with changes in secondary-particle sphericity and compactness. The reduction in secondary-particle size was attributed to accelerated precipitation and nucleation at the elevated temperature, which may increase the number of nuclei and distribute the available metal ions among a larger number of nucleation sites, thereby limiting individual particle growth. These observations indicate that increasing the co-precipitation temperature effectively suppressed excessive secondary-particle growth but simultaneously altered primary-particle development and aggregation behavior. XRD analysis confirmed the formation of the O3-type layered structure under the 50 ℃ condition, while ICP-OES analysis showed that the Ni, Fe, and Mn composition remained close to the targeted equimolar ratio. Further rate-capability and cycling evaluations of the 50 ℃ sample will be conducted to clarify the relationship between secondary-particle size reduction and electrochemical performance. Overall, the sequential experiments demonstrate that pH control, ammonium oxalate solution preparation, and stirring during co-precipitation influence primary-particle development and aggregation, whereas co-precipitation time and temperature strongly regulate secondary-particle formation and growth. The results further indicate that secondary-particle size should not be considered independently from primary-particle development, secondary-particle sphericity and compactness, composition, and crystal structure when optimizing O3-NaNFM." "This study demonstrates that the morphology and growth behavior of O3-NaNFM precursors can be systematically regulated through stepwise control of co-precipitation conditions. Sequential modification of pH, ammonium oxalate solution preparation, and stirring during co-precipitation improved the development and aggregation of platelet-like primary particles. Subsequent adjustment of the solution feed conditions and extension of the co-precipitation time to 11 h promoted the formation of spherical secondary particles but also resulted in substantial particle growth to approximately 30 μm. Electrochemical evaluation of this material showed substantial capacity recovery when the C-rate was returned to 0.2 C after high-rate testing, although pronounced capacity loss at higher rates and gradual capacity decay during long-term cycling at 1 C indicated the need for further improvement in high-rate and cycling performance. Increasing the co-precipitation temperature to 50 ℃ while maintaining the 11 h co-precipitation time reduced the characteristic secondary-particle size to approximately 8 μm. However, this size reduction was accompanied by less-developed and more irregular platelet-like primary particles and changes in secondary-particle sphericity and compactness. These results indicate that particle-size reduction should be balanced with the preservation of well-developed primary particles and compact spherical secondary-particle morphology. XRD and ICP-OES analyses further confirmed the formation of the O3-type layered structure and transition-metal compositions generally close to the targeted equimolar ratio. Therefore, optimization of the co-precipitation process for O3-NaNFM should focus not simply on minimizing secondary-particle size but on identifying an optimal processing window that balances secondary-particle size, sphericity, compactness, primary-particle development, composition, and crystal structure. Further rate-capability and cycling evaluations of the 50 ℃ sample will be conducted to clarify the relationship between secondary-particle size reduction and electrochemical performance. Further quantitative particle-size-distribution (PSD) and primary-particle size analyses will be conducted to determine the mean particle size and size distribution more accurately. Tap density and electrode density will also be evaluated to determine whether morphology control translates into improved particle packing and electrode-level density. Overall, this study establishes the relationship between co-precipitation conditions and primary- and secondary-particle development in O3-NaNFM and provides a basis for further process optimization of morphology-controlled O3-NaNFM cathodes."

P1-100.k: Hard Carbon; Marine Biomass; Sodium-ion Batteries (SIB)
P1-100.a: "Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are considered promising candidates for large-scale energy storage because of the natural abundance and economic advantages of sodium resources. Nevertheless, the relatively large ionic radius of Na+ restricts reversible intercalation into conventional graphite, motivating the development of alternative anode materials. Hard carbon has therefore attracted considerable attention owing to its disordered carbon structure and enlarged interlayer spacing, which are favorable for Na+ storage. In particular, minimizing irreversible Na+ consumption and solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation during the initial cycle is essential for achieving a high initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE), a critical parameter for the practical application of hard-carbon anodes in SIBs. In this study, marine biomass was explored as a sustainable carbon precursor by utilizing its intrinsic CaCO3-rich architecture as a natural template for controlling carbon microstructure and pore formation. This approach also enables the conversion of marine biomass into functional carbon materials for energy-storage applications, providing opportunities for resource valorization and the development of resource-circular electrode materials. To complement carbon-framework formation and enhance electrochemical performance, pitch was incorporated as an additional carbon source and co-carbonized with the marine biomass. Subsequent HCl treatment was employed to remove residual Ca-based inorganic species and control the structural characteristics of the resulting hard carbon. The effects of precursor design and impurity removal on Na⁺ storage behavior were systematically investigated, with particular emphasis on reversible capacity, ICE, and rate capability, to establish processing–structure–performance relationships and identify effective strategies for optimizing marine biomass–pitch-derived hard-carbon anodes for SIBs." "Marine biomass was washed, dried, and pulverized before being mixed with pitches having softening points of 200 or 250 ℃ as additional carbon sources. The resulting marine biomass–pitch mixtures were co-carbonized under an N2 atmosphere at 800, 1000, and 1200 ℃ to investigate the evolution of the carbon structure and Ca-based inorganic phases as a function of carbonization temperature. The two pitches were comparatively evaluated to determine the influence of pitch characteristics on the structural and electrochemical properties of the resulting hard carbons. Following carbonization, HCl treatment was performed to remove residual Ca-based inorganic impurities. The carbonized samples were immersed in HCl solution and continuously stirred for 6, 12, or 24 h to evaluate the effect of treatment duration on impurity removal. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used to examine changes in the carbon structure and residual Ca-based crystalline phases, with particular attention to changes in CaCO3-related peak intensities after HCl treatment. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was employed to investigate morphological evolution, including changes in hierarchical features and pore formation at different carbonization temperatures. Electrochemical performance was evaluated using Na-metal half-cells with 1.0 M NaPF6 in EC/DMC/EMC (1:1:1, v/v/v) containing 1 wt% fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) as the electrolyte. Galvanostatic charge–discharge measurements were conducted over a voltage range of 0.01–2.0 V vs. Na/Na+. Initial cycling was performed at 0.03C, followed by rate-capability measurements at sequential rates of 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 5, and 10C. The current rate was subsequently returned to 0.1C to evaluate capacity recovery after high-rate testing. Reversible capacity, ICE, initial cycling behavior, and rate capability were evaluated to compare the electrochemical responses of the prepared hard carbons." "Structural characterization revealed a clear dependence of carbon morphology and residual inorganic phases on carbonization temperature. At 800 ℃, SEM observations showed that hierarchical features were not well developed and that pore formation remained relatively limited. Based on these observations, the carbonization temperature was increased to 1000 ℃ to promote further structural development. Although the carbon morphology became more developed at 1000 ℃, XRD analysis indicated that pronounced Ca-based crystalline phases remained. The carbonization temperature was therefore further increased to 1200 ℃ to examine additional structural evolution and changes in the residual inorganic phases, and 1200 ℃ was subsequently selected as the carbonization temperature for further purification and electrochemical evaluation. The influence of pitch selection was evaluated using pitches with softening points of 200 and 250 ℃. At 0.1C, the sample prepared with the 200 ℃-softening-point pitch delivered a reversible capacity of approximately 125 mAh g-1, whereas the sample prepared with the 250 ℃-softening-point pitch exhibited a higher reversible capacity of approximately 145 mAh g-1. Based on this electrochemical comparison, the 250 ℃-softening-point pitch was selected as the additional carbon source for subsequent processing. The HCl-treatment duration was then systematically varied to improve the removal of residual Ca-based inorganic species. After 6 h of treatment, pronounced CaCO3-related XRD peaks remained, indicating substantial retention of inorganic impurities. Extending the treatment duration to 12 h resulted in a noticeable decrease in the CaCO3-related peak intensity. A further reduction was observed after 24 h, with substantially weaker CaCO3-related peaks than those observed after 12 h. These results demonstrate that prolonged HCl treatment progressively enhanced the removal of residual CaCO3 within the investigated treatment range. Accordingly, 24 h was selected as the acid-treatment duration for subsequent electrochemical evaluation. Based on these structural and electrochemical comparisons, the selected processing conditions were identified as the use of the 250 ℃-softening-point pitch, carbonization at 1200 ℃, and HCl treatment for 24 h. Under these conditions, the resulting hard carbon exhibited an ICE of approximately 93% and a reversible capacity of approximately 145 mAh g-1 at 0.1C. The galvanostatic charge–discharge profiles measured at 0.1C maintained similar shapes during the initial cycles, indicating reproducible electrochemical behavior during early cycling. During rate-capability testing, reversible capacities of approximately 145, 120, and 80 mAh g-1 were obtained at 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5C, respectively. A pronounced decrease in capacity was observed as the rate was further increased to 1, 5, and 10C. Upon returning the current rate to 0.1C, the reversible capacity recovered to approximately 145 mAh g-1, demonstrating capacity recovery after high-rate operation when the cell was returned to a low current rate." "Marine biomass–pitch-derived hard carbon was prepared through co-carbonization followed by HCl purification, and the effects of carbonization temperature, pitch selection, and acid-treatment duration on its structural and electrochemical properties were systematically investigated. SEM and XRD observations guided the progressive adjustment of the carbonization temperature from 800 to 1200 ℃, while electrochemical comparison of the two pitches and analysis of residual CaCO3 after different HCl-treatment durations were used to establish the processing conditions. Among the conditions investigated, the 250 ℃-softening-point pitch, carbonization at 1200 ℃, and HCl treatment for 24 h were selected for the final electrochemical evaluation. The hard carbon prepared under these conditions exhibited an ICE of approximately 93% and a reversible capacity of approximately 145 mAh g-1 at 0.1C. Moreover, the capacity recovered to approximately 145 mAh g-1 when the current rate was returned to 0.1C after high-rate testing. Nevertheless, the current reversible capacity remains below the approximately 250–300 mAh g-1 range reported for hard-carbon anodes, and a pronounced capacity loss was observed at higher C-rates. These limitations may be associated with incomplete removal of Ca-based inorganic species as well as insufficiently optimized carbon microstructure, interlayer spacing, and pore characteristics. Residual inorganic phases may reduce the fraction of electrochemically active carbon and limit accessible Na+ storage sites, while unfavorable carbon and pore structures may restrict Na+ storage and transport, particularly under high-rate conditions. Further optimization will therefore focus on improving the removal of residual Ca-based species through systematic control of acid concentration, treatment duration, and washing conditions. SEM-EDS and thermogravimetric analysis will be employed to quantify residual inorganic species, while BET, Raman spectroscopy, and XRD will be used to investigate specific surface area, pore characteristics, structural disorder, and d002 interlayer spacing. These analyses will enable correlations between impurity removal, carbon microstructure, ICE, reversible capacity, and rate capability to be established. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy may also be employed to further clarify charge-transfer and interfacial limitations associated with the pronounced capacity loss at high rates. Ultimately, integrated optimization of pitch selection, carbonization, and purification is expected to minimize residual inorganic species and establish a carbon microstructure more favorable for Na+ storage, with the goal of increasing the reversible capacity from the current approximately 145 mAh g-1 toward 250 mAh g-1 while improving rate and long-term cycling performance. Beyond electrochemical optimization, this study demonstrates the potential of converting CaCO3-rich marine biomass into functional carbonaceous electrode materials and provides a basis for the resource-circular utilization of marine biomass in sustainable sodium-ion battery anodes."

P1-101.k: Pitch Precursor; Oxidative Cross-linking; Interlayer Spacing
P1-101.a: Hard carbons with non-graphitizable microstructures represent primary anode candidates for sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) owing to the thermodynamic instability of sodium–graphite intercalation compounds. Although pitch serves as a cost-effective precursor with high carbon yield, its susceptibility to liquid-phase carbonization triggers the coalescence of aromatic mesophase domains. This spontaneous graphitic alignment diminishes structural defects and constricts the interlayer distance, significantly impeding sodium-ion insertion kinetics and storage capability. Herein, a microstructural modulation strategy integrating tailored oxidative cross-linking with internal pore engineering is investigated to govern the carbonization trajectory of pitch precursors. The pre-oxidation-induced cross-linked networks effectively restrict the orientational restructuring and mobility of aromatic segments, thereby suppressing mesophase growth. Consequently, the resulting hard carbon exhibits an expanded interlayer spacing (d002) of 3.76 Å, an extensively developed closed-pore architecture, and an attenuated specific surface area of 5.7 m² g⁻¹. Electrochemical evaluations demonstrate an initial Coulombic efficiency of 93.7% and a reversible capacity of 372 mAh g⁻¹. Furthermore, the electrode delivers enhanced rate capability, retaining 88% of its reversible capacity at 5C relative to 0.1C, coupled with extended cycling stability. These findings establish that precisely modulating cross-linking kinetics allows simultaneous control over short-range crystallite ordering and enclosed void formation, offering a mechanistic framework for pitch-derived carbon architectures for high-rate, durable sodium storage.

P1-102.k: : LiMn0.65Fe0.35PO4 Cathode; Mn Dissolution; Selective Ion Transport
P1-102.a: Blending cathodes offer a promising strategy for enhancing energy density, cycling stability, and cost-effectiveness by integrating different cathode materials. Among olivine-type cathodes, LiMnₓFe₁₋ₓPO₄ (LMFP) has attracted considerable attention owing to its high operating voltage enabled by the Mn²⁺/Mn³⁺ redox reaction. However, its long-term cycling stability remains severely limited by inherent Mn dissolution, posing a critical challenge to its practical application. Herein, we investigated the suppression of Mn dissolution by employing solid electrolytes that selectively transport Li⁺ while restricting Mn²⁺ migration. Electrochemical characterization and post-mortem analyses were performed using a Mn metal/solid electrolyte/current collector configuration to evaluate Mn-ion migration. Furthermore, Rietveld refinement was conducted to compare the structural stability of LMFP in liquid- and solid-electrolyte systems during cycling. Electrochemical and post-mortem analyses confirmed that the solid electrolyte effectively restricted Mn-ion migration, suppressing the solvation-mediated Mn dissolution pathway typically observed in liquid electrolytes. Rietveld refinement revealed a significant reduction in the LMFP unit-cell volume in liquid-electrolyte cells, whereas the solid-electrolyte system preserved its initial unit-cell volume, indicating superior structural stability. Consequently, the solid-state LMFP/LiNi₀.₈Co₀.₁Mn₀.₁O₂ (NCM811) blended cathode achieved a high electrode-level volumetric energy density while maintaining excellent capacity retention during prolonged cycling. This work demonstrates that selective ion transport in solid electrolytes provides an effective strategy for overcoming the inherent Mn dissolution challenge in LMFP. By suppressing Mn-ion migration and preserving structural stability, the solid-state system enables the development of high-energy-density blended cathodes with improved long-term cycling stability.

P1-103.k: Ni-rich Layered Cathodes; Thermal Safety; Thermal Runaway
P1-103.a: The growing demand for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries has driven the development of Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes owing to their high specific capacities. However, increasing Ni content is often accompanied by reduced thermal stability, promoting structural degradation and lattice oxygen release at elevated temperatures. To address these thermal safety concerns, extensive efforts have focused on improving the thermal stability of individual cell components, including delaying oxygen evolution from cathodes, enhancing the thermal stability of electrolytes, and improving the thermal integrity of separators. Nevertheless, recent studies have reported that oxygen-mediated cross-talk reactions among cell components can account for over 80% of the total heat generation during thermal runaway in certain Ni-rich cathode/graphite cells. These findings underscore the importance of extending conventional material-level stabilization approaches toward system-level strategies aimed at mitigating exothermic cross-talk reactions among cell components. In this context, direct scavenging of cathode-derived oxygen represents a promising approach to suppress oxygen-mediated cross-talk reactions and potentially mitigate thermal runaway. Herein, we propose a thermally activated oxygen-scavenging strategy to capture cathode-derived oxygen and potentially mitigate exothermic cross-talk reactions. Oxygen scavengers were incorporated into Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes through physical compositing and mechanofusion-assisted surface coating. The thermal decomposition behavior and oxygen-scavenging mechanisms were systematically investigated using thermogravimetric analysis coupled with mass spectrometry (TGA–MS), temperature-dependent X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). Additional heat-treatment experiments were conducted in the presence of electrolytes to examine chemical reactions and phase evolution under electrolyte-containing conditions. Furthermore, the electrochemical performance of the modified cathodes was evaluated through galvanostatic cycling and rate capability measurements. TGA–MS screening of various oxygen-scavenging candidates incorporated into Ni-rich layered cathodes identified promising materials that significantly reduced oxygen evolution during thermal decomposition. Ex-situ temperature-dependent XRD and XPS analyses further elucidated the oxygen-scavenging mechanism, confirming that cathode-derived oxygen was captured through thermally activated oxidation reactions. Following surface coating, the oxygen-scavenging functionality was maintained even in the presence of electrolytes, demonstrating its potential for application under practical battery conditions. Furthermore, the modified cathodes exhibited improved capacity retention and rate capability, indicating favorable electrochemical performance. These findings highlight the potential of oxygen scavenging to control cathode-derived oxygen and mitigate exothermic cross-talk reactions, providing a promising strategy for enhancing the thermal safety of high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries. This study demonstrates the potential of thermally activated oxygen scavenging as an effective strategy for controlling cathode-derived oxygen while maintaining favorable electrochemical performance. Unlike conventional approaches focused primarily on stabilizing individual cell components, the proposed strategy aims to mitigate oxygen-mediated cross-talk reactions by directly capturing oxygen during cathode decomposition. Notably, this approach offers the potential to effectively reduce heat generation associated with oxygen-mediated cross-talk even at low scavenger loadings. These findings highlight the importance of system-level thermal safety strategies and provide a promising pathway toward safer, high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries.

P1-104.a: The development of next-generation lithium-ion batteries requires a deep mechanistic understanding of the structural and kinetic behaviors of layered transition metal oxide cathodes under non-equilibrium conditions. Challenges such as sudden anisotropic volume changes, apparent phase instabilities, and the difficult utilization of high-valent redox couples severely limit the cycle life and energy density of these materials. The primary objective of this work is to elucidate how electrochemically driven dynamics and partial structural disorder can be engineered to stabilize layered cathodes and unlock high-capacity redox mechanisms. By utilizing a comprehensive suite of advanced multi-dimensional imaging and operando analytical platforms, we investigated the real-time structural evolution and charge compensation mechanisms across various layered oxide chemistries, including LiNixMnyCo(1-x-y)O2, dopant-free LiNi0.9Mn0.1O2, Li4FeSbO6. Our findings highlight three distinct phenomena that fundamentally reshape conventional understandings. First, we demonstrated that the widely reported phase separation in LiNixMnyCo(1-x-y)O2 during delithiation is a fictitious kinetic artifact driven by electro-autocatalysis, where an interfacial exchange current increases with the extent of delithiation, rather than equilibrium phase behavior. Second, we leveraged irreversible oxygen oxidation to electrochemically induce partial cation disorder in dopant-free LiNi0.9Mn0.1O2. Introducing ≥12% transition-metal ions into lithium sites eliminated the deleterious c-axis collapse, significantly preserving microstructural integrity and extending cycle life. Finally, we explored the charge compensation mechanism in Li4FeSbO6, revealing a formal FeIII/V redox couple. Through controlled cation ordering and a templated phase transition, this unique high-valent iron state was stabilized without forming oxygen dimers, enabling reversible high-voltage operation. These insights challenge conventional equilibrium-based assumptions and provide new materials design strategies for next-generation systems. By controlling non-equilibrium population dynamics, induced intrinsic disorder, and earth-abundant high-valent redox couples, we establish a robust pathway toward highly stable, energy-dense battery architectures.

P1-105.k: High-entropy; Voltage Decay; Lithium-rich And Manganese-rich Cathode Materials (LMR)
P1-105.a: Lithium-rich and manganese-rich cathode materials (LMR) have attracted considerable attention as promising cathode materials for next-generation lithium-ion batteries owing to their high specific capacity and energy density enabled by anionic redox reactions at high voltages in addition to conventional cationic redox reactions. However, irreversible structural changes and voltage decay associated with transition-metal migration during repeated charge–discharge cycling remain major obstacles to their practical application. In this study, a high-entropy design strategy based on multielement doping was employed to enhance the structural stability and electrochemical performance of LMR cathodes. High-entropy LMR (HE-LMR) cathodes incorporating Ti, Al, Fe, Zn, and an additional dopant were synthesized via a co-precipitation process followed by a solid-state reaction. Their structural characteristics and electrochemical behavior were systematically investigated as a function of dopant composition. Furthermore, an additional doping strategy involving partial substitution of Li⁺ with Na⁺ was introduced to improve the rate capability of HE-LMR cathodes. The multielement-doped HE-LMR cathodes exhibited significantly suppressed voltage decay compared with conventional LMR cathodes. However, reductions in initial discharge capacity and rate capability were observed. The introduction of Na doping improved the rate capability of HE-LMR cathodes, suggesting that Na substitution could enhance lithium-ion transport and mitigate the limitations associated with multielement doping. The combination of structural stabilization through multielement doping and enhanced lithium-ion transport through Na substitution could mitigate the trade-off between structural stability and electrochemical reaction kinetics. This study provides insights into the effects of multielement doping and alkali-ion substitution on the structural and electrochemical properties of LMR cathodes and presents an effective compositional design strategy for developing high-performance LMR cathode materials.

P1-106.k: Lithium- And Manganese-Rich Layered Oxide (LMR); Co-free; Single-crystal
P1-106.a: Li- and Mn-rich (LMR) cathodes offer high specific capacities and cost-effectiveness, but their practical application is limited by structural degradation and interfacial side reactions during cycling. This study investigates micron-sized single-crystal LMR cathodes prepared by controlling precursor morphology and lithium stoichiometry to improve cycling stability. Co-free Mn0.65Ni0.35(OH)2 precursor with thick primary particles and minimized structural interlocking was synthesized by co-precipitation at 55 °C and pH 10.9, with an ammonia concentration of 0.1 M for 10 h. The precursor was mixed with LiOH·H2O at Li/TM ratios of 1.43-1.625, then calcined at 500 °C for 5 h and 900 °C for 15 h. The powders were subsequently ball-milled and annealed at 600 °C for 5 h to obtain SC-LMR10, SC-LMR20, and SC-LMR25. Among the prepared samples, SC-LMR20, with a Li/TM ratio of 1.56, exhibited the most favorable balance of structural characteristics. It retained 94.8 % of its specific capacity and 89.3 % of its specific energy after 100 cycles. Even after 200 cycles, surface and structural analyses revealed less accumulation of electrolyte-decomposition products and better preservation of the layered structure in SC-LMR20 than in the polycrystalline LMR(PC-LMR). After 600 cycles, SC-LMR20 retained 49.3 % of its capacity and 42.9 % of its specific energy, compared with 34.2 % and 30.7 %, respectively, for PC-LMR. Compared with PC-LMR, SC-LMR20 exhibited superior long-term capacity and energy retention, reduced interfacial side reactions, and better preservation of its structural features. These results demonstrate that co-regulating precursor morphology and lithium stoichiometry is an effective strategy for improving the structural and interfacial stability of micron-sized Co-free single-crystal LMR cathodes.

P2-001.k: Perovskite Solar Cells; Zwitterion; Interface Engineering
P2-001.a: Interface engineering is an effective strategy for improving the efficiency and stability of perovskite solar cells, particularly through the defect passivation at the perovskite crystals. Zwitterionic molecules are one of the favorable passivation materials because their intrinsic positive and negative charges can effectively interact with defect sites in perovskite. However, strong intermolecular electrostatic interactions between zwitterions often lead to poor solubility and aggregation, limiting their processability and uniform interfacial layer formation. Therefore, regulating the intermolecular interactions of zwitterions is essential for overcoming their processability limitations and enabling effective interface engineering in perovskite solar cells To regulate the intermolecular interactions of zwitterions, a modified zwitterion (LTZ) was synthesized from 3-(1-pyridinio)-1-propanesulfonate and LiTFSI. The effects of this molecular interaction modulation on the solubility, processability, and film formation were investigated. LTZ was subsequently introduced at the perovskite buried interface to form a uniform passivation layer, and its effects on perovskite film, carrier dynamics, and photovoltaic performance were compared with those of the conventional zwitterion. The scalability of the LTZ-based device was further demonstrated by fabricating a large-area perovskite module. The suppression of intermolecular interactions significantly improved the solubility and processability of the zwitterionic material, enabling the formation of a more uniformly distributed LTZ passivation layer. Compared with the conventional zwitterion, LTZ treatment resulted in better-distributed interfacial passivation and improved electrical properties of the perovskite layer, leading to enhanced photovoltaic performance. As a result, LTZ-treated perovskite solar cell achieved an improved efficiency of 24.9% and maintained over 80% of their initial efficiency for 1968 h under 60 °C and N₂ atmosphere. Furthermore, the LTZ-based perovskite module with an active area of 32.7 cm² achieved an enhanced efficiency of 19.86%, demonstrating the applicability of this strategy beyond small-area devices. This work demonstrates that controlling intermolecular interactions is an effective strategy for overcoming the intrinsic solubility and processability limitations of zwitterionic passivators. The synthesized LTZ enables uniform film and enhanced charge dynamics, thereby improving the efficiency and thermal stability of perovskite solar cells. The successful demonstration of a 32.7 cm² module further highlights the potential of molecularly engineered zwitterions for scalable interface engineering toward commercialization.

P2-002.k: Wide Bandgap Perovskite; Low Dimension Perovskite; MA-free Passivation
P2-002.a: Two-dimensional (2D)/three-dimensional (3D) perovskite heterostructures have emerged as a promising route to simultaneously realize high power conversion efficiency and enhanced operational stability in perovskite solar cells. In this architecture, a thin 2D perovskite layer formed on the 3D absorber can effectively passivate surface defects, suppress nonradiative recombination, and improve moisture tolerance. However, the conventional 2D surface treatments typically rely on isopropyl alcohol (IPA) as a processing solvent for bulky organic spacer ligands. Such IPA-based deposition often induces non-uniform interfacial reactions and promotes the formation of quasi-2D perovskites with a broad and poorly controlled distribution of n phases. This heterogeneous phase landscape can introduce additional instability pathways and complicate charge transport across the 2D/3D interface. Moreover, incomplete or spatially inhomogeneous conversion at the perovskite surface may aggravate residual PbI2 accumulation, which can negatively impact both device reproducibility and stability. To address these challenges, we employ a solvent-engineering strategy by incorporating N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) into the passivation formulation to enhance wetting and enable more homogeneous interfacial reactions between the passivator and the perovskite surface. Furthermore, we introduce an A-site cation into the passivation system to suppress PbI2 excess by rebalancing local stoichiometry and facilitating more complete surface reconstruction. This combined approach is designed to yield a more uniform 2D/3D heterointerface while mitigating quasi-2D phase heterogeneity and PbI2 residues, thereby offering a practical pathway toward simultaneously improved efficiency and durability. We developed a Low dimensional passivation strategy combining a A-site material with a long-chain monoammonium. Solution-phase association was probed by PL. Surface coverage and distribution were characterized by XPS and KPFM and interfacial energetics by UPS. Devices were fabricated in an inverted architecture. In our approach, a DMF-containing formulation improves wetting and reaction uniformity at the 3D perovskite surface, while the simultaneous introduction of an A-site cation suppresses PbI2 excess, aiming to form a more controlled, single-phase 2D capping layer (targeting n=2). Optical and interfacial analyses support the improved capping quality. Steady-state photoluminescence collected from film side shows enhanced emission after 2D capping, indicating reduced interfacial nonradiative recombination, and time-resolved photoluminescence suggests prolonged carrier lifetime. Importantly, device trends indicate that increasing the alkyl spacer chain length systematically improves photovoltaic performance, with the C12 ligand (dodecylammonium) delivering the highest efficiency among the tested series (BA/HA/OA/DA), consistent with more effective interfacial defect passivation and a better-defined n=2 interlayer. Device stability results further highlight the role of A-site engineering. Replacing the A-site cation with FA leads to markedly improved thermal durability during long-term aging compared with MA-based counterparts. Consistently, KPFM analyses of surface photovoltage (SPV) distributions before and after stressing show that FA-based films retain a more similar SPV response after degradation, indicating reduced photo-induced potential loss and better preservation of the initial interfacial charge-separation performance. These findings suggest that FA-based 2D surface passivation is a viable pathway to realize thermally robust 2D/3D perovskite solar cells and provide a design guideline for next-generation stable perovskite interfaces.

P2-003.k: Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs); Gel Chromatography; Semiconducting SWNTs
P2-003.a: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are promising materials for solar cells due to their excellent electrical, optical, and mechanical properties. Their large surface area and high conductivity expand the donor–acceptor interface for exciton dissociation while forming conductive pathways for charge transport. CNTs also offer tunable energy levels via diameter and chirality control, improving charge extraction through energy-level alignment with the electrode. However, as-synthesized CNTs are inevitably obtained as a mixture of semiconducting and metallic tubes, limiting device performance. Thus, separating high-purity semiconducting SWNTs is essential before practical application. As a preliminary step toward CNT-based solar cells, this study separated semiconducting SWNTs from CoMoCAT-synthesized SWNTs, known for their narrow diameter distribution. Using the differential interaction between surfactant-wrapped tubes and the gel medium, semiconducting SWNTs were isolated via gel chromatography. Samples were characterized by UV-Vis-NIR absorption and Raman spectroscopy, and compared with separated (6,5) SWNTs from HiPco SWNTs. UV-Vis-NIR spectra showed pronounced semiconducting peaks in CoMoCAT-derived (6,5) SWNTs, indicating higher semiconducting yield than HiPco-derived samples. Raman analysis under 532nm and 633nm excitation showed a lower D/G peak ratio for CoMoCAT-derived (6,5) SWNTs, indicating fewer defects and higher crystallinity. These results show CoMoCAT SWNTs outperform HiPco SWNTs in both semiconducting purity and structural quality, supporting their potential for CNT-based solar cells. Future work will incorporate these separated SWNTs into photovoltaic devices to assess power conversion efficiency and stability.

P2-004.k: Perovskite Solar Cells; Passivation; Glyoxylic Acid
P2-004.a: Current defect passivation strategies have explored various long-chain alkylamine salts, which have demonstrated efficacy in reducing non-radiative recombination and improving device performance. Multifunctional additives capable of engaging in diverse interactionssuch as Lewis acid-base interactions, coordination, and hydrogen bonding with the perovskite lattice are highly desirable. Among these, the carboxylic acid (–COOH) group is particularly promising, functioning as a Brønsted acid to donate protons to potential bases such as cationic amines, while the carbonyl group can also form strong Lewis acid–base interactions with undercoordinated Pb2+, simultaneously. The incorporation of –COOH-containing additives, whether through post-treatment or direct precursor modification, has been shown to reduce trap densities, extend carrier recombination lifetimes, and ultimately mitigate losses in VOC, short-circuit current density (JSC), and FF, leading to improved PCEs in PSCs. Various spectropic analyses, film morphology, and device characterizations were conducted to investigate the influence of glyoxylic acid (GXA) for multivalent passivation of peorvksite films. Unlike conventional carboxylic acid additives, GXA undergoes spontaneous Brønsted acid–base proton transfer with formamidinium (FA+), generating an in situ carboxylate species that serves as the active passivation motif. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations combined with spectroscopic analyses reveal that the activated carboxylate simultaneously forms strong hydrogen bonds with FA cations and coordination bonds with undercoordinated Pb2+ defect sites, thereby suppressing defect formation while relieving lattice microstrain during crystallization. The optimized devices achieve a high power conversion efficiency of 25.03% with minimal VOC loss and retain over 95% of their initial efficiency after 2500 h under ambient storage conditions.

P2-005.k: Tin-lead Perovskite; Solar Cell; Quantum Dots
P2-005.a: Perovskite materials are widely regarded as promising candidates for emerging optoelectronic technologies, owing to their favorable charge-transport properties, strong light absorption, and highly tunable electronic structures. However, the high efficiencies achieved in conventional perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are often associated with the use of lead. Sn-Pb mixed perovskites have therefore been investigated as an alternative approach to reduce the lead content while retaining efficient near-infrared light absorption. However, the incorporation of Sn introduces a significant stability concern, as Sn is readily oxidized under ambient conditions. We present a surface engineering strategy employing perovskite quantum dots to simultaneously improve the photovoltaic performance and stability of Sn-Pb PSCs. CsPbI3 (LQD) and CsSnPbI3 (TLQD) were synthesized using a hot-injection method and subsequently deposited onto the Sn-Pb perovskite films to form a surface modification layer, followed by washing with IPA to remove residual ligands. Compared with LQD, the partial substitution of Pb with Sn within the crystal lattice can alleviate lattice distortion associated with the larger ionic size of Pb, thereby contributing to enhanced structural stability. During the IPA washing, dissociated ligands can interact with and passivate surface defects present in the underlying Sn-Pb perovskite layer. The TLQD-modified layer exhibited the highest water contact angle of 106°, indicating enhanced moisture resistance. This modification led to a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 21.76%, the LQD-modified layer achieved a PCE of 20.75%. These results demonstrate the potential of QD-based interfacial modification as an effective strategy for simultaneously enhancing the efficiency and stability of next-generation optoelectronic devices.

P2-006.k: Ionic Materials; Perovskite Solar Cells; Batteries
P2-006.a: Functional ionic materials have attracted considerable attention for applications in next-generation energy conversion and storage devices, including perovskite solar cells and batteries. Naphthyl ether-based ammonium iodide salts with different alkyl chain lengths were designed and synthesized. Their potential applications as functional ionic materials for energy devices were investigated, with a primary focus on perovskite solar cells. The synthesized ammonium salts were successfully incorporated into perovskite solar cells, and the fabricated devices showed promising photovoltaic characteristics. Triple-cation perovskite devices exhibited power conversion efficiencies approaching 17%. Molecularly designed ammonium salts represent versatile ionic materials with potential applications in both energy conversion and storage systems. Further studies will explore their application to perovskite solar cells and battery-related materials.

P2-007.k: Organic Solar Cells; Self-Assembled Monolayers; Phenothiazine
P2-007.a: Organic solar cells (OSCs) have emerged as promising photovoltaic technologies owing to their lightweight, flexibility, low-cost fabrication, and compatibility with solution processing. Although power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) have exceeded 20%, conventional hole transport layers (HTLs) such as PEDOT:PSS and MoOₓ suffer from drawbacks including acidity, vacuum processing, and limited long-term stability. This study employed phenothiazine-based self-assembled monolayers (SAMs), namely brominated BrPZPA and non-halogenated PZPA, as hole transport layers for conventional organic solar cells. Both compounds were synthesized through identical reaction pathways starting from phenothiazine. Bromobutyl groups were first introduced by alkylation of the phenothiazine core, followed by bromination at the 3- and 7-positions for BrPZPA. Phosphonic acid anchoring groups were subsequently attached through Michaelis–Arbuzov and McKenna reactions. The sulfur-containing phenothiazine core downshifts the HOMO level, enhances charge delocalization, and enables the formation of an ordered monolayer on ITO. Devices based on PM6:Y6BO achieve a power conversion efficiency of 18.2% with excellent thermal and UV stability, showing only 1.09% degradation under prolonged illumination. Moreover, PM6:L8-BO devices reach a PCE of 19.7%, highlighting phenothiazine-derived SAMs as efficient interfacial materials for high-performance OSCs. These findings demonstrate that phenothiazine-derived SAMs are robust, efficient, and stable interfacial materials, providing a promising pathway for developing next-generation OSCs with enhanced performance and durability.

P2-008.k: Indium Tin Oxide; Oxygen Vacancy; Interfacial Engineering
P2-008.a: Recent advances in buried-interface engineering have enabled certified efficiencies exceeding 27% for inverted metal halide perovskite solar cells. However, the role of indium tin oxide (ITO), which forms the starting layer of the buried interface, remains underexplored. As a heavily doped n-type semiconductor, ITO inherently contains oxygen vacancies that can influence SAM assembly, interfacial energetics, and charge extraction. Here, we reveal the contrasting roles of surface and bulk oxygen vacancies in ITO. Surface oxygen vacancies promote hydroxyl formation and facilitate dense and uniform SAM assembly, whereas excessive bulk oxygen vacancies strengthen the n-type character of ITO, resulting in unfavorable energy-level alignment and inefficient hole extraction. These findings establish ITO defect states as active regulators of buried-interface formation, rather than passive features of a transparent electrode. Building on this understanding, we developed an oxygen-vacancy reconciliation (VRC) strategy that preserves beneficial surface vacancies while suppressing detrimental bulk vacancies. This approach simultaneously improves SAM assembly and interfacial energy-level alignment, enabling a power conversion efficiency of 27.24% (certified 26.70%, with a short-circuit current density of 26.44 mA cm-2), together with enhanced operational and thermal stability. The VRC strategy is applicable across multiple commercial ITO substrates and wide-bandgap perovskite systems. Its simplicity and low cost make it readily transferable to a broad range of ITO-based inverted PSC architectures.

P2-009.k: Perovskite/silicon Tandem Solar Cells; Molecular Co-assembly; Surface Passivation
P2-009.a: Perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells offer a realistic route to efficiencies well beyond single-junction silicon, with the wide-bandgap (~1.68 eV) perovskite top cell as the performance-limiting component. Defects and non-radiative recombination at the perovskite/C₆₀ interface in inverted (p-i-n) devices erode both efficiency and operational stability. Surface passivation with organic ammonium salts is the established remedy, yet a single passivator molecule struggles to deliver strong chemical passivation and effective field-effect passivation simultaneously: short-chain diammonium salts anchor well but lack the inter-molecular interactions needed to pack densely, leaving an incomplete and disordered surface layer. We developed a synergistic co-assembly passivation (SynAP) strategy combining 1,3-propanediammonium iodide (PDAI₂), a short diammonium passivator, with dodecylammonium iodide (DAI), a long-chain (C12) monoammonium. Solution-phase association was probed by 1H NMR and DOSY; surface adsorption configurations and co-adsorption energies were calculated by density functional theory (DFT) with Bader charge analysis. Surface coverage and distribution were characterized by XPS and ToF-SIMS; carrier recombination by PL mapping, TRPL, and absolute PLQY; and interfacial energetics by UPS and KPFM. Devices were fabricated in an inverted architecture and integrated into two-terminal perovskite/silicon tandems. DAI alone was ineffective as a passivator, lowering efficiency below the control, yet became indispensable in combination with PDAI2. NMR revealed that the two molecules associate in solution through N–H···I···N–H bridging between their ammonium head groups, and DFT confirmed that the co-assembled configuration is thermodynamically favoured over isolated adsorption, whereas two PDAI₂ molecules gain no such stabilization. ToF-SIMS and XPS showed a markedly higher surface density of PDAI2 in the presence of DAI, and PL mapping confirmed more spatially uniform passivation. Device efficiency increased monotonically with the alkyl chain length of the co-assembling monoammonium (C2→C12), identifying chain length as a critical structural parameter. UPS and DFT consistently showed a super-additive work-function reduction upon co-assembly. SynAP delivered 24.01% for single-junction wide-bandgap cells and 34.09% (certified 33.64%) for perovskite/silicon tandems, retaining 89% of initial performance after 800 h of maximum power point tracking. Molecular co-assembly can activate a passivator that is ineffective on its own by directing a second molecule into a denser, more uniformly packed surface layer. This establishes molecular packing density — rather than the intrinsic passivating ability of any single molecule — as a key lever for interface engineering, offering a broadly applicable route to high-performance wide-bandgap perovskite interfaces and efficient tandem solar cells.

P2-010.k: Intrinsically Stretchable Polymer Semiconductors; Bulk Heterojunction; Organic Photodetectors
P2-010.a: Intrinsically stretchable organic photodetectors (OPDs) require photoactive layers that simultaneously provide efficient photogeneration and charge transport under large mechanical deformation. However, conventional bulk heterojunction (BHJ) active layers generally require a substantial fraction of molecular acceptors to achieve efficient charge generation, which can compromise the mechanical stretchability of the resulting films. Controlling the crystalline structure of polymer semiconductors therefore offers a potential route to reconcile the conflicting optoelectronic and mechanical requirements of stretchable BHJ systems. Stretchable block copolymer semiconductors with controlled crystalline structures were used to fabricate BHJ thin films with varying donor–acceptor compositions. Two-dimensional grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray diffraction (GIWAXD) was performed to investigate the effects of polymer structure and acceptor content on crystalline structures. Their optical, electrical, and mechanical properties were systematically evaluated, and OPDs were fabricated to assess photodetection performance under mechanical deformation. Optimization of the polymer crystalline structure enabled efficient charge transport and photoresponse even at reduced acceptor content. Importantly, the reduced acceptor content substantially improved the mechanical compliance of the BHJ films while preserving the optoelectronic functionality required for photodetection. The optimized BHJ films exhibited high stretchability and maintained their electrical and photoresponsive characteristics under large tensile deformation. OPDs incorporating these active layers consequently demonstrated stable photodetection performance under mechanical strain, revealing a close relationship between polymer crystalline organization, BHJ composition, and mechanical robustness. These results demonstrate that crystalline structure engineering of stretchable block copolymer semiconductors enables BHJ active layers with reduced acceptor content to simultaneously achieve efficient photodetection and high mechanical stretchability. These findings establish a structure–composition–property relationship for mechanically compliant BHJ systems and provide a materials design strategy for intrinsically stretchable organic optoelectronic devices.

P2-011.a: To mitigate internal degradation in perovskite solar cells, a dual-functional polymer, 12C4@PEI, was designed by combining the specific chemical properties of crown ether and polyethyleneimine (PEI). The 12-crown-4 (12C4) unit is utilized to capture mobile Li⁺ ions. Because the cavity size of 12C4 perfectly matches the ionic radius of Li⁺ (~0.76 Å), its oxygen atoms can form strong and selective coordination bonds with Li⁺. Concurrently, the PEI backbone acts as an effective proton scavenger to suppress the formation of detrimental HTFSI. The abundant secondary and tertiary amine sites within PEI donate their lone pair electrons to react with H⁺, readily becoming protonated into aminium forms (NH₂⁺, NH⁺). Perovskite solar cells were fabricated with a device structure of ITO / SnO₂ / Perovskite / Spiro-OMeTAD / Au. To verify the synthesis and properties of the target material (12C4@PEI), various analytical techniques were employed, including XRD, ToF-SIMS, NMR (¹H, ⁷Li), XPS (O 1s, Li 1s), J-V curves, energy band alignment (KPFM), AFM, and DFT calculations. XRD patterns reveal that the 12C4@PEI-treated perovskite films exhibit suppressed δ-phase formation and enhanced phase stability compared to the pristine sample. AFM images further demonstrate that the incorporation of 12C4@PEI leads to a reduction in surface roughness for both the perovskite layer (RMS from 39.62 to 35.24 nm) and the HTL (RMS from 18.06 to 11.21 nm), indicating a smoother and more uniform film formation. In XPS analysis, the treated sample shows a clear shift in binding energies toward higher values, suggesting strong coordination between the functional groups of 12C4@PEI and Pb²⁺/I⁻ ions, which leads to effective defect passivation and enhanced interfacial stability. Furthermore, ToF-SIMS depth profiling reveals that while the pristine sample suffers from significant Li⁺ diffusion from the HTL into the perovskite layer, the 12C4@PEI-treated device markedly suppresses this migration. As a result, Li⁺ is effectively confined near the HTL, decreasing the Li⁺ ratio (ETL/HTL) from 4.86 to 1.80. Energetically, the incorporation of 12C4@PEI slightly shifts the energy levels of both the perovskite and Spiro-OMeTAD, resulting in improved band alignment at the perovskite/HTL interface. This facilitates more efficient hole extraction and reduces interfacial energy barriers, contributing to enhanced charge transport and suppressed recombination. Consequently, the 12C4@PEI-treated device exhibits an increasing trend in efficiency over time after 30 days, indicating improved long-term stability, whereas the pristine device shows a decrease in efficiency. The incorporation of 12C4@PEI effectively suppresses Li⁺ migration from Li-TFSI-doped HTLs by capturing Li⁺ ions through the crown ether moiety while simultaneously reducing protonation via the amine groups of PEI. This dual functionality minimizes the formation of hygroscopic byproducts such as LiOH and HTFSI, thereby blocking moisture ingress pathways and improving the chemical stability at the perovskite/HTL interface. Structural analyses reveal suppressed δ-phase formation and enhanced α-phase stability, while morphological and depth-profiling results confirm uniform film formation and the effective confinement of Li⁺ ions near the HTL. Ultimately, these improvements in physicochemical stability translate into enhanced device performance, where the 12C4@PEI-treated devices maintain or even improve their efficiency over time. Overall, this work demonstrates that 12C4@PEI is an effective strategy for suppressing Li⁺ migration, offering a viable pathway toward high-performance and long-term stable perovskite solar cells.

P2-012.k: Perovskite Solar Cells; Additives; Small Organic Molecule
P2-012.a: Defect states and non-radiative recombination remain major limitations to the photovoltaic performance of triple-cation perovskite solar cells. In this study, a synthesized molecular additive was incorporated into Cs₀.₁₇₅FA₀.₇₅₀MA₀.₀₇₅Pb(I₀.₈₈₀Br₀.₁₂₀)₃ perovskite films as a passivating agent to improve their optoelectronic properties and device performance. Different concentrations of the molecular additive (0.25–1.00 mM) were introduced into the perovskite precursor solution. Structural, optical, morphological, thermal, and chemical properties were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD), UV–Vis spectroscopy, photoluminescence (PL), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), contact-angle measurements, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). Perovskite solar cells with the architecture ITO/NiOₓ/perovskite/PCBM/ZnO/Ag were fabricated and their photovoltaic characteristics were evaluated. Among the investigated concentrations, 0.75 mM provided the most effective defect passivation. Additive incorporation reduced trap-state density, increased grain size, suppressed non-radiative recombination, and improved charge-transport properties. The optimized device achieved a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.3%, corresponding to an approximately 9% improvement compared with the pristine device. Molecular additive-assisted passivation effectively improves the structural and optoelectronic quality of triple-cation perovskite films and enhances photovoltaic performance. These findings demonstrate that additive engineering is a promising strategy for developing high-efficiency triple-cation perovskite solar cells.

P2-013.a: Oxide/metal/oxide (OMO) electrodes are promising low-resistance and hightransmittance alternatives to single transparent conducting oxide layers. Although ITO/Ag/ITO is widely used, ITO often requires high processing temperatures and Its polycrystalline surface can hinder the wetting of ultrathin Ag, leading to islandlike growth below a critical thickness. Here, amorphous IZO is introduced as a low-temperature alternative. Unlike previous symmetric IZO/Ag/IZO designs, this study considers the distinct roles of the two oxide layers: the bottom IZO controls Ag nucleation and growth, while the top IZO affects Ag protection and optical interference IZO/Ag/IZO electrodes were fabricated by sputtering with asymmetric oxygen flow ratios for the bottom and top IZO layers. The bottom IZO was deposited under a low oxygen fraction to improve Ag wetting and reduce the critical thickness for continuous film formation. The top IZO was deposited under a higher oxygen fraction to enhance Ag stability and tune optical properties, especially NIR reflection. Contact angle measurements were used to evaluate surface wettability. AFM and SEM analyses were performed for Ag films with different thicknesses to examine morphology and continuity. Sheet resistance, transmittance, and reflectance spectra were also measured. The wetting behavior of Ag on the bottom TCO was first evaluated by measuring the contact angle under different oxygen fractions. Improved wetting promoted earlier formation of a continuous Ag layer, which was confirmed by comparing the critical Ag thickness using AFM and SEM. The transparent electrode performance was then optimized by varying the oxygen fraction of both bottom and top TCO layers, and the figure of merit was calculated from sheet resistance measured by a multimeter and optical transmittance obtained by UV–vis spectroscopy. Finally, the oxygen fraction of the top IZO layer was controlled to tune the onset wavelength of near-infrared reflection, demonstrating adjustable optical selectivity. Asymmetric oxygen-content control in IZO/Ag/IZO electrodes is expected to enable independent optimization of Ag growth and optical response within a single OMO stack. A low-oxygen bottom IZO layer can improve Ag wetting and reduce the critical thickness for continuous conductive pathway formation, while a higheroxygen top IZO layer can tune NIR reflection through optical interference. This strategy may overcome the limitations of conventional symmetric IZO/Ag/IZO electrodes and provide low-temperature, low-resistance, and high-transmittance electrodes for semi-transparent, bifacial, and building-integrated perovskite photovoltaics.

P2-014.k: AS-ALD; Perovskite/Si Tandem Solar Cells; Interface Passivation
P2-014.a: Incomplete coverage of self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) on NiOx hole-transport layers exposes underlying defect sites that promote non-radiative recombination and chemical degradation at the perovskite interface. Area-selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD) of AlOx has recently been shown to passivate such SAM-uncovered regions on planar substrates by exploiting the chemical contrast between hydroxyl-rich NiOx and inert SAM. However, perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells rely on micron-scale pyramidal texturing of the silicon bottom cell, where SAM coverage is expected to be more heterogeneous, leaving this passivation strategy unexplored in textured, tandem-relevant architectures. NiOx/SAM-modified textured silicon substrates are treated with AS-ALD AlOx under systematically varied deposition conditions to identify a texture-appropriate process window. Nanoscale chemical mapping and surface-sensitive spectroscopy are used to examine SAM defect distribution and AlOx selectivity across the textured surface, and the resulting films are integrated into complete perovskite/silicon tandem devices for photovoltaic and stability evaluation against our laboratory's reference tandem cell. Preliminary considerations suggest that SAM coverage on textured NiOx is more defect-prone than on planar surfaces, particularly near regions of high curvature, and that AS-ALD AlOx can selectively remediate these defects while preserving SAM functionality elsewhere. Device- and stability-level outcomes are expected to reflect improvements in charge extraction and interfacial durability relative to the SAM-only control; full quantitative results will be presented at the conference. This work aims to extend SAM-induced area-selective ALD passivation from planar perovskite solar cells to textured perovskite/silicon tandem architectures, offering a scalable, template-free strategy for buried-interface engineering that is broadly relevant to next-generation tandem photovoltaics.

P2-015.k: Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis; Direct Slurry Bar Coating; Alkaline Seawater Electrolysis
P2-015.a: Catalyst-coated membrane (CCM) fabrication is a key factor governing performance, durability, and scalability of anion-exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE). Herein, we developed a scalable direct slurry bar-coating process assisted by an adhesive film to fabricate high-quality CCMs with enhanced membrane–electrode interfacial adhesion. Compared with the conventional spray-coating method, the proposed process significantly improved interfacial shear adhesion by 146% and 135% at anode and cathode, respectively. Furthermore, the combination of direct bar coating and a 5-μm dot-patterned membrane created a three-dimensional interlocking interface, improving electrode integrity and electrochemical performance. The optimized CCM achieved 38% higher current density at 1.85 V than the spray-coated reference. Durability was evaluated under alkaline seawater electrolysis conditions (1 M KOH + seawater) at 60°C, where the direct-coated patterned CCM exhibited only a 9% decrease in current density after 100 h at 0.25 A cm⁻², whereas spray-coated reference showed a 39% decrease. In addition, the increase in high-frequency resistance was limited to 4.3%, compared with 18% for the reference CCM. Post-mortem SEM and EDS analyses further confirmed superior catalyst layer retention and significantly reduced localized chlorine-containing salt accumulation at the membrane–electrode interface. Moreover, the direct slurry bar-coating process was successfully extended to a 150 cm² CCM with highly uniform catalyst loading, exhibiting spatial relative standard deviations of approximately 1.2% for both Ni and Fe. These results demonstrate that scalable interfacial engineering through direct slurry bar coating provides an effective route toward durable and high-performance CCMs for next-generation AEM water electrolysis, particularly under harsh alkaline seawater operating conditions.

P2-016.a: Hydrogen (H₂) is a promising clean fuel, but its wide flammable range, low ignition energy, and high diffusivity pose safety risks and detection challenges. Conventional electrical sensors require external power, pose ignition hazards, and fail to visually map leak origins. To address these limitations, we present a colorimetric H₂ sensor providing a direct visual response. The sensor consists of a cholesteric liquid crystal (CLC) polymer exhibiting Bragg-reflection and catalytically reactive palladium (Pd) film deposited onto an elastomeric substrate. Upon H₂ exposure, the Pd layer absorbs H₂ molecules to form palladium hydride, causing volumetric expansion. Constrained by the elastomer, the Pd film undergoes mechanical buckling, creating a wrinkled surface. This morphological transition shifts the reflective properties of the Pd film from specular reflection to multidirectional light scattering. Interacting with the CLC's Bragg-reflection, our sensor exhibits distinct color shift from the Bragg-reflection color to its complementary color. The sensor detects 1% H₂ within 10 seconds and the color shift remains stable across various viewing angles. Also, we establish the roll-to-roll (R2R) manufacturing process of the sensor, demonstrating its scalability. We wrapped the R2R-processed large-area sensor around the leakage site of H₂ pipe, demonstrating in-situ leak detection. Finally, we developed a real-time monitoring system that detects the colorimetric transition via CCTV and triggers an alert upon H₂ leakage. Our system enables spatial mapping without ignition risks, providing a solution for H₂ leak monitoring in the upcoming hydrogen economy. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea grant (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, RS-2024-00411809)

P2-017.a: Accelerated durability testing (ADT) protocols are widely used to evaluate electrocatalyst stability, but the degradation pathways activated by different potential programs remain insufficiently understood. In particular, carbon corrosion and Pt dissolution are often treated independently despite their strong dependence on the potential-dependent surface state of Pt. We investigated Pt/C degradation under systematically varied ADT conditions using multimodal in situ analysis. Differential electrochemical mass spectrometry was used to monitor CO₂ evolution from carbon corrosion, while inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry quantified Pt dissolution in real time. Potential-cycling and potential-step protocols were compared, with particular emphasis on the lower potential limit and the duration of each potential segment. Carbon corrosion was governed by the dynamic surface state of Pt. Metallic Pt promoted carbon oxidation, whereas Pt oxide suppressed this pathway, resulting in transient carbon corrosion during conventional potential cycling. Lowering the potential to regenerate metallic Pt markedly increased carbon corrosion; however, this condition also enhanced Pt dissolution, revealing an intrinsic trade-off between the two degradation pathways. Importantly, the extent of this trade-off depended not only on the potential limits but also on the time spent at each potential. By tuning the temporal profile of the potential program, carbon corrosion could be selectively intensified while limiting Pt loss. ADT does not simply accelerate degradation uniformly. Instead, it selectively activates degradation pathways through coupled Pt surface-state dynamics and time-dependent electrochemical processes. Rational control and interpretation of potential limits and dwell times are therefore essential for designing reliable ADT protocols and accurately assessing electrocatalyst durability.

P2-018.k: Fe3C; Carbon Quantum Dot; Oxygen Reduction Reaction
P2-018.a: Recently, interest in energy storage devices has been rising due to the increasing use of fossil fuels and global warming. While representative energy storage devices include lithium-ion batteries, supercapacitors, and fuel cells, next-generation energy storage devices such as lithium-air batteries is being researched to achieve more efficient energy storage. In particular, devices that primarily utilize oxygen-based electrochemical reactions, such as lithium-air batteries, are significantly affected by the oxygen reduction reaction. After fabricating CQDs by hydrothermal synthesis, they were electrospun with a CNF precursor. Subsequently, they were stirred with an Fe-containing hydrate, vacuum dried, and then heat-treated. LSV, CV, ADT, etc. were used to measure ORR performance, and electrochemical performance was verified by applying them as a catalyst in LAB.
