The catalyst with an appropriate amount of CQDs exhibited onset and half-wave potentials at 0.951 V and 0.851 V in an alkaline electrolyte, respectively, and displayed an excellent Tafel slope of 59.7 mV/dec. The number of electron transfers measured via LSV approached 4, confirming that the 4-electron reaction pathway was predominant. It was confirmed that the addition of CQDs increased carbon defects and improved the dispersibility of Fe3C, leading to higher activity and enhanced lifetime stability. (1) enhanced catalytic activity due to Fe–Nₓ sites, Fe3C/Fe nanoparticles, and CQD-induced defects synergistically boosting the intrinsic ORR activity (2) the optimized CQD content expand the ECSA and creates a tailored mirco-mesoporous structure (3) the transition to a 4-electron pathway via CQD minimizes peroxide-induced degradation, resulting in significantly enhancing long-term structural and electrochemical durability.

P2-019.k: Flow Battery; Iron Complex; Sugar Alcohol
P2-019.a: Iron-based complexes are promising redox-active materials for aqueous flow batteries (AFBs) because of the high abundance, low cost, and environmental compatibility of iron. However, the use of conventional organic ligands can substantially increase electrolyte cost and may also induce undesirable side reactions, thereby limiting the economic advantages of iron-based systems. Sugar alcohols, such as xylitol, sorbitol, and mannitol, offer attractive alternative ligands because they are inexpensive, widely available, and possess multiple hydroxyl groups capable of coordinating with iron ions. In this study, iron-sugar alcohol complexes are prepared under alkaline conditions, and their coordination characteristics are investigated using spectroscopic analyses. Their electrochemical behavior is evaluated using cyclic voltammetry and related electrochemical techniques, while the effects of ligand structure, metal-to-ligand ratio, and electrolyte composition on complex formation and redox activity are examined. The multiple hydroxyl groups of the sugar alcohol ligands enable multidentate coordination with iron and suppress the precipitation of iron hydroxide under alkaline conditions. The resulting complexes exhibit reversible redox reactions at approximately -1.0 V vs. Hg/HgO, indicating their suitability as negative active materials. Optimization of the complex composition further enhances the overall electrochemical performance. Iron-sugar alcohol complexes are subsequently evaluated as negative electrolytes in AFBs with ferrocyanide as the positive electrolyte, demonstrating stable charge-discharge behavior and sustained cycling performance. These results suggest that sugar alcohols can serve as low-cost, nitrogen-free ligands for developing economical and sustainable iron-based electrolytes for AFBs.

P2-020.a: While platinum (Pt) remains the benchmark electrocatalyst for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in fuel cells, its operation in chloride-rich environments, such as marine systems, leads to severe performance decay. Adsorbed chloride ions block catalytic sites and trigger Pt degradation. To date, traditional mitigation methods overlook the potential of the catalyst-ionomer interface to address this poisoning issue. To overcome this, we introduced a sequential interfacial design using a bilayer of cation- and anion-exchange ionomers. Specifically, Nafion and Sustainion were sequentially deposited on the Pt surface to construct an electrostatic shield. This local environment was extensively tested for its ability to regulate anion transport and preserve both the activity and stability of the catalyst under chloride-contaminated conditions. The engineered bilayer successfully repelled detrimental chloride ions via charge-based exclusion, preventing catalyst poisoning. This tailored configuration delivered outstanding ORR activity retention and highly suppressed Pt dissolution rates compared to conventional catalyst layers in corrosive environments. Notably, the dual-ionomer barrier maintained its protective capability and structural robustness even when exposed to other competitive, strongly-adsorbing species such as phosphate anions. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that sequential ionomer engineering is a highly promising strategy for safeguarding noble-metal catalysts. By finely tuning the electrostatic properties at interfaces, this approach offers a versatile and scalable pathway to extend the lifetime of energy conversion devices.

P2-021.k: Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis; Non-PGM Electrode; Direct Membrane Deposition
P2-021.a: Minimizing the use of precious-metal catalysts in proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) is critical for the large-scale production of green hydrogen. Addressing this challenge requires careful engineering of the electrode–membrane interface. In particular, inadequate contact at the interface increases ohmic resistance, resulting in a higher cell voltage and lower energy efficiency. In this study, we developed a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) incorporating a non-precious-metal anode and direct membrane deposition (DMD) to reduce interfacial ohmic resistance. An MnO2 catalyst layer was deposited onto a Pt-coated porous transport layer (PTL) via anodic electrodeposition. Subsequently, a diluted Nafion dispersion was directly spray-coated onto the electrode, followed by thermal treatment to form a well-integrated membrane–catalyst interface. The membrane thickness was controlled to approximately 60 um, comparable to that of Nafion 212. Imaging analyses confirmed the formation of a uniform membrane–catalyst interface and the infiltration of Nafion into the voids between the MnO2 structures grown on the PTL fibers. High-frequency resistance (HFR) measurements showed that the DMD-based MEA had lower ohmic resistance than an MEA fabricated with a commercial membrane. The I-V curve shows the non-precious-metal anode and DMD achieved a cell voltage of 1.95 V at 2.0 A cm-2 and 80 °C. These results demonstrate that an integrated electrode architecture can reduce ohmic resistance in a non-precious based MEA. Although further studies are required, this interface-engineering strategy could also be extended to Ir-based MEAs to reduce ohmic losses and improve PEMWE performance.

P2-022.k: Atomic Layer Deposition; Cerium Oxide; Proton Conducting Fuel Cell
P2-022.a: Protonic ceramic electrochemical cells (PCECs) offer low-temperature operation and dry hydrogen production, advantages over SOFC/SOEC. However, sluggish oxygen electrode kinetics at 400-600C and Ba/Sr surface segregation forming BaCO3 under humid conditions degrade performance. This study introduces an ALD-derived CeO2 nanolayer on PBSCF air electrodes to suppress segregation and enhance activity. CeO2 nanolayers were deposited onto PBSCF air electrodes via atomic layer deposition using 10 and 20 cycles. XPS confirmed Ce3+/Ce4+ mixed states and self-limiting growth. SEM-EDS, XRD, and TEM characterized microstructure. Ba/Sr segregation was compared after steam/air annealing. EXAFS and Raman probed local bonding changes; electrochemical performance was evaluated at 550-650C. A conformal ~2-3 nm CeO2 layer formed after 10 cycles without altering the PBSCF crystal structure. Bare PBSCF showed pronounced Ba segregation after steam annealing, while CeO2-coated samples maintained a stable Ba/Sr distribution, indicating markedly improved chemical stability under humid conditions. EXAFS and Raman analysis revealed local bonding rearrangement without any bulk phase change or secondary phase formation. The CeO2(10-cycle) cell achieved 1.89 W/cm2 in fuel cell mode (bare: 1.56) and 4.72 A/cm2 in electrolysis mode (bare: 3.78), with reduced polarization resistance confirmed by impedance analysis, whereas 20 cycles noticeably degraded performance across the entire 550-650C range tested. ALD-derived CeO2 nanolayers effectively suppress Ba/Sr surface segregation, improve chemical stability, and enhance oxygen electrode reaction kinetics without bulk phase transformation. This surface modification strategy significantly improves fuel cell and electrolysis performance, with an optimal coating thickness of approximately 10 cycles critical for maximizing electrochemical benefits without introducing transport limitations.

P2-023.k: Daylight Saving Time; Net-Load; Energy Storage System
P2-023.a: As photovoltaic (PV) penetration rises, lithium-ion energy storage systems (ESS) are increasingly essential to address the grid's primary operational challenge: managing net load rather than gross load. This net load—gross load minus PV generation—creates a midday trough and a steep evening ramp that dictate the level of flexibility these battery resources must provide. Yet Daylight Saving Time (DST), by shifting electricity demand an hour against solar time, reshapes this net-load profile directly. This study proposes a net-load-based framework of five metrics---net-load peak, valley, and range, and the maximum upward and downward ramp rates---capturing the level and the rate of clock-induced change. It is applied to South Korea under standard time, seasonal DST, and permanent DST at three PV levels (32, 56, 77 GW), and compared with CAISO, 2023-2025. DST systematically redistributes net-load within the day: it lowers the peak, raises the valley, and narrows the daily range, while steepening the morning downward ramp at every PV level. Both the size of that trade-off and the sign of the effect on the critical evening ramp depend on PV penetration: that ramp worsens at current capacity and eases at projected capacity, and the steepest ramp becomes an almost exclusively evening event. The redistribution holds on average but not every day: the worst-case evening ramp persists even at high penetration, so procurement-setting metrics improve less than annual means suggest. Permanent DST also raises the winter peak, a cost seasonal DST avoids. Because these quantities are the inputs to capacity, flexibility, and energy storage (ESS) procurement, clock policy should be judged not only on consumption totals but on this redistribution, and settled before that procurement is committed rather than after.

P2-024.a: Over the past decades, extensive efforts have been devoted to developing high-performance Pt-based catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs). For heavy-duty vehicle (HDV) applications, a key challenge is maintaining high performance and long-term durability under prolonged operation and harsh conditions. This requires platinum group metal catalysts that combine high ORR activity with robust stability at the membrane electrode assembly level. Commercial acetylene black (AB) carbon was heated to 600℃ in air. For the preparation of L10-PtM intermetallic catalysts, 0.1g of modified AB carbon support was impregnated with metal precursor solutions, which were added dropwise with vigorous agitation. The impregnated samples were heated to 900℃ for 2h under 10% H2/90% N2. After cooling to room temperature, the L10-PtM powder was subjected to acid leaching (0.1 M HClO4, 60 °C). The acid-leached catalyst was filtered out and washed with DIW and acetone. The catalyst was dried overnight and heat-treated at 400 °C under 5% H2/Ar for 2h. In this study, structurally ordered L10-PtM intermetallic alloy catalysts, with M including Co, Cu, Mn, Ga, Sn, etc., are introduced as high-performance PEMFC cathode catalysts. Graphitic AB carbon with an initial surface area of about 120 m2/g was thermally activated in air to produce a high-surface-area mesoporous carbon support of about 440 m2/g. L10-PtM intermetallic nanoparticles, with an average size of 5-6 nm, were uniformly dispersed within the mesopores, thereby mitigating catalyst poisoning. The PtM catalysts were further evaluated using a lab-made half-electrode evaluation system (HEES) to examine ORR performance and sulfonate coverage on the catalyst surface in the electrode. Half catalyst-coated-membrane electrodes with 1 cm2 were prepared by coating the catalyst layer on one side of a Nafion® membrane, enabling rapid assessment of catalyst-layer performance and optimization of ionomer content. This platform enabled better translation of intrinsic catalyst activity into MEA performance and narrowed the gap between rotating disk electrode and MEA evaluations. In conclusion, the L10-PtM intermetallic catalysts exhibited improved electrochemical durability and significantly enhanced performance, demonstrating their strong potential as practical PEMFC electrocatalysts for HDV applications.

P2-025.a: The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is a crucial cathodic reaction in electrochemical energy-conversion and energy-storage devices, such as fuel cells and metal–air batteries. However, its intrinsically sluggish kinetics require highly active electrocatalysts, and Pt-based catalysts, although highly efficient, suffer from high cost, limited durability, and poor tolerance to fuel crossover. Therefore, developing efficient and durable metal-free ORR catalysts has attracted considerable attention. Boron-based carbon materials are promising because the electron-deficient nature of boron can modify the electronic structure of neighboring carbon atoms and facilitate oxygen-related reactions. However, previous studies have mainly focused on in-plane B–C bonds within doped carbon structures, while the catalytic role of out-of-plane interfacial B–C bonds has remained largely unexplored. In this study, the authors constructed a boron nanosheet/reduced graphene oxide (B@rGO) heterostructure and demonstrated that the interfacial B–C bonds formed between the two components can serve as highly active catalytic sites for ORR. The boron nanosheets were first obtained by exfoliating bulk boron powder through prolonged tip sonication, followed by centrifugation and freeze-drying. The resulting boron nanosheets were then mixed with GO under continuous stirring to promote uniform assembly between the two-dimensional components. After lyophilization and subsequent calcination, a porous B@rGO heterostructure was obtained, in which out-of-plane B–C bonds were formed at the interface between boron nanosheets and rGO. The morphology, crystal structure, chemical composition, and bonding states of the materials were characterized using various spectroscopic and microscopic techniques. Their ORR performance was evaluated using cyclic voltammetry and rotating-ring/disk electrode measurements in alkaline electrolyte, with parameters such as onset potential, half-wave potential, limiting current density, Tafel slope, and electron-transfer number used to assess catalytic activity and reaction kinetics. In addition, durability and methanol tolerance tests were conducted, and a Zn–air battery was assembled to demonstrate practical applicability. Density functional theory calculations were also employed to investigate the electronic structure of the interfacial B–C bonds and their effects on oxygen adsorption and O–O bond cleavage. The experimental results demonstrate that the B@rGO heterostructure possesses substantially enhanced ORR performance compared with pristine boron nanosheets, rGO nanosheets, and the physical B+rGO mixture. Structural and spectroscopic analyses confirmed the formation of out-of-plane B–C chemical bonds at the B/rGO heterointerfaces, indicating that the two components were chemically coupled rather than simply physically mixed. Electrochemical measurements showed that B@rGO exhibited a more positive half-wave potential, higher diffusion-limiting current density, a lower Tafel slope, a favorable electron-transfer number, and a larger electrochemical active area, confirming its improved ORR kinetics and catalytic activity. Importantly, B@rGO also showed better durability and methanol tolerance than commercial 20 wt% Pt/C, demonstrating the advantages of the metal-free heterostructure. Theoretical calculations further revealed that electron transfer from B to C at the interfacial B–C bonds modifies the local electronic structure and facilitates the activation of the O₂ intermediate, particularly the cleavage of the O–O bond, which was identified as the key origin of the enhanced ORR activity. Finally, the practical performance of B@rGO was demonstrated in a primary Zn–air battery, which achieved a peak power density of 131 mW cm⁻² and a specific capacity of 639.3 mAh gZn⁻¹, and was capable of powering LEDs. These results collectively indicate that engineering interfacial out-of-plane B–C bonds is an effective strategy for creating highly active metal-free ORR catalysts. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that interfacial out-of-plane B–C bonds in a boron nanosheet/rGO heterostructure can function as highly active catalytic sites for the ORR. Compared with pristine boron, rGO, and their physical mixture, the B@rGO heterostructure exhibited significantly enhanced ORR activity, indicating that the improvement originated from the chemical interaction at the B/rGO interface rather than simple physical contact between the two materials. The interfacial B–C bonds induced favorable electronic redistribution, which enhanced oxygen activation and facilitated O–O bond cleavage during the ORR process. Furthermore, B@rGO showed excellent durability and methanol tolerance and demonstrated promising performance when applied as an air-cathode catalyst in a Zn–air battery. Overall, the work provides a useful strategy for designing metal-free electrocatalysts by engineering three-dimensional interfacial chemical bonds, rather than relying solely on conventional heteroatom doping within a carbon lattice.

P2-026.a: Efficient and low-cost bifunctional electrocatalysts are required to improve alkaline water electrolysis by reducing the overpotentials of the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Although Pt-, Ir-, and Ru-based catalysts show excellent activity, their high cost limits practical application. Therefore, Ni–Fe-based transition-metal catalysts have been investigated as promising alternatives, and the introduction of Cr can further improve catalytic activity by modifying the electronic structure Porous Ni–Fe–Cr electrocatalysts were fabricated on Ni mesh by a one-step electrodeposition process using a bath containing Ni, Fe, and Cr precursors. The structure, morphology, composition, pore distribution, and chemical states were analyzed by SEM, EDS, XRD, TEM, X-ray micro-tomography, and XPS. OER and HER performances were evaluated in 1 M KOH using LSV, Tafel analysis, EIS, ECSA measurement, and long-term stability testing. The optimized porous Ni–Fe–Cr electrocatalyst showed a coral reef-like three-dimensional porous structure formed by hydrogen bubble-templated electrodeposition. SEM and micro-CT analyses confirmed that increasing the deposition time enlarged the catalyst thickness and increased the number of micro- and macropores, which contributed to a higher electrochemically active surface area. The porous Ni–Fe–Cr catalyst exhibited an ECSA of 396.4 cm², approximately 22 times higher than that of the flat Ni–Fe–Cr film. One-step electrodeposition successfully produced a porous Ni–Fe–Cr bifunctional electrocatalyst with excellent OER and HER activity. The improved performance was attributed to the porous structure, increased ECSA, enhanced charge-transfer kinetics, and Cr-induced changes in the Ni–Fe electronic/chemical state.

P2-027.k: Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis (PEMWE); Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER); Pulse Electrodeposition
P2-027.a: Hydrogen produced by proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) is attracting attention as a sustainable energy carrier because it enables high-purity hydrogen production with rapid response to fluctuating renewable energy sources [1]. Despite these advantages, the large-scale commercialization of PEMWE is still constrained by the high cost and limited availability of platinum-group-metal (PGM) electrocatalysts. Among various PGM candidates, ruthenium (Ru) has emerged as a promising cathode catalyst for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) [2,3] because of its Pt-like catalytic properties and relatively lower cost. Nevertheless, reducing PGM loading while maintaining high HER performance remains a major challenge. To overcome this challenge, a growth-controlled two-step pulse electrodeposition strategy was developed to fabricate low-loading Ru cathodes. The deposition process was designed to regulate catalyst nucleation and subsequent growth, enabling the formation of a uniform catalyst layer with improved active-site accessibility. The resulting electrodes exhibited enhanced HER activity and stable electrochemical performance under acidic conditions. In addition, the optimized deposition process was successfully applied to large-area electrodes, producing uniform catalyst coverage and consistent electrochemical performance across the electrode surface. These results demonstrate that pulse electrodeposition is an effective and scalable approach for fabricating low-loading cathodes for PEMWE and provide a practical strategy for reducing noble metal usage while maintaining high catalytic performance. <References> [1] N. Sezer, S. et al., Materials Science for Energy Technologies 8 (2025), 44–65 [2] R. Milazzo,N et al., ACS Applied Energy Materials, 8 (2025) 5698−5707 [3] K.-R. Yeo et al., Applied Catalysis B: Environment and Energy 346 (2024), 123738

P2-028.k: Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis (AEMWE); Oxygen Evolution Reaction (OER); Electrodeposition
P2-028.a: Water electrolysis is a promising technology for sustainable hydrogen production [1]. Anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE) operates under alkaline conditions, enabling the use of cost-effective transition-metal catalysts [2]. However, the sluggish oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and insufficient catalyst durability remain major obstacles to the practical implementation of AEMWE [2]. To address these challenges, considerable efforts have been devoted to developing efficient and durable transition-metal-based OER catalysts. Among them, Co-based catalysts have emerged as promising candidates owing to their abundance, low cost, and tunable electronic structure [3]. In this study, Co-based transition-metal (Co-TM) alloy catalysts were synthesized through a one-step electrodeposition process. A secondary transition metal was incorporated into Co to tailor the electronic structure and optimize the surface properties of the catalyst. Subsequently, potentiostatic dealloying was employed to selectively remove the secondary metal, generating a porous structure with increased electrochemically active surface area. To further improve catalyst stability, post-heat treatment was introduced by optimizing the processing conditions. The structural and chemical characteristics of the prepared catalysts were systematically investigated and their OER performance was evaluated under alkaline conditions. This study demonstrates that the combined electrodeposition–dealloying strategy provides an effective approach for designing non-precious catalysts with improved activity and durability for AEMWE. References [1] S Wang et al., Nano Convergence, 8 (2021) 4 [2] N Du et al., Chemical reviews, 122 (2022) 11830-11895 [3] W Zhang et al., Journal of alloys and compounds, 821 (2021) 153542

P2-029.a: Uniform flow distribution of air and fuel to each unit cell is critical for stable operation and performance of solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) stacks. Non-uniform flow induces cell-to-cell current density deviation, accelerates localized overheating and electrode degradation, and shortens stack lifetime. Ansys Fluent-based CFD analysis was used to quantitatively evaluate the effects of cathode and anode chamber geometry on flow distribution uniformity across 40 cell outlets, as well as internal pressure and velocity fields, in an actual stack configuration, to derive an optimized geometry. For the cathode chamber, flow rate standard deviation was calculated to quantify uniformity, which varied with lower chamber geometry; altering this space changed local velocity and recirculation zones, thereby affecting overall uniformity. For the anode chamber, the baseline geometry showed localized pressure rise near the inlet due to a narrow flow path and abrupt direction change, causing flow concentration at lower outlets. Introducing a lower expansion section buffered internal pressure and velocity gradients, altering flow deviation among the 40 outlets. Systematic CFD-based parametric analysis of cathode and anode chamber geometries provided effective design guidelines for improving flow uniformity in SOFC stacks. Stabilization of internal pressure and velocity distribution was identified as the key mechanism governing outlet flow uniformity. These findings serve as practical design data for enhancing SOFC stack performance and durability, with validation testing planned as a next step.

P2-030.k: Magnetron Sputtering; Thin-Film Solid Oxide Fuel Cell (TF-SOFC); Electrochemical Stability
P2-030.a: Nanostructured Ni–YSZ anodes fabricated by sputtering possess distinct microstructural characteristics compared with conventional sintered cermet anodes, requiring independent optimization of the Ni/YSZ composition for durable thin-film solid oxide fuel cells (TF-SOFCs). However, conventional co-sputtering using Ni and YSZ targets inevitably changes both the anode composition and nanostructure simultaneously, making it difficult to identify the intrinsic effect of YSZ content on electrochemical durability. In this study, metallic Y/Zr co-sputtering was employed as an alternative approach to control the anode composition while minimizing nanostructural variation through in-situ oxidation during cell operation. Ni and Y/Zr thin films were co-deposited by DC/RF magnetron sputtering, and the Y/Zr deposition condition was systematically varied to obtain different anode compositions. Thin-film SOFC single cells incorporating the fabricated anodes were evaluated by current–voltage measurements, galvanostatic durability testing, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), distribution of relaxation time (DRT) analysis, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Among the investigated compositions, the optimized Y/Zr content exhibited the highest voltage stability during galvanostatic operation at 500 °C under a current density of 0.3 A cm⁻², whereas excessive Y/Zr incorporation resulted in accelerated degradation despite comparable initial electrochemical performance. The improved durability is attributed to the optimized anode composition achieved with minimal nanostructural variation, enabling stable maintenance of the electrochemically active Ni network during long-term operation. This work demonstrates that metallic Y/Zr co-sputtering provides an effective platform for independently optimizing the composition of sputtered Ni–YSZ anodes and offers a practical strategy for developing durable TF-SOFCs.

P2-031.k: Metallic Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes (SWNTs); Spontaneous Pt Deposition; Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells (PEMFCs)
P2-031.a: Platinum (Pt) is the benchmark electrocatalyst for proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), but its high cost requires improved Pt utilization. Metallic single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) are promising catalyst supports because of their high electrical conductivity and electron mobility. Metallic-enriched SWNTs were separated from commercially available HiPco SWNTs by gel chromatography and used for Pt deposition without acid treatment or chemical reducing agents. UV–Vis–NIR spectroscopy confirmed the separation of metallic- and semiconducting-enriched fractions. Pt deposition was achieved through spontaneous electron transfer from metallic SWNTs to H₂PtCl 6 precursor ions. Raman spectroscopy with 532 and 633 nm excitation wavelengths was used to investigate the interaction between Pt and SWNTs. The metallic-enriched SWNT film exhibited lower sheet resistance than the unsorted SWNT film. Raman spectroscopy showed that Pt deposition increased the D-band intensity, decreased the radial breathing mode (RBM) intensity, and suppressed the metallic G⁻ band of metallic SWNTs, indicating strong charge transfer and modification of the electronic structure. In contrast, semiconducting SWNTs showed only minor spectral changes, confirming preferential Pt deposition on metallic SWNTs. The electronic structure of SWNTs governs spontaneous Pt deposition through charge- transfer-driven reduction of Pt precursor ions. This reducing-agent-free and acid-free strategy enables selective Pt decoration of metallic SWNTs and provides a simple, environmentally benign route for preparing Pt/SWNT catalysts with improved Pt utilization for PEM fuel cell applications.

P2-032.k: NiMoO₄ Nanofibers; Heteroatom Doping; Bifunctional Electrocatalysis
P2-032.a: The widespread use of transition metal oxides as electrochemical catalysts is attributed to their multiple oxidation states, high electrical conductivity, and environmental friendliness. Among them, NiMoO₄ has attracted considerable attention as a promising electrochemical catalyst because of its high energy density, excellent chemical stability, and high theoretical pseudocapacitance. However, the practical application of NiMoO₄ is limited by its poor long-term stability, which primarily arises from mechanical degradation caused by repeated volume expansion and contraction during redox cycling. To address the limitations of NiMoO₄, heteroatom-doped Ni₀.₉X₀.₁MoO₄ (X = Ca, Sr, Ba) nanofibers were synthesized via electrospinning. The electrochemical properties of the synthesized nanofibers were evaluated to investigate the effects of heteroatom doping and lattice deformation on the redox behavior, mechanical stability, and long-term electrocatalytic performance. Among the doped samples, Ba-doped NiMoO₄ exhibited the greatest suppression of crystal growth and the highest oxygen vacancy concentration. This behavior is attributed to the internal lattice stress generated by the incorporation of Ba²⁺ ions, whose larger ionic radius induces greater lattice distortion. Electrochemical evaluation of the OER and ORR also revealed that the heteroatom-doped samples exhibited superior long-term stability compared with pristine NiMoO₄. The improved durability is attributed to oxygen defect formation induced by doping-related structural stress, which enhances electrochemical catalytic activity while mitigating structural degradation during prolonged redox cycling. In this study, Ca-, Sr-, and Ba-doped NiMoO₄ nanofibers were successfully synthesized by substituting the A-site of the NiMoO₄ lattice, and their bifunctional electrocatalytic performance was evaluated through OER and ORR measurements.

P2-033.k: Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis; OER; Catalysts
P2-033.a: Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis (AEMWE) is gaining attention as a next-generation, eco-friendly water electrolysis technology that produces high-purity hydrogen using non-precious metal-based catalysts instead of noble metals. However, conventional non-precious metal catalysts inherently exhibit low electrochemical activity and suffer from rapid performance degradation during long-term operation due to the structural deformation of the catalyst and support, as well as material dissolution. To commercialize AEMWE, various studies have been conducted, including the introduction of metal oxide supports with high corrosion resistance in strongly alkaline environments and the complexation of multiple transition metals. Nevertheless, the low electrical conductivity of metal oxides and the limited durability and activity of transition metals remain major challenges to be overcome. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel catalyst system that simultaneously secures excellent electrochemical performance and physical durability by hybridizing a transition metal hydroxide catalyst with a metal oxide support featuring significantly enhanced electrical conductivity. By precisely controlling process variables during synthesis, the specific surface area of the composite was maximized, thereby drastically increasing the effective catalyst loading and the actual active reaction area. The evaluation results successfully demonstrated that the composite catalyst developed in this study not only significantly reduced the overpotential due to the enhanced conductivity of the support but also maintained excellent performance durability without degradation under long-term operational conditions. This study is expected to provide important academic and engineering guidelines for the design of non-precious metal electrode catalysts and supports toward the commercialization of highly durable and efficient AEMWEs.

P2-034.k: : Alkaline Water Electrolysis; Bifunctional Electrocatalyst; Galvanic Replacement Reaction
P2-034.a: Water electrolysis combined with renewable energy is a key technology for green hydrogen production, as it generates zero carbon emissions. However, overall water splitting is severely limited by the sluggish kinetics of the anodic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and cathodic hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). The complex four-electron transfer process of OER results in a high overpotential. While noble metal-based catalysts (e.g., Ru, Ir, and Pt) are commercially used to accelerate reaction rates, their high cost and scarcity hinder widespread application. Therefore, developing highly efficient bifunctional electrocatalysts with minimized noble metal loading is crucial for viable water splitting. We report a simple and cost-effective approach to fabricate Ru and Co-based bifunctional electrocatalysts on a porous nickel foam (NF) substrate via electrodeposition followed by a spontaneous galvanic replacement reaction. The uniform coating of Co on the NF substrate, subsequently decorated with a small amount of Ru, was designed to enhance charge and mass transfer. This strategy aims to achieve high electrochemical performance while minimizing the utilization of expensive Ru by exploiting the synergy with earth-abundant Co. The synthesized RuCo/NF electrocatalyst exhibited outstanding performance in alkaline media, requiring low overpotentials both for OER and HER. It also represents a significant improvement over commercial benchmarks such as IrO2 and Pt/C. The catalyst demonstrated excellent durability, maintaining stable performance for both OER and HER over 50 hours of continuous operation with negligible degradation. This work successfully demonstrates a highly efficient, durable, and low-cost RuCo/NF bifunctional catalyst, presenting a promising alternative for large-scale alkaline water electrolysis.

P2-035.k: Alkaline Water Electrolysis; One-step Electrodeposition; Ni Nanotube
P2-035.a: Alkaline water electrolysis is among the most commercially mature technologies for green hydrogen production. However, wider industrial deployment requires further reductions in capital cost through improvements in electrode efficiency, durability, material cost, and manufacturability. Ni-based electrodes are particularly important because their catalytic performance strongly affects the overall efficiency and economic feasibility of alkaline electrolyzers. Although noble-metal incorporation, transition-metal modification, and surface engineering have been widely investigated, achieving high activity and long-term stability under industrially relevant conditions remains challenging. In addition, complex synthesis procedures and multistep surface treatments often limit large-area and high-throughput fabrication. A simplified electrodeposition–dealloying strategy was developed to fabricate a porous nanotubular NiFe electrode directly on Ni foam. Ni, Cu, and Fe were co-electrodeposited onto the Ni foam substrate in a single electrodeposition step. Cu was subsequently removed through selective dealloying, generating a nanotubular porous structure while promoting the formation of catalytically active NiFe species. The fabricated electrode exhibited an overpotential of 274 mV at a current density of 0.1 A cm⁻². Under high-current-density operation, the electrode maintained stable performance at 400 mA cm⁻², with an overpotential increase of only 49 mV after 50 h. The enhanced performance was attributed to the combination of a porous nanotubular architecture and the formation of an active NiFe species. The proposed electrodeposition–dealloying approach enables simultaneous structural and compositional modification of Ni-based electrodes through a streamlined fabrication process. This strategy provides a practical route toward scalable, cost-effective, and high-performance electrodes for industrial alkaline water electrolysis.

P2-036.a: Single-domain ferroelectric photocatalysts spatially separate photogenerated electrons and holes through their internal polarization field; however, sluggish surface charge transfer and recombination limit their catalytic utilization. Metal oxide layers can passivate ferroelectric particles, and surface termination governs cocatalyst electron extraction. Here, we designed a ferroelectric material with a sub-nm metal oxide layer that regulates surface reactions and charge transfer, providing anchoring sites for polarization-directed cocatalyst deposition. Single-domain ferroelectric crystals were prepared hydrothermally, and a sub-nm metal oxide layer was deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD). Diluted organometallic precursors were immobilized via illumination-assisted ionic adsorption and mild fixation to target polarization-selected surface sites while suppressing clustering. The photocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction was used for mechanistic and performance evaluation, complemented by transient absorption spectroscopy and operando characterization to probe charge-carrier dynamics and interfacial electron transfer. Single-domain ferroelectric crystals were successfully synthesized and coated with an optimized number of ALD cycles. The metal oxide layer exhibited a sub-nm thickness, confirming successful incorporation without morphological or structural damage. Single-atom metal cocatalysts were then introduced onto the stabilized layer. Polarization-induced positioning enhanced interfacial electron transfer and lowered the kinetic barrier without increasing metal loading. This study demonstrates synergistic photocatalytic enhancement by combining a single-atom cocatalyst with an ALD-passivated ferroelectric material. The sub-nm metal oxide layer acts both as a passivation layer and as a stable cocatalyst support, providing a general design principle for coupling ferroelectric domains with atomically defined reaction sites.

P2-037.k: Alkaline Water Electrolysis; Oxygen Evolution Reaction; Electroless Plating
P2-037.a: The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is a major kinetic bottleneck in alkaline water electrolysis. Three-dimensional porous nickel electrodes can increase the available reaction area, while Fe incorporation into Ni-based catalysts can enhance OER activity. This study developed a porous Ni electrode coated with electroless Ni–Fe–P. Porous Ni was fabricated on a Ni substrate by dynamic hydrogen bubble templating (DHBT)-assisted electrodeposition. The porous structure was subsequently coated with Ni–Fe–P by electroless plating. Surface morphology and composition were examined by SEM and EDS. OER performance was evaluated in 30 wt% KOH using linear sweep voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and chronopotentiometry. The Ni–Fe–P coating was formed across the DHBT-derived porous Ni structure while preserving its three-dimensional morphology. Compared with uncoated porous Ni and Ni–P-coated electrodes, the Ni–Fe–P-coated electrode showed improved OER activity, with lower overpotential and charge-transfer resistance. The enhancement was attributed to the porous Ni framework, conformal catalyst coverage, and Fe incorporation into the Ni–P layer. Combining DHBT-assisted electrodeposition with electroless Ni–Fe–P plating provides a binder-free route to three-dimensional porous electrodes for alkaline water electrolysis. The resulting electrode integrates a porous Ni framework with a conformal Ni–Fe–P catalytic layer, improving OER kinetics and electrochemical performance.

P2-038.a: The performance of metal-supported thin-film Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (SOFCs) depends heavily on the Ni-GDC (gadolinium-doped ceria) anode, whose composition and microstructure govern the triple-phase boundary density, conductivity, and gas transport. In co-sputtering, these characteristics are determined by coupled process variables such as working pressure, the sputtering power applied to the Ni and GDC targets, and the substrate rotation speed. Conventional optimization relies on a one-factor-at-a-time approach, making it difficult to capture coupled effects and to locate a globally optimal condition. A data-driven framework combining an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and a genetic algorithm (GA) is proposed. Four process variables—working pressure, Ni power, GDC power, and rotation speed—are selected as design variables, and representative sample points are generated to build a training dataset. For each condition, metal support/Ni-GDC/YSZ/Pt single cells are fabricated by sputtering. Cell performance is evaluated using J-V-P and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and the anode is analyzed by SEM and XRD. An ANN surrogate model is trained to predict electrochemical performance as a function of the four variables, capturing the coupled process–performance relationship across the design space. Coupled with a genetic algorithm, the model is expected to derive an optimal process condition while substantially reducing experimental effort. This study introduces a systematic, machine-learning-based strategy that accounts for coupled sputtering variables, providing a direction for efficient and reliable fabrication of high-performance Ni-GDC anodes in metal-supported thin-film SOFCs.

P2-039.k: Metal Support Solid Oxide Fuel Cell; ALD; Sputtering
P2-039.a: Metal-supported solid oxide fuel cells (MS-SOFCs) have attracted considerable attention for low- and intermediate-temperature operation because of their high mechanical durability, rapid thermal response, and reduced use of ceramic components. However, the rough and porous surface of the metal support makes it difficult to form a dense electrolyte and a low-resistance electrode/electrolyte interface. This study investigated an interface-engineering approach combining magnetron sputtering and atomic layer deposition (ALD) to improve the electrochemical performance of MS-SOFCs. A Ni–GDC functional anode and a dense yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) electrolyte were sequentially deposited by magnetron sputtering on a planarized porous stainless-steel support. An ultrathin oxide interlayer was then conformally deposited on the YSZ surface by ALD, followed by the formation of a porous Pt cathode. The ALD interlayer was introduced to seal nanoscale surface defects and modify the cathode/electrolyte interface while minimizing the additional oxygen-ion transport distance. The fabricated cells were characterized using structural, surface, and electrochemical analyses. The sputtered YSZ layer continuously covered the metal-supported anode, while the ALD-derived interlayer uniformly modified the electrolyte surface. Compared with the reference cell without the ALD interlayer, the ALD-modified cell exhibited a higher open-circuit voltage, lower ohmic and polarization resistances, and a higher maximum power density at 500 °C. The improved electrochemical performance was associated with enhanced electrolyte integrity and facilitated oxygen-ion transport at the cathode/electrolyte interface. Combining magnetron sputtering and ALD controlled the electrolyte structure and cathode/electrolyte interface. The ultrathin ALD interlayer enhanced electrolyte integrity and interfacial ion transport, supporting high-performance MS-SOFC operation at reduced temperatures.

P2-040.k: Solid Oxide Fuel Cell; Cathodic Electrochemical Deposition; Praseodymium
P2-040.a: Slow kinetics of oxygen reaction makes the bottleneck during the SOCs operation. So, powerful air electrode is essential for improving SOCs electrochemical performance. In that case, mixed ionic, and electronic conductors(MIEC) are a strong option. Their MIEC properties can enable the increasing of SOCs reaction site not only through the triple phase boundary(TPB) but also the double phase boundary(DPB). Despite these advantages, the performance of MIEC electrode materials still leaves room for further improvement. Conventional MIEC materials generally exhibit lower electrocatalytic activity and electronic conductivity than metal-based electrodes; however, these limitations can potentially be addressed through surface modification. In this study, the surface of a solid oxide cell (SOC) electrode based on lanthanum–strontium–cobalt oxide (LSC), a perovskite-structured MIEC material, was modified via cathodic electrochemical deposition (CELD), and the resulting changes in electrochemical performance were investigated. CELD is a three-electrode-based deposition technique characterized by rapid processing and a simple experimental setup. In addition, the deposition thickness and surface morphology can be readily controlled by adjusting the deposition conditions. Both the stability and electrochemical performance of LSC were increased with CELD deposition CELD coated PrOx can make LSC more efficiency for SOC electrode

P2-041.a: Recent progress has demonstrated that introducing single atoms as dopants can greatly improve both the catalytic performance and durability of transition metal-based materials. However, enhancing metal support interactions through voids or vacancy defects improves metal atom anchoring, but sufficient defect sites are essential. Achieving high coverage of isolated atoms with a defined coordination environment optimizes single-atom catalysts performance. Furthermore, challenges remain in ensuring uniform dispersion, maximizing active sites, and maintaining reproducibility. In comparison to single-atom catalysts, dual-atom catalysts provide enhanced structural versatility and synergistic effects, which facilitate faster kinetics for reactions involving multiple intermediates. The CoSe NWs on NF was straight used as the working electrode, immersed in 100 mL of an solution containing 20 mM of Ni(NO3)2⋅6 H2O, 0.6 mM of Na2MoO4⋅2 H2O, 0.45 mM of Na2WO4⋅2 H2O, and 700 mM of CH4N2S. The resulting Ws/Ni₃S₂@CoSe/NF were washed with purified water and dried in a vacuum oven at 60oC. ﻿The incorporated conductivity and Mo promotes electron delocalization, shifts the d-band center upward, enhances conductivity, and optimizes intermediate adsorption. The assembled electrolyzer operates at just 1.48 V to reach 10 mA cm⁻² and stably delivers 1.0 A cm⁻² for over 1000 h with minimal degradation, surpassing benchmark RuO₂ and Pt/C catalysts. Furthermore, alkaline water electrolysis achieves cell voltages of 1.75 V and 1.88 V at 0.5 and 1.0 A cm⁻² in 6.0 M KOH, highlighting its promise for industrial-scale applications. Atomic-level structural changes are confirmed by scanning transmission electron microscopy and EXAFS analyses. Optimizing substitutional and interstitial doping is an effective strategy for boosting active site utilization, electrochemical efficiency, durability, and scalability in HER and OER technologies.

P2-042.k: Electrochemical Switching; Reversible Nanoparticle Assembly; Redox-state-selective Coordination
P2-042.a: Reversible and well-controlled assembly and disassembly of nanoparticles (NPs) is essential for the development of dynamic nanomaterials. However, most existing stimuli-responsive systems rely on changes in pH, light, or temperature and therefore often suffer from slow response times, limited reversibility, or poor control over the transition direction. We developed an electrochemically controlled strategy that exploits the switchable oxidation states of transition-metal ions to regulate NP assembly and disassembly. The system incorporates two chelating ligand environments with oxidation-state-selective binding affinities: a bidentate ligand anchored to the NP surface that favors tetrahedral, sandwich-type coordination and a complementary ligand system optimized for octahedral coordination. The metal oxidation state was controlled by varying the applied electrochemical potential. Under the oxidation state favoring tetrahedral coordination, sandwich-type metal–ligand complexes formed between neighboring NPs, promoting interparticle bridging and NP assembly. Under the alternative oxidation state, octahedral complexes became dominant, suppressing interparticle bridging and inducing NP disassembly. Switching between the corresponding electrochemical potentials enabled rapid transitions between assembled and dispersed NP states in less than 1 s. These transitions were repeatable and directionally controlled. Moreover, the system exhibited bistability: once an assembled or dispersed state was established by an applied voltage, the state persisted even after removal of the voltage, demonstrating memory-like behavior. This electrochemically switchable coordination strategy enables rapid, reversible, and on-demand control over NP assembly and disassembly. The combination of fast switching, bistability, and oxidation-state-selective coordination provides a promising platform for next-generation optoelectronic, nanophotonic, and memory-related applications.

P2-043.k: Ionomer Blending; Water Management; Proton Transport
P2-043.a: Low-humidity operation simplifies proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) systems but accelerates anode dehydration through electro-osmotic drag, disrupting proton transport and degrading cell performance. Although ionomer blending has been extensively investigated for cathode catalyst layers, the mechanisms governing water management and proton transport in blended anode ionomers remain poorly understood. In this study, long-side-chain (LSC) and short-side-chain (SSC) ionomers were blended in the anode catalyst layer of catalyst-coated membranes (Nafion 212, 0.1 mgPt cm⁻² anode and 0.4 mgPt cm⁻² cathode) at LSC/SSC ratios of 8:2, 7:3, 6:4, 5:5, and 3:7. Electrochemical performance under 50% relative humidity was evaluated using polarization curves, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), water uptake, and proton conductivity measurements. Complementary Distribution of Relaxation Times (DRT) and Voltage Breakdown (VBD) analyses are underway to identify the individual resistance and voltage-loss contributions associated with water management and proton transport. The 5:5 LSC/SSC blend exhibited the highest current density (567 mA cm⁻² at 0.6 V), the lowest high-frequency and charge-transfer resistances, and the highest water uptake and proton conductivity. These findings indicate that balanced LSC/SSC blending suppresses anode dehydration while maintaining continuous proton-conduction pathways under low humidity. Based on electrochemical and physicochemical evidence, we propose that the optimized blend forms a cooperative hydration architecture in which the LSC ionomer promotes water retention and the SSC ionomer establishes interconnected proton-conduction pathways. Ongoing DRT and VBD analyses will further validate the proposed mechanism.

P2-044.k: Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution; Anodic Surface Reconstruction; Interfacial Water Structure
P2-044.a: The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in alkaline media is kinetically bottlenecked by the initial water-dissociation step required to generate adsorbed hydrogen intermediates. While cation-induced polarization of water molecules can facilitate proton transfer at the electrode–electrolyte interface, subsequent hydrogen transfer is often limited by the depletion of solvated water and disrupted hydrogen-bond connectivity within the electrical double layer (EDL). Thus, reconstructing the interfacial water structure to ensure a continuous supply of reactive water molecules is essential to accelerating alkaline HER kinetics Here, we utilize sustainable, microalgae-derived hydrothermal carbon (HC) as a support to immobilize five transition and noble metals, yielding a multimetal catalyst denoted as 5M@HC. Although the pristine 5M@HC electrode requires an overpotential of ~150 mV to reach the target current density (-10 mA cm-2), subjecting the electrode to an in situ anodic polarization pretreatment dramatically boosts its performance. The resulting activated catalyst, A-5M@HC, achieves the same target current density at a remarkably low overpotential of ~40 mV. This pronounced enhancement is driven by anodic-assisted surface reconstruction, characterized by partial metal oxidation and selective metal dissolution, which generates highly oxophilic transition-metal (oxy)hydroxide species on the catalyst surface. These newly formed sites promote water adsorption, polarize nearby water molecules, and reinforce interfacial hydrogen-bond networks, thereby facilitating rapid water replenishment within the EDL. Ultimately, this reconstructed interface accelerates the water-dissociation pathway to bypass the traditional kinetic limitations of alkaline HER.

P2-045.k: Electrochemical Hydrogen Pump; Hydrogen Oxidation Reaction; Ir/IrOx Electrode
P2-045.a: An electrochemical hydrogen pump (ECHP) selectively separates and purifies hydrogen from gas mixtures through the hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR) at the anode and the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at the cathode. Pt electrodes are commonly used for these reactions. However, hydrogen produced through various processes may contain impurities such as CO, CO₂, and CH₄, which can decrease electrode performance and stability. Therefore, electrodes with high HOR activity and impurity tolerance are required for stable ECHP operation. In this study, Ir/IrOx@carbon paper (CP) electrodes are prepared and compared with Pt@CP. IrOx is electrodeposited onto CP and reduced under H₂. The reduction temperature and time are varied to tune the Ir/IrOx interfacial structure and chemical states. The morphology, crystalline structure, and surface chemical states of the electrodes are analyzed by scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, respectively. HOR activities of Ir/IrOx@CP and Pt@CP under pure and impurity-containing H₂ are compared by linear sweep voltammetry and Tafel analysis. The influence of impurity type and concentration on electrode performance is evaluated, together with performance and recovery during gas switching. CO stripping charges are used to estimate the relative amounts of adsorbed CO, and long-term electrochemical stability is also evaluated. Ir/IrOx electrodes prepared under different reduction conditions exhibit enhanced HOR performance and impurity tolerance under impurity-containing hydrogen. These electrochemical characteristics are advantageous for anodes in electrochemical hydrogen pumps operating with impurity-containing hydrogen.

P2-046.k: Solid Oxide Fuel Cell; Dry Reforming of Methane; Perovskite
P2-046.a: SOFC have the advantage of being able to directly use various fuels without an external reformer because they operate at high temperatures (800~1000°C). These benefits facilitate direct CH4 fueling and the internal execution of dry reforming of methane (DRM) for H2 and CO production using greenhouse gases CO2 and CH4. This study compared the performance of La1-xCexCr0.5Ni0.5O3+/-δ (LCCN) perovskite according to the Ce content using it as an alternative fuel electrode. LCCN perovskite was synthesized using the Pechini method. Physical properties were analyzed using TGA/DTA, XRD, BET, XPS, SEM, etc. Catalytic activity for the DRM reaction was analyzed using gas chromatography (GC), and fuel cell cells were fabricated to conduct OCV, impedance, IV curve, and long-term performance tests. At 800℃, the conversion rates of LCCN55, LCCN64, LCCN82 remained high and stable at over 90% for 40 hours. The oxygen defect content was 53.3%, 40.80%, and 34.41% for LCCN55, LCCN64, and LCCN82, respectively. These oxygen defects play an important role in increasing resistance to carbon deposition. LCCN55, a high conversion rate can be observed and at the same time, a small amount of carbon deposition can be confirmed. It is believed that this is due to an appropriate amount of Ce doping increasing the oxygen movement ability and the amount of oxygen defects mentioned above allowing oxygen gas to move smoothly, thereby improving resistance to carbon deposition. The DRM catalytic activity of LCCN perovskite was confirmed, and its potential as an alternative fuel electrode for solid oxide fuel cells was verified.

P2-047.k: Solid Oxide Fuel Cell; Dry Reforming of Methane; Perovskite Catalyst
P2-047.a: Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) are attractive next-generation energy conversion devices, offering high efficiency and fuel flexibility. Dry reforming of methane (DRM) converts CH4 and CO2, two greenhouse gases, into syngas, which can be used as fuel in SOFCs. However, conventional Ni-based anodes suffer from severe carbon deposition during direct fuel operation, leading to rapid degradation. Thus, developing alternative coking-resistant anode catalysts is essential. Perovskite-based anode materials with varying Ru and Ni substitution ratios (Sr0.92Y0.08Ti1-x-yRuxNiyO3-δ) were synthesized via the Pechini method. The samples were characterized by XRD, SEM/TEM, XPS, and BET analyses. DRM performance was evaluated at 800°C under varying CH4/CO2 ratios. Electrochemical properties were evaluated using single cells to measure I-V curves, power density, and EIS. XRD confirmed a single perovskite phase in all samples, with lattice variations reflecting Ru and Ni substitution. SEM/TEM revealed surface exsolution of nanoparticles upon reduction treatment. XPS and BET analyses indicated composition-dependent changes in surface chemical states and specific surface area. DRM evaluation demonstrated that CH4 and CO2 conversion rates were strongly influenced by the Ru/Ni ratio. In single-cell evaluation, the optimal composition exhibited the highest power density and the lowest electrochemical resistance. The Ru-Ni co-doping strategy successfully enhanced catalytic activity and coking resistance in DRM, demonstrating strong potential as a fuel-flexible SOFC anode catalyst. The structural and catalytic baseline data obtained in this study provide a solid foundation for further anode catalyst development and future scale-up for stack-level power generation.

P2-048.k: Porous Yolk-shell; Alkali Resistance; Steam Reforming of Methane
P2-048.a: Hydrogen production from renewable sources or fuel cell applications often faces catalytic deactivation due to alkali impurities and carbon deposition. Core- and yolk-shell structures have emerged to protect active sites, but robust structural stability under harsh alkali conditions remains challenging. Porous yolk-shell Al2O3 (pys-Al2O3) supports were synthesized via spray pyrolysis, selective reduction, and acid etching, followed by Ni impregnation (15 wt%). The catalytic performance of Ni/pys-Al2O3 was evaluated in the steam reforming of methane (SRM) with in-situ alkali exposure at 650 oC and a high space velocity (GHSV = 932,492 mL/g/h). Physical-chemical properties were comprehensively analyzed using H2-chemisorption, H2-TPR, XPS, XAFS, TGA, etc. Ni/pys-Al2O3 exhibited superior catalytic activity and stability, maintaining high CH4 conversion (89.3% initial to 87.5% after 24 h) even under alkali vapor exposure, outperforming non-porous yolk-shell and commercial catalysts. The porous shell effectively preserved structural property, such as high Ni dispersion (3.05%) and small Ni particle size (27.7 nm), which strongly correlated with high turnover frequency (TOF). Furthermore, TGA confirmed complete inhibition of carbon deposition over the yolk-shell structure. The Ni/pys-Al2O3 catalyst demonstrates superior resistance to both alkali poisoning and coking owing to its highly stable porous yolk-shell structure. It offers a promising strategy for highly stable hydrogen production processes under alkali-containing feed gas conditions.

P2-049.k: Two-electron Oxygen Reduction Reaction; Ni Complex; Coordination Environment
P2-049.a: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is widely used in water treatment, paper bleaching, and chemical synthesis. The current anthraquinone process is energy-intensive, generates waste, and involves high transportation costs. The on-site H2O2 electrosynthesis via two-electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e– ORR) is a promising alternative to the anthraquinone process, and atomically dispersed catalysts (ADCs) have emerged as appealing catalysts for the 2e– ORR. Previous studies have synthesized ADCs by heat-treatment-based strategies focusing mainly on efficient H2O2 production. However, these methods inevitably introduce structural heterogeneity in the coordination environment around the metal center, rendering the identification of the structure–selectivity relationship in the 2e– ORR elusive. In this work, we employ a room-temperature synthesis method for Ni ADCs with four different ligands to investigate the impact of π-electron character in the coordination environment on 2e– ORR selectivity. Well-defined Ni complexes were adsorbed on Ketjen Black (KB) to afford Ni ADCs with controlled coordination environments (Ni–N2X2/KB, X = C, N, O, or S). Ni–N2C2/KB with a π-acceptor ligand achieves 95% H2O2 selectivity in 0.1 M KOH, whereas the other three catalysts exhibit selectivity below 85% under the same conditions. This trend is attributed to the withdrawal of d-electron density from the metal center by the π-acceptor ligand, which steers the reaction toward the 2e– ORR. These results suggest that judicious control of coordination structures can serve as a promising method of designing ADCs for highly selective electrocatalysis.

P2-050.k: Chlorine Evolution Reaction; Heteroatom-Doped Carbon Catalyst; Temperature Dependency
P2-050.a: Chlorine, an essential chemical in the chemical industry, is mostly produced by chlor–alkali electrolysis. Dimensionally stable anodes (DSAs) are currently mainstay catalysts for the chlorine evolution reaction (CER). However, DSAs require a high fraction (~30 at%) of expensive and scarce platinum-group metals (PGMs), making them costly. Replacing PGMs with transition metals has been explored, but transition-metal-based active sites are susceptible to corrosion under the harsh conditions of chlor–alkali electrolysis. In this context, metal-free carbon-based materials can serve as promising CER electrocatalysts due to their low cost and intrinsic corrosion resistance. In this work, we present heteroatom-doped carbon black materials as highly active CER electrocatalysts. Commercial carbon black (Ketjen black, KB) was oxidized by annealing in air and subsequently annealed under NH3 or H2S to dope nitrogen or sulfur, respectively, at controlled temperatures. N,O-codoped KBs exhibit higher CER activity with lower annealing temperatures, whereas S,O-codoped KB showed the opposite trend. XPS analysis indicates that the annealing temperature-dependent activity trends are associated with changes in heteroatom functionalities; pyrrolic N and thiophenic S species serve as the active sites in the N,O- and S,O-codoped KB, respectively. Notably, the S,O-codoped KB synthesized at 600 °C exhibits very high activity with an overpotential of 31.9 mV at 10 mA cm−2 and a CER selectivity of 94.1% in 4 M NaCl at 0.01 M HClO4. These findings provide design strategies for high-performance carbon-based electrocatalysts for the CER.

P2-051.k: Li Recyling; Positively Charged CNT; Hydrogen Generation
P2-051.a: Redox-mediated recycling using the ferrocyanide ion couples offers a promising route for lithium iron phosphate battery processing. However, severe electrostatic repulsion and poor wettability on conventional carbon surfaces impede interfacial charge transfer kinetics. To overcome this kinetic barrier, carbon nanotube (CNT) surfaces were functionalized with tris(2-aminoethyl)amine (TAEA). This generated a positively charged, amine-rich interface CNT-COOH/TAEA designed to electrostatically attract negatively charged redox-mediator species. The charge-modulated interface dramatically improved charge transfer performance, achieving a double-layer capacitance of 4.1mF and a diffusion coefficient of 5.85 x 10^(-6) cm^2 s^-1. Integrated into a flow-cell system coupling LiFePO4 recycling with concurrent hydrogen evolution, the modified electrode accelerated reaction kinetics, lowered the specific energy consumption for hydrogen production to 3.26 kWh m^-3, and yielded high-purity LiOH (99.04 wt) alongside FePO4. Amine-based interfacial charge modulation provides a highly effective and scalable design strategy to enhance mass transport, lower energy penalties, and advance closed-loop battery recycling technologies. This research was supported by the Regional Innovation System & Education(RISE) program through the (Chungbuk Regional Innovation System & Education Center), funded by the Ministry of Education(MOE) and the (Chungcheongbuk-do), Republic of Korea.(2026-RISE-11-004-03)

P2-052.k: Water Electrolysis; NiFe-LDH; Oxygen Evolution Reaction
P2-052.a: The rapid deployment of renewable energy has intensified the demand for hydrogen as an energy carrier capable of resolving the temporal and spatial constraints of renewable power. Water electrolysis, which converts electrical energy into hydrogen fuel, consists of two half-reactions: the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Among these, the sluggish four-electron kinetics and high activation energy of the OER remain the major bottleneck of the overall process, making the development of highly active and durable OER catalysts indispensable. Although Ir- and Ru-based noble metal oxides exhibit excellent OER activity, their limited abundance and high cost hinder their large-scale application. Among earth-abundant alternatives, NiFe layered double hydroxides (NiFe LDHs) have emerged as promising candidates owing to their high intrinsic activity in alkaline media. Nevertheless, their practical performance is still limited by the low density of accessible active sites and the poor electrical conductivity of the hydroxide framework. Since the OER proceeds exclusively at the outermost surface, engineering the near-surface region, rather than the bulk composition, offers a direct route to overcome these limitations. In this context, we propose an electrochemical surface treatment as a facile post-synthetic strategy to enhance the OER performance of NiFe LDH. NiFe LDH was grown on a conductive substrate, and the resulting electrode was subsequently subjected to an electrochemical surface treatment under controlled conditions in an aqueous electrolyte. The applied potential and the treatment duration were systematically varied to identify the optimum degree of surface modification. The crystal structure, morphology, and surface chemical states of the electrodes before and after the treatment were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) coupled with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The electrocatalytic properties were evaluated in a three-electrode configuration in alkaline media using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) with iR compensation, Tafel analysis, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) was estimated from the double-layer capacitance measured in the non-Faradaic region in order to assess the contribution of the accessible surface area to the overall activity. Long-term durability was assessed by chronopotentiometry under a constant current density. The pristine NiFe LDH and a commercial noble-metal oxide catalyst were employed as references throughout. XRD confirmed that the layered hydrotalcite-like structure was retained after the electrochemical treatment, indicating that the modification was largely confined to the near-surface region without collapsing the bulk framework. FE-SEM revealed that the interconnected nanosheet morphology was preserved while the surface became noticeably roughened, and XPS showed changes in both the surface cation composition and the binding energies of the constituent species, suggesting that the treatment altered the surface chemical environment rather than the bulk structure. Consistent with these structural features, the treated electrode exhibited a lower overpotential than the pristine counterpart, indicating enhanced OER activity. An increase in the double-layer capacitance was also observed, which could be attributed to a higher density of accessible active sites generated by the surface treatment. Notably, the treated electrode simultaneously displayed a reduced Tafel slope, suggesting that the enhancement originated not only from the enlarged surface area but also from a modification of the interfacial reaction kinetics. EIS further revealed a decreased charge-transfer resistance, which is consistent with the improved kinetics inferred from the Tafel analysis. Under continuous operation, the treated electrode maintained a more stable potential over an extended period, whereas the pristine electrode exhibited a gradual performance decay under identical conditions. In summary, a facile electrochemical surface treatment was developed to enhance the OER performance of NiFe LDH in alkaline media. The treatment reconstructed the near-surface region while preserving the layered bulk framework, thereby integrating two synergistic effects: (i) an increased number of accessible active sites, and (ii) a modified surface chemical environment that facilitates charge transfer and is expected to optimize the adsorption of the oxygenated intermediates. As a result, the treated electrode demonstrated a reduced overpotential, faster reaction kinetics, and improved operational stability compared with the pristine counterpart, achieving a simultaneous enhancement of activity and durability without introducing noble metals. Overall, this work highlights a simple and scalable post-synthetic surface engineering route that is readily applicable to other LDH-based and transition-metal (oxy)hydroxide electrocatalysts. Detailed structural characterization and mechanistic analyses are currently in progress, and the results will be discussed in the presentation.

P2-053.a: Tandem solar cells have attracted significant attention recently due to their ability to absorb light over a wider range of wavelengths by combining two cells with different bandgaps, thus exceeding the theoretical efficiency limit of single-junction solar cells (Shockley-Queissier limit). However, imperfect charge recombination in each cell of tandem solar cells leads to issues such as quasi-Fermi level splitting and reverse diode formation due to charge accumulation, resulting in tandem solar cell efficiencies comparable to those of single-junction solar cells despite extensive research. To address these issues, research has been conducted to apply Au nuclei deposited by a thermal evaporator as a recombination layer between the two cells to facilitate the recombination of charges formed in each cell by achieving high carrier concentration. We aimed to deposit Ru/RuO2 nuclei via sputtering and apply them as a recombination layer in tandem solar cells. By adjusting the flow rate of Ar/O2 plasma during the sputtering process, we confirmed the formation conditions of Ru and RuO2 films and observed the film growth characteristics and properties according to process time adjustment, thereby identifying the nuclei density that maximizes carrier concentration and optical transparency. By applying these Ru and RuO2 nuclei as recombination layers in tandem solar cells and comparing their performance with tandem solar cells applying Au nuclei, we confirmed the potential application of Ru/RuO2 nuclei deposited via sputtering as recombination layers in tandem solar cells.

P2-054.k: Carbon And Ceramic; Graphite Felt; Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries
P2-054.a: Vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) have been widely applied to the energy storage system, attributed to their excellent electrochemical performance, such as non-flammable, long cycle life, large-scale storage, and good cycle stability. In a VRFB, a vanadium-based electrolyte from an external tank circulates into the cell stack, storing energy through redox reactions involving the change of different vanadium valence states at the electrode and electrolyte interface. Carbon-based materials are widely used as electrodes because of their low cost, high electrical conductivity, and good chemical stability. However, these carbon electrodes exhibit insufficient catalytic activity and slow reaction kinetics for vanadium redox reactions. In this study, we proposed graphite felt (GF) electrodes modified with ceramic (transion metal oxide) materials. The carbon coated GF and carbon-ceramic coated GF electrodes were fabricated using an ultrasonic spray coating method with polyacrylic acid (PAA) as a dispersant. The carbon coated GF and carbon and ceramic coated GF electrodes exhibited high energy, coulomb, and voltage efficiency compared to the bare GF. The carbon coated GF electrode increased the specific surface area, providing more active sites for vanadium ion contact. Furthermore, the carbon-ceramic coated GF electrode increased the proportion of oxygen-containing functional groups, which accelerated the vanadium redox reactions and significantly enhanced the catalytic activity of the vanadium ions. This study presents a customized graphite felt interface for ultrafast vanadium redox flow batteries. The carbon and ceramic composite structure was uniformly coated onto a graphite felt using an ultrasonic spray coating method. As a result, the carbon and ceramic coated GF exhibited an energy efficiency of over 90.00%.

P2-055.k: Dry Processed Electrode; Carbon Network; Mechanofusion
P2-055.a: Dry-processed electrodes have attracted considerable attention as a solvent-free and energy-efficient manufacturing strategy for next-generation lithium-ion batteries. However, insufficient conductive pathways and nonuniform conductive-additive distribution in thick electrodes with high active-material content remain major challenges. In this study, we engineered a mechanofused 0D Super P (SP)/1D carbon nanotube (CNT) hybrid conductive network to enhance electron transport and electrochemical performance. Dry LFP electrodes were fabricated through a solvent-free process using LFP, conductive additives, and PTFE at a fixed weight ratio of 95:3:2. Prior to electrode fabrication, 0D Super P and 1D CNTs were hybridized via mechanofusion with controlled SP/CNT ratios. The mixtures were subsequently dry-mixed, kneaded to induce PTFE fibrillation, calendered into free-standing sheets, and laminated onto Al foil. Their structural, electrical, and electrochemical characteristics were systematically evaluated. The mechanofused 0D–1D SP/CNT hybrid provided interconnected conductive pathways and improved electrical contact between LFP particles. Compared with electrodes containing a single conductive additive, the hybrid electrode exhibited lower electrode resistance, enhanced charge-transfer kinetics, higher discharge capacity, and superior rate capability. The synergistic combination of local particle-to-particle contacts provided by SP and long-range electron transport pathways formed by CNTs effectively enhanced the electrochemical performance of the dry-processed LFP electrode. This study demonstrates that mechanofusion-assisted 0D–1D SP/CNT hybridization provides an effective strategy for constructing interconnected conductive networks in dry-processed LFP electrodes. The proposed conductive-network design offers a promising approach for the development of high-performance and scalable dry electrodes for next-generation lithium-ion batteries.

P2-056.a: Gallium-based liquid metals (LMs) are promising electrode materials for electrochemical applications due to their fluidity and metallic conductivity. However, under reductive electrochemical potentials, the removal of the native surface oxide layer alters the interfacial energy, inducing severe electrocapillary deformation, surface area loss, and electrical disconnection. To mitigate this issue, micro/nanoparticle additives were incorporated into the liquid metal matrix. The electrochemical stability and resistance to electrocapillary deformation of the resulting liquid metal composite electrodes were evaluated under reductive bias conditions in comparison with pristine liquid metal electrodes. The composite electrodes demonstrated significantly enhanced morphological and operational stability under reductive bias compared to pristine liquid metals. Rheological analyses indicated that particle size plays a critical role in increasing the viscoelastic properties (storage modulus and yield stress) of the composite, providing mechanical resistance against deformation even at low particle loadings. This study highlights the role of internal oxide structures and particulate interactions in reinforcing liquid metal composites against electrocapillary instability. The presented approach offers a versatile design strategy for developing morphologically robust liquid metal electrodes for long-term electrochemical operations.

P2-057.k: Aqueous Two Phase System; Ion Conductivity; Hydrogoles
P2-057.a: Aqueous two-phase systems (ATPSs), composed of two immiscible aqueous phases, provide a unique platform for constructing fully aqueous materials with compartmentalized and interconnected structures. Their high water content and compatibility with hydrophilic components make ATPSs particularly attractive as templates for functional hydrogels. However, their potential for constructing ion-conductive materials with controlled aqueous transport pathways remains largely unexplored. In this study, we develop stable all-aqueous emulsions as templates for the fabrication of ion-conductive hydrogels with interconnected aqueous networks. By controlling the emulsion structure and selectively polymerizing the aqueous phases, hydrogels with tunable internal architectures and mechanical properties are fabricated. Ionic species are directly incorporated during the fully aqueous fabrication process to impart ionic conductivity. The resulting hydrogels possess interconnected water-rich domains that provide continuous pathways for efficient ion transport. Consequently, the hydrogels exhibit high ionic conductivity while maintaining excellent stretchability and mechanical stability under large deformation. The internal aqueous architecture can also be tailored through control of the emulsion structure, enabling simultaneous regulation of ion transport and mechanical properties. These results demonstrate that all-aqueous emulsion templating provides a versatile strategy for designing soft ion-conductive materials that combine continuous ion-transport pathways with highly deformable polymer networks. This approach offers potential for the development of flexible and stretchable materials for electrochemical systems.
