P2-058.a: Acrolein and acrylic acid are important chemical intermediates widely used in the production of polymers and various value-added chemicals. Their conventional production relies on high-temperature (523–623 K) thermocatalytic oxidation of propylene. Replacing this process with an electrocatalytic process could enable allylic oxidation of propylene under mild conditions and provide a way to control product selectivity through the electrode potential. In this context, the electrochemical oxidation of propylene at ambient conditions has been studied over various catalysts. However, selective oxidation at the allylic position has been mainly limited to fundamental studies on Pd catalysts, with low activity and challenges associated with a limited potential range and uncontrolled surface coverage. In this study, we investigate various Pd-based catalysts and propose electrolysis strategies to improve the activity of electrochemical allylic oxidation of propylene. A series of alloys with varying compositions of Pd and other metals were synthesized on various support materials. The catalysts were characterized by high-resolution elemental mapping using field-emission transmission electron microscopy coupled with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Electrochemical experiments were conducted using a sandwich-type PEEK cell with a gas diffusion electrode system for propylene and O2 supply. HClO₄, NaClO₄, and NaOH solutions with a total ionic strength of 0.1 M were used to control the electrolyte pH. After electrolysis, the products were analyzed by ¹H NMR. Initial catalyst screening showed that Pd was active for the allylic oxidation of propylene, while other metals showed negligible activity. The activity of carbon-supported Pd varied nonlinearly with Pd loading, suggesting that catalyst properties such as Pd particle size and dispersion affect the activity. In particular, PdPt showed 1.7-fold higher activity than Pd (1.62 vs 0.95 μmol gmetal⁻¹ h⁻¹), indicating that alloying can be an effective strategy for tuning Pd-based catalysts. The effect of electrolyte pH was also investigated. The formation of allylic oxidation products was maintained at pH 7 or below, while the activity decreased at higher pH. Allylic oxidation products were also formed under open-circuit conditions, indicating that continuous anodic polarization is not required for product formation. This observation motivates further investigation of dynamic potential control as a strategy for regulating surface species and enhancing activity. Based on these findings, various Pd-based alloy catalysts, support materials, and dynamic electrolysis strategies are being investigated. Pd showed activity for the electrochemical allylic oxidation of propylene, while PdPt exhibited higher activity than Pd alone. Product formation under open-circuit conditions motivates further investigation of dynamic potential control. These findings highlight catalyst design and optimization of electrolysis conditions as promising strategies for improving allylic oxidation.

P2-059.k: 2D Magnetic Semiconductor; Hydrogen Evolution Reaction; Surface Engineering
P2-059.a: Activating the catalytically inert basal planes of two-dimensional (2D) materials through defect formation and atomic substitution is a widely explored strategy for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). CrSBr, an air-stable 2D magnetic semiconductor, has been studied mainly for its magnetic and optoelectronic properties, and its surface catalytic activity remains largely unexplored. Moreover, defect-generation methods applied to CrSBr, such as Ar+ sputtering and thermal annealing, treat the entire sample and cannot localize active sites. Here, we use focused laser irradiation as a localized thermal treatment to engineer the CrSBr basal plane within targeted submicrometer areas and evaluate its local HER activity. We prepared CrSBr flakes of different thicknesses using mechanical exfoliation. Then, laser irradiation was conducted on these exfoliated CrSBr flakes on SiO2/Si substrate with a focused 532 nm continuous-wave laser at different laser powers and exposure times. We characterized laser-induced structural and chemical changes by confocal Raman spectroscopy (XperRam, Nanobase, Republic of Korea), scanning photoemission microscopy (8A1 SPEM beamline, PAL, Republic of Korea), and nano-X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (21A, NSRRC, Taiwan). Local HER activity of laser-treated flakes was evaluated by scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM, NITech, Japan). Mild irradiation (≤ 1.5 mW) preserved the A2g Raman mode of CrSBr (~242 cm-1) without oxidation signatures, while SPEM showed reduced Br 3d and S 2p signals in the irradiated regions, indicating the formation of Br and S vacancies. Harsh irradiation (≥ 2.0 mW) sharply suppressed the A2g mode and produced a Cr2O3-related peak (~550 cm-1) that grew with laser power. An increased O 1s signal, shifted and broadened relative to that of the SiO2 substrate, confirmed surface oxidation confined to the targeted area, and XRF mapping consistently showed Br loss and thinning there. In SECCM, the vacancy-rich basal plane exhibited enhanced HER activity compared with pristine CrSBr, and the oxidized surface yielded the highest current density among the investigated areas. Laser irradiation enables site-selective control of vacancy formation and surface oxidation in CrSBr, both of which activate its inert basal plane for HER, with surface oxidation being the most effective. Localized laser-assisted surface engineering thus offers a route to activating catalytically inert basal planes of 2D materials within targeted submicrometer areas.

P2-060.a: ﻿Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have attracted considerable attention as promising electrocatalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) owing to their atomically thin geometry, tunable electronic structures, and diverse structural phases. ﻿However, the relatively low catalytic activity of their semiconducting 2H basal planes limits their overall HER performance. Researchers have explored strategies such as defect engineering, strain modulation, phase transitions, and alloying to activate their basal planes for various electrocatalytic reactions. ﻿Among these, alloy engineering offers a promising approach to tailoring electronic structures and catalytic activity through atomic-scale compositional controls. ﻿Nevertheless, complex thermodynamic and kinetic factors, including phase separation, structural phase transitions, and phase stability, create a rich landscape of structural and compositional configurations in TMD alloys, offering diverse opportunities to tailor their physical and chemical properties. ﻿These factors can contribute to local compositional and structural heterogeneity, potentially modifying electronic states, charge-transfer behavior, and hydrogen adsorption energetics. Despite their importance, the relationship between local compositional heterogeneity and electrocatalytic activity remains poorly understood. ﻿MoS2–WS2 alloy flakes were synthesized by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) using sodium molybdate dihydrate and sodium tungstate dihydrate as Mo and W precursors, respectively. The precursors were mixed in an aqueous solution and spin-coated onto Si/SiO2 substrates prior to CVD growth. ﻿The morphology and thickness distribution of the as-grown MoS2–WS2 alloy flakes were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM). Spatially resolved Raman and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy were performed to investigate the distributions of MoS2- and WS2-related spectral features and variations in optical emission characteristics. ﻿Scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) was employed to map local HER activity across individual flakes, enabling spatial correlation between compositional heterogeneity and electrocatalytic performance. ﻿The as-grown MoS2–WS2 alloy flakes exhibited polygonal morphologies, including triangular and hexagonal shapes, with a distinct core–shell-like thickness distribution characterized by a thicker central core and a thinner outer shell region. AFM measurements revealed that the outer shell region was about two layers thick, with the thickness gradually increasing toward the central core region. Consistent with these observations, Raman spectroscopy showed spatial variations in the frequency separation between the characteristic E¹₂g and A₁g vibrational modes of MoS2, corresponding to the observed thickness gradient. Spatially resolved Raman spectral mapping further revealed a nonuniform distribution of MoS2 and WS2, preferentially localized along the boundaries of the core regions and the edges of the shell regions. PL spectral mapping revealed a progressive blue shift in the emission peak from the central core region toward the outer shell regions, suggesting spatial variations in optical transition energies that may be associated with thickness and local composition. Notably, SECCM measurements revealed that the alloyed regions exhibited enhanced HER activity compared with pristine MoS2 and WS2, establishing a spatial correlation between local composition and electrocatalytic performance. ﻿MoS2–WS2 alloy flakes exhibited a distinct thickness gradient and spatially heterogeneous alloy distribution, with MoS2 and WS2 preferentially localized along specific edges and internal boundaries rather than uniformly distributed throughout the flakes. We observed enhanced local HER activity in regions associated with these alloy-related features, revealing a spatial correlation between local compositional heterogeneity and electrocatalytic performance. These findings highlight the role of compositional heterogeneity in determining local HER activity and provide insights into the rational design of compositionally engineered 2D TMD electrocatalysts.

P2-061.k: ULTCC; Microwave dielectric properties; Electrode compatibility
P2-061.a: With the rapid development of 5G/6G communications and autonomous driving systems utilizing millimeter-wave radar at 77 GHz and above, there is an increasing demand for substrate materials with low dielectric loss and high thermal stability at high frequencies. Ultra-low-temperature co-fired ceramics (ULTCCs) have attracted considerable attention because they can be co-fired with low-cost metal electrodes at temperatures below 650 �C. ZnMoO4 is a promising Mo-based microwave dielectric ceramic with a relatively low dielectric constant and high quality factor (Q�f). However, its relatively high sintering temperature remains a major challenge for ULTCC applications. Therefore, this study aims to reduce the sintering temperature while maintaining favorable microwave dielectric properties of ZnMoO4-based ceramics through the incorporation of a low-temperature sintering aid. ZnMoO4-based ceramics were prepared via a conventional solid-state reaction method and sintered at 575-700 �C. The starting powders were ball-milled with zirconia balls in ethanol for 48 h and calcined at 500 �C to synthesize the ZnMoO4 phase. TeO2 was subsequently added as a sintering aid, followed by secondary ball milling for 48 h. The resulting powders were uniaxially pressed into pellets and cold isostatically pressed (CIP) at 200 MPa. Phase formation, densification behavior, and microstructure were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Raman spectroscopy. Microwave dielectric properties, including relative permittivity (?r), quality factor (Q�f), dielectric loss (tan?), and temperature coefficient of resonant frequency (?f), were evaluated. Dielectric properties at 77 GHz were also measured to evaluate the millimeter-wave characteristics. Compatibility with metal electrodes was examined to assess the applicability of the developed ceramics to ULTCC technology. TeO2 addition effectively promoted the low-temperature densification of ZnMoO4 ceramics. The ZnMoO4 phase was maintained over the investigated composition range, whereas excessive TeO2 addition resulted in the formation of a secondary phase. SEM observations showed that TeO2 addition promoted grain growth and densification, while excessive addition induced abnormal microstructural evolution and increased porosity. Raman analysis revealed systematic changes in Raman shift and FWHM with increasing TeO2 content, showing a correlation with the Q�f behavior. The optimized composition exhibited ?r = 8.53, Q�f = 54,522 GHz, and tan? = 3.2 � 10-4 at 16 GHz. However, excessive TeO2 addition resulted in degradation of the microwave dielectric properties, which was attributed to excessive liquid-phase formation and secondary-phase development. At 77 GHz, the optimized ceramic exhibited ?r = 8.0427 and tan? = 2.0 � 10-3, confirming its dielectric response in the millimeter-wave frequency range. Electrode compatibility tests revealed that the Ag electrode reacted with the ZnMoO4-based ceramic, as confirmed by XRD and EDS analyses, whereas no detectable reaction with the Al electrode was observed by either XRD or EDS. The results demonstrate that the incorporation of a low-temperature sintering aid is an effective strategy for reducing the sintering temperature of ZnMoO4-based ceramics while maintaining favorable microwave dielectric properties. Optimizing the additive content is critical for promoting densification while suppressing excessive liquid-phase formation and secondary-phase development that degrade dielectric performance. The optimized composition exhibited favorable microwave dielectric properties and maintained its dielectric response at 77 GHz. These findings demonstrate the potential of ZnMoO4-based ceramics as ULTCC substrate materials for next-generation high-frequency communication and millimeter-wave applications. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) Grant funded by the Korean Government (Ministry of Education) [NRF-2018R1A6A1A03025761] and [RS-2026-25620852], the Technology Innovation Program [20024235] and [RS-2024-00431899] funded By the Ministry of Trade, Industry & Energy (MOTIE, Korea), and the Civil-Military Convergence Core Materials Self-Reliance Technology Development Program [25611481].

P2-062.a: KNN-based lead-free piezoelectric ceramics have attracted considerable attention as promising alternatives to lead-based piezoelectric materials owing to their excellent ferroelectric properties and high phase transition temperatures. However, achieving superior piezoelectric performance requires precise control of phase coexistence and polarization behavior near room temperature. In this study, multi-element co-substitution was employed to introduce lattice distortion and local structural heterogeneity through cations with different ionic radii and off-centering tendencies. This approach aims to promote multiphase coexistence and facilitate polarization responses, thereby enhancing the piezoelectric properties of KNN-based ceramics. The objective was to investigate the relationship between composition-induced structural changes and piezoelectric performance and establish an effective composition design strategy. KNNS-based lead-free piezoelectric ceramic powders with systematically varied multi-element substitution contents were prepared using a conventional solid-state reaction method. The starting materials were weighed according to the designed compositions and subjected to primary ball milling for 24 h to ensure homogeneous mixing. The mixed powders were subsequently calcined at 950 �C for 6 h, followed by secondary ball milling for 72 h to obtain fine and homogeneous ceramic powders. The synthesized powders were then compacted into cylindrical green bodies using a 16 mm diameter die through uniaxial pressing. Finally, the green bodies were subjected to two-step sintering, with first-step sintering temperatures of 1160-1170 �C and second-step sintering temperatures of 1070-1090 �C, to obtain KNNS-based lead-free piezoelectric ceramics. The piezoelectric properties initially improved with increasing multi-element substitution content and subsequently deteriorated at higher substitution levels. The maximum piezoelectric coefficient (d33) of 620 pC/N was achieved at a composition with a configurational entropy of approximately 1.36R. This composition also exhibited a planar electromechanical coupling factor (kp) of approximately 0.60, a relative dielectric permittivity (?r) of approximately 4400, and a dielectric loss (tan ?) of approximately 0.025. XRD analysis revealed the coexistence of multiple crystalline phases in this composition, suggesting that the formation of a phase boundary near room temperature may contribute to the enhanced piezoelectric properties. These results indicate that appropriate multi-element co-substitution can effectively modulate the phase structure, leading to enhanced piezoelectric and dielectric performance in KNNS-based lead-free piezoelectric ceramics. Multi-element co-substitution provides an effective approach to tailoring the structural and piezoelectric properties of KNNS-based lead-free piezoelectric ceramics. The enhanced piezoelectric performance observed at a configurational entropy of 1.36R suggests that an appropriate degree of compositional complexity and the resulting structural modifications play important roles in optimizing piezoelectric responses. In particular, the observed multiphase coexistence may facilitate polarization rotation and domain switching, thereby contributing to the enhanced piezoelectric properties. These findings suggest that optimizing the phase structure through controlled multi-element co-substitution, rather than simply increasing configurational entropy, is important for achieving superior piezoelectric performance. This study provides insights into the relationship between composition-induced structural evolution and piezoelectric properties and offers a composition design strategy for developing high-performance KNNS-based lead-free piezoelectric ceramics. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) Grant funded by the Korean Government (Ministry of Education) [NRF-2018R1A6A1A03025761] and [RS-2026-25620852], the Technology Innovation Program [20024235] and [RS-2024-00431899] funded By the Ministry of Trade, Industry & Energy (MOTIE, Korea), and the Civil-Military Convergence Core Materials Self-Reliance Technology Development Program [25611481].

P2-063.a: Piezoelectric nanocomposites consisting of a polymer matrix and ceramic fillers are candidate components of flexible, wearable, and self-powered electronic devices. The physical discrepancy between ferroelectric polymers and ceramics in a piezoelectric interface makes it difficult to assemble efficient hybrid piezoelectric nanocomposites without polarization and extraneous artifacts. Here, we describe the effect of a relaxor ferroelectric terpolymer matrix on the piezoelectric output, which can enhance the energy harvesting or sensor performance of piezoelectric composite device of nanocomposite generators with filler nanoparticles of lead zirconium titanate. Piezoelectric nanocomposites consisting of a polymer matrix and ceramic fillers are candidate components of flexible, wearable, and self-powered electronic devices. The physical discrepancy between ferroelectric polymers and ceramics in a piezoelectric interface makes it difficult to assemble efficient hybrid piezoelectric nanocomposites without polarization and extraneous artifacts. Here, we describe the effect of a relaxor ferroelectric terpolymer matrix on the piezoelectric output, which can enhance the energy harvesting or sensor performance of piezoelectric composite device of nanocomposite generators with filler nanoparticles of lead zirconium titanate. The dielectric property and reduced ferroelectric hindrance of the proposed terpolymer matrix provides more poling to align the polarization of piezoelectric ceramic fillers compared with a normal ferroelectric copolymer matrix. Therefore, relaxor ferroelectric polymers can be better than normal ferroelectric polymers as the matrix of hybrid polymer-ceramic piezoelectric nanocomposite. This research provides important physical information about the interface between a polymer matrix and ceramic fillers in flexible piezoelectric nanocomposite applications.

P2-064.k: Triboelectric Nanogenerator; Poly(vinyl Chloride); Fluorine-free Dielectric Polymer
P2-064.a: Fluorinated polymers such as poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) have been widely employed as negative triboelectric materials because of their high electronegativity. However, increasing environmental concerns regarding PFAS have driven the development of fluorine-free alternatives. In this study, poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) was investigated as a sustainable dielectric polymer for triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs). The triboelectric performance of PVC was optimized by controlling the molecular weight, film thickness, and annealing temperature, and its dielectric and electrical properties were compared with those of PVDF. The triboelectric performance was strongly influenced by both film thickness and thermal treatment. The optimum film thickness was approximately 17 μm for low-molecular-weight PVC and 9 μm for high-molecular-weight PVC, while both samples exhibited the highest output after annealing at 100 °C. Under the optimized conditions, high-molecular-weight PVC achieved an open-circuit voltage of 72 V, a short-circuit current of 0.52 μA, and a maximum power density of 9.7 μW cm⁻², outperforming both low-molecular-weight PVC and conventional PVDF. Dielectric characterization further revealed that PVC exhibited a higher dielectric constant than PVDF (7.2 vs. 5.9), indicating enhanced dipolar polarization. The increased dielectric polarization promoted charge generation, storage, and retention at the triboelectric interface, thereby enhancing the triboelectric output. These findings demonstrate that optimizing the molecular weight, film thickness, and annealing conditions effectively enhances the triboelectric performance of PVC. Owing to its superior dielectric polarization and charge storage capability, PVC represents a promising fluorine-free alternative to conventional PVDF for environmentally friendly, high-performance triboelectric nanogenerators.

P2-065.k: Transition Metal Dichalcogenide; Hot Carrier Injection; In-plane Seebeck Effect
P2-065.a: Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) are considered highly promising materials for small-scale thermoelectric (TE) energy harvesting and micro-cooling applications due to their large energy bandgap and atomic-scale thickness. However, evaluating the Seebeck coefficient for monolayer or few-layer TMDC thin films (e.g., 2 nm PtSe2) is extremely challenging; their exceptionally high electrical resistance (> 10 MΩ) prevents measurements using conventional direct current-based equipment. We refer to the effect as the interface-induced Seebeck effect. Exploiting this effect by directly attaching multilayer PtSe2 over high-resistance few layer PtSe2 thin films as a hybridized single structure, we obtained the highly challenging in-plane Seebeck coefficient for PtSe2 films with extremely high resistance. This direct attachment further enhanced in-plane thermal Seebeck coefficients of the PtSe2/PtSe2 van der Waals homostructure on sapphire substrate. Consequently, we successfully enhanced in-plane Seebeck coefficients for PtSe2 (10 nm) /PtSe2 (2 nm) homostructure approximately 42% compared to pure 10 nm PtSe2 layer at 300 K. These new findings represent a significant achievement in understanding the interface-induced Seebeck effect and pave the way toward an effective strategy for promising large-area thermoelectric energy harvesting devices providing ideal thermoelectric platforms with high figure of merit in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenide materials.

P2-066.a: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) are promising self-powered devices for flexible and wearable electronics, but their performance is often limited by inefficient interfacial charge generation and difficulties in controlling film morphology. Liquid-crystalline block copolymers are attractive materials because their nanoscale ordered structures can tune surface morphology, dipole orientation, and contact electrification. In this study, PDMS–PAzo polymer bilayers were designed to enhance TENG output through nanoscale morphology control. PAzo monomers, PDMS macroinitiators, and PDMS–PAzo block copolymers with different LC volume fractions and terminal groups were synthesized and characterized by NMR and GPC. Annealed bulk films were observed by TEM. TENG devices were fabricated by spin-coating the polymer layers onto PET/ITO, PE, and PTFE substrates. The synthesized block copolymers exhibited controlled molecular weights and compositions, confirming successful synthesis. TEM analysis showed that the polymer morphology varied depending on the LC volume fraction. PNC0.55, PNO0.50 mainly formed cylindrical nanostructures, whereas others exhibited lamellar ordering. These ordered nanostructures are expected to influence interfacial polarization and charge-transfer behavior. TENG measurements revealed that the spin-coating speed strongly affected output performance. For both NC- and NO₂-terminated films, the highest voltage and current were obtained at 1000 rpm, indicating the presence of an optimal film formation condition. Substrate-dependent measurements also demonstrated that interfacial structure and surface contact quality are important factors for improving TENG performance. These results demonstrate that nanoscale morphology control in PDMS–PAzo liquid-crystalline block copolymer bilayers can enhance triboelectric performance. The optimized bilayer system shows potential for flexible wearable energy-harvesting devices and photo-responsive sensor applications.

P2-067.k: Hydrovoltaic Generation; PAN Nanofiber; Wastewater Treatment
P2-067.a: Hydrovoltaic generators harvest electricity through water–material interactions and offer a sustainable route for converting low-grade environmental energy into usable electrical energy. However, their practical application remains limited by insufficient electrical output and performance degradation during prolonged operation. Integrating hydrovoltaic generation with pollutant removal could provide a multifunctional platform for sustainable water treatment and self-powered environmental applications. Electrospun polyacrylonitrile (PAN) nanofiber membranes were coated with an aqueous dispersion containing carbon black (CB) and zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8). A CB-only-coated PAN membrane was prepared under equivalent conditions as a reference. Hydrovoltaic output and long-term operational stability were evaluated continuously for approximately 30 h. Methylene blue (MB)-contaminated water was treated with the CB/ZIF-8-coated membrane for 24 h, and its removal efficiency was determined from the change in MB concentration. The CB/ZIF-8-coated PAN device achieved maximum open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current values of 0.54 V and 492 μA, respectively. Following initial stabilization, the device maintained average outputs of approximately 0.30 V and 230 μA after approximately 30 h of continuous operation. The interconnected nanofiber network supported continuous water transport, while CB provided conductive pathways and porous ZIF-8 increased the water-accessible interfacial area. The composite-coated membrane also achieved ~ 90% MB removal after 24 h and exhibited superior hydrovoltaic performance and long-term stability compared with the CB-only-coated membrane. The CB/ZIF-8-coated PAN nanofiber membrane combines stable hydrovoltaic generation with effective dye removal, demonstrating its potential as a dual-functional material platform for wastewater treatment, environmental remediation, and self-powered systems.

P2-068.a: Hydrovoltaic energy harvesting generates electricity through evaporation- and moisture-driven water transport. In porous hydrovoltaic devices, continuous water transport and a sufficient solid–liquid interfacial area are important for maintaining electrical output. Three-dimensional (3D) printing provides a useful approach for controlling the geometry and porous structure of hydrovoltaic devices. However, polymer-based 3D-printed structures generally have limited intrinsic water-transport capability, which can restrict continuous hydrovoltaic generation. In this study, a carbon coated 3D-printed structure was combined with a porous sponge to improve water supply and maintain hydrovoltaic output during long-term operation. A Menger-type porous structure was fabricated by 3D printing and dip-coated three times using a carbon black suspension containing 0.25 g carbon black, 0.6 g CTAB, and 40 mL deionized water. Hydrovoltaic output was first evaluated using the carbon-coated 3D structure alone. A sponge coated under the same conditions was then integrated at the bottom of the 3D structure to provide continuous water supply. A 3 M CaCl₂ solution was used as the electrolyte, and open-circuit voltage (Voc) and short-circuit current (Isc) were measured using a potentiostat under different water-supply conditions. The electrical output of the 3D-printed structure strongly depended on the water-supply condition. Droplet feeding produced only 0.01 V and 0.2 μA, whereas continuous water supply from the bottom increased the output to 0.38 – 0.39 V and 52.2 – 83.1 μA. However, the 3D structure alone showed difficulty in maintaining continuous water transport during extended operation. After integrating the carbon-coated sponge, the hybrid generator produced an initial output of 0.48 V and 50.2 μA. After drying and water resupply, the device showed outputs of 0.47 V and 53.1 μA and 0.41 V and 59.0 μA in subsequent measurements. The hybrid structure also maintained hydrovoltaic output for 20 h of continuous operation. These results indicate that the sponge improved water supply to the 3D-printed structure and helped maintain electrical output over extended periods. The hydrovoltaic performance of the carbon-coated 3D-printed structure was strongly influenced by water transport within the porous architecture. Integration of the sponge improved water supply and helped maintain the moisture gradient, while the 3D-printed structure provided an evaporation-active region for electricity generation. The hybrid generator maintained an output of approximately 0.4–0.5 V and 50–60 μA during repeated measurements and sustained electricity generation for 20 h. These results indicate that combining controlled 3D porous architecture with continuous water transport can provide both stable electrical output and extended operation in hydrovoltaic generators.

P2-069.k: Lead Free Piezoelectric; KNN; Grain Growth
P2-069.a: KNN-based ceramics have attracted considerable attention as lead-free alternatives to Pb-based piezoelectric materials. However, alkali volatilization during sintering can cause compositional deviations and poor reproducibility, resulting in different microstructures even for nominally identical compositions. Dopant incorporation can further modify grain growth behavior, in some cases enabling the formation of centimeter-scale single crystals. In this study, the initial particle size, dopant species, and dopant concentration were systematically varied to investigate their effects on microstructural evolution. Depending on these variables, normal grain growth, abnormal grain growth, and single-crystal growth were observed. The mechanisms underlying these distinct growth behaviors were interpreted within the framework of the two-dimensional (2D) nucleation model. K0.5-xNa0.5NbO3 (x = 0, 0.005, and 0.01) and (K0.48Na0.5AE0.02)NbO₃ (AE = Ca, Sr, and Ba) powders were prepared by solid-state reaction. K₂CO₃ and Na₂CO₃ were dehydrated before use. The starting powders were weighed to the target compositions and ball-milled for 24 h in a nylon jar with zirconia balls and anhydrous ethanol. After drying, the K0.5-xNa0.5NbO3 and alkaline-earth-substituted powders were calcined at 800 °C for 2 and 3 h, respectively, and subsequently ball-milled for 24 and 72 h using the same milling setup. For particle size control, powders calcined at 800 °C for 2 h were subjected to planetary milling instead of conventional secondary ball milling. A 300 mL alumina jar, ethanol, and zirconia balls with a loading volume of 150 mL were used. The ball diameter (1–10 mm), rotational speed (200–400 rpm), and milling duration (10–60 min) were varied. All milled powders were dried and uniaxially pressed at 100 MPa into 16 mm disks. K0.5-xNa0.5NbO3 specimens and specimens with controlled particle size distributions were sintered for 2 h at 1040–1100 °C and 1080–1100 °C, respectively. Alkaline-earth-substituted specimens were sintered at 1100 °C for 0, 2, 5, 10, and 30 h. Within the framework of the two-dimensional (2D) nucleation grain growth mechanism, the initial particle size distribution, A-site vacancy formation induced by alkali volatilization, and changes in diffusion coefficients and interfacial properties associated with donor-type dopants such as Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, and Ba²⁺ collectively modified the effective relationship between the growth driving force (ΔG) and the critical driving force (ΔG꜀). These factors governed the transition between normal and abnormal grain growth and the emergence of dual growth paths. In Ba²⁺ substituted KNN, controlling the Ba content promoted pronounced abnormal grain growth, enabling rapid single-crystal formation. The growth of giant single crystals along an n-type reduction layer exhibiting electrochemical blackening was interpreted using Narayan’s defect-thermodynamic model. This interpretation suggests that the enrichment of A-site vacancies and donor electrons in the reduction layer maximizes the combined chemical and space-charge contributions to the total driving force, thereby enabling rapid growth of centimeter-scale single crystals. To suppress electrical defects associated with donor electrons, MnO₂ was introduced as an acceptor dopant for electron compensation, reducing leakage current and dielectric loss. The resulting [100]꜀-oriented single crystals exhibited a piezoelectric charge coefficient (d₃₃) of 328 pC/N and a piezoelectric voltage coefficient (g₃₃) of 187 × 10⁻³ V·m/N. This study establishes an integrated approach to developing high-performance KNN-based lead-free piezoelectric ceramics through coordinated control of grain growth mechanisms, defect chemistry, composition, and sintering processes. The findings provide design guidelines for microstructural optimization and rapid single-crystal growth, highlighting the potential of KNN-based systems as environmentally friendly alternatives to lead-based piezoelectric ceramics.

P2-070.a: Ultra-low-temperature co-fired ceramics (ULTCCs) with low dielectric loss and compatibility with cost-effective metal electrodes are highly desirable for high-frequency electronic applications. CuMoO4 is a promising low-permittivity ULTCC material owing to its low sintering temperature and favorable microwave dielectric properties. In this study, Mg substitution was employed to regulate the crystal and local structures of CuMoO4 and to clarify their relationship with microwave dielectric performance. Cu1-xMgxMoO4 (x = 0–0.10) ceramics were synthesized via a conventional solid-state reaction method and sintered at 680–720 °C. Their phase evolution, densification behavior, microstructure, and local lattice vibrations were investigated using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy. Microwave dielectric properties, including relative permittivity (εr), quality factor (Q×f), and temperature coefficient of resonant frequency (τf), were evaluated at 16–18 GHz. The chemical compatibility of the optimized composition with Al electrodes was also examined after co-firing at 700 °C. All compositions sintered at 700 °C exhibited a single triclinic CuMoO4 phase, while the systematic diffraction-peak shift indicated lattice contraction caused by the substitution of Mg2+ for Cu2+. The Cu0.96Mg0.04MoO4 ceramic achieved the highest relative density of 96.5% and exhibited excellent microwave dielectric properties of εr = 8.02, Q×f = 41,034 GHz, and τf = −53.28 ppm/°C. Raman analysis revealed a strong correlation between Q×f and the ν1(A1) symmetric stretching vibration of the [MoO4] tetrahedra near 970 cm-1. The minimized peak splitting at x = 0.04 indicated reduced local structural distortion, corresponding to the maximum Q×f value. In contrast, further Mg substitution increased peak splitting and spectral broadening, resulting in increased local structural disorder and deterioration of Q×f. In addition, no detectable secondary reaction phase or significant elemental interdiffusion was observed between the optimized ceramic and Al electrode after co-firing at 700 °C. Mg substitution effectively regulates the local structural distortion and microwave dielectric properties of CuMoO4 ceramics. The optimized Cu0.96Mg0.04MoO4 composition exhibited a combination of high densification, low permittivity, high Q×f, and ultra-low-temperature sinterability. Its excellent chemical compatibility with Al electrodes further demonstrates its potential as a low-permittivity dielectric material for Al-based high-frequency ULTCC applications.

P2-071.k: ULTCC; Dielectric Ceramics; Microwave Dielectric Properties
P2-071.a: The trend toward higher operating frequencies and greater integration in next-generation wireless communication systems has increased the demand for microwave dielectric ceramics with low relative permittivity (εr), a high quality factor–frequency product (Q×f), and low firing temperatures. Materials for ultra-low-temperature co-fired ceramics (ULTCC) must combine excellent dielectric properties with low firing temperatures, while chemical compatibility between the ceramic and electrode must also be considered when using metal electrodes such as Al. AMoO₄ ceramics (A = Ba, Mg, Mn, and Zn) have been widely investigated as microwave dielectric materials because of their relatively low sintering temperatures and high Q×f values. In particular, MgMoO₄ ceramics sintered at approximately 900 °C have been reported to exhibit εr = 7.07 and Q×f = 79,100 GHz. However, a further reduction in sintering temperature is required for ULTCC applications. In this study, MgMoO₄-based compositions with controlled Mg contents were designed, and the effects of sintering temperature and Mg content on phase composition, density, microstructure, and lattice vibrational characteristics were examined in relation to microwave dielectric properties. Chemical compatibility with Al electrodes was also evaluated. MgMoO₄-based ceramic powders were synthesized by a solid-state reaction method using MgO and MoO₃ as starting materials. The powders were weighed according to the target compositions, wet ball-milled for 24 h using zirconia balls and ethanol, dried, and calcined at 650 °C for 6 h. The calcined powders were ball-milled for an additional 48 h, pressed into disks, and sintered for 12 h at temperatures ranging from 650 to 750 °C in 25 °C increments. Phase composition and microstructure were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), respectively, while density was measured using the Archimedes method. Raman spectroscopy was used to analyze the peak positions and full widths at half maximum (FWHM) of the Mo–O symmetric stretching modes. The microwave relative permittivity (εr), dielectric loss tangent (tan δ), and quality factor–frequency product (Q×f) were evaluated using the Hakki–Coleman method with the TE₀₁₁ resonant mode. XRD and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) were also used to examine possible reactions between the ceramics and Al electrodes. The Q×f of Composition 3 increased markedly from 14,779 GHz at 650 °C to 132,007 GHz at 675 °C. MgMoO₄ and β-MgMo₂O₇ coexisted at 650–675 °C, whereas a phase transformation from β-MgMo₂O₇ to α-MgMo₂O₇ was identified at 700 °C and above. Beyond the maximum attained at 675 °C, Q×f decreased with increasing sintering temperature. Phase composition and dielectric properties were therefore compared as a function of Mg content at 675 °C. The compositions with reduced Mg contents contained a β-MgMo₂O₇ secondary phase in addition to the primary MgMoO₄ phase and exhibited higher relative densities and Q×f values than the reference composition, Composition 1. Whereas Composition 1 exhibited Q×f = 11,922 GHz, Composition 3 achieved the best dielectric properties within the investigated range, with εr = 7.11, Q×f = 132,007 GHz, tan δ ≈ 1.31 × 10⁻⁴, and a relative density of approximately 94%. Further reduction in Mg content decreased Q×f despite relative densities remaining above 93%, with Composition 6 exhibiting Q×f = 112,095 GHz. These results indicate that the differences in Q×f among the compositions cannot be explained by density variations alone. To relate the changes in dielectric properties to lattice vibrational characteristics, the Raman symmetric stretching modes (ν₁) at approximately 956 and 968 cm⁻¹ were analyzed. For Composition 3, the peaks shifted slightly toward higher wavenumbers as the sintering temperature increased from 650 to 675 °C, but shifted toward lower wavenumbers at 700 °C, where the phase transformation was identified. This shift toward lower wavenumbers suggests a reduction in the effective Mo–O bond stiffness and was interpreted as being associated with the decrease in Q×f at higher sintering temperatures. In the compositional comparison at 675 °C, Composition 3 exhibited slightly higher peak wavenumbers and narrower FWHM values than the reference composition, whereas Composition 6 exhibited lower peak wavenumbers and broader FWHM values than Composition 3. Changes in peak position can be associated with changes in the effective Mo–O bond stiffness, while changes in FWHM may reflect variations in structural disorder or vibrational damping. These Raman results were consistent with the lower dielectric loss of Composition 3 and the increased dielectric loss of Composition 6 following further reduction in Mg content. No additional reaction phases were detected by XRD in the specimens incorporating Al electrodes, supporting chemical compatibility with Al under the conditions examined. MgMoO₄-based ceramics with excellent microwave dielectric properties at 675 °C were developed by controlling the Mg content. The optimal composition, Composition 3, exhibited εr = 7.11, Q×f = 132,007 GHz, and tan δ ≈ 1.31 × 10⁻⁴. The dependence of dielectric properties on sintering temperature and composition indicates that both extrinsic and intrinsic loss contributions should be considered to achieve high Q×f values. XRD results also supported chemical compatibility with Al electrodes under the conditions examined. These findings provide an important experimental basis for the compositional design of ULTCC substrate materials that combines favorable dielectric properties with electrode compatibility and are expected to contribute to the development of high-performance microwave dielectric ceramics.

P2-072.a: "KNN-based ceramics are promising lead-free alternatives to PZT because of their relatively high Curie temperature and favorable piezoelectric properties. However, their performance is limited by insufficient piezoelectric response, alkali volatilization, and microstructural instability during sintering. To overcome these limitations, this study focuses on phase-boundary engineering through compositional modification and optimization of the sintering process. By stabilizing multiphase coexistence near room temperature and suppressing excessive grain growth and alkali loss, enhanced piezoelectric performance is expected." (0.96−x)(K0.454Na0.546)(Nb0.95Sb0.05)O3 – xBaZrO3 – 0.04(Bi0.5Sm0.5)0.5(Na0.7K0.2Li0.1)0.5HfO3 (0.00~0.03) ceramics were synthesized using a conventional solid-state reaction method, and a two-step sintering (TSS) process was employed for densification. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed to investigate the crystal structure and phase evolution as a function of BaZrO3 content. In addition, temperature-dependent dielectric properties, the piezoelectric coefficient (d33), P–E hysteresis loops, and S–E curves were measured to evaluate the piezoelectric and ferroelectric properties. Increasing BaZrO₃ content induced a gradual structural evolution from the O phase to O–T, R–O–T, and finally a pseudo-cubic phase, accompanied by a continuous shift of the dielectric anomaly toward lower temperatures and progressive peak broadening. Consistent with this phase evolution, the Curie temperature(Tc) decreased from approximately 215 °C at (x = 0.00) to about 85 °C at (x = 0.03). In contrast, the piezoelectric coefficient (d33) initially increased from approximately 330 pC/N at (x = 0.00) to 550 pC/N at (x = 0.01), reaching a maximum of approximately 680 pC/N at (x = 0.02). This pronounced enhancement is associated with the formation of an R–O–T multiphase coexistence region, which can facilitate polarization rotation and domain switching. However, a further increase in BaZrO₃ content to (x = 0.03) resulted in a significant decrease in (d33) to approximately 220 pC/N, together with the evolution toward a pseudo-cubic structure. These results indicate that (x = 0.02) provides an optimal balance between phase-boundary engineering and piezoelectric performance, whereas excessive BaZrO₃ addition leads to reduced phase anisotropy and deterioration of the piezoelectric response. Various elements were substituted at the A- and B-sites to design a composition with enhanced piezoelectric properties. By further optimizing the BaZrO3 content, a multiphase coexistence region was formed near room temperature, resulting in a significantly enhanced(d33). However, the Curie temperature((TC) tended to decrease with increasing compositional modification, indicating that further optimization is required to achieve both high piezoelectric performance and thermal stability. These results are expected to serve as a useful foundation for the compositional and phase-boundary design of high-performance KNN-based lead-free piezoelectric ceramics.

P2-073.a: Halide perovskite nanocrystals are promising optoelectronic materials with tunable bandgaps through size and morphology control. Representative conventional methods for synthesizing these nanocrystals include hot-injection and ligand-assisted reprecipitation (LARP). However, LARP often yields broad size and morphology distributions, requiring purification. Conversely, hot-injection provides uniform crystals but requires complex preparation, high temperatures (>140 °C), and inert conditions. Crucially, both methods result in low synthetic yields and suffer from batch-to-batch property variations. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new synthetic strategy combining a microfluidic system with a liquid crystal (LC)-based soft template. The microfluidic platform minimizes concentration and temperature gradients within a small volume, enabling continuous synthesis under reproducible conditions. Meanwhile, the responsive, elastic nature of the LC guides nanocrystal formation and restricts uncontrolled growth. This integrated approach produces halide perovskite nanocrystals with improved size and morphology uniformity without extensive post-synthetic purification. Continuous flow operation enables real-time control of injected precursors, offering superior reproducibility within a reactor and between batches. The proposed microfluidic–LC-assisted synthesis successfully addresses key limitations of conventional methods. This strategy provides a scalable platform for producing uniform halide perovskite nanocrystals for optoelectronic applications. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, and RS-2024-00411809)

P2-074.k: Liquid Crystal Template,; Anisotropic Growth Mechanism; Halide Perovskites
P2-074.a: Halide perovskite nanorods have attracted substantial attention for next-generation optoelectronic devices due to their exceptional optoelectrical properties governed by aligned dipole orientations. However, precisely controlling their morphology and size remains a major challenge. Conventional synthetic strategies heavily struggle to regulate nanocrystal shapes because uncontrolled fluid convection at typical fluid interfaces leads to broad size distributions and poor structural reproducibility. Here, we report an advanced synthetic strategy to direct the anisotropic growth of uniform perovskite nanorods by employing a nematic liquid crystal template as an adaptive oil phase at oil-aqueous interfaces. This soft-matter system leverages long-range molecular ordering and unique environmental elasticity to systematically guide the crystallization dynamics. We quantitatively evaluated the thermodynamic energy landscape, surface disclinations, and defect fields to investigate the seed localization and orientation paths. The liquid crystal matrix effectively confined the crystal regrowth, restricting lateral expansion while permitting longitudinal propagation. This physical constraint yielded highly uniform nanorods with a tightly centered aspect ratio distribution. Thermodynamic calculations confirmed that anisotropic growth parallel to the liquid crystal preferred director vector represents the lowest energy state, proving it to be the most energetically stable pathway. Furthermore, this template approach dramatically accelerated phase transition kinetics and enhanced photoluminescence quantum yield. This highly versatile liquid crystal-mediated framework successfully bridges soft-matter physics with nanoscale material engineering. These insights provide a programmable framework for shape-controlled halide perovskite nanocrystals, significantly advancing the structural design for high-performance optoelectronic devices.

P2-075.k: Transfer Pirnting; Quantum Dot; Quantum Dot Light-emitting Diode
P2-075.a: As next-generation displays evolve toward high-resolution, flexible, and deformable form factors, quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QLEDs) have attracted considerable attention. Quantum dots (QDs) offer high photoluminescence quantum yields, narrow emission spectra, and wide color gamuts; however, achieving high-definition RGB subpixel patterning without compromising device performance remains challenging. We developed transfer-printing strategies for high-definition patterning of QD emissive layers and their integration into QLEDs. The printing process enables precise spatial control of QD layers while preserving their optical properties and promoting densely packed emissive films. Transfer-printed QD layers exhibit improved film uniformity and close packing, suppressing leakage current and enhancing external quantum efficiency. The approach enables high-resolution RGB patterning and can be further extended to ultrathin and intrinsically stretchable QLED platforms. Patterned multicolor QLEDs were demonstrated in mechanically compliant form factors relevant to wearable applications, including electronic tattoos. Transfer printing provides a versatile route to simultaneously achieve high-definition patterning, efficient electroluminescence, and mechanical deformability in QLEDs. These capabilities establish transfer-printed QLEDs as a promising platform for next-generation high-resolution displays beyond conventional foldable and rollable technologies.

P2-076.a: Ultrahigh-resolution QD-LEDs require effective electrical isolation to suppress pixel crosstalk and parasitic emission. We developed photo-assisted self-insulating patterning, where selective UV oxidation converts QDs into highly resistive regions without addtional dielectric layers. Self-insulating patterning suppressed leakage current and parasitic emission, enabling monochrome QD-LEDs up to 8,000 PPI and RGB devices exceeding 4,000 PPI with stable electrical and optical performance. Photo-assisted SIP provides a simple and scalable route toward ultrahigh-resolution full-color QD-LED microdisplays.

P2-077.k: Chiral Perovskite Nanocrystals; Ligand Exchange; Circular Dichroism (CD)
P2-077.a: Chirality, which enables the selective absorption and emission of circularly polarized light (CPL), is essential for next-generation photonic applications. Halide perovskite nanocrystals (PNCs) exhibit excellent optical properties such as high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) and narrow full width at half maximum (FWHM), leading to superior color purity. When PNCs acquire chirality, they can serve as promising sources of CPL. One of the most widely used methods for introducing chirality into achiral PNCs is ligand exchange. It can transfer chirality from organic molecules to inorganic PNCs, resulting in chiroptical responses. Most previous studies on chiral PNCs have primarily focused on chiral amine ligands for inducing chirality. As a result, the influence of carboxylic acid ligands on chirality transfer remains poorly understood. CsPbX3 (X = Br and I) NCs were synthesized using a hot-injection method. Then, a chiral solution was added to the purified CsPbX3 NCs solution. A chiral carboxylic acid ligand was introduced onto the surface of CsPbBr3 NCs via post-treatment. The PLQY of chiral ligand-treated CsPbBr3 NCs increased to ~93%, compared with ~54% for the pristine CsPbBr3 NCs. The ligand post-treatment induced a distinct circular dichroism (CD) signal near ~330 nm for CsPbBr3 NCs and ~400 nm for CsPbI3 NCs, while preserving the characteristic excitonic absorption and photoluminescence (PL) near ~510 nm and ~680 nm, respectively. X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) results revealed no significant changes in the crystal structure or morphology after ligand post-treatment. But, Raman analysis suggested the attachment of chiral ligands onto the PNC surfaces. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) revealed a shift of the Pb 4f peaks toward lower binding energies and a decrease in the Pb0 component, suggesting effective surface defect passivation by the chiral ligands. These findings demonstrate that chiral carboxylic acid ligands can effectively induce chiroptical responses, providing insight into the role of carboxylic acid ligands in chirality transfer. In this study, a chiral carboxylic acid ligand was introduced onto the surface of PNCs to investigate the influence of a carboxylic acid ligand on chirality transfer. Chiral ligand binding induces a chiral surface environment and electronic interactions, resulting in distinct CD responses while preserving the crystal structure and morphology of the PNCs. The halide composition influences the absorption and CD signals. Also, effective ligand exchange passivates surface defects, resulting in enhanced PLQY. These results highlight the important role of surface ligand chemistry in controlling chirality transfer and chiroptical properties in PNCs.

P2-078.k: Flexible QLED; High Brightness; Single Wall Carbon Nanotube
P2-078.a: Flexible quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (QLEDs) are promising for next-generation wearable and outdoor displays owing to their high brightness, color purity, and mechanical flexibility. For outdoor applications, stable operation at luminance above 100,000 cd m⁻² is required to ensure visibility under intense ambient light. However, achieving such high luminance requires high current density (j), which generates substantial Joule heat and accelerates thermal degradation. This issue is particularly severe in flexible QLEDs using polymer substrates such as polyethylene naphthalate (PEN), whose low thermal conductivity limits heat dissipation. In this work, we employ single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) as a transparent bottom electrode integrated with an Al heat sink on a flexible PEN substrate. The SWCNT electrode combines high optical transparency, electrical conductivity, and mechanical flexibility with efficient heat spreading. This thermally managed architecture enables stable high-brightness flexible QLEDs for next-generation wearable and outdoor display applications. Flexible QLEDs were fabricated on PEN substrates incorporating an Al heat sink and SWCNT bottom electrodes. A 100-nm-thick Al layer was deposited by thermal evaporation to form the heat sink structure, followed by direct deposition of SWCNTs grown by floating-catalyst chemical vapor deposition (FC-CVD). PEDOT:PSS (Al4083) was subsequently spin-coated at 3,000 rpm for 40 s as the hole injection layer and annealed at 120 °C for 20 min. TFB was then spin-coated at 3,000 rpm for 30 s as the hole transport layer and annealed at 120 °C for 20 min. Commercial CdSe/ZnS red quantum dots were spin coated at 2,000 rpm for 30 s as the emissive layer and annealed at 100 °C for 10 min. A ZnMgO nanoparticle layer was then spin coated at 3,000 rpm for 30 s as the electron transport layer and annealed at 100 °C for 10 min. Finally, a 100-nm-thick Al cathode was deposited by thermal evaporation. The current density–voltage–luminance characteristics of the QLEDs were characterized using a Keithley 2400 source-measure unit combined with an Ocean Insight HR6 spectrometer. Thermal transport in the flexible QLEDs was analyzed using COMSOL Multiphysics. The thermal conductivity of the flexible polymer substrate was set to 0.3 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, and heat dissipation to the surrounding air was incorporated through a convective heat transfer boundary condition. COMSOL heat transfer simulations were performed to evaluate the thermal-management capability of the SWCNT electrode. At an applied heat power of 30 mW, the maximum temperature of the SWCNT-based device was approximately 17% lower than that of the device employing a conventional ITO electrode. The reduced maximum temperature indicates that the SWCNT electrode effectively facilitates heat spreading and suppresses localized heat accumulation during high j operation. Flexible QLEDs employing SWCNT bottom electrodes were subsequently fabricated, and their current density–voltage–luminance (J–V–L) characteristics were evaluated. The SWCNT-based flexible QLEDs maintained stable operation up to a current density of 1.4 A cm⁻² without noticeable thermally induced degradation and achieved a maximum luminance of 110,571 cd m⁻². A clear difference in EQE roll-off behavior was also observed between the ITO- and SWCNT-based devices. The ITO-based QLED exhibited the onset of EQE roll-off at approximately 300 mA cm⁻² and showed an EQE droop of approximately 22% at 1 A cm⁻², whereas the SWCNT-based QLED exhibited only approximately 9% EQE droop at the same current density. All these observations indicate that SWCNT electrodes suppress device overheating even under high j operation.

P2-079.a: Silver, gold, and their alloyed chalcogenide quantum dots (QDs) offer heavy-metal-free access to the second near-infrared (NIR-II) window, but silver chalcogenide QDs (Ag2S, Ag2Se) suffer from limited stability due to the high mobility of Ag⁺ ions within their vacancy-rich lattice. This same mobility also frustrates direct, well-defined core/shell growth, as interdiffusion obscures the compositional interface before a stable shell forms. We synthesized alloyed Ag–Au–Se/Ag–Au–S core/shell QDs via a sequential, topotactic cation-exchange strategy that decouples anion-sublattice formation from cation incorporation, bypassing the interdiffusion limitations of direct synthesis. Gold precursor reactivity was tuned to control phase selectivity, with a less reactive precursor favoring the intended alloy phase. Pairing an alloyed Ag–Au–Se core with an alloyed Ag–Au–S shell markedly increased PLQY relative to the bare core and improved colloidal stability. By adjusting core size and shell thickness, we obtained QDs emitting at approximately 1150 nm with an absolute PLQY of up to 85%, among the highest reported for heavy-metal-free NIR-II emitters. Precursor-reactivity-controlled, sequential cation exchange is established as a general strategy for accessing compositionally complex, vacancy-rich chalcogenide QDs inaccessible by direct synthesis, with potential applications in bioimaging, infrared LEDs, and NIR photodetection.

P2-080.k: Perovskite Quantum Dot Light-Emitting; Transition Dipole Moment; Ligand Engineering
P2-080.a: Perovskite quantum dot light-emitting diodes (PeQLEDs) have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation displays and lighting applications. As the internal quantum efficiency of state-of-the-art PeQLEDs approaches unity, further improvements in device performance increasingly depend on enhancing photon extraction by reducing optical losses. In particular, the orientation of transition dipole moments (TDMs) plays a critical role in determining the light outcoupling efficiency (ηout). Here, we investigate how nanocrystal (NC) shape and stacking behavior influence TDM alignment within the emissive layer. To regulate TDM orientation, a facile ligand-exchange strategy using bifunctional 1,5-naphthalenedisulfonic acid (NDSA) was employed. The NDSA ligand simultaneously passivates surface defects, improves charge transport, promotes long-range NC stacking, and modifies the dielectric environment of the emissive layer. The combined effects of NDSA treatment increase the fraction of in-plane TDMs from 60% to 70%, leading to an enhancement of the calculated light outcoupling efficiency (ηout) from 16.15% to 20.09%. Consequently, the optimized PeQLEDs achieve a peak external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 22.63% at a luminance of 5,127 cd m⁻² and a maximum luminance of 13,950 cd m⁻², significantly outperforming untreated devices. Furthermore, the EQE remains above 20% over a wide luminance range of 400–8,000 cd m⁻², while the operational lifetime under ambient conditions with encapsulation is extended by approximately 400%. These results demonstrate that engineering nanocrystal stacking and TDM orientation through ligand design is an effective strategy for simultaneously enhancing photon extraction, device efficiency, and operational stability. This work provides new insights into transition dipole engineering and offers a practical design strategy for developing high-performance PeQLEDs.

P2-081.a: Diagnosing selective IgA deficiency (SIgAD) requires the highly reliable detection of IgA below 0.07 μg/mL in 1,000-fold diluted serum. Conventional ratiometric fluorescence assays typically rely on dye/QD-loaded carrier beads where reference signals merely reflect bead quantity rather than probe activity. To overcome this limitation, we developed a novel ratiometric sandwich immunoassay utilizing "antibody-barcoded probes" with a built-in inner reference, where green quantum dots (GQDs) are directly conjugated to capture antibodies and red QDs (RQDs) to detection antibodies. By utilizing these functional antibodies as active fluorescent probes themselves, rather than relying on passive fluorescent beads, the green reference signal directly monitors the density of active, functionalized capture probes on magnetic beads (MB@GQD-anti-hIgA). The MB@GQD-anti-hIgA capture probe was prepared via direct conjugation of GQDs to the capture antibody. The two-color sandwich immunoreaction involving the target IgA and the detection probe ("RQD-anti-hIgA" ) was performed in microtubes, followed by magnetic separation and washing. The resulting immunocomplexes were transferred to a black 96-well plate, and dual emissions (λₑₘ = 522/618 nm) were simultaneously monitored under a single excitation wavelength (λₑₓ = 370 nm) using a microplate reader. With increasing IgA concentration, the GQD reference signal representing the active probe density remained highly stable, while the RQD reporter signal increased in a dose-dependent manner. The ratiometric signal (I₆₁₈/I₅₂₂) exhibited excellent linearity (R² > 0.99) in the range of 0 to 2.5 µg/mL with a limit of detection (LOD) of approximately 0.08 µg/mL, closely approaching the critical SIgAD diagnostic threshold. This self-calibrating, antibody-barcoded platform successfully minimizes physical and matrix variations by directly linking the reference signal to functional target-binding events, offering a robust and highly reliable tool for clinical diagnostics.

P2-082.a: Colloidal semiconductor nanoplatelets (NPLs) possess highly anisotropic geometries that strongly influence their interparticle interactions. Their large basal faces can promote aggregation, making colloidal stability an important issue for solution processing. In this study, we investigated how NPL thickness affects dispersion stability by altering the relative contributions of face and edge interactions. CdSe/CdS core/shell NPLs with systematically varied thicknesses were synthesized by colloidal atomic layer deposition. Their morphology and surface ligand coverage were characterized by transmission electron microscopy and thermogravimetric analysis. Dispersion stability was quantified from absorbance changes after RM257-induced aggregation, and pair interaction potentials were calculated for face-to-face and edge-to-edge configurations. Thicker NPLs retained a larger dispersed fraction under depletion-inducing conditions. The calculated face-to-face attractive potential showed only a minor dependence on thickness, whereas the edge-to-edge steric barrier increased substantially. These results indicate that increasing thickness enhances the contribution of repulsive edge interactions, thereby hindering close interparticle contact and suppressing aggregation. The dispersion stability of semiconductor NPLs is governed by the geometry-dependent balance between attractive face interactions and repulsive edge interactions. NPL thickness therefore provides a practical structural parameter for tuning colloidal stability and improving the solution processability of anisotropic nanocrystals.

P2-083.k: Magnetic Induction Heating; Dry Reforming of Methane; Core-shell Catalyst
P2-083.a: Dry reforming of methane (DRM) converts CH4 and CO2 into synthesis gas, but its high reaction temperature and catalyst deactivation remain major challenges. Magnetic induction heating (MIH) directly heats magnetic materials under an alternating magnetic field and may reduce heat-transfer losses associated with conventional furnace heating. A structured catalyst consisting of a Co magnetic core, a Ni active phase, and a CeO2-based oxide layer was prepared for MIH-driven DRM. Catalytic tests were performed in a fixed-bed induction reactor at 650 °C with 30 mg of catalyst and a GHSV of 100 L g−1 h−1. Product gases were analyzed by online gas chromatography. The same catalyst was also tested using conventional thermal heating for comparison. Under MIH, approximately 80% CH4 conversion was achieved at 650 °C, whereas conventional thermal heating required 850 °C to reach a similar conversion. During a 100 h stability test, CH4 conversion, CO2 conversion, and the H2/CO ratio decreased by 14.8%, 6.3%, and 12.1%, respectively. Characterization of the spent catalyst indicated carbon deposition and changes in the catalyst structure, suggesting that deactivation and side reactions remain important issues. The Co-based magnetic catalyst enabled rapid heating and high DRM activity under MIH at a lower measured temperature than conventional heating. These results demonstrate the potential of MIH for energy-efficient DRM. Further work will focus on improving catalyst stability, suppressing the reverse water-gas shift reaction, and identifying the role of magnetic induction in the observed catalytic performance.

P2-084.k: Dry Reforming of Methane; Magnetic Induction Heating; Catalyst Design
P2-084.a: Dry reforming of methane (DRM) is a promising process for syngas production and greenhouse gas utilization. However, conventional heating requires high reaction temperatures, which can promote excessive methane decomposition, carbon deposition, and metal sintering, thereby limiting long-term catalyst stability. Magnetic induction heating (MIH) enables localized heat generation through selective energy delivery to magnetic materials, potentially allowing DRM operation at relatively low bulk temperatures. Therefore, the design of interfaces between heating components and catalytic active sites is important for efficient DRM under MIH conditions. A nanostructured catalyst was prepared and evaluated for DRM under MIH. The reaction was carried out in a fixed-bed quartz reactor equipped with a high-frequency induction heating system. Catalyst stability was evaluated by continuous operation for over 70 h. The physicochemical properties of the catalyst before and after the reaction were characterized by XRD, Raman spectroscopy, TGA, and TEM-EDX. The catalyst, consisting of magnetic Co as the heating component, Ni as the active metal, and basic La2O3, showed stable DRM activity under MIH. The catalyst maintained its activity without significant deactivation during more than 70 h of continuous operation. The combination of magnetic Co, active Ni, and basic La2O3 allowed stable DRM operation under MIH. These results demonstrate the potential of combining localized induction heating with interfacial catalyst design for low-temperature DRM.

P2-085.k: Crystal Growth Kinetics; 2D Ruddlesden Popper Phase Perovskite; Critical Radius of Nuclei
P2-085.a: Ruddlesden–Popper (RP)-phase perovskite nanoplatelets (NPLs), with formula (RNH3)2An−1BnX3n+1, form layered structures of alternating 2D metal-halide octahedral sheets and organic spacer layers via RNH3 ligands at the A-site along the (100) plane. This reduced dimensionality induces quantum and dielectric confinement effects, yielding a larger bandgap than 3D ABX3 perovskite nanocrystals (PNCs) of identical halide composition [1]. Conventional low-temperature syntheses suppress (100)-plane growth but promote nucleation via Pb0 metal clusters instead of ABX3 nuclei, generating intrinsic Pb0 defects and low photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQY) [2]. However, raising the synthesis temperature makes it difficult to control the crystal growth rate. Synthesis of CsPbBr3 nanocrystals CsPbBr3 NCs were synthesized using a hot-injection method under various parameters (synthesis temperature, chain length of ligand, and the concentration of ligand). In this study, we apply the critical radius of nuclei from classical nucleation theory to analyze CsPbBr3 growth kinetics and the 3D-to-2D dimensionality transition. Tuning ligand chain length, temperature, and concentration adjusts the critical radius: larger values suppress (100)-plane growth, producing NPLs with emission blue-shifted relative to ~510 nm 3D CsPbBr3, whereas smaller values favor 3D nanocrystals This behavior arises because a small critical radius impedes (100)-plane suppression, limiting growth-rate control and promoting 3D structures, while a large critical radius enables effective (100)-plane suppression, facilitating 2D RP-phase NPL formation.

P2-086.k: PbS Quantum Dots; Photoelectrochemical Hydrogen Production; Annealing And Chemical Reconstruction
P2-086.a: PbS quantum dots (QDs) are promising sensitizers for photoelectrochemical (PEC) hydrogen production because of their broad light absorption and tunable electronic properties. However, structural imperfections and charge recombination limit their performance. This study investigates annealing and chemical reconstruction (ACR) as a strategy to improve ZnS-passivated, PbS QD-sensitized TiO₂ photoanodes. PbS QDs were deposited on mesoporous TiO₂ by successive ionic layer adsorption and reaction, followed by ZnS passivation. The photoanodes were annealed at 200–300 °C and subsequently reconstructed in a sulfide-containing electrolyte. Structural and spectroscopic characterization was combined with PEC measurements under AM 1.5G illumination (100 mW cm⁻²) in a sulfide/sulfite electrolyte, electrochemical analyses, and direct hydrogen quantification. Annealing induced PbS oxidation to PbSO₄, whereas chemical reconstruction restored the PbS phase with increased crystallite size. The optimized treatment at 250 °C for 30 min followed by reconstruction increased the photocurrent density from 9.8 to 23.8 mA cm⁻² at 0.6 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode. The treated photoanode exhibited enhanced incident-photon-to-current conversion efficiency, prolonged electron lifetime, and reduced interfacial charge-transfer resistance. Hydrogen measurements yielded an average production rate of 239.8 μmol cm⁻² h⁻¹ with a Faradaic efficiency of approximately 87–91%. Controlled annealing followed by chemical reconstruction improves the structural and interfacial properties of PbS QD-sensitized photoanodes. This approach enhances charge utilization and PEC hydrogen production, providing a practical strategy for improving QD-based photoelectrodes.

P2-087.k: Electrotactile Feedback, Wearable Haptics, Electronic Textiles, Conductive Hydrogel, Extended Reality
P2-087.a: Electrical stimulation holds significant promise for applications ranging from tactile feedback to tissue regeneration, wound healing, and pain management. At a full-body scale, such systems can simultaneously provide spatiotemporal haptic feedback and serve as therapeutic platforms in extended reality (XR). However, consistent stimulation across the body is hindered by anatomical variability, individual differences in sensory thresholds, and pressure-dependent skin–electrode impedance, while conventional adhesive or non-breathable materials cause sweat accumulation and skin irritation. We developed a textile-based electrical stimulation suit (TESS) on a lightweight, breathable compression garment. Stretchable Ag–PU interconnects were printed directly into the textile, and dehydration-mitigating conductive hydrogel (DMCH) electrodes were laminated onto them and positioned according to region-specific two-point discrimination thresholds. Integrated pressure sensors enabled real-time calibration of stimulation based on local garment pressure and impedance. DMCH electrodes maintained low impedance and resisted dehydration without encapsulation. The functional components added only 14.5% to the textile weight while preserving breathability. Four distinct sensations—touch, tickling, roughness, and pressure—were recognized with 89.4% average accuracy. Under sweating, current increased only 1.1–1.2×, versus up to 9.9× for commercial TENS electrodes. Pressure-based feedback yielded uniform perceived intensity across body regions and users, and the suit was demonstrated in VR gaming, AR interaction, and VR-assisted tremor suppression. The proposed suit enables consistent, comfortable, and personalized full-body electrical stimulation, offering a practical route toward combining haptic feedback and therapy in XR environments.

P2-088.a: Photovoltaics for buildings, mobility, and wearable systems must conform to curved and deformable surfaces. Yet planar modules and monolithic stretchable designs face limitations in geometric adaptability, active-area utilization, scalable fabrication, and interconnect reliability. These studies explore mechanical architecture as a route to programmable and scalable freeform photovoltaics. Two complementary platforms were developed. A mechanically origami-coded interlocked 3D kirigami structure, reconfigured planar photovoltaic units through a single extension–release cycle. In parallel, standardized auxetic units comprising rigid device islands, compliant hinges, folding-enabled interconnectors, and selectively activatable interconnects were assembled into topology-tunable arrays. Mechanical and photovoltaic performance was evaluated. The origami-coded platform enabled controlled three-dimensional transformation while preserving photovoltaic operation under large and repeated deformation, thereby mitigating the conventional trade-off between mechanical stretchability and active-area utilization. The modular auxetic platform supported scalable expansion, geometric reconfiguration, and conformal deployment on curved surfaces without redesigning the fundamental building unit. In both systems, mechanically compliant composite interconnects maintained stable electrical pathways across deformation-intensive regions and supported reliable device- and system-level operation. Together, these studies establish a multiscale framework in which geometric programming mitigates the deformability–active-area trade-off, while modular assembly decouples unit fabrication from system size and shape. This strategy provides a route toward deployable photovoltaic systems for complex architectural, mobile, and wearable surfaces.

P2-089.a: Electrical stimulation is a well-established strategy for accelerating wound healing, as endogenous electric fields direct cell migration and proliferation via galvanotaxis. However, existing electrically active wound dressings require external power sources or complex circuitry, significantly limiting their practicality in wearable and point-of-care applications. A self-powered, battery-free platform that autonomously generates therapeutic electric fields remains highly desirable. An alginate/polyacrylamide double network hydrogel was formulated as the base matrix, providing mechanical toughness and conformal skin adhesion. Zn and Ti microparticles were homogeneously dispersed into the hydrogel ink and patterned onto a flexible substrate via screen printing, enabling scalable and spatially controlled fabrication of the wound patch. In the moist wound environment, the Zn–Ti galvanic pair drives spontaneous redox reactions Zn undergoes anodic oxidation, releasing Zn²⁺ ions while Ti serves as the cathodic site, generating a sustained, self-powered electric field of 350 V/m across the wound bed, which falls within the physiologically relevant range for electrotaxis. This autonomous electric field promoted directional fibroblast migration, keratinocyte proliferation, and angiogenesis, accelerating wound closure. This work demonstrates a battery-free wound healing platform that integrates redox-driven bioelectricity, mechanical compliance, and antibacterial functionality into a single screen-printed hydrogel patch. The approach offers a practical and scalable route toward next-generation self-powered wound care devices.

P2-090.a: Liquid metal (LM)-based stretchable electrodes offer high conductivity but suffer from uncontrolled aggregation and direct contact between conductive domains, leading to local short-circuiting and unstable electrical pathways. Ultrasonic treatment was applied to modulate the dispersion and surface state of LM, followed by integration with MXene within an elastic polymer matrix to construct a hybrid conductive network. The ultrasonically structured LM suppressed excessive direct contacts while enabling strain-induced reconnection of conductive pathways. Combined with the MXene percolation backbone, the hybrid electrode exhibited reduced resistance variation, suppressed hysteresis, and stable electrical performance under repeated deformation. This work demonstrates that ultrasonic programming of LM connectivity, coupled with MXene-LM hybridization, provides an effective strategy for suppressing short-circuiting while enabling dynamically reconfigurable conduction in stretchable electrodes.

P2-091.k: Functional Polymers; Wearable Electronics; Organic Electronics
