P2-091.a: Wearable and skin-integrated electronics require functional materials that combine electrical performance with softness, flexibility, and mechanical adaptability. Functional polymers are particularly attractive because their electrical, mechanical, and interfacial properties can be engineered to meet the diverse requirements of soft electronic systems, including energy conversion, sensing, and information processing. Functional polymer materials and device structures were strategically designed by controlling material composition, morphology, interfaces, and processing conditions. Various fabrication and structural engineering approaches were employed to achieve mechanically compliant and electrically functional devices. Their electrical, mechanical, and device-level characteristics were systematically evaluated under conditions relevant to wearable and soft electronic applications. The engineered polymer systems demonstrated effective integration of electrical functionality with mechanical compliance. Material and structural engineering enabled improvements in device performance, mechanical durability, and operational functionality. These approaches were applicable across different classes of soft electronic devices, including energy-harvesting, sensing, and memory-related systems. Strategic engineering of functional polymers provides a versatile route toward high-performance wearable and skin-integrated electronics. By jointly considering material properties, device architecture, and manufacturing processes, polymer-based electronics can support increasingly integrated, adaptive, and multifunctional platforms for future healthcare, robotics, and human–machine interfaces.

P2-092.k: Polymer Semiconductors; Stretchable Electronics; Skin-Integrated Devices
P2-092.a: Skin-integrated electronics require active materials that can simultaneously provide reliable electronic functionality, mechanical compliance, and long-term stability under complex deformation. Conventional semiconductor materials, however, are intrinsically rigid and are therefore difficult to integrate with soft, deformable biological interfaces. Functional polymer semiconductors offer a promising materials platform for overcoming this limitation by combining charge transport with molecularly engineered mechanical and interfacial properties. We developed intrinsically stretchable polymer semiconductor systems through molecular and nanoscale engineering of semiconducting polymers, elastomeric matrices, dielectric interfaces, and compliant electrodes. Nanoconfinement and polymer-network engineering were employed to preserve charge-transport pathways during uniaxial and biaxial deformation. Dynamic intermolecular interactions and chemically functionalized elastomers were further incorporated to introduce self-healing, biocompatible, memory, and neuromorphic functionalities into stretchable transistor platforms. The resulting polymer transistors maintained stable electronic characteristics under large uniaxial and biaxial strains and repeated mechanical deformation. By tailoring the semiconductor-elastomer and semiconductor-dielectric interfaces, additional functionalities including autonomous self-healing, environmental stability, charge storage, and synaptic dynamics were realized without sacrificing mechanical compliance. These materials enabled stretchable transistor arrays and functional circuits for skin-integrated applications, including implantable bioelectronics, photo-responsive memory and logic devices, and neuromorphic computing systems capable of processing temporal signals under mechanically deformed conditions. These results demonstrate that polymer semiconductors can evolve beyond their conventional role as mechanically compliant sensing materials and serve as multifunctional active materials integrating sensing, memory, and computing capabilities. Such skin-inspired semiconductor platforms provide a materials foundation for future wearable and bio-integrated electronic systems that can conform to, interact with, and ultimately process information directly on soft biological surfaces.

P2-093.a: Global population growth, climate change, and plant disease outbreaks are intensifying pressure on food security, underscoring the need for advanced plant health monitoring technologies. Conventional imaging, spectroscopic, and wearable sensors suffer from low sensitivity/selectivity, complicated signal processing, or capture only ambient microclimate rather than the plant's own physiological status. We developed electronic plant (e-plant) devices for real-time physiological monitoring. A leaf-attachable multimodal sensor patch integrating volatile organic compound, transpiration/humidity, and temperature sensors was applied to the stomata-rich abaxial leaf surface of tomato plants under abiotic stresses (drought, overwatering, salinity, darkness) and biotic stress (Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus infection). A photo-curable deep eutectic solvent gel electrode was attached to the stem for impedance-based sap flow/hydration monitoring with machine-learning diagnosis. A micro-cracked, dome-patterned strain sensor was wrapped around the stem to track diameter growth and diurnal turgor fluctuations. The leaf sensor detected distinct, stress-specific patterns in VOC emission, humidity, and temperature during abiotic and biotic stress events. The gel electrode showed strong adhesion, biocompatibility, and long-term stability, with impedance tracking dehydration, rehydration, and salinity level. The strain sensor accurately captured stem growth and day-night diameter oscillations, consistent with vernier caliper and LVDT references. These e-plant devices, combined with wireless transmission, provide a real-time, physiology-based platform for monitoring plant health, establishing a materials and device foundation for translating wearable electronics toward precision, sensor-driven smart agriculture.

P2-094.a: Metal-halide perovskites have emerged as highly promising emitters for next-generation light-emitting diodes (LEDs), a key technology for energy-efficient lighting and displays, owing to their high photoluminescence quantum yield, high color purity, and facile color tunability. However, perovskites inherently suffer from internal defects, which quench charge carriers through non-radiative recombination and limit the efficiency of perovskite LEDs (PeLEDs). Owing to their ionic nature, these defects migrate under operation, giving rise to peculiar behavior such as luminance overshooting and accelerated degradation. Critically, these defects reside both within the perovskite bulk and at the interfaces. We develop molecular and structural defect-engineering strategies that span the bulk and the interface of perovskite emitters. Molecular approaches include a strong-nucleophile dithiol additive, a series of sulfonyl-chloride additives with varied substituent positions, and a mixed self-assembled monolayer (SAM) for the buried hole-transport-layer/perovskite interface. As a structural approach, a corner-sharing 6H perovskite polytype is introduced to intervene coherently at the halide position. Passivation efficacy and recombination dynamics are examined through steady-state and time-resolved photoluminescence, transient electroluminescence analysis, and device-level characterization of PeLEDs. The dithiol additive simultaneously suppresses non-radiative recombination within the grains and at the buried interface, affording single-cation polycrystalline PeLEDs with an external quantum efficiency (EQE) of up to 23.46% (Small 2025, 21, 2405272). The substituent position of the sulfonyl-chloride additive governs its passivation efficacy in the bulk, enabling efficient sky-blue PeLEDs. The mixed SAM overcomes the incomplete surface coverage and phosphonic-acid self-association that limit single-component SAMs, reducing interfacial non-radiative recombination and improving the efficiency and operational stability of green PeLEDs. The 6H perovskite polytype screens the shallow-level iodide vacancy (VI+) conventionally regarded as benign, yielding ultra-long carrier lifetimes together with high efficiency and stability (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 5632). These results show that resolving defect passivation across both bulk and interface, and across both molecular and structural levers, provides a coherent design framework for high-performance perovskite light-emitting diodes. This framework offers a general route toward efficient and stable perovskite optoelectronic devices for energy-efficient light sources.

P2-095.a: Upconversion phosphors have attracted significant attention due to their ability to convert near-infrared light into visible emissions through energy transfer processes. In this study, chemically stable Yb³⁺/Er³⁺ co-doped YMoO₄ phosphors were synthesized and investigated for their luminescence properties and potential applications in flexible photonic devices and anti-counterfeiting systems. Yb³⁺/Er³⁺ co-doped YMoO₄ phosphors were synthesized by a co-precipitation method using Y(NO₃)₃·6H₂O, Na₂MoO₄, Yb(NO₃)₃·H₂O, and Er(NO₃)₃·H₂O as starting materials. After mixing the precursor solutions and stirring for 30 min at room temperature, the obtained precipitates were collected by centrifugation, washed with deionized water, and dried at 80 °C overnight. The dried powders were subsequently calcined at 800 °C for 2 h to obtain crystalline YMoO₄ phosphors. XRD analysis confirmed the formation of a single-phase tetragonal YMoO₄ structure and revealed lattice distortion induced by Yb³⁺/Er³⁺ doping. Strong green upconversion emission was observed under 980 nm excitation, with temperature-dependent luminescence enabling reliable optical thermometry. Flexible PDMS composites retained their UC characteristics and demonstrated excellent performance in IR-LED integration and anti-counterfeiting applications. Yb³⁺/Er³⁺ co-doped YMoO₄ phosphors exhibited strong green upconversion emission under 980 nm excitation. Rare-earth doping induced lattice distortion, influencing energy transfer and thermally coupled level populations, resulting in reliable optical thermometry with high sensitivity. Flexible PDMS composites retained their UC properties and demonstrated potential for temperature sensing, photonic devices, and anti-counterfeiting applications.

P2-096.k: Amorphous Boron Oxynitride; RF Sputtering; Moisture Stability
P2-096.a: Flexible electronic devices are subjected to repeated mechanical deformation, moisture, and temperature fluctuations, requiring thin insulating and passivation layers with reliable electrical and environmental stability. Boron nitride-based films are promising for such applications because of their wide bandgap, excellent dielectric properties, and low dielectric constant. However, conventional CVD and ALD routes may face limitations in processing time, precursor handling, and large-area productivity. In this study, amorphous boron oxynitride (a-BON) thin films were deposited by radio-frequency sputtering. The effects of RF power, substrate temperature, process gas composition, and gas flow rate on film composition and moisture stability were systematically investigated. Raman spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy were used to analyze chemical bonding states and moisture-induced reaction products. The moisture reactivity of the a-BON films varied markedly with the sputtering conditions. Films with lower relative contributions of B–O and boron oxide-like bonding exhibited improved environmental stability. Current–voltage measurements were used to evaluate electrical insulation, while optical bandgaps were extracted from Tauc plots. These results established correlations among deposition conditions, chemical composition, moisture stability, and electrical and optical properties. Appropriate control of RF sputtering parameters effectively improved the moisture stability of a-BON thin films. The optimized films show potential as multifunctional insulating and passivation layers that simultaneously provide electrical isolation and environmental protection for future flexible electronic devices.

P2-097.k: Molybdenum Disulfide; Flexible PH Sensor; Functionalized Nanomaterial
P2-097.a: Continuous and noninvasive monitoring of physiological information is essential for wearable healthcare systems. Among various biomarkers, pH in human body fluids provides valuable information on physiological homeostasis and can support real-time health assessment. Molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) is attractive for chemical sensing because of its large surface-to-volume ratio, excellent electrical properties, and good compatibility with flexible media. However, the limited surface reactivity of pristine MoS2 can restrict ion adsorption and reduce sensitivity. Wearable pH sensors were fabricated using functionalized MoS2 as the active sensing layer. Their pH-dependent electrical characteristics were investigated in electrolyte conditions relevant to human body fluids and evaluated over the physiological pH range. The sensing behavior of functionalized MoS2 was directly compared with that of pristine MoS2 to determine the effect of material modification. Functionalization promoted stronger interactions between the MoS2 and hydrogen ions, resulting in a more distinct pH-dependent electrical response than that of pristine MoS2. The modified sensing layer enabled improved discrimination of pH variations under physiologically relevant ionic conditions while maintaining stable device operation. Its thin and flexible configuration further supported conformal integration with wearable substrates. Functionalized MoS2 provides an effective approach for improving pH sensitivity in wearable chemical sensors. The proposed platform shows potential for continuous monitoring of physiological pH variations in sweat, tears, and other body fluids, contributing to the development of sensitive, conformable, and skin-compatible bioelectronic systems.

P2-098.k: Single-walled Carbon Nanotubes (SWCNTs); Azide-functionalized Conjugated Polymer; UV-induced Crosslinking
P2-098.a: Stretchable semiconducting single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) networks have attracted considerable attention for next-generation wearable and deformable electronics. However, further improving their mechanical robustness and stretchability while maintaining high semiconducting purity remains a significant challenge. In this work, we introduce a conjugated polymer bearing azide functional groups that selectively wraps semiconducting SWCNTs, allowing them to be separated from metallic tubes and assembled into networks of high semiconducting purity. After the material is coated onto elastomeric substrates, exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light activates the azide groups, generating reactive nitrene intermediates. These nitrenes drive covalent bond formation both at SWCNT–SWCNT junctions and across the SWCNT–substrate interface, producing an interconnected network that adheres strongly to the underlying elastomer. As a result, the UV-crosslinked thin films exhibit markedly greater stretchability than their non-crosslinked counterparts, as confirmed through film-on-elastomer testing. We attribute this improved stretchability to the formation of covalent linkages at the SWCNT–SWCNT and SWCNT–substrate interfaces. Taken together, our results demonstrate that combining azide-functionalized polymer wrapping with UV-induced crosslinking provides a versatile and effective route to simultaneously obtain highly purified semiconducting SWCNT networks and mechanically robust materials for stretchable electronics.

P2-099.k: Neuromorphic Devices; Conducting Polymers; Nanocorrugated Structures
P2-099.a: Electrolyte-gated organic transistors are promising biosensing platforms because mixed ionic–electronic conduction enables strong coupling between electrolyte ions and the conducting polymer channel. However, biomolecular detection in physiological media remains challenging because ionic screening and inefficient interfacial coupling can limit sensitivity. This study explores nanoscale geometric engineering of PEDOT channels as a strategy to strengthen ion–channel interactions and improve label-free detection. Nanocorrugated SiO₂/Si substrates were prepared and coated with PEDOT to form electrolyte-gated transistor channels, while flat devices served as controls. Surface morphology, molecular organization, and electrochemical properties were examined using complementary structural and spectroscopic techniques. Electrical transistor characteristics were measured under liquid gating, and the devices were functionalized with suitable recognition elements for nucleic-acid and protein biomarker detection in buffer and biological fluids. Additional electrochemical measurements were used to examine charge storage, ion transport, and redox behavior associated with the modified morphology. Nanoscale corrugation reorganized the PEDOT network and enhanced ionic accessibility, electrochemical coupling, and gate-induced channel modulation. Compared with planar devices, the nanocorrugated transistors exhibited stronger electrical responses to biomolecular binding and enabled highly sensitive detection of nucleic acids and clinically relevant protein biomarkers. The sensing response was maintained in complex physiological environments, including serum and whole blood, with clear discrimination from negative controls. Geometric engineering of conducting-polymer channels provides an effective approach for improving mixed ionic–electronic transduction without fundamentally changing the polymer chemistry. Nanocorrugated PEDOT combines enhanced ion transport, structural reorganization, and amplified electrical modulation, offering a scalable platform for sensitive bioelectronic detection and potential future diagnostic applications.

P2-100.k: Covalent Triazine Framework; Ion Selectivity; Transpiration-driven Electrokinetic Power Generation
P2-100.a: Transpiration-driven electrokinetic power generators offer a simple route for harvesting electrical energy from spontaneous water evaporation, but their performance is often limited by insufficient ion selectivity and inefficient ion transport. This study explores charge-regulated covalent triazine frameworks (CTFs) as porous, chemically tunable additives for controlling ion migration and improving electrokinetic energy conversion. Three CTFs bearing neutral, anionic, and cationic pendant groups were synthesized and incorporated into conductive, hygroscopic active layers. Their chemical structures, surface charge, porosity, microstructure, and ion-transport characteristics were examined using spectroscopic, electrochemical, and structural characterization. CTF-coated cotton fabrics were then integrated into transpiration-driven generators and evaluated under different humidity conditions using an aqueous electrolyte. The CTFs exhibited distinct charge-dependent ion-selective transport governed by Donnan-type interactions. Charged frameworks preferentially promoted transport of oppositely charged ions, while their porous structures provided ion-accessible pathways. When incorporated into the generators, framework charge controlled both the magnitude and polarity of the electrical output. The cationic CTF produced the strongest anion-selective transport and the highest overall electrokinetic output, while the anionic CTF reversed the voltage polarity through preferential cation transport. Molecular regulation of fixed charge within porous CTFs provides an effective strategy for tuning ion selectivity and transpiration-driven electrokinetic power generation. By combining chemically defined ionic functionality with stable porous transport pathways, this approach offers a rational materials platform for improving evaporation-based energy harvesting and guiding future development of durable, scalable hydrovoltaic power systems. A series-connected device demonstration further confirmed the potential of the approach for practical low-power energy applications.

P2-101.k: Tellurium; Atomic Layer Deposition; Thin Film Transistor
P2-101.a: Tellurium (Te) has attracted considerable attention as a promising p-type semiconductor for next-generation electronic devices owing to its high carrier mobility, ambient stability, and compatibility with low-temperature processing. However, the electrical performance of Te thin films can be affected by the deposition process, and the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, Te thin films were deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD) and thermal evaporation to investigate the effects of the deposition method on their electrical properties. The thermally evaporated Te exhibited a higher on-current and lower off-current than the ALD-derived Te. XPS, XRD, AFM, and SEM analyses were performed to examine the chemical, structural, and morphological properties of the resulting films. Hall measurements were further conducted to evaluate their carrier transport properties and correlate them with the observed device characteristics. This study provides insight into the relationship between deposition process, material properties, and electrical performance, offering a basis for optimizing the fabrication of high-performance Te-based electronic devices.

P2-102.k: PEDOT:PSS; Protic Ionic Liquids; Conductive Nanomesh
P2-102.a: Conductive polymer electrodes are promising for wearable electronics owing to their high electrical conductivity, mechanical compliance, and solution processability. However, conventional film-type electrodes often exhibit limited breathability and conformability when interfaced with soft, curved, and dynamically deforming surfaces. Conductive nanomesh architectures can overcome these limitations by providing interconnected electrical pathways while maintaining an open and mechanically compliant structure. Freestanding conductive nanomesh electrodes were fabricated by coating electrospun polyurethane (PU) nanomeshes with a PEDOT:PSS/protic ionic liquid (p-IL) composite. The nanomesh structure and coating conditions were systematically varied to investigate their effects on the structural, optical, and electrical properties. Optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy were used to characterize the morphology and network of nanomeshes, while optical and electrical measurements were performed to evaluate the characteristics of the conductive nanomesh. The PEDOT:PSS/p-IL composite formed continuous conductive pathways along the interconnected PU nanofibers while preserving the highly porous nanomesh architecture. Control over the nanomesh structure and coating conditions enabled the electrical and optical properties to be tuned without compromising the structural openness of the network. The optimized conductive nanomesh electrodes exhibited a favorable combination of electrical conductivity, breathability, and mechanical conformability. Moreover, its freestanding and ultrathin architecture enabled intimate contact with curved and soft surfaces, demonstrating its suitability for conformal electrode integration. These results demonstrate a simple solution-based approach for fabricating breathable and conformal conductive nanomesh electrodes by integrating PEDOT:PSS/p-IL with electrospun PU nanofibers. The resulting electrodes combine electrical functionality, structural permeability, and mechanical compliance within a freestanding architecture, providing a promising platform for wearable electronics and conformal sensing applications.

P2-103.k: Liquid Crystalline Elastomers; Low-Dimensional Nanomaterials; Composites
P2-103.a: Integrating inorganic 2D nanomaterials into liquid crystalline and elastomeric matrices is critically limited by severe aggregation and phase disruption due to thermodynamic incompatibility. Conventional exfoliation methods require non-volatile solvents or foreign surfactants that degrade the liquid crystalline order and composite processability. Here, we present a mesogen-assisted exfoliation (MAE) strategy that utilizes reactive mesogens as both exfoliant and dispersant, enabling surfactant-free, high-concentration dispersion of 2D nanomaterials within liquid crystal networks. The MAE strategy leverages reactive mesogens as dual-function exfoliants and dispersants through thermally driven intercalation into bulk layered nanomaterials. By conducting intercalation at temperatures where mesogens exhibit high molecular mobility, the mesogenic molecules effectively penetrate and expand the interlayer galleries. Subsequent liquid-phase shear in a volatile solvent directly yields surfactant-free, highly concentrated 2D nanosheet dispersions ready for polymer/elastomer processing without phase segregation. The MAE approach achieved molecular-level, homogeneous dispersion of various 2D nanosheets in the liquid crystal matrix with remarkable long-term stability. The resulting flexible composites exhibited substantial mechanical reinforcement and strong photothermal responsiveness, enabling rapid mechanical actuation even under extreme low-temperature environments. Furthermore, aligning high-aspect-ratio 2D nanofillers along the liquid crystalline director facilitated highly efficient, anisotropic thermal dissipation pathways. The MAE platform offers a universal and effective solution to the long-standing dispersion bottleneck of inorganic nanomaterials in liquid crystalline polymers. By combining enhanced mechanical strength with tailored photothermal and directional heat-dissipation functionalities, this material system demonstrates broad versatility for high-performance flexible devices and extreme-environment soft actuators.

P2-104.k: Ionic Actuator; Artificial Muscle; Ion Transport Network
P2-104.a: Nafion-based ionic actuators have been widely investigated for artificial muscle applications owing to their favorable ionic conductivity and excellent mechanical durability. However, enhancing ion transport through increased ionic liquid loading often induces matrix plasticization, resulting in a trade-off between ionic conductivity and mechanical stiffness. This trade-off limits stable force generation, particularly at high operating frequencies, and remains a critical challenge for achieving high-performance ionic actuation over a broad frequency range. To address this challenge, we developed a PEG-silica-hybridized ionic electroactive Nafion (Ps-iEN) with an interfacial ion-transport network. PEG-functionalized silica particles were incorporated to improve the balance between ion transport and mechanical stiffness while suppressing ionic liquid-induced matrix softening. The mechanical, ionic, and structural properties of Ps-iEN were characterized, and its electromechanical performance was evaluated using sandwich-type ionic actuators with PEDOT:PSS/AgNW composite electrodes. PEG-silica incorporation enhanced the mechanical stiffness of the Nafion matrix while facilitating interfacial ion transport. The optimized Ps-iEN composition provided a favorable balance between ionic mobility and mechanical stiffness, resulting in enhanced blocking force at low driving voltages. The Ps-iEN actuator maintained stable and reproducible force generation up to 50 Hz and sustained consistent actuation for more than 30,000 cycles. Furthermore, frequency-dependent actuation produced distinct motion patterns that qualitatively resembled different contraction behaviors of skeletal muscle. PEG-silica-mediated interfacial engineering effectively mitigates the long-standing trade-off between ionic conductivity and mechanical stiffness in Nafion-based ionic actuators. The resulting Ps-iEN electrolyte enables enhanced force generation and frequency-robust actuation at low driving voltages, together with long-term operational stability. This strategy offers a promising electrolyte platform for high-bandwidth artificial muscles, wearable haptic interfaces, and soft robotic systems requiring rapid and frequency-tunable mechanical responses.

P2-105.k: Ion Dynamics; Organic Electrochemical Transistor; Neuromorphic Computing
P2-105.a: The human brain achieves efficient learning system through its synaptic plasticity, are converted into long-lasting changes in synaptic strength. Inspired by this mechanism, OECTs have emerged as promising artificial synapse platforms because ion injection and retention within the channel can induce long-term conductance modulation, enabling the emulation of potentiation and depression. However, back-diffusion of injected ions after gate stimulation causes unstable memory states, leaving only volatile characteristics behind. Therefore, stabilizing penetrated ions is essential for realizing robust long-term potentiation in OECT synapses Here, we present ion-affinity modulation of channel phase as a molecular approach to control synaptic plasticity in organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs). To manipulate the residence time of implanted ions, we incorporated organosilicate interpenetrating networks (IPNs) with different functional groups into the P3HT active layer, without compromising the crystaline structure of the P3HT. The Si-OH IPN offers high anion-affinity sites that electrically stabilize the injected ions. As a result, interactions between ions and the IPN network suppress the back-diffusion of anion even after the gate stimulus is removed, allowing the doped state to be maintained for long time. On the other hand, the amine-functionalized Si-NH₂ IPN created a repulsion of injected anion that promoted ion release from the P3HT channel, thereby reducing ion retention and enabling faster recovery of the channel conductance. Consequently, the low ion-affinity channel exhibits a shortened potentiation duration, causing synaptic responses to become more transient. These results demonstrate that engineering ion–channel interactions through IPN networks provides a molecular strategy to precisely regulate ion retention, thereby enabling programmable control over synaptic plasticity by tuning ion affinity.

P2-106.k: Tin Perovskite; Lewis-Base Additive; Thin-Film Transistor
P2-106.a: Tin (Sn²⁺)-halide perovskites are promising lead-free semiconductors for high-performance optoelectronic devices, including thin-film transistors (TFTs). Although solution processing enables low-temperature and scalable fabrication, the high Lewis acidity of Sn²⁺ accelerates crystallization, often resulting in structural defects, non-uniform morphology, and Sn²⁺ degradation. Here, we introduce poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC) as a non-volatile polymeric Lewis-base additive for the two-dimensional perovskite (PEA)₂SnI₄ and systematically compare its effect with monomeric propylene carbonate (PC). PC or PPC was incorporated into (PEA)₂SnI₄ precursor solutions, and the resulting films were investigated using structural, morphological, spectroscopic, and chemical analyses. Bottom-gate, top-contact TFTs were fabricated to evaluate charge transport, device uniformity, and operational stability. Both additives preserved the characteristic layered perovskite structure while improving film continuity and suppressing pinhole-related defects. Especially, PPC produced a compact and uniform morphology with less pronounced grain boundaries and markedly delayed the solution-to-film conversion. Spectroscopic analyses supported coordination between the carbonate groups of PPC and Sn-containing precursor species, consistent with the formation of a persistent macromolecular Lewis acid–base intermediate that moderates rapid crystallization and promotes more complete precursor conversion. PPC incorporation also reduced residual precursor species and Sn degradation. Consequently, PPC-treated TFTs exhibited substantially enhanced field-effect mobility, improved on/off characteristics, better device-to-device uniformity, and superior bias-stress and switching stability. These results demonstrate that polymeric Lewis-base coordination provides an effective strategy for regulating rapid crystallization, suppressing Sn-related degradation, and improving the structural and electrical reliability of solution-processed 2D Sn-perovskite TFTs.

P2-107.a: Stretchable organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) have emerged as promising platform for skin-like electronics due to ion-to-electron signal transduction and in situ amplification with deformability. However, challenges still remain in simultaneously achieving (1) high electrochemical ion–electron coupling efficiency, (2) high stretchability, and (3) compatibility with high-resolution microfabrication. Direct photopatterning of ionic elastomers can be a promising strategy; however, the resulting crosslinked network can restrict chain segmental motion and suppress ion mobility, while solvent development can cause partial extraction of ionic species. In parallel, although ethylene oxide (EO)-based side chain engineering of organic semiconductors can promote ion transport, such systems suffer from limited stretchability and remain incompatible with microfabrication processes. Herein, we demonstrate stretchable OECT arrays based on ionic elastomer network (IEN) and polymer semiconductor network (PSN), in which a thermoplastic polyurethane matrix containing ionic liquid and a polymer semiconductor matrix are photo-crosslinked using ethylene oxide (EO)-combined crosslinker. The EO moieties provide two major capabilities: i) ion compatibility, and ii) intrinsic stretchability. The IEN and PSN with stretchability enable reduced ionic resistance, fast ion diffusion, and high channel capacitance. The chain segmental motion served by EO can impart high stretchability to crosslinked systems, enabling effective relaxation of external mechanical stress while also improving ion mobility, resulting in higher transconductance and switching characteristics. Even during the photo-patterning process, partial extraction of ionic species from elastomer may occur, but it is prevented by EO-ion interaction. Through this non-destructive lithography, they can achieve high resolutions down to 5 um and 2 um for IEN and PSN, respectively. Leveraging this materials platform, we demonstrate high-density stretchable OECT arrays that simultaneously realize stretchability, high device performance, and scalable integration. Consequently, we designed a novel photo‑patternable ion elastomer and polymer semiconductor network applicable to stretchable electronics, and this material approach can offer new insights into highly integrated stretchable iontronics.

P2-108.a: Skin-integrated bioelectronics capable of delivering controlled thermal stimuli over large body areas offer new opportunities for sensory augmentation and continuous bio-signal monitoring. Conventional wearable thermal devices typically employ thermoelectric components for rapid temperature control, but their rigid, bulky, and power-intensive properties hinder flexible, large-area integration. Therefore, developing a highly efficient, flexible thermal interface that enables low-power operation remains essential for next-generation skin-integrated bioelectronics. We propose a skin-integrated platform combining an epidermal Joule heater, passive cooling hydrogel, and switchable thermal barrier for power-efficient bidirectional thermal control. For continuous biofluid monitoring, evaporative cooling foam replaces Joule heaters, enabling flow detection through temperature gradients induced by flow-induced thermal anisotropy on the skin. A zero-energy thermochromic bio-stamp further provides direct, naked-eye visualization of thermal-flow variations without external power. In this presentation, a set of ideas form the foundations of a skin-integrated technology for power-efficient generation of thermal sensation over the large area of the skin. Wireless control enables spatiotemporally tunable thermal stimuli, expanding immersive experiences beyond those traditionally supported by audiovisual and haptic inputs. Non-contact device-to-device communication further enables active thermoregulation and remote safety notifications. In addition, an evaporative-cooling platform enables real-time, on-skin monitoring of cerebrospinal fluid flow through localized cooling and temperature-gradient sensing. Theoretical and numerical models inform materials selection and system-level design optimization. These highly conformal, power-efficient wearable thermal devices hold immense potential for numerous future applications, ranging from immersive virtual reality platforms to advanced prosthetics and remote clinical diagnostics, where providing realistic, low-power, and continuous thermal feedback is absolutely essential for a seamless user experience.

P2-109.a: Ionic materials have attracted considerable interest for electronic sensing applications because they can convert external stimuli into measurable electrical signals through ion transport. However, incorporating ionic liquids into polymer networks remains challenging when the components exhibit poor miscibility, potentially leading to heterogeneous structures and unstable sensing performance. Combining operational stability with degradability is another important challenge in developing sustainable electronic materials. Vanillin-based building blocks offer a promising starting point, but their limited compatibility with ionic liquids requires further molecular modification. To address this limitation, fluorinated groups were introduced into a vanillin-based building block to promote interactions with an ionic liquid and improve compatibility between the components. The modified building block was used to prepare an ionic material that integrates the ionic liquid within a vanillin-based network. The resulting material was subsequently applied as the active sensing component of an electronic sensor. Its sensing behavior, operational stability, and capacity for degradation were evaluated to assess its suitability for stable yet degradable sensing applications. Introducing fluorinated groups improved the compatibility of the vanillin-based material with the ionic liquid, enabling the preparation of an ionic sensing material. The resulting sensor exhibited stable sensing performance under the tested conditions, demonstrating its potential for electronic applications. In addition to its operational stability, the material could undergo degradation, indicating that reliable sensing and degradability can be achieved within the same material platform. These findings highlight the importance of molecular design in overcoming compatibility limitations between vanillin-based networks and ionic liquids. This work presents a molecular functionalization strategy for developing vanillin-based ionic materials with improved ionic-liquid compatibility. The resulting material combines stable sensing performance with degradability, offering a promising approach to sustainable electronic sensors. More broadly, the strategy provides a basis for designing ionic materials that balance functional reliability during use with degradation after their intended service life.

P2-110.a: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) amplifies the Raman signals of analytes through localized electromagnetic field enhancement generated by metallic nanostructures. SERS performance is strongly affected by the number and uniformity of hotspots. Drop-casting metal nanoparticles onto a support is a representative method for fabricating SERS substrates; however, nonuniform particle distribution and aggregation can occur during drying, resulting in position-dependent signal variation and poor reproducibility. To overcome these limitations, Au-SSM substrates were designed by directly growing Au nanostructures on a stainless-steel mesh (SSM). The three-dimensional structure of the SSM provides a large effective surface area, and Au nanostructures can be directly formed via galvanic replacement. In addition, the pretreatment method of the mesh and the reaction conditions with the Au precursor were controlled to optimize substrate reproducibility. Analysis of the Au-SSM substrates revealed that the gold nanostructures were uniformly distributed on both sides of the mesh, forming protruding structures composed of aggregated nanoparticles. In contrast to bare SSM, distinct Raman peaks of 4-ATP, a model probe, were observed. These results suggest that the Au nanostructures enhanced the Raman signal by generating numerous hotspots. Similar Raman peaks were also observed at multiple positions, confirming signal uniformity. In conclusion, Au-SSM substrates exhibited uniform particle distribution and good reproducibility due to the formation of uniform nanostructures. Their large effective surface area and membrane structure are expected to enable the detection of trace analytes.

P3-001.k: Oblique Helicoidal Cholesteric Liquid Crystal; Circularly Polarized Luminescence; Wavelength Tunability
P3-001.a: Circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) encodes optical handedness in addition to intensity, wavelength, and phase, creating opportunities for optical communication, security, encryption, and three-dimensional imaging. Conventional CPL generation requires external polarizers and quarter-wave plates, which increase complexity and volume. Cholesteric liquid crystals (CLCs) can generate CPL intrinsically through chiral helical structures, but their fixed pitch restricts continuous wavelength control and requires separate filters or materials for different colors. This study develops a full-color CPL platform based on an oblique helicoidal cholesteric liquid crystal (ChOH) containing white-emitting quantum dots. Unlike CLCs, ChOH adopts a conical helix whose cone angle and pitch can be adjusted by a stimulus. Stimulus-induced modulation shifts the circularly selective reflection band, while broadband quantum-dot emission supplies light throughout the visible spectrum. The design links the tunable helical structure to wavelength-selective reflection and emission behavior within a single system. The ChOH configuration enables a continuously adjustable reflection band without exchanging optical filters or replacing emissive materials. Combining the photonic structure with broadband quantum-dot emission is expected to generate wavelength-selective CPL across multiple visible colors within one platform. The device architecture preserves intrinsic handedness selection, supporting compact operation compared with assemblies that require polarization components. This integrated liquid-crystal platform offers a compact route to externally tunable, full-color CPL generation. It may facilitate miniaturized photonic systems for wearable optics, secure communication, encryption, displays, and three-dimensional imaging in next-generation optical devices and sensing applications. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2024-00411809, RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586).

P3-002.k: Cellulose Nanocrystals (CNCs); UV Protection; Lyotropic Liquid Crystal
P3-002.a: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation accelerates skin photoaging and increases the risk of skin cancer, while environmental concerns regarding conventional UV filters have driven the search for sustainable UV-shielding materials. Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs), derived from the most abundant renewable natural polymer on Earth, spontaneously self-assemble into chiral nematic structures that selectively reflect light through Bragg reflection. Here, we introduce CNCs exhibiting a chiral nematic phase as a renewable photonic component into conventional oil-in-water (O/W) sunscreen formulations to enhance UV protection. Aqueous CNC suspensions with various concentrations were prepared to determine the concentration range exhibiting a chiral nematic phase. CNC suspensions were incorporated into commercial O/W sunscreen formulations, and their UV-protection performance was evaluated by UV reflectance and in vitro Sun Protection Factor (SPF) measurements. CNC suspensions formed a chiral nematic phase above the critical concentration. O/W sunscreen formulations containing CNCs exhibited enhanced UV reflectance and improved UV-protection performance compared with the CNC-free formulation. The in vitro SPF reached a maximum value of 76.4 at 4 wt% CNC, corresponding to an approximately 155% increase over the CNC-free formulation (SPF 30). These findings demonstrate that the chiral nematic structure of CNCs effectively enhances UV protection in conventional sunscreen formulations. Our findings demonstrate that the chiral nematic structure of CNCs provides a renewable photonic platform for enhancing UV protection in conventional sunscreen formulations. Beyond sunscreen applications, this approach offers a sustainable platform for developing functional photonic materials. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, and RS-2024-00411809).

P3-003.a: Reconfigurable flat optics use a passive, wavelength-multiplexed metasurface addressed by a tunable narrowband reflector. The metasurface is mature, but the selector remains an instrument—synthetic liquid crystals needing electrodes and AC driving, or benchtop filters. Hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC), a water-based, bio-derived cholesteric liquid crystal, Bragg-reflects a narrow band tuned by temperature alone, yet has been dismissed as broadband and not device-grade. An HPC gel (68 wt% in water) was sealed in a 48-μm glass cell and its RCP reflection measured from 25–55 °C; we extracted λ(T), FWHM, and hysteresis, and fed the measured R(λ,T) into inverse design of wavelength-multiplexed TiO₂ metasurfaces (hologram and metalens) with a crosstalk penalty. The reflection band swept 419→744 nm by temperature alone, with FWHM 21–34 nm and near-zero hysteresis. The fractional bandwidth was constant (Δλ/λ = 0.046) with a Gaussian shape, showing that the width is set by texture, not an intrinsic limit—cellulose is not inherently broadband. Modulator-aware design gave five channels at ~10⁻³ crosstalk, extended toward eight, enabling temperature-addressed holography, a tunable metalens, and (concentration, temperature) two-factor optical encryption. A renewable cellulose gel acts as an electrode-free, temperature-only spectral selector, reducing the tunable optic to a passive material and opening a sustainable route to reconfigurable flat optics. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, and RS-2024-00411809).

P3-004.k: Hydrovoltaic Generation; Electrode Configuration; Green Hydrogen
P3-004.a: Hydrovoltaic generation is a promising approach that converts the energy associated with water transport, evaporation, or moisture adsorption into electricity. It uses ambient water and natural evaporation without an additional external power source, showing the potential to drive eco-friendly electrochemical processes such as water electrolysis. However, long-term output instability at the electrode-device interface often limits its practical application. In a wet environment containing ionic electrolytes, electrochemical interactions between carbon-based conductive coating and metal electrodes can induce oxidation and corrosion, leading to increased contact resistance and gradual performance degradation. In this study, we investigate the effect of electrode material and electrode-device attachment method on the long-term stability of a cellulose-based hydrovoltaic generator. By applying different electrode materials and contact methods, we monitored their electrical output and contact resistance over 100 hours of operation. The generator incorporating the optimized electrode configuration achieves an open-circuit voltage of 0.3 V and a short-circuit current of 300 μA. We connected multiple generators in series and parallel to construct a hydrovoltaic module that consistently generates 2.0 V and 1.0 mA. We utilize the module’s output to drive a water electrolysis cell, enabling hydrogen production without an additional external power source. These results demonstrate that optimizing electrode materials and contact configurations is an important factor in implementing a modular system for green hydrogen generation.

P3-005.k: Memory Device; Lead-free Double Perovskite; Neuromorphic Computing
P3-005.a: The development of environmentally sustainable materials has become increasingly important for next-generation functional electronics. Although halide perovskites have attracted considerable attention as active materials for memory devices owing to their mixed ionic–electronic transport and tunable electrical properties, conventional Pb-based perovskites raise serious environmental and toxicity concerns. Therefore, replacing Pb-based compositions with lead-free perovskites is essential for developing sustainable electronic devices. A memory device incorporating a lead-free double perovskite active layer will be fabricated. Its fundamental electrical characteristics will be analyzed through current–voltage measurements, while synaptic responses will be evaluated by applying repetitive voltage pulses. The resistive switching behavior between high- and low-resistance states will be presented. In addition, gradual conductance modulation and multiple resistance states under pulse stimulation will be discussed to demonstrate the functional potential of the device for memory and artificial synaptic applications. This presentation will demonstrate the potential of lead-free double perovskites as environmentally sustainable active materials for functional memory devices. The proposed approach is expected to provide a promising strategy for developing sustainable electronic devices and expanding their applicability to future neuromorphic systems.

P3-006.k: Triboelectric Nanogenerator; Ethanol Sensor; Electrospinning PVDF
P3-006.a: Self-powered gas sensors have attracted increasing attention because they eliminate the need for external power sources while enabling portable and sustainable sensing systems. In this study, a self-powered triboelectric ethanol sensor (TEES) is proposed by integrating a freestanding-mode TENG and an ethanol sensing layer into a single device. The sensing layer consists of electrospun poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) fibers embedded with CuO nanoparticles. The CuO nanoparticles provide abundant oxygen vacancies that promote oxygen ion adsorption, allowing ethanol molecules to modulate the surface charge density through redox reactions and consequently change the triboelectric output. The proposed TEES generated an open-circuit voltage of 50.88 V at 500 rpm and a maximum short-circuit current of 7.94 μA at 800 rpm. The device exhibited excellent mechanical durability with only 4.82% degradation after 240,000 operating cycles. Ethanol sensing performance was systematically investigated by optimizing the CuO concentration in the electrospun PVDF fibers. The optimized device achieved a 10 ppm limit of detection with a 6 s response time at 1000 ppm, outperforming previously reported integrated triboelectric ethanol sensors. These results demonstrate that the proposed TEES provides a highly integrated, self-powered, and high-performance ethanol sensing platform with excellent sensitivity, durability, and practical applicability. The proposed strategy offers a route toward compact self-powered gas sensing systems for wearable electronics, environmental monitoring, and intelligent healthcare applications.

P3-007.k: Hyperspectral Optical Filter; Oblique Helicoidal Cholesteric; Broadband Reflection
P3-007.a: Hyperspectral optical filters, which transmit light within specific wavelength bands, are increasingly important for object identification in autonomous vehicles and infrared-based plastic sorting. However, conventional filters have inherent limitations: IMEC linescan filters require physical movement to switch wavelengths, acousto-optic filters offer low spectral resolution, and Lyot filters exhibit reduced transmittance owing to multiple polarizers. Stacked cholesteric liquid crystal (CLC) filters eliminate mechanical motion, but their transmission wavelengths are fixed, and broad spectral coverage requires many cells, degrading transmittance. We developed a hyperspectral optical filter based on an electrically tunable, broadband oblique helicoidal cholesteric formed by a twist-bend nematic liquid crystal, whose heliconical pitch and selective reflection wavelength are continuously tunable by an electric field. To achieve a broadband response without sacrificing tunability, a pitch gradient was induced by an electric-field gradient rather than polymerization: a cell was assembled from circularly patterned indium tin oxide (ITO)-coated glass, in which the vertical field component is strongest at the pattern center and decays outward. The field gradient produced a spatial pitch gradient, and a broadband reflection peak was experimentally confirmed at the pattern center. This reflection band shifted continuously with the applied electric field, demonstrating both broadband coverage and wavelength tunability without polymerization. Owing to the broadband coverage, only two stacked cells are required, minimizing transmission loss. This approach enables a mechanically static, highly transmissive, and continuously tunable hyperspectral optical filter. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, RS-2024-00411809).

P3-008.a: All-inorganic cesium lead bromide perovskites are promising for optoelectronic and radiation-detection applications because of their strong optical absorption, favorable carrier transport, and high sensitivity to ionizing radiation. Integrating CsPbBr3 with wide-bandgap GaN provides a potential route toward robust heterostructure devices with efficient photocarrier generation and extraction. This study investigates chemical vapor deposition (CVD)-grown CsPbBr3 on GaN for photodetector and X-ray detector applications. CsPbBr3 layers were directly grown on GaN substrates by a vapor-phase deposition process. Their structural, morphological, and optical properties were characterized using complementary microscopic, diffraction, and spectroscopic techniques. A single device was operated in two modes by electrode selection: a lateral photodetector on the CsPbBr3 surface, and a vertical X-ray detector across the CsPbBr3/GaN heterojunction, evaluated under optical illumination and 6 MV photon irradiation from a medical linear accelerator (LINAC). Electrical and photoresponse characteristics were analyzed to assess carrier transport, interfacial charge separation, and radiation-induced signal generation. CVD growth produced crystalline CsPbBr3 layers with well-defined interfaces on GaN. The heterostructures exhibited distinct photoresponses under optical excitation, demonstrating effective photogenerated carrier collection. Under X-ray irradiation, measurable radiation-induced electrical signals were observed, indicating the capability of the CVD-grown CsPbBr3/GaN architecture for high-energy photon detection. The device responses were closely associated with crystalline quality, lateral carrier transport, and vertical interfacial charge separation. CVD-grown CsPbBr3/GaN heterostructures provide a promising platform for integrated photodetection and dosimetry. These results demonstrate the potential of direct vapor-phase perovskite growth on wide-bandgap semiconductors for developing scalable and multifunctional radiation-sensitive optoelectronic devices.

P3-009.k: Chemically Immobilized; Photolithography Free; Patterned Field-effect Transistors
P3-009.a: Semiconducting carbon nanotube (CNT)-based field-effect transistors (CNT-FETs) are promising candidates for next-generation electronics because of their excellent carrier transport properties. However, conventional CNT channel fabrication based on physical adsorption often suffers from poor reproducibility, non-uniform CNT network formation, and complicated photolithography processes, limiting scalable device fabrication. A photolithography-free chemical immobilization strategy was developed using benzophenone-functionalized self-assembled monolayers (BPS-SAMs). Semiconducting SWNTs wrapped with poly(9,9-didodecylfluorene) (PFDD) were deposited onto the BPS-modified substrates. Upon UV irradiation, benzophenone generated reactive radicals through hydrogen abstraction from the PFDD chains, inducing covalent crosslinking between the SAM and the SWNT-wrapping polymer. The resulting chemically immobilized SWNT networks were evaluated after removal of unbound SWNTs by solvent washing. The UV-induced covalent immobilization enabled robust adhesion of ultrathin SWNT networks while maintaining their morphology after washing and device fabrication. SWNT network density could be readily controlled by adjusting the SWNT solution concentration. Compared with physically adsorbed SWNT networks, the chemically immobilized networks exhibited improved uniformity, enhanced device-to-device reproducibility, and superior electrical characteristics. The proposed UV-induced chemical immobilization strategy provides a simple, scalable, and photolithography-free approach for fabricating uniform ultrathin semiconducting SWNT networks. This technique offers an effective route toward reproducible, high-performance SWNT-FETs and has significant potential for future solution-processed electronic devices.

P3-010.k: Hexagonal Boron Nitride; Charge-trapping Layer; Synaptic Transistor
P3-010.a: Neuromorphic devices require reliable charge trapping mechanisms to emulate synaptic functionalities such as hysteresis, memory retention, and weight modulation. However, conventional oxide semiconductor-based devices often suffer from limited stability due to the absence of well-defined trapping layers. Here, we demonstrate that defect-engineered hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) grown by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) can serve as an effective charge-trapping interlayer in indium–gallium–zinc oxide (IGZO) synaptic transistors. The PECVD-grown hBN exhibits significant structural disorder, oxygen-related bonding, increased Urbach energy, and reduced film density, indicating the presence of abundant defect-induced localized states that provide energetically favorable sites for charge trapping and retention. When the hBN film is integrated with IGZO semiconducting channel layer, it significantly enhances charge trapping efficiency, resulting in a pronounced increase in the hysteresis window from 0.8 V to 4.7 V, along with improved synaptic characteristics such as enhanced potentiation/depression behavior and stable long-term memory retention. These results highlight the potential of PECVD-grown defect-rich hBN as a functional charge-trapping layer for high-performance oxide semiconductor-based neuromorphic devices.

P3-011.k: Ag Nanometal Composite; Supercritical Fluid; Expanded Graphite
P3-011.a: Monoclinic VO2(M) is useful for energy-saving smart windows as its reversible phase transition controls NIR solar radiation. However, conventional VO2 films are brown from their narrow bandgap, limiting aesthetics and building integration. Here, solution-processable VO2 nanoparticle–PVP composites were combined with an ultrathin Ag layer to enable structural color and thermochromic solar modulation in one platform. Monoclinic VO2 nanoparticles were synthesized by an annealing-free hydrothermal method and mixed with PVP to form thermochromic inks. The inks were coated on Ag substrates to form optical cavities, with thickness varied to tune Fabry–Pérot interference and visible color. Structural and optical properties were characterized, and visible/NIR transmittance measurements and simulations assessed the thermochromic response. Performance was evaluated through mock-house experiments and building energy simulations. The VO2–PVP/Ag bilayers produced vivid, tunable structural colors via thickness-dependent interference, overcoming the brown appearance of VO2 films. Across the VO2 phase transition, optical-constant changes altered cavity response and reduced near-infrared transmittance, enabling temperature-responsive color and solar regulation. The optimized film showed 47.15% luminous transmittance and 6.09% solar transmittance modulation. The films retained thermochromic performance on flexible substrates, while mock-house trials and energy simulations indicated lower solar heat gain and annual building energy use. This study demonstrates a room-temperature, solution-processed strategy for functional VO2 films combining tunable structural color with passive thermochromic solar control. The VO2–PVP/Ag cavity enables visible-color adjustment through thickness control while preserving near-infrared modulation during the VO2 phase transition. The bilayer architecture offers a useful platform for customizable smart windows, flexible thermochromic coatings, and temperature-adaptive optical devices.

P3-012.k: Ag Nanometal Composite; Supercritical Fluid; Expanded Graphite
P3-012.a: Expanded graphite–silver (EG–Ag) composites were synthesized via a supercritical CO2 fluid process (SCFP), enabling uniform dispersion of silver (Ag) particles within the expanded graphite (EG) matrix. AgNO3 as a source of Ag particles was dissolved in the mixed co-solvent composed of ethanol, methanol, and deionized water, adsorbed onto the EG surface through SCFP, and followed by thermal treatment to form the EG–Ag composites. The effects of reaction time, co-solvent composition, and post thermal treatment on the structural morphology and its thermal properties of EG–Ag composites were investigated. The SCFP showed the performance of improved Ag particle dispersion on EG surface, and yielded the formation of a continuous thermal conduction network on the Eg-Ag composites. Optimization of the co-solvent composition and post thermal treatments further enhanced thermal conductivity in both the through-plane and in-plane directions. These results demonstrate that SCFP is a promising method for fabricating EG–Ag composites with high structural integrity and superior thermal dissipation properties, offering great potential for usage in thermal interface materials for high-power electronic and optoelectronic systems.

P3-013.k: Colloidal Nanocrystals; NIR Optoelectronics; Hierarchical Structure
P3-013.a: Bismuth-based nanomaterials are attracting considerable attention as promising optoelectronic materials spanning the visible to near-infrared region because of their relatively low toxicity, earth-abundant constituents, high absorption coefficients, and good stability. In particular, bismuth chalcohalides enable bandgap tuning through precise control of their composition and stoichiometry. Hierarchically ordered Bi13S18Br2 nanorod superstructures were synthesized through a two-step, single-batch colloidal process. BiOBr nanodisk templates were first formed via a heat-up reaction, followed by delayed hot injection of a sulfur precursor to induce template-guided topotactic transformation.The structural, compositional, optical, and electronic properties of the resulting superstructures were characterized using electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, elemental analysis, and spectroscopic techniques. NIR photoconductors were subsequently fabricated through solution deposition and solid-state ligand exchange under ambient conditions. The transformation yielded orthogonally ordered Bi13S18Br2 nanorod networks while retaining template-derived architectures. Nanoframes, woodpile-like structures, and multipods were selectively obtained with size and shape uniformity. The nanoframes exhibited a trigonal crystal structure, broadband NIR absorption, n-type characteristics, and an indirect bandgap of approximately 0.80 eV. Under 980 nm illumination, the devices showed reproducible intensity-dependent photocurrent, a responsivity of 1.03 A W⁻¹, and an external quantum efficiency of 131.26% at 5 V bias. Stable switching was maintained over repeated illumination cycles without noticeable degradation. Template-guided topotactic transformation provides a low-temperature, morphology-controllable, and potentially scalable route to narrow-bandgap Bi13S18Br2superstructures. Their hierarchical connectivity, solution processability, and NIR photoresponse support their use as environmentally preferable active materials for infrared photodetectors and optoelectronic devices.

P3-014.a: Waste plastics and biomass represent two of the most important global issues due to their huge generation and environmental risks. Recently, co-carbonization has gained attention as an excellent opportunity for the simultaneous valorization of them into adsorbents and/or catalysts. The advantages of co-carbonized chars have been demonstrated in limited literature; however, the roles of the components of biomass, such as cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, have rarely been investigated. This study investigated the co-carbonization of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and cellulose, which play key roles in the development of porous, graphitic structures in pyrolysis. Chars were prepared by pyrolysis (700 °C, 2 hours) of ultrasonicated cellulose (UC) and PET at different mass ratios of 0-3. UC was used because it has more surfaces than cellulose without an alteration of chemical properties, which maximizes the reactions of cellulose during co-carbonization. Acetaminophen (ACT) removal rate in the presence of peroxydisulfate (PDS) and specific surface area were increased as the mass ratio of PET to UC was increased from 0 (UC) to 1 (UC-1PET), but were reduced greatly with further PET addition (UC-3PET). ACT removal was 93.65% in 15 minutes under 50 mg/L UC-1PET, 0.1 mM PDS, and 5 mg/L ACT. UC-1PET showed the highest contents of PDS activating sites, such as C-Cprimary, C-Chigh/Csp²-N, ID/IG, and I2D/IG. The results of quenching experiments, electron spin resonance spectroscopy, and chemical probes conversion indicated that ACT removal in UC+PDS and UC-1PET+PDS was commonly governed dominantly by electron transfer and 1O2 generated from O2•−, which induced coupling to dimers, hydroxylation, demethylation, deamination, and ring cleavage. The results demonstrated that the chars derived from the co-carbonization of UC and PET hold great potential as a catalyst in organic pollutants degradation and that the reactive sites and pore structures of them can be controlled by PET:UC ratio.

P3-016.k: Microwave Synthesis; Metal Doped SnO2; H2 Gas Sensing
P3-016.a: Hydrogen (H2) is regarded as an important clean energy carrier, but accidental leakage can cause serious safety issues because H₂ is highly diffusive and flammable. Therefore, the development of sensitive and reliable H₂ gas sensors is essential. SnO2 is a representative n-type oxide semiconductor for gas sensing. However, its sensing performance is often limited by insufficient surface activity and inefficient charge modulation. In this study, metal-decorated SnO2 nanosheets were fabricated using a microwave-assisted interfacial engineering process. SnO2 nanosheet powder was dispersed in DI water, and a metal precursor was introduced with ascorbic acid as a reducing agent. After magnetic stirring and sonication, the mixed solution was exposed to repeated microwave irradiation cycles. The obtained powder was washed, filtered, and dried. The structural, chemical, and surface properties of the samples were analyzed, and their H2 sensing characteristics were evaluated under controlled gas concentrations and operating temperatures. Compared with bare SnO2 nanosheets, the metal-decorated SnO2 nanosheets showed enhanced H2 sensing behavior. The improved performance is mainly associated with the two-dimensional nanosheet morphology, enlarged surface reaction area, catalytic activation by metal nanoparticles, and effective charge transfer at the metal/SnO2 interface. This work demonstrates that microwave-assisted metal decoration is a simple and effective approach for improving the H2 sensing performance of SnO2 nanosheets. The proposed strategy can provide a useful platform for highly sensitive oxide semiconductor-based H2 gas sensors.

P3-017.k: Radiative Cooling; Phase Change Material; Thermal Energy Storage
P3-017.a: Passive daytime radiative cooling (PDRC) has emerged as an energy-efficient cooling technology. Integrating phase change materials (PCMs) into PDRC coatings enables simultaneous radiative cooling and thermal energy storage. n-Octadecane/SiO₂ core-shell nanobeads were synthesized via emulsion polymerization and spray-coated with PVDF-HFP onto glass substrates. Their morphology, phase-change behavior, optical properties, and outdoor radiative cooling performance were characterized using SEM, DSC, FT-IR, UV-Vis-NIR, infrared thermal imaging, and outdoor cooling measurements. The coating exhibited a solar reflectance of 91.8% and an atmospheric-window emissivity of 95.5%. The encapsulated PCM effectively stored and released latent heat during phase transition, suppressing temperature rise. Under an average solar irradiance of 894 W m⁻², the coating achieved a daytime temperature reduction of 9.0 °C with a calculated cooling power of 107.8 W m⁻². The phase-change PDRC coating combines excellent optical performance with thermal energy storage through a simple and scalable spray-coating process. This multifunctional coating provides a promising strategy for passive thermal management and energy-efficient cooling applications.

P3-018.k: Inkjet Printing; Phosphorescent OLED; Self-Assembled Monolayer
P3-018.a: Inkjet printing is a scalable and material-efficient approach for fabricating organic light-emitting devices. However, solution-processed phosphorescent OLEDs (PHOLEDs) remain limited by interfacial instability, poor solvent orthogonality, and insufficient ambient processability. A high-performance, hole-transport-layer (HTL)-free PHOLED was fabricated entirely under ambient conditions using an eco-friendly inkjet-printing strategy. A dual self-assembled monolayer (SAM) consisting of 2,3,4,5,6-pentafluorobenzoyl phosphonic acid and tricosafluorododecanoic acid was introduced on the ITO anode to enable efficient charge injection without a conventional HTL. To improve film quality, an environmentally benign binary solvent system was developed to suppress the coffee-ring effect and produce highly uniform emissive films. Furthermore, a newly designed heteroleptic Ir(III) emitter with tailored solubilizing groups was employed to enhance ink compatibility and charge-transport properties. The synergistic integration of dual-SAM interfacial engineering, binary solvent optimization, and emitter design enabled the fabricated PHOLEDs to achieve a record-high external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 16.8% under ambient processing conditions, establishing a new benchmark for ambient inkjet-printed PHOLEDs. This work demonstrates an effective strategy for realizing high-efficiency, HTL-free PHOLEDs through eco-friendly inkjet printing. The proposed approach provides a scalable, vacuum-free, and environmentally sustainable manufacturing platform for next-generation OLED technologies.

P3-019.a: CuNb2O6 represents a distinctive class of intrinsic p-type metal oxide semiconductors wherein hole transport is mediated by copper-derived electronic states embedded within a structurally ordered framework, rendering it a promising heterogeneous catalyst for Fenton-like reactions. Given that its surface charge transfer efficiency heavily depends on lattice alignment, selective modulation of monoclinic and orthorhombic crystalline phases serves as a critical determinant of active site exposure and subsequent reactive oxygen species generation. CuNb2O6 powders were prepared via a sol–gel synthetic pathway, subsequently undergoing systematic thermal annealing to precisely dictate the phase transition between monoclinic and orthorhombic structures for optimized catalytic reactivity. The temperature-dependent development of these specific crystal structures and corresponding electronic states was rigorously characterized utilizing X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The empirical data resolve discrete, temperature-dependent crystallization regimes, elucidating the structural transitions from the low-temperature monoclinic phase to the high-temperature orthorhombic framework. Interrogations via XRD and XPS confirm that this polymorphic evolution drives the progressive stabilization of the Cu2+ and Nb5+ oxidation states, directly correlating with enhanced long-range lattice ordering and distinct surface-mediated catalytic behaviors during Fenton pathways. In summary, we clarify how the thermal evolution of CuNb2O6 coordinates its crystal and electronic structures, and evaluate these effects on Fenton catalytic efficiency. By defining the precise thermodynamic and kinetic windows essential for stabilizing either the monoclinic or orthorhombic architectures, these insights provide a fundamental baseline for the rational design and optimization of copper-niobium oxide catalysts tailored for advanced oxidation processes.

P3-020.a: Microwave-assisted Fenton oxidation offers rapid volumetric heating and efficient hydroxyl radical generation for wastewater treatment. Copper germanates are promising catalysts because their Cu2+/Cu2+ redox couple facilitates H2O2 activation. However, the influence of crystal structure on microwave-responsive Fenton activity remains unclear. This work compares CuGeO3 and Cu2GeO4 to establish the relationship between crystal structure, surface chemistry, and catalytic performance. CuGeO3 and Cu2₂GeO4 nanomaterials were synthesized hydrothermally. Their structures and surface properties were characterized by XRD, SEM, TEM, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS. Microwave-assisted Fenton degradation was evaluated using H2O2. Catalytic behavior was interpreted by correlating crystal structure, Cu oxidation states, and oxygen defects with the reaction mechanism. XRD confirmed phase-pure CuGeO3 and Cu2GeO4 with distinct crystal frameworks. SEM and TEM revealed different particle morphologies and crystallinities. Raman spectra showed variations in Cu–O and Ge–O bonding associated with lattice distortion. XPS identified differences in Cu2+/Cu+ ratios and oxygen defect concentrations, indicating distinct surface electronic structures. These characteristics governed microwave-assisted Fenton activity by influencing microwave energy coupling, Cu2+/Cu+ redox cycling, H2O2 activation, and hydroxyl radical generation. The catalyst possessing more favorable redox characteristics and abundant oxygen defects exhibited superior degradation efficiency. The catalytic performance of CuGeO3 and Cu2GeO4 is governed by crystal-structure-dependent surface chemistry rather than phase composition alone. Structural differences modify copper redox behavior and oxygen defect formation, thereby controlling microwave-assisted radical generation. This study provides mechanistic insight into the design of microwave-responsive ceramic catalysts for advanced oxidation processes.

P3-021.a: Memristor is a two-terminal device whose internal state and resistance change according to the history of the applied voltage. Its simple structure and low power consumption make it attractive for next-generation memory. Moreover, the ability to integrate data storage and computation within the same system reduces unnecessary data movement, enabling energy-efficient neuromorphic information processing. This study aims to explore a common material platform in which process control produces distinct switching mechanisms for binary memory and analog synaptic computing, facilitating their integration into neuromorphic computing systems. The study consists of three main stages: fabricating devices tailored for data storage and computing, elucidating their operating mechanisms, and quantitatively evaluating their application-specific performance. To implement this device concept, we employ sputter-deposited Sb2Te3 as the switching layer. Its structurally flexible bonding network and tunable amorphous-crystalline phase transition are advantageous for controlling defect distribution. Defect engineering is achieved through metal doping and by controlling working pressure and post-deposition annealing conditions. We found that as deposited amorphous Sb2Te3 exhibited non-filamentary switching behavior with gradual conductance modulation suitable for analog computing. In contrast, metal doping or post-deposition annealing promoted crystallization, indicating a possible transition toward filamentary switching behavior favorable for binary memory applications. This strategy enables binary memory and analog computing devices to be independently optimized for their respective applications. Therefore, our approach may support the integration of individually optimized binary memory and analog computing devices on a common platform while maintaining material and process compatibility, thereby promoting high performance and energy efficient operation.

P3-022.a: Heteroepitaxial growth of β-Ga₂O₃ on c-plane sapphire by metal–organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) is highly sensitive to gas-phase reactions between gallium precursors and oxygen. Premature reactions and substantial lattice mismatch can deteriorate film quality and reduce growth efficiency. Therefore, precise reactor flow-field control is essential for large-area oxide semiconductor growth. We investigated the effects of flow-field control on β-Ga₂O₃ films grown on 6-inch c-plane sapphire using a multi-zone showerhead MOCVD reactor. Growth temperature, V/III ratio, and oxygen push-gas flow rate were systematically varied. The precursor-injection configuration was optimized by reducing gallium-precursor dilution and introducing controlled N₂ flow through an intermediate showerhead stage. Film properties were evaluated using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, atomic force microscopy (AFM), and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM). XRD revealed characteristic diffraction reflections of monoclinic β-Ga₂O₃ in addition to the dominant sapphire peak, confirming β-phase formation. Raman spectra exhibited characteristic β-Ga₂O₃ vibrational modes distinct from those of sapphire, supporting phase-pure film formation. Under optimized conditions, FE-SEM showed progressively coalesced, faceted grains with substantially improved surface uniformity compared with earlier nucleation-dominated films. AFM further confirmed a smooth, low-roughness surface. These improvements are attributed to suppressed premature gas-phase reactions and a transition toward surface-reaction-limited growth. These results indicate that precise control of growth temperature, V/III ratio, and oxygen push-gas flow, combined with multi-zone showerhead flow-field engineering, enables phase-pure, smooth-surfaced β-Ga₂O₃ heteroepitaxy on 6-inch c-plane sapphire. The findings provide practical guidelines for wafer-scale oxide semiconductor growth for next-generation wide-bandgap devices.

P3-023.a: Salivary ion analysis is a promising non-invasive approach for monitoring physiological conditions because major ions, including K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, and Cl⁻, play essential roles in body metabolism. Organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) based on ethylene glycol-modified PEDOT:PSS (EGPP) have attracted considerable interest as sensing platforms owing to their high sensitivity, excellent electrical properties, and biocompatibility.
