This study aimed to develop a multi-ion detection sennsor (MIDS) incorporating an EGPP-based OECT for simultaneous salivary ion detection. The MIDS was designed, fabricated, and characterized using a semiconductor wafer-scale batch process. EGPP was selectively deposited onto patterned source and drain electrodes to form the OECT channel, while ion-selective membranes (ISMs) were integrated for selective detection of K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, and Cl⁻. The fabricated 10 × 10 mm² device consisted of four sensing channels for multi-ion detection and one additional channel for glucose sensing. Device performance was evaluated by measuring ion detection sensitivity, selectivity, interference resistance among analytes, and sensing performance in artificial saliva. The MIDS successfully detected K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, and Cl⁻ at concentrations below 10⁻⁵ M with a resolution of approximately 2 × 10⁻³ log concentration. The multi-channel architecture enabled simultaneous and selective detection with minimal cross-interference between analytes. Stable responses obtained in artificial saliva further demonstrated the reliability and practical applicability of the sensing platform. The EGPP-based MIDS provides sensitive, selective, and simultaneous multi-ion detection through a scalable wafer-scale fabrication process. Its reliable performance in artificial saliva highlights its potential for personalized point-of-care healthcare, non-invasive salivary diagnostics, and environmental water quality monitoring.

P3-024.a: With the rapid advancement of wireless technology and the ubiquity of electronic devices, exposure to electromagnetic waves has become an inevitable part of modern life. While these waves enable global connectivity, prolonged or high-level exposure poses several significant risks, which can be categorized into biological health hazards and technical interferences. MXene is a promising electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding material due to its high electrical conductivity, two-dimensional structure, and abundant surface functional groups. However, its insufficient oxidative stability and mechanical properties necessitate hybridization with processable materials, such as polymers, for commercialization. Epoxy resin, possessing excellent mechanical strength, chemical resistance, and processability, is widely utilized as a matrix for stealth coatings in the extreme environments of the aerospace and defense industries. In this study, to implement practical, high-performance stealth technology, highly conductive MXene and magnetic materials were dispersed in epoxy to fabricate multilayer structured films. To ensure dispersion stability and interfacial bonding strength, the surface of the composite materials was modified to induce uniform dispersion within the epoxy matrix. Furthermore, the optimal reflection loss value was achieved by adjusting the mixing ratio of MXene and the magnetic material to balance dielectric loss and magnetic loss. The fabricated multilayer structure of MXene and magnetic materials exhibited superior EMI shielding and absorption performance compared to the single-layer structure. This is attributed to the electromagnetic synergy between the dielectric loss of MXene and the magnetic loss of magnetic materials, which optimizes impedance matching and promotes multiple interfacial scattering. These results demonstrate that a high electromagnetic wave absorption performance can be secured even in thin coating structures through laminated structure design. Consequently, this approach is expected to contribute to eco-friendliness by simplifying the coating process for electromagnetic shielding coatings and improving application weight.

P3-025.k: Laser Doping; Back-Contact Solar Cell; Annealing
P3-025.a: Laser technology has attracted significant attention in silicon solar cell fabrication due to its capability for precise localized pattern formation without lithography. In silicon back-contact solar cells, localized rear-side doping is essential for carrier-selective contacts, but conventional thermal diffusion has limitations in spatial doping control and may degrade interface quality because of its high thermal budget. Therefore, laser doping combined with thermal annealing is a promising approach for forming localized doped regions while preserving interface quality. In this study, laser doping was investigated for silicon back-contact solar cells incorporating poly-Si-based passivating contacts. The effects of p-a-Si thickness, boron supply, laser energy density, and subsequent thermal annealing on doping characteristics were systematically evaluated. Electrical properties and passivation quality were characterized by quasi-steady-state photoconductance(QSSPC), while dopant profiles were analyzed using secondary ion mass spectrometry(SIMS). Laser doping behavior strongly depended on thin-film composition and laser-induced melting conditions. Increasing laser energy density enhanced dopant activation and reduced sheet resistance; however, excessive energy degraded the poly-Si/SiOx interface and decreased iVoc. SIMS confirmed dopant redistribution within the laser-melted region. A 100 nm p-a-Si layer provided stable dopant activation over an intermediate laser energy density range of 0.3–0.7 J/cm². Subsequent thermal annealing further improved electrical properties and interface quality. In addition, a SiNx/Al₂O₃ passivation stack effectively suppressed laser-induced defects, achieving a maximum iVoc of 716 mV. These results demonstrate that optimized laser doping and thermal annealing provide an effective route to achieving stable dopant activation, improved interface quality, and enhanced performance of high-efficiency silicon back-contact solar cells.

P3-026.a: The continued miniaturization of semiconductor devices demands deep-ultraviolet (DUV)-responsive photobase generators (PBGs) for high-resolution photoresist patterning. Herein, we report two carbamate-based PBGs with blue-shifted chromophores: 1-naphthylmethyl N,N-diethyl carbamate (PBG-2) and Benzyl N,N-diethyl carbamate (PBG-3). Their DUV absorption characteristics and photobase-generation efficiencies were evaluated and compared with that of 9-anthrylmethyl N,N-diethyl carbamate (PBG-1) as a reference. PBG-1 exhibits strong absorption near 365 nm because of its anthracene chromophore, whereas PBG-2 shows enhanced absorption in the 200–300 nm region relevant to krypton fluoride (KrF) lithography. PBG-3 displays an even greater blue shift, extending its absorption further into the DUV region relevant to both KrF and argon fluoride (ArF) lithography. Photo-base generation was quantified using a phenol red assay. Under DUV irradiation, both PBG-2 and PBG-3 generated significantly larger amounts of base than PBG-1, with PBG-3 exhibiting the highest photo-base generation efficiency. The enhanced DUV absorption and efficient photo-base generation of PBG-2 and PBG-3 demonstrate the effectiveness of chromophore engineering for developing DUV-responsive PBGs. These findings provide valuable molecular design guidelines for next-generation KrF and ArF photoresist systems.

P3-027.k: Reverse Electrodialysis; Pulse Electrodeposition; Electrode Microstructure
P3-027.a: Reverse electrodialysis (RED) is a sustainable energy conversion technology that generates electrical power from salinity gradients through the selective transport of ions across ion-exchange membranes. In this study, the structural and surface properties of electrodes were tailored to improve the electrochemical performance and energy conversion efficiency of RED systems. Pulse electrodeposition, consisting of periodically alternating current-on and current-off periods, was employed to regulate metal-ion reduction and mass transport near the electrode surface. The pulse duration was systematically varied to investigate the effects of ion redistribution and diffusion-layer relaxation during the current-off period. This relaxation period facilitated the replenishment of metal ions at the electrode-electrolyte interface, thereby alleviating local concentration depletion and maintaining a more stable deposition environment. Repeated ion supply and reduction promoted spatially uniform nucleation while suppressing excessive grain growth and particle agglomeration. Consequently, pulse parameter optimization facilitated controlled Pt nucleation and growth, resulting in a thin catalytic layer with improved Pt utilization. microstructure compared with conventional continuous electrodeposition. The resulting structural improvements are expected to increase the electrochemically active surface area, facilitate charge transfer, and enhance electrode reaction kinetics in the RED system. This study presents a controlled electrode fabrication strategy for reducing electrode reaction resistance, improving long-term operational stability, and minimizing catalyst loading. By establishing relationships among pulse conditions, electrode morphology, and electrochemical characteristics, this work provides a foundation for designing efficient RED electrodes with improved material utilization. Ultimately, the proposed approach may contribute to enhanced energy conversion performance and economic feasibility in the fabrication and practical application of RED systems.

P3-028.k: Reverse Electrodialysis; Low-Grade Heat Utilization; Electrochemical Diagnostics
P3-028.a: Reverse electrodialysis(RED) converts the Gibbs free energy of mixing high and low salinity solutions into electrical energy. Increasing feed temperature can enhance ionic mobility and conductivity while reducing solution channel and ion exchange membrane resistance. Low-grade heat sources, including hot spring, low temperature geothermal water, industrial cooling water, and warm effluents could be used through external heat exchangers to preheat RED feeds with minimal high-grade energy input.However, the effects of feed temperatures above 50℃ on continuous RED performance and internal resistance remain insufficiently understood. In this study, 30 and 0.5 g/L NaCl solutions were used as high-and low-salinity feeds respectively. Both feeds were indirectly heated in a temperature controlled water bath to 25,40,50,60 and 70℃ and supplied to a single cell RED device at 5 mL/min for 180 min. Open-circuit voltage, maximum current density, maximum power density and in situ electrochemical impedance were periodically meaured. The water bath reproduced feed-temperature conditions achievable through indirect heat exchange with low grade heat sources. RED preformance improved as feed temperature increased from 25 to 60℃ because of enhanced ion transport and reduced ohmic resistance. The highest performance occurred at 60℃. At 70℃ power generation decreased despite low ohmic resistance, while polarization-related resistance increased, indicating interfacial or mass-transfer losses. These results demonstrate that indirect feed preheating using low-grade heat can improve RED performance, whereas excessive heating may offset conductivity benefits through increased polarization. Therefore, conductivity enhancement and polarization losses should be considered when optimizing feed temperature for RED systems coupled with low-grade heat sources.

P3-029.a: Doped tungsten oxide nanocrystals (NCs) have demonstrated localized surface plasmon resonance absorption ranging from the visible to the near-infrared (NIR) spectrum, enabling their use in electrochromic applications. The hexagonal tunnels in these NCs allow larger cations to move quickly and be charged, serving as optically active sites. While dopants are necessary in these tunnels to maintain structural stability, they hinder the insertion of sodium electrolyte ions. Previous research has shown that rod-shaped Cs:WO3-x NCs, with fewer accessible tunnels, exhibit low charge capacity compared to plate-shaped NCs. To address this issue, dopants are typically removed via acidic treatment; however, this process etches the NCs. In this work, we overcome this limitation by synthesizing NH₄⁺/NH₃-doped hexagonal tungsten oxide nanorods and systematically removing the dopants via a simple thermal annealing process. Thermal treatment at 400 °C increases the charge capacity by more than fourfold relative to Cs⁺-doped nanorods. Coupled with the intrinsically high coloration efficiency of the nanorod architecture, a 150 nm-thick film delivers an optical modulation of 74% at 1200 nm, approaching the performance of Li⁺-based electrochromic systems. This suggests that increasing the number of hexagonal tunnels with negligible dopants through a simple annealing process can help resolve the issue of lower charge capacity. Based on these findings, we propose the use of thermally removable dopant-doped tungsten oxide NCs as a promising material for modulating the NIR region through optically active hexagonal tunnels.

P3-030.k: Residual Stress; ; NF₃/H₂ Remote Plasma Dry Cleaning; Raman Spectroscopy
P3-030.a: With the continuous scaling of semiconductor devices and the advent of three-dimensional (3D) integration technologies, the fabrication of high-aspect-ratio (HAR) contact holes with minimal defects has become essential to ensuring device performance and reliability. A critical challenge in HAR contact formation is the effective removal of the native oxide layer, particularly the non-uniform Angstrom-thick oxide film formed at the bottom of the contact, which degrades device reliability and increases contact resistance. To overcome these issues, remote plasma-based dry cleaning has emerged as a promising alternative, offering high selectivity between the native oxide and underlying substrate materials, along with enhanced process efficiency. atomic force microscopy was employed to characterize the surface morphology and to acquire force–distance (F–D) curves. A SiO₂ colloidal probe was used as the AFM probe for F-D curve measurement in ambient condtions. Prior to the measurements, calibration of the force slope, cantilever sensitivity, and spring constant was performed. Surface bonding states under different process stages and temperatures were further examined using XPS, while adhesion at the film–residue interface was quantified from AFM force–distance curves, which revealed relatively stronger adhesion on Si₃N₄ substrates. The formation and removal of ammonium fluorosilicate layers during NF₃/H₂ remote plasma dry cleaning were quantitatively analyzed in terms of residual stress. Importantly, the Raman shift of the Si LO phonon peak was interpreted not only as a measure of the intrinsic stress in the Si substrate, but also as an indirect indicator of the interfacial stress transferred from the overlying SiO₂ or Si₃N₄ films.

P3-031.k: Optofluidic Device with Functional Plasmonic Nanomaterials; Monitoring of Biological Conversion; Carbon Monoxide
P3-031.a: The monitoring of biological conversion of carbon monoxide has so far been conducted by chromatographic analysis with offline sampling. However, such conventional indirect method often causes microbial contamination during repeated sampling, which leads to the failure of the bioconversion and also suffers from poor sensitivity. Here, I would like to present an optofluidic device with functional plasmonic nanomaterials for the real-time direct and sensitive detection of bioconversion of carbon monoxide in large-scale gas-liquid reactors. The optofluidic device is systematically designed based on fluid dynamics simulations to (i) prevent the loss of plasmonic nanomaterials by the shear stress caused by the impeller agitation, (ii) avoid the optical interference by the gas bubbles, and (iii) enable the free diffusion of target dissolved molecules onto the nanomaterials. Under dynamic conditions, the concentration of dissolved carbon monoxide is precisely determined down to 20 μM in bioconversion media from the measured Raman signals by employing machine learning. Finally, the biological conversion by carbon monoxide dehydrogenase has been successfully tracked by the proposed method, which cannot be achieved by the conventional indirect method. The proposed work could contribute to the advancement of gas bioconversion by enabling process optimization at an industrial scale and facilitating the screening and discovery of high-performing microorganisms at a lab-scale.

P3-032.a: Area-selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD) has emerged as an important bottom-up patterning technique, enabling self-aligned fabrication without the edge placement error inherent to conventional lithography-based patterning, while offering a potential route toward more resource- and process-efficient fabrication by reducing reliance on repeated lithography and etching steps. Its success relies on establishing a sufficient reactivity contrast between growth and non-growth areas, which in small molecule inhibitor (SMI)-based approaches has conventionally been attributed to the difference in acidity between oxide surfaces. However, this acidity-based criterion does not extend to trimethylaluminum (TMA), whose high reactivity and small molecular size make it the most demanding precursor for blocking the non-growth area. Here, we elucidate the inhibition mechanism of acetylacetone in Al2O3 AS-ALD on Pt and SiO2 surfaces, where TMA adsorbs through dissociation at catalytic sites and through hydroxyl-mediated ligand exchange, respectively. Utilizing this difference in adsorption pathway, selective deposition was achieved using a three-step (ABC-type) cycle of acetylacetone, TMA, and H2O pulses. The selectivity window extended with increasing deposition temperature, indicating that the temperature dependence arises from the inhibitor rather than from the TMA-H2O surface reactions. The same behavior was observed on Pd, another noble metal on which TMA adsorbs through dissociation, supporting that the inhibition is governed by the adsorption pathway of the precursor. By demonstrating inhibition on the most challenging precursor, our work establishes a new design rule for inhibitor selection, one governed by the adsorption pathway of the precursor rather than by the acidity of the surface. Such mechanistic design of selective surface reactions could facilitate more material-efficient and environmentally sustainable atomic-scale fabrication by minimizing unnecessary deposition, patterning, and material removal, while extending AS-ALD to a wider range of precursor systems.

P3-033.k: Titanium Carbide; Self-propagating High-temperature Synthesis; Free Carbon
P3-033.a: Titanium carbide (TiC) is used for cutting tools and wear parts, but conventional synthesis methods suffer from high temperatures, long reaction times, and complex equipment. Self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS), utilizing exothermic heat without external energy, offers an efficient alternative. This study aimed to determine the optimal carbon input ratio in the SHS process to synthesize high-purity TiC powder by suppressing unreacted free carbon. Using TiO₂, Mg, and C, simultaneous reduction and carburization were induced with Mg fixed at 4 moles. To minimize free carbon, the carbon molar ratio was varied in five levels from 1.1 to 1.5 moles. After synthesis, acid leaching removed residual MgO and unreacted materials. Samples were evaluated using a carbon/sulfur analyzer, with phase and microstructural analyses performed via XRD and SEM. As the C molar ratio increased from 1.3 to 1.5, the carbon content increased (22.0–25.1 wt%), indicating residual free carbon. However, the 1.1 mole condition (TiO₂ + 4Mg + 1.1C) yielded 20.4 wt% carbon. This value is closest to the theoretical TiC carbon content of 20.06 wt% (a +0.34%p deviation), demonstrating the lowest free carbon generation and highest phase purity among all conditions. The results confirm that the SHS process can efficiently produce high-purity TiC powder in a single step. Optimizing the carbon ratio minimizes free carbon, offering significant advantages in process simplification and cost reduction.

P3-034.a: Efficient electron transfer and stable enzyme integration remain key challenges in constructing high-performance biofuel cell (BFC) anodes. Ferritin provides a redox-active protein nanostructure capable of promoting electronic communication within enzyme-based biointerfaces. Here, we integrate ferritin with glucose oxidase (GOx) and citrate-capped gold nanoparticles (citrate–Au NPs) to construct stable electron-transfer biointerfaces on three-dimensional metallic cotton fiber (MCF) electrodes. Conductive MCF hosts were first prepared using tetraoctylammonium bromide-capped Au nanoparticles (TOABr–Au NPs), providing a three-dimensional conductive framework for biointerface assembly. Ferritin/GOx multilayers were constructed through layer-by-layer assembly and compared with tris(2-aminoethyl)amine (TREN)/GOx reference systems to evaluate the contribution of ferritin. Citrate–Au NPs were subsequently incorporated to form Ferritin/citrate–Au NP/GOx/citrate–Au NP multilayers. Their hydrophilic surface provides favorable interactions with the enzyme layers while introducing nanoscale conductive components within the multilayer architecture. Ferritin-containing GOx electrodes exhibited higher electrochemical activity than TREN-based reference electrodes, supporting the contribution of ferritin to enhanced electronic communication within the biointerface. Incorporation of citrate–Au NPs further promoted electron-transfer pathways while facilitating stable integration of the enzyme-containing multilayers. Combined with the three-dimensional conductive framework established by TOABr–Au NPs, the Ferritin/citrate–Au NP/GOx/citrate–Au NP architecture exhibited enhanced glucose-oxidation performance and improved operational stability. These results demonstrate that ferritin-mediated electron transfer can be cooperatively integrated with citrate–Au NP-assisted enzyme stabilization and a three-dimensional conductive MCF framework. This multifunctional interfacial design provides a promising strategy for constructing high-performance and durable BFC anodes.

P3-035.a: Chemical and biosensing semiconductor platforms still face challenges in achieving reliable and reproducible surface functionalization. A key bottleneck is the effective introduction of chemical functionalities onto semiconductor surfaces while maintaining high sensing performance. In this study, we investigate the surface functionalization of polymer-like amorphous carbon (PAC) and its relationship with sensing performance through optical characterization. The PAC was employed as a surface modification layer for ZnO FET sensors using plasma deposition, a dry and scalable fabrication technique. PAC layers were deposited onto ZnO FET devices using a plasma deposition process, and their surface properties were investigated using optical characterization. Copper (Cu2+) solution was subsequently drop-cast onto the functionalized surface, and Raman spectroscopy was performed to investigate the changes in the Raman spectra induced by Cu binding. In parallel, electrical responses to Cu ions were measured using the ZnO FET devices, and the Raman results were compared with the electrical sensing signals to elucidate the sensing mechanism. Upon Cu binding to the PAC surface, distinct changes in the Raman spectra were observed, including the disappearance of specific peaks and the emergence of new peaks. These spectral changes provided evidence of interactions between Cu ions and surface functional groups and enabled the prediction of Cu binding on the surface. In addition, the FET devices exhibited measurable electrical responses to Cu ions. The correlation between the Raman spectral changes and the electrical sensing signals demonstrated that the observed optical changes were closely associated with the sensing process. This study demonstrates that Raman spectroscopy can be effectively employed to investigate the surface interactions underlying ZnO FET-based Cu ion sensing. By correlating Cu-induced Raman spectral changes with electrical sensing responses, the binding behavior and sensing mechanism at the PAC surface were elucidated. These findings provide fundamental insight into the relationship among surface modification, optical properties, and sensing performance, and highlight the potential of plasma-deposited PAC as a scalable surface modification strategy for FET-based chemical and biosensing platforms.

P3-036.k: ZnO Nanoplate; Colloidal Syntheis; Ligand-controlled Growth
P3-036.a: Metal-oxide nanocrystals are attractive building blocks for nanocomposites and for assembly into ordered arrays, but this requires control over their size and exposed facets, which remains difficult in solution-phase synthesis. Wurtzite ZnO grows fastest along the c axis, so plate-like habits run against its intrinsic tendency; obtaining well-faceted hexagonal nanoplates exposing the polar (0001) basal facet while maintaining sufficiently small lateral dimensions for use as building blocks is therefore challenging. Ligands in colloidal ZnO synthesis act on nucleation and growth at the same time, so changes made to tune one feature tend to alter the others. ZnO nanoplates were prepared by a colloidal heat-up route from zinc acetate as the zinc source, dissolved in 1-octanol with oleylamine, which solubilizes the precursor and coordinates to zinc from the outset. The synthesis was deliberately staged: oleic acid, the second ligand, was withheld from initial stirring and injected only after the reaction temperature had stabilized, and water, which promotes precursor hydrolysis and initiates ZnO formation, was injected as a separate second step. This strategy separated pre-nucleation ligand conditioning from water-triggered nucleation, allowing these variables to be systematically investigated: aging time between the two injections, the amount of oleic acid, and the reaction temperature. A synthesis without oleic acid was carried out for comparison. Morphology and size distribution were followed by scanning electron microscopy, and dispersibility was assessed in nonpolar solvents. Increasing the aging time before water injection enabled systematic tuning of the lateral size between approximately 50 and 300 nm, consistent with a gradual evolution of the zinc-ligand coordination environment. Increasing the amount of oleic acid gave more regular hexagonal outlines, and raising the reaction temperature both sharpened the facets and narrowed the size distribution within a batch. Without oleic acid, the synthesis still gave hexagonal plates, but with a broad size distribution, poorly developed facets, and no dispersibility in nonpolar solvents; the ligand therefore controls how uniform and well-defined the plates become, not whether they form at all. Size, faceting, and dispersibility respond to different experimental parameters in this system: the aging time before nucleation primarily determines the lateral size, while oleic acid governs uniformity, facet development, and colloidal stability. Together these parameters enable the preparation of ZnO nanoplates that are size-tunable and readily dispersible in organic media. Work now underway is aimed at confirming the facet assignment by diffraction, and resolving how the ligand is bound at the surface. Because the plates are synthesized under relatively mild conditions and disperse readily in organic solvents, they are also well suited to solution-processed device fabrication and to further assembly into ordered arrays.

P3-037.k: Plasma Etching; High-Aspect-Ratio Structures; Surface Charge Accumulation
P3-037.a: Charge accumulation on dielectric surfaces is an important factor affecting plasma etching in high-aspect-ratio (HAR) structures. During plasma exposure, the difference in transport behavior between ions and electrons induces local surface charging, which modifies the electrostatic potential and electric field inside the feature. These fields can alter the trajectories and incident energies of charged particles, leading to nonuniform ion fluxes and potentially causing profile distortions such as bowing, notching, and reduced bottom etch rates in HAR etching processes. Therefore, a self-consistent description of charge accumulation and charged-particle transport is required to accurately predict plasma–surface interactions in HAR etching. A three-dimensional charge-up model was incorporated into a feature-scale plasma etching simulator. The electrostatic potential was calculated using the Boundary Element Method (BEM), in which the vacuum and dielectric regions were treated as separate domains and coupled through electrostatic interface conditions. Surface charge density was updated according to the local accumulation of incident ions and electrons. The resulting electrostatic potential and electric field were then used to modify subsequent charged-particle trajectories, establishing an iterative coupling between particle transport, surface charging, and the electrostatic field. This framework enables the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of charge-induced electric fields to be evaluated without discretizing the entire simulation volume. The simulation demonstrated the dynamic development of surface charge and electrostatic potential within high-aspect-ratio structures. Because ions and electrons exhibit different transport characteristics, their local imbalance resulted in spatially nonuniform charge accumulation along the dielectric surface. The accumulated charge generated localized variations in electrostatic potential and electric field, particularly along the sidewalls and near the feature bottom. These electrostatic fields subsequently modified the trajectories and surface incidence of charged particles, leading to spatial variations in ion flux and incident conditions. As the charge distribution evolved, the local ion and electron fluxes were continuously redistributed, forming a feedback mechanism between particle transport, surface charging, and the electrostatic field. Consequently, nonuniform charge accumulation produced localized differences in surface reactions and etching behavior, resulting in spatial nonuniformity and distortion of the etch profile. These results indicate that the evolution of the etch profile is strongly coupled to the local charge distribution and the resulting electrostatic environment within the feature. A self-consistent three-dimensional charge-up model was developed to describe the coupled evolution of surface charge, electrostatic potential, and charged-particle transport during plasma etching. The results show that the imbalance between local ion and electron fluxes produces nonuniform surface charging, which generates internal electric fields capable of significantly modifying subsequent particle trajectories. This charge–field–particle feedback governs the spatial evolution of the electrostatic environment inside high-aspect-ratio features and can lead to nonuniform ion incidence and localized differences in surface reactions. Consequently, charge-up effects were found to contribute to spatial nonuniformity and asymmetry in the resulting etch profile. These results demonstrate that charge accumulation is an important mechanism for understanding charge-induced profile distortion in high-aspect-ratio plasma etching, and the proposed model provides a framework for quantitatively investigating these effects in advanced semiconductor structures.

P3-038.a: Thermoacoustic (TA) loudspeakers are promising solid-state acoustic devices for flexible and conformal electronics because they generate sound through periodic Joule heating without conventional vibrating diaphragms. However, their practical applications are still limited by inefficient thermal dissipation, thickness-dependent acoustic performance, and insufficient mechanical adaptability. In particular, conventional planar graphene-based TA loudspeakers typically require ultrathin films to achieve high sound pressure levels (SPLs), which compromises mechanical robustness and limits their integration into shape-adaptive and three-dimensional acoustic systems. We developed vertically aligned reduced graphene oxide (VrGO) thermoacoustic loudspeakers using a dual-laser processing strategy. Continuous-wave CO₂ laser irradiation was employed to simultaneously reduce graphene oxide and create vertically oriented, porous graphene microstructures, thereby enhancing out-of-plane thermal transport and increasing the effective air-contact area. Subsequently, nanosecond pulsed laser ablation was used to introduce programmable kirigami, auxetic, and three-dimensional patterns without additional lithographic processes. The structural, chemical, thermal, mechanical, and acoustic properties of the resulting VrGO devices were systematically evaluated and compared with conventional planar reduced graphene oxide (PrGO) loudspeakers. The laser-engineered VrGO structure exhibited enhanced graphitization and improved heat dissipation compared with PrGO. The specific heat capacity of VrGO was reduced to 0.503 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, compared with 0.718 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for PrGO, facilitating efficient thermoacoustic conversion. The VrGO loudspeaker achieved an SPL of 85.0 dB at 10 kHz, exceeding the 78.9 dB of the planar PrGO device. Moreover, VrGO substantially suppressed the conventional thickness-dependent degradation in acoustic performance: even a substantially thicker VrGO device maintained an SPL of 82.6 dB at 10 kHz, whereas the corresponding planar structure decreased to 66.1 dB. Kirigami-patterned VrGO loudspeakers retained approximately 75% of their original SPL under 500% strain and showed stable acoustic performance over 1000 stretching–releasing cycles. Furthermore, auxetic and prismoid configurations enabled conformal attachment, reversible 2D-to-3D transformation, and spatially distributed acoustic emission. Laser-engineered vertical graphene provides an effective strategy for simultaneously improving thermal management, acoustic performance, and mechanical reconfigurability in thermoacoustic loudspeakers. The integration of vertical graphene architectures with programmable laser patterning enables mechanically robust, shape-adaptive, and three-dimensional sound emitters, providing a promising platform for future wearable audio systems, conformal electronics, and adaptive human–machine interfaces.

P3-039.a: Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) are compositionally tunable layered materials whose physicochemical properties can be tailored through the selection of constituent metal ions. However, the direct synthesis of multi-component LDHs can make it difficult to independently control the composition and structural characteristics of individual layers. In this study, we investigated a compositionally controlled nanosheet assembly strategy to construct multi-component layered superstructures from preformed binary LDHs with distinct metal compositions. Nitrate-intercalated Ni–Fe, Mg–Al, Mg–Fe, and Ni–Al binary LDHs were synthesized by coprecipitation. The synthesized LDHs were exfoliated by dispersing the wet filter cakes in formamide (1 g/L) for at least 72 h, followed by ultrasonication. The resulting nanosheets were subsequently reassembled through carbonate-induced restacking, either individually or as mixed dispersions containing compositionally distinct LDHs. The structural and compositional characteristics of the exfoliated and reconstructed products were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD), atomic force microscopy (AFM), scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM–EDS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). XRD confirmed the formation of well-defined hydrotalcite-like phases for all binary LDHs. After exfoliation, the disappearance of the basal (003) and (006) reflections indicated disruption of long-range layer stacking, while AFM confirmed the formation of ultrathin LDH nanosheets. Following carbonate-induced restacking, the characteristic basal reflections were recovered, demonstrating the reconstruction of the layered structure, although with a moderate decrease in stacking order. XPS confirmed the presence of Mg²⁺, Ni²⁺, Al³⁺, and Fe³⁺ in the representative mixed-restacked product, and SEM–EDS elemental mapping revealed a homogeneous spatial distribution of the four constituent metals throughout the reconstructed particles. In contrast, the directly coprecipitated quaternary LDH exhibited elemental segregation, indicating improved compositional homogeneity through the nanosheet restacking approach. These results demonstrate that compositionally distinct binary LDH nanosheets can be successfully integrated into a common multi-component layered architecture through exfoliation and subsequent restacking. By separating the formation of individual binary LDH nanosheets from their multi-component assembly, this strategy enables greater control over the composition and structural organization of complex LDH systems than direct multicomponent coprecipitation. The exfoliation–restacking approach therefore provides a versatile platform for constructing compositionally controlled multi-material layered structures and may offer opportunities for the rational design of functional nanomaterials with tailored properties.

P3-040.k: Layered Double Hydroxide; Surface Functionalization; Antifouling
P3-040.a: Surface fouling can reduce material performance and lifetime. Hierarchical surface structures and surface energy control offer approaches to improving antifouling properties. Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) are two-dimensional materials with hydroxyl-rich surfaces and ion-exchange properties. This study investigated how ZnAl-LDH growth on alumina microparticles and subsequent stearic acid treatment affect wettability, surface energy, and antifouling performance. Alumina microparticles with a diameter of 30 μm were pretreated with NaOH, followed by urea-assisted hydrothermal synthesis to grow ZnAl-LDH platelets perpendicularly on their surfaces (alumina@LDH). The crystalline phase and surface structure were characterized by X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy. Alumina and alumina@LDH particles were separately cast onto glass substrates using a polymer as a binder. Static contact angles were measured with water and diiodomethane, and the surface energies of the coatings were calculated using the Owens–Wendt–Rabel–Kaelble (OWRK) model. Both coatings were subsequently treated with stearic acid to compare their water repellency and antifouling performance. ZnAl-LDH platelets grew on the alumina surfaces, forming hierarchical structures composed of microparticles and surface nanostructures. After LDH growth, the water contact angle increased from 46.2 ± 1.2° to 59.5 ± 1.0°, while the surface energy calculated using the OWRK model decreased from 60.4 to 50.5 mN/m. These results indicate that LDH growth modified the wettability and interfacial properties of the particle-based coatings. Following stearic acid treatment, the alumina@LDH coating exhibited enhanced water repellency and antifouling performance compared with the similarly treated alumina coating. The direct growth of ZnAl-LDH on alumina microparticles effectively introduced hierarchical surface structures and modified the interfacial properties of the coatings. Combining these structures with stearic acid treatment improved water repellency and antifouling performance. This study provides an approach to designing functional antifouling coatings by combining surface nanostructure formation with chemical modification of inorganic microparticles.

P3-041.k: Ammonia Electrolysis; Ternary Metal Oxide Electrocatalyst; Hard Templating Method
P3-041.a: Ammonia electrolysis is a promising route for low-energy hydrogen production and simultaneous treatment of ammonia-containing wastewater, but its practical application is limited by sluggish ammonia oxidation kinetics and the high cost of noble-metal catalysts. a non-precious trimetallic Ni–Co–Cu oxide catalyst with a nanorod-bundle structure was developed through metal composition control and hard templating. SBA-15 was used as a silica template, and Ni, Co, and Cu nitrate precursors were introduced through a two-solvent impregnation method, followed by calcination and alkaline template removal. Transmission electron microscopy and elemental mapping confirmed nanorod bundles with homogeneous metal distribution, while nitrogen adsorption–desorption analysis showed mesoporous characteristics originating from inter-rod voids. X-ray diffraction identified NiO, Co₃O₄, and CuO phases, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed composition-dependent modulation of Ni and Co oxidation states and the presence of Cu²⁺, demonstrating electronic interactions among the metals. Among the compositions, Ni₈₀Co₁₅Cu₅ oxide exhibited the highest ammonia oxidation activity in 1 M KOH containing 0.5 M NH₄OH. The optimized catalyst showed a lower onset potential, the lowest Tafel slope of 129.98 mV dec⁻¹, reduced charge-transfer resistance, and the largest electrochemically active surface area of 17.3 mm². It also maintained the highest current density during 24 h chronoamperometry and showed current recovery upon periodic ammonia replenishment over 50 h. The enhanced performance is attributed to abundant Ni-based active sites, Ni–Cu synergistic interactions, and balanced electronic-structure modulation by Co and Cu. These results highlight the importance of metal composition in determining the ammonia electrooxidation performance of Ni–Co–Cu oxide catalysts, with Ni₈₀Co₁₅Cu₅ exhibiting the most favorable activity and stability among the tested compositions.

P3-042.k: Lithium-mediated Nitrogen Reduction; Interfacial Ion Distribution; Solid Electrolyte Interphase
P3-042.a: Lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction (Li-NRR) is a promising electrochemical route for sustainable ammonia synthesis under mild conditions. During Li-NRR, electrolyte decomposition produces a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), whose composition and transport properties strongly influence lithium deposition and ammonia selectivity. Although LiF-rich, anion-derived SEI is beneficial, the highly negative potentials required for lithium deposition induce electrostatic repulsion of anions from the cathode, limiting their participation in SEI formation. Highly charged cationic additives were introduced into the Li-NRR electrolyte to mitigate electrostatic anion repulsion and enrich anions at the cathode interface. Electrochemical measurements and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were employed to investigate Li-NRR performance, the interfacial ion concentration, and SEI properties. Screening of various cationic additives consistently improved the Faradaic efficiency (FE) compared with the additive-free electrolyte. The best-performing additive increased the FE by up to 20.1 %. Double-layer capacitance measurements indicated enhanced interfacial ion accumulation in the presence of the additives. XPS analysis further revealed increased formation of a LiF-rich, inorganic SEI, supporting greater anion participation in SEI formation. These results demonstrate that cationic additives can mitigate interfacial anion depletion and promote anion-derived SEI formation. Direct regulation of interfacial ion distribution offers an effective strategy for improving the selectivity and efficiency of Li-NRR without extensive modification of the bulk electrolyte.

P3-043.a: Electrochemical nitrate reduction has emerged as a promising strategy for simultaneously removing nitrate contaminants from water and producing value added ammonia under ambient conditions. However, achieving high activity and selectivity requires a fundamental understanding of the reaction mechanism and catalyst active sites. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations provide an effective approach for rational catalyst design. DFT calculations were performed to investigate the nitrate reduction mechanism on transition metal based electrocatalysts. Adsorption energies, Gibbs free energy profiles, charge transfer, and electronic structures were systematically analyzed to identify favorable reaction pathways and active sites. Structure–activity relationships were established to understand the origin of catalytic performance. The calculations identified energetically favorable reaction pathways for ammonia formation and revealed the key intermediates governing catalytic activity. Electronic structure analysis demonstrated that the adsorption characteristics of reaction intermediates strongly influence the reaction energetics. These insights enabled the identification of promising catalyst candidates with enhanced theoretical nitrate reduction performance. This study demonstrates that DFT based computational screening provides an efficient strategy for understanding the nitrate reduction mechanism and accelerating the development of high performance electrocatalysts for sustainable ammonia production. The proposed computational framework offers practical design principles for future catalyst optimization.

P3-044.k: Lithium-mediated Nitrogen Reduction Reaction; Green Ammonia Synthesis; Solid Electrolyte Interphase
P3-044.a: Lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) has emerged as a promising alternative to the energy-intensive Haber-Bosch process for green ammonia synthesis. Despite its high ammonia production rates and Faradaic efficiencies, Li-NRR still suffers from parasitic side reactions due to instability of organic solvents. Since the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), an ion-conducting and electron-insulating layer, plays a critical role in regulating reactant transport and determining NH3 selectivity, engineering Li+ solvation structure has become a key strategy for enhancing Li-NRR performance. The Li+ solvation structure strongly influences SEI formation, because species in the primary solvation shell preferentially access the Helmholtz plane and undergo electrochemical reduction. In particular, anion-derived SEI has exhibited superior performance in Li-NRR, because inorganic SEI components such as LiF facilitate the lateral diffusion of Li+ and promote uniform Li plating. Although increasing Li salt concentration is an effective strategy for inducing anion-rich solvation structures, it suffers from high material costs and high viscosity, which hinders N2 diffusion through the electrolyte. For sustainable and economically viable green ammonia production, electrolyte engineering strategies that balance the material cost and performance are required. In this work, we systematically tailored Li+ solvation structures using a series of solvents ranging from antisolvents to weak solvents. A localized high-concentration electrolyte (LHCE) was first introduced into the Li-NRR, by using fluorinated ether as the optimal antisolvent. This strategy successfully formed anion-rich solvation structures by imitating the advantages of HCEs while maintaining a low overall salt concentration. Owing to its low viscosity and high N2 solubility, the LHCE achieved high Faradaic efficiency (73.6 ± 2.5%), which significantly surpasses the performance of conventional electrolyte (34.3 ± 2.8%). Building on this concept, weakly solvating electrolytes (WSEs) were further developed to reduce power consumption and electrolyte cost. Using electrostatic potential (ESP) as a descriptor of solvating ability, acetal-based weak solvents were selected to promote anion-rich solvation structures while maintaining partial coordination with Li+. Beyond tailoring the solvation environment, the unique molecular structure of the acetal solvent enables proton donor regeneration during the reaction, thereby stabilizing the batch system for over 40 h even under HH+-limited conditions. A combination of Raman spectroscopy, FT-IR, and NMR analyses validated systematic changes in Li+ solvation structures, while SEM and XPS confirmed the formation of distinct SEI chemistries and morphologies. These results demonstrate that solvation structure engineering provides an effective strategy for constructing anion-derived SEIs without relying on high concentration electrolytes, enabling high performance, cost-effective, and durable Li-NRR systems for sustainable green ammonia production.

P3-045.k: Lithium-mediated Nitrogen Reduction; Lithium Metal Battery; Electrochemical Ammonia Production
P3-045.a: Lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) is one of the most promising electrochemical routes for ammonia synthesis which could potentially replace energy-intensive conventional Haber-Bosch process. However, its practical development is still limited by several coupled challenges, including poor reaction selectivity, unstable operation, and parasitic electrolyte decomposition. Although these issues arise from multiple origins, many of them are closely associated with uncontrolled lithium deposition and dynamic solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation during operation. This interfacial nature of Li-NRR suggests a close conceptual similarity to lithium metal batteries (LMBs), suggesting the potential of extending battery-derived interfacial design concepts to Li-NRR. We’ve realized artificial SEI as a particularly promising yet underexplored strategy for Li-NRR, which have been widely investigated and proven effective for regulating lithium deposition, suppressing parasitic electrolyte decomposition, and improving interfacial stability in battery literatures. Motivated by this opportunity, we sought to implement artificial SEI engineering in a Li-NRR system, particularly in a gas-diffusion-electrode (GDE)-based continuous-flow configuration. Poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) was introduced onto the GDE by electrospinning to form a porous artificial SEI scaffold. This scaffold promoted the formation of a LiF-enriched interphase during Li-NRR operation, which regulated local Li⁺ transport and guided more uniform lithium plating. As a result, the PVDF-HFP scaffold GDE exhibited improved ammonia production efficiency compared with the bare GDE. In addition, the electrospun porous architecture contributed to maintaining the gas–electrode–electrolyte triphase interface, thereby enhancing gas-phase ammonia recovery and better utilizing the intended advantages of the continuous-flow system. Overall, this work establishes artificial-SEI-based interfacial regulation as a general GDE design principle for Li-NRR and demonstrates the broader validity of translating lithium metal interface strategies from battery research to electrochemical nitrogen reduction.

P3-046.k: Chemical Looping Ammonia Production; Biomass Gasification; Allam Cycle
P3-046.a: Ammonia is attracting attention as a carbon-free energy carrier, but conventional synthesis routes remain energy-intensive and largely dependent on fossil-based inputs. Chemical looping ammonia production (CLAP) enables synthesis under milder conditions; however, its economic and environmental performance is strongly tied to the cost and availability of renewable electricity. This work presents two integrated configurations that address these limitations: a three-stage CLAP coupled with a dual-type air separation unit (CLAP–2ASU), and an extended self-powered variant (CLAP–2ASU–Biomass–Allam) in which a biomass-fueled Allam cycle supplies internal electricity, thereby lowering dependence on external renewable power and improving robustness against electricity price fluctuations. Both configurations were modeled and assessed in terms of energy efficiency, carbon emissions, and levelized cost of ammonia (LCOA). A sensitivity analysis was performed to quantify how key parameters, particularly the renewable electricity price, influence economic performance, and the resulting LCOAs were benchmarked against prevailing green and blue ammonia market prices. The CLAP–2ASU process achieved an energy efficiency of 63.2% with carbon emissions of 0.11–0.14 tCO2/tNH3 when powered by photovoltaic electricity. The LCOA was estimated at $461.6/tNH3 for CLAP–2ASU and $515.0/tNH3 for CLAP–2ASU–Biomass–Allam, and both values were highly responsive to changes in renewable electricity cost. Across nearly all scenarios examined, the LCOA stayed below the green ammonia market range ($722–875/t); when the renewable electricity price fell to $0.061/kWh or lower, all pathways became cost-competitive with blue ammonia as well. Integrating CLAP with a dual-type ASU, and further with a biomass-fueled Allam cycle, yields a green ammonia route that is both environmentally favorable and economically viable across a wide range of electricity price conditions. The proposed systems therefore represent a sustainable and cost-effective pathway toward decarbonized ammonia production.

P3-047.k: CO2/N2 Separation; High Humidity; ZnO-Derived CALF-20
P3-047.a: Efficient CO2/N2 separation under humid conditions remains a critical challenge for post-combustion carbon capture, as water vapor can strongly compete with CO2 adsorption in many porous adsorbents. Herein, ZnO-derived CALF-20/polymer composites were prepared using ZnO nanorods as the zinc source and sacrificial precursor, followed by in situ integration with hydrophobic fluorinated polymers, including poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) and poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP). The resulting CALF@PVDF and CALF@PVDF-HFP composites retained the crystalline CALF-20 framework while showing different CO2 capture behaviors under humid conditions. Under dry equilibrium conditions, the polymer-modified composites preserved the intrinsic CO2-selective adsorption behavior of CALF-20, with high CO2/N2 selectivity and moderate isosteric heat of adsorption. Dynamic breakthrough experiments using a CO2/N2 mixture under different relative humidities further revealed the role of the polymer matrix in regulating humidity tolerance. CALF@PVDF maintained higher CO2 breakthrough capacity than the reference CALF-20 under humid conditions, whereas CALF@PVDF-HFP exhibited stronger capacity retention at elevated relative humidity, associated with lower water uptake. These results demonstrate that hydrophobic polymer integration provides an effective strategy to tune the balance between CO2 capture capacity and humidity resistance in CALF-20-based adsorbents. This study highlights ZnO-derived CALF-20/polymer composites as promising candidates for humid CO2/N2 separation in post-combustion carbon capture.

P3-048.k: Direct Air Capture; Macroporous MOF Beads; Mass Diffusion
P3-048.a: Direct air capture (DAC) demands sorbents that integrate high affinity for CO2 at ultradilute concentrations with efficient mass transport and structural compatibility with practical contactors. However, most amine-functionalized metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are evaluated as fine powders, where shaping into macroscopic bodies introduces transport limitations that suppress amine accessibility and cyclic performance. Here, we report a morphology-engineered strategy to construct hierarchically porous MIL-100(Al) beads that simultaneously enhance amine loading and mitigate intraparticle diffusion resistance. Macroporous γ-alumina beads are sacrificially converted into fully intergrown MIL-100(Al) architectures, followed by diethylenetriamine (DETA) incorporation throughout the macro–microporous network. The resulting beads achieve an amine loading of 2.46 mmol g−1 (1.5 DETA per Al3 cluster), exceeding that of the powder analogue, while exhibiting approximately two-fold reduced diffusion resistance. At 400 ppm CO2 and 298 K, the beads deliver a CO2 uptake of 0.51 mmol g−1 and a six-fold enhancement in dynamic breakthrough capacity relative to DETA-functionalized MIL-100(Al) powder. The partial mass-transfer zone is significantly narrowed, leading to nearly doubled cyclic CO2 productivity (19.8 vs. 9.5 mg g−1 day−1). Importantly, the hierarchical architecture preserves structural integrity and maintains over 94% capacity after repeated adsorption–desorption cycles. These findings demonstrate that morphology engineering at the synthesis stage provides a viable pathway to reconcile adsorption thermodynamics with transport kinetics, establishing a general design principle for diffusion-optimized, process-ready MOF sorbents for DAC and related separations.

P3-049.k: High-Entropy Dichalcogenide; Urea Oxidation Reaction; Hydrogen Production
P3-049.a: Replacing the sluggish oxygen evolution reaction with the urea oxidation reaction (UOR) can reduce the energy demand of hydrogen production while simultaneously valorizing urea-containing wastewater. However, conventional transition-metal dichalcogenides often exhibit insufficient activity and poor durability under oxidative conditions. An anion-vacancy-rich high-entropy dichalcogenide, MoCrSnSSe, was synthesized on reduced graphene oxide through a hydrothermal method. Its structure, defect chemistry, UOR activity, interfacial kinetics, reaction mechanism, and device-level performance were investigated using physicochemical characterization, electrochemical measurements, in situ Raman spectroscopy, distribution-of-relaxation-time analysis, density functional theory calculations, and a zero-gap electrolyzer. MoCrSnSSe formed a single-phase, 1T-rich high-entropy structure with a configurational entropy exceeding 1.74R and abundant anion vacancies. The catalyst required only 1.352 V vs. RHE to reach 10 mA cm-1, exhibited a Tafel slope of 23.6 mV dec-1 and an apparent activation energy of 16.4 kJ mol-1, and maintained 97.1% of its initial performance over 300 h. Mechanistic analyses showed that urea promoted faster interfacial charge transfer, while anion-vacancy-associated Cr-dominant coordination environments strengthened urea adsorption and lowered the reaction barrier through a favorable alternating pathway. In a zero-gap electrolyzer, urea-assisted electrolysis reduced energy consumption by 14.4% compared with conventional water electrolysis. High-entropy engineering combined with vacancy modulation creates catalytically favorable local coordination environments for accelerated UOR. MoCrSnSSe is therefore a promising anode material for durable, energy-efficient hydrogen production coupled with urea-containing wastewater utilization.

P3-050.k: Nitrate Reduction Reaction; Ammonia Electrosynthesis; Multimetallic Electrocatalyst
P3-050.a: Electrochemical nitrate reduction provides a sustainable route for ammonia production while simultaneously removing nitrate pollutants from water. However, achieving high ammonia selectivity, energy efficiency, and stable performance remains challenging because nitrate reduction involves multiple reaction intermediates and competes with hydrogen evolution. Quaternary CoNiCuRu alloy nanoparticles were uniformly supported on multi-walled carbon nanotubes through microwave-assisted reduction. Their structural and electronic properties were characterized, and nitrate reduction performance was evaluated under ambient conditions using both H-type and zero-gap electrolysis cells. Potential-dependent electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and in situ Raman spectroscopy were employed to investigate interfacial kinetics and reaction intermediates. CoNiCuRu/MWCNT achieved an ammonia yield of 3.11 mg h-1 cm-2, a Faradaic efficiency of 90.6%, and a half-cell energy efficiency of 43.3% at 0.1 V vs. RHE. The favorable performance was attributed to synergistic interactions among Co, Ni, Cu, and Ru, which promoted nitrate activation, interfacial hydrogen transfer, and subsequent hydrogenation toward ammonia while limiting hydrogen evolution. Impedance measurements revealed accelerated interfacial charge transfer following nitrate reduction activation, and in situ Raman spectroscopy identified nitrate consumption and NOH-, NH-, and ammonia-related species. In a 3 × 3 cm2 zero-gap electrolyzer, the catalyst achieved a maximum Faradaic efficiency of 97.2%, a full-cell energy efficiency of 30.3%, and stable operation for 100 h. The multimetallic CoNiCuRu catalyst combines efficient nitrate activation, favorable hydrogenation kinetics, and high ammonia selectivity. Its strong half-cell performance and scalable zero-gap operation demonstrate its potential for energy-efficient ammonia electrosynthesis and nitrate remediation.

P3-051.k: Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks; Structural Engineering; CO2 Separation
P3-051.a: As global efforts to capture CO2 from point sources and ambient air increase, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have attracted attention due to their tunable pore structures and chemical functionalities. This study aimed to enhance CO2 affinity and molecular sieving ability in ZIF-67 through post-synthetic modification (PSM) using two amine-functionalized triazole ligands, 3-amino-5-methylthio-1,2,4-triazole (Amtz) and 3,5-diamino-1,2,4-triazole (Dtz), which also differ in molecular volume. ZIF-67, composed of Co2+ ions and 2-methylimidazole (2-MIm), was subjected to post-synthetic modification (PSM) via ligand exchange with Amtz and Dtz to produce Amtz-67 and Dtz-67 series. Pore structures and gas adsorption behavior were characterized via 77 K N2 and CO2 adsorption isotherms. The optimized fillers were then incorporated into a 6FDA-DAM polymer matrix to fabricate mixed matrix membranes (MMMs), and gas permeability was evaluated. Amtz showed low incorporation efficiency due to its large van der Waals volume, and even small amounts led to decreased N2 and CO2 uptake. For Dtz-67, N2 uptake decreased with increasing PSM time, while CO2 uptake decreased at low pressure (~400 ppm) but increased at higher pressures, indicating chemisorption at low pressure and physisorption at high pressure—confirming the contribution of the amine-rich Dtz ligand to enhanced CO2 affinity. The engineered ZIF-67s exhibited excellent CO2/N2 selectivity and high CO2 adsorption capacity under low-concentration conditions, and the resulting MMMs overcame the typical permeability–selectivity trade-off. Multi-ligand structural engineering of MOFs offers an effective strategy for simultaneously tuning pore structure and CO2 affinity, providing a promising platform for next-generation adsorbents and hybrid membranes for targeted gas separation applications.

P3-052.k: Porous Aromatic Framework; Amine Functionalization; CO2 Adsorption
P3-052.a: The continuous increase in atmospheric CO2 concentrations driven by rapid industrialization and extensive fossil fuel consumption has intensified the need for efficient carbon capture technologies to mitigate global climate change. Among porous adsorbents such as Zeolites, Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs), and Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs), porous aromatic framework (PAF) has attracted considerable attention owing to its exceptionally high surface area, permanent microporosity, and outstanding chemical stability. Although amine functionalization has been widely employed to enhance CO2 adsorption, previous studies have primarily focused on increasing amine loading or nitrogen content, while the influence of amine molecular architecture on adsorption behavior has received comparatively little attention. PAF-1 was functionalized via post-synthetic modification (PSM) using two classes of amines: flexible aliphatic polyamines and rigid triazole-based cyclic amines. Gas adsorption analysis was performed to systematically investigate the influence of different amine molecular architectures on CO2 adsorption performance and CO2-selective adsorption properties. Comparative analysis revealed that the molecular architecture of grafted amines significantly influenced the CO2 adsorption performance of functionalized PAF-1. Distinct differences between flexible aliphatic polyamines and rigid triazole-based cyclic amines were observed in CO2 uptake, CO2/N2 selectivity, and the isosteric heat of adsorption, demonstrating that amine architecture governs both adsorption capacity and adsorption energetics. This study demonstrates a combined experimental and computational strategy for elucidating the role of amine molecular architecture in PAF-1. The results are expected to provide design principles for developing highly CO2-selective porous adsorbents for carbon capture applications.

P3-053.a: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) waste is an increasing environmental concern, creating demand for sustainable upcycling strategies. Biological conversion of PET-derived terephthalic acid (TPA) into value-added chemicals is promising, but inefficient TPA uptake limits microbial bioconversion efficiency. Pseudomonas putida KT2440 was metabolically engineered by introducing the Comamonas sp. E6 tphBAabc operon and deleting pcaHG to establish TPA catabolism. Nine heterologous TPA transporters were screened to improve substrate uptake. The best-performing transporters were combined with engineered pathways for catechol and cis,cis-muconic acid (MA) biosynthesis. Commercial and post-consumer PET-derived TPA were evaluated in flask cultures, and fed-batch fermentation was performed to assess process scalability. Transporter screening identified TpaK from Rhodococcus opacus and MucKmut from Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 as the most effective TPA transporters. The TpaK-expressing strain completely consumed 9.89 mM TPA and produced 8.51 mM catechol with an 86.0% molar yield. Extension of the pathway enabled production of 8.45 mM MA with a 93.1% molar yield. Comparable conversion efficiencies were achieved using chemically depolymerized post-consumer PET-derived TPA. Fed-batch fermentation further demonstrated scalability, producing 15.04 mM catechol from 16.76 mM TPA. Engineering high-affinity TPA transport substantially enhanced PET-derived TPA assimilation and enabled efficient production of catechol and MA in P. putida. The engineered platform provides a scalable and sustainable strategy for biological PET upcycling into value-added aromatic chemicals.

P3-054.a: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are biodegradable bioplastics with significant potential to replace petroleum-derived plastics. However, their commercialization is limited by the high cost of carbon substrates. This study aimed to expand the substrate spectrum of Pseudomonas putida for efficient PHA production from sucrose, an inexpensive and abundant renewable carbon source. A sucrose-utilization pathway was established by introducing the sacC gene encoding β-fructofuranosidase, enabling extracellular hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose. Recombinant strains were further engineered to produce either medium-chain-length PHA (MCL-PHA) or poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) [P(3HB)]. PHA production was evaluated through flask, batch, and fed-batch cultivations under nitrogen-limited conditions. Extracellular secretion of β-fructofuranosidase enabled complete hydrolysis of 20 g/L sucrose within 48 h. In flask cultivation, the engineered strain accumulated 10.52 wt% MCL-PHA, while the P(3HB)-producing strain accumulated 9.16 wt% P(3HB). During batch fermentation, sucrose-derived glucose and fructose were completely consumed, resulting in 3.02 g/L P(3HB) with a 31.4 wt% polymer content. Fed-batch fermentation using sucrose feeding achieved a final cell density of 79.4 g/L and produced 30.2 g/L P(3HB) with a polymer content of 38.1 wt%, demonstrating efficient conversion of sucrose into biodegradable polyester. Engineering P. putida with a β-fructofuranosidase-mediated sucrose-utilization pathway enabled efficient production of both MCL-PHA and P(3HB) directly from sucrose. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using low-cost renewable sucrose as a feedstock for industrial PHA production while highlighting opportunities for further improvement through enhanced fructose utilization and reduced byproduct formation.

P3-055.a: 5-Hydroxyvaleric acid (5-HV) is a valuable C5 platform chemical for producing biodegradable polymers, solvents, and specialty chemicals. However, microbial production of 5-HV is often accompanied by substantial accumulation of byproducts, including L-lysine, 5-aminovaleric acid (5-AVA), and glutaric acid (GTA), which complicates downstream processing. This study aimed to develop a highly selective 5-HV production system in Corynebacterium glutamicum by minimizing byproduct formation through systematic metabolic engineering. Multiple metabolic engineering strategies were evaluated, including deletion of endogenous GTA biosynthesis genes, construction of a GTA recycling pathway, disruption of the L-lysine exporter (lysE), and chromosomal integration of an L-lysine conversion module. The engineered strains were assessed through flask, batch, and fed-batch fermentations, and fermentation-derived 5-HV was further converted into δ-valerolactone (DVL) by acid treatment. The combined engineering strategies synergistically improved both 5-HV selectivity and production. The final engineered strain produced 88.23 g/L 5-HV in fed-batch fermentation with a 0.51 mol/mol yield and 0.68 g/L/h productivity. Byproduct formation was substantially reduced to 3.28 g/L GTA, 1.16 g/L 5-AVA, and no detectable L-lysine, representing a marked improvement over the parental strain. Furthermore, fermentation-derived 5-HV was successfully converted into DVL, achieving a 65% conversion efficiency through a simple acid-catalyzed process. Combinatorial metabolic engineering enabled highly selective biosynthesis of 5-HV in C. glutamicum by effectively minimizing competing metabolic pathways and recycling GTA. The resulting platform achieved high-titer 5-HV production while simplifying downstream purification and demonstrated the feasibility of sustainable DVL production from fermentation-derived 5-HV, providing an efficient route for industrial C5 chemical biomanufacturing.

P3-056.a: 1,5-Pentanediol (1,5-PDO) is an important C5 platform chemical used in the production of biodegradable polymers, polyurethanes, and specialty materials. However, microbial production of 1,5-PDO remains limited by inefficient pathway enzymes, intermediate accumulation, and redox imbalance. This study aimed to establish an efficient 1,5-PDO biosynthesis platform in Corynebacterium glutamicum through systematic metabolic and enzyme engineering. A lysine-derived biosynthetic pathway was constructed by introducing heterologous enzymes for 5-hydroxyvaleric acid (5-HV) production and evaluating CoA-dependent and CoA-independent conversion pathways to 1,5-PDO. Metabolic flux was optimized through chromosomal integration of pathway modules and elimination of competing pathways. Carboxylic acid reductases (CARs) were screened and engineered to improve catalytic performance, while a deep learning-based cofactor prediction model was employed to identify an NADH-dependent aldehyde reductase that alleviated NADPH limitation during 1,5-PDO biosynthesis. The CoA-independent CAR pathway outperformed the CoA-dependent pathway for 1,5-PDO production. Genome integration of the 5-HV biosynthetic pathway improved precursor supply and reduced byproduct formation. Screening of 14 CARs identified MAP1040 as the most effective enzyme, and its M296E variant further increased batch production to 23.5 g/L 1,5-PDO without detectable intermediate accumulation. Finally, replacement of the terminal reduction step with a deep learning-guided NADH-dependent aldehyde reductase eliminated the redox bottleneck, enabling the engineered strain to produce 43.4 g/L 1,5-PDO during fed-batch fermentation without 5-HV accumulation. Systematic metabolic engineering, enzyme optimization, and deep learning-guided cofactor engineering enabled high-level microbial production of 1,5-PDO in C. glutamicum. The developed platform effectively addressed pathway inefficiency and redox imbalance, providing a promising strategy for sustainable industrial production of C5 diol platform chemicals.

P3-057.k: Carbon Circularity; Lignin Valorization; Biocatalytic Upcycling
P3-057.a: Gallic acid (GA) is a high-value lignin-derived triphenolic compound with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and selective anticancer activities, making it attractive for pharmaceutical, cosmetic, food, and chemical applications. Conventional GA production relies on acid hydrolysis of botanical tannins, which suffers from low purity, toxic byproducts, and high energy consumption. Therefore, a sustainable biomanufacturing route from lignin-derived feedstocks is highly desirable. A microbial catalyst was engineered to convert lignin-derived aromatic monomers into GA through metabolic pathway optimization. The degradation pathway of the key intermediate, protocatechuic acid (PCA), was disrupted to promote its accumulation, while glycerol was supplied as an auxiliary electron donor for the subsequent hydroxylation step. Medium composition was optimized using yeast extract and ascorbic acid to suppress GA degradation. The optimized process was evaluated in a 2.5 L batch bioreactor under controlled pH and feeding conditions. Metabolic engineering enabled a 77% molar conversion of p-coumaric acid (CA) to PCA. The addition of glycerol successfully drove the hydroxylation of PCA to GA, while medium optimization improved product stability, achieving a GA molar yield of 65% with 90% product retention. Process scale-up in a 2.5 L batch reactor resulted in the production of 11.1 mM GA from 30 mM CA under optimized operating conditions. This study demonstrates an efficient microbial platform for the sustainable upcycling of lignin-derived aromatic compounds into GA. The integration of metabolic engineering, medium optimization, and bioprocess optimization enhanced GA production and provides a promising basis for the sustainable biosynthesis of high-value lignin-derived chemicals.

P3-058.k: Gas Separation; Decarboxylation Cross-linking; Plasticization Resistance
P3-058.a: Glassy 6FDA-based polyimides are promising for gas separation but suffer from CO2-induced plasticization. Although thermal cross-linking via decarboxylation mitigates this, studies on how diamine structural variations affect cross-linking and plasticization resistance remain scarce. Novel copolymers were synthesized by incorporating distinct diamines (mPDA, ODA, 3,4'-ODA, MDA) into a 6FDA-DABA backbone via a precise two-step imidization. Dense flat films were fabricated to evaluate the effects of diamine structures on free volume, chain packing, and sub-/above-Tg thermal decarboxylation behaviors. Diamine structures significantly influenced the fraction of free volume and gas permeation characteristics. Chain packing and flexibility altered the cross-linking onset temperature and kinetics. The resulting covalent networks restricted chain swelling under high-pressure CO2, demonstrating enhanced plasticization resistance and structural stability. This study demonstrates that integrating diamine modification, two-step imidization, and optimized thermal cross-linking successfully improves plasticization resistance. The structure-property relationships established herein offer crucial academic insights for designing advanced cross-linkable polymeric membranes for demanding gas separations.

P3-059.a: Porous metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) with openly accessible Lewis basic sites have attracted considerable attention as CO2 sorbents because of their strong affinity for CO2 and high adsorption selectivity. However, the molecular origin of their exceptionally high CO2 adsorption enthalpy remains unclear. The CO2 adsorption behavior of the 2D Zn-MOF [Zn(3,3′-TPDC)(DABCO)]·2DMF (1) was investigated by combining low-pressure CO2 adsorption measurements with density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The experimental isosteric heat of adsorption (Qst) was correlated with calculated binding energies to elucidate the adsorption mechanism. Experimentally, solvent-free 1 exhibits an exceptionally high low-pressure CO2 adsorption enthalpy (Qst = −76.8 kJ mol−1). DFT calculations reveal that each cage-shaped micropore accommodates two CO2 molecules. While adsorption of one CO2 molecule yields a binding energy of −29.9 kJ mol−1, adsorption of a second CO2 molecule within the same cage increases the binding energy to −71.0 kJ mol−1, in excellent agreement with the experimental Qst. The enhanced adsorption arises from cooperative confinement and Lewis acid–base interactions between CO2 and the uncoordinated nitrogen atoms of DABCO, which also induce bending of the adsorbed CO2 molecules. The excellent agreement between experiment and DFT demonstrates that the unusually high CO2 adsorption enthalpy originates from cooperative adsorption of two CO2 molecules within a single cage-shaped micropore rather than an isolated adsorption event. These findings provide molecular-level insight into the role of Lewis basic sites and offer a rational design strategy for high-performance MOF sorbents for CO2 capture.

P3-060.k: Media Preparation; Gas Conversion; Automated Algorithm
P3-060.a: Culture media are critical for bioprocess performance, making their design and optimization vital. However, applying new media presents challenges such as salt precipitation and thermal degradation from multi-ingredient interactions. These difficulties are intensified in biological gas conversion, where key enzymes often require specific metal ions as cofactors. We developed an application that automatically proposes preparation protocols based on media compositions. By incorporating multi-component thermodynamic and physicochemical equilibrium models, the algorithm evaluates recipe feasibility under targeted conditions. Utilizing logical screening and optimized clustering strategies, it automatically partitions ingredients into stable stock solutions and base mixtures while assigning safe sterilization pathways. The algorithm was validated against hundreds of established defined media, successfully replicating empirical segregation guidelines. It proactively identified latent precipitation risks during stock concentration and autoclaving, proposing safer alternative strategies. The system was practically validated on a medium for Methylocystis sp. MJC1, a promising biocatalyst that converts methane, a greenhouse gas, successfully resolving metal precipitation risks securing reproducible cell growth. This systematic digital framework eliminates empirical trial-and-error in media preparation, serving as a valuable tool to enhance the reliability and reproducibility of biological gas conversion bioprocesses.

P3-061.k: CO2 Mineralization; Hierarchical Calcium Carbonate; Hydrogen-Assisted Conversion
P3-061.a: CO2 mineralization can permanently store captured CO2 while converting it into solid materials. However, CaCO3, the major product of many mineralization processes, is naturally abundant and generally has low economic value. Hydrogen-assisted thermal conversion offers a potential route for utilizing mineralized carbon by lowering the decomposition temperature of CaCO3 and converting the evolved CO2 into CO. Nevertheless, the required temperature remains high, and the structural factors governing this reaction are poorly understood. Here, we examine how aspartic acid enantiopurity and CO2-induced internal etching affect the hierarchical structure and hydrogen-assisted reactivity of mineralized CaCO3. CO2 was bubbled into Ca(OH)2 slurries containing L-, D-, or racemic DL-aspartic acid. Particles collected at different carbonation stages were characterized by scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and N2 adsorption.
