Hydrogen-assisted thermal behavior and evolved gaseous products were evaluated using temperature-programmed surface reaction coupled with mass spectrometry (TPSR–MS) and temperature-programmed reaction (TPx) analysis. Continued CO2 bubbling transformed initially solid, cocoon-like particles into hollow structures through internal etching. The L- and DL-aspartate samples had similar initial phase compositions of approximately 86% calcite and 14% vaterite, became fully calcitic after etching, and showed comparable increases in BET surface area. Nevertheless, the etched racemic sample exhibited the largest decrease in the CO2-evolution peak temperature and the most pronounced increase in the relative CO indicator (m/z 28/44). The smaller changes observed for the enantiopure samples indicate that the racemic enhancement cannot be explained solely by bulk phase composition, morphology, or surface area. Internal etching enhanced the hydrogen-assisted reactivity of hierarchical CaCO3, with the greatest effect observed for racemic DL-aspartate. This difference suggests that local structural features established during growth and exposed or modified by etching may govern the reaction. Ligand enantiopurity therefore offers a potential parameter for tuning the reactivity of carbonate products obtained through CO2 mineralization.

P3-062.k: Magnesium Silicate; Sodium Ion; High-Salinity Water
P3-062.a: The increasing demand for seawater desalination and the utilization of high-salinity water resources have raised concerns regarding the effective management of concentrated brine. In parallel, mineral carbonation has attracted considerable attention as a carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) approach because it enables stable CO₂ sequestration through the formation of inorganic carbonate minerals. In mineral carbonation processes using concentrated brine from seawater desalination, NaOH is often added to enhance carbonation efficiency; however, this can result in residual solutions containing high concentrations of Na⁺, creating an additional challenge for subsequent water treatment and resource recovery. In this study, magnesium silicate was investigated as a potential adsorbent for Na⁺ removal due to its porous structure, high surface area, thermal stability, and surface-active functional groups. Batch adsorption experiments were conducted to evaluate the Na⁺ adsorption performance and adsorption characteristics of magnesium silicate in aqueous solutions. The ability of magnesium silicate to reduce Na⁺ concentrations was examined under controlled adsorption conditions, and the experimental equilibrium data were analyzed using the Langmuir and Freundlich adsorption isotherm models. In addition, to improve the practical applicability of magnesium silicate in industrial water treatment processes, pelletized adsorbents were fabricated using water glass and bentonite as binders. The Na⁺ adsorption performance of the pelletized magnesium silicate was subsequently evaluated to assess its potential for application in continuous or large-scale treatment systems. The adsorption experiments demonstrated that magnesium silicate effectively adsorbed Na⁺ from aqueous solutions, indicating its potential as an adsorbent for sodium removal. The observed adsorption behavior was attributed to the porous structure and active surface sites of magnesium silicate, which can facilitate interactions between Na⁺ and the adsorbent surface. The equilibrium adsorption data showed good agreement with both the Langmuir and Freundlich isotherm models, suggesting that Na⁺ adsorption on magnesium silicate may involve both surface-specific and heterogeneous adsorption characteristics. Furthermore, the pelletized magnesium silicate retained Na⁺ adsorption capability, demonstrating the feasibility of converting the powder adsorbent into a form more suitable for practical process applications. Magnesium silicate exhibited promising Na⁺ adsorption performance and was successfully applied in pelletized form using water glass and bentonite as binders. The agreement of the experimental data with the Langmuir and Freundlich models confirmed its suitability as an adsorbent for Na⁺ removal from aqueous solutions. These results suggest that magnesium silicate could be applied as a post-treatment adsorbent for Na⁺-rich solutions generated from high-salinity water treatment and mineral carbonation processes. The proposed approach may contribute to more effective brine management and facilitate the integration of water treatment, resource recovery, and CO₂ mineralization processes.

P3-063.a: Unrefined glycerol, an abundant byproduct of biodiesel production, has emerged as a potential waste resource for microbial biorefineries. we report engineering of extremophilic microorganism Deinococcus radiodurans R1 for efficient β-carotene production from unrefined glycerol. To establish a base strain, the crtY gene was overexpressed, and the crtLm genes were deleted to complete the β-carotene biosynthetic pathway. The base strain was able to produce 0.46 ± 0.03 mg/L (0.098 ± 0.011 mg/g DCW) from glucose. Further pathway optimization through deleting the crtO gene and fine-tuning of rate-limiting steps by gene overexpression and promoter replacement enhanced β-carotene production to 5.97 ± 0.35 mg/L (2.03 ± 1.03 mg/g DCW), representing a 33.2-fold increase. To enable glycerol utilization, the glpK, glpD, and tpiA genes were integrated into the genome, which resulted in the production of 11.56 ± 1.03 mg/L (2.27 ± 0.20 mg/g DCW) β-carotene from 10 g/L unrefined glycerol, approximately three-fold and 64-fold higher than the yields obtained using glucose and the base strain, respectively. In fed-batch fermentation, the engineered strain achieved 27.23 mg/L (2.60 mg/g DCW) from 25.45 g/L unrefined glycerol within 102 h. These findings demonstrate that the final engineered strain is promising and worthy of as a robust platform for cost-effective and sustainable biorefinery applications.

P3-064.k: Cement Hydration; Carbonation Curing; Raman Spectroscopy
P3-064.a: In-situ mineral carbonation technology applied during ready-mixed concrete (RMC) production has garnered significant interest for carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) and improving mechanical properties. However, the incorporation of carbon dioxide sources into fresh cement mixtures can substantially alter hydration kinetics, water molecule dynamics, and slurry rheological/flow behavior. Traditional ex-situ and destructive analytical methods lack the temporal resolution required to observe rapid, early-stage phase transitions and molecular interactions in real time. Non-destructive in situ Raman spectroscopy offers molecular-level chemical sensitivity, making it an ideal tool to track the evolution of hydration products (e.g., calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)2, calcium silicate hydrate [C-S-H] gel, and ettringite) alongside carbonation products (such as crystalline calcite and amorphous carbonates) directly within fresh slurries. This study investigates the applicability of in situ Raman spectroscopy for real-time monitoring of hydration and carbonation characteristics in cement slurries subjected to two distinct CO2 delivery methods: solid sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) incorporation and direct gaseous (CO)2 injection. Raw Materials and In Situ Raman Apparatus - Materials: Commercial Portland cement (OPC) and analytical grade sodium bicarbonate NaHCO3. - Raman Spectrometer: An Acton Raman spectrometer equipped with a 532 nm laser source (laser power: 50 mW, integration time: 30 s, wave number range: 255–4600 cm⁻¹). - Optics Optimization: Focal length sensitivity tests were performed across a probe-to-sample distance range of 5–12 mm, with 10 mm established as the optimal focal distance to ensure maximal peak intensity and reproducibility. Slurry Preparation and Reaction Monitoring NaHCO3-Incorporated Cement Slurry: - Mix Proportions: Cement (2000 g), water (600 g; water-to-cement ratio w/c = 0.30). NaHCO3 was added at varying dosages: Control (0 wt%, 0 g), N0.1 (0.1 wt%, 2 g), N0.3 (0.3 wt%, 6 g), N0.5 (0.5 wt%, 10 g), N0.7 (0.7 wt%, 14 g), and N1.0 (1.0 wt%, 20 g). - Mixing Procedure: Dry mixing of cement and NaHCO3 was conducted for 6 min to ensure homogeneity. Water was introduced gradually during slow stirring. After 2 min of wet mixing, scrape-down mixing was performed, followed by 1 min of additional mixing. - Time-Resolved Sampling: Samples were drawn and flattened into molds at designated hydration intervals (0, 10, 20, 30, 60, and 90 min) for instantaneous in situ Raman analysis. Gaseous CO2 Injection Slurry: - Reactor Setup: A stainless steel mixing vessel modified with bottom-fitted gas injection nozzles connected to a high-purity CO2 cylinder and an automated precision balance system. - Mix Proportions & Exposure: Cement (2000 g), water (600 g), and a continuous gaseous CO2 flow rate of 20 g/min. Injection times evaluated were: Control (0 s, 0 g), N30 (30 s, 10 g), N90 (90 s, 30 g), and N180 (180 s, 60 g). Sampling: Identical sampling intervals (0 to 90 min) were monitored. Baseline Raman Identification of Raw Powders - Cement Raw Powder: Displayed broad vibrational bands in the 780–920 cm⁻¹ region, characteristic of isolated SiO44 tetrahedra vibrations in alite (C3S) and belite (C2S) silicate phases. - Sodium Bicarbonate Powder: Exhibited three distinct diagnostic bands: 1066 cm⁻¹ (symmetric stretching of CO32-), 1350 cm⁻¹ (asymmetric stretching), and 1542 cm⁻¹ (C-O asymmetric stretching). Hydration and Carbonation in NaHCO3-Mixed Slurries Carbonate Region (800–1150 cm⁻¹): - In the control (0 wt%), a baseline peak around 1000–1025 cm⁻¹ was maintained. - At 0.1–0.7 wt% NaHCO3, the peak initially observed at 1025 cm⁻¹ (amorphous carbonate phase) split into two distinct bands at 1000 cm⁻¹ and 1025 cm⁻¹ after approximately 10–20 min of hydration. Over time (60–90 min), these converged into a single sharp band at ~1010 cm⁻¹ representing the crystallization of ettringite and ordered carbonate phases. - At 1.0 wt% NaHCO3, the amorphous carbonate peak (1025 cm⁻¹) was largely bypassed, and the major crystalline peak at 1010 cm⁻¹ emerged earlier, indicating an altered, highly accelerated precipitation mechanism at higher bicarbonate concentrations. Hydration and Hydroxyl Region (3100–4400 cm⁻¹): - A sharp, diagnostic O-H stretching peak of crystalline portlandite (Ca(OH)2) emerged prominently at 3620 cm⁻¹. Across 0.1–0.7 wt% conditions, this 3620 cm⁻¹ peak reached maximum intensity around 20 min and subsequently diminished as Ca(OH)2 reacted rapidly with available bicarbonate to form CaCO3. The broad band at 3000–3600 cm⁻¹ (free/bulk water) exhibited continuous intensity growth up to 30–60 min, consistent with the release of byproduct water during the carbonation reaction (Ca(OH)2 + HCO3- → CaCO3 + H2O + OH-. - The broad envelope at 3850–4250 cm⁻¹ corresponded to bound water within the a morphous C-S-H gel network. Reaction Dynamics under Gaseous CO2 Injection - Carbonate Region (800–1100 cm⁻¹): - Gaseous CO2 injection produced up to four distinct spectral components: 840 cm⁻¹ (unhydrated alite), 980 cm⁻¹ (monosulfate), 1005 cm⁻¹ (gypsum), and 1085 cm⁻¹ (calcite CaCO3). Significantly, no ettringite band (~1010 cm⁻¹) was formed under direct gaseous CO2 addition across all exposure conditions (30s, 90s, and 180s). Hydration/Hydroxyl Bands: - For 30s CO2 exposure, the Ca(OH)2 peak (3620 cm⁻¹) peaked at 20 min before declining. Increasing CO2 exposure to 180s shifted this peak maximum earlier to 10 min. - The C-S-H gel band (3850–4250 cm⁻¹) exhibited delayed or fluctuating growth characteristics due to the slower dissolution kinetics of gaseous CO2 compared to fully dissolved ionic bicarbonate. Comparative Analysis: NaHCO3 vs. Gaseous CO2 - Carbonation Rate & Water Availability: Solid NaHCO3 rapidly dissolves into aqueous bicarbonate ions, enabling instantaneous chemical reaction with Ca2+/Ca(OH)2 to yield CaCO3 and local byproduct water. This excess free water readily promotes ettringite formation (C3A + 3CSH2 + 26H → C6AS3H32). - Phase Differences: NaHCO3 promotes early ettringite precipitation (1010 cm⁻¹), whereas direct gaseous CO2 injection bypasses ettringite development and predominantly generates calcite (1085 cm⁻¹), maintaining a prolonged portlandite formation–carbonation loop. - High-Frequency Bands (4360 & 4390 cm⁻¹): Sharp doublet features observed at 4360 and 4390 cm⁻¹ were identified as transient intermediate complexes formed between cementitious hydroxyls and carbon species during early paste setting. This study successfully demonstrates that in situ Raman spectroscopy is an effective, non-destructive analytical method for real-time, molecular-level tracking of early-stage hydration kinetics, carbonation behavior, and water molecule dynamics in cementitious slurries. By continuously monitoring the characteristic vibrational bands of portlandite (3620 cm⁻¹), free and bound water (3000–3600 cm⁻¹ and 3850–4250 cm⁻¹), and carbonate-related phases (1000–1085 cm⁻¹), significant differences in reaction pathways between chemical bicarbonate incorporation and direct gaseous CO2 injection were clearly elucidated. The addition of NaHCO3 rapidly accelerates the conversion of calcium hydroxide to calcium carbonate and generates abundant byproduct water, which subsequently promotes the crystallization of ettringite (~1010 cm⁻¹) and leads to accelerated early matrix stiffening and hydration termination. In contrast, direct gaseous CO2 injection primarily drives calcite formation (1085 cm⁻¹) while completely suppressing ettringite precipitation, thereby sustaining a continuous dissolution-carbonation cycle with calcium hydroxide. These findings confirm that time-resolved in situ Raman spectroscopy can serve as a robust monitoring and quality-control framework for capturing microstructural transformations and governing the rheological properties of fresh concrete during CO2 cured manufacturing processes.

P3-065.k: Cell-surface Display; Whole-cell Cascade Biocatalysis; Carbon Circularity
P3-065.a: Carbon circularity requires not only CO₂ capture and reduction, but also downstream platforms that upgrade fixed-carbon intermediates into stable, high-value products. Starch is an attractive carbon carrier in this context, yet its conversion to functional chemicals still relies on multi-step enzymatic cascades requiring separate enzyme expression, purification, and intermediate recovery. Each of these unit operations imposes an energy and carbon penalty that erodes the net benefit of upstream capture. We constructed a whole-cell biocatalytic platform in which the microbial cell envelope itself serves as an engineered catalytic interface. A Bacillus-derived α-amylase was anchored on the Pseudomonas putida surface for extracellular starch depolymerization, and a trehalose synthase (TreS) from P. putida KT2440 was displayed on a second engineered strain for maltose isomerization. Surface localization was verified by whole-cell activity assays and immunofluorescence, and the two strains were co-cultured to operate the cascade in a one-pot system without intermediate separation. The α-amylase-displaying strain achieved a maltose productivity of 2.83 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ from starch. Co-culture of the two surface-engineered strains enabled direct starch-to-trehalose conversion without catalyst purification or intermediate recovery, with an overall conversion efficiency of approximately 55%. Replacing purified enzyme cascades with a self-immobilized, self-regenerating biological interface removes the most cost- and carbon-intensive steps of conventional multi-enzyme bioprocessing. The displayed-enzyme interface is modular, and the same anchoring strategy is extendable to other cascade-driven carbohydrate and C1-derived transformations.

P3-066.k: Corrosion; Pipeline Materials; LCO2 Cargo Transportation Systems
P3-066.a: As Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) technologies become increasingly important for achieving carbon neutrality, interest in the large-scale marine transportation of liquefied carbon dioxide (LCO₂) has grown substantially. LCO₂ transport pipelines operate under low-temperature and high-pressure conditions. Depending on the operating conditions, gas–liquid phase transitions, dry ice and CO₂ hydrate formation, and multiphase flow phenomena such as slug flow may occur. These phenomena can cause flow instability and pipeline blockage while accelerating localized corrosion and damage to carbon steel pipelines through pressure fluctuations and condensation. Therefore, the combined effects of flow behavior and material degradation under actual LCO₂ transport conditions must be evaluated to ensure the safety and reliability of LCO₂ transport systems. An experimental facility capable of simulating the low-temperature and high-pressure operating conditions of LCO₂ pipelines was designed and constructed. Experiments were conducted using carbon steel specimens under various flow-velocity conditions. Changes in the gas–liquid distribution and flow patterns were observed, with particular attention given to the operating conditions associated with unstable two-phase flow and slug flow. The potential formation of dry ice and CO₂ hydrates and their effects on pipeline blockage and localized flow disturbance were also evaluated. Corrosion and material degradation were quantitatively assessed by measuring the mass changes of the specimens before and after testing. In addition, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed to examine microstructural surface changes, localized damage, and the formation of corrosion products. he gas–liquid distribution and flow patterns varied with flow velocity, and unstable two-phase flow and slug flow were identified under specific operating conditions. The results also indicated the potential formation of dry ice and CO₂ hydrates under certain low-temperature conditions, which could increase localized flow disturbances and the risk of pipeline blockage. SEM observations revealed increased surface roughness and localized damage on the carbon steel specimens under specific conditions. In particular, repeated dry ice and hydrate formation was associated with an increased tendency toward surface damage and microcrack formation. Relatively severe surface changes were also observed under slug-flow conditions because of intense flow disturbances and pressure fluctuations. Mass measurements showed slight mass-loss trends under certain low-temperature multiphase-flow conditions, suggesting that repeated phase transitions and flow disturbances in the LCO₂ environment may induce corrosion and degradation of the carbon steel surface. Material degradation in LCO₂ transport pipelines is affected not only by conventional static corrosion conditions but also by the combined effects of multiphase flow, slug flow, and phase-transition phenomena involving dry ice and CO₂ hydrates. Repeated phase transitions and unstable flow conditions may promote localized surface damage and microcrack formation, potentially reducing the long-term structural integrity of pipelines. The findings of this study provide fundamental data for evaluating the corrosion resistance of pipeline materials, establishing material-selection criteria, and optimizing the operating conditions of LCO₂ cargo transport systems. They may also contribute to predicting and mitigating corrosion and blockage problems during the commercialization of large-scale CO₂ transport infrastructure.

P3-067.a: Carbon dioxide capture from post-combustion flue gas is essential for reducing anthropogenic CO2 emissions, but adsorbents intended for practical applications must maintain high separation performance under humid conditions while also enabling rapid adsorption and desorption. CALF-20 has attracted considerable attention as a promising CO2 adsorbent because of its high CO2 capacity, favorable CO2/N2 selectivity, and good structural stability. Nevertheless, competitive water adsorption can reduce its dynamic CO2 capture performance, while mass transfer resistance may further limit its efficiency during cyclic operation. Surface modification with a hydrophobic porous layer offers a potential strategy to improve moisture resistance without severely compromising CO2 accessibility. In this work, CALF-20 was synthesized by a solvothermal reaction of zinc oxalate dihydrate and 1,2,4-triazole. ZIF-8 was subsequently grown on the CALF-20 surface using two different synthesis conditions to control its morphology. A 2D ZIF-8 coating was formed in aqueous solution using SDS as a morphology directing agent, whereas 3D ZIF-8 particles were grown in methanol without SDS. The resulting CALF-20@2D-ZIF-8 and CALF-20@3D-ZIF-8 materials were characterized and evaluated for CO2 adsorption, mass transfer behavior, and humidity resistance. Both materials retained the structural characteristics of CALF-20 while incorporating approximately 28 wt% ZIF-8. Morphological characterization confirmed a relatively continuous interconnected ZIF-8 layer for CALF-20@2D-ZIF-8, whereas CALF-20@3D-ZIF-8 consisted of discrete ZIF-8 nanoparticles surrounding the CALF-20 core. Although ZIF-8 growth moderately decreased the equilibrium CO2 uptake because of the lower intrinsic adsorption capacity of ZIF-8, the 2D-ZIF-8 coating substantially improved dynamic CO2 transport, reducing the mass transfer zone width from about 25 min.g-1 for both pristine CALF-20 and CALF-20@3D-ZIF-8 to 17.81 min.g-1. Furthermore, the CO2 uptake retention at 60% relative humidity of CALF-20@2D-ZIF-8 reached nearly 90%, higher than the 82.1% and 84.8% of pristine CALF-20 and CALF-20@3D-ZIF-8, respectively. In conclusion, morphology-controlled ZIF-8 growth provides an effective approach for tuning the dynamic adsorption performance of CALF-20. In particular, the interconnected 2D-ZIF-8 shell offers the best balance between rapid CO2 mass transfer and improved resistance to humidity.

P3-069.a: Recognition of biomolecular phenomena at interfaces represents a significant scientific challenge because of their importance in theoretical understanding and practical applications. In this study, we report the unique interfacial dynamics of glutamic acid (Glu) and aspartic acid (Asp) at the liquid crystal (LC)-aqueous interface. These biomolecules undergo distinct adsorption-desorption processes, dynamically driving the homeotropic-to-tangential anchoring transition of interfacial LCs. Through optical retardation measurements and DFT calculations, we reveal that these events are dictated by the pH condition of the aqueous solution, which shifts the amino acids' charge states and governs their electrostatic coupling with the LCs. In addition, these adsorption-desorption dynamics are profoundly modulated by bacterial byproducts, including Salmonella lipopolysaccharides (LPS), Staphylococcus aureus lipoteichoic acids (LTA), and Escherichia coli LPS. These biomolecules electrostatically form stable complexes with Glu and Asp and promote their adsorption at the interface and hinder the desorption, significantly accelerating the macroscopic optical transition of LCs. Furthermore, to realize the full potential of this LC system, we optimized key parameters—including Salmonella concentration, structure of surfactant decorated at the LC-aqueous interface, and LC geometry. Consequently, the optimized LC system autonomously recognizes and optically reports presence of Salmonella cells at trace concentrations (100 cfu/ml) with a recognition time of less than 1 minute. The comprehensive understanding of interfacial biomolecular dynamics will hint at practical viability of the LC-based transducers in a wide variety of fields including biological sensors, medical diagnostics, and environmental monitoring. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea grant (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, RS-2024-00411809).

P3-070.k: Molecular Dynamics; Interfacial Adhesion; Biomimetic Materials
P3-070.a: Robust interfacial adhesion in underwater environments remains a significant challenge for science and engineering. It is fundamentally limited by interfacial hydration and surface-bound ion layers at aqueous interfaces, which collectively block intimate adhesive contact. In nature, mussel foot protein type 5 (fp-5), a polyphenolic interfacial adhesive, has evolved strategies that overcome these barriers and inspire routes to improved adhesion. Here, we use coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations with an fp-5-inspired adhesive model to uncover how sequence-specific architectures can be leveraged to precisely control and enhance interfacial adhesion properties. We confirm that the interfacial adhesion mechanism proceeds through four steps: floating, approaching, zipping, and adhesion, and that local charge distributions systematically influence adhesion at hydrated, ion-decorated interfaces. Initial electrostatic interactions between localized charged segments of the adhesive and the surface-bound ion layers facilitate a stepwise approach that enables intimate adhesive contact. These insights provide a versatile framework for designing advanced biomimetic materials tailored for wet conditions. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korea government (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, RS-2024-00411809).

P3-071.a: In dense bacterial suspensions, individual swimmers rarely move independently; the hydrodynamic stresses they exert on the surrounding fluid couple their motions and drive large-scale, turbulent-like collective flows. Confining such a suspension within a microscale droplet reorganizes this active turbulence into coherent vortical motion, making confinement a natural route to controlling collective bacterial behavior. The confining boundaries, however, are almost always rigid and isotropic, defining the interface by scalar properties alone: they carry no preferred direction and cannot respond to the enclosed activity. Here we replace such a boundary with a nematic liquid crystal and examine the coupling across the resulting soft interface. Dense bacterial suspensions are confined as cylindrical droplets within a nematic host, where surfactants impose planar or homeotropic anchoring at fixed geometry, isolating the boundary condition on the director. Optical flow reveals that the enclosed suspension settles into stable vortices, reversing vortices, or sporadic patterns, whose populations shift with the anchoring, whereas isotropic hosts under identical geometry show no comparable dependence. Conversely, the anisotropic interface responds: at higher bacterial volume fraction, the active stress transmitted across the interface distorts the surrounding director field, with the distortion again shaped by the anchoring condition. These observations reveal a dynamic coupling in which anchoring biases the collective state while activity reorganizes the host, providing a way toward reconfigurable control of active matter through responsive anisotropic fluids. This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea grant funded by the Korea government (RS-2023-00212739, RS-2023-00302586, RS-2024-00411809).

P3-072.a: Growing outdoor activity and UV awareness increase demand for effective sun protection. UV damages skin, causing sunburn, pigmentation, wrinkles, DNA damage, photoaging, and cancer. Sunscreens must be water-resistant for sweat and water activities. Traditional water-in-oil(W/O) feels heavy and hard to cleanse, while oil-in-water(O/W) washes off and redistributes filters, reducing efficacy. A new approach should form a durable film on skin and anchor UV filters. We propose a novel oil-in-water (O/W) sunscreen formulation with improved moisturizing and water resistance properties by exploiting the ion-responsive crosslinking mechanism of sodium alginate, a natural polysaccharide derived from brown algae. Stable film formation was optimized depending on calcium concentrations and the molecular weight of sodium alginate. Stable Ca²⁺–alginate “egg-box” ionic cross-linking forms a dense 3D hydrogel that entraps oil droplets without turbidity, preventing leakage and re-emulsification. FTIR confirms carboxylate coordination, while alginate molecular weight(MW) is critical: low-MW causes film tearing and droplet leakage, whereas high-MW yields stronger networks and superior stability. Cross-linking also reduces water evaporation via an occlusive barrier, enhancing moisturization. In real O/W sunscreen and seawater, multivalent cations drive synergistic densification, achieving high water resistance (91.24%). In vivo, higher alginate content and robust film retention maintain UV filter and SPF after frictional challenge. We successfully developed an ion-responsive O/W sunscreen film using alginate that rapidly forms a robust 3D “egg-box” hydrogel network with marine multivalent ions. Our findings indicate that the developed formulation maintains the favorable sensory characteristics of O/W emulsions while delivering high-performance water resistance particularly optimized for marine environments.
