P3-074.a: Injectable hydrogels are attractive biomaterials for cartilage tissue engineering because they can be delivered through minimally invasive systems and conform to irregular defect sites. They also provide a three-dimensional environment that supports tissue regeneration. However, many thermogels exhibit poor mechanical stability, which limits their long-term application in cartilage repair. In this study, a biomimetic injectable hybrid hydrogel composed of octanoyl glycol chitosan (OGC), cartilage-derived extracellular matrix (cECM), and dibenzaldehyde-terminated poly(ethylene glycol) (DP) was developed. OGC undergoes a temperature-triggered sol-gel transition near physiological temperature through hydrophobic interactions, enabling rapid in-situ gelation after injection. cECM was incorporated to provide cartilage-specific biochemical cues, while DP served as a dynamic crosslinker by forming Schiff base bonds with the amine groups of OGC. The physicochemical characteristics of the hydrogels were confirmed by FT-IR and 1H-NMR spectroscopy, and their gelation behavior, rheological properties, degradation profile, and mechanical properties were thoroughly characterized and evaluated. Incorporation of DP significantly enhanced the mechanical strength and structural stability of the OGC/cECM hydrogels by introducing a dynamically crosslinked network. The hydrogels exhibited rapid in-situ gelation and retained excellent injectability. In addition, they demonstrated self-healing behavior, indicating efficient network reconstruction through dynamic Schiff base interactions. The DP-crosslinked hydrogels also showed tunable degradation profiles while maintaining a biomimetic microenvironment provided by cECM. The dynamically crosslinked OGC/cECM hydrogel combines thermoresponsiveness, mechanical reinforcement, injectability, self-healing capability, and a biomimetic cartilage-specific microenvironment, highlighting its potential as an injectable platform for cartilage regeneration and minimally invasive tissue engineering applications.

P3-075.k: Octanoyl Glycol Chitosan; Mesenchymal Stem Cell-conditioned Medium; Wound Healing
P3-075.a: Mesenchymal stem cell-derived conditioned medium (MSC-CM) has attracted considerable interest as a cell-free therapeutic owing to its rich content of bioactive factors involved in tissue regeneration and angiogenesis. However, its therapeutic efficacy is often limited by rapid diffusion and insufficient retention at wound sites. To address these limitations, MSC-CM was incorporated into a thermoresponsive octanoyl glycol chitosan (OGC) system to fabricate an MSC-CM-loaded thermogel film (OGC-CM). The physicochemical properties, tissue adhesion, antibacterial activity, cytocompatibility, wound healing efficacy, and angiogenic activity of the films were systematically evaluated in vitro. The OGC-CM thermogel film maintained thermoresponsive sol-gel transition behavior and exhibited stable hydration and enhanced tissue adhesion under wet conditions. In vitro studies demonstrated excellent cytocompatibility toward NIH3T3 fibroblasts without observable cytotoxic effects. Furthermore, the OGC-CM thermogel film significantly promoted fibroblast migration compared with the OGC film and the control group, indicating enhanced wound healing efficacy. Angiogenic activity was also markedly improved in HUVEC cultures, as evidenced by increased tube formation parameters, including the number of nodes, junctions, branches, and total vessel length. In addition, the film exhibited antibacterial activity against both Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus. These findings demonstrate that OGC-CM thermogel films serve as a multifunctional wound dressing platform capable of localized delivery of stem cell-derived paracrine factors, providing antibacterial activity while promoting cell migration and angiogenesis. This strategy offers considerable potential for next-generation bioactive wound dressings and regenerative biomaterial systems.

P3-076.a: Porous β-type titanium alloys have attracted considerable attention for biomedical implants because of their low elastic modulus, excellent biocompatibility, and recoverable deformation behavior. In this study, the recovery behavior of porous Ti–15Nb–5Sn alloys (at. %) fabricated by Material Extrusion Additive Manufacturing (MEAM) was systematically investigated by varying the infill density. Filaments were prepared by homogeneously mixing spherical Ti–15Nb–5Sn alloy powder with a binder system, and porous specimens with different porosities were fabricated by MEAM through variation of the infill density. After debinding, sintering, and solution treatment, the microstructure and mechanical properties were systematically characterized. Increasing the infill density resulted in a higher area fraction of β-phase and lower porosity, accompanied by an increase in oxygen content. A distinct transition in recoverable strain was observed at approximately 65% porosity. Below this critical porosity, local plastic deformation became dominant, leading to reduced recoverable strain, whereas above it, local softening associated with the porous architecture promoted enhanced strain recovery. Furthermore, the recovery behavior was governed not only by stress-induced martensitic transformation but also by bending-induced recoverable deformation of the porous struts. This result demonstrates that MEAM is not only a cost-effective manufacturing technique but also an effective approach for tailoring microstructure and pore architecture to achieve desirable mechanical and biomechanical properties. This study provides valuable insights into the design of porous β-type titanium implants with improved recovery performance for customized biomedical applications.

P3-077.a: Material Extrusion Additive Manufacturing (MEAM) has attracted increasing attention for fabricating porous biomedical implants. However, developing binder systems that simultaneously provide stable printing, efficient debinding, and shape retention remains a significant challenge. In this study, a thermoplastic polyurethane/polypropylene (TPU/PP) binder system was developed for fabricating porous Ti–15Nb–5Sn alloy (at. %). For comparison, filaments containing either the TPU/PP binder system or only TPU as the binder were prepared by homogeneously mixing them with spherical Ti–15Nb–5Sn alloy powder. Porous specimens were fabricated by MEAM, followed by debinding, sintering, and solution treatment. The extrusion behavior, debinding characteristics, microstructure, phase constitution, and mechanical properties were investigated. An extrusion temperature of 150 °C was identified as the optimum condition, and stable printing was achieved at 220–230 °C without nozzle clogging or interlayer defects. Solvent debinding removed 99.2% of TPU after 12 h, forming interconnected pore channels that increased the total binder removal ratio to 99.5% while suppressing swelling, cracking, and collapse. In contrast, the specimen fabricated using only TPU collapsed because decomposition gases could not escape during thermal debinding. The TPU/PP specimens exhibited a porosity of 41.1%, consisted predominantly of the β phase with only trace amounts of oxygen-stabilized α phase, and showed a compressive strength of 113.9 MPa, an elastic modulus of 2.6 GPa, and a maximum recoverable strain of 3.4%. These results demonstrate that the proposed TPU/PP binder system provides an effective processing strategy for fabricating porous β-type Ti–15Nb–5Sn alloys for biomedical implant applications.

P3-078.a: Conventional plasma treatment can restore surface activity, but post-treatment exposure and handling may permit recontamination. Here, we developed a sealed in-package dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma system that reactivates aged titanium implants within a disposable dielectric ampoule. Aged untreated, conventional open-plasma-treated, and in-package-plasma-treated surfaces were compared using water contact-angle measurements, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, atomic force microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Osteogenic cell and gingival fibroblast responses were evaluated in vitro, and early osseointegration was assessed in rabbit calvarial defects after 4 weeks. An optimized condition of 8.6 kV, 24 kHz, 1 min, He/O₂ (0.5%), and a 1.5-mm gap produced a stable, reproducible discharge. Surface carbon decreased from 23.62 to 19.06 at.% without significant changes in roughness or micro/nanotopography. In-package-reactivated surfaces enhanced osteogenic cell attachment, spreading, viability, alkaline phosphatase activity, mineralized matrix formation, and expression of RUNX2, OCN, and COL1A1. Gingival fibroblast viability, proliferation, spreading, and migration were also increased. In vivo, plasma-treated implants showed higher implant stability quotient (62.1 ± 11.3 vs. 49.7 ± 12.6), bone-to-implant contact (62.8 ± 9.6% vs. 49.7 ± 11.8%), bone volume fraction (0.454 ± 0.134 vs. 0.405 ± 0.138), and removal torque (28.6 ± 4.3 vs. 24.5 ± 4.1 N·cm) than aged controls. These findings demonstrate that in-package DBD plasma reactivation restores the physicochemical and biological activity of aged titanium while minimizing handling-related recontamination, thereby providing a practical strategy to improve early soft-tissue responses and osseointegration (No. RS-2023-00222390).

P3-079.k: PVA/Alginate/Gelatin Hydrogel; Wet-surface Retention; Compressive Durability
P3-079.a: Oral dressings require structural and mechanical stability to withstand the complex, dynamic fluid environment of the oral cavity. While polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)/alginate hydrogels offer flexibility, their susceptibility to saliva-induced deterioration limits baseline efficacy. This study evaluates the systematic influence of gelatin content on modulating network architecture to enhance wet-state resilience Composite hydrogels were prepared with 10% w/v PVA, 2% w/v sodium alginate, and varying gelatin concentrations (0, 1, 3, 5% w/v; PA, PAG-1, PAG-3, PAG-5) via freeze-thaw cycles and CaCl2 crosslinking. Pore morphology, swelling, and degradation kinetics were analyzed in artificial saliva. Wet-state mechanical durability, 10-cycle compressive recovery, oral wash-off surface retention, and preliminary in vitro HGF-1 cytocompatibility were systematically quantified. Gelatin incorporation refined the internal pore structure, reducing average pore size in a concentration-dependent manner. The 3% gelatin formulation (PAG-3) demonstrated an optimal structural equilibrium, minimizing mass leaching and maintaining superior water retention. Crucially, PAG-3 achieved the highest compressive modulus retention after 7 days of artificial saliva aging, alongside excellent dynamic shape recovery and prolonged wet-surface adherence without inducing cytotoxicity. Modulating gelatin content directly dictates the physicomechanical performance of PVA/alginate networks. The PAG-3 patch successfully balances flexibility and environmental durability, effectively resisting hydration-induced softening and dynamic fatigue. These findings validate the PAG-3 composite not as an active biological regenerator, but as a physically durable, mechanically reliable localized barrier optimized for oral mucosal protection (No. RS-2023-00222390).

P3-080.k: Diabetic Periodontitis; 3D Organotypic Model; Methacrylated Collagen (ColMA).
P3-080.a: Diabetic periodontitis causes severe tissue breakdown and impaired healing, partly driven by advanced glycation end-products (AGEs). Traditional 2D cultures fail to replicate the complex architecture of native gingiva. To address this, we developed a 3D organotypic co-culture model using a methacrylated collagen (ColMA) hydrogel at an air-liquid interface (ALI) to simulate diabetic gingival conditions. The model was fabricated using UV-crosslinked 4% ColMA, with human gingival fibroblasts embedded in the stroma and keratinocytes seeded on top to form a stratified epithelium. Constructs were cultured for 21 days under normoglycemic (NG) or diabetic (high-glucose and AGE-BSA) conditions. We evaluated tissue architecture using H&E staining, measured cytotoxicity via LDH release, and quantified inflammatory cytokines (IL-6 and IL-1β) using ELISA. By Day 21, both groups successfully developed a stratified epithelium overlying the stromal compartment. However, diabetic constructs exhibited impaired tissue maturation, characterized by altered epithelial thickness and stromal organization compared to NG controls. Furthermore, the diabetic group exhibited significantly higher LDH-based cytotoxicity and progressively elevate10382d levels of the inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-1β throughout the culture period. We successfully established a 3D ColMA-based organotypic model that reproducibly mimics a diabetic gingival phenotype across structural, cytotoxic, and inflammatory metrics. This stratifying tissue construct serves as a robust in vitro platform for exploring periodontal disease mechanisms and evaluating future therapeutic interventions, such as cold atmospheric plasma treatments (No. RS-2023-00222390).

P3-081.k: Dynamic Hydrogel; Oxidized Alginate (ADA); Gelatin Methacryloyl (GelMA)
P3-081.a: Developing biomimetic scaffolds for oral soft tissue regeneration requires replicating the natural dynamic mechanical microenvironment. Traditional statically crosslinked hydrogels form irreversible covalent networks, restricting cell spreading and proliferation. To overcome this, we propose a stress-relaxing, dynamic hydrogel engineered from alginate dialdehyde (ADA) and gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA). Driven by reversible Schiff base linkages, this matrix dissociates under cellular traction and rapidly self-heals, allowing cells to extend without compromising scaffold structural integrity. ADA was synthesized by sodium periodate oxidation and blended with GelMA to construct a dual-crosslinked hydrogel through reversible Schiff-base interactions and visible light-induced photocrosslinking (405 nm, LAP photoinitiator). The physicochemical properties were characterized by FTIR, swelling test, degradation, and scanning electron microscopy. Mechanical performance was evaluated using compression, rheological, stress-relaxation, and self-healing tests. Human gingival fibroblasts were encapsulated to assess cell viability, proliferation, morphology, and extracellular matrix deposition. The ADA-GelMA hydrogel exhibited a porous architecture, tunable degradation, and enhanced viscoelastic behavior (compressive modulus: ~25 kPa) while maintaining sufficient mechanical stability. Compared with GelMA alone, the dynamic hydrogel demonstrated improved stress relaxation (half-relaxation time, τ1/2: ~90 s), structural recovery after mechanical damage, and prolonged structural integrity during culture. Encapsulated fibroblasts showed high viability, enhanced spreading, and increased extracellular matrix deposition, indicating improved cell–matrix interactions. The integration of dynamic Schiff-base chemistry with photocrosslinked GelMA generated a viscoelastic hydrogel that balances adaptability and mechanical stability. This dynamic biomaterial provides a promising platform for physiologically relevant 3D oral soft tissue disease models and offers new opportunities for oral tissue engineering (No. RS-2023-00222390).

P3-082.k: Atomic Layer Deposition; Mechanotransduction; Oral Soft Tissue Regeneration
P3-082.a: Establishing a durable soft tissue seal around dental implant abutments requires precise isolation of surface chemical cues from physical properties. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) enables precise decoupling of nanoscale surface chemistry from macroscopic topography and bulk stiffness. By utilizing Al2O3 as a model oxide, this study investigates how cycle-dependent nanoscale nucleation governs chemical surface energy and regulates fibronectin adsorption, focal adhesion maturation, and YAP/TAZ signaling in human gingival fibroblasts (HGF-1). Silicon wafers were coated with Al2O3 at 1, 3, 5, 10, 15, and 20 ALD cycles, with uncoated Si as a control. Surface properties were characterized via XPS, ellipsometry, AFM, and water contact angle analyses. Serum protein and fibronectin adsorption were quantified by BCA, ELISA, and fluorescence assays. HGF-1 cells were cultured to assess initial adhesion, cytoskeletal spreading, filamentous actin organization, focal adhesion maturation, including Vinculin and FAK, and YAP and TAZ nuclear localization using immunofluorescence. Low cycles produced incomplete discrete oxide coverage, whereas higher cycles yielded continuous Al2O3 nanofilms. While macroscopic topography remained constant, the nanoscale structural evolution dynamically modulated the chemical surface energy and wettability profiles. Intermediate and high cycle surfaces promoted enhanced cell spreading, increased focal adhesion maturation, and elevated YAP/TAZ nuclear localization compared to low cycles. Early extracellular matrix responses strongly correlated with cycle-dependent surface energy. These findings demonstrate that ALD-defined Al2O3 nanointerfaces can regulate fibroblast mechanotransduction independently of topography and stiffness. Precisely controlled oxide nucleation and surface energy offer a robust platform for mechanobiology-driven oral soft tissue regeneration and improved implant abutment design. (No. RS-2023-00222390)

P3-083.k: Duodenal Metallic Bypass Sleeve; Nitinol Biomaterial; Nutrient Absorption
P3-083.a: Endoscopic bariatric and metabolic therapies are minimally invasive alternatives that bridge the gap between pharmacological treatment and bariatric surgery. A novel duodenal metallic bypass sleeve (DMBS) was developed to induce nutrient malabsorption while preserving ampullary patency and modulating incretin hormones. This study aimed to evaluate the technical feasibility, safety, and efficacy of the DMBS to suppress weight gain in a porcine model. The DMBS consisted of a disk-part, a sleeve-part, and four connecting wires. The characteristics of the DMBS were analyzed. Twelve pigs were randomly assigned to the control, DMBS@4wks, rebounding, and DMBS@8wks groups (n=3 per group). The efficacy and safety of the DMBS were assessed by comparing the results of weight changes, follow-up radiological and endoscopic, hematologic, and histological examination. DMBS placement and removal were technically successful in all study groups. The mean percentage of total body weight gain (%TBWG) in the DMBS-treated groups were significantly lower than that in the control group (all p<0.05). The mean %TBWGs at 8 weeks were 51%, 46%, and 29% in the control, rebounding, and DMBS@8wks groups, respectively. DMBS-induced tissue hyperplasia and mucosal injury markers were significantly increased. In the DMBS-treated groups, increased glucose transporter type 1 (GLUT1) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and decreased glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) levels were observed. The DMBS was technically feasible, effective, and safe in suppressing weight in the porcine model. This device seems to be a novel, minimally invasive endoscopic bariatric therapeutic option for obesity management.

P3-084.k: Anti-restenosis; Bioresorbable Scaffold; Mesenchymal Stem Cells-derived Nanovesicles
P3-084.a: Stent-based revascularization remains limited by the competing demands of restenosis prevention and vascular healing. Although drug-eluting-stents reduce neointimal hyperplasia by suppressing vascular-smooth-muscle-cell (VSMC) proliferation, their cytostatic mechanisms can delay re-endothelialization and compromise vascular repair. This unresolved therapeutic trade-off underscores the need for a regenerative scaffold strategy that preserves antirestenotic efficacy while actively restoring vascular healing. We developed a nanovesicle-eluting bioresorbable-scaffold (NVE-BRS) by non-covalently loading MSC-derived nanovesicles (MSC-NVs) onto a PMB30W-functionalized, honeycomb-structured thin-strut PLLA-scaffold, followed by lyophilization for off-the-shelf use. Lyophilization stability, coating and release behavior, shear retention, NV diffusion, radial expansion mechanics, in-vitro vasculomodulatory activity, and in-vivo efficacy were evaluated using computational analyses, vascular cells and a balloon-injured rabbit iliac artery model with angiography, OCT, histology, and immunofluorescence. The PMB30W-based amphiphilic interface enabled uniform non-covalent MSC-NV loading and localized release without chemical conjugation, while lyophilization preserved EV-mimetic morphology, particle and cargo profiles, and bioactivity. Computational analyses supported transmural NV delivery and scaffold mechanical integrity after expansion. In vitro, MSC-NVs promoted endothelial recovery and angiogenic activity while suppressing VSMC inflammatory activation, proliferation, and pro-atherogenic macrophage responses. In vivo, NVE-BRS maintained vascular patency and reduced neointimal thickness from 0.40 ± 0.02 mm to 0.17 ± 0.01 mm and stenosis area from 48.8 ± 1.56% to 19.38 ± 1.67% compared with bare BRS. Histology further showed increased CD31-positive endothelial coverage and reduced VCAM-1, PDGFR-β, α-SMA, and CD68 signals. NVE-BRS establishes an off-the-shelf regenerative scaffold platform that decouples antirestenotic efficacy from impaired vascular healing by coordinating endothelial repair, VSMC suppression, and inflammatory modulation.

P3-085.a: Cardiovascular disease has become increasingly prevalent with the aging population, and drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty is increasingly favored for lesions unsuitable for conventional stenting. Although various coating agents—paclitaxel, sirolimus (SRL), everolimus, and nitric oxide (NO)—have been proposed, current single-layer coating strategies each carry distinct advantages and limitations. We fabricated a novel dual-layer DCB combining a NO-releasing bionanomatrix with SRL, designed to provide potent antiproliferative activity and promote rapid endothelialization while minimizing cytotoxicity through optimized SRL dosing. In vitro cell studies assessed effects on endothelial and smooth muscle cell proliferation. Coating transfer and retention within the vessel wall were evaluated using an ex vivo porcine artery bioreactor model under physiological flow. The in-vivo therapeutic efficacy and safety of the SRL@NO-coated balloon angioplasty was investigated in a balloon injury-induced stenosis rabbit iliac artery model. Follow-up angiography, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and histology were examined to assess the therapeutic outcomes of SRL@NO-coated balloon angioplasty for 28 days. In vitro study, combined NO and SRL simultaneously enhanced endothelial cell proliferation while suppressing smooth muscle cell proliferation. The dual-layer coating, including the bionanomatrix and SRL-encapsulated liposomes, was effectively transferred into the porcine artery wall and retained for at least 14 days. In the rabbit model, Dual-layer SRL@NO-coated balloon effectively suppressed neointimal hyperplasia; notably, low-dose SRL combined with NO induced intact re-endothelialization with minimal cytotoxicity and inflammation (all variables, p < 0.05). Taken together, pro-healing dual-layer DCB represents a promising therapeutic strategy for enhanced vascular repair, particularly in impaired vascular healing including diabetic populations.

P3-086.a: High-pressure drug-coated balloon (HP-DCB) angioplasty enhances vascular drug delivery by overcoming the limitations of passive diffusion-based conventional non-compliant DCB (NC-DCB) systems. We developed a dual-layer HP balloon catheter composed of an outer Nylon 12 layer and an inner Pebax® 7233 layer, and evaluated its feasibility and therapeutic efficacy as a paclitaxel (PTX)-coated platform. The HP balloon was designed to withstand pressures up to 12 atm while maintaining an expanded diameter identical to that of the NC balloon at 6 atm. Shellac-based PTX coating was uniformly applied to HP-DCB and NC-DCB, and coating thickness, drug amount, release behavior, and mechanical properties were compared. Pressure-assisted drug penetration was assessed in a vascular-mimicking agarose gel phantom using fluorescent PTX and confocal microscopy. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in a balloon injury-induced rabbit iliac artery stenosis model using angiography, optical coherence tomography, histology, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence examinations. Drug amount, coating thickness, and sustained drug release did not differ between groups. The mechanical robustness in HP-DCB was significantly greater than that in NC-DCB. HP-DCB produced significantly greater penetration depth and fluorescence-positive area, indicating enhanced pressure-driven drug transfer. HP-DCB resulted in superior luminal patency, reduced neointimal hyperplasia, and favorable biological responses compared with that in NC-DCB and the sham control. These findings support DCB use based on a dual-layered HP balloon platform as a promising next-generation strategy for stenotic vascular lesion treatment.

P3-087.k: Ursodeoxycholic Acid; Biocatalytic Cascade; Pharmaceutical Biomanufacturing
P3-087.a: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is a clinically important bile acid used for the treatment of hepatobiliary diseases, including primary biliary cholangitis and cholestasis. Because the 7β-hydroxyl configuration of UDCA differs from the 7α-hydroxyl configuration of its precursor, chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), highly stereoselective synthesis is essential to ensure product purity and therapeutic efficacy. Biocatalytic cascade reactions offer an environmentally friendly alternative to conventional chemical synthesis owing to their high regio- and enantioselectivity under mild reaction conditions. However, the industrial implementation of large-scale biocatalytic UDCA production remains challenging. Biocatalysts were engineered using genetic modification and sequence-guided optimization to improve catalytic activity and stability. The optimized biocatalysts were produced in 20–200 L bioreactors to evaluate scalability. A 100 L-scale biocatalytic process was subsequently established for the conversion of CDCA to UDCA. In addition, an integrated downstream process comprising precipitation, filtration, and freeze-drying was developed for product purification and recovery. The engineered biocatalysts maintained catalytic performance and production yield during scale-up from 20 to 200 L. Using the manufactured biocatalysts, the 100 L biocatalytic process achieved a 90% conversion yield from 5 kg of CDCA to UDCA. The optimized downstream purification process enabled the recovery of approximately 4 kg of highly pure UDCA with an overall recovery yield of 82%. This study demonstrates a scalable and sustainable biocatalytic manufacturing platform for the industrial production of high-purity UDCA. The integration of biocatalyst engineering, large-scale bioprocessing, and efficient downstream recovery provides a practical strategy for environmentally friendly pharmaceutical manufacturing of stereochemically demanding bile acid therapeutics.

P3-088.k: Cyclic Peptide; Tyrosinase Inhibition; Antioxidant Activity
P3-088.a: Excessive melanin production and accumulation are the primary causes of various hyperpigmentation disorders, including melasma, age spots, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; therefore, the development of treatment strategies that can effectively regulate these processes is essential. Tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin biosynthesis, is a primary target for the treatment of hyperpigmentation, and research on peptide-based inhibitors to suppress it has been actively pursued. However, conventional linear peptides have limitations in therapeutic applications due to their low in vivo stability. Therefore, in this study, we designed a cyclic peptide, CsPP (Cyclic SYRV Pentapeptide), by incorporating a cyclization strategy to enhance structural stability, and evaluated its skin-lightening and antioxidant activities. CsPP was synthesized using solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), and its successful synthesis and purity of over 98% were confirmed via MALDI-TOF MS and HPLC. In addition, we conducted cytotoxicity assays using RAW 264.7 cells, evaluated tyrosinase inhibitory activity and DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging activity, and performed molecular docking simulations. As a result, CsPP exhibited a cell survival rate of over 90%, confirming its excellent biocompatibility. Furthermore, its tyrosinase inhibitory activity was approximately 1.6 times greater than that of arbutin and approximately 3.4 times greater than that of the linear peptide (IC50 = 336.7 ± 5.79 μM), its DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging activities also demonstrated IC50 values of 30.27 ± 1.06 μM and 282.4 ± 11.45 μM, respectively, confirming its excellent antioxidant activity. Molecular docking results showed that CsPP formed a stable interaction with His263, the active site of tyrosinase, supporting the enzyme inhibition mechanism. By elucidating the mechanisms by which CsPP enhances biological activity through a cyclization strategy and inhibits tyrosinase, this study suggests that CsPP has the potential to serve as a candidate functional peptide for the treatment of hyperpigmentation disorders.

P3-089.k: Layered Double Hydroxide; Radioisotope; Surface Charge
P3-089.a: Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) are promising two-dimensional drug-delivery carriers with biocompatibility and tunable surface charge. However, how surface charge and administration route govern their in vivo fate remains unclear. This study investigated the biological pathways of surface-charge-controlled LDH nanoparticles using cobalt-55 (Co-55) radiolabeling and positron emission tomography (PET). MgAl-LDH was synthesized by coprecipitation and surface-modified with citrate and succinate to obtain negative and moderately positive surface charges. Co-55 was incorporated into the framework via isomorphous substitution. Samples were characterized by PXRD, FT-IR, SEM, zeta potential, and DLS. Labeling stability in PBS and human serum, CT-26 cellular uptake, and in vivo PET biodistribution following oral and intravenous administration in mice were evaluated. Surface modification preserved the hydrotalcite crystal structure and morphology while shifting the zeta potential from +33.6 mV (pristine) to −25.6 mV (citrate) and +20.4 mV (succinate). Co-55 labeling reached ~100% efficiency, with over 80% remaining stable in PBS and serum for 48 h. Cellular uptake in CT-26 cells increased with charge tuning (25%, 27%, and 36% for LDH, LDH-Cit, and LDH-Suc). PET imaging revealed that biological pathways depended on both charge and route: orally administered particles showed charge-dependent gastrointestinal transit, whereas intravenous injection produced distinct liver- and lung-dominant distributions. Surface charge and administration route jointly govern the in vivo behavior of Co-55-labeled LDH nanoparticles. Controlling surface charge through simple surface coating offers a practical strategy for designing organ-specific theragnostic nanomaterials—for example, negatively charged LDH for oral delivery and positively charged LDH for lung targeting via intravenous injection.

P3-090.k: Layered Double Hydroxide; Metal-Organic Framework; 2D Janus Nanohybrid
P3-090.a: Conventional drug delivery carriers suffer from low drug-loading efficiency, premature drug leakage, and poor control over drug release, resulting in reduced therapeutic efficacy and increased side effects. Layered double hydroxides (LDH) have attracted considerable attention as drug delivery carriers due to their biocompatibility and ion-exchange capability, while metal–organic frameworks (MOF) provide high surface areas, tunable pore structures, and pH-responsive degradation. Although Janus nanostructures have been widely investigated for asymmetric functionalization, most reported systems are based on three-dimensional (3D) structure. Two fabrication strategies will be systematically compared: an in-situ direct growth approach using Pickering emulsions and an ex-situ self-assembly approach at immiscible liquid–liquid interfaces. The effects of these methods on Janus formation, MOF coverage, and interfacial stability were investigated to establish an effective strategy for fabricating 2D Janus nanohybrids. LDH-MOF Janus nanohybrids were successfully fabricated with in-situ and ex-situ strategies. The morphology and physicochemical properties of the nanohybrids were confirmed by SEM, TEM, XRD, FT-IR, BET, contact angle, and zeta potential analyses. Both in-situ and ex-situ fabrication strategies were investigated for the development of 2D Janus LDH-MOF nanohybrids. This study provides an effective interfacial engineering strategy for constructing asymmetric 2D nanohybrids with potential for advanced drug delivery applications.

P3-091.a: Clinical applications of exosomes have been limited because they are mostly accumulated in and removed by the liver and spleen, resulting in short biological half-lives (<6 hours) in the body after systemic administration. To develop effective, exosome-based therapeutics, an efficient surface-editing strategy that does not cost their intrinsic biological functions and/or yield is crucial. Here, we report an easy-to-adapt and highly versatile methodology to control the in vivo fate of exosomes by altering their surfaces, based on bioorthogonal copper-free click chemistry (BCC) and metabolic glycoengineering (MGE) of exosome-secreting donor cells For the surface modification of exosomes, unnatural sialic acids containing an azide group (-N3) were exogenously introduced on the donor cells via MGE using tetraacetylated N-azidoacetyl-d-mannosamine (Ac4ManNAz). Then, dibenzocyclooctyne-terminated targeting moieties such as DBCO-PHA were prepared to specifically label the exogenously generated N3 group on the cells via BCC. The surface-edited exosomes effectively accumulated into the target tissues of the animal models with rheumatoid arthritis and tumour, primarily owing to prolonged circulation in the bloodstream and the active targeting mechanism. BCC combined with MGE is highly useful as a simple and safe approach for the surface modification of exosomes to modulate their in vivo fate.

P3-092.k: Interfacial Assembly; Electron Transfer; Hydrogel Bioanode
P3-092.a: Flexible hydrogels provide soft and hydrated matrices suitable for bioelectrochemical interfaces, but efficient integration of enzymes with conductive components remains challenging. Here, we engineer the hydrogel biointerface through sequential assembly of glucose oxidase (GOx) and gold nanoparticles (Au NPs) to establish an organized enzyme–nanoparticle architecture for enhanced electron transfer. A conductive Au NP layer was formed on the hydrogel surface while preserving its flexible and hydrated characteristics. GOx and Au NPs were subsequently assembled through sequential deposition to construct multilayer biointerfaces with controlled interfacial organization. The effects of multilayer number on structural, electrical, mechanical, and electrochemical properties were systematically evaluated to identify the optimal bioanode architecture. Sequential enzyme–nanoparticle assembly produced well-integrated multilayer biointerfaces while maintaining the structural flexibility of the hydrogel electrode. Increasing the multilayer number enhanced bioelectrocatalytic activity up to an optimal assembly condition, beyond which additional deposition provided limited improvement. The optimized architecture promoted effective electronic communication between GOx and the conductive hydrogel electrode, resulting in enhanced glucose-oxidation performance while retaining robust electrochemical activity under mechanical deformation. These results demonstrate that sequential enzyme–nanoparticle assembly provides an effective strategy for engineering flexible hydrogel biointerfaces. Controlled integration of catalytic and conductive components enables efficient electron transfer while preserving mechanical compliance, offering a versatile platform for flexible bioelectrochemical energy-conversion systems.

P3-093.k: Kelp-derived Bioelectrode; Hierarchical Architecture; Biofuel Cell
P3-093.a: Kelp possesses a naturally interconnected and hydrated hierarchical architecture that offers favorable pathways for electrolyte infiltration and molecular transport. These intrinsic structural features make kelp an attractive renewable scaffold for bioelectrochemical applications without requiring artificial microstructuring. Here, we exploit this native architecture as a functional bioelectrode platform for sustainable biofuel cells (BFCs). Kelp scaffolds with thicknesses of 400, 500, and 600 μm were converted into conductive hosts through gold nanoparticle (Au NP) incorporation while preserving their native porous structure. Glucose oxidase (GOx)/Au NP multilayers were subsequently assembled, and the effects of scaffold thickness and multilayer number on structural, mechanical, electrochemical, and BFC performance were systematically evaluated. The processed kelp scaffolds retained their interconnected porous morphology and hydrated characteristics. Bioelectrochemical performance exhibited a distinct thickness dependence, with the 500 μm scaffold providing the optimal balance among conductive-network connectivity, accessible porous volume, transport distance, and mechanical integrity. The optimized (GOx/Au NP)₇ bioelectrode achieved a current density of 9.68 mA cm⁻². The resulting BFC delivered a maximum power density of 2.15 mW cm⁻² and retained 83.2% of its initial performance after 14 days of operation in 300 mmol L⁻¹ glucose. These results establish naturally hierarchical kelp as a viable renewable scaffold for high-performance bioelectrodes. Coupling native porous transport pathways with optimized conductive and catalytic interfaces provides a simple and sustainable strategy for constructing durable BFCs.

P3-094.a: Transient bioelectronics are devices that decompose in the environment or the body after use, and they draw growing attention as a next-generation electronic technology. As the core electrode component of these devices, biodegradable conductive ink must simultaneously satisfy electrical conductivity, biocompatibility, and biodegradability. However, existing biodegradable conductive inks exhibit high electrical conductivity (approximately 6.4 kS/m), yet they readily delaminate from the substrate under mechanical deformation or external force and lose electrical connectivity. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a multifunctional conductive ink that simultaneously achieves electrical conductivity, flexibility, biodegradability, and interfacial adhesion. This ink employs the flexible biodegradable polymer polycaprolactone (PCL) as a matrix and incorporates tungsten nanoparticles (500 nm) as a conductive filler to form a conductive network based on particle-to-particle contact. The formulation further incorporates tannic acid, a naturally derived polyphenolic compound, and its abundant hydroxyl groups (–OH) strengthen adhesion between the ink and the substrate. A stencil-based process patterns the ink onto the substrate, and solvent evaporation then forms the conductive pattern. The conductive ink exhibits an electrical conductivity of approximately 2 kS/m and maintains electrical connectivity even after 1,000 cycles of repeated bending at a 7.5 mm bending radius. The addition of tannic acid further enhances adhesion across a range of organic and inorganic substrates, including chitosan film, polyimide film, and magnesium foil. The ink also shows gradual degradation behavior in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) at 37°C, a condition that simulates the physiological environment. Electronic devices fabricated with this ink operate stably: a resistive heater generates Joule heat under applied voltage, while temperature and pressure sensors achieve sensing functionality based on resistance changes. This biodegradable conductive ink simultaneously demonstrates electrical conductivity, stability under repeated deformation, adhesion to diverse substrates, and degradation behavior under physiological conditions. These properties, together with functional responses across various electronic devices, indicate that this ink holds strong potential as an electrode material for bioelectronic devices in natural and biological environments.

P3-095.k: Microalgal EVs; Stress-responsive Targeting; Photooxidative Stress
P3-095.a: UVB radiation-induced lipid peroxidation reduces membrane fluidity and attenuates endocytic activity in keratinocytes, limiting the delivery efficiency of conventional passive nanocarrier systems. Building on this rationale, we engineered Laminin-332 peptide-functionalized Dunaliella salina (D. salina)-derived extracellular vesicles (DsEVLam332) to operationalize stress-selective intracellular delivery. D. salina was selected for its capacity to hyperaccumulate β-carotene within plastid lipid globules; upon vesicular delivery, this enriches the recipient cell membrane with antioxidant cargo capable of scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inhibiting lipid peroxidation. This study describes a stress-responsive delivery approach in which UVB-induced integrin α3β1 upregulation is utilized as a targeting cue for selective antioxidant delivery to photodamaged keratinocytes. Laminin-332 peptide-functionalized Dunaliella salina-derived extracellular vesicles (DsEVLam332) demonstrated enhanced cellular uptake in UVB-irradiated keratinocytes through integrin α3β1-mediated endocytosis, supporting intracellular β-carotene delivery under conditions where passive carrier uptake is attenuated. Real-time near-infrared nanosensor measurements provided quantitative insight into the relationship between receptor upregulation and oxidative stress attenuation, and antioxidant efficacy was corroborated in a reconstructed human epidermis model. Taken together, these findings suggest that stress-associated receptor remodeling may serve as a useful basis for designing delivery systems capable of discriminating between damaged and healthy tissue. The microalgal origin of the vesicle platform offers practical compatibility with biological environments, and the targeting strategy may be applicable to other oxidative stress-associated skin conditions, pending further validation in more complex physiological settings

P3-096.a: Disease management requires continuous treatment and reliable long-term monitoring. Recently, optical technologies have gained increasing attention as noninvasive tools for tracking disease progression. However, in conventional optical sensing systems, light scattering and absorption by biological tissues attenuate optical signals and limit measurement accuracy. To address this limitation, we propose an implantable polymer-based bio-reflector designed to enhance the utility of reflected optical signals. We fabricate the reflector by molding a photocurable polymer with a microprism-patterned polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) mold. The resulting microstructured surface redirects incident light toward its original optical path, thereby improving the collection of reflected signals. The reflector maintains a reflectance above 50% over the 400–1000 nm wavelength range. Moreover, it preserves its microstructure for 30 days under degradation conditions and maintains both structural integrity and optical performance. The reflector also operates reliably under in vitro conditions, where its presence produces a distinct increase in photocurrent measured by a photodetector. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed bio-reflector as an implantable optical platform for long-term monitoring and support its integration with optical sensors for noninvasive acquisition of biological information.

P3-097.k: Ion-electron Coupling; Low Frequency Wireless; Ionic Sensor
P3-097.a: Wireless bioelectronics require transduction that is sensitive, noise-resilient, and biologically safe. Conventional inductive sensors rely on dielectric capacitors with inherently low capacitance, forcing operation in the MHz range. Such high-frequency coupling introduces electromagnetic interference, tissue heating, and unstable signal fidelity under physiological conditions, limiting safe implantable use. We developed a wireless low-frequency electrochemical sensing (WiLECS) platform that couples ionic dynamics with a low-frequency LC resonant circuit. A biocompatible ion gel was prepared from a choline-malate ionic liquid embedded in a chitosan matrix, incorporating 2-mercaptoethanol-functionalized Au nanoparticles as ion trap sites. The ionic capacitive sensor was integrated with a miniaturized double-layer FPCB antenna, and pressure sensing was validated in an artificial artery model with a balloon catheter simulating normal and plaque-laden arteries. Pressure disrupted hydrogen bonds between the ionic liquid and functionalized nanoparticles, releasing trapped ions to form an electric double layer through piezo-driven redistribution. This mechanotransduction yielded high pressure sensitivity (17.36 kPa⁻¹) and a signal-to-noise ratio of 78 dB, over four times that of a conventional dielectric gel sensor (15 dB). The platform achieved stable wireless transduction below 1 MHz, resolved subtle blood-pressure variations between normal and plaque conditions, and maintained reliable readout through a 5 mm spacer and 7 mm porcine skin. WiLECS directly bridges ionic transport and electronic resonance, enabling sensitive, noise-resilient, and biologically safe wireless monitoring in the sub-MHz regime. This ionic-electronic coupling strategy provides a generalizable framework for next-generation implantable bioelectronics.

P3-098.a: The accumulation of microplastics in the environment has emerged as a critical environmental concern driven by the increasing consumption of plastic products. Microplastics, defined as plastic particles ranging from 1 μm to 5 mm in diameter, not only contribute to environmental contamination but can also enter the human body through food ingestion, potentially posing adverse health effects. Conventional microplastic detection techniques typically require multistep sample pretreatment, costly analytical instrumentation, and time-consuming analysis, limiting their applicability for the quantitative determination of microplastic concentrations in complex environmental matrices. Therefore, the development of a low-cost sensing platform capable of rapid and facile detection and quantitative analysis of microplastics in real-world environmental samples is highly desirable. ) LC resonator-based sensor comprising a gold (Au) electrode, an inductor, and an interdigitated capacitor (IDC) is fabricated via a photolithographic patterning process. Polystyrene (PS) and polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) particles are employed as representative microplastic materials, and PS particles with diameters of 3 and 10 μm are prepared at concentrations ranging from 10⁴ to 10⁶ particles/mL. Each microplastic sample contacts the IDC capacitor region, inducing changes in the local electrical environment and enabling characterization of the resulting electrical response of the sensor. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) characterizes impedance variations as a function of microplastic concentration and polymer type in wired measurements. A vector network analyzer (VNA) characterizes the resonant response of the LC circuit, including shifts in resonant frequency, in wireless measurements. Systematic comparison of the measured electrical responses evaluates the feasibility of the proposed sensor for microplastic detection and quantitative analysis. Electrical characteristics of the LC resonator-based sensor are analyzed using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and a vector network analyzer (VNA). Sensor responses are evaluated as a function of microplastic concentration and polymer type. EIS measurements reveal increasing impedance response with increasing PS particle concentration. This impedance change originates from variations in the effective capacitance of the LC resonant circuit, leading to corresponding shifts in resonant characteristics. VNA measurements consistently show concentration-dependent shifts in resonant frequency and variations in reflection coefficient (S11) with increasing PS particle concentration. The EIS and VNA measurements demonstrate consistent concentration-dependent responses both methods.Sensor responses are compared using PS particles with diameters of 3 and 10 μm to investigate the effect of particle size. Larger PS particles produce a greater impedance change. Larger PS particles produce a more pronounced impedance change. Stronger perturbation of the local electric-field distribution within the IDC structure and at the electrode surface increases the impedance change. PS and PMMA particles enable assessment of microplastic detection performance under both wired and wireless measurement conditions. The LC resonator-based sensor distinguishes electrical responses according to microplastic concentration and polymer type. The sensor shows potential for microplastic detection and quantitative analysis. LC resonator-based sensor platform incorporating an interdigitated capacitor (IDC) enables detection and quantitative analysis of microplastics. The system evaluates impedance and resonant changes across PS and PMMA concentrations and polymer types. Wired EIS and wireless VNA measurements characterize microplastic-induced electrical responses through impedance variations and resonant behavior. The LC resonator-based platform provides a simple and cost-effective approach for microplastic detection and quantitative analysis compared with conventional analytical methods.

P3-099.a: Molecular diagnostics offer non-invasive alternatives to tissue biopsies, yet identifying sequence mutations remains a significant challenge in nucleic acid detection. While polymerase chain reaction serves as a gold standard, its cost, time consumption, and mutation accumulation necessitate amplification-free point-of-care testing approaches. Field-effect transistor biosensors combined with eukaryotic argonaute 1 provide high-resolution sequence recognition without target cleavage. Precise analysis of microRNAs within the same family is crucial for utilizing peritoneal fluid as a biomarker for various clinical conditions. This study introduces a novel biosensor integrating the natural properties of eAgo1 with a complementary metal-oxide semiconductor inverter. MXene is applied to the extended gate to amplify biosensing signals and minimize external environmental interference through noncontact measurements. Response surface methodology is utilized to statistically optimize the in vitro programming and RNA-induced silencing complex assembly conditions of eAgo1. The biosensor's sequence-recognition capability is systematically evaluated for single-nucleotide mismatch resolution under clinically relevant interference conditions. The platform successfully recognizes target microRNAs directly by shifting the switching threshold voltage according to molecular charge characteristics. The eAgo1 biosensor demonstrates remarkable sequence-recognition capability with single-nucleotide mismatch resolution among closely related microRNA families. Performance evaluation confirms its high reproducibility, resolution, and reliability in distinguishing complex single-nucleotide variations. Practical potential is validated through successful sequence identification and performance comparison with quantitative real-time PCR using exosomal microRNAs from peritoneal dialysis fluid. The eAgo1-based biosensing system successfully overcomes conventional technical limitations and amplification-induced mutation accumulation. It provides a robust, simplified, and non-invasive alternative for clinical diagnostics requiring exceptional analytical precision. The platform establishes a breakthrough approach for high-resolution single-nucleotide variation detection in complex biological fluids. Ultimately, this system serves as a reliable milestone for advanced point-of-care precision medical diagnostics in clinical settings.

P3-100.a: Plasmonic nanoparticles have been widely employed in surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS)-based molecular sensing and photothermal applications because of their strong light–matter interactions arising from localized surface plasmon resonance. However, liquid-phase SERS detection remains challenging because effective signal enhancement requires analytes to be localized within abundant electromagnetic hot-spots. Meanwhile, the photothermal properties of plasmonic nanostructures have been primarily exploited for photothermal therapy and light-triggered drug delivery, with limited integration of their molecular sensing capabilities. Therefore, combining SERS-based molecular sensing and photothermal drug delivery within a single plasmonic platform could enable simultaneous biochemical analysis and spatiotemporally controlled therapeutic delivery. Here, we present overgrown plasmonic hybrid nanogels (O-PHNs) that integrate label-free SERS-based molecular and cellular sensing with near-infrared (NIR)-responsive drug delivery by simultaneously harnessing electromagnetic enhancement and photothermal conversion. O-PHNs were synthesized through the radical polymerization of N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM) in the presence of seed plasmonic nanoparticles, followed by a facile overgrowth process that reinforced plasmonic coupling and extend the optical response into the NIR region. Seed plasmonic hybrid nanogels (seed-PHNs) were prepared by photopolymerizing P(NIPAM)-based hydrogels in the presence of metal precursors (Au or Ag). The seed-PHNs were subsequently subjected to seed-mediated metal overgrowth, followed by stabilization and purification, to produce NIR-responsive overgrown PHNs (O-PHNs). The optical properties, hydrodynamic sizes, morphology, elemental composition, and surface chemistry of O-PHNs were characterized using spectroscopic and microscopic techniques. Their wavelength-dependent photothermal conversion performance was evaluated by monitoring temperature changes during visible and NIR laser irradiation. For intracellular applications, O-PHNs were delivered into cells through either conventional co-incubation or hydroporation. Spatially resolved SERS spectra were then acquired from cells containing O-PHNs using a Raman mapping system. The resulting SERS maps were analyzed over selected spectral regions to visualize the intracellular distributions of nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins. To evaluate their drug-delivery capability, normal and tumor-mimicking cellular spheroids were generated in non-adhesive elastomeric microwells. The spheroids were treated with doxorubicin-loaded O-PHNs, and the intratumoral distribution of doxorubicin was visualized by confocal fluorescence imaging. The hydrodynamic diameters of the seed-PHNs ranged from 65.1 to 89.8 nm, whereas those of the corresponding O-PHNs increased to 121.6–209.3 nm. Among the tested formulations, O-Au@Ag-PHN exhibited the strongest NIR absorption, with a distinct peak at approximately 790 nm. This enhanced NIR responsiveness was attributed to nanoparticle growth and the red-shifted plasmonic response arising from Au–Ag interactions. XPS confirmed the presence of the hydrogel components and embedded metal nanoparticles, although the Au and Ag signals were relatively weak because of their confinement within the hydrogel. TEM revealed star-like or spiky spherical nanostructures within O-Au@Ag-PHNs, while SEM-EDS confirmed the coexistence of Au and Ag. Based on its strong NIR absorption and distinctive overgrown morphology, O-Au@Ag-PHN was selected for subsequent experiments and is hereafter referred to as O-PHN. Under 785 nm NIR irradiation, lyophilized O-PHN powder exhibited a substantially greater temperature increase than Ag-PHN, confirming its enhanced photothermal performance. A similar response was observed in aqueous suspensions, where O-PHN produced a temperature increase approximately 10 °C greater than that of Ag-PHN under identical conditions. This enhancement was attributed to the strong NIR absorption of O-PHN resulting from heterometallic overgrowth. O-PHN also maintained a consistent thermal response during repeated irradiation cycles, demonstrating favorable photothermal stability. First, O-PHNs were employed as intracellular SERS probes. To improve the intracellular delivery of O-PHNs, hydroporation based on microfluidic vortex flow was employed. Hydroporation increased O-PHN uptake into cells by approximately 4-fold compared with conventional co-incubation, as confirmed by dark-field imaging and scattering-spot analysis. No significant reduction in cell viability was observed with increasing O-PHN concentrations, regardless of NIR irradiation. Following intracellular delivery, SERS mapping was performed to visualize cellular components. Distinct Raman signals were detected in O-PHN-treated cells but were negligible in cells without O-PHNs. Maps generated using representative bands for nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins revealed spatially distinct molecular distributions within the cells. These results demonstrate that O-PHNs enables sensitive, label-free compositional mapping of intracellular biomolecules. Next, the drug-delivery performance of O-PHNs was evaluated using normal cell-only spheroids and cancer cell co-cultured spheroids as a tumor-mimicking model. Without light irradiation, drug penetrated more deeply into the co-culture spheroids than into the normal cell spheroids. This enhanced passive penetration may result from the heterogeneous cellular architecture and reduced diffusion barriers of the tumor-like spheroids. Light irradiation further increased drug penetration in both spheroid models, with the irradiated cancer cell spheroids exhibiting the greatest penetration depth. Quantification of the drug-positive area at different Z-planes confirmed this trend. These results indicate that both the intrinsic spheroid microenvironment and photothermally triggered drug release contribute to enhanced drug transport. In conclusion, we developed a simple strategy for fabricating light and thermoresponsive plasmonic hybrid nanogels that integrate molecular sensing with controlled cargo delivery. Ag-containing seed-PHNs were prepared through photoinitiated radical polymerization, followed by seed-mediated heterometallic overgrowth to produce O-PHNs with strong NIR absorption and enhanced photothermal conversion. NIR irradiation promoted localized O-PHN assembly in aqueous environments, generating plasmonic hot-spots that enhanced SERS-based molecular detection. O-PHNs enable label-free SERS mapping of nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins within cells. In addition, Drug-loaded O-PHNs also enhanced light-triggered drug penetration into three-dimensional spheroids, particularly in the tumor-mimicking co-culture model. Collectively, these results demonstrate that O-PHNs provide a multifunctional platform combining label-free molecular sensing, intracellular analysis, and spatiotemporally controlled therapeutic delivery. This platform may facilitate the investigation of molecular changes associated with different cell types, cellular states, and external stimuli while supporting the development of light-responsive therapeutic systems.

P3-101.a: Hydrogels attract growing attention as implantable biosensor materials because of their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and stimuli responsiveness. In particular, pH-responsive hydrogels detect changes in the in vivo microenvironment through pH variations within tissues. Tissue pH varies locally with physiological and pathological conditions, including tumors, inflammation, infection, and wound healing, and therefore serves as an important biomarker of the tissue microenvironment. Current pH-responsive hydrogel sensors still face several limitations. Sensor responses to pH changes often exhibit hysteresis, which limits complete reversibility, while narrow sensing ranges, typically pH 4–8, restrict their applicability. In vivo pH monitoring also still requires invasive measurement methods. Therefore, this study presents a biodegradable hydrogel that simplifies signal interpretation through unidirectional swelling, shows linear swelling over a broad pH range from 1 to 8, and maintains stable reversible swelling under repeated pH changes. This study fabricates a biodegradable hydrogel with unidirectional swelling behavior using sacran, agarose, acrylic acid (AA), and acrylamide (AM) through UV curing and heat treatment. After complete drying, 24 h immersion in buffer solutions from pH 1 to 8 allows measurement of the equilibrium weight, height, and width. Changes in weight reveal the pH-dependent swelling behavior and linearity, while comparison of height and width changes confirms unidirectional swelling along the thickness direction. In addition, repeated immersion between pH 5 and pH 7, which represent physiologically relevant conditions, confirms the reversibility of hydrogel swelling and shrinkage. This study analyzes the pH responsiveness of the hydrogel using the weight swelling ratio (WSR) and length swelling ratio (LSR). The WSR increases linearly with increasing pH from 1 to 8 and reaches approximately 2,390% at pH 8. Eight alternating immersions between pH 5 and pH 7 maintain similar swelling responses under each condition, demonstrating high reversibility. At pH 8, the width LSR reaches only approximately 34%, whereas the thickness LSR increases to approximately 1,327%, demonstrating distinct unidirectional swelling. This study develops a sacran-based hydrogel with unidirectional swelling, a broad pH-responsive range, high reversibility, and biodegradability. Therefore, the sacran-based hydrogel provides an implantable pH-sensing platform for monitoring changes in the in vivo microenvironment. Future studies aim to apply this hydrogel as a diagnostic platform for monitoring tumor microenvironment acidification and pH changes associated with inflammation.
